source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: non-occupational hiv exposure other than rape
condition_aliases: non-occupational hiv exposure other than rape
recommended_advice: For non-occupational HIV exposure other than rape, PEP provision should be decided on a case-by-case basis by the clinician.
PEP should not be provided for chronic HIV exposure or recreational exposure cases.
PEP may be provided in some cases such as condom breakage in a discordant couple.
fact_text: PEP for non-occupational HIV exposure other than rape is decided case-by-case; not recommended for chronic or recreational exposure but may be given for episodes like condom breakage in discordant couples.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Risk factors for IRIS include CD4 count <100 before ART, first-time or restart of HIV therapy, large viral load drops, presence of other infections before ART especially if ART started soon after infection diagnosis, and severe TB with high pathogen burden and ART started within 30 days of TB treatment.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
recommended_advice: Most IRIS cases resolve within weeks; severe cases may require stopping ART temporarily and treating underlying infection before restarting ART.
Milder/moderate IRIS can be managed symptomatically or with NSAIDs.
Delaying ART start by 2-8 weeks after TB treatment initiation may reduce IRIS incidence but must be balanced against benefits of early ART.
fact_text: IRIS is an inflammatory syndrome occurring shortly after ART initiation or restart, especially in patients with TB; it can be unmasking or paradoxical, with symptoms ranging from mild to life-threatening; management includes symptomatic treatment, NSAIDs, or ART interruption in severe cases; timing of ART initiation in TB patients affects IRIS risk.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
recommended_advice: Both TB therapy and ART should be continued during IRIS for long-term patient health
contraindications_or_cautions: Do not stop TB therapy or ART in presence of IRIS unless life-threatening conditions occur
fact_text: In patients with IRIS, neither TB therapy nor ART should be stopped as both are necessary for long-term health unless life-threatening conditions arise.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Because cotrimoxazole and antiretroviral therapy (especially nevirapine and efavirenz) can both cause rash, start cotrimoxazole prophylaxis first and delay ART initiation by two weeks if the patient is stable and has no rash; do not start cotrimoxazole and ART simultaneously.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for HIV-infected adults and adolescents with CD4 count less than 350 cells/mm3, or who have had an episode of PCP, or have symptomatic HIV disease or WHO clinical stage 2, 3, or 4.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Duration of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in adults and adolescents is lifelong if not on ART; if on ART and CD4 count is above 350 cells/mm3 on two consecutive samples 6 months apart, cotrimoxazole can be discontinued; if prophylaxis was stopped but CD4 falls below 350 or new/recurrent WHO clinical stage 2, 3, or 4 conditions occur, cotrimoxazole should be restarted.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Recommended cotrimoxazole prophylaxis dose for adults and adolescents is one double strength tablet (160 mg trimethoprim/800 mg sulfamethoxazole) once daily or two single strength tablets (80 mg trimethoprim/400 mg sulfamethoxazole) once daily.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Clients on cotrimoxazole prophylaxis should be monitored for toxicity, clinical events, and adherence. Lab tests for hemoglobin and white blood counts are done only if indicated. Adherence counselling is important to prepare clients for future ART and address medication barriers. Alternative antibiotics should be used for breakthrough bacterial infections while continuing cotrimoxazole prophylaxis. For toxoplasmosis and PCP infections, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis should be suspended and full active treatment initiated; prophylaxis can be recommenced after treatment completion.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
source_section: Cotrimoxazole desensitization chart for adults and adolescents
fact_text: Cotrimoxazole desensitization dosing schedule for adults and adolescents: Day 1: 80 mg sulfamethoxazole + 16 mg trimethoprim (2 ml oral suspension); Day 2: 160 mg + 32 mg (4 ml); Day 3: 240 mg + 48 mg (6 ml); Day 4: 320 mg + 64 mg (8 ml); Day 5: 400 mg + 80 mg (one single-strength sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim tablet); Day 6 and after: 800 mg + 160 mg (two single-strength tablets or one double-strength tablet). Note: each 5 ml suspension contains 40 mg trimethoprim and 200 mg sulfamethoxazole.
source_figure_or_table: Cotrimoxazole desensitization chart for adults and adolescents

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: For patients with cotrimoxazole intolerance, consider dapsone 100 mg once daily as first choice. For non-life-threatening adverse reactions, stop cotrimoxazole for 2 weeks then re-challenge with TMP/SMX by gradually increasing oral dose under surveillance, as up to 70% may tolerate TMP/SMX again.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
source_section: Initiation of cotrimoxazole in relation to ART in children
fact_text: Because rash is a common initial side effect of cotrimoxazole and ARVs (especially nevirapine and efavirenz), cotrimoxazole prophylaxis should be started first and ART initiated two weeks later if the individual is stable on cotrimoxazole and has no rash.
source_figure_or_table: Initiation of cotrimoxazole in relation to ART in children

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: children 6 months to 5 years requiring cotrimoxazole prophylaxis
condition_aliases: children 6 months to 5 years requiring cotrimoxazole prophylaxis
source_section: Dose of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in children
fact_text: For children aged 6 months to 5 years, cotrimoxazole dose is 200 mg SMX/40 mg TMP daily, given as 5 ml suspension or two pediatric tablets (100 mg/20 mg each).
source_figure_or_table: Dose of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in children

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: children 6 to 14 years requiring cotrimoxazole prophylaxis
condition_aliases: children 6 to 14 years requiring cotrimoxazole prophylaxis
source_section: Dose of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in children
fact_text: For children aged 6 to 14 years, cotrimoxazole dose is 400 mg SMX/80 mg TMP daily, given as 10 ml suspension or four pediatric tablets or one single strength adult tablet (400 mg/80 mg).
source_figure_or_table: Dose of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in children

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: children older than 14 years requiring cotrimoxazole prophylaxis
condition_aliases: children older than 14 years requiring cotrimoxazole prophylaxis
source_section: Dose of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in children
fact_text: For children older than 14 years, cotrimoxazole dose is 800 mg SMX/160 mg TMP daily, given as two single strength adult tablets or one double strength adult tablet (800 mg/160 mg).
source_figure_or_table: Dose of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in children

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
source_section: Dose of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in children
fact_text: For children under 6 months, cotrimoxazole dose is 100 mg SMX/20 mg TMP daily, given as 2.5 ml suspension (5 ml syrup 200 mg/40 mg).
source_figure_or_table: Dose of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis in children

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
source_section: Recommendations for starting Cotrimoxazole in infants and children
fact_text: All HIV-exposed infants and children should start cotrimoxazole prophylaxis at 4-6 weeks after birth and continue for at least 3 months after stopping breastfeeding with a confirmed negative HIV test.
source_figure_or_table: Recommendations for starting Cotrimoxazole in infants and children

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
source_section: Recommendations for starting Cotrimoxazole in infants and children
fact_text: For HIV-infected children aged 1-4 years, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended if symptomatic HIV disease is present and/or CD4 count is less than 25% or absolute CD4 count is below 1000/mm3.
source_figure_or_table: Recommendations for starting Cotrimoxazole in infants and children

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
source_section: Recommendations for starting Cotrimoxazole in infants and children
fact_text: For HIV-infected children older than 5 years, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended if symptomatic HIV disease is present and/or CD4 count is less than 350/mm3.
source_figure_or_table: Recommendations for starting Cotrimoxazole in infants and children

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
source_section: Recommendations for starting Cotrimoxazole in infants and children
fact_text: For HIV-infected infants and children less than 1 year of age, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended regardless of CD4 count or clinical status.
source_figure_or_table: Recommendations for starting Cotrimoxazole in infants and children

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Primary cotrimoxazole prophylaxis can be stopped in older children on ART after at least 12 months of good adherence, no WHO stage 2, 3, or 4 conditions, and sustained high CD4 counts on two measurements done at least six months apart (>25% CD4 between 1-5 years, >350 CD4 for children above 5 years).

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Children on cotrimoxazole prophylaxis should have clinical monitoring by health staff at regular intervals with lab tests or referral as needed; caregivers must be informed to recognize jaundice and rash, stop the drug, and report to clinic; children already under lab monitoring for HIV or ART need no additional tests for CTX.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: In children with adverse reactions to cotrimoxazole, desensitization with small doses is not recommended; dapsone is the preferred alternative prophylaxis at 2 mg/kg/day orally, max 100 mg/day, but dapsone is less effective against toxoplasmosis and lacks cotrimoxazole's broad antibacterial activity.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Pregnant women meeting criteria for cotrimoxazole prophylaxis should continue cotrimoxazole throughout pregnancy; if starting during pregnancy, initiate regardless of gestational age; folic acid supplementation at 5 mg daily is recommended at higher dose for pregnant PLHIV on cotrimoxazole.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
source_section: Side effects of cotrimoxazole, grading of toxicity and the recommendations
fact_text: Grade 1 toxicity (erythema) from cotrimoxazole: continue CPT; Grade 2 toxicity (maculopapular rash, dry desquamation): monitor closely and consider antihistamines; Grade 3 toxicity (vesiculation, ulceration): stop CPT and try desensitization after recovery, but desensitization not recommended for children; Grade 4 toxicity (exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, erythema multiforme, moist desquamation): stop CPT permanently and document reason.
source_figure_or_table: Side effects of cotrimoxazole, grading of toxicity and the recommendations

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
alternative_medicines: Triple NRTI regimen AZT+3TC+ABC if PI unavailable
followup_monitoring: Viral load monitoring and NNRTI use recommendations do not apply to HIV-2 infection
fact_text: For HIV-2 infection, protease inhibitors are recommended as active agents; triple NRTI regimen AZT+3TC+ABC can be used if PI is unavailable but has higher virological failure risk; NNRTIs are not active and should be avoided; viral load monitoring and NNRTI use recommendations do not apply; treatment response should be monitored by CD4+ counts and clinical signs of immune deterioration.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: hiv infection in infants and children
condition_aliases: hiv infection in infants and children
source_section: Annex 1 WHO Clinical Staging of HIV for Infants and Children
fact_text: WHO clinical staging for HIV in infants and children defines stage 1 as asymptomatic or persistent generalized lymphadenopathy; stage 2 includes conditions such as unexplained persistent hepatosplenomegaly, papular pruritic eruptions, extensive wart virus infection, recurrent oral ulcerations, herpes zoster, and recurrent upper respiratory infections; stage 3 includes moderate malnutrition not responding to therapy, persistent diarrhea ≥14 days, persistent fever >37.5°C for >1 month, persistent oral candidiasis after 6 weeks of life, pulmonary and lymph node TB, severe recurrent bacterial pneumonia, and hematologic abnormalities; stage 4 includes severe wasting or malnutrition not responding to therapy, pneumocystis pneumonia, recurrent severe bacterial infections excluding pneumonia, chronic herpes simplex infection >1 month, extrapulmonary TB, Kaposi sarcoma, oesophageal candidiasis, CNS toxoplasmosis after neonatal period, HIV encephalopathy, CMV infection with organ involvement after 1 month of age, and extrapulmonary cryptococcosis including meningitis.
source_figure_or_table: Annex 1 WHO Clinical Staging of HIV for Infants and Children

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: cerebral or b cell non-hodgkin lymphoma
condition_aliases: cerebral or b cell non-hodgkin lymphoma
fact_text: Cerebral or B cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma is classified as an AIDS-defining malignancy.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Chronic cryptosporidiosis presenting with diarrhoea is classified as an AIDS-defining illness.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Chronic isosporiasis is included as an AIDS-defining condition.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: disseminated endemic mycosis (extrapulmonary histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, penicilliosis)
condition_aliases: disseminated endemic mycosis (extrapulmonary histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, penicilliosis)
fact_text: Disseminated endemic mycosis including extrapulmonary histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, and penicilliosis is recognized as an AIDS-defining condition.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection is an AIDS-defining illness.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: HIV-associated cardiomyopathy or nephropathy is recognized as an AIDS-defining condition.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Penicillinosis is included as an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is an AIDS-defining neurological condition.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
source_section: Annex 2 Diagnostic criteria for HIV-related clinical events (adults)
fact_text: Diagnostic criteria for adult HIV-related clinical events include: Asymptomatic (no symptoms/signs, no definitive diagnosis); Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy defined as painless lymph nodes >1 cm in two or more noncontiguous sites excluding inguinal, persisting ≥3 months without known cause, confirmed by histology; Moderate unexplained weight loss under 10% body weight (or failure to gain weight in pregnancy) documented by weight loss under 10%; Recurrent bacterial upper respiratory infections (≥1 in last 6 months) with symptoms such as unilateral facial pain with nasal discharge, painful inflamed eardrum, or tonsillopharyngitis without viral features, confirmed by lab studies and culture; Herpes zoster diagnosed clinically by painful vesicular rash in dermatomal distribution not crossing midline; Angular cheilitis diagnosed clinically by splits/cracks at mouth angle not due to iron/vitamin deficiency and usually responding to antifungal treatment; Recurrent oral ulcerations (≥2 episodes in 6 months) with aphthous ulceration and yellow-grey pseudomembrane clinically diagnosed; Papular pruritic eruption with papular pruritic lesions and postinflammatory pigmentation clinically diagnosed; Seborrhoeic dermatitis as itchy scaly skin affecting scalp, axillae, upper trunk, groin clinically diagnosed; Fungal nail infections with paronychia or onycholysis confirmed by fungal culture; Severe unexplained weight loss over 10% body weight with visible wasting or BMI <18.5 documented, noting pregnancy may mask weight loss.
source_figure_or_table: Annex 2 Diagnostic criteria for HIV-related clinical events (adults)

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: acute necrotizing ulcerative stomatitis, gingivitis or periodontitis
condition_aliases: acute necrotizing ulcerative stomatitis, gingivitis or periodontitis
fact_text: Acute necrotizing ulcerative stomatitis, gingivitis or periodontitis is diagnosed clinically by severe pain, ulcerated gingival papillae, loosening of teeth, spontaneous bleeding, bad odor, and rapid loss of bone and/or soft tissue.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Oral candidiasis diagnosis is clinical, based on persistent or recurring creamy white curd-like plaques that can be scraped off (pseudomembranous) or red patches on tongue, palate, or lining of mouth, usually painful or tender (erythematous form).

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Oral hairy leukoplakia is diagnosed clinically by fine white small linear or corrugated lesions on lateral borders of the tongue which do not scrape off.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Pulmonary TB diagnosis requires chronic symptoms (lasting 2-3 weeks) including cough, haemoptysis, shortness of breath, chest pain, weight loss, fever, night sweats plus either positive sputum smear or negative sputum smear with compatible chest radiograph (upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation, fibrosis, shrinkage) and no extrapulmonary disease; definitive diagnosis requires isolation of M. tuberculosis on sputum culture or lung biopsy histology with compatible symptoms.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: severe bacterial infection (e.g. pneumonia, meningitis, empyema, pyomyositis, bone or joint infection, bacteraemia, severe pelvic inflammatory disease)
condition_aliases: severe bacterial infection (e.g. pneumonia, meningitis, empyema, pyomyositis, bone or joint infection, bacteraemia, severe pelvic inflammatory disease)
fact_text: Severe bacterial infection diagnosis is based on fever with specific symptoms or signs localizing infection and response to appropriate antibiotics; definitive diagnosis requires isolation of bacteria from appropriate clinical specimens, usually sterile sites.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Unexplained chronic diarrhoea is defined as loose or watery stools three or more times daily for longer than 1 month; definitive diagnosis requires confirmation of three or more stools observed and documented as unformed, with two or more stool tests showing no pathogens.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Unexplained persistent fever is defined as fever or night sweats for more than 1 month, intermittent or constant, with no response to antibiotics or antimalarials and no other obvious infection focus; definitive diagnosis requires documented fever >37.6°C with negative blood culture, Ziehl-Nielsen stain, malaria slide, normal or unchanged chest X-ray, and no other infection focus.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Chronic HSV infection diagnosis requires painful, progressive anogenital or orolabial ulceration lasting more than 1 month or visceral HSV at any site, with positive culture or PCR for HSV or compatible cytology/histology, and history of recurrent episodes.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: HIV wasting syndrome diagnosis requires documented weight loss >10% plus two or more unformed stools negative for pathogens, or documented fever >37.6°C with no other cause, negative blood culture, negative malaria slide, and normal or unchanged chest X-ray.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Oesophageal candidiasis diagnosis requires recent onset of retrosternal pain or difficulty swallowing food and fluids with oral candidiasis, confirmed by macroscopic appearance at endoscopy or bronchoscopy or by microscopy/histology.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Definitive diagnosis of Pneumocystis pneumonia requires cytology or immunofluorescent microscopy of induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), or histology of lung tissue in patients with dyspnoea on exertion or nonproductive cough within past 3 months, tachypnoea, fever, and chest X-ray showing diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates without evidence of bacterial pneumonia.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Recurrent bacterial pneumonia diagnosis requires current episode plus one or more episodes in last 6 months with acute onset (<2 weeks) of symptoms (fever, cough, dyspnoea, chest pain), new consolidation on clinical exam or chest X-ray, and response to antibiotics, plus positive culture or antigen test of compatible organism.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Unexplained anaemia (Hb <8 g/dl), neutropenia (<0.5 x 10^9/L), or chronic thrombocytopenia (<50 x 10^9/L) for more than 1 month requires diagnosis by laboratory testing excluding other non-HIV causes and failure to respond to standard treatments including haematics, antimalarials, or anthelmintics as per national and WHO guidelines.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: CNS toxoplasmosis clinical diagnosis requires recent focal neurological abnormality or reduced consciousness with response to specific therapy within 10 days.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Definitive diagnosis of CNS toxoplasmosis requires positive serum toxoplasma antibody AND single/multiple intracranial mass lesion on neuroimaging (CT or MRI).

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: cytomegalovirus disease (retinitis or infection of other organs excluding liver, spleen, lymph nodes)
condition_aliases: cytomegalovirus disease (retinitis or infection of other organs excluding liver, spleen, lymph nodes)
fact_text: CMV retinitis clinical diagnosis includes typical fundoscopic lesions with discrete retinal whitening, distinct borders, spreading centrifugally, retinal vasculitis, hemorrhage and necrosis.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: cytomegalovirus disease (retinitis or infection of other organs excluding liver, spleen, lymph nodes)
condition_aliases: cytomegalovirus disease (retinitis or infection of other organs excluding liver, spleen, lymph nodes)
fact_text: Definitive diagnosis of CMV disease requires compatible histology or CMV demonstrated in CSF by culture or PCR.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: No presumptive clinical diagnosis for disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection; diagnosis requires finding typical mycobacterial species from stool, blood, body fluid or tissue excluding lung.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Definitive diagnosis of disseminated TB requires compatible symptoms/signs plus culture or histology from respiratory specimen and evidence of extrapulmonary disease.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Disseminated TB clinical diagnosis includes pleural, pericardial, peritoneal involvement, meningitis, mediastinal or abdominal lymphadenopathy, osteitis; miliary TB shows diffuse small miliary shadows or micronodules on chest X-ray; discrete cervical lymph node M. tuberculosis infection is less severe extrapulmonary TB.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Definitive diagnosis of extrapulmonary cryptococcosis requires isolation of Cryptococcus neoformans from extrapulmonary site or positive cryptococcal antigen test (CRAG) on CSF or blood.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Extrapulmonary cryptococcosis clinical diagnosis includes meningitis with subacute onset, severe headache, meningism, confusion, behavioral changes responsive to cryptococcal therapy.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Definitive diagnosis of HIV encephalopathy is by exclusion and, if available, neuroimaging (CT or MRI).

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: HIV encephalopathy clinical diagnosis includes disabling cognitive and/or motor dysfunction interfering with daily living activities, progressing over weeks or months without other illness explaining findings.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Definitive diagnosis of Kaposi sarcoma requires macroscopic appearance at endoscopy or bronchoscopy or histology.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Kaposi sarcoma clinical diagnosis is typical persistent flat pink or blood-bruised patches on skin or oropharynx that develop into violaceous plaques or nodules.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: No presumptive clinical diagnosis for PML; definitive diagnosis requires progressive neurological disorder with cognitive, gait, speech, visual, limb weakness and cranial nerve palsies plus hypodense white matter lesions on neuroimaging or positive JC virus PCR on CSF.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Atypical disseminated leishmaniasis has no presumptive clinical diagnosis; definitive diagnosis requires histology showing amastigotes or culture from any appropriate clinical specimen.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Chronic isosporiasis has no presumptive clinical diagnosis; definitive diagnosis requires identification of Isospora.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: cryptosporidiosis with diarrhea lasting more than 1 month
condition_aliases: cryptosporidiosis with diarrhea lasting more than 1 month
fact_text: Cryptosporidiosis with diarrhea lasting more than 1 month has no presumptive clinical diagnosis; definitive diagnosis requires identification of cysts on modified Ziehl-Neelsen microscopic examination of unformed stool.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Disseminated mycosis has no presumptive clinical diagnosis; definitive diagnosis requires histology, antigen detection, or culture from clinical specimen or blood culture.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: HIV-associated cardiomyopathy has no presumptive clinical diagnosis; definitive diagnosis requires cardiomegaly and evidence of poor left ventricular function confirmed by echocardiography.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: HIV-associated nephropathy has no presumptive clinical diagnosis; definitive diagnosis requires renal biopsy.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Invasive cervical carcinoma has no presumptive clinical diagnosis; definitive diagnosis requires histology or cytology.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition: lymphoma (cerebral or b cell non-hodgkin) or other solid hiv-associated tumours
condition_aliases: lymphoma (cerebral or b cell non-hodgkin) or other solid hiv-associated tumours
fact_text: Lymphoma or other solid HIV-associated tumours have no presumptive clinical diagnosis; definitive diagnosis requires histology of relevant specimen or for CNS tumours neuroimaging techniques.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Recurrent septicemia has no presumptive clinical diagnosis; definitive diagnosis requires blood culture.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
recommended_tests: Repeat HBsAg, HBeAg, or HBV DNA testing after 6 months to confirm chronic infection
fact_text: Chronic HBV infection can be confirmed by positive HBsAg, HBV DNA, or HBeAg on two occasions at least 6 months apart.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Chronic HBV infection diagnosis requires negative IgM anti-HBc and a positive result on at least one of HBsAg, HBeAg, or HBV DNA tests.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
trigger_evidence: single positive HBsAg or HBV DNA or HBeAg lab result without IgM anti-HBc results
recommended_tests: Multiple laboratory tests for HBV infection may be performed simultaneously on the same specimen as part of a hepatitis panel
fact_text: Probable chronic HBV infection can be diagnosed with a single positive HBsAg, HBV DNA, or HBeAg lab result if IgM anti-HBc is unavailable; discordant test results are acceptable for diagnosis.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: Chronic HBV infection clinical patterns include: 1) immunotolerant phase with high viral replication but mild hepatitis (HBeAg-positive), 2) active infection with high viral replication and raised ALT (wild-type HBeAg-positive), 3) active infection with variant HBV unable to secrete HBeAg (HBeAg-negative or precore mutant), and 4) inactive HBeAg-negative disease.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: The virological pattern of chronic hepatitis B infection is evolving globally, with a shift from predominantly HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B to a higher prevalence of HBeAg-negative infection characterized by HBV variants unable to secrete HBeAg.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
condition_aliases: hbv dna persistence in hbsag negative patients
fact_text: Occult HBV infection is defined by persistence of HBV DNA in liver tissue in patients who are HBsAg negative, representing a clinical profile of uncertain significance.

source_title: National Guidelines of Antiretroviral Therapy, Bangladesh, 2011
fact_text: In Bangladesh, HBV diagnostic testing includes IgM antibodies to hepatitis B core antigen (anti-HBc), hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) by ELISA, and HBV DNA detection by PCR at specialized centers.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Chikungunya fever should be suspected when a person develops sudden onset of fever, joint manifestations, and rash.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Confirmed case: patient meeting laboratory criteria irrespective of clinical presentation.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Possible case: patient meeting only clinical criteria.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Probable case: patient meeting both clinical and epidemiological criteria.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Clinical criteria include acute onset of fever >38.5°C and severe arthralgia/arthritis not explained by other medical conditions.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Epidemiological criteria include residing or having visited epidemic areas and reported transmission within 15 days prior to symptom onset.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Four-fold rise of IgG antibody in samples collected at least three weeks apart (first sample after 7 days) confirms infection.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Laboratory criteria require at least one test in the acute phase: virus isolation by cell culture, or viral RNA by RT-PCR within 5 days of illness onset.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Presence of viral specific IgM antibody in a single serum sample collected within 5 to 28 days of fever onset confirms infection.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Chikungunya joint pain tends to be worse in the morning, relieved by mild exercise, exacerbated by aggressive movements, may improve for 2-3 days then reappear in a saddle back pattern; early and more significant joint involvement occurs with trauma or degeneration.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Common clinical features of chikungunya fever include fever, arthritis/arthralgia, backache, headache, and rash; infrequent features include stomatitis, oral ulcers, exfoliative dermatitis, and photosensitive hyperpigmentation; rare in adults but seen in children are photophobia, retro-orbital pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, mental confusion, and signs of meningeal irritation.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Fever in chikungunya varies from low to high grade, usually lasting 24 to 48 hours, may abruptly rise to 39-40°C with chills and rigor, no diurnal variation, and usually subsides with antipyretics.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Joint symptoms usually start with arthralgia or arthritis, symmetric, often involving ankles, wrists, and small hand joints; migratory polyarthritis with effusions may occur but usually resolves; larger joints like knee, shoulder, and spine can be involved.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
source_section: images showing joint pain, fever thermometer reading 103.5°F, rash on skin, headache, and labeled diagram with fever, arthritis, and rashes
fact_text: Key clinical features of chikungunya fever include acute fever, severe arthritis/arthralgia, and rash.
source_figure_or_table: images showing joint pain, fever thermometer reading 103.5°F, rash on skin, headache, and labeled diagram with fever, arthritis, and rashes

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Mild chikungunya fever is characterized by low grade fever, mild arthralgia, mild focal myalgia, general weakness, and skin rash or itching.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Neurologic manifestations of chikungunya include meningo-encephalitis, encephalitis, acute encephalopathy, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and myelitis.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Ocular manifestations of chikungunya may include neuro-retinitis and uveitis in one or both eyes, with granulomatous and nongranulomatous anterior uveitis, optic neuritis, retrobulbar neuritis, and dendritic lesions reported.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Transient maculopapular rash commonly seen in chikungunya, usually disappears within 48 hours; other skin lesions include vesiculobullous eruptions, angiomatous lesions, purpuras, epidermolysis bullosa in children, stomatitis, and oral ulcers.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Acute chikungunya symptoms typically resolve within 7–10 days.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: High risk chikungunya patients include those with co-morbid conditions (hypertension, diabetes, CAD/CVD, geriatric age, pregnancy, COPD) or co-infections (dengue, tuberculosis, enteric fever, pneumonia, HIV, malaria).

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Moderate chikungunya includes low to high grade persistent fever, moderate arthralgia/arthritis, generalized myalgia, hypotension, mild bleeding, retro-orbital pain, and oliguria.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Severe chikungunya includes persistent high grade fever, severe arthralgia/arthritis, persistent vomiting or diarrhea, altered sensorium, bleeding (GI bleeding due to analgesics), and shock from persistent vomiting and diarrhea.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Dengue fever should be considered in differential diagnosis when severe back pain with purpuras or active bleeding is present; confirmatory lab diagnosis is possible.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Reactive arthritis is a differential diagnosis when arthritis follows febrile gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection lasting less than six months, with enthesitis and oral mucosal ulcers.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Rheumatic fever is a differential diagnosis more common in children, presenting with fleeting migratory polyarthritis predominantly affecting large joints.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Rickettsial disease can present with fever, rash, and joint pains and should be confirmed by serology.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Serum sickness illness may mimic chikungunya with polyarthritis associated with vaccine, medication, or other viral infections.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
source_section: Clinical and laboratory features of chikungunya virus infections compared with dengue virus infections table
fact_text: Chikungunya typically presents with high fever (>39°C), severe arthralgia, rash, and lymphopenia; dengue more often has thrombocytopenia, hemorrhage, shock, and hemoconcentration.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical and laboratory features of chikungunya virus infections compared with dengue virus infections table

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Leptospirosis suggested by severe calf muscle myalgia, conjunctival congestion or hemorrhage, oliguria or jaundice, with history of skin contact with contaminated water.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Malaria can present with high fever and joint pain; periodic fever and altered consciousness/seizures suggest malaria diagnosis.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Mild and moderate chikungunya cases can be managed at home; severe cases require hospital management.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
recommended_advice: Consume plenty of water with electrolytes (approx. 2 liters of home fluids with salt in 24 hours)
Adequate rest in a warm environment
fact_text: Home management includes consuming about 2 liters of water with electrolytes daily and adequate rest in a warm environment.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Patients with suspected chikungunya should be managed as dengue until dengue has been ruled out.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Chikungunya and dengue viruses are transmitted by the same mosquitoes and can co-infect the same patient.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Dengue virus more likely causes neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, hemorrhage, shock, and death.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Chikungunya virus more likely causes high fever, severe polyarthralgia, arthritis, rash, and lymphopenia.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Aspirin and other NSAIDs can increase hemorrhage risk in patients with dengue and should be avoided when dengue is not excluded.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
dose_or_duration: up to 1000 mg tablets four times daily for adults; children 50-60 mg/kg/day in divided doses
contraindications_or_cautions: only if no preexisting liver or kidney disease
fact_text: Paracetamol is recommended for fever up to 1000 mg four times daily in adults without liver/kidney disease; children 50-60 mg/kg/day divided doses.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
admission_criteria: hemodynamic instability (frequent syncopal attacks, systolic BP <90 mmHg, pulse pressure <30 mmHg)
oliguria (urine output <500 ml in 24 hours)
altered sensorium
bleeding manifestations
persistent joint pain or disabling arthritis after 3 days symptomatic treatment
age >60 years
infants <1 year
pregnancy
high risk group
warning_signs: hemodynamic instability (frequent syncopal attacks, systolic BP <90 mmHg, pulse pressure <30 mmHg)
persistent joint pain or disabling arthritis after 3 days symptomatic treatment
fact_text: Admission is indicated for hemodynamic instability, oliguria, altered sensorium, bleeding, persistent joint pain after 3 days, age >60, infants <1 year, pregnancy, or high risk group.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
recommended_advice: Cold compresses may help reduce joint damage but heat should be avoided during acute stage as it may worsen joint pain
Refrain from exertion; mild exercise and physiotherapy are recommended during recovery
fact_text: Cold compresses may reduce joint damage but heat should be avoided during acute stage; mild exercise and physiotherapy are recommended during recovery.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Avoid self medication with aspirin or NSAIDs in chikungunya patients.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
dose_or_duration: Up to 1000 mg paracetamol tablets four times daily for adults; children 50-60 mg/kg/day in divided doses
contraindications_or_cautions: no preexisting liver or kidney disease
fact_text: Paracetamol dosing: adults up to 1000 mg four times daily; children 50-60 mg/kg/day divided doses; avoid if liver or kidney disease present.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Antibiotics can be used to treat secondary bacterial infections in chikungunya patients.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Antihistamines can be used to treat itching in chikungunya patients.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
recommended_medicines: rehydration therapy (5% DNS, Normal Saline, baby saline for pediatric cases)
fact_text: Assess dehydration and institute proper rehydration therapy using 5% DNS, Normal Saline, or baby saline for pediatric cases.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Cold compresses may help reduce joint damage but heat should be avoided during the acute stage as it may worsen joint pain.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Mild forms of exercise and physiotherapy are recommended during recovery from chikungunya.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Patients should refrain from exertion during the acute stage of chikungunya.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: In cases with ophthalmic symptoms or complications, consultation with ophthalmologists is recommended.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Aspirin or NSAIDs should be avoided during the first 10 days of chikungunya illness and NSAIDs can be used only when dengue fever is adequately excluded.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Steroids have no role in the acute stage of chikungunya fever.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Anti-neuralgic drugs such as Amitryptiline, Carbamazepine, Gabapentin, and Pregabalin may be used in standard doses for disturbing neuropathies.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Antihistamines can be used for itching in chikungunya patients.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Cutaneous manifestations may require topical or systemic drugs; neuro-psychiatric problems require specialist care and drugs.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Hypotension should be treated with fluids and inotropics; acute renal failure may require dialysis; contractures and deformities may need physiotherapy or surgery.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Patients with myo-pericarditis or meningoencephalitis may require intensive care with monitoring, inotropic support, and ventilation.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Platelet transfusions are indicated for bleeding with platelet counts less than 50,000/cu mm; fresh frozen plasma or Vitamin K injections if INR > 2.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
recommended_advice: Chikungunya fever appears to have a direct impact on pregnancy with rare spontaneous abortions and mother-to-child transmission in the perinatal period.
fact_text: Chikungunya fever may directly impact pregnancy with rare spontaneous abortions and mother-to-child transmission in the perinatal period.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
recommended_advice: Mothers with chikungunya fever in perinatal period (-4 to +1 days delivery) can transmit virus to neonates by vertical transmission.
Caesarean section does not prevent transmission.
Neonatal chikungunya fever is associated with fever, poor feeding, pain, distal edema, skin manifestations, seizures, meningoencephalitis, and echocardiographic abnormalities.
No infants found infected through breastfeeding; breastfeeding is encouraged.
fact_text: Perinatal chikungunya transmission can occur; neonatal disease includes fever, poor feeding, seizures, and other complications; breastfeeding is safe and encouraged.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Preferred specimens for chikungunya diagnosis are blood or serum; CSF is preferred if neurological features are present.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Hyperpigmentation and papular eruptions may be managed with zinc oxide cream and/or calamine lotion.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
recommended_medicines: chloroquin phosphate 300 mg orally once daily
dose_or_duration: 4 weeks
fact_text: Use hydroxychloroquine 200 mg once daily or chloroquin phosphate 300 mg once daily for 4 weeks if arthralgia is refractory to other drugs.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: Routine labs in chikungunya include CBC showing leucopenia, rare thrombocytopenia, usually elevated ESR, increased CRP during acute phase, and elevated SGPT.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
recommended_tests: RT-PCR within 5 days of illness onset
Viral specific IgM antibody in single serum 5-28 days after fever onset
Four-fold rise of IgG in paired samples at least 3 weeks apart
fact_text: Specific chikungunya tests include virus isolation, RT-PCR within 5 days of onset, IgM antibody 5-28 days after fever onset, and four-fold IgG rise in paired samples at least 3 weeks apart.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
recommended_tests: ICT kit for IgM and IgG
fact_text: Diagnostic validity of currently available ICT kits for chikungunya IgM and IgG detection is very poor.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
fact_text: RT-PCR for chikungunya is performed only at IEDCR in Bangladesh.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
recommended_advice: Minimize chikungunya transmission by reducing vector density through community participation and hospital control measures
fact_text: Chikungunya transmission can be minimized by community participation, risk communication to household members, vector control, minimizing vector-patient contact (Aedes mosquito bites mostly morning and late afternoon), and reporting to public health authorities.

source_title: National Guideline on Clinical Management of Chikungunya Fever
recommended_advice: No need to isolate or segregate chikungunya patients at home as household members share the same environment
Important to reduce vector population in the household to prevent spread
fact_text: Household members do not need to isolate chikungunya patients but should focus on reducing vector population in the household.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Close contact: person not in household but shared enclosed space with index case for extended daytime periods during 3 months before current treatment episode

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Contact: any person exposed to an index TB case

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Index case: initially identified person with new or recurrent TB in a household or comparable setting, focus of contact investigation but not necessarily the source

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Contact screening is a systematic process to identify contacts at increased TB risk by interviewing the index case to obtain names, ages, and assess contacts' risk to determine who needs clinical evaluation
fact_text: Contact screening involves systematic identification and risk assessment of contacts through index case interview to prioritize clinical evaluation

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Estimated childhood TB cases in Bangladesh in 2019 were 43,320 (12% of total cases), with 30,970 missing cases (71% of child cases missing). Children under 5 years are grossly underdiagnosed.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: UNHLM targets for childhood TB cases in Bangladesh: 2019 target 16,300 (achievement 12,350), 2020 target 23,900 (achievement 9,367), 2021 target 28,000, 2022 target 29,800

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Household contact defined as sharing same enclosed living space for one or more nights or frequent/extended daytime period during 3 months before current treatment episode

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Bacteriologically confirmed TB case defined as patient with biological specimen positive by WHO-approved rapid diagnostics (Xpert MTB/RIF), smear microscopy, or culture

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Clinically diagnosed TB case defined as patient without bacteriological confirmation or smear not done, diagnosed as active TB by clinician based on X-ray abnormalities or suggestive histology or extrapulmonary cases without bacteriological confirmation

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Presumptive TB defined as patient presenting with symptoms or signs suggestive of TB (previously TB Suspect)

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Child exposure to M. tuberculosis occurs by contact with infectious TB patient; risk depends on infectiousness, proximity, closeness, and duration of contact; children more likely infected if household member is bacteriologically positive

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Infection occurs by inhalation of aerosol droplets from infectious adolescent/adult pulmonary TB cases; extrapulmonary TB rarely spreads disease; host immune response usually contains spread; dormant bacilli may reactivate if immunity compromised

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Notification of TB patients is mandatory in Bangladesh since January 30, 2014; all children with TB must be registered/notified in the NTP system including bacteriologically confirmed, clinically diagnosed pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB, new or previously treated, and drug-resistant cases.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Extra-pulmonary TB (EPTB) includes bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed TB involving organs outside lung parenchyma and bronchial tree such as pleura, lymph nodes, abdomen, and genitourinary system.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Intrathoracic TB classification: Pulmonary TB involves lung parenchyma, tracheobronchial tree, and miliary TB; Extra-pulmonary TB involves pleural effusion and intrathoracic lymphadenopathy; Both pulmonary and extra-pulmonary TB can coexist and should be classified as pulmonary TB.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Pulmonary TB (PTB) includes bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed TB involving lung parenchyma or tracheobronchial tree; miliary TB is classified as PTB due to lung lesions; tuberculous intra-thoracic lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion without lung abnormalities is classified as extra-pulmonary TB.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: TB cases are classified by anatomical site, drug resistance, history of previous anti-TB treatment, and HIV status to guide treatment and reporting.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Features of a child suspected of drug-resistant TB include contact with known drug-resistant TB case, non-response to treatment, or TB recurrence after adherence.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Features suggestive of drug-resistant TB in source case include contact with known drug-resistant TB case, sputum smear positivity after 3 months treatment, previous TB treatment, or treatment interruption.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Children with tuberculosis outside lung parenchyma and bronchial tree are classified as extrapulmonary TB (EPTB); children with both pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB are classified under pulmonary TB.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: New patient: never treated for TB or taken TB drugs less than one month; Previously treated patient: received ≥1 month anti-TB drugs, sub-classified as relapse, treatment after failure, treatment after loss to follow-up.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Drug-resistant TB diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation by drug susceptibility testing (DST) or phenotypic/genotypic methods.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: In screening contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB cases, all drug-resistant TB cases and index child TB cases should be prioritized.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Sputum induction, nasopharyngeal aspirate, gastric aspirate, BAL, and stool samples are effective for MTB-Xpert or Ultra testing in children.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Any child with pneumonia, pleural effusion, or cavitary/mass lung lesion not improving with standard antibacterial therapy should be evaluated for TB.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Children with fever of unknown origin, failure to thrive, significant weight loss, severe malnutrition, immunosuppression, or unexplained lymphadenopathy should be evaluated for TB.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Diagnosis of TB in children requires careful history, clinical exam, and investigations including Mantoux TST, CXR, smear microscopy, MTB-Xpert/RIF or Ultra, culture or LPA.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Childhood TB diagnosis is difficult due to paucibacillary disease, frequent negative Mantoux in malnourished children, and non-specific X-rays.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: A trial of anti-TB medicine is not recommended as a method to diagnose or rule out TB in children.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: BOX I: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children
fact_text: History of close contact with a sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB case within the past year is the most important diagnostic clue in children, especially under 5 years or immunosuppressed.
source_figure_or_table: BOX I: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: BOX I: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children
fact_text: Careful history including symptoms suggestive of TB and serial weight monitoring are essential in diagnosing TB in children.
source_figure_or_table: BOX I: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
referral_criteria: Refer child for drug-resistant TB evaluation if index case is drug-resistant or not responding to treatment
fact_text: If the index case is not responding to TB treatment or is drug-resistant, the child contact is likely to have drug-resistant TB and needs evaluation.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: BOX I: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children
recommended_tests: Bacterial confirmation (sputum smear microscopy) whenever possible
fact_text: Bacterial confirmation by sputum smear microscopy is recommended whenever possible in children suspected of TB.
source_figure_or_table: BOX I: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: BOX I: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children
recommended_tests: Chest X-ray and other radiological evaluation
fact_text: Chest X-ray and other radiological evaluations are recommended investigations for suspected pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB in children.
source_figure_or_table: BOX I: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: BOX I: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children
recommended_tests: HIV testing for all children suspected of TB
fact_text: HIV testing is recommended for all children suspected of having TB.
source_figure_or_table: BOX I: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: BOX I: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children
fact_text: Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) is recommended as part of investigations to diagnose TB in children.
source_figure_or_table: BOX I: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: Figure 1: Approach to contact management when chest X-ray and TST are not readily available
trigger_evidence: child in close contact with smear-positive pulmonary TB source case
dose_or_duration: 6 months
recommended_advice: Children under 5 years old in close contact with smear-positive pulmonary TB who are well should receive 6 months of Tuberculosis Preventive Therapy (TPT).
Children under 5 years old in close contact who are symptomatic should be evaluated for TB.
Children aged 5 years or older who are symptomatic should be evaluated for TB.
Children aged 5 years or older who are well should receive no treatment but be monitored for symptoms.
fact_text: Contact management flowchart: Under 5 years well contacts get 6 months TPT; symptomatic children any age get TB evaluation; well children 5+ years get no treatment but monitored.
source_figure_or_table: Figure 1: Approach to contact management when chest X-ray and TST are not readily available

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Screening should also be available for contacts of smear-negative pulmonary TB cases.
fact_text: Screening should be available for contacts of smear-negative pulmonary TB cases.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: If a contact of a smear-negative pulmonary TB source case is symptomatic, TB diagnosis should be investigated regardless of contact's age.
fact_text: Symptomatic contacts of smear-negative pulmonary TB source cases require TB diagnostic evaluation regardless of age.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Clinical assessment alone is sufficient to decide if a contact is well or symptomatic; routine CXR or Mantoux test is not required for exposed contacts of smear-positive pulmonary TB cases.
fact_text: Clinical assessment alone suffices to determine if a child contact of smear-positive pulmonary TB is well or symptomatic; routine CXR or Mantoux test is not required for these contacts.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: Box II - Symptom criteria for PTB
referral_criteria: any one of the above symptom criteria in a child <15 years in close contact with known bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed TB should be regarded as presumptive TB and referred for physician evaluation
fact_text: Presumptive pulmonary TB in children <15 years includes any one of: persistent cough >2 weeks not responding to antibiotics/bronchodilators; persistent fever >38°C >2 weeks after excluding common infections; documented weight loss or failure to gain weight over 3 months especially if not responding to deworming/nutrition; fatigue or reduced activity. Such children with close contact to confirmed TB should be referred for evaluation.
source_figure_or_table: Box II - Symptom criteria for PTB

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: TB presentation in children varies by age: infants <1 year mainly pneumonia-like; children 1-9 years usually chronic cough; adolescents 10-19 years similar to adults.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Cervical TB lymphadenitis in children presents as a painless, visible neck mass of matted lymph nodes not fixed to underlying tissues, sometimes with sinus formation; systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss are usually minimal or absent.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Symptoms suggestive of extrapulmonary TB include painless enlarged matted lymph nodes (>2x2 cm) in neck (TB lymphadenitis), cough and shortness of breath (pleural/pericardial TB), neurological signs with meningitis symptoms (TB meningitis), abdominal pain with altered bowel habit or ascites (abdominal TB), gibbus deformity (spinal TB), and chronic single joint pain/swelling (TB arthritis).

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: Chest X-rays showing right-sided TB pleural effusion
fact_text: Pleural TB in children <6 years presents with intermittent fever, localized chest pain, shortness of breath, stony dull percussion, diminished breath sounds, and restricted chest movement; pleural effusion is rare before 2 years and child is not sick-looking.
source_figure_or_table: Chest X-rays showing right-sided TB pleural effusion

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: Chest X-ray showing pericardial TB with enlarged cardiac silhouette
recommended_tests: Chest X-ray showing enlarged cardiac silhouette
fact_text: Pericardial TB in children is rare, presents with pericardial effusion, non-specific symptoms (low-grade fever, malaise, weight loss), and signs including distant heart sounds, pericardial friction rub, raised JVP, and pulsus paradoxus; chest X-ray shows enlarged cardiac silhouette.
source_figure_or_table: Chest X-ray showing pericardial TB with enlarged cardiac silhouette

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: TB meningitis in children <4 years presents with progressive neurological symptoms over weeks; diagnosis requires CSF study and Xpert MTB/RIF if available; early treatment is critical.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Miliary TB is a disseminated TB form in children <3 years with systemic symptoms, characteristic chest X-ray pattern, and physical signs including enlarged lymph nodes and purpuric skin or eye lesions.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Abdominal TB in children presents with non-specific GI symptoms including fever, abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea, weight loss, anorexia, malaise, abdominal distension from ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, doughy abdominal mass, enterocutaneous fistula, and malnutrition.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: TB meningitis is an important form of extrapulmonary TB in children.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: Figure showing clinical gibbus deformity and spinal X-ray
recommended_tests: Spinal X-ray showing vertebral destruction and gibbus
recommended_advice: Suspect spinal TB in any child with local spine pain and tenderness
Recognize rapid onset gibbus as almost always due to tuberculosis
referral_criteria: Neurological deficits such as paraplegia or quadriplegia require urgent referral
fact_text: In children, spinal TB commonly presents with back pain, tenderness, night pain, and rapid onset gibbus deformity; neurological complications require urgent referral.
source_figure_or_table: Figure showing clinical gibbus deformity and spinal X-ray

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: BOX-III: Danger signs requiring urgent hospitalization
fact_text: Urgent hospital referral is required for children with severe respiratory distress (TB pneumonia +/- bacterial superinfection, pleural effusion), severe wheezing unresponsive to bronchodilators, signs of TB meningitis, disseminated TB, pericardial effusion, spinal deformity/paraplegia, or severe anemia/malnutrition.
source_figure_or_table: BOX-III: Danger signs requiring urgent hospitalization

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Congenital TB is rare, manifests at 2-3 weeks with nonspecific symptoms in neonates born to TB-infected mothers or with persistent pneumonia and hepatosplenomegaly.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Uncommon signs indicative of recent TB infection include phlyctenular conjunctivitis (raised red nodule at sclera/cornea junction) and erythema nodosum (raised tender purple patches on shin).

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: False negative TST may occur in severe malnutrition, immunosuppressive conditions (measles, whooping cough, HIV, steroids, anti-cancer drugs), disseminated/miliary TB or TB meningitis, and recent TB exposure within 3 months.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_tests: Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) with 5 TU PPD-S or 2 TU PPD RT23 injected intradermally on left forearm
fact_text: TST is positive if induration ≥10 mm or ≥5 mm in children with PEM, HIV, or immunosuppression; negative TST does not exclude TB; test done by intradermal injection of 5 TU PPD-S or 2 TU PPD RT23 on left forearm.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_tests: Chest X-ray (CXR) is useful for diagnosis of TB in children along with other criteria (signs/symptoms, history of exposure, TST)
Good-quality CXRs are essential and should preferably be read by a radiologist or trained health-care worker
fact_text: Chest X-ray is recommended for diagnosis of TB in children with pulmonary symptoms and suggestive signs; should be good quality and read by radiologist or trained health worker.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Less common radiological signs in child TB include airway compression by lymph nodes, miliary opacification (especially in HIV-negative children), and unilateral pleural effusions in children over 5 years.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Radiological features requiring urgent hospital referral include widespread millet-sized lesions (disseminated/miliary TB), severe airway obstruction, severe lung involvement, and acute spinal angulation (gibbus).

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Chest X-ray should always be done in all forms of TB in children; common radiological patterns include increased hilar density and persistent lung opacities not improving after antibiotics.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Appropriate clinical samples for bacteriological confirmation in children include sputum, gastric aspirates, nasopharyngeal aspirate, stool, lymph node biopsy material, and cerebrospinal fluid; samples should be properly collected and sent for microscopy, culture, and histopathology where available.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Bacteriological confirmation in children should use available clinical samples and tests including Xpert MTB/RIF, Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, smear microscopy, culture, and Line Probe Assay.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Bacteriological confirmation is important in all TB cases but especially in children with suspected drug-resistant TB, severe immunosuppression including HIV, complicated or severe disease, or uncertain diagnosis.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
