source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Children usually have paucibacillary pulmonary TB with rare cavitation; children develop extrapulmonary TB more often than adults, especially severe forms like TB meningitis and miliary TB in children under 3 years.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Effective anti-TB treatment requires bactericidal drugs that kill metabolizing organisms and combinations to target extra- and intra-cellular bacilli, with therapy duration of at least 6 months.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Treatment outcomes in children are generally good, including in young and immune compromised children who are at higher risk of disease progression and dissemination.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Regular weight-based dose adjustment is important, especially in young or malnourished children during the intensive phase when weight gain may be pronounced.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Ethambutol is bacteriostatic/bactericidal at higher concentration, acts on actively growing bacilli, reduces rifampicin resistance in high bacillary load, but has limited blood-brain barrier penetration.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Ethambutol penetrates cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) only in presence of meningeal inflammation; CSF penetration of streptomycin is unpredictable, explaining why EMB replaces SM in TB meningitis treatment.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: In extensive disease excluding TB meningitis, HIV co-infection, or suspicion of INH resistance, add ethambutol as a fourth drug during the intensive phase to improve outcome and reduce drug resistance risk.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Pyrazinamide is bactericidal, effective against dormant intracellular bacilli within acidic centers of caseating granuloma, and achieves good CSF levels.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Standard drug-susceptible TB treatment includes 3 drugs (INH, RMP, PZA) during 2-month intensive phase and 2 drugs (INH, RMP) during 4-month continuation phase.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
dose_or_duration: Child-friendly fixed-dose combination tablets contain 60 mg Rifampicin, 30 mg Isoniazid, and 150 mg Pyrazinamide per tablet; new FDC contains 75 mg Rifampicin, 50 mg Isoniazid, and 150 mg Pyrazinamide per tablet.
contraindications_or_cautions: Some uncertainty in dosing for weight bands due to tablet breaking
fact_text: Child-friendly FDC tablets contain 60 mg Rifampicin, 30 mg Isoniazid, and 150 mg Pyrazinamide per tablet; new WHO-aligned FDC contains 75 mg Rifampicin, 50 mg Isoniazid, and 150 mg Pyrazinamide per tablet.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
dose_or_duration: Isoniazid 10 mg/kg (range 7-15 mg/kg), max 300 mg daily; Rifampicin 15 mg/kg (range 10-20 mg/kg), max 600 mg daily; Pyrazinamide 35 mg/kg (range 30-40 mg/kg), max 2000 mg daily; Ethambutol 20 mg/kg (range 15-25 mg/kg), max 1200 mg daily
contraindications_or_cautions: Higher dosage (mg/kg) required for young children to achieve effective bactericidal activity
No increased risk of drug-related hepatotoxicity or optic neuritis with revised dosages
fact_text: Recommended daily doses for first-line anti-TB drugs in children: Isoniazid 10 mg/kg (7-15), Rifampicin 15 mg/kg (10-20), Pyrazinamide 35 mg/kg (30-40), Ethambutol 20 mg/kg (15-25), with specified maximum daily doses.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
dose_or_duration: Weight band dosing for child FDC tablets: 2-3.9 kg: 0.5 tablet RHZ + 0.5 tablet Ethambutol (E) in intensive phase, 0.5 tablet RH in continuation; 4-7.9 kg: 1 tablet RHZ + 1 tablet E intensive, 1 tablet RH continuation; 8-11.9 kg: 2 tablets RHZ + 2 tablets E intensive, 2 tablets RH continuation; 12-15.9 kg: 3 tablets RHZ + 3 tablets E intensive, 3 tablets RH continuation; 16-24.9 kg: 4 tablets RHZ + 4 tablets E intensive, 4 tablets RH continuation; ≥25 kg: switch to adult dosages and preparations.
contraindications_or_cautions: Ethambutol (20 mg/kg/day) may be added on physician's decision if extensive lung involvement or disseminated TB
fact_text: Weight band dosing table for child FDC tablets: tablets per day increase with weight bands from 0.5 to 4 tablets in intensive and continuation phases; ethambutol may be added at 20 mg/kg/day if extensive lung or disseminated TB.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Children aged ≥8 years and/or weighing ≥25 kg are routinely treated with adult TB regimens.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
contraindications_or_cautions: Ethambutol is considered safe in children at a dose of 20 mg/kg (range 15-25 mg/kg) daily
fact_text: Children with extensive pulmonary disease (cavitary lesion, miliary TB) and severe EPTB (disseminated TB) in low HIV prevalence/low INH resistance settings should be treated with 2 months HRZE followed by 4 months HR regimen.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
contraindications_or_cautions: Ethambutol is considered safe in children at a dose of 20 mg/kg (range 15-25 mg/kg) daily
fact_text: Children with presumptive or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis in low HIV prevalence/low INH resistance settings and HIV-negative children can be treated with 2 months HRZ followed by 4 months HR regimen.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: For children with TB meningitis and osteoarticular TB, treatment may be extended up to 12 months based on clinical judgment.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text:
Table 11: Treatment regimens for children by TB diagnostic category and setting: 
- Low HIV prevalence and low INH resistance: 
  * Smear negative pulmonary TB and TB lymph node (intrathoracic and peripheral): 2 months intensive phase HRZ, 4 months continuation HR.
  * Smear positive pulmonary TB, extensive pulmonary disease, severe EPTB (except TB meningitis and osteoarticular): 2 months intensive HRZE, 4 months continuation HR.
- Any status/setting: TB meningitis and osteoarticular TB: 2 months intensive HRZE, 10 months continuation HR.
- MDR TB and XDR TB: specially designed standardized treatment (2nd line anti-TB drugs).

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: WHO recommends a 4-month treatment regimen (2HRZ/2HR) for children and adolescents under 16 years with non-severe presumed drug-susceptible TB.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: WHO recommends a 6-month intensive treatment regimen (6HRZEto) for children and adolescents with drug-susceptible TB meningitis.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_medicines: Corticosteroids may be used in complicated TB forms including CNS TB (TB meningitis), TB pericarditis, and adrenal TB.
dose_or_duration: Prednisolone 2-4 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg) for 4 weeks, then tapered over 1-2 weeks
contraindications_or_cautions: Sudden withdrawal of corticosteroids can cause serious side effects such as adrenal crisis.
fact_text: Corticosteroids (prednisolone 2-4 mg/kg/day max 60 mg for 4 weeks, then tapered) are recommended for CNS TB including meningitis, TB pericarditis, and adrenal TB; sudden withdrawal risks adrenal crisis.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_medicines: Ethambutol should be added additionally with the fixed-dose combination (FDC) when indicated.
dose_or_duration: Drugs dosages depend on body weight and are given daily (7 days per week); doses adjusted as weight changes during treatment.
fact_text: Ethambutol is added with the FDC when indicated; drug doses depend on body weight and are given daily, adjusted as weight changes.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_medicines: Pyridoxine should be given with isoniazid in HIV-infected and severely malnourished children to prevent isoniazid-associated neuropathy.
dose_or_duration: 12.5 mg/day for children 5-11 years; 25 mg/day for children ≥12 years
fact_text: Pyridoxine is recommended with isoniazid in HIV-infected and severely malnourished children to prevent neuropathy; dose 12.5 mg/day for 5-11 years, 25 mg/day for ≥12 years.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) is essential to ensure patients take the right drugs, doses, intervals, and duration for TB treatment completion and recovery.
followup_monitoring: Children should be weighed at 1, 2, 3 months and at 6 months to adjust drug doses; weight should be documented on the TB treatment card.
fact_text: DOT is essential for TB treatment adherence; children must be weighed at 1, 2, 3, and 6 months to adjust doses and document weight on treatment card.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_medicines: Pyridoxine is not routinely used in general treatment initiation but should be added if a child develops neuropathy symptoms after treatment.
fact_text: Pyridoxine is not routinely used at treatment start but should be added if neuropathy symptoms develop during treatment.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
referral_criteria: Refer children urgently to a competent physician if there is poor response to therapy defined as no weight gain or persistent symptoms after 2-3 months of treatment.
fact_text: Children with no weight gain or persistent symptoms after 2-3 months of TB therapy should be urgently referred for assessment.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
referral_criteria: Refer to physician if drug resistance suspected or poor response
fact_text: Suspect drug-resistant TB in children with poor response, no weight gain after 2-3 months, HIV infection, severe malnutrition, or index case with drug resistance; refer for evaluation.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_tests: Weight monitoring on IPHN growth chart at each visit
Repeat sputum exams at 2, 5, and 6 months for sputum smear-positive children

Routine follow-up chest X-rays not required unless persistent symptoms or poor response
followup_monitoring: Monthly clinical follow-up for first 3 months
Weight gain expected within 2-3 months
Repeat sputum exams for smear-positive cases at 2, 5, and 6 months
Chest X-rays only if persistent symptoms or poor response
fact_text: Children on TB treatment should be followed monthly for 3 months with weight monitoring and sputum exams for smear-positive cases; chest X-rays only if poor response or new symptoms.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
referral_criteria: All children with severe forms of TB (TB meningitis, tuberculoma, cavitary PTB, miliary TB, TB peritonitis, genital, spinal or osteoarticular TB)
Children with presumptive MDR-TB or XDR-TB or in contact with MDR-TB or XDR-TB case and not responding to first-line therapy
Children with poor response to therapy (no weight gain, persistent symptoms after 2-3 months of treatment)
Children with severe adverse effects of anti-TB drugs
fact_text: Children with severe TB forms, presumptive or contact MDR/XDR-TB not responding to first-line therapy, poor treatment response after 2-3 months, or severe drug adverse effects should be referred for expert management.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: TB drugs have specific main toxicities: Isoniazid (hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy), Rifampicin (hepatitis, orange secretions, drug interactions), Pyrazinamide (hepatitis, arthralgia), Ethambutol (visual disturbance), Aminoglycosides (ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity), Fluoroquinolones (arthralgia, insomnia, confusion), Ethionamide (vomiting, hypothyroidism, hepatitis), Capreomycin (oto- and nephrotoxicity), Cycloserine (psychosis, depression, convulsions), PAS (diarrhea, vomiting, hypothyroidism).

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: Figure 3: Management of Drug Induced Hepatitis
recommended_advice: Repeat liver function test after interval to confirm normalization before restarting anti-TB drugs
referral_criteria: Urgent referral if liver tenderness, hepatomegaly, or jaundice present
followup_monitoring: Follow up clinically and biochemically until resolution of hepatitis
contraindications_or_cautions: Stop anti-TB drugs immediately if significant hepatotoxicity occurs
fact_text: In children, hepatotoxicity from TB drugs (mainly PZA, then INH, RMP) is rare but serious; stop medication if SGPT >3x normal symptomatic or >5x asymptomatic, check viral markers, refer if needed, and restart anti-TB drugs gradually after resolution with monitoring.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Treatment failure or relapse within 6 months after treatment completion in children should prompt evaluation for retreatment and drug susceptibility testing to identify MDR-TB.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Mycobacterial culture and drug susceptibility testing (DST) should be performed for all retreatment cases in children before starting treatment to guide regimen choice.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: If drug-resistant TB is identified in a child retreatment case, treatment should be based on the drug susceptibility pattern of the source case strain or isolate from the child if available.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Occurrence of liver tenderness, hepatomegaly or jaundice in children on anti-TB drugs should prompt urgent referral and liver function testing to detect hepatotoxicity; anti-TB drugs should be stopped until liver function normalizes.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
dose_or_duration: Isoniazid (INH) may cause peripheral neuropathy, especially in severely malnourished, HIV-infected children on HAART, chronic liver disease or renal failure; supplemental pyridoxine (12.5-25 mg daily) is recommended in older children and multi-vitamin syrup in infants.
fact_text: Isoniazid (INH) may cause peripheral neuropathy, especially in severely malnourished, HIV-infected children on HAART, chronic liver disease or renal failure; supplemental pyridoxine (12.5-25 mg daily) is recommended in older children and multi-vitamin syrup in infants.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: In genuine treatment failure cases, two or more new drugs should be added to the retreatment regimen and treatment duration should be at least 9 months.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Criteria for presumptive child DR-TB include recent treatment history, close contact with DR-TB cases or treatment failure/non-adherence, and lack of clinical improvement after 2-3 months of first-line treatment.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_tests: rapid molecular testing (GeneXpert or GenoType MTBDRplus line probe assay)
fact_text: Child DR-TB diagnosis relies on clinical and radiological grounds plus risk factors; bacteriological confirmation via smear, culture, pathology, or molecular tests (Xpert MTB/RIF, line probe assay) is recommended when possible, with rapid DST prioritized.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_tests: drug susceptibility testing (DST) for isoniazid and rifampicin
second-line DST to exclude XDR-TB in confirmed DR-TB cases
fact_text: In confirmed child DR-TB cases, second-line DST should be performed to exclude XDR-TB and guide effective treatment regimen.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: Figure 4: Algorithm for presumptive DR-TB in a child
fact_text: For presumptive DR-TB in children, clinical assessment and MDR-TB diagnostics (sputum, rapid tests, fluid sampling) are required; treatment decisions depend on diagnostic results and clinical stability, with unstable children considered for MDR-TB therapy while awaiting confirmation.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Children with DR-TB should be managed using the same principles as adults, including treatment based on the DST pattern of the most likely source case if the child lacks their own DST.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: For children with DR-TB, injectable-free regimens are recommended, especially for very young children.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Severe TB disease in children <15 years is defined by presence of cavities, bilateral chest disease, extra-pulmonary disease other than lymphadenopathy, advanced malnutrition, or advanced immunosuppression/positive bacteriology.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
dose_or_duration: Treatment duration depends on disease severity: 9-11 months for non-severe disease; 12-18 months for severe disease depending on clinical progress.
fact_text: Duration of treatment in children is 9-11 months for non-severe disease and 12-18 months for severe disease depending on clinical progress.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_medicines: Bedaquiline for children aged 6 years and above
Delamanid for children aged 3 years and above with careful monitoring
Avoid Efavirenz in children needing bedaquiline
Amoxicillin-Clavulanic acid with imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem (not counted as separate agent)
Linezolid use associated with frequent toxicity
recommended_advice: Use child-friendly formulations when possible
Monitor and manage adverse events
followup_monitoring: Audiometry for Amikacin
Adverse event monitoring
contraindications_or_cautions: Use of Amikacin requires audiometry monitoring
Linezolid use caution due to toxicity
Careful monitoring with delamanid use
fact_text: DR-TB regimens in children should include at least 3 effective drugs, prioritize WHO Group A and B drugs, use Amikacin with audiometry, bedaquiline for age ≥6 years, delamanid for age ≥3 years with monitoring, avoid Efavirenz if on bedaquiline, and use pyrazinamide only if susceptible.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Current WHO guidelines do not recommend preventive therapy for contacts of drug-resistant TB patients.
Close contacts of DR-TB patients who develop TB usually have drug-resistant disease.
fact_text: Preventive therapy is not recommended for child contacts of drug-resistant TB patients according to current WHO guidelines.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
followup_monitoring: Close monitoring of children on MDR-TB treatment is essential to evaluate therapeutic efficacy and mitigate adverse events.
Monitoring and follow-up are major challenges in pediatric MDR-TB management.
fact_text: Children treated for MDR-TB require close monitoring and follow-up to ensure treatment efficacy and to detect adverse events.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
dose_or_duration: Not specified; regimen depends on age and drug resistance pattern
fact_text: Children with MDR-TB are treated similarly to adults with MDR-TB; regimens vary by age group and include combinations of Lzd, Cfz, Cs, Dlm, PAS, Eto, Lfx, and Bdq with additional drugs as needed.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: All children with an infectious TB contact should be screened for TB disease, especially children living with HIV and child household contacts of DR-TB.
followup_monitoring: Careful clinical follow-up of asymptomatic children is recommended every 2-3 months for the first 6 months, then every 6 months for at least 2 years.
fact_text: Children with infectious TB contact, especially HIV-positive and DR-TB contacts, should be screened and asymptomatic children followed clinically every 2-3 months for 6 months, then 6-monthly for 2 years.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: If TB disease develops in a child contact, treatment with an appropriate DR-TB regimen based on the DST pattern of the presumed source case should be initiated.
fact_text: Treatment of child DR-TB cases should be based on DST pattern of the presumed source case.

fact_text: Weight-band dosing table for second-line DR-TB medicines in children under 14 years includes levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, and cycloserine with specified doses by weight and formulation.

fact_text: Child TB medicines dosing by weight bands for Ethambutol, Delamanid, Pyrazinamide, Amikacin, Ethionamide/Prothionamide, PAS, and high-dose Isoniazid are specified with formulations and usual upper daily doses.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
dose_or_duration: Isoniazid 300 mg tablets can be used in patients over 20 kg; full dose can be given once daily if tolerated
fact_text: Isoniazid 300 mg tablets may be used in children >20 kg; full dose can be given once daily if tolerated.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
dose_or_duration: Moxifloxacin dose: 10 mg/kg for children under 6 months
fact_text: Moxifloxacin dose is 10 mg/kg in children under 6 months of age.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
dose_or_duration: For children aged 3 years or more: Moxifloxacin doses are 25 mg twice daily (bd) for 3-5 years, 50 mg bd for 6-11 years, and 100 mg bd for 12-17 years
fact_text: Moxifloxacin dosing for children ≥3 years: 25 mg bd (3-5 years), 50 mg bd (6-11 years), 100 mg bd (12-17 years).

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_medicines: Pyridoxine is always given with high dose isoniazid in children (12.5 mg once daily in children under 5 years, 25 mg once daily in children over 4 years)
dose_or_duration: Pyridoxine supplementation is mandatory with high-dose isoniazid in children: 12.5 mg daily if <5 years, 25 mg daily if >4 years.
fact_text: Pyridoxine supplementation is mandatory with high-dose isoniazid in children: 12.5 mg daily if <5 years, 25 mg daily if >4 years.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_medicines: Bedaquiline recommended as part of shorter all-oral regimens or longer treatment regimens for children with MDR/RR-TB of all ages
Delamanid recommended as part of longer treatment regimens for children with MDR/RR-TB of all ages
fact_text: Bedaquiline is recommended for all-age children with MDR/RR-TB as part of shorter all-oral or longer regimens; Delamanid is recommended for longer regimens.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Active TB disease in children is defined by infection with M. tuberculosis plus clinical signs/symptoms and optionally laboratory or radiologic evidence suggestive of TB.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Children under 8 years rarely develop cavitary or highly infectious pulmonary TB; children over 8 years often develop sputum smear-positive TB and can transmit infection.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_tests: Positive Mantoux test (MT) or IGRA usually indicates LTBI
MT and IGRA have limitations, especially in HIV-infected or malnourished children
MT may be false negative in these groups
Positive test may take up to 3 months after TB exposure
fact_text: Latent TB infection (LTBI) in children is defined as persistent immune response to M. tuberculosis antigens without active TB symptoms; usually indicated by positive Mantoux or IGRA test, but tests have limitations especially in HIV or malnourished children.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Risk of progression to pulmonary TB disease after primary infection is highest in children under 1 year (30-40%), with 10-20% risk of disseminated disease or tubercular meningitis; risk decreases with age.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Key risk factors for TB disease in children include close contact with smear or culture positive pulmonary TB cases, age under 5 years, severe malnutrition or immunosuppression (including recent measles, whooping cough, HIV, steroids), and development of disease mostly within first year after exposure.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Risk of developing TB among TST or IGRA positive children is highest in <5 years (19%) and lower in older age groups (5-9 years 9%, 9-14 years 8%, 15-18 years 12%).

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Priority groups for TB preventive treatment include household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB, children under 5 years, adults over 60 years, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, anti-TNF treatment, transplantation candidates, substance abuse, and silicosis.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Bangladesh national TB preventive treatment targets for 2021-2023 are 185,560 (2021), 285,300 (2022), and 349,340 (2023) including under-5 children and household contacts.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Symptoms suggestive of TB include any of: cough for two weeks or more, haemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss, chest pain, shortness of breath, fatigue.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: FIGURE: 5 ALGORITHM FOR DIAGNOSIS OF LTBI
fact_text: Algorithm for LTBI diagnosis in household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB patients: Age <5 or ≥60 years old or PLHIV with any TB clinical feature (cough, fever, weight loss) require TB and other disease investigations; if no clinical features, do chest X-ray and if no abnormality, treat for LTBI. For contacts aged ≥5 but <60 years with diabetes, smoking, or clinical vulnerabilities, if clinical features present, investigate TB; if no clinical features, do TST/IGRA test and treat LTBI if positive, no treatment if negative.
source_figure_or_table: FIGURE: 5 ALGORITHM FOR DIAGNOSIS OF LTBI

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
contraindications_or_cautions: Exclude active TB by clinical features and abnormal radiological findings before providing TPT
fact_text: TPT is provided to people with comorbidities (diabetes, CKD, smoking, prolonged steroid use) after excluding active TB by clinical and radiological assessment.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Educate parents/relatives about potential adverse events
Agree on follow-up plan by phone or community visit
Monitor body weight and adverse events
Monthly liver function tests for high-risk or elevated baseline patients
Monthly contact with patient by community health worker or telephone
Ensure continuous drug supply
Regularly screen and manage adverse events
Correctly record and report treatment
followup_monitoring: monthly follow-up
monitor body weight
monitor adverse events
monthly liver function tests if high risk
fact_text: Regular monthly follow-up for people on TB preventive treatment includes education on adverse events, agreed follow-up plan, monitoring weight and adverse events, monthly liver function tests for high-risk patients, monthly contact by community health worker or phone, ensuring drug supply, and proper recording and reporting.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Preventive treatment for contacts of MDR-TB cases is not routinely recommended due to limited evidence; it may be considered in selected high-risk household contacts based on individualized risk assessment and drug susceptibility profile of the source case with strict clinical observation and monitoring for at least two years.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
dose_or_duration: LTBI treatment regimens include 3HP weekly for 12 weeks with isoniazid 300mg and rifapentin 300mg for adults >15 years; 3HR daily for 90 days with rifampicin 75mg and isoniazid 50mg for children <10 years; 3HR daily for 90 days with rifampicin 150mg and isoniazid 75mg for children 10 to <15 years; and INH 300mg daily for 180 days for PLHIV adults.
fact_text: LTBI treatment regimens include 3HP weekly for 12 weeks with isoniazid 300mg and rifapentin 300mg for adults >15 years; 3HR daily for 90 days with rifampicin 75mg and isoniazid 50mg for children <10 years; 3HR daily for 90 days with rifampicin 150mg and isoniazid 75mg for children 10 to <15 years; and INH 300mg daily for 180 days for PLHIV adults.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
dose_or_duration: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg body weight 3 times daily; Domperidone 1 mg/kg/day; Pyridoxine 50 mg if mild peripheral neuropathy in children; Chlorpheniramine oral up to 1 mg for 1 year old, 1-2 mg for 1-5 years, 2-4 mg for >5 years
recommended_advice: Advise hydration with water and juice for flu-like symptoms and nausea
Avoid spicy and greasy food with nausea
Prescribe oral rehydration solution if mild dehydration present
followup_monitoring: Regular screening for adverse events during follow-up in person or by phone if patient cannot attend
contraindications_or_cautions: Do not reintroduce TPT after severe hypersensitivity or Stevens-Johnson syndrome
fact_text: Regularly screen for adverse events during TPT; manage flu-like symptoms with hydration and paracetamol 15 mg/kg thrice daily; treat nausea with domperidone 1 mg/kg/day and hydration; monitor hepatotoxicity by AST/ALT levels and stop TPT if >3 times ULN with symptoms or >5 times ULN; treat mild peripheral neuropathy with pyridoxine 50 mg; manage mild skin hypersensitivity with calamine lotion or steroids and chlorpheniramine; withhold TPT for generalized rash or mucosal swelling; reassure orange-red discoloration of body fluids is harmless.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Trace and investigate household contacts of index TB cases
Prioritize children under 5 years and adolescents for active case finding and outreach sputum smear centers
All child household contacts of smear-positive or DR TB patients should be examined for TB signs
If contacts cannot attend health facility, health workers or community volunteers should visit homes to identify symptomatic persons
fact_text: Active case finding should prioritize household contacts, especially children under 5 and adolescents; child contacts of smear-positive or DR TB patients must be examined for TB signs, with home visits if needed.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Adherence to full course and completion of preventive treatment is critical for clinical benefit and prevention of TB disease
fact_text: Adherence and completion of the full course of TB preventive treatment are essential for individual clinical benefit and prevention of progression from infection to disease.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
referral_criteria: If active TB disease occurs during TPT, stop TPT and provide DS-TB or DR-TB treatment as appropriate
For any TPT regimen change due to severe adverse events, consult national experts before switching
fact_text: If any TB signs or symptoms occur during TPT, investigate for active TB; if active TB is confirmed, stop TPT and start appropriate DS-TB or DR-TB treatment; consult national experts before changing TPT regimen for severe adverse events.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: Figure 6: Community Based Active Case Findings flowchart
recommended_advice: Contact investigation identifies people exposed to infectious TB to evaluate for active TB and LTBI and provide appropriate treatment.
Contact investigation aims to find active TB cases and identify eligible contacts for TB Preventive Treatment (TPT) among children and adults.
Contact investigation is important for early case finding including drug-resistant TB and preventing ongoing transmission in households and communities.
Close follow-up of contacts of MDR-TB and XDR-TB patients is essential to prevent further spread.
fact_text: Contact investigation is used to identify and evaluate household contacts of pulmonary bacteriologically positive TB patients for active TB or LTBI, including drug-resistant TB contacts, to provide treatment and prevent transmission.

recommended_advice: Symptomatic contacts are referred to health facility for TB rule-out and if TB disease is confirmed, treated per national guidelines.
Asymptomatic contacts undergo chest X-ray evaluation; if abnormal, further evaluation is done; if no abnormality, treat for LTBI.
referral_criteria: Symptomatic contacts referred to health facility for TB rule-out
Contacts with abnormal chest X-ray referred for further evaluation
fact_text: Household contacts of pulmonary bacteriologically positive TB patients undergo symptom screening; symptomatic contacts are referred for TB rule-out and treatment if confirmed; asymptomatic contacts get chest X-ray, with abnormal findings leading to further evaluation and normal findings leading to LTBI treatment.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Common adverse events following BCG immunization include adenitis, local abscess, lymphadenopathy (non-suppurative and suppurative), wart-like nodules, large ulcers, osteomyelitis, local bacterial infections, and lupoid reactions.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Two forms of BCG adenitis exist: non-suppurative (benign) and suppurative (afebrile axillary lymphadenopathy developing 2-5 months post vaccination, size 1-5 cm, minimal tenderness).

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: BCG vaccination is recommended to avoid life-threatening TB diseases in children despite incomplete protection against TB disease
fact_text: BCG vaccination is recommended in children to prevent severe forms of TB such as TB meningitis and miliary TB despite incomplete protection against pulmonary TB.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: A baby born to a mother diagnosed with TB in last 2 months of pregnancy or without documented sputum smear conversion needs careful management including referral for evaluation if symptomatic and full TB treatment if diagnosed.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: If baby is asymptomatic, withhold BCG at birth and give BCG after completion of 3 months of 3HR therapy; if symptoms develop during TPT, refer for evaluation to exclude TB.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: If no BCG scar is present, give BCG again with the third dose of pentavalent vaccine as per Bangladesh EPI policy.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: In children with high risk of disseminated TB (e.g. HIV positive), treatment with multiple drugs is required; BCG is resistant to PZA and may be intermediately resistant to INH depending on strain.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Non-suppurative BCG adenitis should be left alone; suppurative and fluctuating adenitis requires needle aspiration or total excision to reduce scar from rupture.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Anti-TB drugs are secreted in breast milk at low concentrations that do not affect the baby; breastfeeding should be encouraged.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: BCG vaccine should not be given at birth to patients receiving TPT or TB treatment and is contraindicated if the infant is known HIV-infected; BCG should be given after completion of 6 months TPT or TB treatment.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Apply administrative, environmental (engineering), and personal protection controls for TB infection control in patient and staff areas.
Provide health education on TB transmission without stigmatizing patients.

Encourage proper cough hygiene: cover nose/mouth with hand, arm, tissue, cloth, or mask when coughing/sneezing; turn head away from others; dispose used tissues properly; spit in covered container; perform hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions.
Ensure natural or cross ventilation and sunlight in TB clinics and health facilities; keep doors/windows open on opposite sides for air circulation.
Segregate children from adult TB patients if possible; keep windows open with ventilation fans; advise TB patients to do the same at home and health facilities.
Screen healthcare workers and caregivers for TB symptoms.
Use respirator devices (e.g., N-95 or FFP2 masks) for healthcare workers during aerosol-generating procedures like sputum induction, bronchoscopy, BAL.
Prompt recognition and treatment of TB patients in community settings reduces TB transmission.
fact_text: TB infection control includes administrative, environmental, and personal protection measures; cough hygiene; ventilation; segregation of children from adult TB patients; screening of healthcare workers; use of respirators during aerosol procedures; and prompt community TB treatment.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Use the following standardized forms and registers for TB recording and reporting: TB Treatment Card (TB 01), TB Identity Card (TB 02), TB Register (TB 03), TB Laboratory Register (TB 04), Request form for AFB Microscopy/Spert MTB/RIF (TB 05), Form DR TB 06 for diagnosis/follow-up of drug resistant TB, TB referral/transfer form (TB 07), Requisition form for drugs (TB 08), Absentee Tracing form (TB 09), Quarterly Reports on case finding (TB 10), treatment results (TB 11), sputum conversion (TB 12), Laboratory Performance Report (TB 13), and Presumptive TB cases Referral Form (TB 14).
fact_text: NTP recommends using specific standardized TB recording and reporting forms and registers (TB 01 to TB 14) for consistent data collection and monitoring.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Use standardized recording and reporting system for monitoring and evaluation of TB patient outcomes and program performance.
fact_text: Standardized TB recording and reporting system is essential for monitoring patient outcomes, program performance, and policy development in the National TB Programme.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Monitoring is the systematic ongoing collection, collation, analysis, and interpretation of data to detect deviations from expected norms and provide feedback for corrective actions.
followup_monitoring: Monitoring tracks progress toward program objectives, permits informed decisions on program effectiveness and resource use, and facilitates early identification of deviations for timely solutions.
fact_text: Monitoring in TB programs involves systematic data collection and analysis to detect deviations and enable corrective actions for program effectiveness.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Methods of monitoring include routine report review focusing on data management, supply, finance, training, quality assurance, and drug use.
followup_monitoring: Supervisory visits reinforce routine reporting requirements and provide on-the-spot training, informal and direct monitoring.
fact_text: Monitoring methods include routine report review, supervisory visits for training and monitoring, and sentinel reporting to detect rapid changes or unexpected outcomes.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Sentinel reporting supplements routine reporting and is most useful when a system is undergoing rapid or substantial change to detect unexpected or unintended outcomes.
fact_text: Sentinel reporting supplements routine TB program reporting to detect unexpected outcomes during rapid or substantial system changes.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Supervision is a key element of TB control, focusing on on-the-job training, coaching, mentoring, coordination, motivation, facilitation, and guidance to achieve national TB program targets.
followup_monitoring: Supervisory visits aim to ensure effective implementation, provide technical and administrative support, validate reported data, review bottlenecks and take corrective measures, ensure patient and staff satisfaction, and strengthen relationships between central, intermediate, and peripheral levels.
fact_text: Supervisory visits in TB control include on-the-job training, coaching, mentoring, and coordination to ensure effective implementation and data validation.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: ANNEX 1: Frequency of symptoms and signs of pulmonary TB stratified by patient age
fact_text: Frequency of pulmonary TB symptoms/signs varies by age: Fever common in infants and adolescents, uncommon in children; Night sweats rare in infants/children, uncommon in adolescents; Cough common in all ages; Productive cough common only in adolescents; Haemoptysis rare in children/adolescents, never in infants; Dyspnoea common in infants, rare in older children/adolescents; Crepitations common in infants, uncommon in children, rare in adolescents; Wheezing common in infants, uncommon in older groups; Fremitus and dullness to percussion rare in infants/children, uncommon in adolescents; Decreased breath sounds common in infants, rare/uncommon in older groups.

recommended_tests: Administer 0.1 ml tuberculin intradermally on forearm, 5-10 cm below elbow, using 27 gauge needle with short bevel
recommended_advice: Ensure wheal of 8-10 mm appears after injection
Repeat test 5 cm away if wheal not visible or less than 5 mm
Do not cover injection site with band aid
fact_text: Mantoux test administration requires intradermal injection of 0.1 ml tuberculin on forearm with visible wheal 8-10 mm; repeat if wheal absent or <5 mm.

fact_text: Mantoux test administration requires recording location, tuberculin lot number, expiration date, date/time, and health professional signature.

Palpate for induration
Mark edges of induration with pen at 45° angle
Measure induration with ruler on inside-left edge and read on inside-right edge
Record induration in millimeters; do not record as positive or negative
fact_text: Mantoux test reading requires inspection, palpation, marking, and measurement of induration 48-72 hours post-injection; record size in millimeters without positive/negative labels.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Children producing sputum may be infectious and should be asked to produce sputum outside or in well-ventilated areas, not in enclosed spaces.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Gastric aspiration is used to collect gastric contents for TB diagnosis by microscopy and culture, recommended only where culture is available due to distress and low smear positivity.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Sputum collection procedure for children includes rinsing mouth with water, instructing deep breaths and cough, and collecting sputum in a container held close to lips; if insufficient sputum, encourage repeated coughing.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Sputum smear microscopy is valuable and should be performed in any child able to produce sputum, especially older children with pulmonary TB symptoms; three sputum specimens are recommended: on-spot, early morning, and second on-spot at follow-up.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: procedure should be done first thing in the morning when child wakes up
position child on back or side; assistant helps hold child
measure nose to stomach distance to guide tube insertion
use nasogastric tube (usually 10 French or larger) and syringe to aspirate 2-5 ml gastric contents
contraindications_or_cautions: gastric aspiration requires two people (tester and assistant) for proper performance
fact_text: Gastric aspiration procedure for TB diagnosis in children requires two people, fasting, proper positioning, measuring tube length, and aspirating 2-5 ml gastric contents using nasogastric tube and syringe.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_tests: gastric aspirate microscopy and culture for young children unable to expectorate sputum
recommended_advice: perform gastric aspiration on three consecutive mornings to maximize smear positivity
first morning gastric aspirate has highest yield
children should fast at least 4 hours (3 hours for infants) before procedure
contraindications_or_cautions: children with low platelet count or bleeding tendency should not undergo gastric aspiration
fact_text: Gastric aspirates are recommended for microscopy and culture in young children unable to expectorate sputum; perform on three consecutive mornings with fasting prior, as first morning aspirate has highest yield; negative results do not exclude TB.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_tests: Sputum induction is an aerosol-generating procedure requiring isolation room with negative pressure, UV light, and extractor fan; it is low risk but requires specialized training and equipment.
contraindications_or_cautions: Children with inadequate fasting (less than 3 hours) or severe respiratory distress (rapid breathing, wheezing, hypoxia) should not undergo sputum induction.
fact_text: Sputum induction in children is aerosol-generating, requires isolation room and infection control, is low risk but contraindicated in children with less than 3 hours fasting or severe respiratory distress.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_tests: Gastric aspiration for sputum collection in children involves inserting a nasogastric tube, checking position with litmus paper (blue litmus turns red in acidic stomach contents), aspirating 5-10 ml gastric contents, adding sodium bicarbonate to neutralize acid, and transporting specimen to lab within 4 hours or refrigerating if delayed.
dose_or_duration: Gastric aspiration for sputum collection in children is a low-risk procedure for TB transmission, involves checking tube position with litmus paper, aspirating 5-10 ml gastric contents, adding sodium bicarbonate to neutralize acid, and transporting specimen to lab within 4 hours or refrigerating if delayed.
recommended_advice: After gastric aspiration, wipe specimen container with alcohol/chlorhexidine to prevent cross-infection, label container, fill lab requisition, transport specimen promptly, and give child usual food.
contraindications_or_cautions: Do not repeat gastric aspiration more than three times if no fluid is aspirated.
If nasogastric tube is incorrectly positioned or saline/water enters airways, risk of adverse events is very small.
Gastric aspiration is low risk for TB transmission and can be safely performed at child's bedside or routine procedure room.
fact_text: Gastric aspiration for sputum collection in children is a low-risk procedure for TB transmission, involves checking tube position with litmus paper, aspirating 5-10 ml gastric contents, adding sodium bicarbonate to neutralize acid, and transporting specimen to lab within 4 hours or refrigerating if delayed.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_tests: sputum collection by expectoration or nasal suction/nasopharyngeal aspiration in children unable to expectorate
contraindications_or_cautions: Administer bronchodilator (e.g. salbutamol) before sputum collection to reduce wheezing risk
Disinfect and sterilize reusable equipment before use on another patient
fact_text: For sputum collection in children able to expectorate, follow standard procedures; for children unable to expectorate (e.g. young children), collect sputum by nasal suction or nasopharyngeal aspiration after bronchodilator and nebulized hypertonic saline administration.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: In children with palpable peripheral lymph node masses, FNAC is the diagnostic modality of choice to confirm TB and rule out malignancy; if FNAC is unavailable, provisional TB diagnosis may be made after excluding other causes and monitoring treatment response.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: Full-size chest radiographs, including lateral views if possible, are essential for childhood TB diagnosis; systematic evaluation includes checking patient ID, rotation, penetration, inspiration, and examining soft tissue, bony structures, and heart shadow.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
source_section: two chest X-ray images with captions
fact_text: Normal chest X-ray in children with TB should show good inspiration, no rotation, and good penetration; lateral view pulmonary artery should not be mistaken for enlarged lymph nodes.
source_figure_or_table: two chest X-ray images with captions

fact_text: In young children, a widened mediastinum on chest radiograph may be caused by a large thymus, producing the 'sail sign', which can be mistaken for hilar lymphadenopathy.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children

fact_text: Poor-quality chest radiographs with insufficient penetration, poor inspiration, or rotation can lead to misinterpretation of hilar lymph nodes in children.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
dose_or_duration: 20 doses vial
recommended_advice: BCG vaccine should be given intradermally in the upper left arm
Dose per injection is 0.05 ml
Vaccination site should be checked for scar formation after vaccination
If no scar or adverse reaction, revaccination may be needed at 3rd dose of DPT/pentavalent vaccine
referral_criteria: Refer to medical officer if severe adverse reaction occurs
followup_monitoring: Check vaccination site for scar formation after BCG vaccination
contraindications_or_cautions: Do not use other vaccines simultaneously with BCG
Do not use BCG vaccine after 6 hours of reconstitution
Do not use BCG vaccine if there is severe immunosuppression or HIV infection
fact_text: BCG vaccine is given intradermally at 0.05 ml dose in the upper left arm to prevent TB; vaccine must be used within 6 hours after reconstitution and not given with other vaccines simultaneously; local adverse reactions require medical referral.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
fact_text: A child is eligible for IPT if they are aged 0-5 years and have been in close contact with a pulmonary smear positive TB patient.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children
recommended_advice: Treatment Completed: Full course of 6 months IPT.
Treatment Interrupted: Treatment stopped for 2 consecutive months or more; need to be re-registered for 6 months IPT.
Transferred out: Child who has been transferred to another center; name of the center where the child was transferred should be written in remarks column.
Died: Child known to have died during the course of IPT.
Developed active TB: Child who has developed active TB disease during the course of IPT.
fact_text: IPT outcomes include treatment completion (6 months), interruption (≥2 months), transfer out, death, and development of active TB during IPT; these should be recorded in the register.

source_title: National Guidelines for Tuberculosis in Children

fact_text: Warning signs in dengue include persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, bleeding manifestations, lethargy, reduced urine output, liver enlargement, and rising hematocrit >20%.
Presumptive dengue diagnosis requires live/travel to endemic area plus fever and two of: anorexia & nausea, rash, aches or pain, warning signs, leucopenia, or positive tourniquet test.

Dengue cases are classified as: Group A (dengue without warning sign, mild, may be sent home), Group B (dengue with warning sign, moderate, referred for hospital care), and Group C (severe dengue, require emergency treatment).
Lab confirmed dengue is important when there is no sign of plasma leakage.

Compensated shock signs include prolonged capillary refill (>2 sec), cool extremities, tachycardia, postural hypotension, narrowing pulse pressure, tachypnoea, and reduced urine output; decompensated shock signs include mottled skin, very prolonged capillary refill, cold clammy extremities, severe tachycardia with late bradycardia, hypotension/unrecordable BP, metabolic acidosis, and oliguria/anuria.

Warning signs include persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, lethargy/restlessness, bleeding signs (epistaxis, black stool, haematemesis, haematuria), giddiness, pale/cold/clammy hands and feet, reduced urine output for 4-6 hours, liver enlargement >2cm, and haematocrit >20%.
Laboratory tests for all dengue groups include full blood count (FBC) and hematocrit (HCT); severe dengue cases also require other organ function tests as indicated.
Group A patients (dengue without warning sign) who are able to tolerate adequate oral fluids and pass urine at least once every 6 hours may be sent home.

Group C patients with severe dengue features (severe plasma leakage with shock or fluid accumulation, severe bleeding, severe organ impairment, severe metabolic dysfunction) require emergency treatment and hospital admission.

Group B patients (dengue with warning sign) with co-existing conditions (pregnancy, infancy, old age, diabetes), social circumstances (living alone, far from hospital), or warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restlessness, liver enlargement >2cm, rising hematocrit) should be referred for hospital care.
Discharge criteria require all: no fever for 48 hours, improvement in clinical picture, increasing trend of platelet count, no respiratory distress, and stable hematocrit without intravenous fluids.
Advise adequate rest, adequate fluid intake including oral fluids and paracetamol 4 grams per day in divided doses; patients with stable hematocrit can be sent home.

Daily review for disease progression including temperature pattern, volume of fluid intake and losses, urine output volume and frequency, warning signs, hematocrit, white blood cell and platelet counts, vital signs and peripheral perfusion every 1-4 hours until patient is out of critical phase, urine output every 4-6 hours, hematocrit before and after fluid replacement every 6-12 hours, blood glucose, and other organ functions as indicated.

If hematocrit remains high (>50%) after second bolus, continue colloid infusion at 10-20 ml/kg as third bolus over 1 hour; if improving, reduce rate to 7-10 ml/kg/hr for 1-2 hours then taper; if unstable, repeat hematocrit after second bolus.

If patient improves after initial fluid bolus, reduce IV fluids gradually to 5-7 ml/kg/hr for 1-2 hours, then 3-5 ml/kg/hr for 2-4 hours, then 2-3 ml/kg/hr or less depending on hemodynamic status; maintain IV fluids for 24-48 hours.

If patient still unstable after initial bolus, check hematocrit after first bolus; if Hct increases or remains high (>50%), repeat second bolus of crystalloid at 10-20 ml/kg/hr for 1 hour; if improvement after second bolus, reduce rate to 7-10 ml/kg/hr for 1-2 hours then reduce further; if Hct decreases, indicates bleeding and need for blood transfusion.

Reassess clinical status and repeat hematocrit (Hct); if Hct remains the same or rises only minimally, continue IV fluids at 2-3 ml/kg/hr for another 2-4 hours; if worsening vital signs and rapid rising Hct, increase IV fluids to 5-10 ml/kg/hr for 1-2 hours.

Reassess clinical status, repeat hematocrit and review fluid infusion rates accordingly; reduce IV fluids gradually when plasma leakage decreases towards end of critical phase, indicated by adequate urine output and/or fluid intake and stable or decreased Hct below baseline.

Encourage oral fluids; if not tolerated, start IV fluids with 0.9% saline or Ringer Lactate at maintenance rate; use isotonic solutions such as 0.9% saline or Ringer lactate starting at 5-7 ml/kg/hr for 1-2 hours, then reduce to 3-5 ml/kg/hr for 2-4 hours, then reduce to 2-3 ml/kg/hr or less based on clinical response.
Treatment of compensated shock: start IV fluids with isotonic crystalloid solutions at 5-10 ml/kg/hr over 1 hour; reassess patient condition.
Treatment of haemorrhagic complications: give 5-10 ml/kg of fresh packed red cells or 10-20 ml/kg fresh whole blood.

Treatment of hypotensive shock: initiate IV fluid resuscitation with crystalloid or colloid solution at 20 ml/kg as bolus over 15 minutes; give 10 ml/kg crystalloid bolus over 1 hour then reduce gradually; reassess hematocrit and clinical status.

Fluid requirement based on ideal body weight (kg) example: for 25 kg IBW, maintenance 1600 ml, M+5% deficit 2850 ml; for 30 kg IBW, maintenance 1700 ml, M+5% deficit 3200 ml.

IV fluid rates: children half maintenance (M/2) 1.5 ml/kg/hr, maintenance 3 ml/kg/hr, M+5% deficit 5 ml/kg/hr, M+7% deficit 7 ml/kg/hr, M+10% deficit 10 ml/kg/hr; adults half maintenance 40-50 ml/hr, maintenance 80-100 ml/hr, M+5% deficit 100-120 ml/hr, M+7% deficit 120-150 ml/hr, M+10% deficit 300-500 ml/hr.
In obese patients, use ideal body weight (IBW) to calculate fluid volume.

Maintenance plus 5% dehydration deficit fluid volume should be given to maintain 'just adequate' intravascular volume; duration of IV fluid therapy is usually 24-48 hours for shock patients, but 60-72 hours for patients entering plasma leakage phase without shock.

Normal maintenance fluid per hour calculation formula: 4 ml/kg/hr for first 10 kg body weight + 2 ml/kg/hr for next 10 kg + 1 ml/kg/hr for subsequent kg; for overweight/obese adults, calculate based on ideal body weight (IBW).

Total fluid volume (oral + IV) is maintenance plus 5% deficit administered over 48 hours; example: child 20 kg with 5% deficit = 1000 ml, total 2500 ml over 48 hours; adjust IV replacement rate based on plasma loss, clinical condition, vital signs, urine output, and hematocrit.
Give only isotonic solutions such as 0.9% saline, Ringer's lactate or Hartmann's or Lactate solution for fluid therapy.

Hyper-oncotic colloid solutions (osmolarity >300 mOsm/l) such as dextran 40 or starch solutions may be used in patients with massive plasma leakage or not responding to minimum crystalloid volume; iso-oncotic colloids like blood and blood components may be less effective.

Dengue virus infection may be asymptomatic or cause undifferentiated fever, dengue fever, dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) with plasma leakage, or dengue shock syndrome (DSS); collectively defined as Dengue Syndrome.
Dengue epidemiology depends on complex interactions among host, mosquito, virus, and environment factors including temperature, humidity, and water collections.
There are four dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4); secondary infection with different serotypes or DENV-2 may increase risk of severe disease.

Dengue shock syndrome (DSS) is hypovolemic shock caused by plasma leakage with increased systemic vascular resistance and narrow pulse pressure (e.g. systolic BP maintained with increased diastolic pressure ~100/90 mmHg).

Goals of fluid resuscitation in dengue shock include improving central and peripheral circulation (decreasing tachycardia, improving BP and pulse volume, warm extremities), improving end-organ perfusion (stable consciousness), and urine output ≥0.5 ml/kg/hour or decreasing metabolic acidosis.
Presence of hypotension in DSS suggests severe bleeding or concealed gastrointestinal bleeding in addition to plasma leakage.
Excessive fluids in DSS cause massive effusions due to increased capillary permeability.

Discharge criteria include no fever for at least 24 hours without antipyretics, at least 2 days after shock recovery, good general condition with improving appetite, normal or near-normal hematocrit, no pleural effusion or ascites, platelet count above 50,000/mm3, and no other complications.

Signs of recovery include stable pulse, blood pressure, breathing rate, normal temperature, no bleeding, return of appetite, no vomiting or abdominal pain, good urine output, stable hematocrit, and convalescent rash or itching on extremities.

Additional investigations for fluid overload include blood gas and lactate analysis, chest X-ray for cardiomegaly/pleural effusion/heart failure, ECG to exclude ischemic changes and arrhythmia, echocardiogram for left ventricular function, and cardiac enzymes.
Hyperchloraemia from large volumes of 0.9% sodium chloride may cause metabolic acidosis despite normal lactate levels.
Sodium bicarbonate is not recommended for metabolic acidosis caused by tissue hypoxia if pH ≥ 7.10.
Compensated metabolic acidosis is an early sign of hypovolemia and shock in dengue.
Correction of shock and adequate fluid replacement will correct metabolic acidosis in dengue shock.

Causes of excessive fluid overload include excessive or too rapid IV fluids during critical phase, incorrect hypotonic crystalloid use, large volumes in unrecognized severe bleeding, inappropriate transfusions, prolonged IV fluids after plasma leakage, and comorbid heart/lung/renal diseases.

Clinical features of fluid overload include rapid breathing, suprasternal in-drawing and intercostal recession (children), respiratory distress, wheeze, crepitations, tense ascites, persistent abdominal pain/tenderness, raised jugular venous pressure, pulmonary oedema, irreversible shock, and puffy face and leg oedema.

Infants with dengue may present with fever, runny nose, cough, loose motion, vomiting, seizures, high fever, sore throat, dehydration, bulged fontanel, neck rigidity, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly.

In infants, leukopenia is unlikely; NS1 positive during febrile period; IgM positive during defervescence; hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, and raised AST may be present; USG may show hepato-splenomegaly and ascites; CXR may show pleural effusion.
Avoid lower uterine segment Caesarean Section (LUCS) or induction of labour during the critical plasma leakage phase unless life-saving.
Caution on overhydration and frequent evaluation of oral fluid intake and urinary output (catheterization needed) in infants.
Frequent assessment and adjustment of fluid regimen required in elderly to avoid congestive heart failure and pulmonary oedema.
If spontaneous labour occurs during critical phase, take steps to prevent vaginal tears by performing episiotomy.

In infants, fluid therapy during plasma leakage phase includes half strength normal saline in 5% dextrose for <6 months and normal saline in 5% dextrose for >6 months; colloids (dextran 40) considered if high crystalloid rates needed.
Maintain platelet count above 50,000/mm3 in pregnant patients with DF/DHF close to delivery; single donor platelet transfusion preferred if available.

fact_text: Dengue epidemics in Bangladesh have shown high case numbers and deaths, with dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) comprising a significant portion of cases and a case-fatality rate of 1.7% in early 2000s outbreaks.
Dengue fever and dengue hemorrhagic fever are leading causes of hospitalization and death in South-East Asia, including Bangladesh.
Dengue virus serotypes DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4 circulate in Bangladesh, with DENV-3 most commonly linked to dengue fever and DHF.

fact_text: Activated memory T cells and proinflammatory cytokines contribute to plasma leak and severe dengue manifestations.
Antibody-dependent enhancement causes increased viral biomass and higher risk of severe disease by facilitating infection of Fc-receptor bearing cells.
Complement activation and cytokines (C3a, C5a) increase vascular permeability leading to dengue hemorrhagic fever/dengue shock syndrome (DHF/DSS).

Dengue virus has 4 serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4) transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes; infection with one serotype confers lifelong immunity to that serotype and short cross-immunity to others for 2-3 months.
Severe dengue pathogenesis involves antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), T-cell mediated immunopathology, complement activation, and cytokine abundance.

Causes of bleeding in dengue syndrome include abnormal coagulogram, thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, liver-related prothrombin deficiency, endothelial injury, DIC, prolonged APTT, low fibrinogen, elevated FDP and D-Dimer, consumptive coagulopathy, and platelet sequestration.
Factors increasing risk for DHF/DSS include enhancing antibodies, age under 12 years, female sex, Caucasian race, infection sequence and serotype (type 3 and Asian type 2 genotype more dangerous).

fact_text: Dengue virus infection pathophysiology involves antibody production, complement activation, vessel deposition causing bleeding and organ involvement, and T cell activation causing increased vascular permeability and capillary leakage.
