fact_text: The total number of diabetic people in Bangladesh is nearly 13.1 million with a prevalence of 14.2% in adults aged 20 to 79 years.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Hyperglycemia first detected during pregnancy includes diabetes mellitus in pregnancy and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Other genetic syndromes sometimes associated with diabetes include Down syndrome, Friedreich’s ataxia, Huntington’s chorea, Klinefelter’s syndrome, myotonic dystrophy, porphyria, Prader-Willi syndrome, and Turner’s syndrome.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
source_section: Table 1.2 Difference between T1DM, T2DM and GDM
fact_text: Type 1 DM: beta cell destruction markers may be present; onset before 30 years; normal to wasted body habitus; sudden classical symptoms; less genetic link; ketoacidosis common; insulin mandatory. Type 2 DM: beta cell destruction usually absent; onset after 30 years; obese/overweight; gradual atypical symptoms; more genetic link; hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state common; insulin reserve declines slowly; treatable with non-insulin agents. GDM: associated with pregnancy; placental hormones antagonize maternal insulin; more common if maternal age ≥25 years; obesity/overweight favors GDM; family history of T2DM is risk factor; ketosis may develop; insulin is treatment of choice.
source_figure_or_table: Table 1.2 Difference between T1DM, T2DM and GDM

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Unclassified diabetes category is used temporarily when there is no clear diagnostic category, especially near diagnosis time.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Uncommon specific forms of immune-mediated diabetes include insulin autoimmune syndrome, anti-insulin receptor antibodies, and stiff man syndrome.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
source_section: Section 1.4 Initial steps for classifying DM
fact_text: Initial classification of diabetes includes confirming diagnosis, excluding secondary causes, assessing age at diagnosis, family history, obesity, metabolic syndrome features, ketosis presence, and performing β-cell autoantibodies and C-peptide tests if available.
source_figure_or_table: Section 1.4 Initial steps for classifying DM

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Type 1 diabetes is caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, leading to severe insulin deficiency; genetic susceptibility and environmental factors contribute; some cases are idiopathic.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Type 2 diabetes is characterized by insulin resistance and beta cell failure; patients lose about 50% of beta cell function; multiple organs contribute to glucose intolerance including muscle, liver, fat, gut, alpha cells, kidney, and brain.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Atypical DM manifestations include non-specific symptoms like non-healing infection, infertility, repeated pregnancy loss, pruritus vulvae, and undue fatigability, common in T2DM.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: T1DM is always symptomatic with classical hyperglycemia features; T2DM and other types are often asymptomatic and diagnosed by biochemical tests or routine check-up.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: T2DM and other diabetes types may remain asymptomatic for a long time, delaying diagnosis and intervention; T1DM is usually diagnosed before chronic complications develop.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Typical DM features start with glycosuria after blood glucose exceeds renal threshold; symptoms include polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss, and generalized weakness, mostly seen in T1DM.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Gestational diabetes mellitus is caused by placental hormones (beta hCG, human placental lactogen, estrogen, progesterone) antagonizing insulin action.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Prediabetes includes impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) and impaired fasting glucose (IFG); persons with prediabetes have high risk of developing diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: About 30% of impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) cases may revert to normal with proper intervention.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: About 40% of impaired fasting glucose (IFG) cases may revert to normal with proper intervention.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Prediabetes persons are treated by lifestyle modifications; drugs may be used if indicated.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: All pregnant women should be screened at the first antenatal visit with 3 samples of 75 g OGTT; if negative, re-screen during 24-28 weeks of gestation.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: If screening test results are normal, repeat testing should be done at 1-year intervals or as relevant.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Screening for prediabetes and diabetes should be considered in all asymptomatic adults aged 30 years or older, regardless of risk factors.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Screening for prediabetes and diabetes should be considered in asymptomatic adults under 30 years who are overweight or obese (BMI ≥23 kg/m²).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Screening for prediabetes and diabetes should be considered in asymptomatic adults under 30 years with BMI <23 kg/m² who have one or more risk factors including: first-degree relative with diabetes, history of GDM, history of CVD with hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg or on therapy), low HDL (<35 mg/dL), high triglycerides (>250 mg/dL), polycystic ovary syndrome, or physical inactivity.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Screening should be considered after onset of puberty or after 10 years of age in all asymptomatic children and adolescents with BMI ≥85th percentile.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Screening should be considered before 10 years of age in children and adolescents with BMI ≥85th percentile who have additional risk factors for diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Testing for prediabetes and diabetes should be considered in all women planning pregnancy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Procedures for documenting glucose intolerance include 2-sample oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), fasting plasma glucose (FPG), HbA1c, and random plasma glucose (RPG) with symptoms.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diabetes testing is advised in all patients with HIV.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Immediate diabetes testing is required in symptomatic cases.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: People with prediabetes (HbA1c >5.7-6.4%, IGT or IFG) and women with prior GDM should be tested yearly.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Children with prediabetes should be tested yearly, with repeat testing every 2 years if normal, or more frequently if risk deteriorates or symptoms appear.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Immediate diabetes testing is required in symptomatic children and adolescents.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Testing for prediabetes/diabetes should be considered after puberty onset or after 10 years of age in asymptomatic children/adolescents with BMI ≥85th percentile or obese (BMI ≥95th percentile).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Testing for prediabetes/diabetes should be considered before 10 years of age in asymptomatic children/adolescents with BMI ≥85th percentile or obese (BMI ≥95th percentile) plus additional diabetes risk factors including history of diabetes or GDM in gestation, parental diabetes, family history of type 2 diabetes, or signs of insulin resistance.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Testing for prediabetes/diabetes should be considered in all women planning pregnancy; if preconception test is negative, test all women at first antenatal visit with 3-sample 75 gm OGTT.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Plasma glucose rather than HbA1c should be used to diagnose acute onset T1DM in individuals with hyperglycemia symptoms.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: After organ transplantation, OGTT testing should be performed once patient is stable on immunosuppressive therapy and no infection.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: If early screening is negative, screen pregnant women at 24-28 weeks gestation with 3 sample 75 gm OGTT.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In patients with hemoglobinopathies, annual screening with standard OGTT should begin at 10 years of age; HbA1c has limited role.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Screening for T1DM risk with autoantibody panel can be done in first-degree relatives of T1DM probands where facility is available.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Women with GDM should be tested with 2 sample 75 gm OGTT and non-pregnant diagnostic criteria at 4-12 weeks postpartum, preferably at 6th week.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diagnosis of prediabetes and diabetes is based on documentation of glucose intolerance using OGTT, FPG, HbA1c, or RPG tests.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Fasting plasma glucose can be used to label diabetes but cannot exclude it

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: HbA1c test must be highly standardized for use in diabetes diagnosis

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
trigger_evidence: classical symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis
dose_or_duration: No preparation required
fact_text: RPG without preparation can confirm diabetes if classical hyperglycemia symptoms or crisis are present

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: 75 g anhydrous glucose for adults (1.75 g/kg body weight for children, max 75 g) in 250-300 ml water, drink within 5 minutes
contraindications_or_cautions: No smoking, tea, or physical stress during test
fact_text: OGTT requires overnight fasting 8-14 hours, unrestricted diet with ≥150 g carbs for 3 days prior, 75 g glucose load in 250-300 ml water, blood samples at fasting and 120 minutes, no smoking/tea/stress during test

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diabetes diagnosis in non-pregnant adults and children requires FPG ≥7.0 mmol/L, or 2-h OGTT ≥11.1 mmol/L, or HbA1c ≥6.5%, or random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L with classical symptoms; prediabetes defined by IFG or IGT glucose and HbA1c thresholds.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Gestational diabetes mellitus diagnosed by FPG 5.1-<7.0 mmol/L, 1-h OGTT ≥10.0 mmol/L, or 2-h OGTT 8.5-<11.1 mmol/L; diabetes in pregnancy diagnosed by FPG >7.0 mmol/L or 2-h OGTT ≥11.1 mmol/L.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Classical symptoms of hyperglycemia include polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss, and generalized weakness; random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L with these symptoms supports diabetes diagnosis.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
contraindications_or_cautions: Presence of complications or comorbidities such as ASCVD, CKD, and heart failure influences therapy choice.
fact_text: Complications or comorbidities like ASCVD, CKD, and heart failure must be considered when selecting diabetes therapy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_advice: Monitoring of glycemic control by SMBG and CGM is important in diabetes management.
fact_text: Self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) are important components of diabetes management.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Insulin is the only pharmacotherapy for T1DM; T2DM treatment may include sulfonylureas, meglitinides, biguanides, TZDs, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, and insulin.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
source_section: Table 3.1 Factors to be considered before selection of antidiabetic agent
fact_text: Factors to consider before selecting antidiabetic agents include: type of DM, age, body weight/BMI, associated conditions (acute/chronic complications, pregnancy/lactation, major surgery, life expectancy), socio-economic status/cost, personal preference, degree of hyperglycemia, job and lifestyle, previous antidiabetic agents, caregiver support, and potential side effects like hypoglycemia risk.
source_figure_or_table: Table 3.1 Factors to be considered before selection of antidiabetic agent

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Treatment of diabetes mellitus is individualized; T1DM always requires insulin, while T2DM management requires appropriate decision-making considering glycemic control, CVD risk, comorbidities, and complications.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Medical nutrition therapy for diabetes and prediabetes should be individualized, preferably by a registered dietitian, with a balanced diet of approximately 50% carbohydrate, 10-20% protein, and less than 30% fat.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Education and empowerment regarding lifestyle changes, self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG), and treatment adjustment should be targeted in diabetes management.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: BMI target is <23 kg/m² in non-pregnant adults with diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Blood pressure target is systolic <130 mm Hg and diastolic <80 mm Hg in non-pregnant adults with diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Fasting/pre-meal blood glucose target is <7.0 mmol/L; post-meal target is <10.0 mmol/L (1-2 hours after beginning of meal) in non-pregnant adults.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: HDL cholesterol target is >40 mg/dL in males and >50 mg/dL in females.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: HbA1c target is <7% in non-pregnant adults; less stringent target (7-8%) may be considered in elderly with multiple comorbidities.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: LDL cholesterol target is <100 mg/dL; <70 mg/dL if history of cardiovascular disease.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Triglyceride target is <150 mg/dL in non-pregnant adults with diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Waist circumference target is <90 cm in males and <80 cm in females with diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Calorie allowance calculated as Ideal body weight (height in cm - 100) multiplied by calorie factor (20 to 45) based on BMI and physical activity status.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diet rich in monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, including long-chain n-3 fatty acids (EPA, DHA) and nuts/seeds (ALA), is recommended to improve glucose metabolism and prevent/treat cardiovascular disease.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diet should contain sufficient protein from both animal and plant sources.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diet should emphasize nutrient-dense carbohydrates high in fiber such as vegetables, fruits, legumes, whole grains, and dairy products.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Meal frequency: three main meals and two snacks with a bedtime snack recommended for patients on multiple daily insulin injections or with tendency for midnight hypoglycemia.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: No clear evidence that dietary supplementation with vitamins, minerals (chromium, vitamin D), herbs, or spices improves diabetes outcomes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Non-nutritive sweeteners can reduce calorie and carbohydrate intake but people are encouraged to decrease both sweetened and non-nutritive sweetened beverages and increase water intake.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: People with diabetes and at risk should avoid sugar-sweetened beverages including fruit juices to control glycemia, weight, and reduce cardiovascular and fatty liver risk.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: People with diabetes should limit salt consumption to 5 gm/day, same as general population recommendations.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Weight loss ≥5% by calorie reduction and increased physical activity benefits overweight or obese adults with T2DM and prediabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Adults with diabetes should engage in 2-3 sessions per week of resistance exercise on non-consecutive days.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Adults with diabetes should perform at least 150 minutes per week of moderate intensity aerobic activity, spread over at least 5 days/week, with no more than 2 consecutive days without activity.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: All adults, especially those with type 2 diabetes, should reduce daily sedentary behavior by interrupting prolonged sitting every 30 minutes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Physical activity or exercise is encouraged to be done at the same time each day.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Shorter durations (minimum 75 minutes/week) of moderate intensity or interval training may be sufficient for younger and more physically fit individuals with diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Bed-ridden persons should receive physiotherapy, passive movement, and posture change exercises.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: During pregnancy, moderate exercise such as walking at moderate speed for 30 minutes a day (continuous or divided) is advised if no obstetric contraindication exists.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Exercise session should include warm up (5-10 min aerobic low intensity), muscle stretching (5-10 min gentle stretching), main exercise (30 min moderate to high intensity), and cool down (5-10 min low intensity).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Exercise should be postponed if blood glucose is >16.7 mmol/L; if blood glucose is <3.9 mmol/L, extra 15-30 grams carbohydrate should be taken before exercise.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Exercise should be withheld until blood pressure is controlled in patients with uncontrolled hypertension.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Patients with peripheral neuropathy, loss of protective sensation, Charcot's joint, or osteoarthritis of back and knee should avoid repetitive weight bearing exercises (e.g. prolonged walking, treadmill, jogging) due to risk of blistering, ulceration, and fracture; non-weight-bearing exercises like swimming, cycling, rowing are preferred.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
trigger_evidence: moderate to severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy
fact_text: Patients with proliferative or moderate to severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy should avoid anaerobic exercise and physical activity involving straining, jarring, or Valsalva-like maneuvers (e.g. weight lifting, boxing, heavy competitive sports) due to risk of vitreous hemorrhage or retinal detachment; low impact exercises like swimming (not diving), walking, or stationary cycling are recommended.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Patients with significant acute illness or uncompensated major chronic illness should not exercise during the illness.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Patients with stable coronary heart disease should perform moderate intensity exercise.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_advice: lifestyle modification
fact_text: For T2DM adults with FPG 10-14 mmol/L, HbA1c 8.5-10%, or RPG 11.1-16.6 mmol/L, start lifestyle plus metformin and subcutaneous insulin or other agent.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_advice: lifestyle modification
fact_text: For T2DM adults with FPG <10 mmol/L, HbA1c <8.5%, and RPG <11.1 mmol/L, initial treatment is lifestyle plus metformin.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: For symptomatic T2DM adults with FPG ≥14 mmol/L, HbA1c >10%, or RPG >16.6 mmol/L, start lifestyle plus basal/split/mix insulin and metformin.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_medicines: adjust insulin or treatment at any point
fact_text: If HbA1c is <7% after 3 months of treatment, adjust insulin or treatment at any point as needed.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_medicines: add 3rd oral agent of different action or add insulin
recommended_advice: titrate and optimize treatment
fact_text: If HbA1c ≥7% after 2 oral agents, add a third oral agent of different action or add insulin.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_advice: titrate and optimize treatment
fact_text: If HbA1c ≥7% after 3 oral agents, intensify insulin regimen.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_medicines: add 2nd oral agent of different action
recommended_advice: titrate and optimize treatment
fact_text: If HbA1c ≥7% on treatment, add a second oral agent of different action and optimize treatment.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
contraindications_or_cautions: Oral antidiabetic drugs are not recommended in type 1 diabetes mellitus, and during pregnancy and lactation.
fact_text: Oral antidiabetic drugs are not recommended in type 1 diabetes mellitus, and during pregnancy and lactation.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_medicines: DPP4 inhibitors: Vildagliptin, Sitagliptin, Linagliptin, Saxagliptin, Alogliptin
SGLT2 inhibitors: Dapagliflozin, Canagliflozin, Empagliflozin, Ertugliflozin
fact_text: Classes of oral antidiabetic drugs include sulfonylureas, non-sulfonylureas, biguanides, thiazolidinediones, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, DPP4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, and oral GLP1 receptor agonists.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Two secretagogues should not be prescribed together; one secretagogue cannot be replaced by another if glycemic target is not achieved; secretagogues must be discontinued when twice daily insulin is started.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors are weight friendly and reduce post-prandial blood glucose but cause GI upset and are limited by impaired hepatic function, inflammatory bowel disease, and malabsorption states.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Biguanides improve insulin sensitivity, are weight friendly, reduce mostly pre- and post-prandial blood glucose, and have favorable effects on lipid and NAFLD; contraindicated if eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73m2 and not initiated if eGFR <45.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: DPP4 inhibitors are weight friendly, reduce mostly pre- and post-prandial blood glucose, but cause GI upset, upper respiratory tract infection, and pancreatitis; dose adjustment needed in renal impairment with specific eGFR thresholds for vildagliptin and sitagliptin.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: GLP1 receptor agonists reduce weight and provide cardiovascular safety but cause GI upset and pancreatitis; contraindicated in personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Non-sulfonylureas have less hypoglycemia risk and reduce post-prandial blood glucose but cause weight gain; avoid in impaired hepatic or renal function.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: SGLT2 inhibitors are weight friendly, reduce pre- and post-prandial blood glucose, but cause urinary tract infections and genital fungal infections; contraindicated if eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73m2.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Sulfonylureas are potent oral agents that reduce pre- and post-prandial blood glucose but have hazards of hypoglycemia and weight gain; avoid in impaired hepatic or renal function and avoid long-acting SU in CKD.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Thiazolidinediones improve insulin sensitivity, reduce mostly pre- and post-prandial blood glucose, and favorably affect lipid and NAFLD but cause weight gain, fluid retention, and are limited by heart failure risk, bone fracture risk, and bladder cancer.

fact_text: Insulin types classified by onset, peak, duration, and appearance: bolus (prandial) insulin includes short-acting regular and rapid-acting analogues; basal insulin includes intermediate-acting (NPH) and long-acting analogues; premixed insulin combinations and coformulations are also listed with their pharmacokinetics.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Basal Plus regimen combines basal insulin with one or more short-acting insulin doses as needed, offering more meal time flexibility.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Basal only insulin regimen uses NPH once or twice daily or basal analogue once daily; common for insulin initiation and to build patient confidence in self-injection.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Basal-bolus regimen uses long-acting insulin analogue at bedtime as basal dose and rapid-acting insulin analogue before meals as bolus doses; ideal for very active persons with irregular meal times.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Coformulation insulin allows flexibility regarding meal timing and is convenient for twice daily injections.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII) via insulin pump delivers insulin continuously as basal with patient-activated boluses at meals.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Indications for insulin therapy include type 1 diabetes mellitus, severe acute complications or illness (e.g. MI, acute infection), uncompensated chronic complications or illness, and pregnancy or lactation.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Intravenous insulin infusion is indicated in DKA, HHS, critical illness, prolonged NPO, TPN, perioperative period, and during delivery.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Premixed insulin is the most commonly prescribed twice daily insulin regimen; it is convenient but has risk of hypoglycemia if meal times are irregular and is difficult to achieve glycemic control at all times.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Split-mixed insulin regimen adds two or three short-acting doses to twice daily intermediate acting insulin; easier glycemic control at all times but requires multiple injections and dose adjustment can be difficult.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Start insulin at 0.2-0.5 unit/kg/day; premixed insulin dose split two-thirds morning, one-third evening; split-mixed dose two-thirds intermediate acting, one-third short acting; basal insulin 10 units/day or 0.1-0.2 unit/kg/day; increase dose by 2-4 units every 3 days to reach target; decrease dose by 2-4 units if blood sugar below target.
fact_text: Insulin initiation starts at 0.2-0.5 unit/kg/day with dose adjustments every 3 days by 2-4 units to reach glycemic targets; premixed and split-mixed dosing details provided.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
trigger_evidence: T2DM with high insulin dose >10 unit/kg and uncontrolled glycemia
fact_text: Continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII) pump is recommended for children with T1DM having multiple hypoglycemia episodes or uncontrolled diabetes, and T2DM patients requiring >10 unit/kg insulin and not achieving glycemic targets.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Poor glycemic status defined by HbA1c >=10%, FBS >=14 mmol/L, RPG >=18 mmol/L, HbA1c >=7% despite 50% max dose SU and max sensitizer, or symptomatic hyperglycemia indicates need for treatment adjustment.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: For persons not on multiple dose insulin or insulin pump, SMBG should be done as required according to clinical situations.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Self blood glucose testing (SMBG) should be done frequently, preferably once or twice weekly covering pre-meal and post-meal, in persons on multiple dose insulin regimens or insulin pumps, especially in T1DM and pregnancy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: If refrigeration is unavailable in hot climates, use cooling jars, earthenware pitchers, or cool wet cloth around insulin container to preserve insulin activity.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Insulin must never be frozen or exposed to direct sunlight or warming; store unused insulin in refrigerator (4-8°C) to retain potency until expiry; in use, insulin can be kept at room temperature if not too hot but retains potency better if refrigerated.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Cloudy insulin vials or pen devices must be gently rolled 10-20 times to mix suspension; when mixing regular insulin with NPH, draw regular insulin first and administer mixture immediately.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Insulin injections should be given into deep subcutaneous tissue at 45-90° angle using two-finger pinch to avoid intramuscular injection; needles must be fully inserted and a 15-second wait after injection helps complete insulin expulsion.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Preferred insulin injection sites: abdomen for faster, uniform absorption; front and lateral thigh for slower absorption; lateral upper arm as alternative with injection assistance; rotate injection sites within same area.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_advice: Comprehensive diabetes medical evaluation includes past medical/family history, social history, medication/vaccination, psychosocial screening, educational/nutritional support, pregnancy planning, physical exam, lab/imaging investigations, and planning for glycemic/metabolic targets.
fact_text: Comprehensive diabetes evaluation includes history, social factors, medication, psychosocial and educational support, pregnancy planning, physical exam, labs/imaging, and metabolic target planning.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
followup_monitoring: Target time in range (4.0-10.0 mmol/L) >70% (about 17 hours/day)
fact_text: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) measures interstitial glucose every few minutes; target time in range (4.0-10.0 mmol/L) is >70% daily (about 17 hours).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
followup_monitoring: HbA1c testing at least twice a year if stable glycemic control; quarterly if therapy changed or glycemic goals not met
contraindications_or_cautions: RBC turnover (blood loss, hemolysis, blood transfusion, pregnancy) and hemoglobin variants affect HbA1c accuracy
fact_text: HbA1c reflects glycemic status over 2-3 months; target is <7%. Test HbA1c at least twice yearly if stable, quarterly if therapy changed or goals unmet; consider factors affecting HbA1c accuracy such as RBC turnover and hemoglobin variants.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Hypoglycemia is defined biochemically as blood glucose below 3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Level 1 hypoglycemia is blood glucose between 3.0 and <3.9 mmol/L.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Level 2 hypoglycemia is blood glucose below 3.0 mmol/L.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Level 3 hypoglycemia is a severe event with altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Hypoglycemia is defined biochemically with blood glucose below 3.9 mmol/L and clinical features of autonomic overactivity and neuroglycopenia.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Hypoglycemia is more common in T1DM than in T2DM.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Hyperglycemic acute complications require prompt diagnosis, urgent hospitalization, and management with IV fluids, insulin, and frequent clinical and lab monitoring.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Hypoglycemia level 1 and 2 should be promptly treated with oral carbohydrate.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Hypoglycemia level 3 requires treatment with parenteral glucose.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Causes of hypoglycemia include excess insulin dose, excess antidiabetic medications especially insulin secretagogues, delayed or missed meals, unusual exercise, severe renal or hepatic impairment, and excess alcohol intake.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Recurrent hypoglycemia may cause behavioral changes, cognitive impairment, and increased risk of life-threatening cardiovascular events.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Hypoglycemia unawareness occurs in individuals with long-standing T1DM, autonomic neuropathy, use of medications like non-selective beta-blockers, or very tight glycemic control; frequent blood glucose monitoring is recommended to prevent hypoglycemia.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Nocturnal hypoglycemia usually occurs during the night, typically between 2 and 4 am.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Clinical features of hypoglycemia by level: Level-1 autonomic symptoms include palpitation, tremor, sweating, hunger; Level-2 neuroglycopenic symptoms include irritability, headache, visual disturbance; Level-3 neuroglycopenic symptoms include drowsiness, confusion, behavioral abnormality, convulsion, coma.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: After initial recovery from level 3 hypoglycemia, ensure food ingestion and consider modification of treatment to prevent recurrence.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Glucagon 1 mg intramuscularly or subcutaneously can be given in level 2 hypoglycemia if available.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Glucagon 1 mg intramuscularly or subcutaneously can be given in level 3 hypoglycemia if available.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: If hypoglycemia is due to long-acting antidiabetic medications, 10% dextrose infusion should be started and continued to prevent recurrence.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Level 1 and 2 hypoglycemia should be treated by the patient or family with 15 gm glucose or equivalent food, repeated every 15 minutes until stable, with blood glucose monitoring every 15 minutes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Level 3 hypoglycemia requires 100 ml of 25% dextrose intravenously under medical supervision.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
trigger_evidence: hypoglycemia on long acting antidiabetic agents
fact_text: Hospitalization is indicated for level 3 hypoglycemia, recurrent hypoglycemia, or hypoglycemia in people on long-acting antidiabetic agents.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a medical emergency in diabetes, commonly in T1DM, caused by insulin deficiency and increased counter-regulatory hormones leading to hyperglycemia and lipolysis.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Precipitating factors for DKA include infection, insulin discontinuation or inadequacy, pancreatitis, MI, stroke, pulmonary embolism, trauma, pregnancy, and new-onset T1DM.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: DKA develops rapidly over hours to days and is preceded by symptoms of uncontrolled diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Nocturnal hypoglycemia prevention includes reducing evening insulin dose, adjusting timing with dinner, considering bedtime snacks, and monitoring blood glucose.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_advice: Frequent blood glucose monitoring
Proper meal timing and amount
Avoid unaccustomed exercise
Set higher glucose targets for older people, children, and those with hypoglycemia unawareness
fact_text: Prevention of hypoglycemia includes frequent glucose monitoring, proper meal timing and amount, avoiding unaccustomed exercise, and setting higher glucose targets for vulnerable groups.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
fact_text: Diagnostic criteria for DKA and HHS: BG >13.8 mmol/L for DKA (mild to severe), >33.3 mmol/L for HHS; arterial pH <7.00 severe DKA, >7.30 HHS; serum bicarbonate <10 severe DKA, >18 HHS; urine ketone positive in DKA, small in HHS; effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg in HHS; anion gap >10 mild DKA, >12 moderate/severe DKA, variable in HHS; mental status alert to stupor/coma depending on severity.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: HHS is a severe hyperglycemia, dehydration, and hyperosmolarity state without significant ketonuria, usually in elderly T2DM with residual insulin preventing ketosis.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: HHS precipitating factors include compromised fluid intake and drugs such as glucocorticoids and diuretics.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: HHS clinical features include slow development over days to weeks, symptoms of uncontrolled diabetes, profound dehydration, and impaired consciousness.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Fluid infusion start at 0.9% NaCl at 1.0 L/hr; if severe hypovolemia continue 0.9% NaCl 1.0 L/hr; if mild dehydration measure corrected serum Na+; if Na+ ≥155 mmol/L use 0.45% NaCl 250-500 ml/hr; if Na+ <155 mmol/L use 0.9% NaCl 250-500 ml/hr; when plasma glucose <11.1 mmol/L (DKA) or <16.7 mmol/L (HHS) start 10% dextrose at 125 ml/hr.
fact_text: Fluid infusion protocol for adult DKA/HHS starts with 0.9% NaCl at 1.0 L/hr; adjust fluid type and rate based on severity of hypovolemia, serum sodium, and plasma glucose levels as per flowchart.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Start 0.9% NaCl at 1.0 L/hr; adjust fluid type and rate based on serum sodium and clinical status; when plasma glucose <11.1 mmol/L (DKA) or <16.7 mmol/L (HHS), start 10% dextrose at 125 ml/hr
referral_criteria: Immediate hospitalization for DKA or HHS
fact_text: Immediate hospitalization and initial evaluation for adult DKA or HHS includes blood glucose and ketone testing, blood pH, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, CBC, and starting IV fluids at 0.9% NaCl 1.0 L/hr with adjustments based on serum sodium and clinical status; start 10% dextrose at 125 ml/hr when plasma glucose falls below 11.1 mmol/L (DKA) or 16.7 mmol/L (HHS).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: If serum K+ <3.5 mmol/L, give 20-40 mmol KCl per liter infusion fluid, may require more rapid hourly infusion; if K+ 3.5-5.5 mmol/L, give 20-30 mmol KCl per liter infusion fluid; if K+ >5.5 mmol/L, do not administer KCl
recommended_advice: Maintain serum K+ at 4-5 mmol/L; observe renal function and urine output
fact_text: In DKA and HHS, potassium infusion is guided by serum potassium: <3.5 mmol/L give 20-40 mmol/L KCl infusion; 3.5-5.5 mmol/L give 20-30 mmol/L; >5.5 mmol/L do not give KCl; maintain serum K+ 4-5 mmol/L with renal and urine monitoring.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Start with 0.1 U/kg body weight IV bolus then 0.1 U/kg/hr IV infusion; if plasma glucose does not fall by 10% in first hour, give 0.14 U/kg IV bolus then continue infusion; for HHS start 0.14 U/kg/hr IV infusion
fact_text: In DKA and HHS, start regular insulin IV with 0.1 U/kg bolus then 0.1 U/kg/hr infusion; if glucose does not fall 10% in first hour, give 0.14 U/kg bolus then continue; reduce infusion rate when glucose reaches specified thresholds.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: Complications of DKA/HHS include cerebral oedema, circulatory failure, thromboembolism, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: Criteria for improvement of DKA/HHS include: no dehydration, no vomiting and able to take food, well oriented and hemodynamically stable, no ketone in urine and normal anion gap (in DKA), effective serum osmolality <315 mOsmol/kg (in HHS).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: Effective serum osmolality <315 mOsmol/kg indicates improvement in HHS.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: Improvement criteria for DKA/HHS include no dehydration, no vomiting, ability to take food, and hemodynamic stability.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: No dehydration is a criterion for improvement of DKA/HHS.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: No ketone in urine and normal anion gap indicate improvement in DKA.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: No ketone in urine and normal anion gap indicate improvement in DKA; serum osmolality <315 mOsmol/kg indicates improvement in HHS.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: No vomiting and ability to take food are criteria for improvement of DKA/HHS.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: Person should be well oriented and hemodynamically stable as criteria for improvement of DKA/HHS.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: Blood glucose should be checked hourly initially during DKA/HHS management.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: Blood pH, electrolytes, urea, and creatinine should be rechecked frequently as required during DKA/HHS management.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: If blood pH <6.9, infuse 100 mmol sodium bicarbonate in 400 ml normal saline with 20 mmol KCl over 2 hours; repeat every 2 hours until pH ≥7; if pH ≥6.9, no sodium bicarbonate infusion needed.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: Address precipitating cause in DKA/HHS management.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: After resolution of DKA/HHS and ability to eat, start subcutaneous insulin at least 1-2 hours before stopping intravenous insulin.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
condition: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
condition_aliases: diabetic ketoacidosis (dka) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (hhs)
fact_text: During transition to subcutaneous insulin, multiply last 6 hours' intravenous insulin dose by 4 to calculate 24-hour dose; then initiate split-mixed or basal-bolus insulin regimen.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Control of blood glucose, blood pressure and blood lipids along with other factors is the cornerstone of prevention and control of diabetic complications.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Every person with diabetes should be screened periodically for chronic complications.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Every person with diabetes should receive preventive foot care advice.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diabetic nephropathy is a specific form of microangiopathy of the kidney characterized by persistent albuminuria and progressive renal insufficiency (declining eGFR) with or without hypertension.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Ophthalmoscopy of dilated eyes should be performed yearly to screen for retinopathy, with color fundus photography if needed.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Serum creatinine, eGFR and urine albumin excretion should be used for screening diabetic nephropathy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: ACR is calculated by dividing albumin concentration in milligrams by creatinine concentration in grams in urine.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) in a spot urine sample (preferably morning fasting before exercise) is the preferred method to detect elevated proteinuria for diabetic nephropathy screening.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
source_section: Table 5.1 Stages of CKD by eGFR
fact_text: CKD stages defined by eGFR: Stage 1 ≥90, Stage 2 60-89, Stage 3 30-59, Stage 4 15-29, Stage 5 <15 or dialysis

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Markers of renal damage include albuminuria (AER ≥30 mg/24h or ACR ≥30 mg/g), urine sediment abnormalities, tubular disorder abnormalities, histology or imaging abnormalities, and history of kidney transplantation

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
followup_monitoring: serum creatinine and eGFR at least annually
fact_text: Serum creatinine and eGFR should be assessed at least annually for renal function monitoring

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Monitor urinary complications such as asymptomatic UTI and autonomic bladder dysfunction in diabetic patients

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Renal biopsy may be required in nephropathy if retinopathy is absent, heavy proteinuria present, or rapid unexplained renal deterioration occurs

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Screening and follow-up for renal damage includes AER, eGFR or creatinine clearance estimation, and blood tests for urea, creatinine, protein, albumin, electrolytes, uric acid, calcium, and phosphate

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Kidney function tests: at diagnosis and annually in T2DM; yearly at or after 5 years of diagnosis in T1DM; tests include urinary albumin/microalbumin and serum creatinine.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Iron supplementation often fails to correct anemia in renal failure; iron plus erythropoietin provides optimum response.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Protein intake up to 0.8 g/kg/day of body weight is allowed in diabetic nephropathy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Restrict high phosphate and uric acid containing foods if necessary to correct high phosphate and uric acid.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are preferred drugs to reduce or revert early nephropathy but must not be combined; monitor electrolytes and creatinine 2 weeks after starting or dose increase.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Refer to nephrologist if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m2, uncertainty about kidney disease etiology, difficult management issues, or rapidly progressing kidney disease.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In nephropathy with evidence, maintain HbA1c <7% and blood pressure <130/80 mmHg; also look for other microangiopathies/complications.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Target blood pressure for diabetic nephropathy is <130/80 mmHg to prevent rapid progression.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Good glycemic control reduces incidence and delays progression of diabetic nephropathy; SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP1-RA are beneficial if not contraindicated.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Maintain fluid and electrolyte balance in diabetic nephropathy management.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Renal replacement therapy (dialysis and renal transplantation) is done when indicated in diabetic nephropathy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diabetic retinopathy classified as: Early non-proliferative (microaneurysm, dot/blot hemorrhage, hard exudate); Moderate to severe non-proliferative (cotton wool spots, soft exudate, venous beads/loops, IRMA); Proliferative (NVD, NVE, vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment); Maculopathy (edema, exudate, hemorrhage in/around macula).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_tests: initial dilated comprehensive eye examination by ophthalmologist or optometrist within 5 years of diagnosis
dose_or_duration: then annually; more frequent if retinopathy progressing or sight-threatening
followup_monitoring: annual eye exam; more frequent if retinopathy progressing or sight-threatening
fact_text: In T1DM, initial dilated comprehensive eye exam by ophthalmologist or optometrist within 5 years of diagnosis, then annually; more frequent if retinopathy progresses or is sight-threatening.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_tests: initial dilated comprehensive eye examination by ophthalmologist or optometrist at time of diabetes diagnosis
dose_or_duration: then annually; more frequent if retinopathy progressing or sight-threatening
followup_monitoring: annual eye exam; more frequent if retinopathy progressing or sight-threatening
fact_text: In T2DM, initial dilated comprehensive eye exam by ophthalmologist or optometrist at diagnosis, then annually; more frequent if retinopathy progresses or is sight-threatening.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_tests: screening for retinopathy before pregnancy in women with T1DM or T2DM
dose_or_duration: repeat eye examination during pregnancy
followup_monitoring: repeat eye exam during pregnancy
fact_text: Women with T1DM or T2DM planning pregnancy should have retinopathy screening before pregnancy and repeat eye exam during pregnancy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh

followup_monitoring: Eye exam at diagnosis and then annually in T2DM
Eye exam yearly at or after 5 years (or earlier) of diagnosis in T1DM
fact_text: Eye examination recommended at diagnosis and annually in T2DM; yearly at or after 5 years of diagnosis in T1DM; use ophthalmoscopy and fundus photography; refer if retinopathy beyond early NPDR.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh

Vibration sensation testing using 128-Hz tuning fork (large fiber function)
