fact_text: Screen diabetic neuropathy starting at T2DM diagnosis and annually; start 5 years after T1DM diagnosis and then annually; use 10-g monofilament, temperature/pinprick, and 128-Hz tuning fork tests; assess cranial and autonomic neuropathy signs.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diabetic neuropathy types include somatic (sensory, motor, cranial focal neuropathy) and autonomic (gastroparesis, hypoglycemia unawareness, postural hypotension, erectile dysfunction).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_advice: Look for other microangiopathies/complications after evidence of ophthalmopathy
referral_criteria: Refer to ophthalmologist if retinopathy is beyond early NPDR
fact_text: After evidence of ophthalmopathy, maintain HbA1c <7% and BP <130/80 mmHg; assess for other microangiopathies; refer if retinopathy beyond early NPDR.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diabetic foot is the most common cause of non-traumatic amputation and is preventable and treatable.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Prior history of ulceration, amputation, Charcot foot, angioplasty or vascular surgery, cigarette smoking, and retinopathy are important historical risk factors for diabetic foot complications.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Comprehensive foot evaluation should be done initially and at least annually to identify risk factors for ulcers and amputations in diabetic patients.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Individuals with sensory loss or prior ulceration or amputation should have their feet examined at every visit.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Treatment of diabetic autonomic neuropathy includes good metabolic control and symptom-specific therapies: erythromycin, metoclopramide, domperidone for gastroparesis; antibiotics, loperamide for diarrhea; PDE5 inhibitors for impotence; intermittent catheterization or surgery for neurogenic bladder; midodrine, mineralocorticoids, elastic stockings, fluid and salt intake adjustments for orthostatic hypotension; plus physiotherapy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy treatment includes optimum glycemic control and symptomatic treatment with antidepressants (e.g. duloxetine, tricyclics), anticonvulsants (e.g. gabapentin, pregabalin), topical capsaicin, quinine sulfate for cramps, and addressing contributing factors like alcohol, vitamin deficiency, renal failure.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
source_section: Table 5.3 Risk categories of diabetic foot
fact_text: Diabetic foot risk categories: Low risk = normal plantar sensation; Moderate risk = loss of protective sensation (LOPS); High risk = LOPS with high pressure or poor circulation or structural foot deformities or onychomycosis; Very high risk = history of ulceration, amputation, or neuropathic fracture.
source_figure_or_table: Table 5.3 Risk categories of diabetic foot

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Always protect feet with appropriate footwear.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Before wearing shoes, check inside for nails, stones, or any other sharp objects.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Daily foot care advice: check feet daily for cuts, blisters, color changes, swelling, ingrown toenails; use a mirror or help if needed.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Inspect skin, assess foot deformities, perform neurological assessment with 10-g monofilament plus pinprick, temperature, or vibration, and assess vascular status including pulses and ankle-brachial index for diabetic foot risk.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Multidisciplinary approach recommended for diabetic foot management including general preventive foot self-care education for all individuals with diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Specialized therapeutic footwear is recommended for high-risk persons with diabetes, including those with severe neuropathy, foot deformities, or history of amputation.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Annual foot examination by healthcare professional is recommended for people with diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Avoid barefoot walking and avoid tight, torn, or rough shoes with uneven edges.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Avoid shoes with narrow toe box, high heels, or footwear lacking back supports.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Buy new shoes at the end of the day and dry feet carefully after washing, especially between toes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Cut nails straight across and file sharp edges to prevent injury.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Do not let feet become dry and cracked; avoid self-removal of corns using medicine or blades.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Do not use socks with tight tops or rough seams and do not use hot water to wash feet.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: More than 70% of people with diabetes die due to cardiovascular causes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Wear cotton socks with shoes and wash socks daily ensuring no holes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Screening for coronary artery disease should be done in symptomatic persons and people with cardiovascular risk.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Refer to foot care specialists if history of prior lower-extremity complications, loss of protective sensation, structural foot abnormalities, peripheral arterial disease, or presence of ulcer/gangrene/infection.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Screen lipid profile at diabetes diagnosis, initial medical evaluation, yearly, and more frequently if indicated
fact_text: Lipid profile screening and monitoring should be done at diabetes diagnosis, initial evaluation, yearly, and more frequently if indicated.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Blood pressure target for non-pregnant adults with diabetes is less than 130/80 mmHg.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Lipid targets in diabetes: LDL cholesterol <70 mg/dL, triglycerides <150 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol >40 mg/dL (male), >50 mg/dL (female).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Lifestyle modification recommended
fact_text: If blood pressure is between 130/80 and 140/90 mmHg, lifestyle modification is recommended.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Recheck after 1 week; if still high, start lifestyle modification and monotherapy
fact_text: If blood pressure is ≥140/90 mmHg, recheck after 1 week; if still high, start lifestyle modification and monotherapy with ACE inhibitor, ARB, calcium channel blocker, or diuretics.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Start dual antihypertensive therapy
fact_text: If blood pressure is ≥160/100 mmHg, start dual antihypertensive therapy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Selective beta blocker or alpha blocker can be used in special situations
fact_text: Selective beta blockers or alpha blockers may be used in special situations for hypertension in diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Selective beta-blockers should be continued for at least 2 years after the event
fact_text: Treatment of hypertension in diabetes includes ACE inhibitors or ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP1-RA, statins, aspirin/clopidogrel, and continuation of selective beta-blockers for at least 2 years post-event.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Lifestyle modification includes maintaining ideal body weight, avoiding saturated and trans fats, increasing dietary omega-3 fatty acids, fibers, green leafy vegetables and fresh fruits, and increasing physical activity.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Aspirin therapy (75–150 mg/day) is recommended as secondary prevention in diabetes patients with a history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Dual antiplatelet therapy is reasonable for one year after an acute coronary syndrome in diabetes patients.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: For primary prevention of ASCVD in diabetes patients aged ≥50 years with at least one major ASCVD risk factor, aspirin is recommended.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and documented aspirin allergy, clopidogrel 75 mg/day should be used.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: For patients <40 years with ASCVD or 10-year ASCVD risk >20%, high-intensity statin is recommended; if LDL cholesterol ≥70 mg/dL despite therapy, consider combining with ezetimibe.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: For patients ≥40 years with ASCVD or 10-year ASCVD risk >20%, high-intensity statin is recommended; if LDL cholesterol ≥70 mg/dL despite therapy, consider combining with ezetimibe.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: For patients ≥40 years without ASCVD or 10-year ASCVD risk >20%, moderate- or high-intensity statin may be considered based on risk-benefit or ASCVD risk presence.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Pharmacological therapy for ASCVD risk: For patients <40 years without ASCVD or 10-year ASCVD risk >20%, none or moderate intensity statin may be considered based on risk-benefit or ASCVD risk presence.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diabetes education and counselling should be given prior to Ramadan and Hajj.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: During sick days, patients should check blood glucose frequently at home and take plenty of water and fluids.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: All women planning pregnancy or conceived should be screened for diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Hyperglycemia in pregnancy may be due to GDM (diabetes first detected during gestation) or preexisting prediabetes or diabetes in pregnancy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Risk factors for GDM include BMI ≥23 kg/m2, age ≥25 years, first degree relative with diabetes, history of delivery of baby >9 lb or LGA or bad obstetric history, previous GDM, HbA1c ≥5.7%, IGT or IFG, physical inactivity, hypertension or therapy for hypertension, HDL <35 mg/dL, triglycerides >250 mg/dL, PCOS, acanthosis nigricans, and history of cardiovascular disease.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Insulin is the only therapy in children under 10 years of age; metformin can be given after 10 years.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Only insulin is recommended for use in pregnancy and lactation period.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In hospital admitted patients, insulin therapy should be initiated if persistent hyperglycemia >10 mmol/L on two occasions; target blood glucose 7.8 to 10 mmol/L; intravenous insulin preferred in critical setting.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
contraindications_or_cautions: Review medication list for potentially harmful drugs like ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or statins before conception.
fact_text: Review medication list for potentially harmful drugs like ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or statins before conception in women with diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Preconception HbA1c should be below 6.5% in women planning pregnancy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Recommended weight gain during pregnancy varies by pre-pregnancy BMI and singleton or twin pregnancy status as per Table 6.1.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Medical nutrition therapy (MNT) should be started soon after diagnosis of GDM, preferably by a dietitian, and reviewed each trimester.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: The aim of GDM management is to achieve normoglycemia, adequate maternal weight gain, adequate fetal growth, and prevention of ketosis.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Women receiving non-insulin antihyperglycemic agents should switch to insulin before conception.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
trigger_evidence: excessive abdominal muscular contracture during exercise
fact_text: During exercise in pregnancy, excessive abdominal muscular contracture should be avoided.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Physical activity in pregnancy: moderate aerobic and resistance exercise for 20-50 minutes/day, 2-7 days/week of moderate intensity is effective.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
source_section: Caloric intake table by pre-pregnancy BMI and trimester
fact_text: Caloric intake during pregnancy varies by pre-pregnancy BMI: <18.5 BMI requires 35 kcal/kg/day in 1st trimester and 40 kcal/kg/day in 2nd/3rd trimester; BMI 18.5-22.9 requires 30 and 35 kcal/kg/day; BMI 23-27.4 requires 25 and 30 kcal/kg/day; BMI >27.5 requires 30-33% calorie restriction during pregnancy.
source_figure_or_table: Caloric intake table by pre-pregnancy BMI and trimester

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Meal pattern in pregnancy: 3 main meals and 3 snacks daily including 1 snack at bedtime.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Recommended overall total caloric distribution in pregnancy: Carbohydrate 33-40% with low glycemic index; Protein ~20%; Fat <40% with saturated fat <7% and trans fat <1%; avoid simple sugars; encourage complex carbohydrates, high dietary fiber, and whole grains; non-calorie sweeteners (aspartame) may be used safely; increase lean protein, oily fish, and vegetable consumption; daily iron 30 mg, calcium 1000 mg, and folate 0.6 mg recommended.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In first and third trimester pregnancy with FPG 5.1-6.0 mmol/L and/or 2h PPG 6.7-7.8 mmol/L, start lifestyle modification for 1 week; if target not achieved, add pharmacological treatment; if target achieved, continue lifestyle.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In first and third trimester pregnancy with FPG 6.1-7.0 mmol/L and/or 2h PPG 7.8-11.1 mmol/L, start lifestyle modification for 3 days; if target not achieved, add pharmacological treatment; if target achieved, continue lifestyle.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In first and third trimester pregnancy with FPG ≥7.0 mmol/L and/or 2h PPG ≥11.1 mmol/L, start lifestyle modification plus pharmacological treatment immediately.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In second trimester pregnancy with FPG 5.1-6.0 mmol/L and/or 2h PPG 6.7-7.8 mmol/L, start lifestyle modification for 1 week; if target not achieved, add pharmacological treatment; if target achieved, continue lifestyle.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In second trimester pregnancy with FPG 6.1-7.0 mmol/L and/or 2h PPG 7.8-11.1 mmol/L, start lifestyle modification for 3 days; if target not achieved, add pharmacological treatment; if target achieved, continue lifestyle.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In second trimester pregnancy with FPG ≥7.0 mmol/L and/or 2h PPG ≥11.1 mmol/L, start lifestyle modification plus pharmacological treatment immediately.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Every pregnant woman should be offered education and encouraged for self-monitoring of pre- and post-meal glucose at home, twice or thrice a week.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: HbA1c should be used as a secondary measure of glycemic control after blood glucose monitoring in pregnancy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Non-insulin antihyperglycemic agents are not recommended in gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Pre-mixed insulin is usually not preferred in gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Initial daily insulin dose is 0.2 to 0.5 unit/kg body weight; obese women may need higher doses; treatment should be adjusted to reach targets.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Recommended insulins include recombinant human short and intermediate (NPH) acting insulin, rapid acting analogues aspart and lispro, and long-acting analogue detemir.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Glycemic targets in pregnancy: fasting blood glucose <5.3 mmol/L (95 mg/dL) and 2-hour post-prandial glucose <6.7 mmol/L (120 mg/dL).

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Maternal glucose should be maintained between 4.0 to 7.0 mmol/L during labor.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Hospital delivery is mandatory for women with diabetes in pregnancy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Indications for cesarean section (C/S) in women with diabetes are the same as for other women.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Only bolus insulin may be needed in some cases of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) when fasting plasma glucose is well controlled.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Step 1: Raised post-meal blood glucose should be controlled by bolus insulin (regular/short acting human insulin or short/ultra-short acting analogue) with meals, titrated frequently to reach post-meal targets.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Step 2: High fasting plasma glucose (FPG) should be controlled with intermediate acting human insulin (NPH) or basal analogue insulin at lower dose, then titrated to target.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_advice: About 50% of women with GDM may develop type 2 diabetes within 5 to 10 years.
fact_text: Approximately 50% of women with GDM may develop type 2 diabetes within 5 to 10 years postpartum.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_advice: All mothers with history of GDM should be counseled about screening for GDM during every subsequent pregnancy.
fact_text: Mothers with history of GDM should be counseled to screen for GDM in every subsequent pregnancy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
followup_monitoring: Annual re-assessment with 75-g 2h OGTT or HbA1c if blood glucose is normal postpartum.
fact_text: If postpartum blood glucose is normal, annual re-assessment with 75-g 2h OGTT or HbA1c is recommended.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: After delivery, at least 1 fasting and 1 post-meal plasma glucose should be measured before discharge in persons with GDM managed by MNT or insulin.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Blood glucose of newborn should be checked by heel prick within half an hour after birth.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
followup_monitoring: If blood glucose remains elevated after delivery, continued monitoring is warranted.
fact_text: If blood glucose remains elevated after delivery in GDM managed with insulin, continued monitoring is warranted.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_tests: 75-g 2h OGTT using non-pregnant criteria at 6 weeks postpartum
fact_text: Women with GDM (not requiring insulin after delivery) should be screened for diabetes 6 weeks postpartum with 75-g 2h OGTT using non-pregnant criteria.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_advice: All types of insulin can be safely used in lactating women.
contraindications_or_cautions: Oral antidiabetic drugs should be avoided in breastfeeding women.
fact_text: All types of insulin are safe in lactating women; oral antidiabetic drugs should be avoided during breastfeeding.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_advice: Contraception advice should be given postpartum.
contraindications_or_cautions: Progesterone only contraception increases risk of vascular complications.
fact_text: Postpartum contraception advice: low dose estrogen-progesterone can be offered; progesterone-only increases vascular risk.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: If needed, 5% Dextrose infusion with short acting insulin can be maintained but glucose-insulin infusion should be stopped immediately after delivery.
fact_text: 5% Dextrose infusion with short acting insulin can be maintained if needed but must be stopped immediately after delivery.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Mothers on insulin >1 unit/kg/day may reduce dose to 50% postpartum.
fact_text: Postpartum mothers on insulin >1 unit/kg/day may reduce dose to 50%.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Mothers on low dose insulin (<0.5 unit/kg/day) can stop insulin and monitor glucose postpartum.
fact_text: Postpartum mothers on low dose insulin (<0.5 unit/kg/day) can stop insulin and monitor glucose.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
dose_or_duration: Most women requiring <1.0 unit/kg/day insulin can be monitored without intravenous insulin postpartum.
fact_text: Women needing less than 1.0 unit/kg/day insulin postpartum can be monitored without IV insulin.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Postpartum prediabetes should be managed with Medical Nutrition Therapy (MNT) using standard protocol.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diabetes education is essential for children and adolescents, including insulin injection technique, dietary practice, home blood glucose monitoring, and emotional support.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Infants and toddlers with diabetes are fully dependent on parents and caregivers for injections, food, and monitoring; education on prevention and recognition is needed.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Diabetes mellitus in childhood and adolescence is most often type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), but type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) incidence is increasing due to rising obesity rates.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Target plasma glucose levels in children and adolescents: Fasting/pre-meal 5.0-7.2 mmol/L, post-meal 5.0-10.0 mmol/L, pre-bed 5.0-8.3 mmol/L; HbA1c target <7.0%.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In T1DM children and adolescents, insulin is the only treatment choice.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: For T2DM children aged 10-18 years, insulin or metformin is recommended.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: For T2DM children under 10 years, insulin only is recommended.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: For T2DM patients older than 18 years, treatment options include insulin, metformin, or other antidiabetic agents such as sulfonylureas and thiazolidinediones.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Age-specific calorie calculation charts are available for measuring diet allowance in children with diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: All children with diabetes should be referred to a dietitian for counseling at diagnosis and if diet adjustment problems arise.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Children above 10 years and adolescents may take part in complex sports like basketball, football, tennis, and hockey.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Children aged 3-5 years may take part in free play, walking, running, and similar activities.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Children aged 6-9 years may start learning to play team sports such as football and cricket.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Children with T1DM and good glucose control can perform all levels of exercise including leisure, recreational sports, and competitive professional performance.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Exercise is especially important for young obese children with T2DM.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Adolescents with diabetes should be promoted to independent, responsible self-management appropriate to their maturity and understanding.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Children with T1DM should be trained on insulin injections, blood glucose monitoring, hypoglycemia symptom recognition, and self-management adapted to school programs and meals.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Parents and school authorities should be involved in supporting gradual development of independence in diabetes self-management for children and adolescents.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Blood pressure should be monitored at diagnosis and at every follow-up visit in patients with diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Target blood pressure for patients aged 13 years or older is below the 90th percentile for age, sex, and height, and if age ≥13 years, BP <130/80 mmHg.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
trigger_evidence: BP 90-95th percentile for age, sex, height or age ≥13 years with BP 120-129/<80 mmHg
recommended_advice: lifestyle modification
fact_text: Lifestyle modification is recommended for elevated blood pressure defined as 90-95th percentile for age, sex, height or if age ≥13 years with BP 120-129/<80 mmHg.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
followup_monitoring: annual ACR if normal; confirm abnormal by 2 of 3 samples in 6 months
fact_text: Albumin creatinine ratio (ACR) should be measured at puberty or age >10 years, whichever is earlier, and diabetes duration >5 years; if normal, screen annually; if abnormal, confirm by repeating 2 of 3 samples in 6 months.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
followup_monitoring: every 2 years if normal
fact_text: Dilated fundoscopy should be performed to screen for retinopathy at puberty or age >11 years, whichever is earlier, and diabetes duration 3-5 years; if normal, repeat every 2 years.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_tests: foot examination with pulse, pinprick, vibration, ankle jerk, 10-g monofilament if possible
followup_monitoring: annually if normal
fact_text: Foot examination including pulse, pinprick, vibration test, ankle jerk, and 10-g monofilament (if possible) should be performed at puberty or age 11 years, whichever is earlier, and diabetes duration 5 years; if normal, annually.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
followup_monitoring: repeat lipid profile every 3-5 years if LDL <100 mg/dL
fact_text: If LDL cholesterol is <100 mg/dL, repeat lipid profile every 3-5 years.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
followup_monitoring: annual lipid profile if abnormal
fact_text: Lipid profile should be performed in children soon after diabetes diagnosis (preferably after diabetes control or age ≥2 years); if abnormal, annual monitoring is recommended.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: The goal of lipid therapy is to achieve LDL cholesterol <100 mg/dL.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
trigger_evidence: LDL cholesterol >130 mg/dL with cardiovascular risk factor
recommended_advice: lifestyle changes
fact_text: After age 10, statin therapy is recommended for patients with LDL >160 mg/dL or LDL >130 mg/dL plus cardiovascular risk factor despite lifestyle changes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
trigger_evidence: BP ≥95th percentile for age, sex, height or age ≥13 years with BP >130/80 mmHg
recommended_advice: lifestyle modification
fact_text: Lifestyle modification plus ACEI or ARB is recommended for hypertension defined as BP ≥95th percentile for age, sex, height or if age ≥13 years with BP >130/80 mmHg.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Screening for diabetes complications should be individualized in older adults, especially for complications that may lead to functional impairment.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Screening for early detection of mild cognitive impairment or dementia should be performed for adults aged 65 years or older at initial visit, annually, and as appropriate.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Older adults who are otherwise healthy with few coexisting chronic illnesses and intact cognitive and functional status should have glycemic targets: HbA1c <7.5%, FPG <7.2 mmol/L, PPG <10.0 mmol/L.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Older adults with multiple coexisting chronic illnesses, cognitive impairment, or functional dependence should have less stringent glycemic targets: HbA1c 8.0-8.5%, FPG <10 mmol/L, PPG <11.1 mmol/L.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
recommended_tests: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) for celiac disease
fact_text: For patients with type 1 diabetes, advise thyroid function test and IgA anti-tTG for celiac disease soon after diagnosis if possible.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
trigger_evidence: life expectancy at least equal to primary prevention or secondary intervention trial time frame
fact_text: Lipid lowering therapy and aspirin therapy may benefit older adults with diabetes who have life expectancy at least equal to the time frame of primary prevention or secondary intervention trials.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Treatment of hypertension to individualized target levels is indicated in most older adults with diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Modest weight loss of 5-7% is recommended for obese older adults with diabetes.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Older adults with diabetes should have optimal nutrition and protein intake, and be encouraged to perform regular aerobic, weight-bearing, and/or resistance exercise if safe.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: An admission HbA1c value ≥6.5% suggests that diabetes onset preceded hospitalization.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Hyperglycemia in hospitalized patients is defined as blood glucose levels >7.8 mmol/L.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: HbA1c should be measured in all hospitalized patients with diabetes or hyperglycemia if not done in the previous 3 months.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In older diabetic patients, medication classes with low risk of hypoglycemia are preferred due to increased hypoglycemia risk.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Metformin is the first-line oral therapy in older adults but should be used cautiously.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP1 receptor agonists can be used in older adults if tolerated and not contraindicated.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Avoid overtreatment of diabetes in older adults to reduce hypoglycemia risk.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Consider cost of care when developing treatment plans for older adults to reduce risk of cost-related nonadherence.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In older adults on short-acting prandial insulin, if prandial insulin dose >10 units/dose, reduce dose by 50% and add non-insulin agent; if <10 units/dose, discontinue prandial insulin and non-insulin agent.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Simplify complex medication regimens in older adults to reduce hypoglycemia risk and polypharmacy.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: For patients on NG tube or NPO, bedside glucose monitoring every 4-6 hours is recommended.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: For patients on oral feeding in hospital, bedside glucose monitoring is recommended before meals and 2 hours after meals.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In critical patients on IV insulin, glucose monitoring every 30 minutes to 2 hours may be needed.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Use of sliding scale insulin regimen is strongly discouraged in hospitalized patients.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Once insulin therapy is started, target glucose range is 7.8-10.0 mmol/L for most critically ill and non-critically ill patients.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: If oral intake is poor, prandial insulin should be administered immediately after the person eats.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
source_section: Table 6.5 Insulin therapy in critical and noncritical setting
fact_text: In critical setting, continuous IV insulin infusion is preferred with more frequent monitoring and adjustment.
source_figure_or_table: Table 6.5 Insulin therapy in critical and noncritical setting

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
source_section: Table 6.5 Insulin therapy in critical and noncritical setting
fact_text: In non-critical setting, basal or basal plus/NPH or NPH plus short acting insulin is used for poor oral intake; basal-bolus/split mixed plus correctional insulin is used for good intake.
source_figure_or_table: Table 6.5 Insulin therapy in critical and noncritical setting

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: In noncritical hospitalized patients, scheduled insulin regimen is recommended.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Insulin therapy is preferred for treatment of hyperglycemia in all hospitalized individuals.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
fact_text: Insulin therapy should be initiated for persistent hyperglycemia at glucose ≥10.0 mmol/L confirmed on two occasions.

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh
source_section: Table 6.6 Insulin dose adjustment prior and during surgery
fact_text: Day before surgery insulin dose adjustments: For normal diet until midnight, usual dose of glargine/detemir and regular/rapid acting insulin; 80% usual dose of NPH/pre-mixed insulin AM and PM. For only liquid 12-24 hrs prior surgery, usual dose glargine/detemir; 80% usual dose NPH/pre-mixed AM and PM; hold regular/rapid acting insulin.
source_figure_or_table: Table 6.6 Insulin dose adjustment prior and during surgery

source_title: National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus Bangladesh

fact_text: Day of surgery insulin dose adjustments: NPO status; glargine/detemir 80% usual dose if twice daily basal insulin; NPH/pre-mixed 50% usual dose, hold if blood glucose <6.6 mmol/L; regular/rapid acting insulin held.

fact_text: Causes of jaundice in pregnancy are classified as 'Jaundice unique to pregnancy' (e.g. obstetric cholestasis, acute fatty liver, severe preeclampsia/eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, severe hyperemesis gravidarum, endotoxic shock) and 'Jaundice due to inter-current illness' (e.g. viral hepatitis, drug induced, cholelithiasis, haemolytic jaundice, autoimmune hepatitis, CLD, malaria, hepatic neoplasm, pancreatitis).

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: Abdominal examination in jaundice includes checking liver size and tenderness (enlarged/tender in viral hepatitis, firm edge in cirrhosis, smooth enlarged in post hepatic obstructive jaundice), splenomegaly (cirrhosis), and palpable pancreatic tumor.

fact_text: Interpretation of liver enzymes: ALT >1000 IU/L indicates acute parenchymal disease; ALT >400 IU/L viral hepatitis; ALT 150-400 IU/L chronic active or viral/drug hepatitis; ALT <100 IU/L obstructive jaundice; ALT>AST in acute hepatitis; AST>ALT in cirrhosis, hemolytic jaundice, alcoholic hepatitis; alkaline phosphatase and bile acids raised in cholestasis; LDH raised in HELLP syndrome.

warning_signs: Any per vaginal bleeding with or without pain before delivery or severe bleeding after delivery
High blood pressure (≥140/90 mm Hg or rise of 30/15 mm Hg)
Severe headache and blurring of vision
Excessive vomiting, vomiting immediately after eating or drinking for continuous 24 hours

fact_text: Recognize danger signs in pregnancy, labour, and postpartum including bleeding, convulsions, high BP, fever, severe headache, persistent pain, prolonged labour, abnormal presentation, and foul-smelling discharge with fever.

Arrange emergency transport (ambulance, rickshaw, van, boat, bullock cart)
Save money for emergency delivery expenses
Keep contact with at least 2 blood donors or blood bank
fact_text: Birth planning includes deciding place of delivery, birth attendant, emergency referral site, transport, saving money, and blood donor contacts to avoid delays in complications.

fact_text: Latent first stage of labour is characterized by painful uterine contractions with variable cervical changes including some effacement and slower dilation up to 5cm; median duration 6 to 7.5 hours.

fact_text: Diagnosis of labour requires history taking (ask and check current and previous records), general, abdominal and PV examination, and then management accordingly.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: Examination of woman in labour includes general and abdominal exam (appearance, vital signs, pallor, edema, jaundice, dehydration, urine output, abdominal contour, fetal presentation, fetal movements, FHS rate and rhythm).

fact_text: Vaginal examination in labour should include explanation to woman, consent, privacy, dignity, comfort, and checking vaginal bleeding, leaking amniotic fluid, bulging perineum, fetal parts, cervical effacement and dilation, presenting part, station, membrane status, and liquor color if membranes ruptured.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: History taking in labour should include greetings, duration and frequency/severity of labour pain, fetal movement, duration of ruptured membranes, bleeding amount, associated complaints (headache, fever, blurred vision, vomiting, breathing/voiding difficulties), previous pregnancy outcomes, current pregnancy ANC records, tetanus immunization, and birth plan review.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
recommended_advice: Encourage walking and support woman's choice of position in each stage

fact_text: For induction of labour (IOL) in intrauterine death (IUD), assess membrane status (MBS) at time 0; if MBS ≥7 cm, start Oxytocin; if <7 cm, start Prostaglandins or Misoprostol and reassess uterine activity hourly. If contracting, send to labour room and augment with Oxytocin if needed. If not contracting, reassess MBS: if ≥7 cm, start Oxytocin; if <7 cm, insert Foley's catheter. When balloon falls, start Oxytocin; if balloon remains after 12 hours, remove balloon and start Oxytocin.

fact_text: Unsatisfactory progress of labour includes prolonged latent phase (>12h primipara, >8h multipara), prolonged active phase (cervical dilatation <2cm in 4h, delay in fetal head descent/rotation, contraction changes), prolonged 2nd stage (nulliparous ≥3h no progress without epidural or ≥4h with epidural; parous ≥2h no progress without epidural or ≥3h with epidural), secondary arrest (no cervical dilatation and descent despite good contractions), and obstructed labour (delay in descent despite good contractions). Minimum 1cm/hr cervical dilatation rate is not a strict normal labour progression criterion.

fact_text: In prolonged active phase, exclude obstruction or fetal distress; if membranes intact do ARM; assess uterine contractions; if contractions inadequate, augment with oxytocin infusion increasing dose every 30 min by 10 drops; reassess after 2 hours; if no progress do C/S; if progress continue monitoring every 2 hours.

fact_text: Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed when the fetal head is delivered but the shoulders are stuck and cannot be delivered, with signs including head tightly applied to vulva, chin retracting and depressing perineum, and failed traction due to shoulder caught behind pubic symphysis or sacral promontory.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: Risk factors for shoulder dystocia include antepartum factors: excessive weight gain (>35 lb/15.9 kg), maternal obesity (BMI >30), post-term pregnancy, fetal macrosomia, diabetic mother, multiparity; and intrapartum factors: operative vaginal delivery (vacuum, forceps) and prolonged second stage of labour.

fact_text: Management of shoulder dystocia includes: call for help, position woman with buttocks over table edge, perform episiotomy to allow maneuvers, apply continuous downward traction on fetal head avoiding excessive force, use McRobert's maneuver (flex thighs, abduct and rotate legs), then if shoulder not delivered, proceed with RUBIN-1 (suprapubic pressure and rotation), RUBIN II (vaginal hand behind shoulder rotation), Wood's screw maneuver, Jacquemier's maneuver (delivery of posterior arm), and placing woman in all fours position to facilitate delivery.

fact_text: For shoulder dystocia, call for help, position woman with buttocks at bed edge, perform adequate episiotomy, place woman in McRobert's position, apply suprapubic pressure (avoid fundal pressure), deliver anterior shoulder with continuous downward traction, if unsuccessful insert hand to rotate anterior shoulder (Rubin-2), then apply pressure to posterior shoulder to deliver it, use Wood's screw maneuver to rotate shoulders, try Jacquemier's maneuver if shoulder still not delivered, or place woman in all fours position to dislodge anterior shoulder and facilitate delivery.

recommended_advice: Women with one prior uncomplicated lower-segment transverse caesarean and no contraindication to vaginal birth should be counseled about planned VBAC and ERCS options.
Counseling should be documented in notes.
Final decision on mode of birth should be agreed by woman and obstetrician before expected delivery date, ideally by 36 weeks gestation.
Women should be informed that successful planned VBAC chances are 72–76%.

Counsel about maternal and perinatal risks and benefits of planned VBAC and ERCS considering individual circumstances including motivation, attitudes to risks, future pregnancy plans, and prior vaginal birth history.
Review previous caesarean operative notes to identify indication, uterine incision type, and perioperative complications.
fact_text: Antenatal counseling for women with prior caesarean should include discussion of VBAC vs ERCS options, documentation, decision by 36 weeks, success chances, risks/benefits, personal factors, and review of previous caesarean notes.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: Planned VBAC refers to vaginal birth after a prior caesarean birth, planned instead of elective repeat caesarean section (ERCS).

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: Other serious maternal outcomes of VBAC include hysterectomy, thromboembolism, haemorrhage, transfusion requirement, viscus injury (bowel, bladder, ureter), endometritis, and maternal death.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: Uterine rupture is disruption of uterine muscle extending to serosa and adjacent structures; uterine dehiscence is disruption of muscle with intact serosa; both are serious VBAC maternal outcomes.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: Successful VBAC is vaginal birth (spontaneous or assisted) in a woman undergoing planned VBAC; emergency caesarean during labour indicates unsuccessful VBAC.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: Factors associated with unsuccessful VBAC include induced labour, no previous vaginal birth, BMI >30, previous caesarean for dystocia, VBAC at or after 41 weeks gestation, birth weight >4000g, no epidural anesthesia, previous preterm caesarean birth, cervical dilation <4 cm at admission, less than 2 years since previous caesarean, advanced maternal age, non-white ethnicity, short stature, and male infant.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: Previous vaginal birth, especially previous VBAC, is the single best predictor for successful VBAC.

fact_text: Ideal labour analgesia criteria include efficient pain relief, no depression of fetal respiratory center, no effect on labor progress, easy administration, and good therapeutic safety.

fact_text: Relief of pain during labor and delivery is essential for good obstetric care and should allow participation in birthing, minimal motor block, minimal fetal effects, and minimal labor progress interference.

fact_text: Types of labour analgesia include non-pharmacological (psycho prophylaxis, ancillary support such as position and acupuncture) and pharmacological (systemic opioid analgesia, antispasmodic, inhalation agents like Entonox, regional analgesia including epidural, pudendal block, perineal infiltration, and patient-controlled analgesia).

fact_text: In labour, psycho prophylaxis includes allowing ambulation, comfortable positions, breathing techniques, and presence of a companion to reduce fear and anxiety and reduce need for analgesia.

fact_text: Entonox and injectable Pethidine are pharmacological options for labour analgesia when indicated.

Pulse, BP: rapid, low volume (>110/min), low BP (systolic <90 mmHg)
Hydration: dehydrated, low urine output (<30 ml/hr)
P/V exam: findings according to cause of shock
fact_text: Obstetric shock is defined as circulatory failure causing inadequate organ perfusion, with danger signs including coma, cold clammy skin, rapid weak pulse >110/min, low BP <90 mmHg, rapid breathing, dehydration, and low urine output <30 ml/hr.

fact_text: Immediate management of obstetric shock includes shouting for help, left lateral position, IV fluids (normal saline or Ringer's lactate), blood tests (Hb, blood group, cross-match), continuous vital sign monitoring every 5 minutes, catheterization for urine output, warming patient, and foot end elevation.

fact_text: PROM diagnosis requires maternal history of fluid gush, sterile speculum exam showing fluid from cervix, typical amniotic fluid odor, and confirmatory tests like Nitrazine, Fern, fetal fibronectin, or ultrasound.

Ultrasound for fetal wellbeing and amniotic fluid volume
fact_text: PROM general management includes confirming gestational age, assessing maternal symptoms and fetal movement, and investigations including CBC, urine RME, high vaginal swab, CRP, and ultrasound for fetal wellbeing and amniotic fluid volume.

fact_text: Dexamethasone 6 mg every 12 hours for 4 doses over 48 hours is recommended for PROM with gestational age <34 weeks; steroids should not be used if infection is present.

tocolytics for 2 days if uterine contractions present to allow steroid benefit

fact_text: For PROM at 32 to <36 weeks, immediate induction and delivery after antibiotics and steroids is recommended if gestational age <34 weeks and delivery within 24 hours, especially if infection signs or fetal compromise present; otherwise expectant management with hospitalization, antibiotics, antenatal corticosteroids, and monitoring.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
admission_criteria: active management can wait 24 hours for spontaneous labour onset

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts

fact_text: For PROM before 24 weeks, counseling and termination is recommended as no management improves prognosis; follow protocol for pregnancy termination.

fact_text: Chorioamnionitis diagnosis requires fever ≥100.4°F plus two or more signs (maternal pulse >100 bpm, FHR >160 bpm, uterine tenderness, foul smelling discharge, leukocytosis >15000, CRP >2.7 mg/dl, no other infection site); treat with Regimen 1 antibiotics, corticosteroids if <34 weeks, hospitalize and consider NICU transfer.

Ampicillin/Cephalexin IV for 48 hours followed by oral Erythromycin 250 mg qds + Amoxicillin 500 mg tds until delivery; if chorioamnionitis develops, give injectable ampicillin 2 gm IV 6 hourly + gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV daily + metronidazole 500 mg IV 8 hourly until fever free for 24 hours.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: Gestational hypertension is defined as systolic BP ≥140 mm Hg and/or diastolic BP ≥90 mm Hg in a previously normotensive pregnant woman at ≥20 weeks gestation without proteinuria or new end-organ dysfunction, confirmed by two readings 4 hours apart.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
condition: mild preeclampsia / preeclampsia without severe features
condition_aliases: mild preeclampsia / preeclampsia without severe features
fact_text: Mild preeclampsia is defined by systolic BP 140 to ≤160 mm Hg and diastolic BP 90 to <110 mm Hg on two readings >4 hours apart after 20 weeks, with significant proteinuria but no organ dysfunction.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
condition: new-onset hypertension without proteinuria but with severe features
condition_aliases: new-onset hypertension without proteinuria but with severe features
warning_signs: Headache increasing frequency not relieved by analgesics
fact_text: New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria but with any severe feature (thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, liver dysfunction, pulmonary edema, cerebral/visual symptoms, oliguria, upper abdominal pain) defines severe preeclampsia.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
condition_aliases: new-onset hypertension plus proteinuria after 20 weeks
fact_text: Preeclampsia is defined as new-onset hypertension (systolic ≥140 or diastolic ≥90 mm Hg) plus significant proteinuria (≥300 mg/24h urine or protein/creatinine ratio ≥0.3 or dipstick 1+) after 20 weeks gestation.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
condition: severe preeclampsia / severe features of preeclampsia
condition_aliases: severe preeclampsia / severe features of preeclampsia

Impaired liver function (elevated liver transaminases ≥ twice normal)
Cerebral or visual symptoms (headache increasing frequency, not relieved by analgesics, blurred vision)
Upper abdominal pain (epigastric or right upper quadrant)
fact_text: Severe preeclampsia is defined by systolic BP ≥160 mm Hg or diastolic BP ≥110 mm Hg after 20 weeks plus significant proteinuria and/or any severe features including thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, liver dysfunction, pulmonary edema, cerebral/visual symptoms, oliguria, or upper abdominal pain.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
trigger_evidence: high BP detected before 20 weeks gestation
high BP persists more than 12 weeks postpartum
fact_text: Chronic hypertension is defined as high blood pressure known before conception, detected before 20 weeks gestation, or persisting more than 12 weeks postpartum.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
warning_signs: sudden sustained increase in protein excretion
fact_text: Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia is diagnosed if a woman with early gestation hypertension develops proteinuria after 20 weeks or if a woman with hypertension and proteinuria before 20 weeks shows sudden hypertension worsening, liver enzyme rise, thrombocytopenia (<100,000), right upper quadrant pain, severe headache, pulmonary edema, renal insufficiency, or increased protein excretion.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
trigger_evidence: new onset hypertension after 20 weeks gestation
fact_text: Eclampsia is defined by new onset hypertension after 20 weeks gestation, significant proteinuria ≥1+ on dipstick, sometimes altered sensorium or severe preeclampsia signs, and presence of convulsions.

fact_text: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy classification: Gestational hypertension is BP ≥140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks without proteinuria; Chronic hypertension is BP ≥140/90 mmHg before 20 weeks; Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia includes early hypertension plus new proteinuria or severe preeclampsia features; Mild preeclampsia is BP ≥140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks with significant proteinuria.

fact_text: Women with mild or severe preeclampsia and eclampsia must be stabilized and immediately referred to a Comprehensive EmONC centre for management.

warning_signs: Headache (increasing frequency, unrelieved by regular analgesics)
Oliguria (passing less than 400 mL urine in 24 hours)

fact_text: Severe preeclampsia is defined by systolic BP ≥160 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥110 mmHg after 20 weeks gestation with significant proteinuria; danger signs include headache, blurred vision, oliguria, upper abdominal pain, and pulmonary edema.

24 hours total urinary protein (do not repeat quantification)

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: If woman with eclampsia is unconscious or convulsing, shout for help and perform rapid simultaneous airway, breathing, and circulation assessment.

fact_text: In eclampsia, perform investigations including CBC, blood group and Rh typing, serum creatinine, electrolytes, SGPT, bilirubin, urine protein, bedside clotting test, and coagulation profile.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: Oral antihypertensive medications for chronic hypertension in pregnancy include Methyldopa 250 mg tds (max 2g), Labetalol 100 mg bd-tds (max 2400 mg), and Nifedipine 10 mg bd-tds (max 120 mg).

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts
fact_text: In chronic hypertension, do not lower blood pressure below 120/80 mmHg to maintain renal and placental perfusion; if BP≥150/100, start antihypertensive treatment; if proteinuria or preeclampsia signs present, manage as preeclampsia.

monitor FHR, urine output, auscultate lung bases
continuous catheterization to monitor urine output and proteinuria

never leave woman alone
fact_text: In eclampsia, protect airway, do not restrain convulsing woman, provide oxygen 4-6 L/min if breathing, assist ventilation if not breathing, establish IV access with normal saline or Hartmann's solution, give anticonvulsant drugs, and monitor vital signs and urine output closely.

source_title: Bangladesh EmONC Standard Clinical Management Protocols and Flowcharts

fact_text: Hypertension is common in renal transplant patients (50-80% adults, 47-82% pediatrics) and contributes to cardiovascular events and graft survival; no specific antihypertensive shown superior for graft or patient survival.
In dialysis patients, hypertension is defined as pre-dialysis BP >140/90 mmHg or post-dialysis BP >130/80 mmHg requiring antihypertensive treatment.

In peritoneal dialysis patients, hypertension is defined as average home BP ≥135/85 mmHg over 7 consecutive days in recumbent and supine positions, with measurements 1-2 minutes apart if ABPM unavailable.

If ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM) is unavailable in dialysis patients, diagnosis is based on office/home BP measured mid-weekday free of hemodialysis, averaging three readings 1-2 minutes apart in sitting position; threshold is 140/90 mmHg.

recommended_medicines: Beta-blockers including carvedilol (especially for cardiovascular disease, stroke, ischemic heart disease)
fact_text: Pharmacological treatment options include CCBs, ACEi, ARBs, vasodilators, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and beta-blockers (carvedilol) especially for patients with cardiovascular disease, stroke, or ischemic heart disease.
Hypertension causes left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and diastolic dysfunction, which predict heart failure even with normal LV systolic function.
Target BP in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) is approximately <130/80 mmHg.

contraindications_or_cautions: CAD with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF <40%)
fact_text: Calcium antagonists (both dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine) are contraindicated in CAD patients with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF <40%).

avoid_medicines: non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers with beta blockers
contraindications_or_cautions: increased risk of bradycardia and AV block
fact_text: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers should be avoided with concomitant beta blocker use due to increased risk of bradycardia and AV block.
If BP is not controlled with beta-blockers and RAS blockers in CAD, alpha-1 blockers can be used.
In STEMI, beta-blockers, RAS blockers, antiplatelet, and statin are treatment of choice.
In hypertensive patients with CAD, beta-blockers and RAS blockers improve post-myocardial infarction outcomes and reduce mortality.
In patients with symptomatic angina, beta-blockers and rate limiting calcium antagonists are preferred drug treatments.
In heart failure patients, it may be wise to avoid actively lowering BP below 120/70 mmHg due to possible poor outcomes.

recommended_medicines: Carvedilol is preferred beta-blocker (combined alpha & beta blocker) in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Other beta blockers for heart failure: Bisoprolol, Metoprolol, Succinate, Nebivolol
fact_text: Carvedilol is the preferred beta-blocker in HFrEF; other beta-blockers used include Bisoprolol, Metoprolol Succinate, and Nebivolol.

recommended_medicines: Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) - sacubitril and valsartan
fact_text: For hypertension in HFrEF patients, recommended drugs include ACE inhibitors, ARBs, ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan), beta-blockers, and MRAs; non-dihydropyridine CCBs, alpha-blockers, and centrally acting agents should not be used.
Antihypertensive treatment is commonly needed in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) using the same BP threshold and target as HFrEF.
In patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), antihypertensive treatment should start if BP is >140/90 mmHg.
Hypertension in children and adolescents is a significant health concern and a key predictor of adult hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and organ damage.
Blood pressure readings obtained in the school setting are not recommended for diagnosis of hypertension in children.

referral_criteria: severe hypertension requires urgent consultation and management
fact_text: Severe hypertension in children requires urgent consultation and management; hypertension with encephalopathy is a medical emergency.
Blood pressure measurement in children follows the same principles as adults but requires special attention to appropriate cuff size related to the child's right upper arm.
Hypertension stages in children and adolescents are defined by percentile-based thresholds for children 1-12 years and fixed mmHg thresholds for adolescents ≥13 years.
Hypertensive emergency in children and adolescents is defined by severe BP elevation with encephalopathy symptoms and possible target organ damage.
Hypertensive urgency in children and adolescents is defined as BP >95th percentile + 30 mmHg (children) or >180/120 mmHg (adolescents) without target organ damage symptoms.
Hypertension in children and adolescents is defined by percentile-based BP thresholds for ages 1-12 and fixed mmHg thresholds for adolescents ≥13 years.
Signs and symptoms that should alert physicians to possible hypertension in neonates include failure to thrive, seizure, irritability or lethargy, respiratory distress, and congestive heart failure.

Important history clues for pediatric hypertension include prematurity, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, umbilical artery catheterization, head/abdominal trauma, family history of heritable diseases (e.g., neurofibromatosis), medications (pressure substances, steroids, tricyclic antidepressants), episodes of pyelonephritis, dietary history (caffeine, high salt), sleep/snoring history, smoking, and irregular eating habits.

Risk factors for hypertension in children/adolescents include overweight/obesity, male sex, family history, low birth weight/intrauterine growth restriction, prematurity, neonatal umbilical procedures, excess dietary salt, physical inactivity, and chronic health conditions like CKD and diabetes.

Examination for hypertension in children should include checking for signs of end organ damage such as hypertensive retinopathy on fundoscopy, apical heave, hepatomegaly, oedema, palpable kidneys, and focal neurological signs like facial nerve palsies.
In older children, signs suggesting secondary hypertension include headache, shortness of breath, chest pain, vomiting, fatigue, blurred vision, epistaxis, and bell's palsy.

Signs suggesting secondary hypertension causes in children include Cushingoid appearance, proptosis, goitre, webbed neck (Turner syndrome), elfin facies (William syndrome), skin changes (cafe-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, acanthosis nigricans, hirsutism, striae, acne, rash), cardiovascular murmurs or radiation, reduced femoral pulses, oedema, hepatomegaly, abdominal masses, palpable kidneys, flank bruits, and ambiguous or virilized genitalia (e.g., CAH).

recommended_tests: CMP (LFT, glucose, HbA1c, calcium, fasting lipids)
fact_text: Consider comprehensive metabolic panel including LFT, glucose, HbA1c, calcium, and fasting lipids in children with BMI above 95th centile.
First-line investigations in hypertensive children include CBC with peripheral blood film, urea/electrolytes/creatinine, urinalysis, and renal ultrasound if indicated.

Management of pediatric hypertension should start with history, physical examination, and appropriate investigations.

Hypertension types: Essential hypertension (no identifiable cause, ~90% cases) and Secondary hypertension (due to identifiable causes like kidney disease or endocrine disorders).
Hypertension is defined as systolic BP ≥140 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥90 mmHg; normal BP is systolic <120 mmHg and diastolic <80 mmHg; prehypertension is systolic 120-139 mmHg or diastolic 80-89 mmHg.
Hypertension diagnosis requires repeated BP measurements on different occasions; one high reading is insufficient for diagnosis.
Blood pressure should be measured multiple times at different occasions to confirm hypertension diagnosis; single high reading is insufficient.
BP measurement should avoid talking by patient during measurement; patient should not have consumed tea, coffee, or smoked before measurement; patient should rest 5-10 minutes before measurement.

Blood pressure should be measured using a sphygmomanometer (digital, aneroid, mercury types allowed) with correct technique and proper cuff size; patient should be seated comfortably with back supported, arm at heart level, legs uncrossed, and after 5-10 minutes rest before measurement.
Cuff should be applied on bare arm, at heart level, with cuff bladder covering two-thirds of upper arm; patient should be seated with feet flat on floor and back supported.
If patient has postural hypertension or is elderly or diabetic, BP should be measured in both sitting and standing positions.
Two BP measurements should be taken 2 minutes apart; if difference is large, additional measurements are needed; average of readings should be used for diagnosis.

Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are effective and safe antihypertensive agents including losartan, valsartan, and telmisartan.
Calcium channel blockers reduce blood pressure via vascular dilation and are commonly used in hypertension, including heart failure patients.
Diuretics reduce blood pressure by promoting renal sodium and water excretion; examples include frusemide, thiazide, spironolactone, and indapamide.
First-line antihypertensive drug classes include calcium channel blockers, ARBs, ACE inhibitors, diuretics, and beta blockers.

contraindications_or_cautions: In patients with severe hypertension, abrupt withdrawal of antihypertensive drugs is not recommended due to risk of rebound hypertension and complications.
fact_text: Abrupt stopping of antihypertensive drugs in severe hypertension patients is unsafe and can cause rebound hypertension; gradual withdrawal under supervision is advised.

contraindications_or_cautions: In government-supplied antihypertensive drugs, there is a risk of shortage or interruption; patients should be advised to continue medication and seek replacement promptly if supply is interrupted.
fact_text: Patients receiving government-supplied antihypertensive drugs may face supply interruptions; they should be advised to continue medication and obtain replacement promptly to avoid treatment gaps.

contraindications_or_cautions: Antihypertensive drug use in severe hypertension requires careful monitoring due to risk of side effects and rebound hypertension if stopped abruptly.
fact_text: Severe hypertension patients require careful antihypertensive drug use and monitoring to avoid side effects and rebound hypertension from abrupt drug withdrawal.
Masked hypertension is defined as normal clinic BP but elevated ambulatory BP on 24-hour ABPM.
White coat hypertension is defined as elevated clinic BP but normal ambulatory BP on 24-hour ABPM.

recommended_tests: 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring using portable device

fact_text: BP should be measured in the right arm in children for consistency and to avoid falsely low readings from the left arm in coarctation of the aorta; arm should be at heart level, supported, uncovered, and patient and observer should not speak during measurement.

For auscultatory BP in children, place stethoscope bell over brachial artery in antecubital fossa; cuff lower end 2-3 cm above fossa; inflate cuff 20-30 mmHg above disappearance of radial pulse; deflate at 2-3 mmHg per second; first and last Korotkoff sounds are SBP and DBP respectively; if sounds disappear at 0 mmHg, use phase IV as DBP or repeat measurement with less pressure.
In children, BP measurement requires seating the child quietly for 3-5 minutes with back supported and feet uncrossed on floor.

To measure BP in legs of children, patient should be prone if possible; use appropriately sized cuff mid-thigh; place stethoscope over popliteal artery; leg SBP is usually 10%-20% higher than brachial artery pressure.
Use correct cuff size in children: bladder length 80%-100% of arm circumference, width at least 40%.

About 50% of hypertensive adults in Bangladesh are unaware of their condition; 35% are under treatment, and only 14% have controlled blood pressure.
Adherence to hypertension treatment in Bangladesh is low due to lack of understanding about need for continued treatment after BP lowers and cost of medication.

Hypertension significantly increases risk of heart, brain, kidney diseases and is leading global cause of death; prevalence in Bangladesh adults 18-69 years is 23.5%, higher in elderly (>60 years) at 49%.

Hypertension treatment in Bangladesh is mainly provided by general practitioners and specialists; screening and referral also done by medical assistants and community health workers at union level clinics.
Updated, country-specific hypertension guidelines are needed for effective management by physicians and healthcare providers at various health system levels in Bangladesh.

Office BP classification for adults: Normal <130/<85 mmHg; High-normal 130-139/85-89 mmHg; Grade 1 hypertension 140-159/90-99 mmHg; Grade 2 hypertension ≥160/≥100 mmHg; Isolated systolic hypertension SBP ≥140 and DBP <90 mmHg.
Hypertension is diagnosed in adults (≥18 years) not on antihypertensive medication and not acutely ill when office SBP ≥140 mm Hg and/or DBP ≥90 mm Hg after repeated measurement.
Hypertension is defined by office BP ≥140/90 mmHg, or ABPM 24-h average ≥130/80, or ABPM daytime ≥135/85, or ABPM night-time ≥120/70, or HBPM ≥135/85 mmHg.
Hypotension is defined as blood pressure less than 90/60 mmHg and is considered benign if no symptoms of oxygen lack are present.
Low blood pressure is considered dangerous if it causes symptoms such as confusion, dizziness, nausea, syncope, fatigue, neck/back pain, headache, blurred vision, or palpitations.

fact_text: Measure BP in both arms at first visit; use higher arm value as reference. If first reading <130/85 mmHg, no further measurement needed. If ≥130/85 mmHg, take two more readings in higher arm 1 min apart and average last two for diagnosis.

fact_text: Hypertension diagnosis requires BP ≥140/90 mmHg on 2-3 separate office visits; record higher BP and arm site for follow-up; communicate readings verbally and in writing with position noted.

For auscultatory BP measurement with aneroid or mercury device, palpate SBP first, place cuff at arm level, stethoscope over brachial artery, inflate cuff 20-30 mmHg above radial pulse disappearance, deflate slowly 2 mmHg/sec, record systolic and diastolic BP at 1st and 5th Korotkoff sounds.
Before BP measurement, the patient should rest physically for at least half an hour and avoid tea, coffee, and smoking; also rest quietly for 5 minutes before measurement.

During BP measurement, the patient should rest and avoid activity; sit with back supported; ensure correct cuff position on the arm; keep arm supported at heart level; avoid crossing legs or feet; remove tight clothing; keep feet flat on floor; and avoid talking or moving.
Ankle BP measurement should be done after 5 minutes rest, and ankle BP is preferred over calf or thigh measurements due to less discomfort and better cuff fit, especially in obese patients.

Ankle blood pressure is measured supine with cuff around ankle/lower calf encircling ≥80% of ankle circumference; readings by oscillometry or Doppler of dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial arteries; ankle BP ≥155/90 mmHg defines hypertension in patients without vascular disease.
Leg blood pressure measurement requires a large cuff (45-52 cm) placed mid-thigh with patient prone and stethoscope at popliteal fossa; leg BP is normally up to 20 mmHg higher than arm BP.
Diagnosis of hypertension requires multiple BP measurements on separate visits, minimum three readings per visit and two to three visits at 1-4 week intervals.
Diagnosis should be confirmed by out-of-office BP measurement if possible and available (HBPM and/or ABPM).
For initial BP 140-159/90-99 mmHg, diagnosis requires repeat measurements on three separate occasions within 1-4 weeks.
Hypertension diagnosis can be made on a single visit if BP ≥160/100 mmHg or if hypertension mediated organ damage is present.
If hypertension is not diagnosed, measure clinic BP at least every 3 years; measure more frequently if BP is close to 140/90 mmHg.
BP measurement should be performed in both arms initially; if difference >10 mmHg, repeat after 1-2 minutes; if difference remains >10 mmHg, use arm with higher reading for subsequent measurements.
If inter-arm BP difference is >20 mmHg, consider further investigation for secondary causes.

For office BP <130/85 mmHg, remeasure within 3 years (1 year if other risk factors). For 130-159/85-99 mmHg, confirm with repeated office visits and if possible out-of-office BP. For >160/100 mmHg, confirm within a few days or weeks.

referral_criteria: Review medication if systolic BP falls by ≥20 mmHg on standing

fact_text: In treated hypertensives with symptoms of postural hypotension or at first visit in elderly/diabetes, measure standing BP after supine/seated; if systolic BP falls ≥20 mmHg on standing, review medication and measure subsequent BP standing.

referral_criteria: Refer to specialist if symptoms of postural hypotension persist despite medication review
fact_text: Postural hypotension is diagnosed by lying BP after 5 minutes rest, then standing BP and pulse at 1 and 3 minutes; a drop in SBP ≥20 mmHg or DBP ≥10 mmHg or symptoms indicates abnormality.
Diagnosis and grading of hypertension require initial clinical evaluation including history, physical exam, and simple labs; confirmation of diagnosis is needed before final diagnosis.
Identify evidence of hypertension-mediated organ damage (HMOD) or existing cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, or renal disease during initial evaluation.

fact_text: While waiting for hypertension diagnosis confirmation, carry out routine simple laboratory investigations to assess for HMOD.
Screen for potential secondary causes of hypertension during initial clinical evaluation.

History of symptoms suggestive of hypertension-mediated organ damage (HMOD) should include brain/eye symptoms (headache, vertigo, syncope, impaired vision, TIA, stroke, cognitive impairment, dementia), heart symptoms (chest pain, SOB, oedema, MI, arrhythmias especially AF, heart failure), kidney symptoms (thirst, polyuria, nocturia, haematuria, UTI), and peripheral artery symptoms (cold extremities, claudication, pain, family history of CKD).
Physical examination should include fundoscopic examination for hypertensive retinopathy and neurological examination with cognitive status assessment.
Physical examination should include palpation and auscultation of heart and carotid arteries, palpation of peripheral arteries, and skin inspection for cafe-au-lait patches (phaeochromocytoma).
Physical examination should include weight and height measurement with BMI calculation, waist circumference, and kidney palpation for renal enlargement in polycystic kidney disease.
Physical examination should include comparison of blood pressure in both arms at least once.
History of antihypertensive drug treatment should include current/past medications, effectiveness, intolerance, side effects, and adherence including reasons for non-compliance.
History should include sleep history (snoring, sleep apnoea), previous hypertension in pregnancy/pre-eclampsia, and oral contraceptive use as clues for secondary hypertension.

Major cardiovascular risk factors include elevated SBP and DBP, tobacco use, dyslipidemia (total cholesterol >5.1 mmol/L, LDL >3 mmol/L, HDL <1 mmol/L men or <1.2 mmol/L women), diabetes mellitus, age >55 years men or >65 years women, family history of premature CVD (men <55 years, women <65 years), and central obesity (waist circumference >90 cm men, >80 cm women).
Auscultation of heart and renal arteries for murmurs or bruits can indicate aortic coarctation or renal artery stenosis as secondary hypertension clues.
Comparison of radial with femoral pulse to detect radio-femoral delay is useful to identify aortic coarctation.
Signs of Cushing’s disease or acromegaly should be assessed as possible secondary hypertension causes.
Signs of thyroid disease should be checked as part of secondary hypertension assessment.
Cerebrovascular HMOD manifestations include transient ischemic attack, stroke, carotid bruits, and motor or sensory defects.

Hypertension mediated organ damage (HMOD) cardiac signs include left ventricular hypertrophy, coronary heart disease, heart failure with forcible displaced apex beat, accentuated aortic second heart sound, abnormal rhythms, S4, ventricular gallop, and pulmonary rales/crackles.
Peripheral vascular HMOD signs include absence of one or more major pulses in extremities (except dorsalis pedis) with or without intermittent claudication.
Renal HMOD signs include GFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m², proteinuria (1+ or greater), microalbuminuria (2 out of 3 positive tests over 4-6 months), and dependent leg edema.
Retinopathy HMOD signs include fundoscopic abnormalities such as haemorrhages or exudates, with or without papilloedema.
