For patients with SBP 130–139 mmHg, cardiovascular risk assessment is important to guide decisions about initiating pharmacological treatment.
If cardiovascular risk assessment may delay treatment initiation or follow-up, treatment should not be postponed but included in follow-up strategy.
Patients with clinic SBP ≥140 mmHg or DBP ≥90 mmHg are at high risk and should start pharmacological treatment without requiring prior cardiovascular risk assessment.

recommended_advice: achieve and maintain ideal body weight with BMI 18.5-24.9 kg/m2 (Asians 18.5-23.5 kg/m2)

recommended_advice: limit total salt intake to less than 5 grams per day
fact_text: Hypertensive patients should limit total salt intake to less than 5 grams per day, with gradual reduction of added salt and use of alternative seasonings to aid taste adaptation.

recommended_advice: Adults should do at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity or at least 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity weekly, or an equivalent combination.

fact_text: Adults should perform 150–300 minutes moderate or 75–150 minutes vigorous aerobic activity weekly plus muscle-strengthening activities on 2 or more days weekly for hypertension management.

recommended_advice: Avoid tobacco use including smoking and smokeless tobacco to reduce cardiovascular risk and acute BP increases.
fact_text: Avoid tobacco use in hypertension management; counsel smokers and smokeless tobacco users; nicotine replacement therapy may be used under medical supervision.

fact_text: For hypertensive emergencies, recommended IV agents include labetalol, esmolol, nicardipine, clevidipine, nitroglycerin, sodium nitroprusside, fenoldopam, hydralazine, and enalaprilat with specified dosing and adverse effects.
BP reduction in hypertensive emergencies must be controlled to prevent organ hypoperfusion and ischemia or infarction.
In hypertensive emergencies, the primary goal is to lower mean arterial pressure by no more than 25% within the first hour, then reduce BP to 160/110-100 mmHg within 2 to 6 hours.
In patients with aortic dissection, blood pressure must be aggressively lowered during hypertensive emergency management.
Common secondary hypertension causes in adults include renal parenchymal disease, renovascular hypertension, primary aldosteronism, chronic sleep apnea, and substance/drug induced causes.
Secondary hypertension is hypertension caused by an identifiable underlying cause, affecting 5-10% of hypertensive patients.

Additional investigations for secondary hypertension are appropriate in patients with: early onset hypertension under 30 years without risk factors, hypertension urgency/emergency, resistant hypertension, abnormal renal function/proteinuria/hematuria, hypokalemia without diuretics, sudden BP increase after control, or sudden hypertension onset.

Renal parenchymal disease secondary hypertension clues include personal/familial CKD history, proteinuria, hematuria, leukocyturia, decreased eGFR, and kidney ultrasound.

Resistant hypertension is defined as uncontrolled BP despite treatment with three or more antihypertensive drugs at optimal or maximally tolerated doses including a diuretic, after excluding pseudo-resistance and secondary causes.

Causes of pseudo-resistant hypertension include improper BP measurement, heavily calcified arteries (especially in elderly), white-coat effect, medication side effects, poor doctor-patient relationship, inadequate patient education, and memory or psychiatric problems.

fact_text: Factors contributing to resistant hypertension include lifestyle factors (inadequate physical activity, excess alcohol intake, excess dietary salt, cocaine and amphetamines misuse), drug-related causes (NSAIDs, contraceptive hormones, adrenal steroids, sympathomimetics, erythropoietin, cyclosporin, tacrolimus, liquorice, herbal supplements), and volume overload (progressive renal insufficiency, high salt intake).

Typical characteristics of patients with resistant hypertension include old age (>75 years), high baseline BP and chronic uncontrolled hypertension, target organ damage, diabetes, obesity, atherosclerotic vascular disease, aortic stiffening, female sex, and excessive dietary salt intake.

Secondary causes of resistant hypertension include primary hyperaldosteronism, renal artery stenosis, renal parenchymal disease, obstructive sleep apnoea, phaeochromocytoma (episodic palpitations, headaches, sweating), thyroid diseases, Cushing's syndrome, coarctation of the aorta, and intracranial tumors.

recommended_advice: All non-pharmacological interventions for hypertension management should be implemented vigorously in resistant hypertension.
fact_text: All non-pharmacological interventions for hypertension management should be implemented vigorously in resistant hypertension.

Device therapy options for resistant hypertension include percutaneous transluminal radiofrequency sympathetic denervation of renal arteries and carotid baroreflex activation to improve blood pressure control without further medication.

fact_text: For resistant hypertension, low dose Spironolactone (25 mg once daily, increasing to 50 mg once daily) is the preferred fourth agent if blood potassium is <4.5 mmol/L; Amiloride or Eplerenone can substitute if Spironolactone causes gynecomastia; centrally acting agents (Methyldopa, Clonidine) or direct vasodilators (Hydralazine, Minoxidil) are options; high-dose beta-blockers (Metoprolol, Bisoprolol, Nebivolol) and loop diuretics (Furosemide) may be needed to counteract side effects; combined alpha- and beta-blockers (Labetalol, Carvedilol) may improve control.

In elderly treated for hypertension, BP target should be <140/80 mmHg but SBP should not be lowered below 130 mmHg.
Isolated systolic hypertension (SBP ≥140 mmHg and DBP <90 mmHg) is more common in elderly.
Hypertension definition in elderly is the same as in general adults.
Co-morbidities are common in elderly hypertensive patients.
In elderly, blood pressure may be falsely elevated due to arterial stiffness (pseudo-hypertension).
Postural hypotension and hypertension are more commonly seen in elderly.
White-coat hypertension is more common in elderly.

fact_text: Elderly patients have higher risk of adverse drug effects and drug interactions with antihypertensive medications.

In elderly patients with milder hypertension, lifestyle modification alone may suffice, including weight reduction, increased physical activity, no added salt, increased potassium intake, stress avoidance, and smoking cessation.
Ambulatory BP monitoring is indicated when hypertension diagnosis or response to therapy is unclear from office visits, or when syncope, hypotensive disorders, vertigo, or dizziness are suspected.
Home BP measurements may be important in elderly patients to avoid hazards of excessive BP reduction.

In elderly patients, BP should be measured in both seated/supine and standing positions to detect postural hypotension; standing BP guides treatment if significant postural drop (>20 mmHg) is present.

General BP target in uncomplicated hypertension is <140/90 mmHg; in older patients (>65 years) target SBP 130-140 and DBP <80 mmHg if tolerated; patients with diabetes, CKD, CAD, or heart failure should have BP <130/80 mmHg.

fact_text: On day of surgery, SBP ≥170 or DBP ≥100 mm Hg likely causes perioperative BP fluctuations needing management.

recommended_medicines: Patients on chronic beta-blocker therapy should continue beta-blockers on day of surgery.
fact_text: Patients on chronic beta-blockers should continue them on day of surgery.

fact_text: In emergent surgery with poorly controlled BP, review recent ECG and echocardiogram or obtain STAT ECG and echocardiogram if unavailable.

Intraoperative BP targets for patients with hypertension or cardiovascular disease are approximately SBP 130 mm Hg, MAP 60-65 mm Hg, and DBP 70-90 mm Hg.
Young healthy patients with baseline BP around 110/65 mmHg can tolerate lower intraoperative BP than patients with hypertension or cardiovascular disease.

contraindications_or_cautions: prolonged intraoperative hypotension increases morbidity and mortality risk even in healthy patients
fact_text: Prolonged intraoperative hypotension may increase morbidity and mortality even in healthy patients and should be avoided.
For intracranial, intrathoracic, or major abdominal surgery, arterial line insertion for beat-to-beat BP monitoring is advisable to manage significant BP fluctuations.
Beat-to-beat arterial line monitoring is recommended for rapid dose adjustment of intravenous agents during severe intraoperative hypertension.

referral_criteria: hospitalization for 24 to 48 hours postoperatively if significant perioperative BP fluctuations occur to start antihypertensive treatment before discharge
fact_text: Significant perioperative BP fluctuations may require hospitalization for 24-48 hours postoperatively to initiate antihypertensive therapy before discharge.
Severe intraoperative hypertension under anesthesia can be treated with intravenous sodium nitroprusside, nicardipine, nitroglycerin, and hydralazine for longer-term control.
Postoperative hypertension is defined as systolic BP >160 mm Hg or diastolic BP >90 mm Hg within 30 to 90 minutes after surgery.
If invasive BP monitoring is unavailable in critically ill patients, non-invasive BP should be repeated every 1 to 2 minutes.
In critically ill patients with severe hypertension, hypotension, or rapid BP changes, invasive arterial catheter BP measurement should be initiated ASAP; radial artery is most common site.
In surgery in sitting position, non-invasive BP at brachial artery underestimates brain perfusion; cuff BP goals should be higher; arterial line transducer should be zeroed at ear level.

Pregnancy induced hypertension (PIH) affects about 10.1% of pregnant women in Bangladesh with gestational age >20 weeks; preeclampsia and eclampsia are common obstetric complications.

Careful monitoring of patient response and adjustment of treatment is essential for safe and effective perioperative hypertension management; after surgery, transition to effective oral antihypertensive regimen is recommended.

Perioperative hypertension treatment goal should be based on patient's preoperative BP; a conservative target is about 10% above baseline, but more aggressive lowering may be needed for very high risk patients such as those with severe heart failure or bleeding risk.

dose_or_duration: Sodium nitroprusside is standard but requires invasive monitoring; newer agents like labetalol, nicardipine, nitroglycerin are preferable in routine practice.
fact_text: Sodium nitroprusside is standard for rapid BP control but requires invasive monitoring; labetalol, nicardipine, nitroglycerin, hydralazine, esmolol, fenoldopam, ACE inhibitors, and clonidine are useful alternatives for perioperative hypertension management.
Mild pre-eclampsia is defined as SBP 140 to <160 mmHg and DBP 90 to <110 mmHg after 20 weeks gestation without significant proteinuria or organ dysfunction.

Severe pre-eclampsia is SBP ≥160 mmHg and/or DBP ≥110 mmHg after 20 weeks gestation with significant proteinuria or new-onset hypertension plus thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, or impaired liver function.

Pregnancy induced hypertension is defined as SBP ≥140 mmHg and/or DBP ≥90 mmHg in a previously normotensive pregnant woman after 20 weeks gestation without proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction, confirmed by BP readings on at least two occasions 4 hours apart.

Pre-eclampsia is new-onset hypertension (SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90 mmHg on two occasions ≥4 hours apart after 20 weeks gestation) plus new-onset proteinuria (≥300 mg/24h urine, protein/creatinine ratio ≥0.3, or dipstick 1+ if quantitative unavailable).
Chronic hypertension in pregnancy is defined as elevated BP ≥140/90 mmHg diagnosed before pregnancy or before 20 weeks gestation and persisting after delivery.

Chronic hypertension with superimposed preeclampsia is diagnosed by new proteinuria after 20 weeks or proteinuria before 20 weeks plus clinical/lab signs including worsening hypertension, liver enzyme rise, thrombocytopenia, symptoms, pulmonary edema, renal insufficiency, or increased protein excretion.
Eclampsia diagnosis requires new onset hypertension after 20 weeks gestation with significant proteinuria or altered sensorium/loss of consciousness plus severe preeclampsia signs and convulsions.
Preeclampsia diagnosis is clinical based on symptoms (headache, nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, swelling, convulsions) and signs (oedema, high BP, proteinuria, retinal changes).

referral_criteria: Pulmonary edema
Cerebral or visual symptoms: headache (increasing frequency, not relieved by analgesics), blurred vision
Oliguria (<400 mL urine in 24 hours)
Upper abdominal pain (epigastric or right upper quadrant pain)

recommended_advice: Delay first pregnancy until age 20 or older
Avoid pregnancy if age 35 or older unless absolutely necessary
Maintain birth spacing of 2-5 years
Control weight gain during pregnancy, especially if overweight at conception (5-7 kg recommended)

Use low dose aspirin during pregnancy
fact_text: Primary prevention of hypertension in pregnancy includes delaying first pregnancy until age 20+, avoiding pregnancy after 35 unless necessary, birth spacing 2-5 years, controlling weight gain, calcium supplementation after 12 weeks, and low dose aspirin use.

serum creatinine (>1.1 mg/dl or doubling indicates renal insufficiency)

Women at risk of preeclampsia are defined by presence of one or more high risk factors (e.g. history of preeclampsia, multifetal gestation, renal disease, autoimmune disease, diabetes, chronic hypertension) or multiple moderate risk factors (e.g. first pregnancy, maternal age ≥35, BMI >30, family history).
Secondary prevention includes measuring blood pressure and urine albumin at all opportunities in 8 ANC visits, including self-measurement.

In diabetes, target BP is generally <130/80 mmHg; lower to <125/75 mmHg if proteinuria >1 g/24 hours is present.

fact_text: In diabetes, caution with beta-blockers and diuretics due to risks of decreased insulin responsiveness, masking hypoglycaemia, worsening peripheral vascular disease, and dyslipidaemia.
Pharmacological treatment in diabetes should start if BP is persistently >130/80 mmHg; ACEI or ARB preferred especially if microalbuminuria or overt proteinuria present.

contraindications_or_cautions: Peripheral alpha blockers may worsen orthostatic hypotension, especially in autonomic neuropathy

In hypertensive nephrosclerosis, ACEi or ARB are first choice if kidney function is normal or near normal; B-blockers if cardiovascular or coronary artery disease present; other drugs include CCB and vasodilators.

fact_text: The IMCI strategy includes both preventive and curative interventions aiming to improve health care practices in health facilities, the health system infrastructure and delivery, and at home.

fact_text: Severe Malaria clinical features include bleeding tendency or abnormal spontaneous bleeding, severe anaemia, oliguria or acute renal failure (<17 ml/hr or <400 ml/24 hrs). Laboratory features include hypoglycemia (<2.2 mmol/L or <40 mg/dl), severe normocytic anaemia (Hb <5 g/dl, PCV <15%), fluid and electrolyte disturbance (hyponatremia), haemoglobinuria, metabolic acidosis (plasma bicarbonate <15 mmol/l), hyperlactataemia (>5 mmol/l), and renal impairment (serum creatinine >265 micromol/l or >3 mg/dl).

fact_text: Uncomplicated falciparum malaria is treated with Artemether + Lumefantrine combination (ACT) given as 6 oral doses over 3 days, starting immediately after diagnosis. Dose timing: 1st dose at 0 hour, 2nd dose at 8 hours, then doses at 24, 36, 48, and 60 hours. Dose varies by weight band: 5-<15 kg (1 tablet per dose), 15-<25 kg (2 tablets), 25-<35 kg (3 tablets), >35 kg (4 tablets). Encourage taking with fatty meal or milk for better absorption.

fact_text: If Artemether + Lumefantrin (ACT) cannot be given for uncomplicated malaria, alternative treatment is Quinine plus either Tetracycline, Doxycycline, or Clindamycin for 7 days, or other WHO recommended ACTs if available. Quinine dose is 10 mg/kg body weight orally every 8 hours for 7 days with dose adjusted by weight bands. Tetracycline 250 mg every 6 hours, Doxycycline 100 mg once daily, Clindamycin 10 mg/kg twice daily, all for 7 days. Tetracycline and Doxycycline are contraindicated in children under 8 years and in pregnant or lactating women.

After initial parenteral treatment for severe malaria, once the patient can tolerate oral therapy, it is essential to continue and complete treatment with a full course of an effective oral antimalarial.

Parenteral treatment options for severe malaria include: (a) IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg stat dose followed by 2.4 mg/kg daily until oral medication tolerated; (b) IM artemether 3.2 mg/kg stat followed by 1.6 mg/kg daily until oral medication tolerated; (c) Quinine dihydrochloride 20 mg salt/kg stat followed by 10 mg/kg every 8 hours by slow IV infusion (max 5 mg/kg/hour); (d) IM quinine injection to anterior thigh diluted to 60 mg/ml, with first 20 mg/kg dose split as 10 mg/kg per thigh.
Hospital treatment for severe malaria prefers intravenous artesunate when available; if not available, intravenous quinine drip is an alternative parenteral antimalarial.

Intramuscular artemether and intramuscular quinine can be used as alternatives to intravenous artesunate or quinine; IM artemether is effective but not superior to IV artesunate due to erratic absorption.
Intramuscular quinine can be given as an alternative pre-referral treatment for severe malaria, with a loading dose recommended.

Pre-referral treatment for severe malaria includes intramuscular quinine dihydrochloride at 20 mg salt/kg stat dose given with half dose in each thigh, or rectal artesunate capsules at 10 mg/kg (containing 100 mg or 400 mg sodium artesunate) when available.
Primaquine should not be given to pregnant women or children under 4 years old.
Tetracycline and doxycycline are contraindicated in children under 8 years old.
Where available, clindamycin may be substituted for doxycycline in children and pregnant women as doxycycline cannot be given to these groups.

A single oral dose of primaquine 0.75 mg base/kg body weight (max 45 mg base for adults) is added at end of treatment with ACT or Q7+ T7/D7/Clin7 to eliminate gametocytes and reduce malaria transmission.
Chloroquine dose schedule for vivax malaria: Day 1: 10 mg/kg (4 tabs adult), Day 2: 10 mg/kg (4 tabs adult), Day 3: 5 mg/kg (2 tabs adult).
Primaquine dose for adults with vivax malaria: 1 tablet daily (1 tab = 15 mg) for 14 days.
Primaquine dose for children with vivax malaria: 0.3 mg/kg daily for 14 days.
For vivax malaria (VM) confirmed by BSE and/or RDT positive for P. vivax, treatment includes chloroquine and primaquine.

condition: child aged 12 months up to 2 years
condition_aliases: child aged 12 months up to 2 years
fact_text: For children aged 12 months up to 2 years, breastfeed as often and as the child wants, day and night. Give family foods at least 3 times per day including rice, lentils, vegetables, fruits (e.g., papaya, jackfruit), and egg yolk. Give 3 meals daily plus 1-2 nutritious snacks. Encourage the child to feed self with hand or spoon. Continue breastfeeding during illness and after recovery.

condition: child aged after 6 months up to 12 months
condition_aliases: child aged after 6 months up to 12 months
fact_text: For children aged after 6 months up to 12 months, breastfeed as often and as the child wants, day and night. Give soft, mashed or semi-solid foods such as rice, lentils, vegetables, fruits (e.g., papaya, jackfruit), and egg yolk. Give 2-3 meals daily plus 1-2 nutritious snacks. Give 120 ml to 250 ml of milk daily. Encourage the child to feed self with hand or spoon. Help the child to drink from a cup. Continue breastfeeding during illness and after recovery.

For children under 6 months, breastfeed as often and as long as the child wants, day and night. Do not give other foods or fluids. Encourage the mother to continue breastfeeding even if the child is sick. Help the mother to recognize feeding cues and to respond to the child's feeding needs.

For a child with persistent diarrhoea, if still breastfeeding, give more frequent and longer breastfeeds day and night. If taking other milk, replace it with breastfeeding or milk with increased nutrient content (e.g., semisolid food). For other foods, follow feeding recommendations for the child's age.

fact_text: At home, caregivers should be taught how to give oral drugs and treat local infections, and counseled about food, fluids, when to return, and their own health.

recommended_advice: At referral health facility, on hospital arrival, rapid screening of sick children for emergency signs should be done according to Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment (ETAT).

Follow-up care should be provided.
fact_text: At referral health facility, rapid emergency screening (ETAT) is required on arrival; diagnosis by clinical evaluation and investigations after admission; appropriate treatment and monitoring; and follow-up care.
IMCI case management is based on two age categories: young infants 0 day up to 2 months, and children aged 2 months up to 5 years.

fact_text: At outpatient health facility, the provider must assess, classify, identify treatment, provide referral or caregiver counseling based on classification, and arrange follow-up care.

Advise the mother to increase the child's fluid intake during illness by breastfeeding more frequently and for longer at each feed; if the child is not breastfeeding, increase the amount of milk given. Also give rice water, chira pani, dub water, yogurt drink, or clean water to increase fluid intake.
Advise the mother to return immediately if the child is not able to drink or breastfeed, becomes sicker, develops fever, fast breathing, difficult breathing, blood in stool, or is drinking poorly.
For a child with diarrhoea, give fluid according to Plan A or Plan B on the TREAT THE CHILD chart; giving extra fluid can be lifesaving.
If the child has diarrhoea, advise the mother to also return immediately if the child develops any immediate return signs.

condition: child with pneumonia, dysentery, malaria, fever, measles, persistent diarrhoea, ear infection, chronic ear problem, anaemia, or malnutrition
condition_aliases: child with pneumonia, dysentery, malaria, fever, measles, persistent diarrhoea, ear infection, chronic ear problem, anaemia, or malnutrition
fact_text: Advise the mother to return for follow-up at the earliest time listed for the child's problem: pneumonia, dysentery, malaria, fever, measles - return in 3 days; persistent diarrhoea, acute ear infection, chronic ear problem - return in 5 days; anaemia, severe acute malnutrition - return in 7 days; moderate acute malnutrition - return in 14 days; other conditions - return in 30 days.
If the child has no pneumonia, cough, or cold, advise the mother to return if the child develops any of the immediate return signs.

recommended_advice: If the child is not feeding well during illness, counsel the mother to: breastfeed more frequently and for longer if possible; use a cup if the child cannot breastfeed; encourage the child to eat as much as possible; and continue to feed the child as much as possible after illness.
If the child has a blocked nose that interferes with feeding, clear the nose to improve feeding.
If the child has poor appetite, plan small frequent meals, feed slowly, and check feeding regularly.
If the child has sore mouth or ulcers, give soft foods that will not burn the mouth such as eggs, mashed potatoes, banana, papaya, mango, etc.
Follow up any feeding problem within 5 days.
followup_monitoring: Follow up any feeding problem in 5 days.
fact_text: If a child is not feeding well during illness, counsel the mother to breastfeed more frequently and longer if possible, use a cup if needed, encourage eating as much as possible, clear blocked nose if present, plan small frequent meals if poor appetite, give soft non-irritating foods if sore mouth or ulcers, and follow up feeding problems within 5 days.

recommended_advice: If the mother reports difficulty with breastfeeding, assess the child’s age and breastfeeding status.

fact_text: For children with shock and severe malnutrition, initial management includes weighing the child, opening an IV line, giving 15 ml/kg IV fluid over 1 hour, broad spectrum antibiotics, and emergency lab tests. Assess vital signs and urine output. If improved, give another 15 ml/kg IV fluid over 1 hour, then oral/nasogastric rehydration with ReSoMal or ORS 10 ml/kg/hr for 10 hours and start feeding as tolerated. If not improved, suspect septic shock, maintain IV fluid at 4 ml/kg/hr, give blood transfusion 10 ml/kg over 3 hours, reassess. If still not improved, stop IV fluids, change antibiotics, and refer to ICU-capable center.

To prevent low blood sugar, if child can breastfeed, ask mother to breastfeed; if child cannot breastfeed but can swallow, give expressed breast milk or breast milk substitute; if neither available, give 30-50 ml sugar water or milk before departure; if child cannot swallow, give 50 ml milk or sugar solution by nasogastric tube.

For shock without severe malnutrition (hypovolemia), give rapid IV fluid boluses of 20 ml/kg normal saline or Ringer's lactate until pulse is palpable and blood pressure recordable; maximum 60-80 ml/kg fluid may be given within 1-2 hours; reassess after initial treatment and treat cause accordingly.

fact_text: Factors influencing growth and development include: 1) Genetic heredity; 2) Nutritional deficiency retards growth; 3) Health status of pregnant mothers positively impacts growth; 4) Hormones like thyroxin, GH, insulin influence growth; 5) Childhood diseases (genetic, chromosomal, chronic illnesses like TB, heart, kidney diseases) adversely affect growth; 6) Emotional trauma, unstable family, loss of parents, inadequate schooling negatively affect growth; 7) Intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) and maternal infections/diseases adversely affect fetus and newborn; 8) Poor socioeconomic conditions affect growth; 9) Physical surroundings (sunshine, living standard, psychological and social interactions) positively affect growth; 10) Smaller birth size usually predicts smaller size in subsequent years.

Growth refers to physical maturation with increase in size of body parts due to tissue hyperplasia, hypertrophy, and differentiation; development means attainment of functional maturity including skills, emotional and social adaptation. A complete child has optimum physical growth and mental development.
Holistic development of a child includes care of both body and mind, ensuring complete physical growth and mental development for overall well-being.

fact_text: Assess other problems beyond the main symptoms during outpatient management of children aged 2 months up to 5 years.

For children aged 2 months up to 5 years, the initial assessment must include greeting the mother/caregiver and asking about the child's problem, specifically about the four main symptoms: cough or difficult breathing, diarrhoea, fever, and ear problem.

When a main symptom (cough/difficult breathing, diarrhoea, fever, ear problem) is present, assess the child further for signs related to that symptom and classify the illness according to the presence or absence of these signs.
Ask if the child has cough or difficult breathing and for how many days; count breaths per minute; assess for fast breathing, chest indrawing/severe chest indrawing, stridor, and wheeze.

Ask if child has fever (history or feels hot, temperature ≥99.5°F/37.5°C), duration of fever, and if fever has been present every day for more than 7 days; ask about travel to high/low malaria risk areas in last 30 days; ask about measles in last 3 months; look and feel for stiff neck, runny nose, bacterial causes of fever, generalized rash, cough/runny nose/red eyes; if measles now or within last 3 months, look for mouth ulcers, eye pus drainage, and corneal clouding.

Look and feel for signs of acute malnutrition including oedema of both feet; determine weight-for-height/length (WFH/L) z score; measure MUAC in children 6 months or older; if WFH/L less than -3 z scores or MUAC less than 115 mm, check for medical complications including general danger signs, severe classification, pneumonia with chest indrawing; if no complications and child is 6 months or older, assess if child is able to finish offered food; if child is less than 6 months, assess breastfeeding and feeding problems.
Look for palmar pallor to assess anaemia; distinguish severe, some, or no pallor.

Ask duration of diarrhoea and presence of blood in stool; look at child's general condition (lethargic/unconscious, restless/irritable), sunken eyes; assess if child is able to drink or drinks poorly, eagerly, or is thirsty; pinch skin on abdomen to assess skin pinch recoil time (very slow >2 seconds or slow).
Ask if there is ear pain or discharge and duration; look for pus draining from ear and feel for tender swelling behind ear.
Ask if the child is able to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, or has had convulsions during this illness; look for lethargy/unconsciousness, convulsions now.

General danger signs may indicate serious diseases such as meningitis, encephalitis, septicaemia, dengue shock syndrome, severe pneumonia, or cerebral malaria; children with these signs are severely ill and need urgent care.
Greet mother/caregiver appropriately and ask her to sit with the child; ask what the child's problems are to open good communication and ensure the mother that the child will receive good care.

Check child's immunization status by verifying vaccines received at birth, 6 weeks, 10 weeks, 14 weeks, 18 weeks, 9 months, and 15 months including BCG, Penta (1-3), PCV (1-3), OPV (1-3), IPV, MR, Vitamin A, and antihelminthic; record vaccines needed today and date for next immunization visit.

Assessment of dehydration in children with diarrhoea includes clinical signs such as lethargy or unconsciousness, restlessness or irritability, inability to be consoled, and sunken eyes; sunken eyes may be less reliable in severely malnourished children but can still be used.
Diarrhoea in children may be classified as acute watery diarrhoea (including cholera), dysentery (blood in stool), or persistent diarrhoea (lasting 14 days or more).

Children with diarrhoea should be assessed for general danger signs, cough or difficult breathing, signs of dehydration, duration of diarrhoea, and presence of blood in stool to determine if dysentery is present.

In children aged 2 months up to 5 years, general danger signs include inability to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions during illness, lethargy or unconsciousness, and current convulsions.

Children aged 2 months up to 5 years with weight-for-height/length Z score -2 or more are classified as having No acute malnutrition.
Children aged 2 months up to 5 years with weight-for-height/length Z score between -3 and -2 are classified as Moderate acute malnutrition (MAM).
Children aged 2 months up to 5 years with weight-for-height/length Z score less than -3 are classified as Severe acute malnutrition (SAM), indicating increased risk of infection and death.

Proper feeding is the most important treatment for persistent diarrhoea; goals include providing sufficient energy, protein, vitamins, and minerals to repair mucosa and improve nutrition, avoiding foods/drinks that aggravate diarrhoea, and reducing animal milk or lactose in diet for non-breastfed children.

Routine antimicrobial treatment is not essential for persistent diarrhoea; antimicrobials should only be used if specific non-intestinal or intestinal infections are diagnosed and treated correctly.
Infant and childhood mortality are sensitive indicators of inequity and poverty; poverty and ill health form a vicious cycle, and quality of care is an important indicator of child health inequities.

Mortality rates defined as: Neonatal mortality = probability of dying within 28 days per 1000 live births; Infant mortality = probability of dying before first birthday per 1000 live births; Under-five mortality = probability of dying between birth and fifth birthday per 1000 live births.
Mortality reductions are linked to improved coverage of vaccines, vitamin A supplementation, oral rehydration therapy for diarrhoea, and antibiotics for pneumonia.
Bangladesh achieved the MDG4 target for under-five mortality (48 per 1000 live births) ahead of the 2015 deadline but has not yet achieved the target for newborn and infant mortality.

Under-five mortality in Bangladesh decreased from 133 to 46 deaths per 1000 live births between 1993 and 2014, with neonatal mortality decreasing from 52 to 28 deaths per 1000 live births and infant mortality from 87 to 38 deaths per 1000 live births.

More than 60% of under-five deaths occur in the neonatal period; main causes of death under 5 years include acute respiratory infections (mostly pneumonia), diarrhoea, measles, malaria, and malnutrition, often in combination.

No palmar pallor indicates no anaemia. If child is less than 2 years old, assess feeding and counsel mother according to feeding recommendations. If feeding problem is present, schedule follow-up in 5 days.

Always start treatment with a first-line oral drug that is less expensive, more available, and easier to administer. Use a second-line drug only if the first-line drug is unavailable or ineffective.
Advise the caregiver that the full course of oral drugs (tablets or syrups) must be completed even if the child appears better, because bacteria may still be present after symptoms resolve.

Explain carefully to the caregiver how to give the drug, including dose amount, frequency (e.g., early morning, lunch, dinner, before bed), and duration of treatment in days. Label and package the drug accordingly.

If a child vomits after taking oral medication, still give the drug. Observe the infant for 30 minutes; if vomiting recurs within 30 minutes, give another dose. If the child is dehydrated and vomiting, wait until rehydration before repeating the dose.

Determine the correct dose and duration of oral antibiotics based on the child's weight; if weight is unavailable, use age. The same antibiotic (e.g., amoxicillin or co-trimoxazole for 5 days) can be used to treat different classifications such as pneumonia and acute ear infection.

fact_text: Counsel the mother or caregiver by asking and listening to understand the infant's problems and current care, praising what has been done well, advising on home care, and checking understanding with open-ended questions.

Use simple, familiar words and teaching aids when talking with the mother; provide feedback on her practice, praise what was done well, make corrections, allow more practice if needed, and encourage questions.

When checking mother's understanding, ask open-ended questions requiring explanation (what, how, how much, how many, when, why), avoid yes/no questions, allow time to answer, praise correct answers, and provide more information or practice if needed.

When counselling the mother or caregiver, advise to continue feeding and increase fluids during illness, teach how to give oral drugs or treat local infection, counsel to solve feeding problems if any, and advise when to return for care.
During counselling, every mother or caregiver must be advised clearly about when to return immediately to a health facility for further care.

For feeding problems, provide tailored advice on nutrition during and after illness, promote breastfeeding especially exclusive breastfeeding for first 6 months, encourage improved weaning with locally appropriate nutrient-rich foods, explain feeding frequency by age, discourage feeding bottles at any age, assess breastfeeding attachment and suckling, and provide specific feeding recommendations for children with persistent diarrhoea.

During illness and health, mothers and caregivers should be counselled to continue feeding and increase fluids, offering age-appropriate foods frequently even if the child takes small amounts, to prevent weight loss and malnutrition and support recovery and future health.

fact_text: Advise caregiver to return immediately if infant has any of these signs: breastfeeding or drinking poorly, becomes sicker, develops fever, or fast breathing.
Counsel mother on feeding problems and her own health; advise to breastfeed frequently at least 8 times per 24 hours, day and night, during sickness and health.
Counsel mother or caregiver of a sick young infant on how to give oral drugs, treat local infection, manage breast or nipple problems, and correct positioning and attachment for breastfeeding.
If the infant has local skin or umbilical infection, any feeding problem, or oral thrush, return for follow-up visit within 2 days.
If the infant has low weight for age, return for follow-up visit within 14 days.
Advise caregiver when to return for the next immunization according to the immunization schedule.
Avoid giving Cotrimoxazole to a young infant less than 1 month old who is premature or jaundiced; instead give Amoxicillin to this infant.

The first dose of oral drugs for a young infant should always be given in the clinic, with caregiver taught how to give oral antibiotics at home, including measuring dose and mixing with breast milk if syrup unavailable.
Ask if the child has cough or difficult breathing and for how many days; count breaths per minute and assess for fast breathing, chest indrawing, stridor, and wheeze.

Ask if the child has diarrhoea and for how many days, and if there is blood in stool; look for lethargy, unconsciousness, restlessness, irritability, sunken eyes, poor drinking, and slow skin pinch return (>2 seconds).
Ask if the child has ear pain or ear discharge and for how many days; look for pus draining from ear and feel for tender swelling behind the ear.

Ask if the child has fever or history of fever (≥99.5°F/37.5°C or above), duration of fever, travel history to high/low malaria risk areas, and signs of measles (generalized rash, cough, runny nose, red eyes, mouth ulcers, pus from eyes, corneal clouding).

Look and feel for oedema of both feet, measure weight-for-height/length z-score or MUAC in children 6 months or older; if WFH z-score < -3 or MUAC < 115 mm, check for medical complications including danger signs, severe classification, pneumonia with chest indrawing; assess feeding problems in children under 6 months or ability to finish offered food in children 6 months or older.
Look for palmar pallor to assess anaemia severity: severe, some, or none.
Ask if the child is able to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, or has convulsions during illness; look for lethargy, unconsciousness, or convulsing now as general danger signs.

recommended_advice: Effective child health care in low-resource settings depends on history and clinical signs rather than sophisticated or expensive technology.
Improvements in child health are not necessarily dependent on the use of sophisticated and expensive technologies.
A holistic, integrated syndromic approach to managing sick children is needed to achieve better outcomes, moving beyond single disease focus to address overall child health and well-being.
fact_text: In low-resource first-level health facilities with minimal diagnostic support, effective child care relies on history and signs rather than sophisticated technology; an integrated syndromic approach addressing overall child health and well-being is recommended over single disease focus to improve outcomes.

Immunization status should be checked for children 2 months to 5 years, verifying receipt of vaccines at birth, 6 weeks, 10 weeks, 14 weeks, 18 weeks, 9 months, and 15 months including BCG, Penta (1-3), PCV (1-3), OPV (1-3), IPV, MR, Vitamin A, and antihelminthic as per national EPI schedule.

For children with anaemia, moderate acute malnutrition, or under 2 years old, assess feeding by asking if breastfeeding is ongoing, frequency in 24 hours, night feeds, intake of other foods or fluids, feeding frequency per day, feeding method, serving size if low weight, and changes in feeding during illness.

fact_text: For children 2 months to 5 years with diarrhoea, assess dehydration by signs: severe dehydration if 2 of lethargic/unconscious, sunken eyes, drinks poorly or not at all, skin pinch goes back very slowly; some dehydration if 2 of restless/irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly/thirsty, skin pinch goes back slowly; no dehydration if none of these signs. Classify diarrhoea as severe persistent if dehydration present and diarrhoea ≥14 days, persistent diarrhoea if no dehydration and diarrhoea ≥14 days, dysentery if blood in stool. Treat severe dehydration urgently with fluids and refer. For some dehydration, give fluids, zinc, and food; advise continued feeding; follow up in 5 days if not improving. For persistent diarrhoea, give zinc and continue feeding; follow up in 5 days. For dysentery, give Cotrimoxazole for 3 days and follow up in 3 days.

referral_criteria: Complicated severe acute malnutrition: oedema of both feet, WHZ less than -3 Z score, MUAC less than 115 mm, medical complications, or danger signs
followup_monitoring: Follow up in 7 days for complicated and uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition and moderate acute malnutrition
Follow up in 30 days for no acute malnutrition
fact_text: For children 6 months to 5 years, assess acute malnutrition by checking for oedema of both feet, measuring MUAC, and WHZ score. Classify as complicated severe acute malnutrition if oedema present or WHZ < -3 or MUAC < 115 mm with medical complications or danger signs; treat urgently in hospital. Uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition if WHZ < -3 or MUAC < 115 mm without complications; treat with oral antibiotics for 5 days, vitamin A, feeding counselling, and follow up in 7 days. Moderate acute malnutrition if WHZ between -3 and -2 or MUAC 115-125 mm; counsel feeding and follow up in 7 days. No acute malnutrition if WHZ between -2 and 2 or MUAC ≥ 125 mm; counsel feeding and follow up in 30 days.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Collect about a spoonful of stool, including portion with mucus, pus, or blood if present; send specimen to lab as early as possible.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Stool container should be clean, dry, leak-proof, disinfectant free, wide-necked; use light plastic box or glass jar with attached spoon and stopper.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Stop drugs/antidiarrheal substances (mineral oil, barium, bismuth, magnesium, antibiotics) at least 1 week before stool collection.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: If stool specimen cannot be cultured within 2 hours, place in Cary-Blair transport medium and refrigerate immediately.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: For children urine sample collection, use sterile adhesive bag or suprapubic tap (tap fingers on suprapubic region 1 hour after feed, 1 tap/sec for 10 sec, repeat after 1 min).

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: For female urine sample collection, clean vulva with cotton plug soaked in water, separate labia, collect morning mid-stream urine in wide mouth sterile container.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: For male urine sample collection, clean urethral meatus with plain tap water, allow to dry, collect at least 30 ml mid-stream urine in sterile container; first MSU of the day preferred.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Suprapubic aspiration may be necessary occasionally in acute retention of urine or unconscious patients for urine sample collection.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Ureteric catheterization is used during urological surgery or examination when necessary for urine sample collection.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Urethral catheterization is rarely used in children or unconscious patients; use fresh sterile catheter and collect urine directly from catheter, not from collecting bag.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing

fact_text: Sputum collection patient instructions: collect early morning specimen before breakfast or mouthwash; rinse mouth with water before collection; do not collect saliva or nasopharyngeal discharge; collect exudate from lungs after deep cough into dry wide-neck leak-proof container; send container early; never refrigerate sample.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Stool specimen collection: use cotton swab to take portion of stool, insert swab in sterile Cary-Blair transport medium, break swab stick to replace bottle top lightly.

fact_text: Precautions for stool specimen: avoid contaminating faeces with urine or water; never store in incubator or refrigerator.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Throat swab collection: collect before mouthwash/food/drink, patient mouth open wide, head fixed, tongue depressed; rub sterile cotton swab vigorously over tonsils, uvula, posterior pharynx avoiding tongue and buccal surfaces; place swab in sterile tube; preferably take two swabs from same patient; dispatch to lab ASAP.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Wound swab collection: sample from base of ulcer or nodule after removing debris or surgical biopsy of deep tissues without touching superficial lesion layer; collect two swabs if possible; place in sterile capped container; send to lab early.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: For infants or other patients, rectal swab may be collected by moistening swab with saline, introducing 1 inch into anal canal, rotating 10 seconds with circular movement, avoiding contamination from anal skin.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Collect cervical swab specimens during pelvic exam using a speculum moistened with warm water (no antiseptics); wipe cervical speculum with cotton wool ball; rotate swab in cervical canal for at least 10 seconds before withdrawal; transport in Amies and Stuart media; refer urethral discharge and genital ulcer to Microbiology Department.

dose_or_duration: Collect blood culture aseptically at spike of febrile illness, before antibiotics or just before next dose if antibiotics started; adult volume 5-10 ml, children 1-3 ml, neonates 1 ml; inoculate blood into culture bottle bedside and send to lab within one hour.

source_section: Core elements of antibiotic stewardship figure
recommended_advice: Improve awareness and understanding of antimicrobial resistance
Strengthen knowledge through surveillance and research
Reduce incidence of infection
Optimize use of antimicrobial agents
Support interdisciplinary approach
Enhance infection prevention and control
Control source of infection
Prescribe antibiotics only when truly needed
Prescribe appropriate antibiotics with adequate dosages
Use shortest duration of antibiotics based on evidence
Reassess treatment when culture results are available
Support surveillance of AMR and healthcare-associated infections and monitor antibiotic consumption
Educate staff
fact_text: Core elements of antimicrobial stewardship include prescribing antibiotics only when truly needed, using appropriate antibiotics with adequate dosages, shortest duration based on evidence, reassessing treatment with culture results, infection prevention and control, and supporting surveillance and education.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Penicillin, amoxicillin/ampicillin, Augmentin/Unasyn, methicillin/oxacillin, piperacillin-tazobactam/ticarcillin-clavulanate, and cephalosporins cover gram positives and gram negatives with varying spectrum; carbapenems cover broad spectrum including resistant organisms; quinolones, aminoglycosides, TMP-SMX, macrolides, tetracyclines, clindamycin, vancomycin, daptomycin, linezolid, fosfomycin, and colistin have specific coverage patterns.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Penicillin-G covers MSSA and E coli; Methicillin (Oxacillin, Nafcillin) covers MSSA; Amoxicillin covers Klebsiella and Proteus; Ampicillin-sulbactam (clavulanate) covers Klebsiella and Proteus; Vancomycin covers MRSA; Linezolid covers VRE; Piperacillin-Tazobactam covers Pseudomonas; Carbapenems cover ESBL E coli/Klebsiella.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Enterobacterales include Klebsiella pneumoniae complex, Klebsiella oxytoca, Proteus mirabilis, Proteus vulgaris, Serratia marcescens, and Yersinia enterocolitica as common members.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Enterobacterales are intrinsically resistant to benzylpenicillin, glycopeptides, fusidic acid, macrolides, lincosamides, streptogramins, rifampicin, linezolid, and lipoglycopeptides.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
fact_text: Empiric antibiotic treatment should be limited to conditions where early initiation is beneficial (e.g. severe sepsis, septic shock, bacterial meningitis, community acquired pneumonia, necrotizing fasciitis).

fact_text: Re-assess patient within 48 hours based on test results and examination; adjust or de-escalate antibiotic regimen to narrowest spectrum and least toxic effective antibiotic.

source_title: Bangladesh STG on Infections and Infectious Diseases Prescribing
