source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
fact_text: Breastfeed exclusively for the first 6 months of life (180 days), giving no other liquid or food, not even water.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
source_section: Table 1: IYCF clinical guidelines, 12-23 completed months
fact_text: From 12+ months, feed one bowl (250 ml size) small solid pieces of family foods three times a day plus 1–2 nutritious snacks; child can feed himself/herself; continue breastfeeding.
source_figure_or_table: Table 1: IYCF clinical guidelines, 12-23 completed months

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
source_section: Table 1: IYCF clinical guidelines, 6 completed - 8 completed months
fact_text: From 6 completed to 8 completed months, start complementary feeding with a feed bowl (250 ml size) mashed semi-solid family foods two times a day plus 1–2 nutritious snacks; continue breastfeeding.
source_figure_or_table: Table 1: IYCF clinical guidelines, 6 completed - 8 completed months

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
source_section: Table 1: IYCF clinical guidelines, 9-11 completed months
fact_text: From 9 to 11 completed months, feed one-half bowl (250 ml size) solid family foods three times a day plus 1–2 nutritious snacks; child can start self-feeding; continue breastfeeding.
source_figure_or_table: Table 1: IYCF clinical guidelines, 9-11 completed months

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
source_section: Table 1: IYCF clinical guidelines, 0-6 months of age
fact_text: In the first 6 months, feed only breastmilk; no liquids or food other than breastmilk; feed frequently day and night.
source_figure_or_table: Table 1: IYCF clinical guidelines, 0-6 months of age

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
fact_text: Initiate breastfeeding immediately within the first hour after birth for all deliveries.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
fact_text: Start complementary feeding at 6 completed months with nutritionally adequate, safe, and hygienically prepared foods while continuing breastfeeding up to 23 months.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
source_section: Table 1: IYCF clinical guidelines, sickness feeding advice
fact_text: During child's sickness, increase frequency and duration of breastfeeding; do not stop breastfeeding; give small frequent feeds of favorite foods; during recovery, increase number of meals and amount of food for 10–15 days or until child regains weight.
source_figure_or_table: Table 1: IYCF clinical guidelines, sickness feeding advice

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
fact_text: Do not give pre- or post-lacteal feeds or feed with a bottle in the first days after birth; only give colostrum, no water, glucose, or other milk.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
source_section: Figure 2: Prolactin and oxytocin secretion mechanism
recommended_advice: Breastfeeding is hormonally controlled by prolactin and oxytocin.
Prolactin is necessary for milk secretion by alveoli cells and is highest in the first two hours after birth.
Prolactin levels increase with baby suckling and at night; breastfeeding at night helps maintain milk supply.
Oxytocin causes alveoli contraction and milk ejection (letdown reflex), stimulated by baby suckling and maternal expectation of feeding.
fact_text: Prolactin and oxytocin hormones regulate breastmilk production and ejection; prolactin increases with suckling and at night to maintain supply, oxytocin triggers milk flow during feeding.
source_figure_or_table: Figure 2: Prolactin and oxytocin secretion mechanism

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
avoid_medicines: any other liquid or food after birth
recommended_advice: Do not give prelacteal feeds such as honey, water with sugar, mustard oil or any other liquid or food after birth
fact_text: Babies should not be given prelacteal feeds including honey, water mixed with sugar, mustard oil or any other liquid or food after birth to prevent illness and interference with breastfeeding.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: Express and feed colostrum to premature and low birthweight newborns if they cannot suckle
fact_text: For premature and low birthweight newborns, colostrum is life-saving and should be expressed and fed if the baby cannot suckle.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: Foremilk is produced early in a feed; it is thinner, lower fat, higher water content and provides protein, lactose and nutrients
Hindmilk is produced later in a feed; it is whiter, higher fat and provides energy
Do not take baby off breast too quickly; allow baby to finish feeding until satisfied
fact_text: Foremilk is produced early in a feed and is lower fat with higher water content; hindmilk is produced later and is higher fat providing energy; baby should be allowed to finish feeding until satisfied.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: Breastfeed early and frequently; mature milk production starts around day 3-4
Breastmilk volume increases and becomes thinner and whiter
Feed newborns on demand or at least 8-10 times in 24 hours to get benefits of colostrum and stimulate mature milk production
Frequent breastfeeding helps prevent breast engorgement
fact_text: Mature milk production starts around day 3-4 with increased volume and thinner consistency; feed newborns on demand or at least 8-10 times per 24 hours to gain colostrum benefits and stimulate milk production; frequent feeding prevents engorgement.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: Initiate breastfeeding within one hour of birth
Put baby to mother’s breast immediately after birth to stimulate suckling reflex
fact_text: Recommended initiation of breastfeeding is within one hour of birth; baby’s suckling reflex is maximum at this stage; putting baby to breast immediately after birth helps quick suckle initiation.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
source_section: Figure 3: Comparison of nutrients in human milk and animal milks
recommended_advice: Human milk contains more lactose and anti-infective protein and less casein than cow’s milk, making it easier to digest
fact_text: Human breastmilk has higher lactose and anti-infective protein and lower casein compared to cow’s milk, making it easier to digest for infants.
source_figure_or_table: Figure 3: Comparison of nutrients in human milk and animal milks

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
fact_text: The International Breastmilk Substitutes (BMS) Code prohibits promotion of pacifiers, artificial nipples, infant formula, water, teas, juices, and distribution of infant feeding product samples or advertisements in health facilities.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
fact_text: All pregnant women should be informed about benefits and hazards of breastfeeding and formula feeding, hazards and restrictions of prelacteal feeds, initiation of breastfeeding within one hour of delivery, colostrum feeding, breastfeeding techniques (position, attachment, expression), exclusive breastfeeding importance, maternity leave, skin-to-skin contact, and rooming-in.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
fact_text: Breastfeeding benefits for baby include providing all necessary energy and nutrients up to six months, antibodies protecting against infections, easy digestion, allergy reduction, and support for brain development and emotional bonding.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
fact_text: Breastfeeding immediately after delivery reduces maternal blood loss and stimulates uterine contraction; exclusive breastfeeding acts as natural family planning with about 2% pregnancy risk; breastfeeding mothers have lower risk of breast, ovarian cancer and osteoporosis.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
fact_text: Feed on demand by responding to early feeding cues; put baby to breast at onset of early hunger signs (early sign - opening mouth; late sign - cycling/limb movement; very late sign - crying); always breastfeed whenever baby wants; wake baby to breastfeed if more than 3 hours between feeds.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
fact_text: Assess adequate milk supply by checking if baby urinates six or more times per day, plays happily with limb movement, sleeps well, and gains weight; reversed signs indicate insufficient milk.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
fact_text: Avoid bottle feeding and formula feeding in infants and children under two years due to multiple harms including interference with bonding, discouragement of suckling, reduced breastmilk supply, infection risk, malnutrition, allergies, and increased chronic disease risk.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
avoid_medicines: No baby product gifts from formula/milk companies to families
No gifts or inducements (scholarships, grants, facilities) to health staff including nurses and doctors
contraindications_or_cautions: Breast Milk Substitute (BMS) Act 2013 restricts marketing of breastmilk substitutes and related products
fact_text: The Bangladesh BMS Act prohibits baby product gifts to families and inducements to health staff to protect breastfeeding promotion.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
source_section: Figure 5: External signs of good and poor attachment
recommended_advice: Signs of good attachment: baby's mouth wide open, lower lip curled outwards, more areola visible above baby's mouth, chin touching breast
Signs of poor attachment: baby's mouth not wide open, lower lip points forward or turned inwards, upper and lower areola visible, chin away from breast
fact_text: Good attachment is indicated by wide open mouth, curled out lower lip, more areola visible above mouth, and chin touching breast; poor attachment shows closed mouth, inward lower lip, visible upper and lower areola, and chin away from breast.
source_figure_or_table: Figure 5: External signs of good and poor attachment

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
source_section: Figure 4: Correct positions during breastfeeding (sitting and lying positions)
recommended_advice: Position mother sitting, lying down, or standing relaxed and comfortable without back strain
Support mother's back if sitting; bring baby towards mother without leaning forward
Position baby across mother's chest and abdomen, under arm or alongside body
Ensure baby's body is straight with head and shoulder in line, facing breast, close to mother, and whole body supported especially buttocks
fact_text: Mother should be relaxed and comfortable in sitting, lying, or standing position with back supported if sitting; baby should be positioned across mother's chest/abdomen with body straight, head and shoulder aligned, facing breast, close to mother, and whole body supported.
source_figure_or_table: Figure 4: Correct positions during breastfeeding (sitting and lying positions)

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
trigger_evidence: mother with sore or cracked nipples
recommended_advice: Express breastmilk manually when mother is away or infant cannot suckle
Wash hands with soap and water before expression
Use a wide mouth cup washed with soap and warm water for collection
Mother should sit comfortably during expression
fact_text: Manual expression of breastmilk is recommended when mother is away, infant is premature/low birth weight/sick, breast is engorged, or mother has sore/cracked nipples; hygiene and comfortable posture are essential.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: When feeding expressed breastmilk with cup/spoon, mother/caregiver should wash hands, hold baby in breastfeeding position, put an amount baby can consume in cup, hold cup/spoon gently against baby's lower lip, tilt slightly so milk reaches lip, and allow baby to open mouth and suckle slowly.
fact_text: Expressed breastmilk should be fed by cup/spoon with careful hygiene and positioning to allow baby to suckle slowly from the cup/spoon tilted against lower lip.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
dose_or_duration: 6-8 hours at room temperature; 2-3 days refrigerated at 8°C
recommended_advice: Expressed breastmilk should be covered in a clean pot; at room temperature it is safe for 6-8 hours; refrigerated at 8°C it remains safe for 2-3 days; warm by placing container in hot water before feeding.
fact_text: Expressed breastmilk should be stored covered in a clean container; safe for 6-8 hours at room temperature and 2-3 days refrigerated at 8°C; warm by placing container in hot water before feeding.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: To express milk manually, mother should hold breast with thumb above areola and four fingers below, press and release areola repeatedly with thumb and index finger, rotating around areola to express milk from all areas without squeezing nipple.
fact_text: Manual expression of breastmilk involves pressing and releasing the areola with thumb and index finger, rotating around the areola to express milk without squeezing the nipple.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
dose_or_duration: first six months postpartum
recommended_advice: Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) is effective for family planning if mother has no menstruation, baby is less than six months old, and baby is exclusively breastfed day and night.
LAM is 98% effective for first six months postpartum but is no longer effective once menstruation returns or baby is older than six months or other foods/fluids introduced.
fact_text: LAM requires exclusive breastfeeding day and night, no menstruation, and baby under six months; it is 98% effective for first six months postpartum but stops being effective if menstruation returns or baby is older than six months or other foods introduced.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
dose_or_duration: first six months postpartum
recommended_advice: Non-hormonal contraception methods (IUDs, condoms, diaphragms, spermicides) are suitable during breastfeeding and do not affect lactation.
Hormonal methods: combined estrogen pill reduces breastmilk and should be avoided within six months postpartum; progesterone-only pills can be used if menstruation has started.
contraindications_or_cautions: Combined pill (mainly estrogen) reduces breastmilk production and should not be used within six months of delivery.
Progesterone-only pills can be used in first six months if menstruation starts.
fact_text: Non-hormonal contraception methods are suitable during breastfeeding; combined estrogen pills reduce breastmilk and should be avoided within six months postpartum; progesterone-only pills can be used if menstruation starts.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
fact_text: Breast engorgement is characterized by swollen, edematous, shiny, reddened breasts, painful, tight flat nipples, poor milk flow, and fever subsiding within 24 hours.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
contraindications_or_cautions: breastfeeding contraindicated in mothers with substance abuse, antineoplastics, radiopharmaceuticals, chemotherapy, radioactive isotope therapy, or antithyroid drugs
fact_text: Breastfeeding contraindicated in mothers using substance abuse, antineoplastics, radiopharmaceuticals, chemotherapy, radioactive isotope therapy, or antithyroid drugs.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
contraindications_or_cautions: galactosemia in baby is the only contraindication for breastfeeding; recommend lactose-free milk feeding in such cases
fact_text: Galactosemia in the baby is the only contraindication for breastfeeding; lactose-free milk feeding should be recommended in such cases.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
contraindications_or_cautions: use caution with drugs associated with ill effects in breastfed infants including acebutolol, atenolol, bromocriptine, aspirin, lithium, phenobarbital, and others
fact_text: Use caution with drugs associated with ill effects in breastfed infants including acebutolol, atenolol, bromocriptine, aspirin, lithium, phenobarbital, and others.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: milk not removed from breast causes engorgement especially in first days after delivery
other causes include delayed initiation, infrequent feeds, poor attachment, ineffective suckling
fact_text: Engorgement is caused by milk not removed from breast, delayed initiation, infrequent feeds, poor attachment, or ineffective suckling.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
trigger_evidence: mother with sore or fissured nipple
recommended_advice: help mother improve baby's position and attachment
pain usually lessens as baby attaches well
continue breastfeeding normally
smear hind milk on nipple and air dry
avoid tight dress
mother may need pain killer
fact_text: For sore or fissured nipple, improve baby's position and attachment, continue breastfeeding, smear hind milk on nipple, air dry, avoid tight dress, and consider painkillers.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: Feed frequently from affected breast
Gently massage breast over lump while baby suckles
Apply warm compresses
Change baby's position to aid milk flow
If thickened milk string appears after massage, allow milk to flow out
fact_text: For blocked duct, recommend frequent feeding from affected breast, gentle massage over lump, warm compresses, and changing baby position to improve milk removal.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: Drain and treat abscess with penicillinase-resistant antibiotics
Mother may continue feeding from affected breast; feeding does not affect baby
If suckling is too painful or mother unwilling, teach expressing milk and advise to resume breastfeeding when pain lessens (usually 2-3 days)
Continue feeding from other breast
fact_text: For breast abscess, drain and treat with penicillinase-resistant antibiotics; mother may continue feeding from affected breast; if painful, teach expressing milk and resume breastfeeding when pain decreases.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_medicines: antibiotics if infected nipple fissure or no improvement after 24h
recommended_advice: Advise mother to rest and breastfeed frequently
Avoid long gaps between feeds
If employed, take sick leave to rest and feed baby
Apply warm compresses to affected breast
Vary baby position to stimulate milk flow
Use analgesics to reduce inflammation and pain
If no improvement after 24 hours, start antibiotics targeting penicillinase-resistant organisms
followup_monitoring: monitor for symptom improvement within 24 hours
fact_text: For mastitis, advise frequent breastfeeding, rest, warm compresses, analgesics, and if no improvement after 24h with infected nipple fissure, start penicillinase-resistant antibiotics.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: If baby cannot attach or suckle effectively, mother should express milk by hand several times until breasts are softer to enable baby to attach
Breastfeed frequently if baby can attach and suckle
Apply warm compresses or take warm shower before expressing to help milk flow
Use cold compresses after feeding or expressing to reduce oedema
fact_text: If baby cannot attach or suckle well in mastitis, mother should hand express milk several times until breasts soften, breastfeed frequently if possible, use warm compresses before expressing, and cold compresses after feeding.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
condition: inverted, flat, large, or long nipples
condition_aliases: inverted, flat, large, or long nipples
recommended_advice: Help mother position and attach baby immediately after delivery
Encourage skin-to-skin contact near breast
Encourage mother to put baby to breast in different positions to stimulate rooting reflex
Explain that babies can often suckle without difficulty from unusual nipple shapes
Avoid feeding bottles or dummies
For flat or inverted nipples, maintain proper position and attachment, ensure child suckles with areola inside mouth, and breastfeed frequently
fact_text: For inverted, flat, large, or long nipples, support mother with positioning, attachment, skin-to-skin contact, frequent breastfeeding, and avoid bottles/dummies to improve breastfeeding success.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: Provide appropriate care including feeding support, temperature maintenance especially skin-to-skin contact (kangaroo care), and hygienic cord care
fact_text: A baby weighing less than 2500 g at birth is low birthweight (LBW) and requires appropriate feeding, temperature maintenance (skin-to-skin kangaroo care), and hygienic cord care.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
condition: candida infection (thrush) in mother and baby
condition_aliases: candida infection (thrush) in mother and baby
trigger_evidence: symptoms of thrush in mother or baby
recommended_medicines: Nystatin suspension 100,000 IU/ml for baby, 1 ml by dropper 4 times daily after breastfeeds for 7 days or longer
Nystatin cream 100,000 IU/ml for mother, apply to nipples 4 times daily after breastfeeds for 7 days after lesions heal
dose_or_duration: 7 days or longer as needed
route_or_site: oral for fluconazole and nystatin suspension; topical for nystatin cream
recommended_advice: Treat both mother and baby if mother has symptoms
If only baby has symptoms, treat baby only
fact_text: Treat candida infection (thrush) in mother and baby with fluconazole 150 mg tablet for mother, nystatin suspension 100,000 IU/ml for baby (1 ml 4 times daily after feeds for 7+ days), and nystatin cream 100,000 IU/ml for mother’s nipples 4 times daily after feeds for 7 days after lesions heal.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
trigger_evidence: LBW infant unable to breastfeed effectively
recommended_advice: If LBW infant unable to breastfeed effectively, feed by alternative oral feeding methods or intra-gastric tube feeding
If mother unable to breastfeed LBW infant, options include expressed breastmilk from mother or donor breastmilk
fact_text: For LBW infants unable to breastfeed effectively, feed by alternative oral feeding methods (cup/spoon/direct expression) or intra-gastric tube; if mother unable to breastfeed, use expressed breastmilk or donor breastmilk.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: Early effective suckling ensures adequate milk supply for both twins
Mothers may need help to hold two babies to suckle simultaneously or one at a time
Mother may give each baby its own breast or vary the side; help may be needed for good attachment
Holding babies in underarm position with pillows or folded clothes support is helpful
Build mother's confidence to produce enough milk for two and encourage family support to avoid formula feeding
fact_text: For breastfeeding twins, support early effective suckling, help mother hold babies to suckle simultaneously or one at a time, encourage good attachment, and build confidence to produce enough milk for two.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: Help mother hold baby upright at breast with baby's legs on either side of mother's thigh to ease swallowing
Mother can express milk and feed baby by cup or spoon until surgical help is available
Refer baby for surgery, usually done in stages after some months
referral_criteria: Refer baby with cleft lip/palate for surgery
fact_text: For babies with cleft lip/palate, support upright feeding position, express and feed milk by cup/spoon until surgery, and refer for staged surgical repair.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: Show mother how to help baby attach to breast using Dancer-hand position
Support baby's chin with 3 fingers below breast to create U-shape with thumb and forefingers and support head to keep mouth close to breast
Mother can express milk and feed by cup or tube
Provide extra support and counseling to mother to bond and persist with breastfeeding
fact_text: For babies with muscular weakness (e.g. Down syndrome, cerebral palsy), teach Dancer-hand position for attachment, support chin and head, express milk for cup/tube feeding, and provide extra mother support and counseling.

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: Mothers known to be HIV-infected should receive lifelong antiretroviral therapy or prophylaxis to reduce HIV transmission through breastfeeding

HIV-infected mothers and infants who are HIV uninfected or unknown status should exclusively breastfeed for first 6 months, introduce complementary foods thereafter, and continue breastfeeding for 12 months
Stopping breastfeeding abruptly is not advisable; if stopping, do so gradually within one month
If stopping breastfeeding, infants should receive safe and adequate replacement feeds to support normal growth
Expressed, heat-treated breast milk or home-modified animal milk is not recommended as replacement food in first 6 months
For infants under 6 months, commercial infant formula milk can be used if home conditions are fulfilled
For children over 6 months, commercial infant formula milk and animal milk (boiled for infants under 12 months) can be part of diet with complementary foods 4-5 times per day

Mothers known to be HIV-infected should only give commercial infant formula milk as replacement feed to HIV-uninfected infants or infants of unknown status if safe water, sanitation, reliable preparation, exclusive formula feeding for first 6 months, family support, and access to comprehensive child health services are assured

HIV-infected mothers may consider expressing and heat-treating breast milk as interim feeding if infant is low birth weight, ill, mother unwell or temporarily unable to breastfeed, has mastitis, or if antiretroviral drugs are temporarily unavailable
Mothers known to be HIV-infected are strongly encouraged to exclusively breastfeed for first 6 months and continue breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond
fact_text: HIV-infected mothers should receive lifelong ART, exclusively breastfeed first 6 months, continue breastfeeding to 12 months, stop gradually if needed, and use safe replacement feeds if stopping; expressed heat-treated breastmilk may be interim feeding in special cases

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: Mother should continue to feed her baby on demand after caesarean section
Mother may need help to hold baby for a few days
Mother should learn to breastfeed lying down and turn over to position comfortably
Hospital staff and family members should support mother
Most mothers can breastfeed normally after caesarean with appropriate help
If baby is too ill or too small to feed at breast soon after delivery, mother should be helped to express milk to establish supply
fact_text: After caesarean section, mother should feed baby on demand, get help to hold baby, learn comfortable breastfeeding positions, and express milk if baby too ill or small to feed at breast

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
trigger_evidence: mother and/or baby with chicken pox
recommended_advice: If both mother and baby have active chicken pox, mother should continue breastfeeding and both isolated together
If mother is ill but baby not exposed, mother should be isolated until no longer contagious and express milk for baby
fact_text: In chicken pox, mother should continue breastfeeding if both mother and baby affected and isolate together; if mother ill but baby not exposed, isolate mother and express milk

source_title: Clinical Guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)
recommended_advice: If mother and baby are infected with pulmonary tuberculosis, mother should continue breastfeeding and both treated for TB
If only mother is infected, she should be isolated until 2 weeks after treatment begins and no longer contagious
Mother should use a mask during this period
