source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Treatment outcomes for TB patients include: Cured - bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB patient completing full treatment with bacteriological response and no failure; Treatment Completed - completed treatment without failure or bacteriological evidence; Treatment Failure - treatment regimen terminated or changed due to bacteriological reversion (two positive smears at least 7 days apart after conversion); Died - patient dies before or during treatment; Lost to follow up - treatment not started or interrupted for 2 consecutive months or more; Transferred out - patient transferred to another unit with unknown outcome; Not evaluated - treatment outcome unknown other than transfer; Treatment success is sum of cured and treatment completed.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Patients during TB treatment may require referral or transfer to another designated DOTS centre for continuation of treatment; referral requires completing Tuberculosis Referral/Transfer Form (TB 07) in triplicate with copies sent to referral centre, patient, and retained at treatment initiation centre.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: When treatment is continued in the receiving DOTS centre, the patient should be registered there as a 'transfer in' case and the lower portion of the form (TB 07) should be returned to the referring centre.

If a patient treated without registration (e.g., hospital or private practitioner) continues treatment at a DOTS centre, this is a referral, not a transfer; the receiving centre registers the patient as per treatment category (new, relapse, treatment after loss to follow-up, failure), not as transfer in.
Efforts should be made to collect treatment outcomes of transferred-out patients from the referred centre and report final outcomes to minimize transfer-out numbers.
Referred centres should inform referring centres about treatment outcomes of transfer-in cases.
fact_text: Patients continuing treatment at a receiving DOTS centre must be registered as 'transfer in' cases with form TB 07 returned; if previously untreated at DOTS, registration is by treatment category as referral not transfer; treatment outcomes of transferred patients must be collected and communicated between centres.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Do not separate a newborn child from a mother with active TB unless the child is acutely ill.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Mothers with TB should be advised on cough hygiene including covering nose and mouth when coughing or sneezing, and encouraged to wear a face mask and breastfeed in a well-ventilated area to reduce transmission risk.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If mother is sputum smear-negative and infant has no congenital TB evidence, give BCG vaccine to infant.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If mother is sputum smear-positive at delivery, infant should be carefully examined for active TB disease.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Mantoux skin test is done after 3 months of prophylactic treatment in infants born to mothers with active TB.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: All pregnant women on anti-TB treatment should receive oral vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) 10 mg/day to prevent isoniazid-related peripheral neuropathy for the entire treatment duration.
fact_text: All pregnant women on anti-TB treatment should receive oral vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) 10 mg/day to prevent isoniazid-related peripheral neuropathy for the entire treatment duration.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: Breastfeeding women on anti-TB treatment should receive oral vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) 10 mg/day to prevent isoniazid-related peripheral neuropathy for the entire treatment duration.
fact_text: Breastfeeding women on anti-TB treatment should receive oral vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) 10 mg/day to prevent isoniazid-related peripheral neuropathy for the entire treatment duration.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: For mothers receiving rifampicin during pregnancy, give vitamin K PO 10 mg/day for 15 days before delivery; for newborns, give prophylactic IM vitamin K 1 mg as a single dose on day of birth to prevent hemorrhagic disease.
fact_text: For mothers receiving rifampicin during pregnancy, give vitamin K PO 10 mg/day for 15 days before delivery; for newborns, give prophylactic IM vitamin K 1 mg as a single dose on day of birth to prevent hemorrhagic disease.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: If infant is well, give prophylactic daily INH and Rifampicin for 3 months (3RH regimen) at recommended doses; BCG is withheld until prophylaxis completion.
fact_text: If infant is well, give prophylactic daily INH and Rifampicin for 3 months (3RH regimen) at recommended doses; BCG is withheld until prophylaxis completion.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Anti-TB treatment should be started as soon as diagnosis is made in pregnancy and full course given; most anti-TB drugs are safe during pregnancy.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Breastfed infants of mothers on ATT should receive INH preventive therapy after ruling out active TB.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Breastfeeding mothers with TB should receive full anti-TB treatment; all anti-TB drugs are compatible with breastfeeding except in TB/HIV co-infection where breastfeeding should be avoided.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If infant is ill at birth and congenital TB is suspected, a full course of anti-TB treatment should be given.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: In previously treated pregnant TB cases, fluoroquinolones like levofloxacin should be avoided; instead, 4FDC (RHEZ) for 6 months should be prescribed.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Anti-TB drugs can cause liver damage; pyrazinamide is most hepatotoxic, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin; monitor liver function and rule out other causes before attributing hepatitis to drugs.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If drug-induced hepatitis is diagnosed, stop anti-TB drugs until symptoms and liver tests normalize; reintroduce drugs gradually or all at once if mild hepatitis; avoid rifampicin and pyrazinamide if severe jaundice.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Alternative regimens for drug-induced hepatitis depend on suspected drug: if pyrazinamide involved use 2HRE/7HR/9HRE; if isoniazid involved use 9RZE; if rifampicin involved use 9Lfx-HZE; if pyrazinamide and rifampicin involved use 10Lfx-HE.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: In acute viral hepatitis, defer TB treatment until hepatitis resolves; after resolution, usual anti-TB regimens can be given if no liver impairment; monitor closely with routine liver function tests.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: In patients with unstable or persistent hepatitis, treat with 8 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol, avoiding pyrazinamide.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Patients with chronic liver disease should not receive pyrazinamide; use isoniazid plus rifampicin plus ethambutol for 9 months (2HRE/7HR).

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Patients with past acute hepatitis or excessive alcohol use but normal liver function can receive usual TB regimen with close monitoring for hepatotoxicity.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Rifamycins induce hepatic enzymes and reduce efficacy of oral contraceptive pills; female TB patients on ATT may choose alternate contraception methods like IM medroxyprogesterone, barrier methods, IUD, or OCP with higher estrogen dose (50 µg) during treatment.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: Initial TB treatment for patients with renal failure or severe renal insufficiency: 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol given three times per week with pyrazinamide 25 mg/kg and ethambutol 15 mg/kg doses, followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin three times per week.
followup_monitoring: Patients with severe renal insufficiency or failure receiving isoniazid should receive pyridoxine 10 mg daily to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
contraindications_or_cautions: Isoniazid and rifampicin do not require dose adjustment in renal insufficiency due to biliary excretion.
Pyrazinamide and ethambutol require dose adjustment in late-stage renal disease (Stage 4 and 5).
fact_text: In patients with severe renal insufficiency, TB treatment uses thrice-weekly dosing of pyrazinamide (25 mg/kg) and ethambutol (15 mg/kg) for 2 months, followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin thrice weekly; pyridoxine 10 mg daily is recommended to prevent neuropathy.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_tests: Blood sugar levels should be strictly controlled during anti-TB treatment, preferably with insulin.
recommended_medicines: TB treatment regimen is the same as for non-diabetics.
recommended_advice: Early diagnosis and management of TB in diabetics is important to improve outcomes.
followup_monitoring: Assess renal function in diabetic TB patients and manage accordingly.
fact_text: Patients with diabetes have increased vulnerability and worse outcomes with TB; TB treatment is the same as non-diabetics but requires strict blood sugar control, preferably with insulin, and renal function assessment.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: At TB treatment start, ask patients about current medications to identify interactions.
Dosages of other drugs may need adjustment during rifampicin treatment and after its discontinuation.
contraindications_or_cautions: Rifampicin induces metabolism of many drugs, decreasing their concentrations and effects.
fact_text: Rifampicin substantially decreases concentrations of many drugs including antimicrobials, hormones, anticoagulants, immunosuppressives, anticonvulsants, cardiovascular drugs, hypoglycemics, lipid-lowering drugs, antipsychotics, anxiolytics, and cytotoxics; dosage adjustments and medication review are required at TB treatment start and after rifampicin discontinuation.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Patients should be clinically monitored for adverse effects during treatment
Counsel patients to self-report symptoms promptly
Health workers and DOT providers should teach patients to recognize common side effects
Routine laboratory monitoring is not necessary for all patients
Minor adverse effects usually do not require stopping drugs; use counseling and ancillary medicines
Major adverse effects may require stopping offending drugs and modifying regimen
followup_monitoring: Enquire about side effects during routine visits and when patients collect drug refills
fact_text: Minor adverse effects of TB drugs include anorexia, nausea/vomiting, arthralgia, burning sensation, and photosensitivity; management includes symptomatic treatment, pyridoxine for isoniazid neuropathy, and patient counseling to report symptoms promptly.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
followup_monitoring: Weekly liver function tests recommended if liver enzymes elevated or jaundice symptoms present during anti-TB therapy.
fact_text: Moderate to severe skin rash requires stopping all anti-TB drugs and sequential reintroduction; jaundice with liver enzyme elevation >5x normal requires stopping drugs and weekly monitoring; ethambutol can cause reversible visual impairment.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
followup_monitoring: Monitor renal function and electrolytes during fluoroquinolone therapy
Monitor for signs of shock, purpura, and hemolytic anemia with rifampicin
fact_text: Ethambutol toxicity first sign is loss of red-green colour distinction; stop causative agent permanently. Rifampicin can cause shock syndrome, purpura, acute renal failure, and hemolytic anemia; stop immediately and treat aggressively; never reuse rifampicin after thrombocytopenic purpura. Fluoroquinolones cause QT prolongation, especially moxifloxacin; monitor renal function, electrolytes, and QT interval; adjust dose if needed.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Children under 15 years represent 10% of TB cases; young children usually infected by adult household member with bacteriologically positive PTB; infants and children under 5 years and those with immunosuppressive illnesses are at higher risk of TB disease.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Key risk factors for TB in children include close contact with smear/culture positive PTB cases, age under 5 years, severe malnutrition or immunosuppression (measles, whooping cough, HIV, steroids), exposure within past year, and comorbidities like HIV/AIDS, diabetes, renal failure, cancer, connective tissue disease, silicosis, gastrectomy, organ transplant, and prolonged steroid use.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
source_section: Age-specific risk of progression to disease after primary infection with M. tuberculosis in immunocompetent children
fact_text: Risk of progression to pulmonary disease and disseminated TB or tubercular meningitis after primary infection with M. tuberculosis varies by age: highest risk in children <1 year (30-40% pulmonary, 10-20% disseminated), decreasing with age.
source_figure_or_table: Age-specific risk of progression to disease after primary infection with M. tuberculosis in immunocompetent children

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Common extrapulmonary TB presentations in children include tubercular lymphadenopathy, pleural or pericardial effusion, tubercular meningitis, spinal TB (Pott’s disease), abdominal TB, and tubercular arthritis.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Any one of the above symptom criteria in a child <15 years in close contact with a known bacteriologically or clinically confirmed TB case should be regarded as presumptive TB and referred for physician evaluation.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Presumptive pulmonary TB in children includes persistent non-remitting cough >2 weeks not responding to antibiotics/bronchodilators, and/or documented fever >38°C for >2 weeks after ruling out common causes, and/or documented weight loss or no weight gain in past 3 months or severe malnutrition, and/or fatigue, reduced playfulness, irritability, refusal to feed.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Recommended approach to diagnose TB in children includes careful history taking (including TB contact and symptoms) and clinical assessment including serial weight monitoring and growth assessment.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Diagnosis of TB in children is difficult due to non-specific symptoms, inability to produce sputum for microscopy or GeneXpert, and often negative Mantoux test in malnourished children.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: PTB is common in children but bacteriological confirmation is often not possible; sputum induction and gastric aspiration are effective specimen collection methods and should be attempted whenever possible.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Diagnosis in children requires careful history including contact history, clinical signs, symptoms, and investigations such as Mantoux test, chest X-ray, smear microscopy, and GeneXpert.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If any EPTB symptoms are associated with a history of contact with TB, the possibility of TB is high.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Symptoms in children are often non-specific and mimic common childhood illnesses; childhood TB is paucibacillary making microbiological diagnosis difficult; CXR and Mantoux test have limitations in malnourished children.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_tests: Chest X-ray and other radiological evaluation
Bacteriological confirmation whenever possible: smear microscopy, Xpert-MTB RIF, culture of respiratory sample or gastric lavage
Other supportive investigations relevant to suspected PTB/EPTB
fact_text: Investigations for TB include Mantoux test, chest X-ray, bacteriological confirmation by smear microscopy, Xpert-MTB RIF, culture of respiratory or gastric lavage samples, other supportive tests for PTB/EPTB, and HIV testing.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
source_section: Table: Recommended daily dose of First-Line Anti-TB
dose_or_duration: Rifampicin 15 mg/kg (10-20 mg/day) max 600 mg/day; Isoniazid 10 mg/kg (7-15 mg/kg) max 300 mg/day; Pyrazinamide 35 mg/kg (30-40 mg/kg) max 2000 mg/day; Ethambutol 20 mg/kg (15-25 mg/kg) max 1500 mg/day; Levofloxacin 15-20 mg/kg
recommended_advice: Counsel parents/guardians to report any vision-related symptoms promptly during treatment
followup_monitoring: Record weight during initial and follow-up visits to monitor treatment response
contraindications_or_cautions: Minimal risk of optic neuritis from Ethambutol in children but visual monitoring and parental counseling for vision symptoms is important
fact_text: Recommended daily doses of first-line anti-TB drugs for children are weight-based: Rifampicin 15 mg/kg (max 600 mg), Isoniazid 10 mg/kg (max 300 mg), Pyrazinamide 35 mg/kg (max 2000 mg), Ethambutol 20 mg/kg (max 1500 mg); Levofloxacin 15-20 mg/kg for H resistant cases; Ethambutol eye toxicity risk is minimal but visual monitoring and parental counseling are advised.
source_figure_or_table: Table: Recommended daily dose of First-Line Anti-TB

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
referral_criteria: All seriously ill children previously treated for TB (relapse, treatment after failure, treatment after lost to follow-up or not improving on new regimen) should be investigated for drug resistant TB
fact_text: All children with TB receive standard treatment; seriously ill children previously treated for TB (relapse, treatment failure, lost to follow-up, or not improving) must be investigated for drug-resistant TB; strict DOT is essential in all pediatric TB cases.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021

dose_or_duration: Children with TB are treated using child-friendly dispersible and flavoured fixed-dose combinations (FDC) of HRZ (50/75/150 mg) and HR (50/75 mg) dosed by weight bands.
fact_text: Children with TB are treated using child-friendly dispersible and flavoured fixed-dose combinations (FDC) of HRZ (50/75/150 mg) and HR (50/75 mg) dosed by weight bands.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021

dose_or_duration: If levofloxacin 100 mg dispersible tablet is unavailable, use 250 mg tablet dosed by weight bands for children 0-14 years: 5-6 kg: ½ tablet/day; 7-9 kg: ¾ tablet/day; 10-15 kg: 1-1½ tablets/day; 16-23 kg: 1½-2 tablets/day; 24-30 kg: 2-2½ tablets/day; 31+ kg: follow adult schedule (up to 1.5 g/day).
fact_text: If levofloxacin 100 mg dispersible tablet is unavailable, use 250 mg tablet dosed by weight bands for children 0-14 years: 5-6 kg: ½ tablet/day; 7-9 kg: ¾ tablet/day; 10-15 kg: 1-1½ tablets/day; 16-23 kg: 1½-2 tablets/day; 24-30 kg: 2-2½ tablets/day; 31+ kg: follow adult schedule (up to 1.5 g/day).

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Pulmonary TB and extrapulmonary TB are treated for 6 months (2 months HRZE intensive phase + 4 months HR continuation phase).

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Severe forms of extrapulmonary TB (including TB meningitis, osteomyelitis, miliary TB, TB pericarditis/effusion) are treated for 9-12 months by extending the continuation phase by 3-6 months (total 2 months HRZE + 7-10 months HR).

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Child contacts on INH preventive therapy should be followed up at least monthly until completion of chemoprophylaxis.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If a child receiving isoniazid develops symptoms, TB assessment is required; if the child was not vaccinated with BCG, BCG should be given after completion of isoniazid prophylaxis.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: Corticosteroids should be used sparingly in children but are beneficial in TB meningitis, some TB pericarditis cases, and airway obstruction due to TB lymphadenitis; prednisolone dose 2 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks, then tapered over 1-2 weeks, max 4 mg/kg/day (60 mg/day) in severe cases.
fact_text: Corticosteroids should be used sparingly in children but are beneficial in TB meningitis, some TB pericarditis cases, and airway obstruction due to TB lymphadenitis; prednisolone dose 2 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks, then tapered over 1-2 weeks, max 4 mg/kg/day (60 mg/day) in severe cases.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: INH preventive therapy for child contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB patients is 10 mg/kg daily for 6 months, irrespective of BCG or nutritional status, after excluding active TB.
fact_text: INH preventive therapy for child contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB patients is 10 mg/kg daily for 6 months, irrespective of BCG or nutritional status, after excluding active TB.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: Pyridoxine should be given with isoniazid in HIV-infected children to prevent isoniazid-associated neuropathy; dose 12.5 mg/day for children 5-11 years, 25 mg/day for children ≥12 years.
fact_text: Pyridoxine should be given with isoniazid in HIV-infected children to prevent isoniazid-associated neuropathy; dose 12.5 mg/day for children 5-11 years, 25 mg/day for children ≥12 years.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Due to serious limitations in evidence, MDR-TB preventive therapy is not recommended as a public health measure; strict clinical observation and close monitoring for active TB development for at least two years is preferred for contacts of MDR-TB cases.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Infants born to mothers with infectious pulmonary TB can be safely breastfed if isoniazid prophylaxis is given.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Drug resistant TB (DR TB) is active TB caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis resistant to one or more anti-TB medicines.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Mono-resistance: resistance to one first-line anti-TB drug only; Poly-resistance: resistance to more than one first-line drug except isoniazid and rifampicin together; Rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB): resistance to rifampicin detected by phenotypic or genotypic methods; Isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB): resistance to isoniazid with rifampicin susceptibility confirmed in vitro; Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR): resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin; MDR TB with quinolone resistance: MDR TB plus resistance to moxifloxacin or levofloxacin; Extensive drug resistance (XDR): MDR TB plus resistance to moxifloxacin or levofloxacin and one of two other group A drugs (BDQ, LZD).

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
source_section: Table of causes of inadequate anti-TB treatment
fact_text: Causes of inadequate anti-TB treatment include: Health care providers - inappropriate guidelines, non-compliance, poor training, poor patient education, no treatment monitoring, poor adverse reaction management, poor treatment support, poorly organized TB control programs; Drugs - poor quality, stock-outs, poor storage, wrong dose or combination, poor regulation; Patients - lack of information, lack of means to adhere (transport, food), adverse effects, social barriers, HIV, diabetes, undernutrition, malabsorption, substance abuse, psychiatric conditions.
source_figure_or_table: Table of causes of inadequate anti-TB treatment

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Presumptive DR TB includes all previously treated (retreatment) cases at diagnosis with failure of category-1 and retreatment regimen, relapse, treatment after loss to follow-up, non-converters at month 2, close contacts of DR TB patients with symptoms, HIV infected persons with or without TB symptoms, and bacteriologically negative pulmonary TB patients with clinical deterioration or no improvement despite treatment as per NTP guidelines.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Diagnostic algorithm for presumptive DR TB: perform GeneXpert; if MTB detected with RR detected, do SL-LPA or phenotypic DST on second specimen; if sensitive, start STR treatment; if resistant, start LTR treatment. If MTB detected without RR, start first line drugs and follow-up by microscopy. If error/invalid/no result, repeat GeneXpert; if positive, treat as per guideline. If MTB not detected, do CXR/clinical evaluation; if negative, treat for other respiratory diseases.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_tests: extended DST for Mfx, BDQ, Lzd, Cfz
fact_text: Rapid DST should be offered to all presumptive TB cases before starting treatment; if unavailable, prioritize DST for previously treated cases, non-converters at month 2, close contacts of DR TB, HIV infected persons, and bacteriologically negative pulmonary TB with clinical deterioration. RR TB diagnosed by GeneXpert should have second-line DST by LPA and phenotypic culture; resistance to fluoroquinolones requires phenotypic DST. Extended DST for high dose Mfx, BDQ, Lzd, and Cfz will be performed to guide treatment.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: Intensive Phase: 4-6 months with 7 drugs (bedaquiline, levofloxacin, clofazimine, ethionamide, ethambutol, high dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide); continuation phase fixed 5 months; intensive phase may extend to 6 months if sputum smear or culture positive at 4-5 months
fact_text: Shorter MDR/RR-TB regimen intensive phase lasts 4-6 months with 7 drugs; can extend to 6 months if sputum smear or culture remains positive at 4-5 months; continuation phase is fixed 5 months.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
trigger_evidence: suspected Hr-TB with close contact to known Hr-TB case without lab confirmation
fact_text: In suspected Hr-TB cases without lab confirmation, start (H) REZ-levofloxacin regimen; modify based on DST results: stop levofloxacin if isoniazid susceptible in new cases, continue with 6HREZ in retreatment cases.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: 6 months
fact_text: For rifampicin-susceptible and isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB), the recommended regimen is rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin for 6 months.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
trigger_evidence: MDR/RR-TB patients with confirmed rifampicin resistance
no documented or suspected resistance to shorter regimen drugs except isoniazid resistance
no prior exposure to shorter regimen drugs >1 month
no extensive or severe extra-pulmonary TB
dose_or_duration: Intensive phase 4-6 months; continuation phase fixed 5 months; total 9-11 months
contraindications_or_cautions: exclude pregnancy
exclude extensive/severe extra-pulmonary TB
fact_text: Shorter MDR/RR-TB regimen (STR) is recommended for eligible patients with confirmed rifampicin resistance, no extensive TB, not pregnant, and children ≥6 years; regimen includes bedaquiline, levofloxacin, clofazimine, ethionamide, ethambutol, high dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide; duration 9-11 months with intensive phase 4-6 months and continuation phase 5 months.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Allowed modifications to shorter all-oral bedaquiline MDR-TB regimen include prolonging initial phase up to 6 months if sputum smear/culture remains positive at 4 months, substituting prothionamide for ethionamide, and substituting moxifloxacin for levofloxacin.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Bedaquiline is used for a fixed duration of 6 months in MDR-TB regimens, taken daily for the first 2 weeks then three times weekly for the remaining 22 weeks (total 24 weeks).

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If a patient on shorter all-oral bedaquiline MDR-TB regimen requires, they can be transferred later to the longer MDR-TB regimen.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Longer MDR/RR-TB regimens are recommended for patients with extensive TB disease, severe extrapulmonary TB, additional resistance to fluoroquinolones or exposure to second-line drugs >1 month, or those ineligible for shorter all-oral regimens.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Patients on shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing MDR-TB regimens should not have regimen composition or duration changed except for specific allowed modifications.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Recommended longer MDR-TB regimens for quinolone resistant patients: 6 months Bdq-Dlm-Lzd-Cfz-Z-Cs / 14 months Lzd-Cfz-Z-Cs.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Recommended longer MDR-TB regimens for quinolone susceptible patients: 6 months Bdq-Lzd-Lfx-Cfz-Z / 14 months Lzd-Lfx-Cfz-Z.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: The continuation phase of the all-oral shorter MDR-TB regimen contains 4 drugs: levofloxacin, clofazimine, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide for 5 months.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: The initial phase of the shorter all-oral MDR-TB regimen lasts 4 to 6 months and includes bedaquiline, levofloxacin, ethionamide, clofazimine, and pyrazinamide.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: In longer MDR/RR-TB regimens, all three Group A agents and at least one Group B agent should be included to ensure at least four effective TB agents at treatment start; if only one or two Group A agents are used, both Group B agents must be included; Group C agents are added if Groups A and B agents cannot be used alone.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Kanamycin and Capreomycin are no longer recommended for use in longer MDR-TB regimens.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
source_section: Grouping of medicines recommended for use in longer MDR-TB regimens
fact_text: Longer MDR-TB regimens group medicines into Group A (Levofloxacin or Moxifloxacin, Bedaquiline, Linezolid), Group B (Clofazimine, Cycloserine or Terizidone), and Group C (Ethambutol, Delamanid, Pyrazinamide, Imipenem-Cilastatin or Meropenem, Amikacin or Streptomycin, Ethionamide or Prothionamide, P-Aminosalicylic Acid).
source_figure_or_table: Grouping of medicines recommended for use in longer MDR-TB regimens

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: The BPaL regimen (Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, Linezolid) is a 6-9 month novel treatment regimen for XDR-TB, pre-XDR, intolerant and non-responsive MDR-TB patients with less than 2 weeks prior exposure to Bedaquiline and Linezolid, used under operational research conditions with ethical approval and patient-centered care.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Adverse effects are a common reason for treatment interruption and must be detected early and managed promptly.
fact_text: Early detection and management of adverse effects is critical to prevent TB treatment interruption.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Use of fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) and shorter treatment courses improves adherence by reducing pill burden and treatment duration.
fact_text: Fixed-dose combinations and shorter treatment courses improve TB treatment adherence by simplifying regimens.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Good treatment adherence is essential for relapse-free cure and to prevent treatment failure or drug resistance.
fact_text: Good treatment adherence is essential to prevent relapse, treatment failure, and drug resistance in TB patients.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Patient comfort, reasonable clinic waiting times, and adequate accommodations improve adherence.
Good patient-health care worker relationship enhances adherence by increasing trust and communication.
Free care including visits, tests, and treatment reduces financial barriers and treatment abandonment.
Co-management of HIV and TB with coordinated services reduces visits and waiting times, improving patient satisfaction and outcomes.
fact_text: Patient comfort, good patient-health worker relationship, free care, and coordinated HIV-TB services improve TB treatment adherence.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Socioeconomic, psychological, and patient perception factors influence adherence and should be addressed individually during patient visits.
fact_text: Socioeconomic, psychological, and patient perception factors affect TB treatment adherence and require case-by-case solutions.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: A package of treatment adherence interventions may be offered to TB patients alongside selection of suitable treatment administration options.
fact_text: A package of treatment adherence interventions may be offered to TB patients alongside selection of suitable treatment administration options.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Health education and counselling on TB disease and treatment adherence should be provided to all TB patients and family members to ensure treatment success and prevent drug resistance.
fact_text: Health education and counselling on TB disease and treatment adherence should be provided to all TB patients and family members to ensure treatment success and prevent drug resistance.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Psychological support should be provided to TB patients to encourage treatment adherence and disclosure of treatment issues.
fact_text: Psychological support should be provided to TB patients to encourage treatment adherence and disclosure of treatment issues.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Social support measures such as assistance with disability allowances, housing, and shelter should be implemented for TB patients with limited resources.
fact_text: Social support measures such as assistance with disability allowances, housing, and shelter should be implemented for TB patients with limited resources.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Hospitalization may be necessary for severe TB cases or complications when ambulatory treatment is not feasible.
referral_criteria: Severe haemoptysis
Spontaneous pneumothorax
TB meningitis
Cardiac tamponade
Other serious associated diseases
fact_text: Hospitalization is indicated for severe TB complications such as severe haemoptysis, spontaneous pneumothorax, TB meningitis, cardiac tamponade, or other serious diseases when ambulatory treatment is not possible.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Medical officers and paramedics must identify and record the DOT provider's name and address on the patient's treatment card and ensure the provider receives the filled-up Treatment Card and drugs at specified intervals.
fact_text: DOT provider details must be recorded on the patient's treatment card and the provider must receive treatment cards and drugs regularly.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: DOT providers can be facility or community-based health workers, including trained community members such as TB & Leprosy Control Assistants, assistant health inspectors, health assistants, community health workers, Shasthya shebikas, village doctors, community leaders, and cured patients.
Non-medical DOT providers must be supervised at least monthly.
fact_text: DOT providers include trained health workers and community members; non-medical providers require monthly supervision.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Directly Observed Treatment (DOT) is essential to ensure correct and complete TB treatment by observing patients swallow their drugs at the right dose, interval, and duration.
followup_monitoring: DOT provides opportunity for early detection of adverse drug reactions and patient counselling.
All patients, regardless of treatment category, should receive all anti-TB drug doses under DOT.
fact_text: DOT requires an observer to watch the patient swallow anti-TB drugs to ensure correct dosing and adherence, essential for treatment success and early adverse reaction detection.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: DOTS providers must ensure patients swallow drugs as prescribed and take prompt action to trace patients missing doses to prevent loss to follow-up.
Patients missing three consecutive doses must be traced immediately and resumed on DOT without delay.
Priority tracing is for smear-positive pulmonary TB patients.
followup_monitoring: Detailed patient address and valid mobile number should be recorded on the Treatment Card and TB Register to facilitate tracing.
Patients should be encouraged to visit the treatment initiation centre fortnightly during the intensive phase for evaluation of adverse events, prognosis, symptom remission, and weight gain.
fact_text: DOTS providers must trace patients missing doses, especially smear-positive pulmonary TB cases, and encourage fortnightly visits during intensive phase for monitoring.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: If DOT is provided at the patient's registered centre, drugs for the whole treatment course should be kept secured at that centre; drugs should be given for two weeks at a time.
If DOT is provided at a sub-centre or community level, drugs should be given for two to four weeks at a time to the DOT provider until treatment completion.
fact_text: Drug supply to DOT providers should be arranged for two weeks at registered centres or two to four weeks at sub-centres/community level until treatment ends.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If patient cannot come daily to treatment or subcentre but a reliable health worker/DOT provider is available, arrange DOT with trained non-medical provider, provide TB 01 card and drug supply for 1-4 weeks, confirm attendance, and supervise provider monthly.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If the patient can be admitted to hospital for intensive phase treatment, admit and provide DOT in hospital.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If the patient can come to the treatment centre every day, give daily DOT and provide 1 day medicine supply for weekends and public holidays.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If the patient cannot be admitted to hospital for intensive phase treatment, reinforce any available DOT method.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If no reliable health worker/DOT provider is available, communicate with responsible centre person to arrange DOT, ensure TB 01 card and drug supply, and confirm patient attendance at microscopy centre for sputum follow-up.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: If the patient cannot come to the treatment centre daily but can come to subcentre/family welfare centre/community clinic daily, arrange DOT at that centre with TB 01 treatment card and ensure drug supply and attendance at microscopy centre for sputum follow-up.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Close contact is a person not in the household but sharing enclosed space with the index patient for extended periods during the day (e.g., social gathering, workplace).

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Contact investigation is a systematic process to identify undiagnosed TB disease and LTBI among contacts of an index TB patient for testing and treatment.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Contact is any individual exposed to a person with TB disease.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Household contact is a person who shared the same enclosed living space with the index patient for one or more nights or frequent/extended periods.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Index patient (index case) of TB is the initially identified person with new or recurrent TB in a household or comparable setting where contact investigation is centered.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Source case or patient is the original source of infection for secondary cases or contacts but may not be the index case.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Active case finding (ACF) involves health workers or volunteers screening individuals for TB symptoms and contact history using a standard questionnaire; positive symptom screening leads to further investigation and treatment.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Contact investigation identifies people exposed to infectious TB to find active TB cases and latent TB infection (LTBI) for treatment.
Contact investigation aims to prevent TB transmission in households and communities, including drug-resistant TB (MDR-TB, XDR-TB).
Close follow-up of contacts of MDR-TB and XDR-TB patients is important to prevent further spread.
fact_text: Contact investigation is a systematic process to identify and evaluate contacts of TB patients for active TB and LTBI, including drug-resistant TB contacts, to provide appropriate treatment and prevent transmission.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: TB preventive treatment (TPT) is offered to individuals at risk of developing TB disease to reduce that risk; it is also called LTBI treatment.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Contact investigation should include all household and close contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB cases; clinically diagnosed pulmonary TB cases should also be included when possible.
Contact investigation should focus on household and close contacts but also consider workplace and other exposure settings.
Contact investigation should start when a presumptive TB case is confirmed bacteriologically positive pulmonary TB, evaluating all household and close contacts.
Index TB cases should be interviewed within 1 week of diagnosis to identify household and close contacts for contact investigation.
Household contacts are defined as persons living in the same home as the TB patient, sharing at least one meal per day.
Close contacts include persons spending prolonged time closely with the TB patient regularly, such as coworkers or friends.
fact_text: Contact investigation must include all household and close contacts of bacteriologically confirmed TB cases and clinically diagnosed pulmonary TB cases when possible, with prompt interview of index case and evaluation of contacts.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Contact investigation forms (CI forms) are initiated by TLCA/DOT centers for each bacteriologically confirmed TB patient; one form per index case.
For multiple patients in one family, separate CI forms are used for each patient.
Drug-resistant TB contact investigation forms are yellow; drug-susceptible TB forms are white.
TLCA/DOT corner fills upper portion of CI form and hands over forms to HI/HI In-charge to distribute to government and NGO field staff.
Health Assistants conduct household visits monthly or weekly to collect further contact information.
fact_text: Contact investigation uses standardized CI forms initiated by TLCA/DOT centers, with color coding for drug-resistant and drug-susceptible TB, and involves coordination between TLCA, HI, and field staff for household visits and data collection.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Community health workers or DOT providers must visit the home of the index TB case to collect information and screen household and close contacts for symptoms, referring symptomatic contacts (adult and child) to government or NGO clinics for evaluation.
All asymptomatic contacts of index drug-susceptible TB cases should be referred for further evaluation and initiation of TB preventive treatment (TPT) at government or NGO clinics.
Only symptomatic contacts of index drug-resistant TB cases should be referred for further evaluation to diagnose possible TB or drug-resistant TB.
Referral slips must be issued to contacts by health assistants or community health workers, and communication with DOT providers should ensure timely referrals.
Contact investigation forms must be returned and preserved at treatment units where contacts are evaluated by physicians.
Contact investigation registers should be maintained and countersigned monthly by UH&FPO, with quarterly reports sent to the National TB Program.
Contact investigation of hospitalized drug-resistant TB patients should be done promptly post-admission under supervision of UH&FPO through TLCA.
NGO workers and managers are responsible for ensuring proper implementation, recording, and reporting of contact investigation.
fact_text: Symptomatic contacts of DR TB cases and all contacts of DS TB cases require referral and evaluation; contact investigation must be documented, supervised, and reported by designated health staff and NGOs.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Contact investigation data must be collected in standardized forms and registers.
National TB control program routinely evaluates contact investigation effectiveness and designs interventions to improve performance.
Data collection supports management and follow-up of index cases and contacts, and epidemiological analysis.
Field level UHFPO is responsible for implementation, recording, reporting, and review of contact investigation data.
HA, HI, AHI, DOTS providers, and TLCA coordinate to ensure prompt visits, referral of symptomatic and asymptomatic contacts for evaluation.
At minimum, collect number of contact investigations, contacts identified by age and sex, contacts completing evaluation, TB cases identified, and contacts started on preventive treatment.
fact_text: Contact investigation data collection and coordination among health staff is essential for monitoring and improving TB contact management and preventive treatment initiation.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Household contacts of pulmonary bacteriologically positive TB patients undergo symptom screening.
Symptomatic contacts are referred to health facility for rule out of TB.
If TB disease is confirmed, treat according to National Guideline.
If no TB disease, consider for TB preventive treatment (TPT).
Asymptomatic contacts are managed according to LTBI algorithm.
fact_text: Household contacts of pulmonary bacteriologically positive TB patients should be symptom screened; symptomatic contacts referred for TB rule out and treatment if confirmed, asymptomatic managed per LTBI algorithm.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Latent TB infection (LTBI) is defined as persistent immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without clinical evidence of active TB disease.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Emphasis on testing and treatment for LTBI in special conditions such as prisoners and co-workers
fact_text: Priority groups for LTBI testing and treatment include PLHIV, TB contacts <5 or ≥60 years, diabetics, CKD, anti-TNF therapy, transplant candidates, silicosis, smokers, substance abusers, and special conditions like prisoners and co-workers.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_tests: Tuberculin skin test (TST) using standardized PPD of recommended strength
recommended_advice: Individuals should be asked about symptoms of TB before testing
fact_text: LTBI testing can be done by TST or IGRA; IGRA should not replace TST and neither test differentiates active from latent TB; symptom screening is required before testing.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Risk factors for LTBI include diabetes, clinical vulnerabilities, CKD, anti-TNF treatment, transplantation, silicosis, smoking, and substance abuse.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Algorithm for LTBI diagnosis: For PLHIV and bacteriologically positive household contacts, symptom screening and chest X-ray are used; TST/IGRA is used if no symptoms and no risk factors; clinical evaluation confirms TB or no TB; initiate TPT if no active TB.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Adherence to full course and completion of LTBI preventive treatment is critical for clinical benefit to the individual and success of the program.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Preventive therapy (TPT) is not recommended for contacts of drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) patients in NTP Bangladesh due to limited quality of evidence.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: For adults >15 years, LTBI treatment regimen 3HP consists of fixed-dose combination tablets of Isoniazid 300 mg plus Rifapentine 300 mg once weekly for 12 weeks (3 months).
fact_text: For adults >15 years, LTBI treatment regimen 3HP consists of fixed-dose combination tablets of Isoniazid 300 mg plus Rifapentine 300 mg once weekly for 12 weeks (3 months).

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: For all adults with PLHIV, LTBI treatment regimen 6H consists of Isoniazid 300 mg daily dose for 180 days (6 months).
fact_text: For all adults with PLHIV, LTBI treatment regimen 6H consists of Isoniazid 300 mg daily dose for 180 days (6 months).

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: For children <10 years, LTBI treatment regimen 3RH consists of Rifampicin 75 mg plus Isoniazid 50 mg daily dose for 90 days (3 months) with weight band dosing.
fact_text: For children <10 years, LTBI treatment regimen 3RH consists of Rifampicin 75 mg plus Isoniazid 50 mg daily dose for 90 days (3 months) with weight band dosing.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
dose_or_duration: For children aged >10 to <15 years, LTBI treatment regimen 3RH consists of Rifampicin 10 mg/kg/day plus Isoniazid 10 mg/kg/day daily dose for 90 days (3 months) with weight band dosing.
fact_text: For children aged >10 to <15 years, LTBI treatment regimen 3RH consists of Rifampicin 10 mg/kg/day plus Isoniazid 10 mg/kg/day daily dose for 90 days (3 months) with weight band dosing.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
source_section: Table 12.4 Treatment options for LTBI (weight band dosing)
dose_or_duration: Isoniazid and Rifampicin (75/50 mg) dosing for children by weight band: 4-7 kg = 1 tab, 8-11 kg = 2 tabs, 12-15 kg = 3 tabs, 16-24 kg = 4 tabs, >25 kg = adult dose.
fact_text: Isoniazid and Rifampicin (75/50 mg) dosing for children by weight band: 4-7 kg = 1 tab, 8-11 kg = 2 tabs, 12-15 kg = 3 tabs, 16-24 kg = 4 tabs, >25 kg = adult dose.
source_figure_or_table: Table 12.4 Treatment options for LTBI (weight band dosing)

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Baseline laboratory testing is mandatory before LTBI treatment for individuals with risk factors (liver disease, alcohol use, HIV, pregnancy, postpartum period) and routine periodic testing if baseline abnormalities exist.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Isoniazid adverse reactions include asymptomatic elevation of liver enzymes, peripheral neuropathy, and hepatotoxicity; Rifampicin and Rifapentine can cause cutaneous reactions, hypersensitivity, gastrointestinal intolerance, and hepatotoxicity.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: TB/HIV collaborative activities aim to reduce HIV-associated TB mortality and morbidity through coordination between National AIDS/STD Program and National Tuberculosis Control Program.
fact_text: Collaborative TB/HIV activities in Bangladesh focus on coordination between TB and HIV programs to reduce TB mortality and morbidity in people living with HIV.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Key TB/HIV collaborative activities include intensified case finding, isoniazid preventive therapy, infection control, provider initiated testing and counseling (PITC), cotrimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT), and HIV treatment and care.
fact_text: TB/HIV collaboration includes intensified case finding, isoniazid preventive therapy, infection control, PITC, CPT, and HIV treatment support.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Implementation strategy for TB/HIV collaboration in Bangladesh includes establishing functional collaboration between NTP, NASP, and partners, integrating TB/HIV services into existing programs, and generating national evidence for burden and interventions.
fact_text: TB/HIV collaboration strategy includes functional coordination, service integration, and evidence generation for implementation.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: PLHIV diagnosed with TB should start TB treatment immediately and be closely monitored by both HIV and TB programs with regular documented follow-up and DOT.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: All HIV-positive patients, suspected TB cases among high-risk groups, and immediate family/partners/contacts of HIV-positive patients should be referred for TB screening.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: In 23 high priority districts, all TB and drug-resistant TB cases should be screened for HIV.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: In other districts, HIV screening is recommended for TB patients with high-risk behavior, complicated EPTB, relapse, treatment failure, clinical HIV suspects, children of HIV-positive mothers, and DR TB patients.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: Patients screening positive for HIV should be referred to the nearest ART center for confirmation, registration, and initiation of ART.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
fact_text: All PLHIV and MDR TB patients should be screened for TB and HIV respectively using rapid diagnostic tools (Xpert MTB/RIF) at least once a year or at treatment initiation.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
contraindications_or_cautions: active tuberculosis
diagnosis and treatment of TB in past 3 years
poor prognosis (terminally ill AIDS patients)
history of poor compliance with treatment
active hepatitis (chronic or acute)
fact_text: Contraindications for TPT include active TB, TB symptoms, abnormal chest X-ray, recent TB treatment (<3 years), poor prognosis, poor treatment compliance history, and active hepatitis.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: Same day ART and TPT initiation is recommended for newly diagnosed PLHIV on ART who are eligible
PLHIV on ART not yet on TPT should be screened for TB at every visit and started on TPT as soon as eligible
PLHIV who completed TB treatment should be assessed for TPT initiation immediately after completing TB treatment
All TPT recipients must have their treatment recorded in TPT/IPT register and patient-held records
TPT status should be recorded in HIV patient care booklet
An outcome should be given to all patients registered for TPT
fact_text: TPT initiation and monitoring in PLHIV includes same-day ART and TPT start, regular TB screening, documentation in registers and patient records, and outcome reporting.

source_title: National Guideline and Operational Manual for Tuberculosis 2021
recommended_advice: patient must be motivated and convinced to complete full TPT course after counseling on benefits, side effects, and risks
contraindications_or_cautions: history of alcoholism
history of active liver disease, liver insufficiency, or jaundice
unwell or unexplained illness

Intracellularly, abacavir is converted by cellular enzymes to the active metabolite carbovir triphosphate, an analogue of deoxyguanosine-5'-triphosphate (dGTP). Viral DNA growth is terminated because the incorporated nucleotide lacks a 3'-OH group, which is needed to form the 5â€² to 3â€² phosphodiester linkage essential for DNA chain elongation.

Although some increase in pulse pressure occurs, there is usually no great elevation in mean blood pressure. Clavulanic acid possesses the ability to inactivate a wide range of beta-lactamase enzymes commonly found in microorganisms resistant to penicillins and cephalosporins. Thus Clavulanic acid in this preparation protects Amoxicillin from degradation by (3-lactamase enzymes and effectively extends the antibiotic spectrum to embrace a wide range of microorganisms.

The pharmacokinetics of the two components of Co-amoxiclav is closely matched. Peak serum levels of both occur about one hour after oral administration. Absorption of Co-amoxiclav is optimized at the start of a meal. Both clavulanate and Amoxicillin have low levels of serum binding; about 70% remains free in the serum. Doubling the dosage of Co-amoxiclav approximately doubles the serum levels achieved.

Canagliflozin is indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Canagliflozin is an inhibitor of subtype-2 sodium-glucose co-transport protein (SGLT2), which is responsible for at least 90% of the glucose reabsorption in the kidney. Blocking this transporter reduces the reabsorption of glucose from renal tubules, leading to more excretion of glucose in urine.

Candesartan Cilexetil-Hydrochlorothiazide combines an angiotensin II receptor blocker, Candesartan Cilexetil and a diuretic, Hydrochlorothiazide.

Candesartan blocks the vasoconstrictor and aldosterone-secreting effects of angiotensin II by selectively blocking the binding of angiotensin II to the AT1 receptor in many tissues (eg, vascular smooth muscle, adrenal gland).
Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic. Thiazides affect the renal tubular mechanisms of electrolyte reabsorption, directly by increasing sodium excreation.

the diuretic action of hydrochlorothiazide reduces plasma volume with consequent increase in plasma renin activity, aldosterone secretion, urinary potassium loss, and decrease in serum potassium.

Capecitabine is a prodrug that is selectively tumour-activated to its cytotoxic moiety, fluorouracil, by thymidine phosphorylase, an enzyme found in higher concentrations in many tumours compared to normal tissues or plasma.
Capecitabine is a prodrug, that is enzymatically converted to fluorouracil (antimetabolite) in the tumour, where it inhibits DNA synthesis and slows growth of tumour tissue.

FdUMP and the folate cofactor, N 5-10 methylenetetrahydrofolate, bind to thymidylate synthase (TS) to form a covalently bound ternary complex. This binding inhibits the formation of thymidylate from 2-deoxyuridylate. Thymidylate is the necessary precursor of thymidine triphosphate, which is essential for the synthesis of DNA, therefore a deficiency of this compound can inhibit cell division.
Fluorouracil is further metabolized to two active metabolites, 5-fluoro-2'-deoxyuridine 5-monophosphate (FdUMP) and 5-fluorouridine triphosphate (FUTP), within normal and tumour cells.

Nuclear transcriptional enzymes can mistakenly incorporate FUTP in place of uridine triphosphate (UTP) during the synthesis of RNA. This metabolic error can interfere with RNA processing and protein synthesis through the production of fraudulent RNA.

Carbetocin is indicated for the prevention of uterine atony and postpartum haemorrhage (excessive bleeding) following delivery of the infant by elective caesarean section under epidural or spinal anaesthesia.

Carbetocin is a drug used to control postpartum hemorrhage, bleeding after giving birth. It is an analogue of oxytocin, and its action is similar to that of oxytocin; it causes contraction of the uterus. Carbetocin binds to oxytocin receptors present on the smooth musculature of the uterus, resulting in rhythmic contractions of the uterus, increased frequency of existing contractions, and increased uterine tone.

Carbocisteine is indicated for- Acute bronchitis, Chronic bronchitis, Bronchial asthma, Upper respiratory tract inflammation (pharyngitis, laryngitis), Cystic fibrosis Bronchiectasis, Pulmonary tuberculosis, Drainage in chronic sinusitis and pneumonia, Drainage in otitis media in children.

Carbocisteine reduces goblet cell hyperplasia and therefore plays a role in the management of disorders characterised by abnormal mucous. Carbocisteine loosens thick sputum effectively by reducing its viscosity and thereby helps to expectorate that mucus more easily from the respiratory tract. The mucolytic action happens in several mechanisms. It breaks the disulphide bonds, which cross-link certain glycoprotein molecules in the mucus, the mucus produced under the influence of Carbocisteine has high sialomucin and low fucomucin content. This combined effect ultimately reduces the viscosity of the sputum and increases its volume.

Carboprost tromethamine administered intramuscularly stimulates in the gravid uterus myometrial contractions similar to labor contractions at the end of a full term pregnancy.

Carboprost tromethamine also stimulates the smooth muscle of the human gastrointestinal tract. This activity may produce the vomiting or diarrhea or both that is common when carboprost tromethamine is used to terminate pregnancy and for use postpartum.

Cephalosporins are bactericidal and have the same mode of action as other beta-lactam antibiotics (such as penicillins). Cephalosporins disrupt the synthesis of the peptidoglycan layer of bacterial cell walls. The peptidoglycan layer is important for cell wall structural integrity, especially in Gram-positive organisms. The final transpeptidation step in the synthesis of the peptidoglycan is facilitated by transpeptidases known as penicillin binding proteins (PBPs).

The transpeptidase enzyme that performs this step is inhibited by penicillins and cephalosporins. As a result the bacterial cell wall is weakened, the cell swells and then ruptures. Clotrimazole acts primarily by damaging the permeability barrier in the cell membrane of fungi. Clotrimazole causes inhibition of ergosterol biosynthesis, an essential constituent of fungal cell membranes. If ergosterol synthesis is either completely or partially inhibited, the cell is no longer able to construct an intact and functional cell membrane. Because ergosterol directly promotes the growth of fungal cells in a hormone-like fashion, rapid onset of the above events leads to dose-dependent inhibition of fungal growth.

Though decreased ergosterol, due to the inhibition of lanosterol 14-demethylase (also known as CYP51) is accepted to be primarily responsible for the antimycotic properties of clotrimazole, this drug also shows other pharmacological effects. These include the inhibition of sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca 2+ ATPase, depletion of intracellular calcium, and blocking of calcium-dependent potassium channels and voltage-dependent calcium channels.

Atrophic vaginitis and Kraurosis Vulvae associated with estrogen deficiency. In the absence of estrogen stimulation, the vulvar and vaginal tissues shrink, the vaginal walls become thin and dry, and rugal folds disappear. Tenderness and pruritus, with resulting dysuria and dyspareunia, may occur. Fissures and ulcerations of tissue with spotting or bleeding may result from coitus. These changes are reversible with the administration of estrogen replacement therapy.

Estrogen replacement therapy is indicated in hypoestrogenism related to female hypogonadism or primary ovarian failure. Primary ovarian failure starting early in life will lead to delayed closure of the epiphyses and retarded bone maturation. Long term estrogen deficiency in any age group will usually lead to osteoporosis (for efficacy with estrogen replacement therapy see osteoporosis). Estrogen therapy is associated with the appearance of female characteristics in these patients.

Estrogen replacement therapy is the most effective single modality for the prevention of osteoporosis (loss of bone mass) in postmenopausal women. Estrogen reduces bone resorption and retards or halts postmenopausal bone loss. One clinical study demonstrated that even when estrogen was started as late as fifteen years after menopause, further loss of bone mass was prevented but no restoration of bone mass was observed. The effect on bone mass conservation is sustained only as long as conjugated estrogen therapy is continued.

Estrogens are important in the development and maintenance of the female urogenital system and secondary sex characteristics. They promote growth and development of the vagina, uterus, and fallopian tubes, and enlargement of the breasts. Indirectly, they contribute to the shaping of the skeleton, maintenance of tone and elasticity of urogenital structures, changes in the epiphyses of the long bones associated with the pubertal growth spurt and its termination, growth of axillary and pubic hair, and pigmentation of the nipples and genital tissues. However, in the preovulatory or anovulatory cycle, estrogen is the primary determinant in the onset menstruation. Eestrogen also affects the release of pituitary gonadotropins. The pharmacologic effects of conjugated estrogens are similar to those of endogenous estrogens. In responsive tissues (female urogenital organs, breasts, hypothalamus, pituitary) estrogens enter the cell and are transported into the nucleus. As a result of estrogenic activity, specific RNA and protein synthesis occurs.

After menopause, most endogenous estrogen is produced by conversion of androstenedione, which is secreted by the adrenal cortex, to estrone in the peripheral tissues. Thus, estrone and the sulfate-conjugated form, estrone sulfate, are the most abundant circulating estrogen in postmenopausal women.

Circulating estrogens modulate the pituitary secretion of the gonadotropins, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), through a negative feedback mechanism. Estrogens act to reduce the elevated levels of these gonadotropins seen in postmenopausal women.
Endogenous estrogens are largely responsible for the development and maintenance of the female reproductive system and secondary sexual characteristics.
Estrogens act through binding to nuclear receptors in estrogen-responsive tissues. To date, two estrogen receptors have been identified. These vary in proportion from tissue to tissue.
The primary source of estrogen in normally cycling adult women is the ovarian follicle, which secretes 70 to 500 mcg of estradiol daily, depending on the phase of the menstrual cycle.
estradiol is the principal intracellular human estrogen and is substantially more potent than its metabolites, estrone and estriol, at the receptor level.

Daunorubicin in combination with other approved anticancer drugs is indicated for remission induction in acute nonlymphocytic leukemia (myelogenous, monocytic, erythroid) of adults and for remission induction in acute lymphocytic leukemia of children and adults.

Daunorubicin has antimitotic and cytotoxic activity through a number of proposed mechanisms of action. It forms complexes with DNA by intercalation between base pairs. It inhibits topoisomerase II activity by stabilizing the DNA- topoisomerase II complex, preventing the religation portion of the ligation- religation reaction that topoisomerase II catalyzes. Single strand and double-strand DNA breaks result. It may also inhibit polymerase activity, affect the regulation of gene expression, and produce free radical damage to DNA.

Daunorubicin is extensively metabolized in the liver and other tissues, mainly by cytoplasmic aldo-keto reductases, producing daunorubicinol, the major metabolite which has antineoplastic activity. Approximately 40% of the drug in the plasma is present as daunorubicinol within 30 minutes and 60% in 4 hours after a dose of Daunorubicin. Further metabolism via reduction cleavage of the glycosidic bond, 4-O demethylation, and conjugation with both sulfate and glucuronide have been demonstrated. Simple glycosidic cleavage of Daunorubicin or Daunorubicinol is not a significant metabolic pathway in man. Twenty-five percent of an administered dose of Daunorubicin is eliminated in an active form by urinary excretion and an estimated 40% by biliary excretion.

Daunorubicin is rapidly and widely distributed in tissues, with the highest levels in the spleen, kidneys, liver, lungs and heart. The drug binds to many cellular components, particularly nucleic acids. There is no evidence that it crosses the blood-brain barrier, but the drug apparently crosses the placenta.

The mechanism of the anti-inflammatory activity of the topical corticosteroids, in general, is unclear. However, corticosteroids are thought to act by the induction of phospholipase A2 inhibitory proteins collectively called lipocortins. It is postulated that these proteins control the biosynthesis of potent mediators of inflammation such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes by inhibiting the release of their common precursor, arachidonic acid. Arachidonic acid is released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2.

Corticosteroids inhibit the inflammatory response to a variety of inciting agents and may delay or slow healing. They inhibit edema, fibrin deposition, capillary dilation, leukocyte migration, capillary proliferation, fibroblast proliferation, deposition of collagen, and scar formation associated with inflammation. There is no generally accepted explanation for the mechanism of action of ocular corticosteroids. However, corticosteroids are thought to act by the induction of phospholipase A2 inhibitory proteins, collectively called lipocortins. It is postulated that these proteins control the biosynthesis of potent mediators of inflammation such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes by inhibiting the release of their common precursor arachidonic acid. Arachidonic acid is released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2. Difluprednate is structurally similar to other corticosteroids.

Docetaxel is an antineoplastic agent, which acts by disrupting the microtubular network in cells that is essential for vital mitotic and interphase cellular functions. Docetaxel promotes the assembly of tubulin into stable microtubules while simultaneously inhibiting their disassembly. Docetaxel binds to free tubulin thereby decreasing the critical intracellular concentration of tubulin. The promoted polymerization of microtubules leads to the production of microtubule bundles without normal function and to the stabilization of microtubules, resulting in the inhibition of mitosis in cells. The binding of Docetaxel to microtubules does not alter the number of protofilaments in the bound microtubules; in that, it differs from other spindle poisons.

Esomeprazole (S-isomer of omeprazole) is the first single optical isomer of proton pump inhibitor, provides better acid control than racemic proton pump inhibitors.

Esomeprazole capsules contain an enteric-coated pellet formulation of esomeprazole magnesium. After oral administration peak plasma levels (C max ) occur at approximately 1.5 hours (T max ). The C max increases proportionally when the dose is increased, and there is a three-fold increase in the area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) from 20 to 40 mg. At repeated once daily dosing, the systemic bioavailability is approximately 90% compared to 64% after a single dose. The AUC after administration of a single dose of esomeprazole is decreased by 33-53% after food intake compared to fasting conditions. Esomeprazole should be taken at least one hour before meals.

Esomeprazole is 97% bound to plasma proteins. Plasma protein binding is constant over the concentration range of 2 20 mmol/L. The apparent volume of distribution at steady state in healthy volunteers is approximately 16 L.
Esomeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that suppresses gastric acid secretion by specific inhibition of the H+/K+-ATPase in the gastric parietal cell.

Esomeprazole is extensively metabolized in the liver by the cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme system. The metabolites of esomeprazole lack anti-secretory activity. The major part of esomeprazoleâ€™s metabolism is dependent upon the CYP2C19 isoenzyme, which forms the hydroxy and desmethyl metabolites. The remaining amount is dependent on CYP3A4 which forms the sulphone metabolite.

Esomeprazole magnesium 40 mg once daily is given in combination with clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily and amoxicillin 1000 mg twice daily for 7 days. The mean steady state AUC and Cmax of Esomeprazole increased by 70% and 18%, respectively, during triple combination therapy compared to treatment with Esomeprazole alone. The pharmacokinetic parameters for clarithromycin and amoxicillin are similar during triple combination therapy and administration of each drug alone. However, the mean AUC and Cmax for 14-hydroxyclarithromycin are increased by 19% and 22%, respectively, during triple combination therapy compared to treatment with clarithromycin alone. This increase in exposure to 14-hydroxyclarithromycin is not considered to be clinically significant.

The plasma elimination half-life of esomeprazole is approximately 1â€“1.5 hours. Less than 1% of parent drug is excreted in the urine. Approximately 80% of an oral dose of esomeprazole is excreted as inactive metabolites in the urine, and the remainder is found as inactive metabolites in the faeces.

corticosteroids are thought to act by the induction of phospholipase A2 inhibitory proteins, collectively called lipocortins. It is postulated that these proteins control the biosynthesis of potent mediators of inflammation such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes by inhibiting the release of their common precursor, arachidonic acid. Arachidonic acid is released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2. Their primary target is the cytosolic glucocorticoid receptor. After binding the receptor the newly formed receptor-ligand complex translocates itself into the cell nucleus, where it binds to many glucocorticoid response elements (GRE) in the promoter region of the target genes. The DNA bound receptor then interacts with basic transcription factors, causing the increase in expression of specific target genes.
