fact_text: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is treated with anti-complement C5 monoclonal antibodies eculizumab and ravulizumab, which reduce haemolysis, transfusion needs, and thrombosis risk; these therapies require vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis due to increased infection risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Sickle-cell disorder results from polymerisation of deoxygenated HbS molecules causing red cell membrane distortion and irreversible sickling.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Painful vaso-occlusive crisis is the most common acute complication of sickle-cell disorder, characterized by bone marrow vessel plugging causing severe bone pain and systemic features including tachycardia and fever.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Stroke or silent stroke occurs in 10-15% of children and adolescents with sickle-cell disorder and about 25% of patients by age 45; screening with transcranial Doppler ultrasound for increased velocity (>200 cm/s) identifies children at risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Sickle-cell disorder causes multisystem complications including ocular (retinopathy, vitreous bleeds), pulmonary (chest syndrome, infection, pulmonary hypertension), renal (haematuria, papillary necrosis, chronic renal failure), bone (dactylitis, osteomyelitis, avascular necrosis), CNS (stroke, subarachnoid bleed, fits), cardiac (cardiomegaly, sickle myocardium, iron overload), and splenic infarction.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Sickle-cell trait is common in tropical Africa (>20%) and African American populations (~8%) and confers relative resistance to falciparum malaria in childhood.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Blood film shows numerous sickle-shaped red cells, confirming sickling.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Electrophoresis gel shows presence of HbS band in sickle-cell disorder compared to normal HbA band.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Haemoglobin C disorder is associated with microcytosis and target cells on blood film; compound heterozygotes for HbS and HbC genes have a milder sickle-cell disorder phenotype.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation in selected patients with matched siblings
referral_criteria: Consider referral for allogeneic stem cell transplantation in patients with matched siblings
fact_text: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation from HLA-matched siblings is potentially curative for sickle-cell disorder and has been performed safely in selected patients, with ongoing monitoring for graft-versus-host disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Simple top-up transfusion or exchange transfusion in selected cases
admission_criteria: Indication for exchange transfusion includes life-threatening crises or preparation for surgery in patients with low HbF levels
fact_text: Management of vaso-occlusive crises in sickle-cell disorder includes aggressive rehydration, oxygen therapy, adequate analgesia often with opiates, and antibiotics; simple top-up or exchange transfusion with ABO-compatible, extended Rhesus and Kell-matched units is indicated in selected cases, especially with recurrent severe complications or cerebrovascular accidents.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: P-selectin inhibitor crizanlizumab to reduce vaso-occlusive crises
fact_text: P-selectin inhibitor crizanlizumab is licensed to reduce vaso-occlusive crises in sickle-cell disorder but is rarely used outside Europe and post-marketing surveillance is ongoing.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Folic acid 5 mg daily throughout pregnancy and postpartum
Hydroxycarbamide discontinued 3 months prior to conception
Discontinue ACE inhibitors prior to conception
Thromboprophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin for at least 10 days post vaginal delivery and 6 weeks post caesarean section
Transfusion with ABO-compatible, extended Rhesus and Kell-matched units at minimum, blood should be cytomegalovirus-negative
dose_or_duration: Folic acid 5 mg daily; Hydroxycarbamide stopped 3 months before conception; Aspirin 75 mg daily throughout pregnancy; Heparin thromboprophylaxis at least 10 days post vaginal delivery and 6 weeks post caesarean
recommended_advice: Pre-conceptual counselling on sickle-cell disorder effects in pregnancy
Vaccination status should be updated before conception
Testing of partner for haemoglobinopathy status is advised
contraindications_or_cautions: Pulmonary hypertension must be excluded before conception
Placental failure risk increased in sickle-cell disorder
fact_text: In pregnancy with sickle-cell disorder, pre-conceptual counselling, vaccination update, partner testing, and folic acid 5 mg daily throughout pregnancy and postpartum are recommended; hydroxycarbamide and ACE inhibitors should be stopped before conception; aspirin 75 mg daily is advised throughout pregnancy; thromboprophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin is recommended for at least 10 days post vaginal delivery and 6 weeks post caesarean; transfusion with ABO-compatible, extended Rhesus and Kell-matched, cytomegalovirus-negative blood is required.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Alpha-thalassaemia diagnosis depends on number of alpha gene deletions on chromosome 16: 1 deletion causes no clinical effect; 2 deletions cause mild hypochromic anaemia; 3 deletions cause haemoglobin H disease; 4 deletions cause stillbirth (hydrops fetalis).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Beta-thalassaemia major diagnosis includes profound hypochromic anaemia, severe red cell dysplasia, erythroblasts presence, absent or grossly reduced haemoglobin A, raised haemoglobin F, and parental evidence of thalassaemia minor.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Beta-thalassaemia minor diagnosis includes mild anaemia, microcytic hypochromic erythrocytes without iron deficiency, presence of target cells, punctate basophilia, and raised haemoglobin A2 fraction.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Haematological malignancies arise from uncontrolled proliferation, differentiation, or apoptosis of blood cells due to acquired mutations in key regulatory genes, with mature differentiated cells producing indolent neoplasms and primitive stem/progenitor cells producing aggressive leukaemias.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Leukaemias are malignant disorders of white cell lineage with increased malignant cells in bone marrow and/or peripheral blood; clinical course varies from days to years depending on type.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 24.46 Haematological malignancy in old age
fact_text: Median age for haematological malignancies is ~70 years; older patients have poorer prognosis due to adverse cytogenetics and resistance; chemotherapy is less well tolerated; cure rates are lower; treatment decisions should consider biological status, comorbidities, patient and family wishes rather than chronological age alone.
source_figure_or_table: Box 24.46 Haematological malignancy in old age

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Iron therapy is contraindicated in beta-thalassaemia major due to risk of iron overload.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) from HLA-compatible sibling
Regular transfusion to maintain haemoglobin >100 g/L
fact_text: Beta-thalassaemia major treatment includes allogeneic HSCT from HLA-compatible sibling, gene editing therapy (experimental), regular transfusions to maintain Hb >100 g/L, and daily folic acid 5 mg.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Splenectomy may be required in beta-thalassaemia major to manage splenomegaly causing mechanical problems and excessive transfusion needs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 24.45 Consequences of haematological malignancy in adolescence
fact_text: Adolescents with leukaemia and lymphoma require tailored management protocols differing from children and adults, with treatment preferably in specialist centres; psychosocial effects may be significant and require multidisciplinary support; late effects from chemotherapy and radiotherapy include growth, cognitive, fertility, and secondary malignancy risks requiring lifelong follow-up.
source_figure_or_table: Box 24.45 Consequences of haematological malignancy in adolescence

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Treatment of haemoglobin H disease is similar to beta-thalassaemia of intermediate severity, including iron supplementation if required and avoiding iron therapy unless iron deficiency is confirmed.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Acute leukaemia diagnosis requires blast cells to be more than 20% of bone marrow cells according to WHO 5th edition and International Consensus Classification.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Leukaemias are classified into four main groups: acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), and chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 24.47 WHO 5th edition classification of acute leukaemia
fact_text: WHO 5th edition classification of acute leukaemia includes: acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) with defining genetic abnormalities, AML defined by differentiation, and acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) subdivided into B-lymphoblastic and T-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma.
source_figure_or_table: Box 24.47 WHO 5th edition classification of acute leukaemia

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Acute leukaemia incidence is highest in children aged 1-5 years and young adults, with chronic leukaemias more common in middle and old age.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Acute leukaemias involve proliferation of mutated haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells with limited accumulation of differentiated cells, leading to bone marrow failure.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cytotoxic drugs, especially alkylating agents, topoisomerase II inhibitors, and industrial exposure to benzene, increase leukaemia risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Genetic factors including identical twins with leukaemia, Down syndrome, other genetic syndromes, and familial single gene disorders (e.g., GATA-2, RUNX1 mutations) increase leukaemia risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Immunological factors such as immune deficiency states (e.g., hypogammaglobulinaemia) are risk factors for leukaemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Incidence of all leukaemia types is about 10 per 100,000 per year, with acute leukaemia more common in males (ratio 3:2 for AML, 2:1 for ALL).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ionising radiation exposure (e.g., atomic bombing, radiotherapy, diagnostic X-rays in pregnancy) is a risk factor for leukaemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Retroviruses such as adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma virus 1 (HTLV-1) are associated with T-cell lymphoproliferative disorders in endemic areas.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diagnosis of acute leukaemia requires abnormal blood count with abnormal white cell count and confirmation by bone marrow examination including morphology, immunophenotyping, cytogenetics, and molecular studies.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In acute leukaemia, the malignant clone can be myeloid or lymphoid lineage; lymphoid leukaemias derive from lymphoid progenitor cells (B and T cells), myeloid leukaemias from myeloid progenitors (red cells, granulocytes, monocytes, platelets).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: WHO ICC classification includes a new category of AML with myelodysplasia-related changes (MDS/AML) defined by some chromosomal and genetic variants with blast counts between 10% and 19%.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Despite raised white cell counts, neutropenia with blast cells predominating is common; severe thrombocytopenia is usual but not invariant.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bone marrow examination is essential to confirm acute leukaemia diagnosis; marrow is usually hypercellular with variable replacement of normal elements by leukaemic blast cells.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Blood count in acute leukaemia usually shows anaemia with normal or raised mean corpuscular volume (MCV); leukocyte count varies widely from very low (<1 x 10^9/L) to very high (>300 x 10^9/L), often below 100 x 10^9/L.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Presence of Auer rods (coalesced granules) in cytoplasm of blast cells indicates myeloblastic type of acute leukaemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Initial AML diagnosis includes history, full blood count, blood film, bone marrow biopsy showing ≥20% blasts and dysplasia, immunophenotyping (CD34 30%, CD33 and CD13 positive), cytogenetics (monosomal karyotype -5, -7, -13), and molecular testing for FLT3 and NPM1 mutations.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) myeloid gene panel is used to detect multiple TP53 mutations to confirm AML-myelodysplasia related diagnosis per WHO 2022 criteria.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Assess and start tumour lysis risk prevention with fluids and allopurinol or rasburicase before therapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Before specific therapy in acute leukaemia, assess comorbidities, performance status, cardiac function (especially before anthracycline use), and treat existing infections including oral and skin infections.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Consider early clinical trial entry for patients starting specific therapy for acute leukaemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Correct anaemia with red cell transfusion and control thrombocytopenic bleeding with platelet transfusions before starting therapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Explain therapy regimen clearly to the patient and obtain informed consent before starting treatment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: If remission is not achieved with induction chemotherapy, alternative drug combinations may be tried, but prognosis remains poor unless remission is attained.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Insert a central venous catheter (e.g., PICC or Hickman line) if possible to facilitate delivery of chemotherapy, fluids, blood products, and supportive drugs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Intensive treatment of acute leukaemia should not be attempted without adequate supportive care, including blood product support and infection management, as this is essential for improved survival.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with acute leukaemia should be treated within a clinical trial when possible; treatment decisions depend on subtype, patient fitness, and comorbidities, with a treatment plan formed after a week of information gathering.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Relapse after treatment or hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) has poor prognosis and is difficult to treat; further treatment may be effective but is often palliative to reduce leukocyte proliferation and maintain quality of life.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The primary treatment goal in acute leukaemia is eradication of the leukaemic clone without destroying normal stem cells, enabling repopulation of haematopoietic tissues.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: AML treatment is increasingly tailored to genetic abnormalities or measurable residual disease; the first decision is whether to give specific treatment to achieve remission.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Consolidation treatment for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia includes daunorubicin IV, cytarabine IV, etoposide IV, methotrexate IV, and oral imatinib or dasatinib if Philadelphia chromosome-positive.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Induction treatment for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia includes vincristine IV, dexamethasone oral, L-asparaginase IM, daunorubicin IV, intrathecal methotrexate, oral imatinib (if Philadelphia chromosome-positive), and blinatumomab.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Maintenance treatment for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia includes prednisolone oral, vincristine IV, mercaptopurine oral, methotrexate oral, and oral imatinib or dasatinib if Philadelphia chromosome-positive.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Relapse treatment for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia includes fludarabine IV, cytarabine IV, idarubicin IV, blinatumomab, and gilteritinib.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Consolidation treatment for acute myeloid leukaemia includes cytarabine IV, amsacrine IV, and mitoxantrone IV.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Induction treatment for acute myeloid leukaemia includes daunorubicin IV, cytarabine IV, Vyxeos liposomal IV, etoposide IV and oral, gemtuzumab ozogamicin IV, all-trans retinoic acid oral, arsenic trioxide IV, midostaurin oral, quizartinib oral, azacitidine oral, venetoclax oral, and ivosidenib oral.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Maintenance treatment for acute myeloid leukaemia includes azacitidine oral, midostaurin oral, and quizartinib oral.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Relapse treatment for acute myeloid leukaemia includes fludarabine IV, cytarabine IV, arsenic trioxide IV, idarubicin IV, and gilteritinib.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Azacitidine is used alone or with venetoclax for AML patients unfit for intensive chemotherapy, given in 28-day cycles; venetoclax combinations are myelosuppressive and require careful monitoring.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: FLT3 inhibitors midostaurin and quizartinib are used in combination with chemotherapy and as maintenance therapy in AML with FLT3 mutations; gilteritinib inhibits mutant FLT3 and is used alone for relapsed patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Remission consolidation in AML involves 1–2 courses of high-dose cytosine arabinoside after remission induction; this reduces relapse risk and is standard for patients fit for further chemotherapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Remission induction in AML aims to kill most tumour cells using chemotherapy combinations; daunorubicin with cytosine arabinoside is standard, given for 7–10 days in 1–2 cycles. Patients with good or standard risk karyotype benefit from adding gemtuzumab ozogamicin, an antibody-drug conjugate targeting CD33, delivering calicheamicin to induce DNA damage.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Remission maintenance therapy in AML is a recent development; maintenance with oral azacitidine improves survival in some patients compared to no maintenance, especially in those not undergoing allogeneic HSCT or with FLT3-mutated AML receiving midostaurin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), favourable cytogenetic risk (promyelocytic leukaemia t(15;17)) has a 5-year survival of 90%, adverse risk (cytogenetic abnormalities -5, -7, del 5q, abn(3q), complex >5) has 21%, and intermediate risk (AML with none of the above) has 48%.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In ALL, adverse risk features include Philadelphia chromosome, high white count >100 x 10^9/L, and abnormal short arm of chromosome 11 (t1;19), with 5-year survival of 20%; standard risk (ALL with none of these) has 37% 5-year survival.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The presence of minimal residual disease (MRD) after treatment is a powerful prognostic indicator in acute leukaemia and guides subsequent consolidation therapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Frequent monitoring of fluid balance, renal, hepatic, and haemostatic function is necessary during acute leukaemia treatment due to common side effects and risk of tumour lysis syndrome.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: HSCT is less effective in patients with isolated FLT3-ITD mutations, which are considered a contraindication for transplant in first remission.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Allogeneic HSCT offers a 5-year survival of 20%-50% in high-risk acute leukaemia patients and is most effective in patients under 70 years with normal karyotype and no NPM1 gene mutations.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Allopurinol and intravenous hydration are used to prevent renal failure from tumour lysis syndrome in acute leukaemia patients at high risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Neutropenic sepsis in acute leukaemia requires empirical antibiotic therapy guided by severity and local resistance; high-risk cases need combination therapy including aminoglycosides and broad-spectrum penicillins or carbapenems.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Oral and pharyngeal Candida infections in acute leukaemia patients are treated with fluconazole; systemic Candida infections require intravenous amphotericin B, caspofungin, or voriconazole for up to 3 weeks.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Prophylactic rasburicase is used in tumour lysis syndrome for acute leukaemia patients with white cell count >100 x 10^9/L to reduce uric acid levels.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia during chemotherapy for acute leukaemia is recommended using co-trimoxazole.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Reactivation of herpes simplex infection in acute leukaemia patients is treated with aciclovir; prophylactic aciclovir is recommended for patients with history of cold sores or low antibody titres.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder from mutated stem cells causing proliferation mainly in granulocytic lineage, with normal blood cell maturation and no bone marrow failure; peak incidence at 55 years, rare with UK incidence 1.8/100,000.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The defining characteristic of CML is the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph), a shortened chromosome 22 from reciprocal translocation with chromosome 9, creating the BCR-ABL fusion gene encoding a tyrosine kinase causing abnormal cell proliferation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Blast crisis in CML is defined by transformation to acute leukaemia (myeloid or lymphoblastic, ~30%), is relatively refractory to treatment, and survival depends on timing of blast crisis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: CML natural history is classically divided into three phases: chronic phase (responsive to treatment, lasting 3-5 years), accelerated phase (disease control more difficult), and blast crisis (acute leukaemia transformation, refractory to treatment).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: BCR-ABL fusion gene detection by molecular techniques (PCR) is diagnostic for CML, especially when conventional karyotyping does not detect the Philadelphia chromosome.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hepatomegaly occurs in about 50% of CML patients; lymphadenopathy is unusual.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with very high white cell count (>300 x 10^9/L) may have symptoms of hyperviscosity including headache, visual changes, somnolence, confusion, hypoxia, and bleeding.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Splenomegaly is present in 90% of CML patients; about 10% have massive enlargement (>15 cm below costal margin).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Symptoms at CML presentation may include lethargy, weight loss, abdominal discomfort, sweating; about 25% are asymptomatic at diagnosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Full blood count in CML shows variable results; usually normocytic normochromic anaemia, leukocyte count from 10 to 600 x 10^9/L, and about one-third have high platelet count, sometimes >2000 x 10^9/L.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, and bosutinib are tyrosine kinase inhibitors used in CML treatment targeting BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase domain.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) target the BCR-ABL fusion protein's tyrosine kinase activity, blocking phosphorylation and downstream signalling, reversing CML pathogenesis and leading to leukemic cell death.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: BCR::ABL1 quantitative PCR for transcript levels
fact_text: Molecular response in CML is monitored by quantitative BCR::ABL1 PCR with milestones: 10% transcript at 3 months (MR1), 1% at 6 months (MR2), 0.1% at 12 months (MR3/MMR), 0.01% at any time (MR4), and 0.001% (MR5) indicating deep molecular response.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with TKI resistance or T315I mutation may benefit from asciminib (STAMP inhibitor) or allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Second-line TKIs: imatinib, nilotinib, dasatinib, bosutinib, ponatinib
contraindications_or_cautions: Ponatinib recommended for patients with T315I kinase domain mutations
fact_text: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors for CML treatment include first-line agents imatinib, nilotinib, and dasatinib; second-line agents include imatinib, nilotinib, dasatinib, bosutinib, and ponatinib; third-line agent is asciminib (STAMP inhibitor). Ponatinib is specifically recommended for patients with T315I kinase domain mutations.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chronic phase CML treatment aims to normalize blood counts and achieve complete cytogenetic response within 3-6 months, defined as disappearance of the Philadelphia chromosome in 90% of patients, using first-line TKIs nilotinib or dasatinib or imatinib.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In accelerated phase or blast crisis CML, second- or third-generation TKIs, hydroxycarbamide, interferon, and FLAG-Ida chemotherapy are used; consolidation therapy includes dexamethasone and cytarabine, with palliative options for older patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In accelerated phase or blast crisis of CML, treatment is more difficult; nilotinib, dasatinib, or ponatinib are frequently used, and blast crisis requires treatment as lymphoblastic or myeloblastic leukaemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with CLL should be vaccinated against pneumococcus and influenza and receive annual influenza and COVID-19 vaccinations to reduce infection risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Clinical stage A (60% patients): no anaemia or thrombocytopenia and fewer than three areas of lymphoid enlargement.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Clinical stage B (30% patients): no anaemia or thrombocytopenia but three or more involved areas of lymphoid enlargement.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Clinical stage C (10% patients): anaemia and/or thrombocytopenia regardless of the number of areas of lymphoid enlargement.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In CLL, history should include symptoms of anaemia, infections, painless lymphadenopathy, systemic symptoms such as night sweats or weight loss, as these may indicate advanced disease or transformation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Disruption of TP53 gene by deletion or mutation is a poor prognostic marker in CLL and predicts resistance to chemotherapy; TP53 status should be assessed before treatment initiation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Somatic hypermutation status of the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene (IGHV) is a prognostic marker in CLL; mutated IGHV (≥2% variation) predicts better prognosis than unmutated cases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diagnosis of CLL requires peripheral blood findings of mature lymphocytosis >5 × 10^9/L with characteristic morphology and immunophenotyping showing monoclonal B cells expressing CD19, CD20, CD23, and either kappa or lambda light chains, with characteristic aberrant T-cell antigen CD5 co-expression.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Flow cytometry is required to confirm CLL diagnosis and to distinguish it from other lymphoproliferative disorders; some patients may have circulating CLL cells at levels <5 × 10^9/L, which requires further assessment for monoclonal B lymphocytosis of uncertain significance (MBL).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: BTK inhibitors have varying degrees of bleeding risk, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and heart failure; acalabrutinib and zanubrutinib may have fewer side effects than ibrutinib but require ongoing therapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In younger fit patients, immunochemotherapy with FCR (fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, rituximab) may be used; in older or frailer patients, BR (bendamustine, rituximab) or ChO (chlorambucil, obinutuzumab) are options, especially if TP53 is not disrupted.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Initial therapy in the UK for CLL is universally chemotherapy-free, using two approaches: continuous therapy with oral BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib) or fixed duration therapy with oral BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax combined with anti-CD20 antibody obinutuzumab.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Targeted therapies for CLL include BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib) that block BCR signaling, PI3K inhibitor idelalisib, BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax inducing apoptosis, and anti-CD20 antibodies rituximab and obinutuzumab used with chemotherapy or venetoclax to enhance cell killing.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Venetoclax-based therapies are given for fixed duration or until disease progression; venetoclax is effective but increases risk of infections, cytopenias, and immunosuppression, and requires careful monitoring for tumour lysis syndrome, especially at initiation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: No specific treatment is required for most clinical stage A CLL patients unless disease progression occurs; patients should be informed about the indolent nature of CLL and reassured.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Treatment is offered for symptomatic or progressive CLL with evidence of bone marrow failure, massive or progressive lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly, systemic symptoms such as weight loss or night sweats, or rapidly increasing lymphocyte count, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia or thrombocytopenia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MDS prognosis is classified by IPSS-R scoring into five groups with median survival 0.5 to >5 years; high-risk patients have median survival 1-1.5 years; IPSS-M includes mutation data and improves risk stratification.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MDS must be differentiated from aplastic anaemia and other causes of bone marrow failure.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MDS presents with bone marrow failure signs including anaemia, recurrent infections, or bleeding; blood film shows cytopenias with dysplastic cells and hypogranular neutrophils; bone marrow is hypercellular with dysplastic changes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: bone marrow biopsy and cytogenetic analysis
mutation analysis for SF3B1 and TP53
fact_text: MDS diagnosis requires bone marrow hypercellularity with dysplastic changes in ≥10% of cells, blasts <20%, and mutation analysis including SF3B1 and TP53; chromosome 5 or 7 abnormalities worsen prognosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: single cycle
fact_text: Hairy cell leukaemia treatment includes a single cycle of cladribine chemotherapy, which can produce long-lasting remissions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) for anaemia in low-risk MDS
avoid_medicines: unlicensed ESA treatments such as erythropoietin-beta and darbepoetin
fact_text: For low-risk MDS, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) are first-line treatment for anaemia; licensed erythropoietin-alpha is preferred; unlicensed ESAs like erythropoietin-beta and darbepoetin are less effective and may delay transfusion dependency.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: alemtuzumab intravenous for T-PLL and BTK inhibitors for B-cell origin PLL
fact_text: Alemtuzumab given intravenously produces responses in about 90% of patients with T-PLL; BTK inhibitors produce responses in B-cell origin PLL; younger patients responding to treatment are considered for allogeneic HSCT.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hodgkin lymphoma is slow-growing, localized, and rarely fatal; nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL is a low-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma subtype with distinct histology and clinical course.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosis requires lymph node biopsy showing Reed-Sternberg cells, which are large malignant B-cells often surrounded by reactive non-malignant cells.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hodgkin lymphoma peak incidence is at 18-35 years; typical clinical features include painless, rubbery lymphadenopathy in the neck, supraclavicular fossae, and mediastinum.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Non-Hodgkin lymphomas are classified as low- or high-grade based on proliferation rate; high-grade lymphomas progress rapidly over weeks and may be life-threatening, while low-grade lymphomas progress slowly over months to years and often disseminate widely.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Lymphomas are neoplasms of lymphocyte lineage cells, involving a more mature lymphocyte stage than acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, diagnosed by lymph node biopsy, with B-cell lymphomas comprising the majority and T-cell lymphomas about 10% of Western cases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MDS classification includes categories based on blast percentage, cytogenetics, and mutations: MDS with defining genetic abnormalities (e.g., MDS with low blasts and isolated 5q deletion, MDS with SF3B1 mutation, MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation) and MDS morphologically defined by blast count and marrow fibrosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MDS morphologically defined categories include MDS with low blasts (<5% BM and <2% PB), hypoplastic MDS, MDS with increased blasts (MDS-IB1: 5-9% BM or 2-4% PB; MDS-IB2: 10-19% BM or 5-19% PB or Auer rods), and MDS with fibrosis (5-19% BM; 2-19% PB).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R) for MDS stratifies risk into five categories (very low, low, intermediate, high, very high) based on blast percentage, cytogenetics, and blood counts, correlating with median survival and progression to acute myeloid leukemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: consider referral for HSCT in suitable patients
referral_criteria: good performance status
high-risk MDS (IPSS-R high and very high)
contraindications_or_cautions: not suitable for some intermediate- and low-risk patients, especially older with marked cytopenias or transfusion dependence
fact_text: Allogeneic HSCT may cure patients with high-risk MDS and good performance status; it is less suitable for some intermediate- and low-risk older patients with marked cytopenias or transfusion dependence.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: azacitidine improves survival by median 9 months compared to supportive care or low-intensity chemotherapy
fact_text: Azacitidine, a hypomethylating agent, improves survival in high-risk MDS patients not eligible for transplantation, extending median survival by 9 months compared to supportive care or low-intensity chemotherapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
contraindications_or_cautions: benefit of adding venetoclax to azacitidine in high-risk MDS is unproven
fact_text: The addition of venetoclax to azacitidine in high-risk MDS is not yet proven beneficial and remains under investigation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) is recommended for short-term use in neutropenic MDS patients with active infection.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Lenalidomide, an immunomodulatory drug, is effective in a rare MDS subtype with isolated del(5q), inducing transfusion independence in about two-thirds of patients for up to 2 years.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with low-risk MDS on long-term red cell transfusions may benefit from iron chelation therapy, most conveniently with oral deferasirox.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Lymph node architecture includes distinct zones: mantle, marginal, paracortex, medulla, and germinal centre; B cells reside in follicles and are selected for antigen in follicle centres; errors in this process can cause B-cell lymphomas, the most common lymphoma type.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Early erythropoiesis stages are regulated by erythropoietin (EPO), while later stages are negatively regulated by TGF-β superfamily ligands via Smad2/3 pathway; Luspatercept binds these ligands to allow erythropoiesis progression and mature red blood cell production.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hodgkin lymphoma aetiology is unknown but is more common in patients with a history of infectious mononucleosis or small family size; a definitive causal link to Epstein–Barr virus is not proven.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hodgkin lymphoma incidence is approximately 4 new cases per 100,000 population per year, with a slight male predominance (1.5:1), except nodular sclerosis subtype which is more common in females; median age at diagnosis is 31 years with two peaks at 20–35 and 50–70 years.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hodgkin lymphoma lymph node biopsy shows large Reed–Sternberg cells with two nuclei and prominent eosinophilic nucleoli, characteristic for diagnosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In Hodgkin lymphoma, lymph nodes may fluctuate in size; young patients with nodular sclerosis subtype often have large mediastinal masses that may be asymptomatic or cause cough and breathlessness; disease spreads contiguously to adjacent lymph nodes and can involve the diaphragm.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Splenomegaly may be present in Hodgkin lymphoma but does not always indicate disease involvement and can be reactive; extranodal disease is rare but can involve bone, brain, or skin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Systemic symptoms in Hodgkin lymphoma include drenching night sweats, fever, and loss of 10% body weight (B symptoms); other symptoms can include pruritus and rarely, pain after alcohol consumption in involved lymph nodes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ann Arbor classification stages Hodgkin lymphoma as: Stage I - single lymph node region or extralymphatic site; Stage II - two or more lymph node regions on same side of diaphragm; Stage III - lymph node regions on both sides of diaphragm with possible extralymphatic involvement; Stage IV - diffuse involvement of one or more extralymphatic tissues such as liver or bone marrow. Each stage is subclassified as A (no systemic symptoms) or B (weight loss >10%, drenching sweats, fever).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: WHO 5th edition pathological classification of Hodgkin lymphoma divides HL into nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL (5% of HL) and classical HL, with classical HL subtypes nodular sclerosing (70%), mixed cellularity (20%), lymphocyte-rich (5%), and lymphocyte-depleted (rare).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: A negative FDG PET-CT after two cycles of ABVD predicts a very good outcome and may allow reduction of chemotherapy cycles to four, reducing lung toxicity risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chest X-ray is used to detect mediastinal masses; a bulky disease defined as >10 cm in a single nodal mass or mediastinal mass > one-third of chest X-ray diameter is an adverse prognostic feature.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) may be raised and is an adverse prognostic factor in Hodgkin lymphoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Full blood count may be normal; presence of normochromic normocytic anaemia or lymphopenia is a poor prognostic factor, especially in advanced disease. Eosinophilia, neutrophilia, or thrombocytosis may be present.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: LDH may be raised in Hodgkin lymphoma and is an adverse prognostic factor.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Liver function tests may be abnormal in Hodgkin lymphoma due to hepatic infiltration or disease and should be assessed.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Lymph node biopsy is essential for diagnosis and should be performed under radiological guidance.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Positron emission tomography–CT (PET-CT) scanning is standard for staging Hodgkin lymphoma, identifying involved nodes and allowing more accurate staging and monitoring of early and end-of-treatment responses.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Renal function tests are required to ensure safe treatment and may be abnormal due to disease or hepatic infiltration.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Long-term toxicity from radiotherapy in Hodgkin lymphoma includes infertility and treatment-related secondary malignancies, necessitating judicious use.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: ABVD regimen (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) remains standard treatment in the UK; more intensive regimens like BEACOPP or BEACOPDAC are more effective but have increased risks of infertility and treatment-related malignancies.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Early-stage Hodgkin lymphoma patients with additional risk factors such as bulky disease or high ESR require four cycles of ABVD chemotherapy without radiotherapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Standard therapy for early-stage Hodgkin lymphoma without additional risk factors is two cycles of ABVD chemotherapy combined with 20 Gy radiotherapy to involved sites.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Careful planning of radiotherapy is required in early-stage Hodgkin lymphoma to limit doses to normal tissues and reduce long-term toxicity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Standard treatment for advanced-stage Hodgkin lymphoma is 6–8 cycles of ABVD chemotherapy followed by response assessment with FDG PET-CT.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Treatment aims to maintain maximum cure rates while minimizing long-term treatment-related toxicity in young and middle-aged patients with Hodgkin lymphoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: Patients treated with ABVD should have cardiac and pulmonary follow-up due to doxorubicin and bleomycin toxicity risks
fact_text: Patients treated with ABVD chemotherapy require cardiac and pulmonary follow-up to monitor for late toxicities from doxorubicin and bleomycin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
trigger_evidence: female patients receiving breast irradiation during chest treatment
recommended_advice: Participate in breast cancer screening programs after chest irradiation
Continue breast screening after completing irradiation due to increased breast cancer risk
fact_text: Young women receiving breast irradiation during Hodgkin lymphoma treatment have increased breast cancer risk and should participate in ongoing breast cancer screening programs after completing irradiation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The Hasenclever prognostic index for advanced Hodgkin lymphoma uses age >45, male sex, serum albumin <40 g/L, hemoglobin <105 g/L, stage IV disease, WBC >15 x10^9/L, and lymphocytes <0.6 x10^9/L to stratify 5-year progression-free and overall survival rates.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: FDG PET-CT scan after 2 cycles of ABVD chemotherapy to assess treatment response
fact_text: Interim FDG PET-CT scan after 2 cycles of ABVD chemotherapy is recommended to assess treatment response in Hodgkin lymphoma; PET-2 negativity predicts better 5-year progression-free survival and guides therapy intensification or de-escalation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: adult-onset still disease, ra, periodic fever syndromes
condition_aliases: adult-onset still disease, ra, periodic fever syndromes
recommended_medicines: {"dose": "100 mg daily SC", "drug": "Anakinra", "indications": "Adult-onset Still disease, RA (rare), periodic fever syndromes", "mechanism_of_action": "Decoy receptor for IL-1; neutralizes IL-1α and IL-1β"}
dose_or_duration: Most frequent use is for adult-onset Still disease and periodic fever syndromes; rarely used in RA
contraindications_or_cautions: Not licensed for RA except when other drugs are ineffective
fact_text: Anakinra, an IL-1 receptor antagonist given 100 mg daily SC, is mainly used for adult-onset Still disease and periodic fever syndromes; it is rarely used in RA and not licensed for RA except when other drugs fail.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition

fact_text: Mepolizumab and benralizumab are IL-5 inhibitors used in EGPA; mepolizumab is given 300–400 mg SC every 8 weeks, benralizumab 30 mg SC every 4 weeks; adverse effects include headache and increased infection risk.

fact_text: ABVD chemotherapy is standard first-line treatment for early-stage Hodgkin lymphoma; four cycles with negative interim PET-2 scan predict good 5-year progression-free survival. Bleomycin pulmonary toxicity risk is higher in elderly; BEACOPP/DAC regimen is not suitable for patients over 60 or with comorbidities.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition

recommended_medicines: Autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) for patients failing initial chemotherapy or relapsing within 1 year
referral_criteria: Refer patients failing initial chemotherapy or relapsing within 1 year for autologous HSCT evaluation
fact_text: Autologous HSCT is recommended for Hodgkin lymphoma patients who fail initial chemotherapy or relapse within 1 year; salvage chemotherapy and achieving FDG PET-CT negativity before transplant improve outcomes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Brentuximab vedotin antibody-drug conjugate targeting CD30 for relapsed or refractory Hodgkin lymphoma
fact_text: Brentuximab vedotin, an anti-CD30 antibody-drug conjugate, is used for relapsed or refractory Hodgkin lymphoma patients who have failed or are unsuitable for autologous HSCT and can serve as a bridge to allogeneic HSCT.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Immunochemotherapy alone for patients relapsing after 1 year
referral_criteria: Refer relapsed patients for immunochemotherapy and possible HSCT
fact_text: Patients relapsing after 1 year may achieve long-term survival with immunochemotherapy alone; those who respond frequently proceed to autologous HSCT.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Immune checkpoint inhibitors pembrolizumab and nivolumab for refractory Hodgkin lymphoma
fact_text: Pembrolizumab and nivolumab, immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting PD-1, are effective in patients with refractory Hodgkin lymphoma after multiple treatment failures and may become future treatment options.

fact_text: Ustekinumab is a combined IL-12/IL-23 inhibitor given 45 mg SC every 12 weeks for PsA; monitor for infections, hypersensitivity, and neutropenia.

fact_text: Rituximab is indicated for RA and ANCA-associated vasculitis with 1000 mg IV every 6–12 months; treatment can be repeated when improvement wanes. Monitor for hypogammaglobulinaemia, infusion reactions, infections including PML, and JC virus reactivation.
