source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 24.60 Epidemiology and aetiology of non-Hodgkin lymphoma
fact_text: NHL incidence is about 12 new cases per 100,000 people per year, with a slight male predominance and median age at diagnosis 65–70 years.
source_figure_or_table: Box 24.60 Epidemiology and aetiology of non-Hodgkin lymphoma

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) is a monoclonal proliferation of lymphoid cells, mostly B-cell (90%) and some T-cell (10%), with incidence increasing with age and an overall rate rising about 3% per year since the 1970s.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Histology of NHL shows low-grade follicular or nodular pattern and high-grade diffuse pattern, aiding pathological classification.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: NHL is classified by cell lineage (B or T cells), histology, and genetic features; high-grade NHL has high proliferation, rapid symptom onset, and is fatal if untreated but potentially curable, whereas low-grade NHL has low proliferation, may be asymptomatic for months or years, often disseminated at diagnosis, and is less curable by conventional therapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 24.60 Epidemiology and aetiology of non-Hodgkin lymphoma
fact_text: NHL aetiology includes no single cause; it is a late manifestation of HIV infection and associated with viruses such as Epstein-Barr virus, human herpesvirus 8, and human T-cell lymphotropic virus-1; gastric lymphoma may be linked to Helicobacter pylori infection; some chromosomal translocations (e.g., t(14;18), t(11;14)) dysregulate oncogenes c-myc and BCL-2, promoting malignant proliferation.
source_figure_or_table: Box 24.60 Epidemiology and aetiology of non-Hodgkin lymphoma

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 24.60 Epidemiology and aetiology of non-Hodgkin lymphoma
fact_text: NHL occurs more frequently in congenital immunodeficiency states and in immunosuppressed patients after organ transplantation.
source_figure_or_table: Box 24.60 Epidemiology and aetiology of non-Hodgkin lymphoma

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 24.40 Massive axillary lymphadenopathy in NHL
fact_text: Massive axillary lymphadenopathy with high-grade diffuse large B-cell lymphoma may present with visible large lymph node masses and skin changes.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 24.40 Massive axillary lymphadenopathy in NHL

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with NHL often present with widespread lymphadenopathy including extranodal sites, systemic symptoms such as weight loss, fever, sweats, and itching, and may have hepatosplenomegaly.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The International Prognostic Index (IPI) for high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma assigns one point each for: age > 60 years, ECOG performance status > 1, Ann Arbor stage III or IV, more than one extranodal site, and presence of LDH above normal.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Measurement of urate levels is recommended in very high-grade NHL to prevent tumour lysis syndrome by starting treatment before urate levels rise.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cytogenetic analysis to detect chromosomal translocations, especially rearrangements of oncogene c-MYC and partners including BCL2, is recommended in Hodgkin lymphoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: For Hodgkin lymphoma, bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy should be performed to identify bone marrow involvement.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: HIV testing is recommended in lymphoma patients as HIV is a risk factor and affects treatment decisions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hepatitis B and C testing should be performed prior to therapy with rituximab in lymphoma patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Immunoglobulin determination is useful in some lymphomas as IgG or IgM paraproteins serve as markers for treatment response.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Immunophenotyping of surface antigens is required to distinguish T-cell from B-cell tumours in Hodgkin lymphoma and to assess bone marrow or nodal material involvement.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: R-CHOP chemotherapy (rituximab plus CHOP) is recommended as first-line therapy for all relatively fit patients with high-grade NHL.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with diffuse large B-cell NHL require initial treatment with intravenous combination chemotherapy, typically CHOP regimen (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) plus rituximab.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Rituximab given over two years delays time to chemotherapy by more than ten years in some asymptomatic advanced stage follicular lymphoma patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chemotherapy and immunochemotherapy are mainstays of treatment for advanced stage low-grade NHL.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Monoclonal antibody therapy with humanised anti-CD20 antibody rituximab can be used to target surface antigens on tumour cells and improve durable clinical responses in low-grade NHL.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Radiotherapy is used for localized stage I disease in low-grade NHL, with a 70% cure rate when confirmed by FDG PET-CT.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Rituximab or second-generation anti-CD20 antibody obinutuzumab combined with chemotherapy regimens including cyclophosphamide, vincristine, prednisone, doxorubicin, and bendamustine are commonly used first-line therapies for low-grade NHL.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Maintenance therapy with single-agent rituximab for two years after first or second response may improve progression-free survival in low-grade NHL, but benefit is less clear if only a partial response is achieved.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Most low-grade NHL patients present with advanced disease and have a waxing and remitting course over several years; asymptomatic patients may be managed by watchful waiting without immediate therapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: High-dose chemotherapy and autologous HSCT can produce long remissions in relapsed disease; decisions on timing are complex and depend on disease progression and response to rituximab maintenance.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Targeted therapy with PI3 kinase inhibitor idelalisib is approved for relapsed follicular lymphoma but is rarely used due to toxicity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ibrutinib, a PI3 kinase inhibitor, is approved for relapsed mantle cell lymphoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ibrutinib and zanubrutinib are used in Waldenström macroglobulinaemia and other B-cell malignancies, often combined with chemotherapy or immunotherapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MGUS is defined by presence of a monoclonal immunoglobulin in blood without other myeloma features, with serum paraprotein <15 g/L, bone marrow plasma cells <10%, and no lytic bone lesions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Paraproteinaemias result from overproduction of one or more immunoglobulin classes, often polyclonal in chronic inflammation or monoclonal in conditions like myeloma, amyloidosis, or MGUS.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Waldenström macroglobulinaemia is a low-grade lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgM paraprotein causing hyperviscosity syndrome and systemic symptoms like anaemia, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, headache, bleeding, and neurological disturbances.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Serum free light chain ratio (SFLCr) is abnormal in MGUS patients at higher risk of progression; abnormal SFLCr and serum paraprotein >15 g/L or IgA paraprotein predict increased progression risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with MGUS require long-term monitoring for progression to myeloma or related disorders, with risk stratification based on serum paraprotein level, paraprotein type, and SFLC ratio.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of Waldenström macroglobulinaemia includes plasmapheresis to remove IgM and reduce blood viscosity in patients with hyperviscosity symptoms and anaemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diagnosis of multiple myeloma requires one or more of: increased malignant plasma cells in bone marrow (>10%), serum and/or urinary paraprotein, or skeletal lytic lesions or other end-organ damage such as renal failure.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bone pain, fractures, hypercalcaemia, anaemia or pancytopenia, renal impairment, and spinal cord compression are clinical red flags indicating advanced multiple myeloma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Renal failure in multiple myeloma may be caused by paraprotein deposition, hypercalcaemia, infection, NSAIDs, or amyloid deposition.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Spinal cord compression in multiple myeloma can result from bony collapse or extradural mass and requires urgent assessment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Paraproteinaemia can cause elevated ESR but is non-specific; absence of light chains in urine does not exclude multiple myeloma diagnosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Examination should include assessment for retinal changes (retinal bleeds, engorged veins) indicating hyperviscosity syndrome in multiple myeloma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bence Jones proteinuria is detected by measuring serum free light chains and urine for light chains in multiple myeloma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bone marrow plasmacytosis >10% is a diagnostic criterion for multiple myeloma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: IgG monoclonal protein is the most common subtype in multiple myeloma (55%), followed by light chain only (22%), IgA (21%), and others (2%).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Laboratory abnormalities in multiple myeloma include anaemia (normocytic or macrocytic), pancytopenia, raised ESR, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, paraproteinaemia, and immune paresis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Paraproteinaemia causes elevated ESR but is a non-specific test; absence of immunoglobulin light chains in urine does not exclude diagnosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bone marrow aspiration, plasma and urine electrophoresis, and skeletal survey are required investigations for multiple myeloma diagnosis; MRI is preferred if available for detecting bone lesions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) International Staging System (ISS) for myeloma at diagnosis: Stage I - serum β2-microglobulin <3.5 mg/L and albumin ≥35 g/L; Stage II - not fitting criteria for stage I or III; Stage III - serum β2-microglobulin ≥5.5 mg/L irrespective of albumin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: High-risk asymptomatic myeloma is defined by one or more of: >20% bone marrow plasma cells, serum monoclonal protein >2 g/dL, serum free light chain ratio >20, or International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) stage III.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bortezomib is associated with significant neuropathy including autonomic neuropathy and constipation; treatment should be stopped if paraprotein levels stop falling.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Thalidomide and lenalidomide have anti-angiogenic and immunomodulatory effects but can cause somnolence, constipation, peripheral neuropathy, and thrombosis; lenalidomide has a better side-effect profile but both are teratogenic.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Asymptomatic myeloma patients without end-organ damage may not require immediate treatment but need close monitoring for progression to symptomatic disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Four main drug groups for myeloma management include chemotherapy (steroids, melphalan, anthracyclines, platinum-based drugs), immune modulators (thalidomide, lenalidomide, pomalidomide), targeted antibodies/small molecules (anti-CD38 antibodies daratumumab, isatuximab; anti-SLAMF7 elotuzumab; histone deacetylase inhibitor panobinostat; BiTE antibodies teclistamab, talquetamab), and proteasome inhibitors (bortezomib, carfilzomib, ixazomib).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Immediate supportive care for symptomatic myeloma includes high fluid intake to prevent renal impairment and hypercalcaemia, analgesia for bone pain, bisphosphonates to delay skeletal-related events, allopurinol to prevent urate nephropathy, plasmapheresis if needed, and antibiotic prophylaxis with levofloxacin during the first 3 months of therapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In older patients unsuitable for autologous HSCT, first-line regimens commonly used in the UK include bortezomib (Velcade), thalidomide or lenalidomide with dexamethasone, with or without daratumumab, and melphalan with prednisone and thalidomide or lenalidomide.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Lenalidomide maintenance therapy can prolong remission after autologous HSCT in patients who have achieved maximal response.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Myeloma is incurable and treatment aims to maximize depth and duration of response to improve symptoms and minimize toxicity, thereby prolonging survival and quality of life.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: HLH results from mutations in immune genes (e.g., PRF-1) causing macrophage and histiocyte infiltration, cytokine storm, and pancytopenia; it presents with fever and multisystem involvement and can be secondary to infections, autoimmune diseases, or malignancies.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is the most common histiocytic disorder caused by MAP kinase pathway mutations (e.g., BRAF 65-70%, MAP2K); it presents with bone, skin, or systemic symptoms including lymphadenopathy and eosinophilic granuloma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: High-risk multiple myeloma patients have adverse cytogenetics (e.g., t(4;14), del(17/17p), t(14;16), t(14;20)), non-hyperdiploidy, or gain(1q); these patients have poorer prognosis and may benefit from autologous HSCT and novel therapies.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) ISS staging uses beta-2 microglobulin and albumin levels to classify prognosis; normal albumin and low beta-2 microglobulin (ISS stage I) predict median survival >62 months.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Solitary plasmacytoma diagnosis requires biopsy confirmation of a monoclonal plasma cell tumour and exclusion of disseminated multiple myeloma by staging.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: CT and PET scans can demonstrate bilateral histiocytic infiltration of kidneys in Langerhans cell histiocytosis, with characteristic 'hair on end' renal cortex appearance and intense PET signal correlating with glucose excretion in urine.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients on long-term bisphosphonates require dental review before starting therapy to reduce risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw, especially with poor oral hygiene or gum sepsis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Treatment of HLH is immunosuppressive with glucocorticoids, chemotherapy or ciclosporin, and aims to inhibit cytokine storm and complement activation; allogeneic stem cell transplantation is considered in refractory cases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of LCH includes surgical excision or radiotherapy for isolated lesions and systemic chemotherapy (methotrexate, etoposide, cladribine) for multisystem disease; BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib) show promise in refractory cases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Long-term bisphosphonate therapy reduces bone pain, skeletal events, and may protect against malignant plasma cell progression in multiple myeloma; zoledronate combined with anti-myeloma therapy improves survival.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Radiotherapy is effective for solitary plasmacytomas not responding to simple analgesia and for pathological fractures; it is also used emergently for spinal cord compression from plasmacytomas.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Severity of aplastic anaemia is graded by Camitta criteria including marrow cellularity <25% and at least two of: neutrophils <0.5 x10^9/L, platelets <20 x10^9/L, reticulocytes <20 x10^9/L.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Very severe aplastic anaemia (VSAA) is defined as severe aplastic anaemia with neutrophils <0.2 x10^9/L.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Primary idiopathic acquired aplastic anaemia is a rare disorder caused by autoimmune destruction of pluripotent stem cells leading to bone marrow failure and pancytopenia, with unknown trigger and exclusion of secondary causes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 24.66 Causes of secondary aplastic anaemia
fact_text: Secondary aplastic anaemia can be caused by drugs (e.g., cytotoxic agents, antibiotics, antirheumatics, antithyroid drugs, anticonvulsants, immunosuppressants), chemicals (benzene, organophosphates, insecticides), radiation, viral hepatitis, pregnancy, and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.
source_figure_or_table: Box 24.66 Causes of secondary aplastic anaemia

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diagnosis requires bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy showing hypocellularity; blood tests show pancytopenia and a proportion have abnormal liver function tests indicating autoimmune hepatitis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Addition of eltrombopag to ATG and ciclosporin improves response rates in refractory aplastic anaemia and is used off-license in some patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: First-line treatment for severe aplastic anaemia in young patients (<35 years) is allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: For patients older than 50 years or those unsuitable for HSCT, immunosuppressive therapy with antithymocyte globulin (ATG) and ciclosporin is the treatment of choice.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Non-severe aplastic anaemia patients require supportive care with blood product support and infection management; severe AA patients need immunosuppressive therapy or allogeneic stem cell transplant.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In HHT, patients with pulmonary or cerebral arteriovenous malformations should be considered for embolisation or ablation to reduce bleeding and embolic stroke risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with myelofibrosis require monitoring for transformation to acute leukaemia or myelofibrosis progression, as about 15% develop acute leukaemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with polycythaemia vera require monitoring for cerebrovascular or cardiovascular events, which occur in up to 60% of patients, and for transformation to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Disorders of primary haemostasis involve initial platelet plug formation failure, causing bleeding tendency as seen in thrombocytopenia, platelet function disorders, and vessel wall abnormalities.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Essential thrombocythaemia diagnosis requires exclusion of secondary causes of thrombocytosis and detection of pathogenic JAK-2, V617F, CALR, or MPL mutations; patients typically present around age 60 with vascular occlusion, acral cyanosis, or isolated high platelet count.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in endoglin and activin receptor-like kinase genes, leading to abnormal angiogenesis and arteriovenous malformations in skin, mucosa, lungs, liver, and brain.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with HHT present with recurrent bleeding, especially epistaxis and iron deficiency anaemia from occult gastrointestinal bleeding; treatment is challenging and often requires regular iron therapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Myelofibrosis is characterized by initially hypercellular marrow with excess abnormal megakaryocytes releasing growth factors, leading to marrow fibrosis and extramedullary hematopoiesis, often presenting after age 50 with symptoms of lassitude, weight loss, night sweats, and splenomegaly.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Characteristic blood picture in myelofibrosis includes leucoerythroblastic anemia with circulating immature red blood cells (increased reticulocytes and nucleated red blood cells) and granulocyte precursors, tear-drop shaped red cells, giant platelets, and often high platelet count initially.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Presence of a pathological JAK-2 mutation supports the diagnosis of myelofibrosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Polycythaemia vera mainly affects patients over 40 years and presents with either incidental high haemoglobin or symptoms of hyperviscosity such as lassitude, headaches, dizziness, pruritus, and epistaxis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Vessel wall abnormalities causing bleeding may be congenital (e.g., hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia) or acquired (e.g., vasculitis or scurvy).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bone marrow biopsy in myelofibrosis shows excess megakaryocytes, increased reticulin and fibrous tissue replacement, confirming marrow fibrosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diagnosis of polycythaemia vera requires demonstration of high haematocrit and presence of a pathogenic JAK-2 mutation in over 95% of cases, with exclusion of secondary erythrocytosis causes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In polycythaemia vera, the spleen may be enlarged and marrow and platelet counts frequently raised; bone marrow culture can demonstrate autonomous growth in absence of growth factors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Intravenous radioactive phosphorus (32P) may be used in essential thrombocythaemia but is rarely available and contraindicated in pregnancy and women planning pregnancy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Low-dose aspirin is likely beneficial in essential thrombocythaemia patients with symptoms or vascular events to reduce risk of occlusive events.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Treatment to reduce platelet count in essential thrombocythaemia is not required for low-risk patients (age <40 years, platelet count <1500 x 10^9/L, no bleeding or thrombosis); for higher risk, platelet count reduction with hydroxycarbamide or anagrelide is indicated.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fedratinib, a JAK-2 inhibitor, is effective in patients refractory or intolerant to ruxolitinib, reducing splenomegaly and symptom burden.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Interferon-alfa may be used to suppress marrow proliferation in myelofibrosis but is rarely available nowadays and mainly used in younger patients, pregnant women, and those with low platelet counts.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Treatment options include hydroxycarbamide for symptom control and cytotoxic therapy, with allogeneic HSCT considered for younger patients; ruxolitinib, a JAK-1 and JAK-2 inhibitor, reduces systemic symptoms, splenomegaly, and transfusion requirements and improves survival.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Aspirin reduces thrombosis risk and venesection relieves hyperviscosity symptoms in myelofibrosis; venesection is repeated every 5–7 days until haematocrit is below 45%, then less frequently until JAK-2 negative or iron deficiency develops.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Aspirin reduces thrombosis risk in polycythaemia vera; venesection removes 400-500mL blood to reduce haematocrit below 45%, repeated every 5-7 days until target achieved, then less frequently until JAK-2 negativity or iron deficiency develops.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hydroxycarbamide or interferon-alfa suppress marrow proliferation in polycythaemia vera; hydroxycarbamide is preferred for most patients, interferon-alfa mainly for younger or pregnant patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The JAK-2 inhibitor ruxolitinib is licensed for polycythaemia vera patients who are resistant or intolerant to hydroxycarbamide, improving survival beyond 10 years.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is an immune-mediated disorder with autoantibodies against platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa causing premature platelet removal; spontaneous bleeding usually occurs only when platelet count is below 20 × 10^9/L.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
referral_criteria: Refer urgently if severe or life-threatening bleeding
admission_criteria: Admit for severe or life-threatening bleeding
fact_text: In ITP, severe, life-threatening, or mucosal bleeding are danger signs requiring urgent referral and admission.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Bone marrow examination in patients over 65 years or if malignancy or connective tissue disease suspected
HIV testing due to implications for therapy
fact_text: In ITP, bone marrow examination is recommended in patients over 65 years or if malignancy or connective tissue disease is suspected; HIV testing should be performed due to treatment implications.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) can raise platelet count by blocking antibody receptors on reticulo-endothelial cells and is used in severe haemostatic failure or before splenectomy
referral_criteria: Consider referral for splenectomy in patients with severe bleeding or failure of medical therapy
fact_text: IVIG is used in ITP to raise platelet count by blocking antibody receptors, especially in severe haemostatic failure or pre-splenectomy, with monitoring of platelet response required.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: First-line therapy for patients with bleeding or platelet count <30 × 10^9/L: corticosteroids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily) or dexamethasone 40 mg daily for 4 days to suppress antibody production and inhibit phagocytosis
dose_or_duration: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily or dexamethasone 40 mg daily for 4 days
referral_criteria: Referral for splenectomy if no response to corticosteroids and immunosuppressants, or if severe bleeding

Consider second-line therapies such as thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag, avatrombopag, romiplostim) or immunosuppressants (rituximab, ciclosporin, mycophenolate, tacrolimus) if corticosteroids fail
admission_criteria: Admission for severe mucosal bleeding or life-threatening bleeding
fact_text: In ITP, corticosteroids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily or dexamethasone 40 mg daily for 4 days) are first-line treatment to suppress antibody production and phagocytosis; splenectomy and second-line immunosuppressants or thrombopoietin receptor agonists are considered if corticosteroids fail or bleeding is severe.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Second-line therapies for ITP include thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag, avatrombopag, romiplostim) and immunosuppressants (rituximab, ciclosporin, mycophenolate, tacrolimus)
fact_text: In ITP, second-line treatments include thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag, avatrombopag, romiplostim) and immunosuppressants such as rituximab, ciclosporin, mycophenolate, and tacrolimus, used when corticosteroids fail.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In neonates with severe haemophilia, avoid head trauma during delivery and first 24 hours; routine caesarean section is not recommended solely to prevent intracranial bleeding.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Acquired coagulopathies arise from underproduction (liver failure, vitamin K deficiency), increased consumption (DIC, immune-mediated like acquired haemophilia, von Willebrand syndrome, factor deficiencies in amyloid or sepsis), and drug-induced inhibition of coagulation factors or post-translational modification (e.g., warfarin).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Congenital coagulopathies include X-linked haemophilia A and B, autosomal von Willebrand disease, combined factor deficiencies (II, VII, IX, X, XI, XII), hypofibrinogenaemia, and dysfibrinogenaemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Haemophilia A and B are X-linked recessive disorders caused by mutations in factor VIII and IX genes on the X chromosome; female carriers have reduced factor VIII/IX due to X inactivation and may bleed mildly.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Severe haemophilia (<1 IU/dL) presents with spontaneous haemarthroses and muscle haematomas; moderate (1–5 IU/dL) with mild trauma or surgery bleeding; mild (5–40 IU/dL) with major injury or surgery bleeding in excess.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Haemophilia severity is classified by factor VIII or IX levels: severe <1 IU/dL, moderate 1–5 IU/dL, mild 5–40 IU/dL.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Large muscle haematomas in haemophilia can compress nerves (e.g., femoral nerve), cause compartment syndrome, ischaemia, necrosis, fibrosis, and Achilles tendon contracture.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Senile purpura in older adults is due to age-related loss of subcutaneous fat and collagen support of small blood vessels, increasing minor trauma bleeding risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Severe haemophilia patients have spontaneous bleeding into joints and muscles, with risk of retroperitoneal and intracranial bleeding; babies with severe disease have increased intracranial haemorrhage risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Thrombocytopenia is common in older adults due to increased disorders and drug causes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Thrombosis incidence rises with age due to stasis, concurrent illness, increased platelet aggregation, and hyperactivity of the haemostatic system.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Older patients are more sensitive to anticoagulants like warfarin, with higher risk of fatal bleeds, especially over age 80.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Prophylaxis with factor VIII or IX concentrates aims to maintain trough levels to prevent spontaneous bleeding; optimal trough levels and dosing schedules (daily, alternate days) remain debated.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management aims to render severe haemophilia patients 'bleed free' using replacement of deficient coagulation factors and adjunct therapies; factor concentrates are preferred in high-income countries.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Thromboprophylaxis should be considered in all immobile older patients to prevent acute illness-related thrombosis, but not routinely in chronic immunosuppression as no increased risk is shown.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Component resolved diagnostics (CRD) use purified native or recombinant allergen proteins to detect specific IgE directed against individual allergenic molecules, improving specificity over total IgE.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Mast cell tryptase is stable in serum and is a convenient biomarker of mast cell activation, unlike total IgE which can be falsely elevated in atopic patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: NK cells contribute to tumour surveillance by killing tumour cells that lose HLA expression, which normally inhibits NK cell activation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tumour cells use HLA molecules to evade immune recognition by T cells, facilitating immune escape.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: CD4 T cells kill infected cells by producing pore-forming molecules like perforin and enzymes that trigger apoptosis; CD8 T cells are key in defense against viral infection.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Naïve T-cell activation requires antigen processing by antigen-presenting cells, antigenic peptide presentation by MHC class II molecules, and co-stimulatory signals; intracellular T-cell signaling then drives proliferation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Th1 cells produce IL-2, IFN-γ, and TNF-α to support delayed-type hypersensitivity and antiviral defense; T-regulatory cells suppress other immune cells to prevent autoimmunity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Th17 cells produce pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-17 and IL-22, playing roles in defense against extracellular bacteria and fungi and in autoimmune disease development.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Intestinal failure (IF) is defined as reduced gut function below minimum needed for adequate absorption of macronutrients, water, and electrolytes, requiring intravenous supplementation to maintain health or growth.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Type 1 intestinal failure is a common, acute-onset, usually self-limiting condition often following abdominal surgery or critical illness, requiring short-term intravenous fluid and electrolyte support.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Type 2 intestinal failure is less common, occurs after acute intra-abdominal events (e.g., ischaemia, trauma, sepsis), and requires multidisciplinary support due to complex nutritional needs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Type 3 intestinal failure is a chronic condition where patients are metabolically stable but require long-term intravenous nutrition support over months to years; reversibility is variable.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Acute cellular rejection after transplantation is mainly mediated by activated B cells.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Failure to control viral infections post-transplant increases risk of malignant transformation and malignancy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: HLA incompatibility does not necessarily predict transplant outcome, but donor-recipient HLA polymorphisms influence rejection risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Major complications of solid organ transplantation include graft rejection, drug toxicity, and infection due to immunosuppression.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Certain antidepressant medications can cause false-negative skin test results and should be discontinued before allergy skin testing.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Immune checkpoint blockade can cause immune-related adverse effects including autoimmune disease and immune toxicity, which may persist despite treatment withdrawal.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Immune checkpoint blockade therapies target CTLA-4 and PD-1 pathways to enhance anti-tumour immunity by preventing tumour-induced T-cell suppression.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of intestinal failure requires multidisciplinary care focusing on maintaining hydration, nutrition, minimizing complications, and preserving quality of life.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 5.26 Likely requirements for support according to length of intact residual small bowel
fact_text: Oral fluid restriction and oral glucose/electrolyte solution use depend on residual jejunum length: <200 cm requires both restrictions and IV fluids; 100-200 cm requires oral restrictions and IV fluids; <75 cm requires oral restrictions, IV fluids, and parenteral nutrition.
source_figure_or_table: Table 5.26 Likely requirements for support according to length of intact residual small bowel

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: short bowel syndrome with high stoma output
condition_aliases: short bowel syndrome with high stoma output
source_section: Box 5.27 Management of patients with short bowel syndrome and a high stoma output
fact_text: Teduglutide 0.05 mg/kg subcutaneously once daily can be considered to reduce intravenous fluid and nutritional support requirements after achieving bowel adaptation in high-output short bowel syndrome.
source_figure_or_table: Box 5.27 Management of patients with short bowel syndrome and a high stoma output

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: short bowel syndrome with high stoma output
condition_aliases: short bowel syndrome with high stoma output
source_section: Box 5.27 Management of patients with short bowel syndrome and a high stoma output
fact_text: Management includes monitoring stoma output for 24 hours on free oral intake and 24 hours on nil by mouth; intravenous fluids restore circulating volume and reduce thirst; intravenous fluids correct ongoing imbalance between oral intake and stool loss.
source_figure_or_table: Box 5.27 Management of patients with short bowel syndrome and a high stoma output

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: short bowel syndrome with high stoma output
condition_aliases: short bowel syndrome with high stoma output
source_section: Box 5.27 Management of patients with short bowel syndrome and a high stoma output
fact_text: To reduce stool volume, restrict oral fluid intake to less than 1000 mL hypotonic fluid per 24 hours, give 1000 mL oral rehydration solution with 90–120 mmol Na/L, consider loperamide 16 mg daily or codeine phosphate 30–60 mg four times daily, and consider omeprazole 20 mg daily or octreotide 50–100 µg three times daily subcutaneously.
source_figure_or_table: Box 5.27 Management of patients with short bowel syndrome and a high stoma output

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Jejunostomy patients have high fluid and electrolyte losses due to absence of ileum and colon; sodium and magnesium losses predominate, requiring early recognition and correction of dehydration and electrolyte disturbances to prevent permanent damage.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: short bowel syndrome with jejunum-colon anastomosis
condition_aliases: short bowel syndrome with jejunum-colon anastomosis
fact_text: Patients with jejunum-colon anastomosis may develop protein-energy malnutrition and weight loss over weeks despite initial good recovery; stool volume is influenced by oral intake and malabsorption of bile acids and fat-soluble vitamins.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Co-stimulatory blockade with CTLA-4 fusion protein belatacept selectively inhibits T-cell activation by binding CD80/86 on antigen-presenting cells and is used in post-transplant immune suppression.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Antibodies against factor IX are much less common (<1%) but can cause severe allergic reactions when they occur.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Desmopressin can cause significant hyponatraemia due to water retention, especially in young children, and may provoke thrombotic events in predisposed patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Factor concentrates can cause development of anti-factor VIII antibodies in about 25% of severe haemophilia patients, reducing treatment efficacy and causing severe allergic reactions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: activated clotting factors (e.g. VIIa or factor VIII)
fact_text: Infusions of activated clotting factors such as factor VIIa or factor VIII may be used in patients with inhibitors to factor VIII.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: 300 µg dose for prophylaxis
fact_text: Desmopressin (arginine vasopressin receptor agonist) raises vWF and factor VIII levels 3- to 4-fold and is effective in mild or moderate haemophilia A; given IV, SC, or intranasally at 300 µg dose for prophylaxis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Factor VIII/IX concentrates for haemophilia are freeze-dried, stored at 4°C, and can be self-administered at home early in bleeding episodes to improve outcomes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Haemophilia A and B prophylaxis is best guided by pharmacokinetic studies to optimize dosing schedules, with treatment evolving from plasma-derived factor concentrates to recombinant factor concentrates with longer half-lives.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: All non-immune recipients of pooled blood products should receive hepatitis A and B immunisation to prevent infection.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with von Willebrand disease present with mucocutaneous bleeding manifestations such as reduced platelet function, superficial bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia, and gastrointestinal haemorrhage; bleeding severity varies within families and can be mild or asymptomatic.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Von Willebrand disease is classified by type of defect (quantitative or qualitative), inheritance pattern (autosomal dominant or recessive), and laboratory findings including von Willebrand factor antigen levels, high molecular weight multimers, ristocetin cofactor activity, and platelet aggregation tests as detailed in Table 24.70.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Measure activity of von Willebrand factor (vWF) and factor VIII
Conduct platelet function tests including ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation (RIPA)
Measure specific antigen levels of vWF and factor VIII
Genetic analysis for mutations in the vWF gene if available
fact_text: Diagnosis of von Willebrand disease requires measurement of vWF and factor VIII activity, multimer analysis, platelet function tests including ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation, and specific antigen assays; genetic testing for vWF mutations can be informative.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Caplacizumab is used in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) to bind the A1 domain of von Willebrand factor, preventing platelet binding and aggregation.
fact_text: Caplacizumab binds the A1 domain of von Willebrand factor to prevent platelet binding and aggregation, used in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Concizumab and marstacimab are anti-tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI) monoclonal antibodies in development for haemophilia A and B to block TFPI binding to factor Xa, allowing ongoing thrombin generation and restoration of haemostasis.
fact_text: Concizumab and marstacimab are anti-TFPI monoclonal antibodies administered by intravenous infusion to block TFPI binding to factor Xa, enhancing thrombin generation in haemophilia A and B.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Emicizumab is licensed for use in patients with moderate to severe haemophilia A, including those with factor VIII inhibitors, as a bispecific monoclonal antibody that mimics factor VIII activity by binding to factor IXa and factor X to activate thrombin and clot formation.
fact_text: Emicizumab is a bispecific monoclonal antibody licensed for subcutaneous use in moderate to severe haemophilia A, including patients with factor VIII inhibitors, by mimicking factor VIII activity to promote thrombin and clot formation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Gene therapy for haemophilia A and B uses recombinant adeno-associated viral vectors delivered intravenously to increase deficient clotting factor expression, potentially reducing or eliminating the need for factor replacement or non-replacement therapies.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bleeding in chronic liver disease is multifactorial, involving reduced hepatic synthesis of coagulation factors, decreased anticoagulant proteins, reduced fibrinolytic activity, and structural abnormalities like varices and sepsis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: DIC causes bleeding due to exaggerated inappropriate intravascular coagulation and is classified under thrombotic disorders.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Non-specific arthralgia and mechanical low back pain are the most common musculoskeletal manifestations in HIV patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Idiopathic inflammatory arthritis may occur in HIV patients and is part of the differential diagnosis of musculoskeletal symptoms.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteomyelitis presents with localised bone pain and tenderness, often accompanied by malaise, night sweats, and pyrexia; adjacent joint pain and sterile effusion or septic arthritis may develop.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Psoriatic arthritis in HIV patients is usually of lower limb joints and may be associated with spondyloarthropathy (SpA) aetiology.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Reactive arthritis occurs especially in men who have sex with men and is a recognized musculoskeletal manifestation of HIV.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Risk factors for venous thrombosis include patient factors (age, obesity, varicose veins, previous VTE, family history, transient risk factors like pregnancy, surgery, immobility), surgical conditions (major surgery, cancer surgery, orthopaedic surgery), medical conditions (heart failure, inflammatory disorders, malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, chronic lung disease, severe infection, neurological immobility, high-dependency admission), and haematological disorders (polycythaemia, thrombocythaemia, anticoagulant deficiencies, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, prothrombotic mutations, myelofibrosis, antiphospholipid syndrome).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: severe factor vii, x, xi deficiency
condition_aliases: severe factor vii, x, xi deficiency
fact_text: Severe deficiencies of factors VII, X, and XI are autosomal recessive, rare, and cause severe bleeding including umbilical stump and intracranial haemorrhage; factor XIII deficiency is linked to recurrent fetal loss.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: MRI for early detection of osteomyelitis
Synovial fluid or biopsy culture if tuberculosis suspected
PCR-based analysis of synovial fluid or biopsy material if tuberculosis suspected
Routine blood tests including neutrophil count and ESR and CRP
recommended_medicines: Intravenous antibiotics as soon as osteomyelitis is suspected
Prolonged course of oral antibiotics after initial intravenous therapy
recommended_advice: Early recognition and treatment of osteomyelitis is critical to prevent chronic infection and complications
referral_criteria: Consider referral for surgical debridement if necrotic tissue or abscess present
admission_criteria: Admission may be required for intravenous antibiotic therapy and surgical management
fact_text: Osteomyelitis primarily affects bone and marrow with haematogenous spread common in children; early MRI is recommended for diagnosis, blood cultures and synovial fluid or biopsy cultures are essential, and treatment requires early intravenous antibiotics followed by prolonged oral therapy with monitoring of ESR and CRP.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Intravenous antibiotics initially, followed by prolonged oral antibiotics
recommended_advice: Early antibiotic treatment is critical to prevent chronic osteomyelitis
Surgical debridement may be required for necrotic bone or abscess
Admission may be necessary for intravenous therapy and surgery
referral_criteria: Refer for surgical debridement if necrotic tissue or abscess present
admission_criteria: Admit for intravenous antibiotics and surgical management
fact_text: Early recognition and treatment of osteomyelitis with intravenous antibiotics followed by prolonged oral therapy is essential; surgical debridement and hospital admission may be required for necrotic bone or abscess.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: PCR-based analysis of synovial fluid or biopsy if tuberculosis suspected
Routine blood tests including neutrophil count, ESR, CRP
fact_text: MRI is the preferred early imaging for osteomyelitis; blood cultures and synovial fluid or biopsy cultures are essential; PCR-based tests should be done if tuberculosis is suspected; routine blood tests show neutrophilia and raised ESR and CRP.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bleeding severity in renal failure correlates with plasma urea concentration; treatment includes dialysis to reduce urea and platelet concentrate infusions for severe bleeding.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: VTE includes deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, with an annual incidence of ~1:1000 and a 30-day mortality of ~10% for DVT and 15% for PE.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: bleeding in young children and type 2b thrombocytopenia
condition_aliases: bleeding in young children and type 2b thrombocytopenia
fact_text: Young children and patients with severe arterial disease or type 2B thrombocytopenia should not receive desmopressin due to risk of thrombocytopenia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In cholestatic jaundice, vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding and should be corrected with parenteral vitamin K administration.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Image-guided biopsy of lesion if blood cultures negative
recommended_medicines: Supportive care and parenteral antibiotics followed by oral antibiotics as for osteomyelitis
fact_text: Discitis presents with back pain, fever, and raised ESR/CRP; MRI is the diagnostic test of choice; blood cultures and biopsy if needed to identify pathogen; treatment includes supportive care and parenteral antibiotics followed by oral antibiotics as for osteomyelitis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Mild haemorrhage episodes can be treated with local measures or desmopressin to raise vWF levels and increase factor VIII.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tranexamic acid may be useful for mucosal bleeding as an adjunct to haemostatic treatment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Desmopressin or cryoprecipitate may be used to increase vWF concentration in renal failure bleeding, but caution is needed due to increased bleeding risk with renal impairment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Serious or persistent bleeding can be treated with selected factor VIII concentrates containing vWF, including plasma-derived and recombinant vWF concentrates.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Synovial fluid or tissue biopsy for histology and culture
PCR testing of synovial fluid or tissue
recommended_medicines: Quadruple anti-tuberculous therapy with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months
Followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin
Extended treatment of 12-18 months may be required depending on disease extent and response
dose_or_duration: Initial 2 months quadruple therapy, then 4 months dual therapy; extension to 12-18 months if needed
recommended_advice: Treatment duration depends on clinical and radiological response
Surgical debridement may be required for resistant organisms or severe disease
Surgical decompression and stabilization may be needed for severe spinal disease
referral_criteria: Refer for surgical management if severe spinal cord compression or resistant disease
warning_signs: Progressive spinal deformity and cord compression
fact_text: Musculoskeletal tuberculosis requires diagnosis by MRI and synovial fluid or tissue biopsy with PCR; treatment is quadruple anti-TB therapy for 2 months followed by dual therapy for 4 months, extended to 12-18 months if needed; surgical intervention may be required for resistant or severe spinal disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: Warfarin treatment should aim for an INR of 2.5 (range 2–3). LMWH treatment should continue until INR is therapeutic. DOACs can be started immediately without bridging with LMWH.
route_or_site: oral for warfarin and DOACs; subcutaneous for LMWH
fact_text: Warfarin anticoagulation for VTE should target an INR of 2.5 (range 2–3), with LMWH continued until INR is therapeutic; DOACs such as rivaroxaban and apixaban may be started immediately without LMWH bridging.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: DOACs such as rivaroxaban and edoxaban have demonstrated efficacy in cancer-associated thrombosis but have higher bleeding rates compared to LMWH.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Dabigatran requires initial treatment with LMWH for a minimum of 5 days before starting the oral anticoagulant for VTE management.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
contraindications_or_cautions: patients with new pulmonary embolism despite therapeutic anticoagulation
fact_text: In patients with VTE who develop new pulmonary embolism despite therapeutic anticoagulation, an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter should be considered to prevent life-threatening PE.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Maintenance anticoagulation with LMWH in patients with active cancer and VTE is associated with a lower recurrence rate than warfarin and is preferred.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Post-thrombotic syndrome complicates 30% of lower limb DVT cases and severe cases may be complicated by ulceration.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The mainstay of treatment for all forms of venous thromboembolism (VTE) is anticoagulation, achievable by several methods including initial low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) followed by oral anticoagulants such as warfarin, or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) like rivaroxaban and apixaban.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Moderate risk of DVT includes major surgery in patients over 40 years or with other risk factors such as heart failure, myocardial infarction with complications, sepsis, inflammatory bowel disease, active malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, stroke, or conditions causing lower limb paralysis; high risk includes major abdominal or pelvic surgery for malignancy or with history of DVT, known thrombophilia, major hip or knee surgery, and neurosurgery.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Factor V Leiden mutation leads to resistance to activated factor V cleavage, resulting in a 5-fold increased risk of venous thrombosis in heterozygotes and 50-fold in homozygotes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Inherited deficiency of protein C or protein S causes a prothrombotic state with approximately fivefold increased risk of venous thromboembolism compared to the background population.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Heterozygous prothrombin G20210A mutation increases venous thrombosis risk by two- to threefold compared to the background population.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: prophylactic or treatment doses over the period of risk
fact_text: Patients with antithrombin deficiency should receive anticoagulation treatment or prophylaxis with unfractionated heparin or LMWH during periods of thrombosis risk, including pregnancy, as they are at high risk of venous thromboembolism.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: doses ≥ 100 U/kg/day during pregnancy
fact_text: Pregnant patients with antithrombin deficiency require aggressive management with LMWH at doses ≥ 100 U/kg/day, with antithrombin concentrate available for cardiopulmonary bypass or perioperative prophylaxis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients at moderate or high risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) should receive specific antithrombotic prophylaxis including mechanical methods (intermittent pneumatic compression, graduated compression stockings) and pharmacological agents such as LMWHs, unfractionated heparin, fondaparinux, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, or warfarin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Antiphospholipid antibodies include lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies; positivity for one or more increases thrombosis risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Conditions associated with secondary APS include systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, Behçet disease, temporal arteritis, and Sjögren syndrome.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: ISTH scoring system for DIC diagnosis uses platelet count, fibrin degradation products, prothrombin time prolongation, and fibrinogen level; a total score ≥5 indicates overt DIC.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Underlying conditions triggering DIC include infection/sepsis, trauma, obstetric complications, severe liver failure, malignancy, tissue destruction, vascular abnormalities, and toxic/immunological causes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: TTP is characterized by a pentad of thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, neurological sequelae, fever, and renal impairment, though not all patients have all five features.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diagnosis of DIC requires clinical suspicion plus coagulation tests including APTT, PT, fibrinogen, platelet count, and fibrin degradation products (e.g., D-dimers).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: APS-associated arterial thrombosis, cerebral stroke, and venous thromboembolism should be treated with anticoagulation rather than antiplatelet therapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In obstetric APS, heparin and aspirin are often prescribed despite limited clinical trial evidence for efficacy in improving pregnancy outcomes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Warfarin is preferred over direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) for patients with APS presenting with thrombotic events due to better evidence of efficacy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with DIC should not, in general, be treated with antifibrinolytic therapy such as tranexamic acid.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Treatment of DIC focuses on addressing the underlying cause and supportive care including blood component therapy; prophylactic heparin is generally not recommended unless clear contraindications are absent.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Glucocorticoids, rituximab, and caplacizumab used in acquired TTP require monitoring for potential adverse drug reactions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
referral_criteria: treat by emergency plasma exchange
admission_criteria: admit for emergency plasma exchange
fact_text: Acquired TTP is an acute autoimmune disorder caused by antibodies against ADAMTS-13, leading to microvascular platelet thrombi mainly affecting brain and kidneys. It requires emergency plasma exchange as primary treatment. Adjunctive therapies include glucocorticoids, aspirin, rituximab, and caplacizumab (a monoclonal antibody against vWF A domain) which improves outcomes, reduces relapse, and shortens recovery time. Untreated mortality is 90% in 10 days; with treatment mortality reduces to 20-30% at 6 months.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Parvovirus B19 infection can precipitate an aplastic crisis in hereditary spherocytosis, characterized by a 'flushed cheeks' rash and severe anaemia with low reticulocyte count and elevated MCV.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Solitary plasmacytoma diagnosis is supported by a persistent localized bone mass with low-level intact IgG paraprotein, absence of multiple lytic bone lesions, hypercalcaemia, marrow involvement, or cytopenias.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In a patient with positive lupus anticoagulant but negative anticardiolipin and anti-β2-GP1 antibodies, APS diagnosis is supported if there is a history of thrombosis; indefinite anticoagulation with warfarin is optimal for APS patients with venous thromboembolism.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: relapsed diffuse large b-cell non-hodgkin lymphoma (dlbcl)
condition_aliases: relapsed diffuse large b-cell non-hodgkin lymphoma (dlbcl)
fact_text: CAR-T therapy for multiply relapsed DLBCL requires achieving a negative FDG PET-CT before treatment; CAR-T cells can be prepared and delivered within one week; CAR-T products use autologous T cells modified to express chimeric antigen receptors; T-cell exhaustion limits efficacy and checkpoint inhibitors may reverse this.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: General Assessment of Locomotor System (GALS) and Schober test
fact_text: GALS examination includes assessment of gait by asking patient to walk a few steps and return, observing for pain or limp.
source_figure_or_table: General Assessment of Locomotor System (GALS) and Schober test

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: General Assessment of Locomotor System (GALS) and Schober test
fact_text: In GALS arm examination, inspect hands for swelling or deformity, test hand function by asking patient to make a fist and open/close fingers, and test for inflammation by squeezing metacarpals.
source_figure_or_table: General Assessment of Locomotor System (GALS) and Schober test

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: General Assessment of Locomotor System (GALS) and Schober test
fact_text: In leg examination, test hip movements by flexing each hip with hand on knee and rotating internally and externally to detect crepitus and range of motion.
source_figure_or_table: General Assessment of Locomotor System (GALS) and Schober test

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition

fact_text: Inspect ankles and feet and squeeze the forefoot to test for metatarsophalangeal synovitis.
source_figure_or_table: General Assessment of Locomotor System (GALS) and Schober test

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition

fact_text: Inspect spine from behind and side for scoliosis, kyphosis, or localized deformity; ask patient to touch toes to assess spinal mobility.

fact_text: Palpate each knee for warmth and swelling to assess for synovitis and effusion.
source_figure_or_table: General Assessment of Locomotor System (GALS) and Schober test

fact_text: Schober test: mark skin 4 cm below and 10 cm above the superior iliac crest in midline; ask patient to bend forward; normal increase in distance between marks is 15 cm, indicating normal lumbar spine flexion.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: General Assessment of Locomotor System (GALS) and Schober test
fact_text: Spine examination includes testing cervical spine flexion and extension by asking patient to look at ceiling then put chin on chest.
source_figure_or_table: General Assessment of Locomotor System (GALS) and Schober test

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: General Assessment of Locomotor System (GALS) and Schober test
fact_text: Test arm joint movements by asking patient to put hands behind head (shoulder movement), flex elbows to touch shoulders (elbow flexion), and turn palms up and down with elbows at side (supination and pronation).

fact_text: Test lateral flexion of cervical spine by asking patient to try to put ear on shoulder.

fact_text: Test lateral spine flexion by asking patient to slide hand down leg to knee.
source_figure_or_table: General Assessment of Locomotor System (GALS) and Schober test

fact_text: To test thoracolumbar rotation, stand behind patient holding their pelvis and ask them to turn from side to side without moving their feet.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bone types are divided by embryonic development: flat bones (e.g., skull) develop by intramembranous ossification from mesenchymal tissue, while long bones (e.g., femur, radius) develop by endochondral ossification from a cartilage template.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: A thin remnant of cartilage called the growth plate or epiphyseal plate remains at the end of long bones, allowing continued growth until the cartilage disappears as longitudinal bone growth ceases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bone lining cells are flattened cells lining bone surfaces that differentiate from osteoblasts after bone formation is complete.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bone marrow stromal cells produce RANKL and macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF) that stimulate osteoclast formation and cytokines supporting haematopoiesis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: During development, cartilage in long bones is invaded by vascular tissue containing osteoprogenitor cells, which are gradually replaced by bone from ossification centers in the middle and ends of bones.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells responsible for bone resorption; osteoblasts are mononuclear cells derived from marrow stromal cells responsible for bone formation; osteocytes are osteoblast-derived cells embedded in bone matrix that sense mechanical stimuli and coordinate bone remodeling via RANKL and sclerostin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Two types of bone tissue exist in normal skeleton: cortical bone, which is dense and forms a hard envelope around long bones, and trabecular (cancellous) bone, which is a meshwork at the bone centre separated by spaces filled with bone marrow.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Musculoskeletal disorders are more common in women and increase in frequency with age, being the most common cause of physical disability in older people and accounting for one-third of physical disability at all ages.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Musculoskeletal system disorders affect all ages and ethnic groups, with about 25% of new UK general practice consultations related to musculoskeletal symptoms; MSK diseases often cause pain and impairment of locomotor function, impacting quality of life and work.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The musculoskeletal system provides movement, structural support for internal organs, and acts as a reservoir for calcium and phosphate to regulate mineral homeostasis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bone matrix is primarily type I collagen with mineral deposits mainly as hydroxyapatite; bone turnover releases biochemical markers useful for monitoring bone formation and resorption.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bone remodelling is a cyclical process with four phases: quiescence, resorption by osteoclasts, reversal, and formation by osteoblasts, taking about 10 days for osteoclast apoptosis to initiate reversal.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteoblast activity is stimulated by Wnt family proteins and coupling factors such as ephrin B2 secreted by osteoclasts; osteocytes produce sclerostin (SOST) which inhibits bone formation and stimulates resorption.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteoclast precursors derive from haematopoietic stem cells and mature under influence of M-CSF, RANKL (produced by osteoblasts, marrow stromal cells, T-cells), and are inhibited by osteoprotegerin (OPG), a decoy receptor for RANKL.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteocytes produce fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), which acts on the kidney to promote renal phosphate excretion, playing a role in phosphate homeostasis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fibrous and fibrocartilaginous joints form simple bridges between bones with little movement, e.g., symphysis pubis and intervertebral discs; the nucleus pulposus in discs acts as a shock absorber due to its high water content.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fibrocartilaginous joints allow limited movement; examples include symphysis pubis, costochondral junctions, intervertebral discs, and sacroiliac joints.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fibrous joints allow minimal movement; example includes skull sutures.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Synovial joints allow large movement; examples include most limb joints, temporomandibular, and costovertebral joints.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: There are three main types of joints: fibrous, fibrocartilaginous, and synovial.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Synovial joint structure includes bone, capsule, synovium, fibrocartilage pad, joint space, hyaline articular cartilage, skin and subcutaneous tissue, bursa, tendon and sheath, ligamentous thickening of capsule, muscle, and bursa.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Synovial joints contain articular cartilage made of chondrocytes producing type II collagen and proteoglycans (mainly aggrecan) that provide shock absorption and structural integrity; aggrecan's negative charge attracts water to maintain cartilage volume and resilience.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ephrin B2 produced by osteoclasts stimulates bone formation via a coupling factor.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Glucocorticoids from the adrenal gland inhibit bone formation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Oestrogen from the ovary inhibits bone resorption.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteoprotegerin secreted by osteoblasts inhibits bone resorption by acting as a decoy receptor for RANKL.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
