fact_text: Parathyroid hormone from parathyroid glands increases both bone resorption and formation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: RANKL produced by osteocytes, activated T cells, stromal cells, and osteoblasts stimulates bone resorption by activating RANK.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Sclerostin produced by osteocytes inhibits bone formation by blocking Wnt effects on LRP receptors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: TGF-β and IGF from bone matrix stimulate bone formation and act as coupling factors released during bone resorption.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Thyroid hormone from the thyroid gland increases bone resorption and formation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Wnt proteins from stromal cells stimulate bone formation by activating LRP receptors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: osteoarthritis, spondyloarthritis, bone cysts, bone sclerosis, enthesopathy
condition_aliases: osteoarthritis, spondyloarthritis, bone cysts, bone sclerosis, enthesopathy
fact_text: Plain X-rays are diagnostic in many bone and joint diseases; osteoarthritis shows focal joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, bone cysts, and calcified loose bodies; spondyloarthritis shows erosions, new bone formation, periosteal reaction, and punched-out erosions in psoriatic arthritis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: suspected septic arthritis, crystal arthritis, intra-articular bleeding
condition_aliases: suspected septic arthritis, crystal arthritis, intra-articular bleeding
recommended_tests: joint aspiration with synovial fluid examination
recommended_advice: joint aspiration should be performed in all patients with suspected septic arthritis, crystal arthritis, or intra-articular bleeding
fact_text: Joint aspiration with synovial fluid examination is essential in suspected septic arthritis, crystal arthritis, or intra-articular bleeding; synovial fluid should be sent for microscopy to identify inflammation, infection, or crystals, with characteristic findings including volume, turbidity, cell count, and crystal morphology.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
trigger_evidence: skeletal anatomy needs defining or MRI contraindicated
contraindications_or_cautions: MRI contraindicated
fact_text: CT is used selectively for bone and joint disease to define skeletal anatomy or assess calcific lesions when MRI is contraindicated or when evaluating articular regions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Ultrasound of temporal or axillary arteries
fact_text: Ultrasound can detect vessel wall thickening in temporal or axillary arteries, aiding diagnosis of giant cell arteritis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Gadolinium contrast in MRI can increase sensitivity for detecting synovitis and erosions by suppressing fat signal and enhancing inflamed tissue.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: MRI with T1- and T2-weighted sequences
fact_text: MRI T1-weighted sequences define anatomy; T2-weighted sequences assess tissue water content and inflammation, useful for diagnosing inflammatory musculoskeletal diseases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MRI with T1-weighted post-contrast imaging shows extensive enhancement consistent with synovitis and is useful for detecting synovitis and erosions in joints.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: metastatic bone disease and paget disease
condition_aliases: metastatic bone disease and paget disease
trigger_evidence: suspected metastatic bone disease or Paget disease
dose_or_duration: Intravenous injection of 99mTc-labelled bisphosphonate
fact_text: Radionuclide bone scintigraphy using 99mTc-labelled bisphosphonate detects active bone turnover in metastatic bone disease and Paget disease; images are taken hours after injection to assess perfusion and bone activity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteoarthritis radiographic features include joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, joint deformity, and subchondral cysts.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteoporosis radiographic features include osteopenia, vertebral fractures, non-vertebral fractures, and cortical thinning, aiding diagnosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Paget disease radiographic abnormalities include bone expansion, abnormal trabecular pattern, osteosclerosis and lysis, and pseudofractures.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Psoriatic arthritis X-ray features include sacroiliitis, syndesmophytes, bone sclerosis, proliferative enthesis erosions, enthesophytes, and juxta-articular new bone formation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In rheumatoid arthritis, X-rays may show periarticular osteoporosis, marginal joint erosions, joint subluxation, and joint space narrowing, useful for diagnosis and monitoring structural damage.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: small joint synovitis and tendon lesions
condition_aliases: small joint synovitis and tendon lesions
fact_text: Ultrasonography with power Doppler is more sensitive than clinical exam for detecting early synovitis and inflammatory tendon lesions, useful for diagnosis and guided injections.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Full blood count (FBC) to detect neutrophil and lymphocyte abnormalities
Direct antiglobulin test to detect intravascular haemolysis in SLE
fact_text: Full blood count abnormalities such as neutrophilia, neutropenia, lymphopenia, anemia, and thrombocytosis are common in inflammatory rheumatic diseases; regular FBC monitoring is essential during DMARD and biologic therapy to detect marrow toxicity. Direct antiglobulin test is useful to detect haemolysis in SLE.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: metabolic bone disease and inflammatory arthritis
condition_aliases: metabolic bone disease and inflammatory arthritis
recommended_tests: Serum urate to help diagnose gout
Serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase for bone disease
C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) for inflammation
Serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) for myopathy or myositis
fact_text: Routine biochemistry including serum urate, calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, CRP, ESR, and creatine phosphokinase is essential for assessing metabolic bone disease, gout, and inflammatory myopathies; normal serum urate does not exclude gout, and CRP is a more specific inflammation marker than ESR, which may be unreliable in connective tissue diseases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Dual X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) at lumbar spine, hip, and sometimes forearm
fact_text: Dual X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is the preferred method to measure bone mineral density (BMD) for diagnosing osteoporosis, with T-scores used to classify normal bone density (> -1.0), osteopenia (-1.0 to -2.5), and osteoporosis (≤ -2.5) in adults over 50; Z-scores are used for younger patients. Serial DXA scans help monitor treatment response by detecting statistically significant BMD changes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Antiphospholipid antibodies, including antibodies to cardiolipin and beta-2-glycoprotein 1, are detected in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome and are used diagnostically in clinical practice.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Elevated serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) can be caused by inflammatory myositis ± vasculitis, muscular dystrophy, motor neuron disease, alcohol or drugs (especially statins), myocardial infarction, trauma or prolonged immobilisation, hypothyroidism, metabolic myopathy, viral myositis, or macro-CK variant.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) is found in 100% of systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease, 90% of systemic sclerosis, 40–70% of Sjögren disease, 30–80% of dermatomyositis or polymyositis, 100% of autoimmune hepatitis, 30–50% of rheumatoid arthritis and autoimmune thyroid disease, and variably in malignancy and infectious diseases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Positive rheumatoid factor is highly associated with rheumatoid arthritis (100% with nodules and extra-articular features, 70% overall), primary Sjögren disease (90%), mixed essential cryoglobulinaemia (90%), and also found in primary biliary cholangitis, infective endocarditis, systemic lupus erythematosus, tuberculosis, and in 20% of people over 65 years.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In rheumatoid arthritis diagnosis, IgM rheumatoid factor is positive in about 70% but has poor specificity; anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPA) are positive in ~70% with >95% specificity and associate with more severe disease and extra-articular features, but ACPA positivity alone does not confirm diagnosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: systemic lupus erythematosus and other autoimmune diseases
condition_aliases: systemic lupus erythematosus and other autoimmune diseases
recommended_tests: Antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing by indirect immunofluorescence assay (ELISA)
fact_text: Antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing by immunofluorescence is highly sensitive but poorly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus; a negative ANA excludes SLE, but positive ANA requires further testing such as anti-dsDNA antibodies which are more specific and correlate with disease severity and relapse.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Typical biochemical patterns in bone diseases include specific changes in calcium, phosphate, ALP, PTH, FGF23, and 25(OH)D levels that help differentiate osteoporosis, Paget disease, renal osteodystrophy, vitamin D–deficient osteomalacia, hypophosphataemic rickets, and primary hyperparathyroidism.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl-tRNA synthetase) antibody is found in polymyositis, dermatomyositis, and polymyositis–systemic sclerosis overlap (20%–30%), especially with interstitial lung disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anti-La antibody (anti-SS-B) is associated with Sjögren syndrome (60%) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (20%–60%).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anti-RNA polymerase antibody is found in 15% of patients with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anti-Ro antibody (anti-SS-A) is associated with SLE (35%–60%), especially with photosensitivity, thrombocytopenia, and subacute cutaneous lupus; also found in maternal anti-Ro antibodies linked to neonatal lupus and congenital heart block, and in Sjögren syndrome (40%–80%).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I antibody) is found in 15% of patients with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and is associated with more severe organ involvement including pulmonary fibrosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is found in 15%–30% of patients with SLE and is associated with renal disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anti-centromere antibody is associated with localized cutaneous systemic sclerosis with 60% sensitivity and 98% specificity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anti-histone antibody is associated with drug-induced lupus with approximately 80% frequency.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anti-ribonucleoprotein antibody (anti-RNP) is found in mixed connective tissue disease (100%) and in SLE (25%–50%), often with anti-Sm antibodies.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Monoarthritis refers to pain and swelling of a single joint; common causes include crystal arthritis, sepsis, reactive arthritis, and oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis; clinical assessment should include history of onset pattern, speed, age, and gender.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Clinical history for monoarthritis should include pattern of joint involvement, speed of onset, age, and gender to guide diagnosis; rapid onset (6–12 hours) suggests either gout or acute calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) arthritis (pseudogout).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 25.63 Features of primary Sjögren disease
fact_text: Sjögren disease typically affects females aged 40–50 years with a 9:1 female-to-male ratio; features include keratoconjunctivitis sicca, xerostomia, salivary gland enlargement, rashes, non-erosive arthralgia, generalized osteoarthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, and fatigue; less common features include low-grade fever, interstitial lung disease, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, cryoglobulinaemia, vasculitis, peripheral neuropathy, lymphadenopathy, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, and renal tubular acidosis.
source_figure_or_table: Table 25.63 Features of primary Sjögren disease

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 25.63 Features of primary Sjögren disease
fact_text: Differential diagnoses for Sjögren disease include systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, coeliac disease, primary biliary cholangitis, chronic active hepatitis, and myasthenia gravis.
source_figure_or_table: Table 25.63 Features of primary Sjögren disease

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Antineutrophil cytoplasm antibodies (ANCA) target cytoplasmic constituents of neutrophils and are useful in diagnosis and monitoring of systemic vasculitis; two main patterns are cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA) caused by antibodies to proteinase-3 and perinuclear ANCA (p-ANCA) caused by antibodies to myeloperoxidase and other enzymes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Autoantibody testing should be performed to support diagnosis when clinical assessment suggests autoimmune disease; routine screening without clinical suspicion is not recommended due to limited sensitivity and specificity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Low complement C3 is an indicator of active SLE and some vasculitis forms; low C3 is less specific for SLE activity, while high C3 and functional complement activation measures are nonspecific inflammation markers.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bone biopsy is occasionally required for infiltrative bone disorders, renal bone disease, suspected chronic infection or malignancy; biopsy should be taken under X-ray guidance or open surgery, often from iliac crest using large-diameter trephine needle under local anesthesia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tissue biopsy is useful to confirm diagnosis in selected musculoskeletal diseases, including synovial biopsy for chronic inflammatory monoarthritis or tenosynovitis to exclude infections, and temporal artery biopsy for suspected giant cell arteritis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Electromyography is valuable in suspected myopathy and inflammatory myositis, showing spontaneous fibrillation, short-duration action potentials in polyphasic disorganized motor units, and repetitive high-voltage oscillations on needle contact with diseased muscle.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Muscle biopsy is important in investigating myopathy and inflammatory myositis, usually taken from quadriceps or deltoid under local anesthesia; immunohistochemical staining helps differentiate primary and secondary muscle and neuromuscular diseases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 25.63 Features of primary Sjögren disease
fact_text: Autoantibodies frequently detected in Sjögren disease include rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, SS-A (anti-Ro), SS-B (anti-La), anticentromere antibody, gastric parietal cell antibody, and thyroid antibody.
source_figure_or_table: Table 25.63 Features of primary Sjögren disease

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: multiple organ function tests including renal, liver, bone, haematology
antinuclear antibodies including anti-Scl70 and anti-RNP antibodies
fact_text: Systemic sclerosis diagnosis and assessment require multiple organ function tests (renal, liver, bone marrow, haematology), urinalysis, antinuclear antibody testing including anti-Scl70 and anti-RNP antibodies, chest X-ray, transthoracic echocardiography, lung function tests, high-resolution lung CT, barium swallow, esophageal manometry, and hydrogen breath test to assess for interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension, and esophageal involvement.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Narrow biopsy of affected tissues (skin, lung, nasopharynx, gut, kidney, muscle) can confirm systemic vasculitis diagnosis; bone marrow biopsy may help diagnose conditions like Vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, Autoinflammatory, Somatic (VEXAS) syndrome.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: hypertensive renal crisis in systemic sclerosis
condition_aliases: hypertensive renal crisis in systemic sclerosis
recommended_tests: antinuclear antibodies including anti-Scl70 and anti-RNP antibodies
referral_criteria: consider referral for HSCT in severe cases
admission_criteria: rapidly developing hypertensive renal crisis
contraindications_or_cautions: HSCT has potential risks including increased mortality
warning_signs: rapidly developing accelerated phase hypertension and renal failure
fact_text: Hypertensive renal crisis in diffuse systemic sclerosis is characterized by rapidly developing accelerated hypertension and renal failure, associated with anti-Scl70 and anti-RNP antibodies; management includes high-intensity immunosuppression (e.g., cyclophosphamide) and possibly autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, though HSCT carries increased mortality risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: interstitial lung disease (ild) in systemic sclerosis
condition_aliases: interstitial lung disease (ild) in systemic sclerosis
trigger_evidence: diagnosis of ILD in systemic sclerosis
recommended_medicines: tyrosine kinase inhibitor nintedanib (150 mg twice daily)
dose_or_duration: nintedanib 150 mg twice daily
fact_text: Interstitial lung disease in systemic sclerosis may be treated with cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate mofetil; tyrosine kinase inhibitor nintedanib (150 mg twice daily) is effective and licensed for SSc-ILD; rituximab and tocilizumab (IL-6 inhibitor) are other options with recent FDA approval for SSc-ILD.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: ambrisentan 10 mg daily; tadalafil 40 mg daily; riociguat 1.5–2.5 mg daily
referral_criteria: consider heart–lung transplant in progressive disease
fact_text: Pulmonary hypertension in systemic sclerosis may be treated with endothelin-1 antagonist ambrisentan 10 mg daily combined with tadalafil 40 mg daily as first-line therapy; riociguat 1.5–2.5 mg daily is an alternative; heart–lung transplant may be considered in progressive disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: calcium channel blockers for Raynaud phenomenon
PDE5 inhibitors such as tadalafil for Raynaud phenomenon
proton pump inhibitors for oesophageal reflux
analgesics and/or NSAIDs for joint involvement
recommended_advice: avoid cold exposure and use thermal insulating gloves/socks to prevent Raynaud attacks
maintain high core temperature to prevent Raynaud phenomenon
use intravenous prostaglandin and iloprost for severe Raynaud phenomenon with digital ischemia
use topical fucidin–hydrocortisone cream for digital tip tissue health
contraindications_or_cautions: HSCT has potential increased mortality risk
fact_text: Management of systemic sclerosis includes immunosuppressants such as methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, and high-intensity immunosuppression with possible autologous stem cell transplantation; Raynaud phenomenon is treated with calcium channel blockers, PDE5 inhibitors, prostaglandins, and avoidance of cold exposure; oesophageal reflux is managed with proton pump inhibitors and antireflux agents; joint symptoms may require analgesics or NSAIDs; hypertension requires ACE inhibitors even if renal impairment is present.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Abdominal organ involvement including hepatosplenomegaly, haematuria, proteinuria, urethritis, fever, and lymphadenopathy is seen in rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, reactive arthritis, and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Heart and lung involvement such as pleuropericarditis, aortic valve/root disease, and interstitial lung disease occur in systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, and related connective tissue diseases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Oral ulcers and nodules are features of systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, and vasculitis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Psoriatic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus are associated with skin, nails, and mucous membrane features such as psoriasis, nail pitting, Raynaud phenomenon, photosensitivity, livedo reticularis, and vasculitis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Uveitis is associated with spondyloarthritis, sarcoidosis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and Behçet disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Xerostomia, dry skin, and various rashes are features of primary Sjögren disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Common causes of monoarthritis include gout, pseudogout, septic arthritis, osteoarthritis, trauma, haemarthrosis, spondyloarthritis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, and enteropathic arthritis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Less common causes of monoarthritis include rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, pigmented villonodular synovitis, foreign body reaction, tuberculosis, leukaemia, gonococcal infection, and osteomyelitis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Axial spondyloarthritis and enteropathic arthritis affect mid-size and large joints and entheses, more commonly lower limbs than upper limbs, and are associated with inflammatory back pain.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Calcium pyrophosphate arthritis causes chronic polyarthritis involving wrists, ankles, knees, and oligoarticular small hand joints.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chronic gout affects more proximal joints than acute attacks and causes polyarthritis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chronic sarcoidosis causes small and large joint polyarthritis, often involving ankles.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis presents with various patterns including polyarticular, oligoarticular, and systemic but usually with enthesitis predominance.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteoarthritis polyarthritis is symmetrical, targets PIP, DIP, and first CMC joints in hands, knees, hips, and neck, and is associated with Heberden and Bouchard nodes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Poncet disease is a reactive arthritis affecting large joints associated with tuberculosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Psoriatic arthritis tends to be asymmetrical, affects PIP and DIP joints in hands and large joints, may involve enthesitis, dactylitis, spondylitis, and nail changes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Rheumatoid arthritis typically causes symmetrical small and large joint polyarthritis affecting upper and lower limbs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus causes symmetrical polyarthritis with small joints affected; clinical evidence of synovitis is unusual.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Viral arthritis causes symmetrical small joint polyarthritis, may be associated with rash and prodromal illness, and is usually self-limiting.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: suspected crystal arthritis or cppd disease
condition_aliases: suspected crystal arthritis or cppd disease
fact_text: If investigations suggest calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD), serum uric acid measurements are of limited value and may be normal; serum calcium and parathyroid hormone should be checked to exclude secondary causes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Aspiration of the affected joint is mandatory in patients with sudden onset of a hot swollen joint; fluid should be sent for culture and Gram stain to detect organisms and examined by polarized light microscopy for crystals.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Blood cultures should be taken in patients suspected of septic arthritis; CRP and ESR should be measured to assess infection and inflammation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with suspected crystal-induced arthritis or reactive arthritis may receive intra-articular glucocorticoid injections to reduce pain and swelling, but if Gram stain and synovial fluid culture are negative after 48 hours, longer-term management should target the underlying cause.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: If septic arthritis is suspected, intravenous antibiotics should be started promptly pending culture results.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anthropometric measurements in nutritional assessment should include body mass index, triceps skinfold thickness or mid-arm circumference, and waist circumference.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Assess affect for fatigue, depression, and dementia as part of nutritional disorder examination.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Clinical examination for nutritional disorders should include observation for signs of weight loss such as prominent ribs, muscle wasting, and decreased skin turgor.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Examine eyes for sunken appearance, pallor, jaundice, and Bitot spots indicating vitamin A deficiency.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Examine hands for muscle wasting (dorsal interossei, thenar eminences), finger clubbing, leukonychia indicating low albumin, and koilonychia indicating iron deficiency.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Examine legs for pitting oedema, ulcers, and bruising which may indicate vitamin K deficiency.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Examine mouth for pallor, angular stomatitis (linked to B12, folate, iron deficiency), glossitis (B12, folate, iron deficiency), gingivitis and bleeding gums (vitamin C deficiency), and poorly fitting dentures.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Skin examination should include assessment for dry, flaky skin or dermatitis, hair loss, and specific abnormalities such as petechiae and corkscrew hairs indicating vitamin C deficiency, and dermatitis of pellagra indicating niacin deficiency.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Axial spondyloarthritis targets the spine asymmetrically, including sacroiliitis, with peripheral joint involvement in an asymmetrical pattern.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fragility fractures occur from fall from standing height or less and are associated with osteoporosis or osteopenia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: High-energy fractures result from major trauma and have no underlying disease association.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pathological fractures occur spontaneously or after minimal trauma and are associated with malignancy, Paget disease of bone, or osteomalacia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Stress fractures occur due to running or excessive training and have no underlying disease association.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Vertebral fractures result from bending, lifting, or falling and are associated with osteoporosis or osteopenia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Presentation of fracture includes localized bone pain worsened by movement, usually with a history of trauma, but spontaneous fractures can occur in severe osteoporosis without trauma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteoarthritis targets proximal and distal interphalangeal joints of hands, first carpometacarpal joint at base of thumb, knees, hips, lumbar and cervical spine.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Rheumatoid arthritis typically targets metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints of hands and metatarsophalangeal joints of feet symmetrically, also affecting other joints symmetrically.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Psoriatic arthritis targets proximal and distal interphalangeal joints of hands, often asymmetrically, with involvement of PIP and DIP joints and may be accompanied by nail pitting or onycholysis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Blood tests for suspected inflammatory arthritis should include routine hematology, biochemistry, ESR, CRP, viral serology, and immunological screen including ANA and ACPA or RF.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: If clinical suspicion of inflammatory arthritis is high but blood tests are inconclusive, ultrasound or MRI may help confirm synovitis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: If clinical suspicion is high but no fracture is seen on X-ray, consider magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Order X-rays in two projections at right angles including whole bone and joints at either end to detect fractures and displacement.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: X-rays may show evidence of underlying disorders such as osteoporosis, Paget disease, or osteomalacia; if suspicion remains high despite negative X-rays, MRI is recommended.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: X-rays should be taken in at least two planes and examined for cortical outline discontinuity to confirm fracture.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Glucocorticoids should generally be avoided until a definitive diagnosis of inflammatory arthritis is established.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of inflammatory arthritis should be tailored to diagnosis; NSAIDs and analgesics are used for symptom control while investigations continue.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Relentlessly progressive generalised pain with weight loss suggests malignant disease; fibromyalgia presents with generalised pain plus fatigue, poor concentration, and focal hyperalgesia; widespread pain may indicate hypermobility syndromes or polymyalgia rheumatica; localised pain suggests inflammatory arthritis or osteoarthritis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Causes of muscle weakness include inflammatory diseases (polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, other autoimmune connective tissue diseases), endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, Cushing syndrome, Addison disease), metabolic disorders (myophosphorylase deficiency, phosphofructokinase deficiency, hypokalaemia, carnitine deficiency, osteomalacia, hypercalcaemia), genetic diseases (muscular dystrophy, mitochondrial disease), drugs/toxins (alcohol, cocaine, glucocorticoids, statins, fibrates, TNF-α inhibitors, zidovudine), and infections (viral, parasitic, bacterial).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Clinical assessment of muscle weakness should document presence, pattern, and severity using the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale (0 to full power 5); proximal muscle weakness suggests myopathy or myositis; worsening with exercise and post-exercise cramps suggest metabolic myopathy; family history and early onset suggest muscular dystrophy; alcohol excess can cause inflammatory myositis and atrophy of type 2 muscle fibres.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bone scintigraphy is valuable in suspected bone metastases or Paget disease; FBC, ESR, CRP, plasma and urine protein electrophoresis should be performed to detect inflammatory disease or myeloma; imaging with X-ray, low-dose CT or MRI is indicated if abnormalities are detected; vitamin D and PTH measurement is recommended if osteomalacia is suspected; ALP elevation is typical in Paget disease but may be normal in fibromyalgia and hypermobility syndromes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Investigations for muscle weakness include routine blood tests (biochemistry, haematology, ESR, CRP, CK, vitamin D, PTH), viral serologies (parvovirus, hepatitis B/C, HIV), streptococcus serology, serum and urine protein electrophoresis, autoimmune markers (ACE, ANA, ENA, anti-dsDNA, RF, myositis-specific autoantibodies), muscle biopsy, MRI of affected muscles, electromyography, and CT chest to screen for malignancy if myositis is suspected.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of fibromyalgia and chronic generalised pain should focus on treating the underlying cause; chronic pain of unknown cause poorly responds to analgesics and NSAIDs but may respond partially to amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, or pregabalin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The main causes of mechanical back pain include soft-tissue lesions (e.g., myofacial pain), intervertebral disc disease, facet joint osteoarthritis, vertebral fracture, Paget disease, axial spondyloarthritis including axial psoriatic arthritis, discitis, bone metastases, and spondylolisthesis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Spinal stenosis presents insidiously with leg discomfort on walking relieved by rest, bending forwards or walking uphill, often with a stooped posture and slight flexion at hips and knees.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: urgent spinal imaging if spinal cord or nerve root compression or cauda equina lesion suspected
referral_criteria: urgent referral to neurosurgical or spinal surgery team if significant neurological lesion or suspicion
warning_signs: clinical evidence of spinal cord or nerve root compression
fact_text: In back pain assessment, urgent spinal imaging and referral to neurosurgical or spinal surgery team is required if clinical signs suggest spinal cord or nerve root compression or cauda equina lesion.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Mechanical back pain is more common in manual workers exposed to heavy lifting and twisting, with a generally good prognosis; 30% recover by 2 days, 80% by 6 weeks, but 10-15% may develop chronic pain.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Mechanical back pain is usually confined to the lumbosacral region, buttock or thigh, is asymmetrical, does not radiate beyond the knee, and is exacerbated by activity and relieved by rest.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: urgent investigations including imaging to assess for systemic illness
referral_criteria: refer according to underlying cause (infection, fracture, malignancy)
fact_text: In acute severe back pain, urgent investigations including imaging should be considered to assess for systemic illness, with referral based on findings such as infection, fracture, or malignancy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: consider investigations if pain becomes chronic
referral_criteria: refer to chronic pain service if investigations are normal and pain persists
fact_text: Mechanical back pain should be managed conservatively initially; investigations are considered if pain becomes chronic, and referral to chronic pain service is appropriate if investigations are normal.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
referral_criteria: refer to rheumatology if inflammatory back pain suspected
fact_text: Inflammatory back pain should be initially treated with a trial of NSAIDs and referred to rheumatology for further management.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Referral for physiotherapy should be considered if patients with mechanical back pain have not returned to normal activities by 6 weeks.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Surgery is required in less than 1% of patients with low back pain but may be needed for progressive spinal stenosis, spinal cord compression, severe spondylolisthesis, severe scoliosis, or nerve root compression.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cauda equina syndrome presents with difficulty in micturition, loss of anal sphincter or faecal incontinence, saddle anaesthesia, gait disturbance, and pain, numbness, or weakness affecting one or both legs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Inflammatory back pain improves with exercise but not with rest, is associated with night pain and stiffness, pain and stiffness are worse with movement, typically involves the sacroiliac joints and posterior thoracic spine, may have systemic features like psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease, and recurrent episodes are common.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Mechanical back pain typically worsens with physical activity and improves with rest, often affects the lumbar area, is precipitated by lifting or bending, presents with recurrent episodes, and usually has no systemic features or neurological root distribution; 90% are self-limiting within 6 weeks.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Radicular pain is characterized by unilateral leg pain worse than back pain, pain radiating beyond the knee, paraesthesia in a dermatomal distribution, nerve irritation signs such as reduced straight leg raising reproducing leg pain, motor or sensory/reflex signs limited to one or adjacent nerve roots, and is often self-limiting with 50% recovery by 6 weeks.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Examination red flags for serious spinal pathology include painful spinal deformity, severe or symmetrical spinal deformity, saddle anaesthesia, progressive neurological signs or muscle wasting, and multiple levels of root signs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Red flags in history for serious spinal pathology include age <20 or >55 years, constant progressive pain unrelieved by rest, thoracic location, past history of carcinoma, tuberculosis, HIV, systemic glucocorticoid use, osteoporosis, systemic symptoms like sweats or weight loss, and major trauma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Investigations are not required in acute mechanical back pain unless symptoms persist beyond 6 weeks or red flags are present; MRI is the investigation of choice to detect spinal stenosis, cord compression, nerve root compression, and inflammatory changes in axial spondyloarthritis or malignancy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Neck pain commonly occurs after injury or falling asleep in an awkward position and may be associated with osteoarthritis; persistent pain with nerve root distribution or neurological signs requires investigation with X-rays and MRI and possible referral to a neurosurgical opinion.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: If metastatic spinal disease is suspected, bone scintigraphy or CT should be considered alongside routine biochemistry, haematology, ESR, CRP, serum protein electrophoresis, and human leucocyte antigen B27 testing for axial spondyloarthritis and prostate-specific antigen for prostate carcinoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants may help with sleep and mood in mechanical back pain; glucocorticoids can be considered in severe acute bouts of inflammatory back pain or if axial spondyloarthritis is suspected and NSAIDs are ineffective.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of mechanical back pain includes patient education emphasizing the self-limiting nature, encouraging exercise over rest, use of regular analgesia and/or NSAIDs to improve mobility, and referral to physiotherapy if normal activities are not resumed by 6 weeks.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Other treatments such as epidural and facet joint injections, traction, and lumbar supports are occasionally used but have limited randomized controlled trial evidence to support their use.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Shoulder pain is common and often associated with varying pain patterns and common lesions; general management includes analgesics, NSAIDs, local glucocorticoid injections, and physiotherapy aimed at restoring normal movement and function.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: shoulder pain with rotator cuff lesions
condition_aliases: shoulder pain with rotator cuff lesions
fact_text: Surgery may be required for patients with debilitating or persistent shoulder symptoms due to rotator cuff lesions or severe acromioclavicular joint arthritis; in immunocompromised patients without complete rotator cuff tear on MRI, subacromial glucocorticoid injection and physiotherapy are preferred.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: rotator cuff tears in people over 40
condition_aliases: rotator cuff tears in people over 40
fact_text: Complete rotator cuff tears in people over 40 years of age may respond well to surgical repair but results are less good in older people.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 25.22 Clinical findings in shoulder pain
fact_text: Pain on full abduction and adduction at about 90° of forward elevation suggests acromioclavicular joint disease.
source_figure_or_table: Box 25.22 Clinical findings in shoulder pain

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 25.22 Clinical findings in shoulder pain
fact_text: Tenderness over the bicipital groove and pain reproduced by resisted active wrist supination or elbow flexion indicate bicipital (long head) tendinitis.
source_figure_or_table: Box 25.22 Clinical findings in shoulder pain

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Radiculopathy of C6, C7, or C8 nerve roots can cause hand and wrist pain.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Carpal tunnel syndrome presents with hand position-dependent and/or nocturnal pain, numbness, and paraesthesia of the thumb and second to fourth digits.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: common local causes of elbow pain
condition_aliases: common local causes of elbow pain
source_section: Table 25.23 Common local causes of elbow pain
fact_text: Lateral humeral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) causes lateral epicondyle pain with tenderness and pain reproduced by resisted wrist extension. Medial humeral epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) causes medial epicondyle pain with tenderness and pain reproduced by resisted wrist flexion. Olecranon bursitis causes olecranon pain with tender swelling.
source_figure_or_table: Table 25.23 Common local causes of elbow pain

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hip joint pain is usually felt deep in the groin with variable radiation to the buttock, anterolateral thigh, or knee. Causes include symphysis pubis lesions, osteitis pubis, and pubic ramus fracture, which can present with groin pain. Patients often localize hip pain to the greater trochanter area.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 25.21 The main causes of neck pain
fact_text: Main causes of neck pain include mechanical (postural, whiplash injury, cervical spondylosis, spondylolisthesis), inflammatory (axial spondyloarthritis, psoriatic arthritis, axial CPPD disease, rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, discitis, infection), neoplastic (metastases, myeloma, lymphoma, intrathecal tumours), and other causes such as fibromyalgia and torticollis. Referred pain sources include pharynx, cervical lymph nodes, dental disease, angina pectoris, aortic aneurysm, pancreatic tumour, and diaphragm.
source_figure_or_table: Table 25.21 The main causes of neck pain

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 25.11 Pain patterns around the shoulder
fact_text: Pain patterns around the shoulder can be localized to acromioclavicular joint disease, rotator cuff and glenohumeral arthritis, and bicipital tendinitis, as indicated by specific shaded areas of maximum pain.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 25.11 Pain patterns around the shoulder

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Raynaud phenomenon is characterized by digital vasospasm triggered mostly by cold exposure.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 25.22 Clinical findings in shoulder pain
fact_text: Pain reproduced by resisted active movement in shoulder abduction indicates supraspinatus involvement; pain on external rotation indicates infraspinatus or teres minor involvement; pain on internal rotation indicates subscapularis involvement.
source_figure_or_table: Box 25.22 Clinical findings in shoulder pain

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tenosynovitis affects flexor or extensor digital tendons causing pain and tenderness localized to tendon lesions, often with early morning 'claw-like' digit stiffness. De Quervain tenosynovitis involves abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons, causing maximal pain over the radial distal forearm and wrist, with pain on forced ulnar deviation of the wrist (Finkelstein sign).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Adhesive capsulitis presents with pain and marked restriction of shoulder elevation and external rotation, commonly associated with diabetes mellitus and neck/radicular lesions. Early treatment includes NSAIDs, short course oral prednisolone, intra-articular glucocorticoid injection, and regular pendulum exercises. Complete recovery may take up to 2 years; hydrodilatation and surgical manipulation under anaesthesia are options for severe or persistent symptoms.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Calcific supraspinatus tendinitis unresponsive to glucocorticoid injection may be treated with barbotage (needle disruption of deposit under ultrasound guidance).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Lateral and medial epicondylitis are caused by repetitive trauma and present with pain and tenderness at respective epicondyles. Management includes rest, analgesics, topical or systemic NSAIDs, and local glucocorticoid injections if resistant. Olecranon bursitis may follow repetitive trauma or infection and requires appropriate treatment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 25.24 Local causes of hip pain
fact_text: Local causes of hip pain include osteoarthritis causing groin pain worse on weight-bearing with limited hip movement; gluteus medius enthesitis causing upper lateral thigh pain worse at night with tenderness over greater trochanter; trochanteric bursitis with similar features; adductor tendinitis causing upper inner thigh pain with tenderness over adductor origin; ischiogluteal bursitis causing buttock pain worse on sitting; and pubic symphysis inflammation causing medial groin pain radiating to inner or outer upper thighs with tenderness over symphysis.
source_figure_or_table: Table 25.24 Local causes of hip pain

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 25.25 Local causes of knee pain
fact_text: Local causes of knee pain include osteoarthritis causing weight-bearing pain with knee joint enlargement and crepitus; pre-patellar bursitis causing tender swelling over patella; superficial and deep infrapatellar bursitis and fat-pad syndrome causing tenderness in front of patella with pain on full knee flexion; anserine bursitis causing tenderness over upper medial tibia; medial collateral ligament lesions causing localized tenderness and pain reproduced by valgus stress; popliteal cyst causing tender swelling in popliteal fossa; patellar ligament enthesopathy causing tenderness over tibial tubercle; and osteochondritis of patellar ligament (Osgood–Schlatter disease) causing pain on resisted active knee extension.
source_figure_or_table: Table 25.25 Local causes of knee pain

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pain in the ankle (tibiotalar joint) just distal to the joint is commonly due to osteoarthritis or osteochondral defect and is worse on weight-bearing; pain around the subtalar joint is also worse on weight-bearing. Inflammatory arthritis such as psoriatic arthritis may cause ankle pain with swelling and tenderness. Plantar fasciitis causes heel pain typically worse on weight-bearing and may be associated with enthesitis of the Achilles tendon.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In middle and older adults, knee pain is most commonly caused by osteoarthritis, characterized by locking and painful inability to fully extend the knee, often due to meniscal tear or osteochondritis dissecans; pain may be referred from the hip or lumbosacral spine.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Excessive impact-loading and repetitive use of joints in arthritis can worsen symptoms; joint protection includes ceasing contact sports, pacing activities with breaks, using shock-absorbing footwear, and walking sticks on the contralateral side.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: education and support of whole family
schooling and psychological support
multidisciplinary team involvement
fact_text: For children and adolescents with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, education and support should include the whole family, schooling, psychological support, and be delivered by a multidisciplinary team.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: aerobic fitness training
local strengthening exercise
weight-bearing exercise
fact_text: Aerobic fitness training reduces pain and disability and improves well-being in rheumatic diseases; local strengthening exercises improve muscle strength and coordination; weight-bearing exercise is beneficial in osteoporosis to increase bone density and slow bone loss.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: education about nature of condition and investigations
information and therapist contact to reduce pain and disability
improve self-efficacy
reduce healthcare costs
fact_text: Education for patients with rheumatic diseases improves outcome by reducing pain and disability, improving self-efficacy, and lowering healthcare costs; it should be delivered via one-to-one discussion, written literature, patient-led groups, or interactive computer programs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: local heat
ice packs
wax baths
other local external applications
fact_text: Local heat, ice packs, wax baths, and other local external applications can induce muscle relaxation and provide temporary relief of symptoms in rheumatic diseases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: physical treatments including heat, cold, aids, appliances
surgery
coping strategies
fact_text: Other management options for rheumatic diseases include physical treatments (heat, cold, aids, appliances), surgery, and coping strategies.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patient-run charitable organisations provide valuable information and support for patients with rheumatic diseases and should be integrated with multidisciplinary care.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Local glucocorticoid injections are an option for managing rheumatic diseases, especially when symptoms persist despite other measures.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Other analgesic drug options for rheumatic diseases include oral NSAIDs, topical agents, opioid analgesics, amitriptyline, and gabapentin or pregabalin, choice depending on severity and diagnosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: education
aerobic conditioning
muscle strengthening
simple analgesics
disease-modifying therapy
fact_text: Core interventions for rheumatic diseases include patient education, aerobic conditioning, muscle strengthening, simple analgesics, and disease-modifying therapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of rheumatological disorders should be individualized and patient-centered, involving a multidisciplinary team, and tailored to the underlying diagnosis, with aims to educate patients, control pain, optimize function, modify disease where possible, and identify/treat comorbidities.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Successful management requires thorough assessment including patient activity, risk factors, perceptions, prior medication and coping strategies, comorbidities, and availability of evidence-based interventions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Surgical interventions can relieve pain and restore function in bone, joint, and periarticular disease when drugs, physical therapy, and injections are insufficient.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Recommended self-help strategies include yoga, Pilates, relaxation techniques, avoiding negative situations, altering beliefs about disease, reducing maladaptive pain behavior, using imagery and distraction, and expanding social contacts.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: chronic pain and disability in rheumatology
condition_aliases: chronic pain and disability in rheumatology
fact_text: Self-help plans including self-assessment, problem-solving, and attitude/health behavior changes can improve coping with chronic pain and disability in rheumatology patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Weight loss and maintenance are important in obese patients with arthritis to reduce mechanical strain and inflammatory symptoms; BMI <20 kg/m2 is associated with increased fracture risk and should be avoided.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Soft tissue release and tenosynovectomy can reduce inflammation and pain in tendon disorders but may only provide temporary relief.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: arthrodesis for joint pain and instability
condition_aliases: arthrodesis for joint pain and instability
fact_text: Arthrodesis recommended for damaged wrist (pain relief, grip improvement) and ankle/subtalar joints (pain relief, hindfoot stabilization).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fracture repair options include hip arthroplasty for fractured neck of femur, external fixation for multiple/open fractures, intramedullary nailing for tibial and femur fractures, and screw/plating/wiring for wrist and other fractures.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Joint replacement arthroplasty indicated for painful damaged joints in osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis affecting knee, hip, shoulder, and elbow.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteotomy indicated for early OA of hip (femoral osteotomy), uni-compartmental knee OA, and deformed tibia in OA or Paget disease (tibial osteotomy).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Other procedures include facetectomy for patello-femoral osteoarthritis, nerve root decompression for spinal stenosis and nerve entrapment, and vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty for painful vertebral fractures with poor efficacy evidence.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Excision arthroplasty indicated for painful hallux valgus (first metatarsophalangeal joint), painful distal radio-ulnar joint (radial head), painful acromioclavicular joint (lateral end of clavicle), and painful subluxed metatarsophalangeal joints (metatarsal head).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Synovectomy indicated for pain relief and prevention of extensor tendon rupture in RA, resistant inflammatory synovitis (wrist and extensor tendon sheath with radial head excision), and resistant inflammatory synovitis in knee.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tendon repairs recommended for extensor tendon rupture (hand extensor tendons) and flexor tendon rupture (thumb and finger flexor tendons).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Soft tissue release procedures indicated for median nerve compression (carpal tunnel), posterior tibial nerve entrapment (tarsal tunnel), relief of 'trigger' fingers (flexor tenosynovectomy), ulnar nerve entrapment at elbow (ulnar nerve transposition), and severe Dupuytren contracture (fasciectomy).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Paracetamol (1g up to 4 times daily) is the oral analgesic of first choice for mild to moderate pain due to its central inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis with minimal peripheral effects and good tolerability.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Paracetamol can be combined with codeine (co-codamol) or dihydrocodeine (co-dydramol) for enhanced analgesic effect, but these combinations have more side effects including constipation, headache, and drowsiness, especially in older adults.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: High risk NSAIDs such as indomethacin have a high incidence of dyspepsia and CNS side effects; medium risk NSAIDs like ibuprofen, naproxen, and diclofenac cause more gastrointestinal adverse effects, especially with COX-2 inhibitors even when combined with proton pump inhibitors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Non-selective NSAIDs can damage gastric and duodenal mucosa, increasing risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding and perforation; risk is higher with non-selective NSAIDs than selective COX-2 inhibitors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Major risk factors for NSAID-induced peptic ulcers include age over 60 years, past history of peptic ulcer, past history of adverse events with NSAIDs, concomitant glucocorticoid use, high-dose or multiple NSAIDs, and use of high-risk NSAIDs such as indomethacin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Two COX enzymes exist: COX-1 is constitutively expressed and protects mucosa, platelets, and kidneys; COX-2 is induced by cytokines and mediates pain and inflammation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Low risk NSAIDs: Celecoxib 100–200 mg daily (1–2 doses), Etoricoxib 60–120 mg daily (1 dose); Medium risk NSAIDs: Ibuprofen 1600–2400 mg daily (3–4 doses), Naproxen 500–1000 mg daily (1–2 doses), Diclofenac 75–150 mg daily (2–3 doses); High risk NSAID: Indomethacin 50–200 mg daily (1–2 doses).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: nsaid use with risk factors for ulcer
condition_aliases: nsaid use with risk factors for ulcer
fact_text: H2 antagonists at standard doses are ineffective in preventing NSAID-induced ulceration and bleeding.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: nsaid use with risk factors for ulcer
condition_aliases: nsaid use with risk factors for ulcer
fact_text: Co-prescription of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) or misoprostol (200 mcg two or three times daily) reduces the risk of NSAID-induced ulceration and bleeding in patients at risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: NSAIDs are widely prescribed for pain treatment but long-term use has declined due to increased cardiovascular risk; they inhibit cyclo-oxygenase (COX) enzymes affecting prostaglandin production.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Paracetamol has few adverse effects but chronic use in patients with cardiovascular disease may increase risk of gastrointestinal events and cardiovascular complications, possibly due to channeling bias.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Strong opioid analgesics such as oxycodone or morphine may be required for severe or intractable pain, as non-opioid analgesics like nefopam have side effects limiting their use.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: NSAIDs have less gastrointestinal toxicity risk when used with low-dose aspirin, but a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) should be co-prescribed with all NSAIDs, especially COX-2 selective NSAIDs, to reduce GI adverse events.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Azathioprine requires monitoring of full blood count and creatinine/eGFR to detect marrow suppression and renal impairment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ciclosporin A requires monitoring of blood pressure and creatinine/eGFR to detect hypertension and renal impairment; full blood count and liver function tests are not routinely required.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cyclophosphamide requires monitoring of full blood count, liver function tests, and creatinine/eGFR to detect marrow suppression, liver toxicity, and renal impairment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Classical synthetic DMARDs require monitoring of full blood count, liver function tests, and renal function (creatinine/eGFR) usually every 2 weeks for 6 weeks, then monthly for 3 months, then every 3 months; specific monitoring varies by drug (e.g., visual function for hydroxychloroquine, blood pressure for leflunomide and ciclosporin).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hydroxychloroquine requires monitoring of visual function regularly to detect retinal toxicity, but does not require routine full blood count or liver function tests.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Leflunomide requires monitoring of full blood count, liver function tests, blood pressure, and creatinine/eGFR to detect marrow suppression, liver toxicity, hypertension, and renal impairment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Methotrexate requires monitoring of full blood count, liver function tests, and creatinine/eGFR to detect marrow suppression, liver dysfunction, and renal impairment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Mycophenolate mofetil requires monitoring of full blood count, liver function tests, and creatinine/eGFR to detect marrow suppression, liver toxicity, and renal impairment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Sulfasalazine requires monitoring of full blood count and liver function tests including creatinine/eGFR to detect marrow suppression and liver or renal dysfunction.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Methotrexate is given orally or subcutaneously at 15–25 mg weekly with folic acid (5 mg/week) to reduce toxicity; benefit usually observed after 4–8 weeks but treatment should continue for 3 months before assessing efficacy; avoid excess alcohol to reduce hepatotoxicity risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: DMARDs, including classical small-molecule inhibitors and targeted synthetic agents, modify disease progression in inflammatory rheumatic diseases by targeting immune system molecules and pathways, requiring regular blood monitoring for marrow suppression or liver dysfunction.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: NSAIDs should be used with great caution in older adults due to increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, renal impairment, and cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Use the lowest effective NSAID dose for the shortest duration to control symptoms; avoid NSAIDs in patients on warfarin; allow 2-3 weeks to assess efficacy before considering alternative NSAIDs; never prescribe more than one NSAID simultaneously; consider proton pump inhibitors for patients at risk of GI adverse effects.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Older adults have increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding and perforation with NSAIDs, especially if they have a history of peptic ulcer; they are also at higher risk of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease and renal impairment, so NSAIDs should be avoided or used with caution in this group.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: treatment of oa and superficial periarticular lesions
condition_aliases: treatment of oa and superficial periarticular lesions
fact_text: Topical NSAID creams and gels, including capsaicin cream, can be used as adjuncts or alternatives to oral analgesics for osteoarthritis and superficial periarticular lesions, with systemic absorption mainly from joint capsule levels.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
warning_signs: Reduced grip strength is associated with increased mortality
fact_text: Reduced grip strength is a danger sign associated with increased mortality and should be assessed during nutritional evaluation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Perform general physical examination including neurological exam, assessment of eyes, teeth, mouth, and grip strength to evaluate nutritional status.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ask about weight gain or loss, physical activity, gastrointestinal symptoms, diet, alcohol, smoking, and medication history including vitamins and supplements as part of nutritional status clinical evaluation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Use specific formulas to calculate height from knee height or demispan measurements, differentiated by sex and including age adjustment for knee height.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Check weight, height, waist circumference, and perform routine biochemistry and haematology tests; consider measuring trace elements and vitamins to assess nutritional status.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Use knee height or demispan measurements to estimate height in patients unable to stand for direct height measurement.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: women of childbearing potential on jak inhibitors
condition_aliases: women of childbearing potential on jak inhibitors
recommended_advice: Treatment with Tofacitinib or Baricitinib must be stopped 3 months before planned pregnancy
contraindications_or_cautions: JAK inhibitors require robust contraception in women of childbearing potential
fact_text: Women of childbearing potential treated with JAK inhibitors such as Tofacitinib or Baricitinib must use robust contraception and stop treatment at least 3 months before planned pregnancy due to potential fetal risks.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) and fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging after 5 years of treatment or annually in high-risk patients
recommended_medicines: {"drug": "Hydroxychloroquine", "use": "alone or in combination with other drugs for inflammatory rheumatic diseases"}
recommended_advice: Safe during pregnancy
Warn patients about possible orange staining of urine and contact lenses
contraindications_or_cautions: Toxicity due to retinal accumulation is dose- and time-dependent
fact_text: Hydroxychloroquine is generally well tolerated and safe in pregnancy; retinal toxicity risk increases with dose and duration, so optical coherence tomography and fundus autofluorescence imaging are recommended after 5 years or annually in long-term users; patients should be warned about orange urine and contact lens staining.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Liver function tests (LFTs) every 4–8 weeks initially
recommended_medicines: {"drug": "Sulfasalazine", "use": "alone or in combination with other drugs for inflammatory rheumatic diseases"}
recommended_advice: Warn patients about possible nausea, GI intolerance, rash, and need for monitoring
contraindications_or_cautions: Nausea and gastrointestinal intolerance are common adverse effects
Leucopenia and abnormal liver function tests may occur
Benefit should be assessed after 4–8 weeks
Treatment should be stopped if no benefit after 3 months
fact_text: Sulfasalazine can be used alone or with other drugs in inflammatory rheumatic diseases; it commonly causes nausea, GI intolerance, leucopenia, and abnormal LFTs; liver function tests should be monitored every 4–8 weeks initially; treatment benefit should be assessed at 4–8 weeks and stopped if ineffective after 3 months.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition

fact_text: Targeted synthetic DMARDs require baseline and 3-month monitoring of full blood count, liver function tests, and lipid profile depending on the drug; Apremilast does not require routine monitoring, while Tofacitinib, Baricitinib, and Upadacitinib require all three tests; Filgotinib requires FBC monitoring; Avacopan requires FBC and LFTs monitoring.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Biologic and targeted synthetic DMARDs act by inhibiting key cytokines and immune cell activation pathways such as JAK-STAT signaling, TNF, IL-6, IL-1, IL-17, and B cell proliferation to reduce inflammation in inflammatory rheumatic diseases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: Warn patients to stop therapy and seek advice if new respiratory symptoms develop
If pneumonitis occurs, withdraw treatment and give high-dose glucocorticoids
fact_text: Pneumonitis is a rare but serious adverse effect of targeted synthetic DMARDs; patients should be warned to stop treatment and seek medical advice if new respiratory symptoms develop; if pneumonitis occurs, treatment should be withdrawn and high-dose glucocorticoids started.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: systemic lupus erythematosus (sle), vasculitis, rheumatoid arthritis (ra), psoriatic arthritis (psa)
condition_aliases: systemic lupus erythematosus (sle), vasculitis, rheumatoid arthritis (ra), psoriatic arthritis (psa)
recommended_medicines: Leflunomide (LEF) inhibits pyrimidine synthesis and is used alone or with other drugs for RA and PsA; requires contraception in women of childbearing potential due to teratogenicity; must be stopped 2 years before planned pregnancy or use cholestyramine washout
Azathioprine (AZA) is used in vasculitis and SLE, often combined with other drugs; requires TPMT genetic testing due to risk of myelosuppression

Cyclophosphamide is a cytotoxic alkylating agent used mainly in ANCA-associated vasculitis and SLE with major organ involvement; given intravenously in pulses; adverse effects include nausea, anorexia, vomiting, bone marrow suppression, cardiotoxicity, alopecia, and haemorrhagic cystitis which can be mitigated by co-administration of mesna
Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) inhibits guanosine nucleotide synthesis and is used in SLE and vasculitis; main adverse effect is haematological toxicity
Ciclosporin A inhibits lymphocyte activation and is used in RA and PsA; adverse effects include nephrotoxicity and hypertension

Glucocorticoids have anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects; used in various inflammatory rheumatic diseases; high doses induce remission in early RA, systemic and polyarticular JIA, giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, vasculitis, and SLE; long-term use requires caution due to side effects and risk of rebound inflammation on withdrawal
Intramuscular methylprednisolone (80–120 mg) is useful for controlling inflammatory arthritis while waiting for new oral drugs to take effect

Targeted synthetic DMARDs (tsDMARDs) inhibit Janus-activated kinase (JAK) enzymes, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine signaling; JAK inhibitors (JAKi) increase risk of infections, DVT, cardiovascular disease, and malignancy; contraindicated in active infections, active hepatitis B or C, and recent thrombocytopenia; require avoidance in patients over 65 years unless no alternatives
