fact_text: Ocular sarcoidosis occurs in 25-50% of patients with systemic sarcoidosis and can involve any eye part; anterior uveitis is most common, but conjunctival granulomas, lacrimal gland enlargement, retinal vasculitis, and optic nerve inflammation also occur.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ocular syphilis occurs in 1-5% of syphilis infections and can present at any disease stage with diverse ocular manifestations; co-infection with HIV is common and requires neuro-syphilis treatment if involved.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ocular toxoplasmosis is the most common cause of posterior uveitis worldwide, presenting with floaters, blurred vision, photophobia, and characteristic white focal retinal lesions with overlying vitreous inflammation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ocular tuberculosis can affect any eye part with varied presentations including anterior scleritis or uveitis, posterior uveitis with granulomas, vasculitis, or choroiditis; diagnosis requires clinical suspicion especially in endemic or immunocompromised patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Posterior uveitis involves inflammation of retina, choroid, and optic nerve; it is less common but sight-threatening and requires thorough clinical evaluation to identify underlying cause.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of aqueous fluid samples enables identification of specific viral pathogens in ARN; intravitreal or intravenous antiviral therapy should be started early to improve outcomes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anterior uveitis presents with eye pain, redness, photophobia, blurred vision, conjunctival injection, keratic precipitates on corneal endothelium, inflammatory cells and flare in anterior chamber; hypopyon may be visible in severe cases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diagnosis of anterior uveitis is primarily clinical using slit-lamp examination to identify cells and flare; full dilated fundus exam is needed to exclude posterior uveitis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In anterior uveitis patients with history >3 months, age <45 years, or joint pains requiring health care, HLA-B27 testing is warranted to identify seronegative spondyloarthropathy association.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diagnosis of ocular sarcoidosis is supported by biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas, chest imaging, and elevated serum ACE levels.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Treatment of anterior uveitis involves glucocorticoid eye drops to reduce inflammation and cycloplegic agents to relieve pain and break posterior synechiae.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Specific treatment for infective anterior uveitis should be given if identified.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Treatment of ocular sarcoidosis involves glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive agents to control inflammation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: HIV co-infection with ocular syphilis requires treatment with neuro-syphilis regimen as outlined in Chapter 15.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Prophylaxis following activation of ocular toxoplasmosis reduces risk of further episodes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Treatment of ocular toxoplasmosis typically involves antiparasitic drugs like pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine combined with glucocorticoids to reduce inflammation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of ocular tuberculosis includes at least 6 to 9 months of anti-tuberculosis therapy combined with glucocorticoids to control ocular inflammation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Endophthalmitis is an ocular emergency with marked intraocular inflammation, usually secondary to infection, presenting with ocular pain, reduced vision, redness, photophobia, conjunctival injection, corneal oedema, and hypopyon; vitreous opacities and reduced red reflex may be seen.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Endophthalmitis causes include exogenous infection after intraocular surgery or trauma, and endogenous infection from haematogenous spread.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 28.4 Causes of optic disc swelling
fact_text: Optic disc swelling differential diagnoses include inflammatory, vascular, tumour, infiltrative, granulomatous, compressive causes, and pseudopapilloedema structural variants.
source_figure_or_table: Box 28.4 Causes of optic disc swelling

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Visual prognosis in endophthalmitis varies with speed of diagnosis, treatment, and virulence of the causative organism.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Gram stain and culture of aqueous and vitreous samples
B-scan ultrasonography if posterior segment visualization is compromised
fact_text: Diagnostic samples for endophthalmitis should include aqueous and vitreous for Gram stain, culture, and sensitivity; B-scan ultrasound is adjunctive if posterior segment is not visible.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Intravitreal broad-spectrum antibiotics, commonly vancomycin and ceftazidime
fact_text: Immediate treatment of endophthalmitis requires intravitreal broad-spectrum antibiotics, typically vancomycin and ceftazidime.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Systemic antibiotics may be indicated in endogenous endophthalmitis or severe/refractory cases
fact_text: Systemic antibiotics may be required in endogenous or severe/refractory endophthalmitis cases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pars plana vitrectomy is considered in severe or refractory endophthalmitis, especially if visual prognosis is poor or infection is unresponsive.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: NAION typically presents in adults over 50 years with sudden painless monocular vision loss, often on waking, with variable severity; visual field defects are common, especially altitudinal defects; patients may report blurred vision or dark spots.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Papilloedema grading (Frisén scale) defines 6 stages (0 to 5) based on optic disc swelling severity, vessel obscuration, peripapillary halo presence, and optic cup visibility, guiding clinical assessment of raised intracranial pressure.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: fundoscopy to confirm optic disc swelling
optical coherence tomography (OCT) for detailed optic nerve head and retinal nerve fibre layer imaging
fluorescein angiography or B-scan ultrasound to exclude optic disc drusen
baseline visual field testing to monitor disease progression
blood pressure measurement to exclude hypertensive papilloedema
body mass index calculation as risk factor for idiopathic intracranial hypertension
CT head and CT venogram to exclude mass lesions, hydrocephalus, venous sinus thrombosis
lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement and cerebrospinal fluid analysis to exclude infection or inflammation
fact_text: Diagnosis of papilloedema requires fundoscopy to confirm optic disc swelling; OCT provides detailed imaging; fluorescein angiography or B-scan ultrasound exclude optic disc drusen; baseline visual field testing monitors progression; CT head and venogram exclude structural causes; lumbar puncture measures CSF pressure and excludes infection/inflammation; blood pressure and BMI assessment help exclude hypertensive papilloedema and assess idiopathic intracranial hypertension risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab (for steroid-sparing therapy)
referral_criteria: urgent diagnosis and treatment initiation to prevent permanent vision loss
fact_text: Giant cell arteritis causes sudden painless monocular vision loss due to ischemic optic neuropathy from short posterior ciliary artery occlusion; symptoms include amaurosis fugax and diplopia; diagnosis requires temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy; treatment is urgent high-dose glucocorticoids with possible steroid-sparing tocilizumab; long-term follow-up is necessary to monitor relapse and prevent permanent vision loss.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Treatment of papilloedema targets underlying raised intracranial pressure; management includes weight reduction, acetazolamide, and diuretics; refractory cases may require surgical intervention such as optic nerve sheath fenestration or CSF shunting; regular visual field and optic disc monitoring is essential to guide treatment and prevent vision loss.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Symptomatic relief of ptosis and diplopia in ocular myasthenia gravis can be achieved with eyelid crutches or prisms.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ocular myasthenia gravis presents with fluctuating ptosis and diplopia due to weakness of extraocular muscles, often worsening with fatigue or sustained activity and usually asymmetric.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Causes of optic atrophy include hereditary (e.g., Leber hereditary optic neuropathy), ischaemic (e.g., anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy), inflammatory/autoimmune (e.g., optic neuritis), compressive (e.g., pituitary adenoma, meningioma), traumatic (e.g., direct optic nerve injury), toxic/nutritional (e.g., amiodarone, methanol poisoning), infectious (e.g., syphilis), degenerative (e.g., glaucoma), vascular (e.g., central retinal artery occlusion), and miscellaneous (e.g., chronic papilloedema).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Optic neuritis presents with acute unilateral eye pain, especially on eye movement, and progressive vision loss over hours to days, often with color vision defects and relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Acetylcholine receptor antibody (AChR-Ab) testing is positive in 50–70% of ocular myasthenia gravis cases; anti-MuSK antibodies are more common in generalized myasthenia gravis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diagnosis of ocular myasthenia gravis involves clinical evaluation and bedside tests such as ice pack test and rest test, which are quick and useful for diagnosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Single-fibre electromyography (SFEMG) is highly sensitive for detecting neuromuscular transmission defects in ocular myasthenia gravis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain and orbits with gadolinium contrast is the most useful investigation to confirm optic neuritis and assess for lesions suggestive of multiple sclerosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressive agents such as azathioprine may be used in ocular myasthenia gravis for more severe or refractory cases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, is often first-line treatment for ocular myasthenia gravis to improve symptoms and prevent progression.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Thymectomy is generally reserved for ocular myasthenia gravis patients with thymoma or generalized disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Intravenous methylprednisolone is typically used for severe optic neuritis cases to speed recovery, but does not affect final visual outcome.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Mild optic neuritis cases may recover spontaneously; glucocorticoids may speed recovery but do not alter final vision.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency characterized by sudden increased intraocular pressure due to impaired aqueous humour outflow from a closed or narrowed anterior chamber angle, presenting with rapid onset severe ocular pain, headache, decreased visual acuity, halos around lights, red eye, corneal oedema, mid-dilated fixed pupil, and hazy cornea.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Optic neuropathy causes visual impairment with sudden or gradual vision loss, often affecting one eye, with central, peripheral, or altitudinal visual field defects; may present with decreased colour vision and relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) in unilateral or asymmetric cases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a common cause of progressive optic nerve damage and visual field loss, often asymptomatic early, with open anterior chamber angle, typically affecting adults over 40 years, more prevalent in African and Hispanic populations, associated with elevated intraocular pressure, myopia, hypertension, and diabetes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Secondary glaucomas are a group of eye conditions with increased intraocular pressure due to underlying ocular or systemic disorders such as trauma, inflammation (uveitis), vascular disorders (central retinal vein occlusion), medications (glucocorticoids), or intraocular tumours.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tense orbit is an ophthalmic emergency caused by soft tissue oedema and retrobulbar haemorrhage within the orbit, leading to increased intraorbital pressure, restricted blood flow, optic nerve injury, and sight loss; clinical features include reduced visual acuity, painful proptosis, and resistance to retropulsion.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Evaluation of optic neuropathy requires detailed ophthalmic exam including visual acuity, colour vision, visual field testing, and fundoscopy to assess optic disc; OCT measures retinal nerve fibre layer thickness to detect optic nerve damage; MRI of brain and orbits is indicated if inflammatory, demyelinating, or compressive lesions suspected; blood tests including inflammatory markers and specific antibodies help diagnose underlying causes like giant cell arteritis or autoimmune conditions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diagnosis of POAG requires comprehensive eye exam including intraocular pressure measurement by tonometry, pachymetry for corneal thickness, gonioscopy to confirm open angle, optic nerve head evaluation by slit-lamp biomicroscopy or OCT, and automated visual field testing to monitor disease progression.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Immediate reduction of intraocular pressure is required in acute angle-closure glaucoma to prevent optic nerve damage and irreversible vision loss; treatment includes intravenous acetazolamide plus topical pressure-lowering agents and pilocarpine to induce miosis; definitive treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy to create an alternative aqueous outflow pathway; surgical lens extraction may be indicated if refractory.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Initial glaucoma management aims to lower intraocular pressure (IOP) to slow disease progression; 360° selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) is first-line treatment if topical treatment is unavailable or declined; topical prostaglandin analogues are preferred first-line agents; beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, sympathomimetics, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are additional options if IOP remains uncontrolled.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Surgical options for glaucoma, including trabeculectomy or drainage implants, are reserved for cases refractory to medical and laser therapy; regular monitoring with IOP checks, visual field analysis, and optic nerve evaluation is required to detect progression and guide treatment escalation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Treatment of optic neuritis includes intravenous glucocorticoids to accelerate recovery; ischemic optic neuropathy management includes addressing cardiovascular risk factors; surgical intervention may be needed in compressive optic neuropathy to relieve pressure; long-term management focuses on monitoring vision changes and treating associated systemic conditions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: In patients receiving parenteral nutrition, phosphate must be provided to prevent deficiency.
Phosphate supplementation is advised in elderly people with poor diet and in severe starvation.
fact_text: Phosphate supplementation is required in patients on parenteral nutrition, elderly with poor diet, and severe starvation to prevent deficiency.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
warning_signs: Muscle pain, weakness, bone pain, neurological symptoms, respiratory failure, heart failure, and seizures are clinical features of phosphate deficiency requiring urgent treatment.
fact_text: Phosphate deficiency can cause muscle pain, weakness, bone pain, neurological symptoms, respiratory failure, heart failure, and seizures, which require urgent treatment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Phosphate deficiency is rare but should be considered in patients with renal tubular phosphate loss, diabetic ketoacidosis, prolonged aluminium hydroxide use, or alcohol misuse with high carbohydrate intake.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 5.36 Cause and clinical features of scurvy
fact_text: Scurvy clinical features include swollen gums that bleed easily, perifollicular and petechial hemorrhages, ecchymoses, haemarthrosis, gastrointestinal bleeding, and anaemia; precipitated by dietary deficiency of vitamin C for more than 2 months or increased requirement states such as trauma, burns, infections, smoking, or drugs like glucocorticoids and aspirin.
source_figure_or_table: Box 5.36 Cause and clinical features of scurvy

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
contraindications_or_cautions: Excessive phosphorus intake (Ca:P ratio <1:3) can cause hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
fact_text: Calcium absorption depends on vitamin D status; deficiency or malabsorption impairs absorption causing hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism; excessive phosphorus intake with Ca:P ratio below 1:3 worsens hypocalcaemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: whole-body status or dietary intake assessment for inorganic micronutrients
fact_text: Assessment of inorganic micronutrient deficiency requires evaluation of whole-body status or dietary intake because toxicity and deficiency can result from self-medication or altered absorption/excretion.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Iron absorption is higher from haem sources than non-haem; vitamin C enhances absorption; dietary calcium inhibits iron absorption from the same meal, risking deficiency in borderline cases; iron homeostasis is regulated by hepcidin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 5.37 Summary of clinically important inorganic nutrients
recommended_medicines: Recommended daily calcium intake is 700 mg from dairy products and tofu.
Recommended daily phosphorus intake is 550 mg from marmite, dry-roasted peanuts, dairy products, cereals, bread, and meat.
Recommended daily magnesium intake is 300 mg for males and 270 mg for females from whole grains and nuts.
Recommended daily iron intake is 8.7 mg for males and 14.8 mg for menstruating females from red meat, liver, vegetables, and wholemeal bread.
Recommended daily zinc intake is 9.5 mg for men and 7 mg for women from red meat, seafood, dairy products, and wholemeal bread.
Recommended daily iodine intake is 140 µg from edible seaweeds, sea fish, dairy products, and seafood products.
Recommended daily selenium intake is 75 µg for men and 60 µg for women from fish, meat, oatmeal, rice, beans, and mushrooms.
Recommended daily copper intake is 1.2 mg from shellfish, liver, bread, and cereal products.
Recommended fluoride intake has no recommended nutrient intake (RNI) but safe intake is 0.5 mg/kg from tea and drinking water.
Recommended daily potassium intake is 3500 mg from dried fruit, potatoes, coffee, fresh fruit, vegetables, meat, and dairy foods.
Recommended daily sodium intake is 1600 mg from table salt, anchovies, processed foods, bread, and bacon.
recommended_advice: Increased amounts of calcium, magnesium, and zinc are required in women during lactation.
Rich sources contain the nutrient in highest concentration but are not generally eaten in large amounts; important sources contain less but contribute most due to larger amounts consumed.
fact_text: Daily recommended intakes for key inorganic nutrients include calcium 700 mg, phosphorus 550 mg, magnesium 300 mg (male) or 270 mg (female), iron 8.7 mg (male) or 14.8 mg (menstruating female), zinc 9.5 mg (men) or 7 mg (women), iodine 140 µg, selenium 75 µg (men) or 60 µg (women), copper 1.2 mg, fluoride safe intake 0.5 mg/kg, potassium 3500 mg, and sodium 1600 mg; increased calcium, magnesium, and zinc are needed during lactation.
source_figure_or_table: Table 5.37 Summary of clinically important inorganic nutrients

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Oral phosphate supplements or dietary modification are recommended for mild to moderate phosphate deficiency.
fact_text: Mild to moderate phosphate deficiency should be treated with oral phosphate supplements or dietary modification.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Children under 2 years with orbital cellulitis should be admitted for IV antibiotics due to poorly developed orbital septum and high risk of progression.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Orbital cellulitis is a serious infection of tissues surrounding the eye within the orbit, often caused by bacterial spread from adjacent sinuses, with risk of vision loss and intracranial extension.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Differentiation between orbital cellulitis and preseptal cellulitis is critical; preseptal cellulitis is more common and less severe, while orbital cellulitis involves deeper tissues and risk of complications.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: For suspected orbital cellulitis, investigations may include temperature measurement, full blood count, blood cultures, and CT scans of orbits and sinuses (pre- and post-contrast) to assess extent.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Oral acetazolamide 250 mg or modified-release acetazolamide is used in a case-dependent manner to decrease aqueous production in glaucoma.

fact_text: Prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost) are used once daily in the evening topically to increase aqueous outflow via the uveoscleral route in glaucoma treatment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Topical ROCK inhibitor netarsudil 0.02% is used once daily in the evening to increase aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork and reduce episcleral venous pressure in glaucoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Topical alpha-2 agonist brimonidine 0.2% is used twice daily to decrease aqueous production and increase aqueous outflow via the uveoscleral route in glaucoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Topical apraclonidine 0.5% is used three times daily and 1% as a stat dose to decrease aqueous production and increase aqueous outflow via the uveoscleral route in glaucoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Topical beta-blocker timolol maleate (0.25%, 0.5%) is used twice daily to decrease aqueous humor production in glaucoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors brinzolamide 1% and dorzolamide 2% are used twice daily (or three times daily if used alone) to decrease aqueous production in glaucoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Topical pilocarpine (1%-6%) is used up to four times daily to increase aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork by inducing miosis in glaucoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Suspected orbital cellulitis requires admission and treatment with intravenous antibiotics, typically ceftriaxone plus metronidazole.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ocular metastasis refers to spread of cancer cells to the eye from a primary tumor located elsewhere in the body, most commonly from breast or lung cancer.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ocular surface malignancies include squamous cell carcinoma, conjunctival melanoma, and lymphoma; squamous cell carcinoma arises from the limbal region and is linked to UV exposure, human papillomavirus infection, and immunosuppression; conjunctival melanoma originates from melanocytes and presents as a pigmented lesion often associated with primary acquired melanosis; mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphomas present as painless salmon-pink lesions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 28.8 Differentiation between orbital and preseptal cellulitis
fact_text: Orbital cellulitis usually presents with fever, eyelid swelling and erythema, proptosis (often subtle), chemosis, eye pain or tenderness, painful eye movements, ophthalmoplegia, late visual acuity reduction, and possible color vision changes; preseptal cellulitis may have fever sometimes, eyelid swelling and erythema, rarely chemosis, no proptosis, no eye pain or tenderness, no painful eye movements, no ophthalmoplegia, no visual acuity reduction, and no color vision affected.
source_figure_or_table: Table 28.8 Differentiation between orbital and preseptal cellulitis

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Sebaceous carcinoma is a rare but highly aggressive eyelid malignancy arising from sebaceous glands, commonly in the upper eyelid; it may mimic benign lesions like chalazia or blepharitis, causing diagnostic delays and has a high recurrence rate with potential for local invasion and distant metastasis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the eyelid accounts for 5-10% of eyelid malignancies, presents as a scaly, erythematous lesion with irregular borders and may ulcerate; it is more aggressive than BCC with higher risk of metastasis to regional lymph nodes and distant organs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) accounts for 85-90% of eyelid cancers, presenting as a slow-growing pearly nodule with rolled edges and often ulceration; it rarely metastasizes but can cause extensive local tissue destruction.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, presenting as a pigmented or non-pigmented dome- or mushroom-shaped lesion with possible subretinal fluid and retinal detachment; diagnosis relies on clinical exam, retinal imaging, and ultrasonography; treatment aims to preserve life and vision, depending on tumor size, location, and metastases, with options including brachytherapy, external beam radiation, surgical enucleation, and systemic therapy for metastases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Melanoma of the eyelid is a rare but highly aggressive cancer with significant metastatic risk, often presenting as a pigmented lesion with irregular borders and rapid growth, requiring prompt diagnosis and management; risk factors include prolonged UV exposure, fair skin, advanced age, and prior skin cancers.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Orbital metastasis most commonly originates from breast cancer due to choroid vascular supply; symptoms vary by location and include proptosis, restricted eye movements, blurred vision, visual field defects, or pain. Diagnosis requires clinical exam plus imaging (ultrasound, MRI). Treatment depends on location and may include excision, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapies to preserve vision and control systemic disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: Early diagnosis is critical to improve outcomes and preserve vision
Treatment choice depends on disease extent and aims to prevent metastasis
referral_criteria: suspected retinoblastoma in child under 5 years with leukocoria or eye swelling
fact_text: Retinoblastoma is the most common malignant intraocular tumor in children under 5, presenting with leukocoria, eye redness, or swelling. Diagnosis requires fundoscopy, ultrasound, and MRI. Treatment options include enucleation, chemotherapy, radiation, laser, or cryotherapy depending on disease extent, aiming to preserve vision and prevent metastasis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Idiopathic anterior uveitis is the most common form, presenting with red eye, pain, photophobia, and pupil constriction; systemic associations include HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, herpesviridae infections, syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Behçet disease, and SLE.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In suspected anterior uveitis, a full systemic history should be taken to identify associated systemic diseases or drug exposures, including trauma and contact lens use.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Dysthyroid optic neuropathy occurs if increased orbital pressure damages the optic nerve, causing visual loss; orbital swelling causing eyelid proptosis without optic nerve damage leads to corneal exposure keratopathy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Optic neuritis presents with reduced visual acuity and retrobulbar pain worsened by eye movement, without proptosis; optic nerve function tests (color vision, visual field, pupillary responses) are abnormal.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Sight-threatening complications of thyroid eye disease include dysthyroid optic neuropathy from increased orbital pressure and corneal exposure keratopathy from eyelid proptosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Thyroid eye disease is the most common cause of unilateral or bilateral proptosis in adults, characterized by ocular pain at rest, exacerbated by eye movements, eyelid/conjunctival swelling and redness, double vision, and proptosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Left homonymous hemianopia results from right cerebral hemisphere stroke affecting optic radiations; bitemporal hemianopia is caused by pituitary or chiasmal pathology; monocular altitudinal defects arise from optic nerve or retinal pathology.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: A dendritic corneal lesion in a patient with history of contact lens wear and burning eye sensation is typical of herpes simplex keratitis and should be treated with topical aciclovir.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: high-resolution MRI to detect luminal stenosis or enhancement of superficial temporal arteries
recommended_medicines: intravenous methylprednisolone for end-organ damage while awaiting diagnostic confirmation
fact_text: In suspected arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy secondary to giant cell arteritis, diagnosis is supported by elevated ESR, CRP, reactive thrombocytosis, and confirmed by temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound; intravenous methylprednisolone should be started promptly if end-organ damage is present while awaiting confirmation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
trigger_evidence: presence of drusen and pigmentary changes
recommended_tests: OCTA or fluorescein angiography to confirm choroidal neovascular membrane
referral_criteria: urgent referral to ophthalmology for diagnosis confirmation and treatment initiation
fact_text: Wet age-related macular degeneration presents with gradual central vision loss, distortion of straight lines, drusen, pigmentary changes, and macular haemorrhage; urgent ophthalmology referral is required for confirmation with OCT and angiography and treatment with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In anorexia nervosa, clinical examination should include checking for thin, dry hair and lanugo hair on skin, yellow skin due to carotenaemia, and dental erosion or caries from self-induced vomiting.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Agitation or overactivity (anxiety, ADHD, hypomania, acute psychosis, schizophrenia, delirium) should be assessed by observing behaviour.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In bulimia nervosa, look for dental erosion or caries from self-induced vomiting and knuckle calluses (Russell sign) on hands.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Look for stigmata of chronic liver disease such as spider naevi and palmar erythema on the skin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In suspected cocaine use, examine for erosion of the nasal septum.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Underactivity with psychomotor retardation (eyes down, hunched posture, little movement or speech) is a key clinical sign in depression, chronic schizophrenia, catatonia, parkinsonism, and dementia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In endocrine conditions, psychomotor retardation (eyes down, hunched posture, little movement or speech) increases risk of anxiety and depression.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Examine arms for injection track marks from intravenous drug use and scars from previous self-harm.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In OCD, examine for skin picking or excoriation lesions and contact dermatitis from excessive cleaning or abrasion.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Examine legs for signs of peripheral neuropathy, which is commonly caused by chronic alcohol excess.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In autism and catatonia, observe for repeating words or postures (echolalia, echopraxia) and bizarre postures characteristic of catatonia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Repeating words or postures (echolalia, echopraxia) are clinical signs seen in autism and catatonia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Underactivity such as psychomotor retardation (eyes down, hunched posture, little movement or speech) suggests depression, chronic schizophrenia, catatonia, parkinsonism, or dementia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Agitation or overactivity is a clinical sign seen in anxiety, ADHD, hypomania, acute psychosis, schizophrenia, and delirium.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In trichotillomania, examine for missing clumps of hair due to hair pulling.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MoCA abstraction tests similarity recognition between pairs of words (e.g., banana-orange as fruit) for 2 points.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MoCA attention is tested by digit span forward and backward, letter tapping (A), and serial 7 subtraction from 100, with scoring based on accuracy and errors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MoCA delayed recall tests recall of five words without cues, scoring up to 5 points, with optional category and multiple choice cues for un-cued recall scoring.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MoCA language test includes repeating two complex sentences and verbal fluency by naming words starting with letter F in one minute (≥11 words required).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MoCA memory test involves reading a list of five words twice and recalling them after 5 minutes, with scoring based on recall trials and cues.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MoCA naming test requires naming three animals (lion, rhinoceros, camel) for up to 3 points.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MoCA orientation tests awareness of date, month, year, day, place, and city for up to 6 points.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MoCA visuospatial/executive function is assessed by copying a cube and drawing a clock showing ten past eleven, scoring up to 5 points for the clock (contour, numbers, hands).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) is a validated screening tool for cognitive impairment with a maximum score of 30; a score of 26 or above is considered normal, with an additional point added for patients with 12 or fewer years of education.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The WHO ICD-11 classification of psychiatric disorders includes neurodevelopmental disorders (e.g., ASD, ADHD), primary psychotic disorders (e.g., schizophrenia), mood disorders (bipolar, depression), anxiety and stress-related disorders (e.g., phobias, PTSD), eating and elimination disorders (e.g., anorexia nervosa), bodily distress disorders, substance misuse disorders, impulse control disorders, personality disorders, factitious disorders, delirium, dementia, and mental disorders associated with pregnancy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: A brief mental state examination can be performed in a few minutes and should be part of the assessment of all patients, not only those with suspected psychiatric illness.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: A full psychiatric history including a detailed mental state examination may take an hour or more due to complexity and is usually reserved for patients with suspected psychiatric illness.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Psychiatric assessment requires a structured clinical history emphasizing detailed symptom history and less reliance on investigations, with a large clinical examination component integrated into history taking rather than as separate procedures.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Psychiatric history taking often includes interviewing an informant (relative or friend) who knows the patient well to improve accuracy, especially when the patient's insight is impaired.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The psychiatric interview aims to establish a therapeutic relationship, elicit symptoms and history, examine mental state, and provide information, reassurance, and advice.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Assessment of alertness and motor behaviour abnormalities such as restlessness or retardation is essential; level of consciousness must be determined especially to assess possible delirium.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: A delusion is a false belief held with strong conviction despite evidence to the contrary, often with a patient's cultural background as context.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hallucinations are sensory perceptions without external stimuli, such as hearing voices when no one is present.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Content of thought should be elicited by asking main concerns, presence of negative, guilty, or hopeless thoughts suggesting depression, thoughts of self-harm, excessive worry, grandiosity or mania; abnormal thinking forms include loosened associations and thought broadcasting in schizophrenia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Mood should be assessed by facial expression, posture, and movements; patients should be asked if they feel sad, depressed, or lack pleasure (anhedonia), or if they feel anxious, worried, tense, or have elevated mood with excess energy and reduced need for sleep.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Speech speed and fluency should be observed, noting slow (retarded) speech, word-finding difficulty, or rapid 'pressure of speech' that is difficult to interrupt.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Psychiatric interview should include presenting problem, reason for referral (who referred and why), presenting complaints (patient's description of main problems and expectations), history of present illness (course, nature, duration, severity, associated factors), family history (mental illness in relatives), personal history (birth, development, education, relationships, social circumstances), previous medical and psychiatric history (including substance use and direct questions about psychiatric history), and previous personality (patterns of behaviour and stress reactions).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Delirium is very common in medical inpatients (+++), rare or absent in general practice and outpatients; alcohol/substance abuse and depression are common across settings; schizophrenia and bipolar disorder are mainly seen in general psychiatric services.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cognitive function assessment includes memory, concentration, visuospatial and executive function; brief orientation tests (person, place, time) and serial 7s subtraction are used to exclude significant impairment; standardized screening tools like the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) cover main cognitive domains and are useful especially when delirium or mild impairment is suspected.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Iron deficiency anaemia is a major global nutritional cause of ill health; in the UK, about 10% of women are iron-deficient, with dietary overload occasionally causing iron accumulation and liver damage.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Selenium is a cofactor for glutathione peroxidase and iodothyronine deiodinase; deficiency can cause hypothyroidism, cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease), and myopathy; selenium deficiency is linked to industrial pollution and dietary selenium intake varies by geography.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chronic zinc deficiency causes dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhoea, growth retardation, and immune dysfunction; zinc supplements may accelerate healing of skin lesions and improve general well-being in malnourished patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Western diets are high in sodium and low in potassium and magnesium; recommended daily salt intake is below 6 g to prevent hypertension; potassium and magnesium intake should be maintained to prevent blood pressure rise and cardiovascular risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fluoride is essential for normal dental enamel formation and repair; deficiency increases dental caries risk, especially in children; fluoride supplementation via water or toothpaste reduces caries but excess fluoride causes dental mottling, skeletal fluorosis, and increased fracture risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chronic fluoride poisoning occurs with water fluoride >10 ppm and can cause dental and skeletal fluorosis; exposure to aluminium sodium fluoride in smelting can cause pitting of teeth; fluoride toxicity should be suspected with dental mottling and bone pain.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Iodine deficiency causes goitre and hypothyroidism; prevention includes iodised salt administration (1–2 mL of iodised poppy seed oil every 3–5 years for children and adults) and fortification of foods with iodine, especially in endemic areas.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Iron absorption is regulated by body iron stores and zinc competes with iron absorption; indiscriminate iron supplementation can be toxic and fatal in overdose, so iron supplements should be used cautiously.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Brain imaging techniques such as PET, MRI, and SPECT reveal structural and functional brain abnormalities in psychiatric disorders, but are currently research tools without established diagnostic or prognostic utility.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Genetic factors contribute to psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, with polygenic inheritance and environmental modulation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Psychiatric disorders arise from complex interactions among psychological, social, environmental, and genetic factors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Psychotic patients often lack insight into their illness and fail to recognize the need for treatment, which should be assessed during history taking.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In anxiety disorders, recommended investigations include full blood count, urea and electrolytes, calcium, urine drug screen, GGT, and serum or urine metanephrines.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: blood tests: full blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, CRP, urea and electrolytes, calcium, liver function tests, thyroid function tests, HbA1c, vitamin B12, folate
structural brain imaging (head CT or MRI)
further brain imaging: FDG PET or perfusion SPECT, DaTscan, Amyloid/Tau PET
microscopy and culture if clinically indicated
chest X-ray, ECG, syphilis and HIV serology
fact_text: In most patients with dementia, recommended investigations include blood tests (full blood count, ESR, CRP, urea and electrolytes, calcium, liver and thyroid function tests, HbA1c, vitamin B12, folate), structural brain imaging (CT or MRI), and further imaging (FDG PET, perfusion SPECT, DaTscan, Amyloid/Tau PET) as well as lumbar puncture and EEG; microscopy, culture, chest X-ray, ECG, syphilis and HIV serology are indicated if clinically relevant; brain biopsy is very rarely performed.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In anorexia nervosa, recommended investigations include full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid and liver function tests, albumin, cholesterol, amylase, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, glucose, ECG, and bone mineral density scan.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In bulimia nervosa, recommended investigations include full blood count, urea and electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, vitamin B12, folate, ferritin, and ECG.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In depression, recommended investigations include full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid and liver function tests, vitamin B12, folate, vitamin D, and Epstein-Barr virus serology.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In mania, recommended investigations include urine drug screen, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function tests, and brain CT.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In psychiatry, laboratory and radiological tests are primarily used to exclude non-psychiatric illnesses rather than confirm psychiatric diagnoses; specific investigations are recommended for conditions like dementia, delirium, substance misuse, and eating disorders.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In psychosis, recommended investigations include urine drug screen, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function tests, HIV and syphilis serology, and brain CT.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, GGT
fact_text: In alcohol misuse, recommended investigations include breath alcohol measurement, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, GGT, brain CT, and FibroScan for liver fibrosis assessment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: HIV, Hepatitis B and C serology
fact_text: For other psychoactive substance misuse, recommended investigations include urine drug screening and serology for HIV, Hepatitis B and C, plus ECG.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Delirium is a common medical disorder in older adults and high-dependency patients; it requires specific causes, assessment, and management as detailed in Chapter 32.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Organic psychiatric disorders are common in older adults and cognitive function should always be assessed; if impaired, an associated medical condition or adverse drug effect should be suspected.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Risk factors for psychiatric disorders are classified into predisposing (e.g., genetic/epigenetic factors, disturbed family background), precipitating (e.g., stressful life events, acute physical illness, substance misuse), and perpetuating factors (e.g., lack of social support, chronic physical illness) that delay recovery.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Certain personality types, including obsessive ('anankastic') personality, increase risk of psychiatric disorders such as obsessive-compulsive disorder; personality disorders may perpetuate psychiatric illness once established.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Early childhood adversity such as emotional deprivation or abuse predisposes to psychiatric disorders including depression, eating disorders, and personality disorders in adulthood.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Excess alcohol use can predispose to psychiatric disorders by causing dependence, anorexia, or phobic avoidance behaviors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Social and environmental stressors such as trauma, loss, or perceived threats can precipitate or worsen psychiatric disorders including post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, and anxiety.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Social isolation predisposes to psychiatric disorders such as depression, especially in older adults, and reduced social support can perpetuate psychiatric illness.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Clinical assessment of alcohol misuse should include quantifying intake over the past week (1 unit = 8 g alcohol, approx. 284 mL beer or small glass of wine); corroboration from GP, records, or family may be needed.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Routine biochemistry and hematology abnormalities, including raised mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and γ-glutamyl transferase (GGT), support diagnosis of alcohol misuse but are abnormal in only about half of problem drinkers; these tests help monitor treatment response.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Transient elastography (FibroScan) is an ultrasound-based technique useful for assessing liver fibrosis and steatosis in alcohol misuse, providing information beyond routine blood tests.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Substance misuse includes misuse of all drug types and is associated with problems linked to administration route (e.g., intravenous injection) and problems from substances prescribed by doctors; assessment and management are detailed later in the chapter.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: clinical assessment of hallucinations and delusions
condition_aliases: clinical assessment of hallucinations and delusions
recommended_medicines: Antipsychotics can reduce psychotic symptoms including hallucinations and delusions
Benzodiazepines may be used adjunctively to reduce acute distress and behavioral disturbance
recommended_advice: Doctors should acknowledge hallucinations and delusions as real experiences to the patient to avoid conflict and provide reassurance
Neutral statements like 'We will have to agree to disagree' may be necessary if patient insight is poor
fact_text: Clinical assessment of hallucinations and delusions requires careful history to identify symptom nature, extent, and time course; auditory hallucinations with running commentary suggest schizophrenia; hallucinations with disturbed consciousness suggest organic causes; antipsychotics reduce psychotic symptoms and benzodiazepines may alleviate acute distress; doctors should acknowledge patient experiences to provide reassurance and avoid conflict.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Delusions are defined as false beliefs held with strong conviction despite evidence to the contrary and can be classified by content into persecutory, hypochondriacal, grandiose, or nihilistic types.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Depressive disorders present with psychological symptoms including depressed mood, low self-esteem, pessimism, guilt, loss of interest, anhedonia, and suicidal thoughts, alongside somatic symptoms such as reduced appetite, weight change, disturbed sleep, fatigue, loss of libido, bowel disturbance, and motor slowing.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Hallucinations are sensory perceptions without external stimuli, commonly auditory or visual, and must be differentiated from illusions and normal hypnagogic/hypnopompic phenomena; their clinical context helps distinguish psychiatric from organic causes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: Differentiate low mood requiring support from depressive disorder requiring specific treatment
Support rather than treatment may be appropriate for mild self-limiting reactive low mood
fact_text: Low mood is common in hospital patients and must be differentiated from depressive disorder by assessing core psychological symptoms and physical symptoms; mild reactive low mood requires support rather than treatment, while depressive disorder requires specific treatment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pressure to prescribe misused substances can involve manipulation, deceit, threats, factitious illness description, or malingering, requiring careful clinical assessment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Complications of substance misuse vary by route: intravenous use risks local abscesses, cellulitis, thrombosis, and systemic infections including bacterial endocarditis, viral hepatitis, and HIV; nasal ingestion can cause nasal septum erosion and epistaxis; smoking increases risk of oral, laryngeal, and lung cancer; inhalation can cause burns, chemical pneumonitis, and rashes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Differential diagnosis of anxiety includes normal response to threat, adjustment disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, phobic disorder, organic causes (e.g., hyperthyroidism, paroxysmal arrhythmias, phaeochromocytoma, alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal, hypoglycaemia, temporal lobe epilepsy).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Symptoms of anxiety disorder include psychological features (apprehension, irritability, worry, poor concentration, fear of impending disaster, depersonalisation) and somatic features (palpitations, fatigue, tremor, dizziness, sweating, diarrhoea, frequent desire to pass urine, chest pain, initial insomnia, breathlessness, headache).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: When assessing low mood, clinicians should ask about symptom presence (nausea, over-sedation, parkinsonism), duration, impact on enjoyment, attribution by patient, and specifically ask about suicidal thoughts, as failure to enquire denies prevention opportunity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Elevated mood is less common than depression and often secondary to drug or alcohol misuse, organic disorders, or medical treatment; mania is a bipolar affective disorder characterized by over-activity, lack of sleep, irritability, recklessness, and sometimes psychotic symptoms like delusions of grandeur.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Organic mood disorders can be caused by neurological diseases (e.g., cerebrovascular disease, cerebral tumour, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease, Huntington disease, Alzheimer disease, epilepsy), endocrine disorders (e.g., hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, Cushing syndrome, Addison disease, hyperparathyroidism), malignant disease infections (e.g., infectious mononucleosis, herpes simplex, brucellosis, typhoid, toxoplasmosis), connective tissue disease (systemic lupus erythematosus), and drugs (phenothiazines, phenylbutazone, glucocorticoids, oral contraceptives, interferon).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Risk factors for psychological problems in medical illness include previous history of depression or anxiety, lack of social support, new diagnosis of serious medical condition, deterioration or failure of treatment for a medical condition, unpleasant or disfiguring treatment, change in medical care such as hospital discharge, and impending death.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anxiety may be a manifestation of medical conditions such as thyrotoxicosis; tests to exclude or confirm these conditions should be considered especially if anxiety is a new symptom without obvious stressor.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In patients with persistent and unexplained elevated mood without bipolar history, initial investigations should exclude drug causes, glucocorticoid use, Cushing syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, syphilis, and encephalitis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Benzodiazepines and related drugs are effective for short-term management of specific anxiety disorders but have poor tolerance and unpleasant withdrawal syndromes if used longer than a few weeks.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of low mood includes supporting the patient by minimizing uncertainty, effective communication, and addressing social isolation by facilitating access to visitors and telephone contact.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of bipolar disorder includes treatment of disturbed or aggressive behavior and addressing the underlying cause of organic mania.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Admission to psychiatric ward is necessary for persons who display or are at risk of: acute psychiatric disorder, high short-term suicide risk, need for temporary respite from intolerable circumstances, or requirement for further mental state assessment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Functional somatic syndromes include irritable bowel syndrome (gastroenterology), pre-menstrual syndrome and chronic pelvic pain (gynaecology), fibromyalgia (rheumatology), atypical or non-cardiac chest pain (cardiology), hyperventilation syndrome (respiratory medicine), chronic post-viral fatigue syndrome (infectious diseases), tension headache and non-epileptic attacks (neurology), temporomandibular joint dysfunction and atypical facial pain (dentistry), globus syndrome (ear, nose and throat), and multiple chemical sensitivity (allergy medicine).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Medically unexplained somatic symptoms (MUS) describe symptoms without identifiable physical disorder, commonly including pain (back, chest, abdominal, pelvic, headache), fatigue, fits, 'funny turns', dizziness, and weakness feelings.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with MUS may have a diagnosis of functional somatic syndrome such as irritable bowel syndrome and often have psychiatric diagnoses like anxiety or depressive disorders; if these are absent, consider bodily distress disorder.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Approximately 20% of patients who self-harm repeat the behavior within the following year, and 1-2% die by suicide; risk factors for suicide after self-harm are listed in Box 29.14.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Self-harm (SH) is a common reason for medical presentation and includes intentional self-injury or overdose; the term 'attempted suicide' is misleading as many patients do not intend to die.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Common methods of self-harm include overdose of prescribed or non-prescribed drugs; less common methods include asphyxiation, drowning, hanging, jumping from height or moving vehicles, and firearms use.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Clinical assessment of self-harm must exclude accidental poisoning and recreational drug overdose; self-harm is not a diagnosis but a presentation that may be linked to adjustment disorder, substance/alcohol misuse, depressive disorder, or personality disorder.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Risk factors for suicide include psychiatric illness (depression, schizophrenia), older age, male sex, living alone, unemployment, recent bereavement/divorce/separation, chronic physical ill health, drug or alcohol misuse, suicide note written, and history of previous attempts especially with violent methods.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: All patients presenting with self-harm should undergo thorough psychiatric and social assessment; some may discharge themselves before assessment, so urgent assessment is needed unless medical or surgical conditions require deferral.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The psychiatric assessment of self-harm aims to establish short-term suicide risk, identify treatable problems (medical, psychiatric, social), and assess the need for admission or further mental health evaluation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Assessment after self-harm should include current attempt details (patient's account, intent degree, method used especially if violent, current intent, psychiatric symptoms), and background history (previous attempts and outcomes, family and personal history, social support, stress response, extent of drug and alcohol misuse).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: establish rapid control to ensure safety of patient and others
determine cause of disturbance to guide treatment
presence of adequate trained staff and physical environment is essential
hospital security and police assistance may be required
warning_signs: behaviour putting patient or others at risk
fact_text: Management of disturbed and aggressive behaviour requires rapid control to ensure safety of patient and others, and determination of cause to guide treatment; adequate trained staff, appropriate physical environment, and sometimes hospital security or police assistance are necessary.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: haloperidol 0.5–5 mg IM/oral; diazepam 5–10 mg IV slowly; lorazepam 1–2 mg orally
recommended_advice: ensure adequate personnel to provide overwhelming force
try to attain safe and quiet environment
referral_criteria: consult senior staff if sedation ineffective or dose increase needed
warning_signs: behaviour putting patient or others at risk
fact_text: In disturbed behaviour likely caused by mental disorder and putting patient or others at risk, ensure adequate personnel and safe environment; consider emergency sedation with haloperidol (0.5–5 mg IM/oral), diazepam (5–10 mg IV slowly), or lorazepam (1–2 mg orally). Monitor effectiveness and review; if ineffective, consult senior staff to consider repeating drug, increasing dose, or using other agents such as midazolam or paraldehyde.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
referral_criteria: psychiatric admission using mental health legislation if necessary
referral to psychiatric outpatient service
admission_criteria: urgent medical treatment needed
immediate and significant suicide risk
fact_text: Patients admitted after deliberate self-harm require urgent medical assessment to determine need for urgent medical treatment; if needed, provide medical treatment first, then psychiatric assessment. If immediate and significant suicide risk is present, plan to minimize risk by removing self-harm methods, arranging special support, and considering mental health legislation. If significant psychiatric illness is suspected, consider psychiatric admission or outpatient referral.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In psychiatric emergencies, obtain detailed history including psychiatric, medical (especially neurological), criminal history, current psychiatric and medical treatment, alcohol and drug misuse, recent stressors, and time course and accompaniments of current episode.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: blood or urine analysis for illicit drugs or alcohol
fact_text: In psychiatric emergencies, investigations should include clinical assessment, routine biochemistry, haematology, and blood or urine tests for illicit drugs or alcohol if indicated.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 29.17 Classification of commonly used psychotropic drugs
fact_text: Psychotropic drugs are classified by action: antipsychotics (phenothiazines, butyrophenones, second-generation) for schizophrenia, bipolar mania, delirium; antidepressants (tricyclics, SSRIs, MAOIs, esketamine) for depression, anxiety, OCD; mood stabilisers (lithium, valproate, lamotrigine) for bipolar disorder; anti-anxiety agents (benzodiazepines, β-blockers) for anxiety and alcohol withdrawal.
source_figure_or_table: Box 29.17 Classification of commonly used psychotropic drugs

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of psychiatric disorders requires addressing biological factors with medication and physical treatments, alongside psychological therapies and social environment changes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: oral haloperidol 0.5 mg for sedation; 10 mg or more IV for acute psychotic episode; similar dose of haloperidol may be required with intravenous diazepam
recommended_advice: use low dose haloperidol for sedation in elderly or patients with emphysema and delirium
consider anticholinergic agents like procyclidine to treat extrapyramidal side effects
flumazenil can reverse benzodiazepine-induced respiratory depression
contraindications_or_cautions: use caution with antipsychotics in patients with lung or liver disease due to respiratory depression and encephalopathy risk
avoid benzodiazepines in patients with risk of respiratory depression
warning_signs: risk of respiratory depression in patients with lung disease
risk of encephalopathy in patients with liver disease
fact_text: Sedation in psychiatric emergencies can be achieved with low-dose oral haloperidol (0.5 mg) or higher intravenous doses (≥10 mg) combined with diazepam; procyclidine may be used to treat extrapyramidal side effects; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine respiratory depression; caution is needed in lung or liver disease due to respiratory and encephalopathy risks.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
referral_criteria: admission to psychiatric facility if patient has acute psychiatric disorder
medical cause must be excluded before psychiatric transfer
admission_criteria: acute psychiatric disorder requiring inpatient care
risk to patient or others not manageable outside hospital
fact_text: In psychiatric emergencies, reduce harm by calm, non-threatening approach, involve relatives, consider drug intoxication, and admit to psychiatric care if acute psychiatric disorder is present after excluding medical causes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The negative cognitive triad in depression includes negative views of self ('I am no good'), the current world ('The world is an awful place'), and the future ('The future is hopeless').

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: chronic psychiatric illness resistant to other treatments
condition_aliases: chronic psychiatric illness resistant to other treatments
fact_text: Psychosurgery has a very limited role and is rarely performed; frontal lobotomies are obsolete and current operations target specific brain subregions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and vagal nerve stimulation (VNS) have limited but potential benefit in depression resistant to conventional treatments.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cognitive therapy targets systematic errors in patients' thinking, aiming to identify and challenge negative cognitive errors common in depression and other disorders.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) combines behavioural and cognitive therapy and is the most widely available and extensively researched psychological treatment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) is a brief psychotherapy focusing on current interpersonal relationships and is effective for mild to moderate depression.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Behaviour therapy is a structured treatment helping patients implement graded exposure to feared stimuli, useful in phobias.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Problem-solving therapy involves defining problems, choosing one to work on, listing and evaluating solutions, trying the best, evaluating results, and repeating until resolution.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: General supportive psychotherapy should be part of all psychiatric treatment, providing empathetic listening, addressing patient fears and concerns, and offering accurate information.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Psychodynamic psychotherapy aims to identify unconscious motivations and negative effects in patient relationships, requiring frequent sessions over months or years.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: psychiatric disorders and some non-psychiatric conditions
condition_aliases: psychiatric disorders and some non-psychiatric conditions
fact_text: Psychological therapies involve talking treatments based on patient contact duration and techniques, often supplemented by homework or tasks, and are useful in many psychiatric and some non-psychiatric conditions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: psychiatric disorders with adverse social factors
condition_aliases: psychiatric disorders with adverse social factors
fact_text: Addressing adverse social factors like unemployment and poor housing can improve psychiatric outcomes; benefits advice, befriending, and housing support should be offered.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) produces a controlled convulsion via high-voltage direct current under anesthesia and muscle relaxation; it is safe with few side effects and effective for severe depression, though transient headaches and amnesia (retrograde and anterograde) may occur.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Problem-solving therapy is a brief form of CBT delivered by trained non-psychiatric staff to help patients self-harm in response to situational crises.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects about 25% of cases with classical infantile regressive autism caused by MECP2 gene variants and fragile X syndrome by FMR1 gene; ASD involves difficulties in communication, social interaction, and restricted repetitive behaviors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Neurodiversity frames high-functioning autism, ADHD, and dyslexia as natural human cognitive variations with strengths in deep focus, lateral thinking, and innovation, rather than just disabilities.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Schizophrenia involves delusions, hallucinations, and lack of insight; acute schizophrenia may present with disturbed behavior, disordered thinking, social withdrawal, and negative symptoms; genetic susceptibility and environmental factors like obstetric complications and brain imaging abnormalities contribute to pathogenesis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
