source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Macrolides may cause major malformations in first trimester and genital malformations in any trimester and are contraindicated in pregnancy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Quinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy due to arthropathy risk in animal studies.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Sulphonamides are contraindicated in pregnancy due to risk of neonatal haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tetracyclines and glycylcyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy due to skeletal abnormalities in animals, fetal dental discoloration, and maternal hepatotoxicity with parenteral doses in second or third trimesters.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Trimethoprim is contraindicated in first trimester due to teratogenicity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Aciclovir, penicillins, cephalosporins, clindamycin, glycopeptides, linezolid, and meropenem are not known to be harmful in pregnancy and should be used only when necessary.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: For HIV occupational exposure (sharps injury), combination tenofovir/emtricitabine and raltegravir is recommended; modification is needed if the index case's virus is known to be resistant.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: For prevention of secondary influenza A cases in adults with chronic respiratory, cardiovascular, renal disease, immunosuppression or diabetes mellitus, oseltamivir is recommended.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: broad spectrum bacterial infections including pseudomonas aeruginosa
condition_aliases: broad spectrum bacterial infections including pseudomonas aeruginosa
fact_text: Fourth-generation cephalosporins such as cefepime have broad-spectrum activity including streptococci, some gram-negatives, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: broad spectrum bacterial infections including resistant organisms
condition_aliases: broad spectrum bacterial infections including resistant organisms
fact_text: Carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem, doripenem) have the broadest antibiotic activity of beta-lactams, including activity against ESBL-producing organisms and anaerobes; often combined with beta-lactamase inhibitors to overcome carbapenemase enzymes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Aztreonam is the only available monobactam, active against gram-negative bacteria except ESBL-producing organisms, but inactive against gram-positive and anaerobic bacteria; it is useful in penicillin-allergic patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Second-generation cephalosporins have enhanced activity against gram-negative bacteria and include cephamycins such as cefoxitin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: gram-negative bacterial infections including pseudomonas spp.
condition_aliases: gram-negative bacterial infections including pseudomonas spp.
fact_text: Third-generation cephalosporins such as ceftazidime and cefotaxime have improved gram-negative coverage including activity against Pseudomonas spp.; cefotaxime and ceftriaxone are effective against Streptococcus pneumoniae and H. influenzae.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: First-generation cephalosporins have excellent activity against gram-positive organisms and some activity against gram-negative bacteria.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: infections caused by legionella, mycoplasma, chlamydia, bordetella
condition_aliases: infections caused by legionella, mycoplasma, chlamydia, bordetella
fact_text: Macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin) are bacteriostatic agents used for infections by Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, and Bordetella; azithromycin is preferred for short-course therapy of genitourinary Chlamydia and Mycoplasma infections.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Erythromycin causes gastrointestinal upset in about 30% of patients; cholestatic jaundice is associated with erythromycin estolate; macrolides can prolong QT interval and clindamycin predisposes to Clostridioides difficile infection.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fifth-generation cephalosporins such as ceftobiprole and ceftaroline have enhanced activity against MRSA and some gram-negative bacteria including Pseudomonas aeruginosa; some agents are inactivated by ESBLs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Clindamycin, a lincosamide, is primarily used for soft tissue, bone, and joint infections.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Aminoglycosides have negligible oral absorption, poor penetration into intracellular fluid and adipose tissue, negligible CSF and corneal penetration, and peak plasma levels occur 30 minutes after infusion; they exhibit a post-antibiotic effect requiring therapeutic level monitoring.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Quinolones are bactericidal agents with broad-spectrum activity against gram-negative bacteria; fluoroquinolones have anti-pseudomonal activity but resistance is emerging; they have good oral absorption, wide tissue distribution, and good intracellular penetration concentrating in phagocytes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, and ofloxacin (IV/oral or topical) are fluoroquinolones active against enteric gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Haemophilus species, and atypical respiratory pathogens.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Levofloxacin (IV/oral) is active against Haemophilus species, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and atypical respiratory pathogens.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Moxifloxacin (oral) is active against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, atypical respiratory pathogens, mycobacteria, and anaerobes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Nalidixic acid is an oral quinolone active against enteric gram-negative bacilli but not Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Gentamicin can cause reversible renal toxicity, which is worsened by other nephrotoxic agents; cochlear toxicity is usually permanent and more common in older patients or those with mitochondrial gene mutations; neuromuscular blockade may occur after rapid IV infusion, especially with calcium channel blockers, myasthenia gravis, or hypomagnesaemia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Gentamicin dosing is based on actual body weight or ideal body weight if obese; usual dose interval is 7 mg/kg every 24 hours, adjusted by drug levels using the Hartford nomogram; in most cases, gentamicin is given twice or three times daily with target peak levels 5-10 mg/L and post-dose levels <1 mg/L.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: gentamicin dosing in endocarditis, pregnancy, severe burns, pediatric patients
condition_aliases: gentamicin dosing in endocarditis, pregnancy, severe burns, pediatric patients
fact_text: In endocarditis, pregnancy, severe burns, and pediatric patients, gentamicin can be administered at 7 mg/kg body weight every 24 hours; dose interval depends on drug clearance and is guided by the Hartford nomogram.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: gentamicin use in streptococcal and enterococcal endocarditis
condition_aliases: gentamicin use in streptococcal and enterococcal endocarditis
fact_text: Gentamicin is used with a cell wall active agent (usually a β-lactam) to provide synergy in streptococcal and enterococcal endocarditis; lower doses and target levels are used in this situation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: gonococcal urethritis in pregnancy or penicillin allergy
condition_aliases: gonococcal urethritis in pregnancy or penicillin allergy
fact_text: Spectinomycin is used intramuscularly to treat gonococcal urethritis in pregnancy or in patients allergic to β-lactam antibiotics, but resistance is common and it is rarely used otherwise.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Plazomicin is a novel aminoglycoside resistant to aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, used to treat complicated urinary tract infections caused by highly drug-resistant strains including multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, often in combination with other agents.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: adverse effects of trimethoprim and sulphonamides
condition_aliases: adverse effects of trimethoprim and sulphonamides
fact_text: Trimethoprim is generally well tolerated but can cause adverse effects; sulphonamides and dapsone may cause haemolysis in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and Stevens-Johnson syndrome or 'dapsone syndrome' (rash, fever, lymphadenopathy).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: adverse effects of vancomycin and teicoplanin
condition_aliases: adverse effects of vancomycin and teicoplanin
fact_text: Vancomycin and teicoplanin are associated with nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; vancomycin can cause red man syndrome and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Vancomycin is used orally to treat Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) because glycopeptides are not absorbed orally; intravenous vancomycin is not effective for CDI.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: infections caused by mycoplasma, chlamydia, rickettsia, coxiella, bartonella, borrelia, helicobacter pylori, treponema pallidum, atypical mycobacteria
condition_aliases: infections caused by mycoplasma, chlamydia, rickettsia, coxiella, bartonella, borrelia, helicobacter pylori, treponema pallidum, atypical mycobacteria
fact_text: Tetracyclines, including doxycycline and minocycline, are indicated for infections caused by Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Rickettsia, Coxiella, Bartonella, Borrelia, Helicobacter pylori, Treponema pallidum, and atypical mycobacteria.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: multi-resistant gram-negative bacterial infections including pseudomonas aeruginosa and acinetobacter baumannii
condition_aliases: multi-resistant gram-negative bacterial infections including pseudomonas aeruginosa and acinetobacter baumannii
fact_text: Colistin is a polymyxin antibiotic active against multi-resistant gram-negative bacteria including Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii; it can be administered orally, intravenously, or by nebulised routes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: multi-resistant gram-positive and gram-negative infections including mrsa and esbl producers
condition_aliases: multi-resistant gram-positive and gram-negative infections including mrsa and esbl producers
fact_text: Tigecycline, a chemical modification of tetracycline, is a broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotic active against MRSA and ESBL-producing gram-negative bacteria; it should be used only when risk-benefit assessment favors it due to higher mortality in some studies.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: pneumocystis jirovecii infection, toxoplasmosis, malaria, leprosy, and prevention of pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
condition_aliases: pneumocystis jirovecii infection, toxoplasmosis, malaria, leprosy, and prevention of pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
fact_text: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) is the first-line treatment for Pneumocystis jirovecii infection and toxoplasmosis, also used for malaria and prevention of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; dapsone is used for leprosy and toxoplasmosis prevention when combined with pyrimethamine.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: serious gram-positive infections including mrsa and glycopeptide-resistant enterococci
condition_aliases: serious gram-positive infections including mrsa and glycopeptide-resistant enterococci
fact_text: Daptomycin is a cyclic lipopeptide with bactericidal activity against gram-positive organisms including MRSA and glycopeptide-resistant enterococci, used intravenously for soft tissue infections and Staphylococcus aureus infective endocarditis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Teicoplanin is administered intravenously or intramuscularly once daily after a loading dose; it has a long half-life allowing once-daily dosing.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Vancomycin is administered by slow intravenous infusion with dosing guided by plasma trough levels aiming for >10 mg/L (15–20 mg/L in serious staphylococcal infections).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Vancomycin and teicoplanin are effective against gram-positive organisms including MRSA and enterococci, used mainly for serious staphylococcal and enterococcal infections resistant to other antibiotics.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Dalbavancin, a semisynthetic glycopeptide, is used primarily for skin and skin structure infections and has a long half-life allowing once-weekly dosing.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: All tetracyclines except doxycycline are contraindicated in renal failure; tetracyclines cause dizziness (minocycline), binding to metals causing teeth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia (avoid in children and pregnancy), oesophageal ulcers, and phototoxic skin reactions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: use of folate antagonists in pregnancy
condition_aliases: use of folate antagonists in pregnancy
fact_text: Folic acid should be given to prevent megaloblastic anemia when folate antagonists are used long term or unavoidably in early pregnancy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: aerobic gram-negative and gram-positive bacterial infections including enterococci
condition_aliases: aerobic gram-negative and gram-positive bacterial infections including enterococci
fact_text: Nitrofurantoin is rapidly eliminated renally and active against aerobic gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria including enterococci, but is used only for lower urinary tract infections and is generally safe in pregnancy and childhood.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fidaxomicin, an RNA synthesis inhibitor introduced in 2012, is used for CDI treatment; it is non-absorbable orally, has lower recurrence rates than vancomycin in non-severe CDI, but its effectiveness in severe CDI is under trial evaluation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Lefamulin is a pleuromutilin antibiotic inhibiting the 50S ribosome and protein synthesis, licensed for community-acquired pneumonia, available orally and intravenously, but should not be used in pregnancy and prolongs the QT interval.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: community-acquired pneumonia and skin and soft tissue infection
condition_aliases: community-acquired pneumonia and skin and soft tissue infection
fact_text: Omadacycline, related to tigecycline, is active against MRSA and ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, licensed for community-acquired pneumonia and skin and soft tissue infections, available in parenteral and oral forms, with gastrointestinal upset as the main side effect.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Eravacycline is a parenteral halogenated tetracycline effective against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria including MRSA and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae, used for complicated intra-abdominal infections but associated with thrombophlebitis as a main side effect.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fusidic acid is active against gram-positive bacteria, available in intravenous, oral, and topical forms; it is lipid-soluble, distributes well to tissues, and interacts with coumarin derivatives and oral contraceptives.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: infection caused by resistant gram-positive bacteria including mrsa and gre
condition_aliases: infection caused by resistant gram-positive bacteria including mrsa and gre
fact_text: Linezolid and tedizolid are oxazolidinones effective against resistant gram-positive bacteria including MRSA and GRE, used intravenously or orally; linezolid is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor and should not be combined with MAOIs or serotonin reuptake inhibitors to avoid serotonin syndrome.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Prolonged nitrofurantoin treatment can cause eosinophilic lung infiltrates, fever, pulmonary fibrosis, peripheral neuropathy, hepatitis, and haemolytic anaemia, requiring careful monitoring.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Prolonged nitroimidazole treatment can cause peripheral neuropathy and a dose-dependent metallic taste; severe vomiting may occur if alcohol is consumed (Antabuse effect).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chloramphenicol is reserved for severe infections when other antibiotics are unavailable or impractical due to toxicity risks including dose-dependent bone marrow depression and severe aplastic anemia occurring in 1 in 25,000–40,000 exposures.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Nitroimidazoles such as metronidazole and tinidazole are highly active against strictly anaerobic bacteria including Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium spp., and protozoa like Giardia lamblia; they are well absorbed orally but 60% after rectal administration and distribute well including CNS and CSF.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ethambutol inhibits arabinogalactan synthesis, a component of the mycobacterial cell wall, and is bacteriostatic; resistance usually occurs with resistance to other TB drugs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Isoniazid is bactericidal against replicating and bacteriostatic against non-replicating Mycobacterium tuberculosis by inhibiting InhA enzyme involved in mycolic acid synthesis; side effects include hepatitis, neuropathy (ameliorated by pyridoxine), and hypersensitivity reactions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pyrazinamide inhibits fatty acid synthase and ribosomal trans-translation, is bactericidal and active against semi-dormant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains; side effects include nausea, hepatitis, asymptomatic hyperuricemia, and myalgia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Rifampicin inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, bactericidal against replicating bacteria including isoniazid-resistant M. tuberculosis; it is well absorbed orally, metabolized by liver cytochrome P450, causes orange discoloration of body fluids, and may cause flu-like symptoms and hypersensitivity reactions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fosfomycin inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis, active against gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria including MRSA in combination with other antimicrobials, used for urinary tract infections and multi-resistant bacteria in other situations.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Imidazoles (miconazole, econazole, clotrimazole) are relatively non-toxic and used topically for Candida spp. and dermatophytes
Ketoconazole is used topically and orally for Malassezia spp., dermatophytes, and agents of eumycetoma
Triazoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole) are used systemically for yeasts and filamentous fungi with varying spectra
Fluconazole is effective against Candida and Cryptococcus spp., has a long half-life (~30 hours), good CSF penetration, and excellent safety
Itraconazole is lipophilic, distributes extensively including to nails and fingernails, but has poor CSF penetration and erratic oral absorption requiring therapeutic drug monitoring

Voriconazole is absorbed orally but has variable levels, requires therapeutic drug monitoring, and is used mainly in aspergillosis; side effects include phototoxicity, hepatitis, and transient retinal toxicity

Posaconazole and isavuconazole are broad-spectrum azoles active against Candida spp., Aspergillus spp., and some mucoraceous moulds; isavuconazole is less effective than voriconazole for invasive aspergillosis but can be used as an alternative when voriconazole is contraindicated

Echinocandins (anidulafungin, caspofungin, micafungin) inhibit fungal β-1,3-glucan synthesis, have few significant adverse effects, and are used IV for Candida spp., Aspergillus spp. (caspofungin and anidulafungin), and Cryptococcus spp. or mucoraceous moulds (no activity for caspofungin)
Polyene antifungals: Amphotericin B (IV) is active against yeasts and most dimorphic and filamentous fungi including mucoraceous moulds; Nystatin is used topically for similar fungi
Other antifungals include 5-fluorocytosine (oral, IV) for yeasts, griseofulvin (oral) for dermatophytes, and terbinafine (topical, oral) for dermatophytes
contraindications_or_cautions: Itraconazole requires therapeutic drug monitoring due to erratic absorption
Voriconazole requires therapeutic drug monitoring due to variable oral absorption and side effects
Voriconazole side effects include phototoxicity, hepatitis, and transient retinal toxicity
Posaconazole and isavuconazole require monitoring; isavuconazole is considered safer and well tolerated
fact_text: Azole antifungals inhibit ergosterol synthesis; imidazoles are used topically for Candida and dermatophytes, ketoconazole topically and orally for Malassezia and dermatophytes, triazoles systemically for yeasts and filamentous fungi with fluconazole effective for Candida and Cryptococcus with good CSF penetration, itraconazole requiring drug monitoring due to erratic absorption, voriconazole used mainly in aspergillosis with variable absorption and phototoxicity risk, posaconazole and isavuconazole broad-spectrum with isavuconazole safer and alternative to voriconazole. Echinocandins inhibit fungal β-1,3-glucan synthesis, used IV for Candida and Aspergillus with few adverse effects. Amphotericin B IV covers yeasts and filamentous fungi including mucoraceous moulds. Monitoring is required for itraconazole and voriconazole.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ganciclovir IV is used for treatment and prevention of CMV infection in immunosuppressed patients; side effects include gastrointestinal symptoms, liver dysfunction, neurotoxicity, myelosuppression, renal impairment, fever, rash, and phlebitis at infusion sites; it has potential teratogenicity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Valganciclovir oral is used for treatment and prevention of CMV infection in immunosuppressed patients; side effects are similar to ganciclovir but neutropenia is predominant.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Nephrotoxicity from Amphotericin B may be reduced by concomitant infusion of normal saline and lipid formulations of Amphotericin B have less nephrotoxicity and infusion reactions than conventional Amphotericin B deoxycholate.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: cmv and aciclovir-resistant hsv and vzv infections in immunosuppressed
condition_aliases: cmv and aciclovir-resistant hsv and vzv infections in immunosuppressed
fact_text: Foscarnet IV is used for CMV and aciclovir-resistant HSV and VZV infections in immunosuppressed patients; side effects include gastrointestinal symptoms, renal impairment, electrolyte disturbances, genital ulceration, and neurotoxicity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Remdesivir (IV) is used for COVID-19 with significant side effects being rare.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Terbinafine is used topically and orally for dermatophyte and onychomycosis infections with a half-life of about 1 week; major adverse effect is hepatic toxicity (approximate incidence 1:50,000 cases), and it is not recommended during breastfeeding.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Griseofulvin is effective for dermatophyte infections except in children where it is contraindicated; it deposits in keratin precursor cells and resistance can develop.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Amphotericin B causes cell death by binding ergosterol and damaging fungal membranes; adverse effects include immediate anaphylaxis, infusion-related reactions, and nephrotoxicity which may be severe and irreversible with large cumulative doses.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Nystatin has a similar antifungal spectrum to Amphotericin B but is limited to topical use due to toxicity, e.g., for oral and vaginal candidiasis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Flucytosine is active against yeasts but should be used only in combination with another antifungal to prevent resistance; adverse effects include myelosuppression, gastrointestinal upset, and hepatitis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Aciclovir is used topically, orally, or IV for herpes zoster, chickenpox (especially in immunosuppressed), and herpes simplex infections; side effects are rare but include hepatitis, renal impairment, and neurotoxicity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Valaciclovir and famciclovir are oral agents for herpes zoster and herpes simplex with similar side effect profiles to aciclovir.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV infection is given orally and adverse effects include CNS symptoms, anaemia, and lipodystrophy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: hiv-associated cmv and other viral infections
condition_aliases: hiv-associated cmv and other viral infections
fact_text: Cidofovir IV or topical is used for HIV-associated CMV infections and other viruses; side effects include renal impairment and neutropenia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Amantadine and rimantadine (oral) are used for influenza A but have CNS side effects and nausea.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Zanamivir (inhalation/IV), oseltamivir (oral), and peramivir (IV, IM) are anti-influenza agents for influenza A and B; side effects include allergic reactions (very rare), gastrointestinal side effects, rash, hepatitis (very rare), CNS side effects, and renal impairment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Penciclovir topical cream is used for labial herpes simplex and may cause local irritation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: lassa fever and rsv infection in infants
condition_aliases: lassa fever and rsv infection in infants
fact_text: Ribavirin (oral/IV/inhalation) is used for Lassa fever (IV) and RSV infection in infants (inhalation); side effects include haemolytic anaemia, cough, dyspnoea, bronchospasm, and ocular irritation (when inhaled).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Most viral infections in immunocompetent individuals resolve without intervention; antiviral therapy is available for a limited number of infections.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cidofovir inhibits viral DNA polymerases including aciclovir-resistant CMV and other viruses; it is used in immunocompromised patients for resistant infections but has significant toxicity including nephrotoxicity and requires monitoring.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Foscarnet is an inorganic pyrophosphate analogue that inhibits viral DNA polymerase without requiring phosphorylation and is effective against CMV and HSV resistant to other drugs; it has variable CSF penetration.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Letermovir is a CMV DNA terminase inhibitor used orally or intravenously for CMV prophylaxis in allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients; it has gastrointestinal side effects and drug-drug interactions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Aciclovir, valaciclovir, penciclovir, and famciclovir are acyclic guanosine analogues that inhibit viral DNA polymerase after phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase; famciclovir is a prodrug of penciclovir.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ganciclovir is a chemical modification of aciclovir that preferentially inhibits CMV and other beta-herpesviruses by targeting viral protein kinases, administered intravenously or orally as valganciclovir.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Doravirine and rilpivirine can cause rashes or abnormal liver function tests and may interact with strong inducers or inhibitors of CYP450 enzymes, such as rifampicin or erythromycin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Abacavir is used to replace tenofovir in patients at risk of tenofovir-induced nephrotoxicity but requires HLA-B*57:01 testing before use due to risk of severe hypersensitivity reaction; if hypersensitivity occurs, abacavir must be stopped and not reused.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Rilpivirine requires gastric acidity for absorption and cannot be used with proton pump inhibitors; it can be co-administered with dolutegravir or cabotegravir as long-acting injectable combinations.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) bind allosterically to reverse transcriptase and are used in combination therapy; first-generation NNRTIs are no longer recommended due to low resistance barrier, while second-generation NNRTIs like doravirine and rilpivirine have higher resistance barriers.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Nucleoside and nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) are nucleoside analogues incorporated into HIV DNA to terminate chain elongation and are used in combination antiretroviral therapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tenofovir, often combined with lamivudine or emtricitabine, is a preferred NRTI with good tolerability but can cause nephrotoxicity, including proximal renal tubulopathy resembling Fanconi syndrome; monitoring renal function is important.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Zanamivir and oseltamivir inhibit influenza A and B neuraminidase and are used for treatment and prophylaxis; oseltamivir is oral with limited use in chronic respiratory or renal disease, while zanamivir is inhaled and under development for critically ill patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Amantadine and rimantadine inhibit influenza A M2 protein ion channel but are only used for oseltamivir-resistant influenza A due to widespread resistance.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
trigger_evidence: COVID-19 patients unable to take oral drugs or with drug interactions
dose_or_duration: five days
fact_text: Molnupiravir is an oral antiviral reserved for COVID-19 patients at risk of severe disease who cannot take Paxlovid due to drug interactions or other reasons; side effects include nausea, diarrhea, and dizziness; limited efficacy data in vaccinated patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: five days
fact_text: Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) is an oral protease inhibitor combination used for COVID-19 patients at high risk of progression who do not require supplemental oxygen; dose is 300 mg nirmatrelvir plus 100 mg ritonavir twice daily for five days; ritonavir causes significant drug interactions; side effects include dysgeusia, diarrhea, skin rash, elevated liver tests, and hypertension.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: 200 mg loading dose then 100 mg daily for 5 days
contraindications_or_cautions: ALT >5 times normal
history of chronic liver disease
fact_text: Remdesivir is an intravenous RNA polymerase inhibitor used for hospitalized COVID-19 patients with pneumonia requiring supplemental oxygen or mild to moderate infection at high risk of progression; dose is 200 mg loading then 100 mg daily for 5 days; avoid if ALT >5 times normal or chronic liver disease; monitor liver function and infusion reactions; watch for CYP3A4 inducer drug interactions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
avoid_medicines: artemisinin derivatives in first trimester pregnancy
contraindications_or_cautions: avoid artemisinin derivatives in first trimester pregnancy
fact_text: Artemisinin derivatives are effective antimalarials used for uncomplicated falciparum malaria in second and third trimesters of pregnancy and in combination for resistant Plasmodium species; avoid use in first trimester pregnancy due to limited safety data.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Atovaquone is an oral antimalarial used for treatment and prophylaxis, often combined with proguanil; it is well tolerated with uncommon significant adverse effects and is an alternative for patients intolerant to co-trimoxazole.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Quinoline-containing compounds (chloroquine, quinine, amodiaquine, mefloquine, primaquine)
fact_text: Quinoline-containing compounds such as chloroquine, quinine, amodiaquine, mefloquine, and primaquine are used for malaria treatment and prophylaxis; primaquine is specifically used for radical cure; these agents inhibit intracellular haem polymerisation by different mechanisms.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Proguanil is a folate synthesis inhibitor used orally for malaria prophylaxis, often combined with atovaquone; pyrimethamine–sulfadoxine is another folate inhibitor used for malaria treatment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: asymptomatic cyst carriage of entamoeba histolytica
condition_aliases: asymptomatic cyst carriage of entamoeba histolytica
fact_text: Iodoquinol is a quinoline derivative active against Entamoeba histolytica cysts and trophozoites, used orally for asymptomatic cyst excretion or intestinal amoebiasis; long-term use is not recommended due to neurological adverse effects including optic neuritis and peripheral neuropathy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bithionol is used orally to treat Fasciola hepatica infections; it is well absorbed and adverse effects are usually mild (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, rashes) but relatively common (~30%).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is an oral agent for filariasis and loiasis treatment; it reduces microfilariae, fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, arthralgia, and prostration; adverse effects are due to host response to dying microfilariae and may be reduced by pre-treatment with glucocorticoids.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: giardiasis, cryptosporidiosis, and other protozoal infections
condition_aliases: giardiasis, cryptosporidiosis, and other protozoal infections
fact_text: Nitazoxanide inhibits pyruvate-ferredoxin oxidoreductase in protozoa and anaerobic bacteria; it is broad-spectrum against nematodes, tapeworms, flukes, intestinal protozoa, and some anaerobic bacteria and viruses; administered orally for giardiasis and cryptosporidiosis; adverse effects are usually mild including nausea, diarrhea, and abdominal pain.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: helminth infections including hookworm, ascariasis, threadworm, strongyloides, trichinellosis, taenia solium, and hydatid disease
condition_aliases: helminth infections including hookworm, ascariasis, threadworm, strongyloides, trichinellosis, taenia solium, and hydatid disease
fact_text: Albendazole and mebendazole inhibit helminth glucose uptake causing depletion of glycogen stores; albendazole is used for multiple helminth infections and is administered orally with absorption increased by fatty meals; significant adverse effects are uncommon.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diloxanide furoate is an oral agent used to eliminate luminal cysts after treatment of invasive amoebiasis or in asymptomatic cyst excreters; it is slowly absorbed and has no hepatic amoebicidal effect; main adverse effect is flatulence.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Paromomycin, an aminoglycoside, is used orally for intestinal amoebiasis and by intramuscular injection for visceral leishmaniasis; it is poorly absorbed orally and not significantly absorbed when administered systemically; it showed promise in HIV-associated cryptosporidiosis but later trials showed limited efficacy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: neurotransmitter helminth infections including ascariasis and threadworm
condition_aliases: neurotransmitter helminth infections including ascariasis and threadworm
fact_text: Piperazine inhibits neurotransmitter function causing helminth muscle paralysis; used orally in ascariasis and threadworm (Enterobius vermicularis); adverse effects are uncommon but may include neuropsychological reactions such as vertigo, delirium, and convulsions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pentavalent antimonials (sodium stibogluconate and meglumine antimoniate) inhibit protozoal glycolysis and are used parenterally for leishmaniasis; adverse effects include arthralgia, myalgias, raised hepatic enzymes, pancreatitis, and cardiotoxicity but death is uncommon.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Praziquantel increases membrane permeability to calcium causing violent muscle contraction; it is the drug of choice for schistosomiasis and is effective orally for cestode and fluke infections; adverse effects are usually mild and transient including nausea and abdominal pain.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: strongyloides infection and cutaneous larva migrans
condition_aliases: strongyloides infection and cutaneous larva migrans
fact_text: Thiabendazole inhibits fumarate reductase required for helminth energy production; it is used orally for Strongyloides infection and topically for cutaneous larva migrans; significant adverse effects are uncommon.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ivermectin binds helminth nerve and muscle cell ion channels causing increased permeability; it is an oral agent used for Strongyloides infection, filariasis, and onchocerciasis; significant side effects are uncommon.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: tapeworm infections (taenia saginata, taenia solium, intestinal taenia), and intestinal trematodes
condition_aliases: tapeworm infections (taenia saginata, taenia solium, intestinal taenia), and intestinal trematodes
fact_text: Niclosamide inhibits oxidative phosphorylation causing paralysis of helminths; it is oral, used in Taenia saginata and solium and intestinal trematodes; systemic absorption is minimal with few significant side effects.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pyrantel pamoate causes spastic paralysis of helminth muscle via a suxamethonium-like action; it is used orally only for threadworm infection; systemic absorption is poor and adverse effects are uncommon.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Measles has a high basic reproduction number (R0), higher than SARS-CoV-2 and Ebola, reflecting its high transmissibility and dependence on vaccine coverage and population behavior.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Echinocandins such as caspofungin are preferred for candidemia in patients with central venous catheter infection and acute kidney injury due to their mechanism inhibiting β-1,3-glucan synthesis in fungal cell walls and lower nephrotoxicity compared to amphotericin B.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In cystic fibrosis patients with Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection and cephalosporin intolerance, ceftazidime is the preferred anti-pseudomonal cephalosporin due to its activity against P. aeruginosa and better tolerance compared to ceftriaxone.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Praziquantel is the preferred treatment for Taenia saginata infection; niclosamide is an alternative when praziquantel is unavailable.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In HIV patients with new symptoms after starting therapy, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) should be considered when chest X-ray lesions are inconsistent with drug side effects and occur after immune recovery, especially with tuberculosis exposure history.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pneumocystis pneumonia is less likely in HIV patients with rising CD4 counts and no prophylaxis, but remains a differential diagnosis in pulmonary infiltrates.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: A cluster of Serratia marcescens bloodstream infections occurring about 4 weeks after a hospital antimicrobial stewardship policy change suggests a common source outbreak rather than a hospital outbreak or epidemic.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Changes in antimicrobial stewardship policy may increase incidence of infections resistant to commonly used antimicrobials, but this is unlikely to explain outbreaks without a common source.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: When cases of bloodstream infection are geographically dispersed across different hospital units and no evidence of hospital outbreak exists, consider a common source outbreak linked to shared environmental factors or contaminated infusions/injected agents.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the cancer patient
referral_criteria: ascites in ovarian carcinoma
fact_text: Ascites is a significant clinical finding in ovarian carcinoma patients and should prompt urgent evaluation and management.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the cancer patient

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the cancer patient
fact_text: Clinical examination of cancer patients should include detailed assessment of: 1) Periphery for calf tenderness, venous thrombosis, rash, and skin changes; 2) Hands for clubbing, smoking signs, and pallor; 3) Breast for asymmetry, lumps, and skin tethering above the nipple; 4) Respiratory system for stridor, consolidation, and pleural effusion; 5) Lymph nodes including cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal; 6) Face for conjunctival pallor, icterus, Horner syndrome, and Cushingoid features; 7) Cardiovascular system for superior vena cava obstruction, atrial fibrillation, pericardial effusion, and hypo/hypertension; 8) Abdomen for surgical scars, umbilical nodules, epigastric masses, visible peristalsis, abdominal distension, ascites, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, renal masses, and pelvic or adnexal masses; 9) Neurological system for focal neurological signs, sensory deficits, spinal cord compression, memory deficits, and personality changes; 10) Skeletal survey for focal bone tenderness (pelvis, spine, long bones) and wrist tenderness (hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy). Observation should also note cachexia, dehydration, and asymmetry or lumps.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the cancer patient

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the cancer patient
referral_criteria: presence of SVCO in cancer patient
admission_criteria: presence of SVCO in cancer patient
warning_signs: superior vena cava obstruction in a patient with mediastinal mass
fact_text: Superior vena cava obstruction (SVCO) is a critical clinical sign in cancer patients, especially those with a mediastinal mass, requiring urgent recognition and referral.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the cancer patient

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Neutropenia is caused by cytotoxics, CDK4/6 inhibitors, and PARP inhibitors; bleeding risk increases with cytotoxics, VEGF inhibitors; anaemia can result from cytotoxics and radiotherapy.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Peripheral neuropathy is caused by cisplatin, oxaliplatin, taxanes, gemcitabine, brentuximab, and immunotherapy; encephalopathy can occur with ifosfamide, cisplatin, and immunotherapy; hearing loss is a known adverse effect of cisplatin; posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is associated with VEGF inhibitors, rituximab, and immunotherapy.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Alopecia is a common side effect of cytotoxic chemotherapy; trichomegaly occurs with EGFR inhibitors; loss of pigmentation can occur with pazopanib.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Cardiomyopathy can be caused by HER2 inhibitors, anthracyclines, and radiotherapy; myocarditis is linked to immunotherapy and cisplatin; myocardial ischaemia may occur with 5-FU, capecitabine, bevacizumab, and radiotherapy; arrhythmia and QTc prolongation are associated with cytotoxic chemotherapy and TKIs.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Hypothyroidism can occur with VEGF inhibitors, immunotherapy, and radio-iodine; hypophysitis is linked to immunotherapy; diabetes may develop with immunotherapy and glucocorticoids; adrenalitis is associated with immunotherapy; adrenal insufficiency can result from glucocorticoid withdrawal.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Uveitis can occur with immunotherapy, BRAF inhibitors, and erlotinib; cataracts may develop with anti-oestrogen therapy; lens changes can occur with steroids.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea can occur with all cancer treatments; colitis is associated with ipilimumab, 5-FU, capecitabine, taxanes, and radiotherapy; paralytic ileus may occur with vinca alkaloids; bowel perforation is a risk with bevacizumab; strictures can develop after radiotherapy.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: hand and foot toxicity from cancer treatment
condition_aliases: hand and foot toxicity from cancer treatment
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Palmar plantar erythrodysesthesia occurs with 5-FU and capecitabine and EGFR inhibitors; paronychia is linked to EGFR inhibitors; finger tip cracks can occur with EGFR inhibitors.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Hepatitis can be caused by cisplatin, vinblastine, rituximab, and immunotherapy; pseudocirrhosis is associated with gemcitabine; sinusoidal obstructive syndrome may occur with cyclophosphamide, oxaliplatin, and vincristine; steatosis is linked to oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and tamoxifen.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Dysgeusia and xerostomia occur with all cancer treatments; stomatitis is common with 5-FU, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, and radiotherapy; osteonecrosis of the jaw is associated with VEGF inhibitors and bisphosphonates.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Pneumonitis can be caused by immunotherapy, taxanes, bleomycin, gemcitabine, tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), and radiotherapy; fibrosis is associated with bleomycin, gemcitabine, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, and radiotherapy; non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema may occur with gemcitabine and methotrexate.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Nephritis can occur with immunotherapy; nephrotic syndrome is linked to VEGF inhibitors; haemorrhagic cystitis is caused by ifosfamide; nephrotoxicity is a known adverse effect of cisplatin.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Arthralgia can occur with anti-oestrogens and mTOR inhibitors; myalgia is associated with taxanes and anti-oestrogens; bone pain may develop with G-CSF.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Dry skin occurs with all cancer treatments; maculopapular rashes are linked to TKIs; acneiform rashes occur with EGFR inhibitors; DRESS syndrome is associated with immunotherapy; telangiectasia may develop after radiotherapy; tattoo point marks can be caused by radiotherapy.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment
fact_text: Venous and arterial thromboembolism can be caused by platinum agents, taxanes, and TKIs; phlebitis is associated with fluorouracil, epirubicin, cisplatin, and gemcitabine.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the patient on cancer treatment

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 8.1 The 20 most common cancers in the UK
fact_text: In the UK, the most common cancers by incidence include breast, prostate, lung, bowel, and melanoma, with breast cancer incidence higher in females and lung cancer incidence higher in males.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 8.1 The 20 most common cancers in the UK

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: TP53 gene mutation testing can identify disrupted apoptosis pathways in cancers, as TP53 mutations occur in over 50% of cancers and impair p53 protein function.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Apoptosis is programmed cell death often reduced in cancers, especially high-grade or treatment-resistant types; TP53 tumor suppressor gene is a key regulator inducing apoptosis in response to genomic damage.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Autophagy is a lysosomal degradation process that can be cytoprotective for malignant cells by removing damaged components, especially when induced by radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cancer cells resist cell death by evading apoptosis, autophagy, and necrosis, which are normal mechanisms of cell death in healthy tissues.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cancer growth involves multiple hallmarks including genome instability and mutation, which cause accumulation of driver genomic aberrations leading to cancer progression.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cancer cells produce growth factors (e.g., TGF-α, PDGF) and overexpress growth factor receptors (e.g., EGFR, HER2/neu), leading to constitutive activation of proliferative pathways like Ras-Raf-MAP kinase.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cancer cells sustain proliferation by producing growth factors that activate surface-bound receptors and intracellular kinase cascades, promoting cell growth and division.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cell cycle progression is regulated by cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), which are controlled by phosphorylation; tumor suppressor genes (e.g., TP53, TP21, TP16) inhibit progression but are often mutated or inactivated in cancer.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cells arrest at checkpoints in G1, G2, and during mitosis in response to DNA damage or incomplete replication, preventing progression until repair occurs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chemotherapeutic agents target specific phases of the cell cycle, including G1 (cyclin D, CDK4/6), S phase (DNA replication), G2 (DNA damage checkpoint), and M phase (mitosis), exploiting cell cycle regulation to inhibit cancer cell proliferation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The cell cycle has four ordered phases: G1 (gap 1), S (DNA synthesis), G2 (gap 2), and M (mitosis); normal cells stop proliferating and enter quiescence (G0) when confluent or deprived of growth factors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The first gap phase (G1) precedes DNA synthesis and is the commitment point for cell division; cells in G0 or G1 respond to growth signals, but after passing the restriction point, they enter S phase for DNA replication.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Necrosis is premature cell death causing release of cellular contents, triggering inflammation and angiogenesis, which promotes tumor growth rather than inhibiting it.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Angiogenesis involves VEGF receptor activation on endothelial cells, leading to new vessel formation; tumour cells also produce urokinase receptor activating plasminogen to plasmin, causing proteolysis and breakdown of extracellular matrix to facilitate invasion and metastasis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cancer initiation involves inherited or acquired oncogene gain and tumour suppressor gene loss, leading to first mutation in normal epithelium, followed by initial proliferation, clonal expansion, and further mutations that promote rapid growth, local invasion through basal lamina, failed apoptosis (e.g. TP53 mutation), angiogenesis, and eventual invasion or metastasis via lymphatic and blood spread.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Normal cells have limited divisions due to telomeric DNA shortening causing senescence or crisis; cancer cells express telomerase enzyme to maintain telomere length, allowing continued cell division and replicative immortality.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The ability of tumour cells to invade neighbouring tissue determines whether a tumour is benign or malignant; presence of metastases clinically determines if cancer can be cured.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tumours require angiogenesis to grow beyond 1 mm³; angiogenesis is driven by vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), with a balance of pro-angiogenic and inhibitory signals such as thrombospondin (TSP)-1; tumour cells produce ectopic growth factors to stimulate new vessel formation supporting tumour growth.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Breast cancer risk in women of Far Eastern heritage is lower, possibly due to environmental factors including diet and lifestyle changes in subsequent generations.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cancer cells evade immune destruction by escaping immune surveillance, including downregulating immune recognition and promoting immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cancer cells reprogram glucose metabolism to favour glycolysis even in oxygen presence ('aerobic glycolysis'), mainly via upregulation of glucose transporter GLUT1, supporting biosynthesis for tumour growth.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Environmental triggers for cancer are identified by epidemiological studies examining cancer distribution patterns and associated factors such as smoking, diet, infections, and lifestyle.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Inherited cancer syndromes account for 5-10% of cancers; genetic testing for mutations such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 can guide screening and preventive treatments.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Most cancers result from complex interactions between genetic factors and environmental exposures rather than a single cause.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tumour-associated inflammatory responses contribute to cancer progression by releasing cytokines, growth factors, and pro-angiogenic factors that promote tumour growth and invasion.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Most cervical cancers are related to infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) subtypes 16 and 18.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Smoking is the main established environmental cause of lung cancer, but other factors also contribute.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In suspected cancer, a full history should include potential risk factors such as smoking, occupational exposures, family cancer history, and complications of the disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The TNM classification system stages cancer by assessing primary tumour size/invasion (TX-T4), regional lymph node involvement (NX-N2/3), and presence of distant metastases (MX-M1), with exact criteria varying by anatomical site.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Inherited cancer predisposition syndromes are associated with specific malignancies, inheritance patterns (autosomal dominant or recessive), and causative genes as detailed in the table, supporting genetic risk assessment and targeted surveillance.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Tumour markers are substances produced by many cancers used to aid diagnosis, assess response to treatment, and detect relapse.
fact_text: Tumour markers are useful adjuncts for diagnosis, treatment response evaluation, and relapse detection but are neither sufficiently sensitive nor specific to be used in isolation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Positron emission tomography (PET) using 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) combined with CT (PET-CT) is recommended to evaluate metabolic activity and extent of tumour spread, especially when radical treatment is planned.
fact_text: PET-CT using 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose is useful to assess metabolic activity and tumour spread extent, but small malignant deposits or lymph nodes may not be detected, limiting sensitivity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Gallium-68 prostate-specific membrane antigen (Ga-PSMA) PET is highly sensitive for detecting prostate cancer recurrence or metastasis.
fact_text: Ga-PSMA PET is a sensitive imaging modality for detecting prostate cancer that has recurred or spread to other body parts.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: CT imaging is used to detect and monitor liver metastases, with repeat imaging after cytotoxic chemotherapy to assess radiological response.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a glycoprotein found in yolk sac and fetal liver tissue; transiently elevated in liver diseases; used in screening for neural tube defects and Down syndrome; elevated in ovarian non-seminomatous germ cell tumours (80%), testicular teratoma (80%), and hepatocellular cancer (50%).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Beta-2-microglobulin is a human leucocyte antigen common fragment elevated in autoimmune and renal glomerular disease; elevated in non-Hodgkin lymphoma and myeloma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Calcitonin is a 32-amino-acid peptide from thyroid C cells and is a marker for medullary cell carcinoma of the thyroid.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cancer antigen 125 (CA 125) is a differentiation antigen of coelomic epithelium, elevated in ovarian epithelial cancer (75%), gastrointestinal cancer (10%), lung cancer (5%), and breast cancer (5%); levels also rise in ascites, pleural effusion, heart failure, and inflammatory conditions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cancer antigen 15-3 (CA 15-3) is part of the MUC1 protein family involved in cell signalling and protective barriers; elevated in breast cancer (especially advanced stage), lung cancer, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, and prostate cancer.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9) is a mucin found in fetal stomach, intestine, and pancreas epithelium; elevated in pancreatic cancer (80%), mucinous tumours of ovary (65%), gastric cancer (30%), and colon cancer (30%).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a glycoprotein found in intestinal mucosa during embryonic and fetal life; elevated in smokers, cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis, ulcerative colitis, pneumonia; tumour marker for colorectal cancer, especially with liver metastasis, gastric cancer, breast cancer, lung cancer, and mucinous ovarian cancer.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) is a glycoprotein hormone from placental syncytiotrophoblasts; used for disease monitoring in hydatidiform mole and pregnancy test; elevated in choriocarcinoma (100%), hydatidiform moles (97%), ovarian non-seminomatous germ cell tumours (50-80%), and seminoma (15%).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP) is an isoenzyme of alkaline phosphatase elevated in seminoma (40%) and ovarian dysgerminoma (50%).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is a serine protease from human kallikrein gene family that liquefies semen; elevated in prostate cancer (95%) and can be elevated in benign prostatic hypertrophy and prostatitis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Thyroglobulin is a matrix protein for thyroid hormone synthesis in normal thyroid follicles; elevated in papillary and follicular thyroid cancer.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: 'Clinical reasoning' is the process of thinking and decision-making in clinical practice, involving evidence-based history and examination, diagnostic test interpretation, problem identification, clinical reasoning concepts, and shared decision-making.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: History taking remains the most important part of clinical decision-making, with 70-90% of diagnoses based on history alone; history should be explored from all available sources including patient, paramedics, emergency notes, eyewitnesses, relatives, or carers if needed.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 1.2 Reasons for errors in clinical reasoning
fact_text: Cognitive biases include accepting a diagnosis without questioning the evidence or framing the problem incorrectly, which can lead to diagnostic error.
source_figure_or_table: Box 1.2 Reasons for errors in clinical reasoning

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 1.1 Root causes of diagnostic error in studies
fact_text: Diagnostic errors are categorized as no fault (e.g., unusual disease presentation, missing information), system errors (e.g., inadequate diagnostic support, poor communication), and human cognitive errors (e.g., inadequate data gathering, reasoning errors).
source_figure_or_table: Box 1.1 Root causes of diagnostic error in studies

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diagnostic errors occur in 10-15% of cases in specialties like emergency medicine and general practice, mainly due to knowledge gaps, misinterpretation of diagnostic tests, and cognitive biases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 1.2 Reasons for errors in clinical reasoning
fact_text: Knowledge gaps as a source of clinical reasoning error include incorrect assumptions such as telling a patient they cannot have biliary colic after gallbladder removal despite possible bile duct stones.
source_figure_or_table: Box 1.2 Reasons for errors in clinical reasoning

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 1.2 Reasons for errors in clinical reasoning
fact_text: Misinterpretation of diagnostic tests can occur when a normal test is incorrectly used to exclude disease, e.g., computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging may not identify an infarct if performed early.
source_figure_or_table: Box 1.2 Reasons for errors in clinical reasoning

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In suspected meningitis, clinical examination should include checking for headache, fever, and meningeal signs such as photophobia, neck stiffness, Kernig and Brudzinski signs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Likelihood ratios (LRs) quantify diagnostic test usefulness: LR >1 increases disease probability; LR <1 decreases it; LRs for classical meningitis signs are about 1, indicating limited diagnostic utility.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In a US study, nearly all adults with meningitis had headache and fever, but only 5% had Kernig and Brudzinski signs; these signs have a likelihood ratio around 1, indicating limited diagnostic value.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In adults with suspected meningitis, headache, fever, and meningeal signs (photophobia, neck stiffness, Kernig and Brudzinski signs) are classical clinical features but have low sensitivity and specificity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Immunohistochemistry uses antibodies to detect tumour antigens aiding diagnosis and classification; examples include ER/PR for hormone sensitivity, AFP/hCG for germ cell tumours, PSA for prostate cancer, cytokeratins for epithelial tumours, T-cell markers for lymphomas, and PD-L1 for immune checkpoint therapy suitability.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Histopathology is essential to identify cancer type by microscopic examination of tissue or cells, differentiating carcinoma subtypes and grading tumour behaviour, including tumour grade, lymphovascular invasion, and mitotic rate.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Molecular pathology testing (proteins, DNA, RNA) supplements histopathology by providing diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive information to guide cancer management, but is time-consuming and costly.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Genomic sequencing (whole genome or targeted gene panels) provides extensive molecular information for cancer diagnosis and treatment selection but is costly and time-consuming; common targets include EGFR mutations in lung cancer and BRAF mutations in colon cancer and melanoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In situ hybridisation (FISH) localises specific nucleic acid sequences in tumour tissue to detect HER2 overexpression in breast cancer (predicting HER2 inhibitor response), ALK or ROS1 rearrangements in lung cancer (predicting ALK inhibitor response), and chromosome 11;22 translocations or MDM2 amplification in sarcoma subtyping.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: Ensure patient comfort and accessibility to lesion
Identify tumour and avoid critical structures
Use local anaesthetic if needed
Label and immobilise lesion
Insert needle with syringe attached, apply negative pressure by pulling syringe and continue to lesion
Make multiple passes varying angles
Stop sampling if blood seen in syringe hub
Release negative pressure before needle removal
Withdraw needle and send cellular material on labelled slides for pathology
fact_text: Fine needle aspiration biopsy technique includes patient positioning, lesion identification, local anaesthesia if needed, needle insertion with negative pressure, multiple passes with angle variation, stopping if blood contaminates sample, and careful withdrawal to preserve sample quality for pathology.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: Detailed clinical history and examination are essential to direct initial investigations and early specialist referral
referral_criteria: Presence of red flag symptoms or signs indicating possible new cancer
warning_signs: Local effects of primary tumour or metastases causing symptoms such as lump, dysphagia, bleeding, or persistent pain
Constitutional symptoms including unexplained weight loss, fatigue, or fevers
Paraneoplastic syndromes due to biologically active hormones or immune response
Symptoms from tumour or immune response causing new cancer presentation
fact_text: Patients presenting with new cancer symptoms often have local tumour effects (lump, dysphagia, bleeding, pain), constitutional symptoms (weight loss, fatigue, fever), or paraneoplastic syndromes; detailed history and exam guide investigations and early specialist referral is required for red flag symptoms.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
trigger_evidence: Patient with advanced or metastatic cancer but no identifiable primary site after history, exam, and imaging
recommended_tests: Prompt investigations to assess patient fitness, disease extent, and comorbidities
Avoid delays in investigations to 'hunt down' primary tumour
recommended_advice: Investigations should be limited to those necessary to assess patient status and guide management
referral_criteria: Patients with advanced cancer and unknown primary should have prompt specialist assessment
fact_text: In patients with advanced metastatic cancer and no identifiable primary site after history, exam, and imaging, investigations should be prompt but limited to assessing patient fitness, disease extent, and comorbidities to avoid delays; specialist assessment is required.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: Cancer incidence rises to about 50% in people over 65 years
Women over 65 in the UK are not routinely invited for breast cancer screening but can request it
Life expectancy for an 80-year-old woman is about 8 years, so cancer may not shorten life or may progress slowly
Histology, stage, and observation period guide treatment decisions in elderly cancer patients
Cancer in elderly often has a more indolent course due to reduced angiogenesis
Treatment response in elderly is similar to younger patients but may be influenced by comorbidities
Toxicity of cancer treatment may be higher in elderly due to baseline organ function decline
Treatment selection in elderly must consider chronic illness and patient preferences; aggressive treatment may not be appropriate
Symptom control may be the main goal in elderly cancer patients
fact_text: Cancer incidence increases with age, reaching about 50% in those over 65; elderly patients often have slower progressing cancers and higher treatment toxicity risk, so treatment should be individualized considering comorbidities, life expectancy, and patient preferences, with symptom control as a key goal.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: Agree on cancer type and final stage
Decide on appropriate primary treatment modality, commonly surgery plus neoadjuvant systemic anticancer therapy and/or radiotherapy
Arrange review by appropriate team to coordinate management
Plan surveillance strategies
Diagnose cancer recurrence or metastases
Ensure appropriate transition from curative to palliative treatment
Promote recruitment into clinical trials
Agree on operational policies to deliver high-quality care
Plan and review audit data to ensure quality care delivery
Identify late effects of cancer treatments
