fact_text: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) has an incidence of 1 in 6000 and presents with early lethality, characteristic skull and facial features, and frequent malformations of heart, kidney, and other organs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition

fact_text: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) occurs in 1 in 1000 males and presents with phenotypic male features, infertility, gynaecomastia, and small testes.

condition: mechanism of recurrent deletions and duplications
condition_aliases: mechanism of recurrent deletions and duplications

fact_text: Recurrent deletions and duplications arise from non-allelic homologous recombination due to abnormal pairing between DNA repeats on maternal and paternal chromosomes, leading to deletion on one chromosome and duplication on the homologous chromosome.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 3.3 Chromosome and contiguous gene disorders
fact_text: Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) occurs in 1 in 15,000 births and is characterized by early lethality, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, small head, and frequent congenital heart disease.
source_figure_or_table: Table 3.3 Chromosome and contiguous gene disorders

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 3.3 Chromosome and contiguous gene disorders
fact_text: Prader–Willi syndrome (15q11–q13 deletion) occurs in 1 in 15,000 and presents with distinctive facial appearance, hyperphagia, small hands and feet, and a distinct behavioral phenotype; imprinting and paternal allele deletions occur in 70% of cases.
source_figure_or_table: Table 3.3 Chromosome and contiguous gene disorders

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 3.3 Chromosome and contiguous gene disorders
fact_text: Smith–Magenis syndrome (17p11.2 deletion) occurs in 1 in 25,000 and is characterized by distinctive facial appearance, behavioral phenotype, self-injury, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep abnormalities; the major gene involved is RAI1.
source_figure_or_table: Table 3.3 Chromosome and contiguous gene disorders

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 3.9 Chromosomal analysis and structural chromosomal disorders
fact_text: Structural chromosomal anomalies include reciprocal translocations, Robertsonian translocations, inversions, and deletions or duplications classified as interstitial, terminal, tandem, or inverted, which can cause disease by disrupting gene dosage or structure.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 3.9 Chromosomal analysis and structural chromosomal disorders

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition

fact_text: Triple X syndrome (47,XXX) occurs in 1 in 1000 females and is usually asymptomatic but may be associated with reduced IQ.
source_figure_or_table: Table 3.3 Chromosome and contiguous gene disorders

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 3.3 Chromosome and contiguous gene disorders
fact_text: Turner syndrome (45,X) occurs in 1 in 5000 females and presents with phenotypic female features, short stature, webbed neck, coarctation of the aorta, and primary amenorrhoea.
source_figure_or_table: Table 3.3 Chromosome and contiguous gene disorders

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 3.3 Chromosome and contiguous gene disorders
fact_text: Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion) occurs in 1 in 10,000 and presents with distinctive facial appearance, supravalvular aortic stenosis, learning disability, and infantile hypercalcaemia; the major gene involved is elastin.
source_figure_or_table: Table 3.3 Chromosome and contiguous gene disorders

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition

fact_text: XYY syndrome (47,XYY) occurs in 1 in 1000 males and is usually asymptomatic but may cause impulse control problems.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Asbestos exposure causes pleural plaques, benign asbestos-related pleural effusions, diffuse pleural thickening, asbestosis, and mesothelioma; pleural plaques are common, usually asymptomatic, and do not impair lung function, identified on chest X-ray or CT.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Asbestosis is lung fibrosis from prolonged asbestos exposure over years, presenting with exertional breathlessness, fine late inspiratory crackles, and finger clubbing; pulmonary function tests and HRCT support diagnosis; asbestos exposure history is essential; lung biopsy is rarely needed; patients have a 10-fold increased risk of lung cancer, especially with smoking history; progression is usually slow with better prognosis than idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; nintedanib may slow lung function decline in progressive cases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Benign asbestos-related pleural effusions are usually small, unilateral or bilateral, often asymptomatic but may cause pleurisy or breathlessness; diagnosis requires exclusion of mesothelioma by thoracoscopy and pleural fluid analysis showing exudate without haemorrhage; treatment is drainage if symptomatic.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diffuse pleural thickening causes thickening of the visceral pleura and may cause restrictive lung impairment, exertional breathlessness, and occasionally persistent chest pain; CT shows pleural thickening of the costophrenic angles and rounded atelectasis; no treatment exists and progression occurs in about one-third of cases; biopsy may be needed to exclude mesothelioma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Predictive factors for hypersensitivity pneumonitis include exposure to a known offending antigen, presence of positive precipitating antibodies to that antigen, recurrent symptom episodes, inspiratory crackles on exam, symptoms occurring 4-8 hours after exposure, and weight loss.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Inhalation fever is caused by contaminated humidifiers or air-conditioning units releasing a fine spray of microorganisms, producing symptoms similar to hypersensitivity pneumonitis but with self-limiting fever and breathlessness; it can be distinguished by the presence of Mycobacterium avium or Acinetobacter/Ochrobactrum species.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chest X-ray shows extensive calcified pleural plaques with a 'candle wax' appearance, especially on the diaphragm and lateral pleural surfaces, characteristic of asbestos exposure.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Prompt recognition and treatment of pulmonary embolism is potentially life-saving; sufficient oxygen should be given to hypoxaemic patients to maintain target oxygen saturations; oxygen may relieve pain and distress but should be used cautiously in hypotensive patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Acute massive pulmonary embolism presents with major haemodynamic effects including cardiac output reduction and acute right heart failure, symptoms of faintness or collapse, crushing central chest pain, apprehension, and severe dyspnoea, signs of major circulatory collapse with tachycardia, hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure, loud P2, cyanosis, and pulmonary outflow murmur; ECG shows S1Q3T3 pattern, anterior T-wave inversion, and right bundle branch block; arterial blood gases show marked abnormality with low PaO2 and PaCO2 and metabolic acidosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Acute small or medium pulmonary embolism causes occlusion of segmental pulmonary artery leading to infarction and pleural effusion; symptoms include pleuritic chest pain, restricted breathing, and haemoptysis; signs include tachycardia, pleural rub, raised hemidiaphragm, crackles, effusion often blood-stained, and low-grade fever; ECG shows sinus tachycardia; arterial blood gases may be normal or show low PaO2 or raised PaCO2.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chronic pulmonary embolism involves chronic occlusion of pulmonary microvasculature causing right heart failure; symptoms include exertional dyspnoea and late signs of pulmonary hypertension or right heart failure; signs progress from right ventricular heave and loud P2 to right heart failure signs; ECG shows right ventricular hypertrophy and strain; arterial blood gases show exertional low PaO2 or desaturation on formal exercise testing.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Differential diagnoses for pulmonary thromboembolism include myocardial infarction, pericardial tamponade, aortic dissection, pneumonia, pneumothorax, musculoskeletal chest pain, and other causes of pulmonary hypertension.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Colour Doppler ultrasound of leg veins is useful in suspected pulmonary embolism, especially if clinical signs in a limb are present, to identify proximal deep vein thrombosis; this is particularly useful in pregnant women to minimize radiation exposure to mother and fetus.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In patients with renal impairment undergoing CTPA, care is needed due to contraindication with iodinated contrast in those with history of iodinated contrast media allergy; ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scanning or single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) may be considered as alternatives.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: V/Q scanning is of limited benefit in patients with abnormal chest X-ray due to likely underlying lung disease rather than pulmonary embolism; echocardiography can be useful bedside to detect right heart dilation and thrombus in transit in massive PE and to exclude differential diagnoses such as left ventricular failure, aortic dissection, and pericardial tamponade.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chest X-ray features suggestive of pulmonary thromboembolism include wedge-shaped opacity, horizontal linear opacities in lower zones, pleural effusion often blood-stained, pulmonary opacities of any size or shape, oligemia of lung field, enlarged pulmonary artery, and elevated hemidiaphragm.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The main principle of treatment for pulmonary embolism is anticoagulation, which is also used for other forms of venous thromboembolism.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: screen for underlying malignancy with detailed history, focused examination, and appropriate imaging if no VTE risk factors identified
fact_text: All patients with venous thromboembolism should be assessed for underlying malignancy by detailed history, focused clinical examination, and targeted imaging if no identified VTE risk factors or family history are present.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 17.66 Algorithm for investigation of suspected pulmonary embolism
fact_text: If deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is suspected in a patient with suspected PE and CTPA is negative, consider proximal leg vein ultrasound scan to confirm DVT before continuing or stopping anticoagulation.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 17.66 Algorithm for investigation of suspected pulmonary embolism

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 17.66 Algorithm for investigation of suspected pulmonary embolism
fact_text: In suspected pulmonary embolism, first determine the two-level PE Wells score; if Wells score >4 (PE likely), perform immediate CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) or start interim therapeutic anticoagulation while awaiting CTPA; if Wells score <4 (PE unlikely), perform quantitative D-dimer test and await result within 4 hours or start interim anticoagulation while awaiting result; if D-dimer positive, proceed to CTPA; if D-dimer negative, PE is unlikely and anticoagulation can be stopped if no other diagnoses.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 17.66 Algorithm for investigation of suspected pulmonary embolism

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: echocardiogram at 3 months post-PE if right ventricular dysfunction present
fact_text: Patients with right ventricular dysfunction at presentation of pulmonary embolism should have a repeat echocardiogram at 3 months to assess for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: CT pulmonary angiography may be performed safely with low radiation dose (0.01–0.06 mGy)
recommended_advice: V/Q scanning has lower fetal radiation dose (0.11–0.22 mGy) but higher maternal breast radiation
In utero radiation exposure estimated childhood malignancy risk about 1 in 16,000 per mGy
contraindications_or_cautions: consider breast tissue radiation risk if family history of breast carcinoma
fact_text: In pregnancy, pulmonary embolism diagnosis may use CT pulmonary angiography safely with low radiation dose; V/Q scanning has lower fetal but higher maternal breast radiation; warfarin is teratogenic and should be avoided; low-molecular-weight heparin is the treatment of choice.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
trigger_evidence: acute massive PE with haemodynamic instability
admission_criteria: acute massive PE with haemodynamic instability
contraindications_or_cautions: absolute contraindication to thrombolysis in some patients
fact_text: Thrombolysis is indicated in patients presenting with acute massive pulmonary embolism accompanied by haemodynamic instability but requires careful screening for haemorrhage risk; surgical or percutaneous pulmonary embolectomy may be considered if thrombolysis is contraindicated but carries high mortality.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
contraindications_or_cautions: IVC filter should be removed when possible
fact_text: Consider an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter in patients with recurrent venous thromboembolism despite anticoagulation or when anticoagulation is contraindicated; retrievable filters are preferred and should be removed when safe.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pulmonary hypertension is classified into pulmonary arterial hypertension (idiopathic, heritable, drugs, connective tissue disease, HIV, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease, schistosomiasis, pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, pulmonary capillary haemangiomatosis), pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease (systolic dysfunction, diastolic dysfunction, valvular disease), and pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease/hypoxia (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, interstitial lung disease, sleep-disordered breathing).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Clinical features of pulmonary hypertension include breathlessness, chest pain, fatigue, palpitations, exertional dizziness, syncope, elevated jugular venous pressure with a prominent 'a' wave, parasternal heave (right ventricular hypertrophy), accentuated pulmonary component of second heart sound, right ventricular third heart sound, peripheral oedema, and ascites; signs of interstitial lung disease or cardiac, liver, or connective tissue disease may suggest underlying cause.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chest X-ray in pulmonary hypertension shows enlarged pulmonary arteries, right ventricle enlargement, and reduced peripheral pulmonary blood vessels.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: ECG for right ventricular strain pattern
Chest X-ray for enlarged pulmonary arteries, peripheral pruning, right ventricle enlargement
Doppler echocardiography to estimate pulmonary artery pressure and assess tricuspid regurgitation
Right heart catheterisation to assess pulmonary haemodynamics and vasodilator responsiveness
Additional tests: pulmonary function tests, V/Q scan, CT thorax, CTPA, MRI, overnight oximetry, exercise testing
fact_text: Suspect pulmonary hypertension if ECG shows right ventricular strain and chest X-ray shows enlarged pulmonary arteries with peripheral pruning and right ventricle enlargement; confirm with Doppler echocardiography estimating pulmonary artery pressure and right heart catheterisation to measure haemodynamics and vasodilator response; additional investigations include pulmonary function tests, V/Q scan, CT thorax, CTPA, MRI, overnight oximetry, and exercise testing.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Diuretics for patients with right heart failure
Supplemental oxygen to maintain PaO2 above 8 kPa (60 mmHg)
Calcium channel blockers (e.g., amlodipine 20 mg once daily) in patients with acute pulmonary vasodilator response
dose_or_duration: Calcium channel blockers: amlodipine 20 mg once daily
recommended_advice: Avoid excessive physical activity causing distressing symptoms
Encourage pneumococcal and influenza vaccination
referral_criteria: Refer for double-lung transplantation in selected patients
Consider pulmonary thrombo-endarterectomy in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
Consider atrial septostomy as bridge to transplantation in refractory right heart failure
contraindications_or_cautions: Digoxin use should be cautious due to risk of atrial tachyarrhythmias
Pregnancy carries high risk and requires counselling
fact_text: Management of pulmonary hypertension includes diuretics for right heart failure, supplemental oxygen to maintain PaO2 >8 kPa, cautious use of digoxin, avoidance of nitrates and beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers (e.g., amlodipine 20 mg daily) only after positive vasodilator test by right heart catheterisation; patients should avoid excessive physical activity causing distressing symptoms and receive pneumococcal and influenza vaccines; pregnancy carries high risk and requires counselling; referral for lung transplantation, pulmonary thrombo-endarterectomy, or atrial septostomy may be needed in selected cases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Overnight studies of breathing, oxygenation, and sleep quality (polysomnography)
Epworth Sleepiness Scale questionnaire to quantify daytime sleepiness
recommended_advice: Careful history to exclude other causes of daytime sleepiness
Drivers with sleepiness sufficient to impair driving should be advised of their responsibility to inform the driving licence authority
referral_criteria: Referral for specialist sleep studies if local resources and probability of diagnosis justify
fact_text: Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome (OSAHS) is diagnosed by recurrent upper airway obstruction during sleep causing sleep fragmentation and daytime sleepiness, with an apnoea–hypopnoea index (AHI) ≥5 events/hour; severity is mild (5–14), moderate (15–30), or severe (>30). Diagnosis requires overnight sleep studies and oxygenation monitoring, with Epworth questionnaire to assess daytime sleepiness.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Excessive daytime sleepiness and habitual snoring are nearly universal in OSAHS; patients often wake unrefreshed, may have choking or gasping episodes, and bed partners report loud snoring with multiple breathing pauses. Associated features include impaired concentration, nocturia, irritability, depression, and early morning headaches.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: OSAHS is associated with male gender, obesity, narrow pharynx anatomy (e.g., recessed mandible), and upper airway narrowing by alcohol, sedatives, and anatomical factors such as large maxilla and mandible.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: OSAHS is linked to increased cardiovascular risk including systemic hypertension, coronary events, and stroke, partly due to sympathetic activation from sleep apnoea and associated metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: OSAHS results from recurrent pharynx occlusion during sleep due to loss of upper airway dilating muscle tone, especially palatoglossus and genioglossus, causing airway collapse and impaired ventilation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnolence are important differential diagnoses of daytime sleepiness; narcolepsy is rare and idiopathic hypersomnolence is characterised by long nocturnal sleep periods.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: Drivers with sleepiness sufficient to impair driving must be advised of their responsibility to inform the driving licence authority
referral_criteria: Patients with sleepiness causing traffic accident risk require specialist assessment and management
fact_text: Patients with OSAHS causing daytime sleepiness that impairs driving should be counselled about their legal responsibility to inform driving authorities; specialist referral is indicated if sleepiness poses a traffic accident risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: central sleep apnoea (csa) and nocturnal hypoventilation
condition_aliases: central sleep apnoea (csa) and nocturnal hypoventilation
fact_text: Central sleep apnoea is episodic reduced ventilation during sleep without airway obstruction, caused by absent ventilatory drive or chest expansion inability, with causes including post-polio, brainstem stroke, opiates, alcohol, and Cheyne-Stokes breathing in heart failure

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: central sleep apnoea (csa) and nocturnal hypoventilation
condition_aliases: central sleep apnoea (csa) and nocturnal hypoventilation
fact_text: Patients with CSA or nocturnal hypoventilation may present with symptoms similar to OSAHS, features of cor pulmonale (fluid retention from chronic hypoxia), or acute type II respiratory failure; early morning headaches are common

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Epworth sleepiness scale quantifies daytime sleepiness by scoring likelihood of dozing in 8 situations from 0 to 3, max 24; normal average 5.9, severe OSA average 16.0

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 17.88 Differential diagnosis of persistent sleepiness
fact_text: Persistent sleepiness differential includes lack of sleep, sleep disruption syndromes, sleepiness with normal sleep (narcolepsy, idiopathic hypersomnolence, neurological lesions, drugs), and psychiatric causes like depression
source_figure_or_table: Box 17.88 Differential diagnosis of persistent sleepiness

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: central sleep apnoea (csa) and nocturnal hypoventilation
condition_aliases: central sleep apnoea (csa) and nocturnal hypoventilation
recommended_tests: Sleep studies to differentiate OSAHS, CSA, and nocturnal hypoventilation
Blood gases to identify type II respiratory failure
Pulmonary function tests to assess ventilatory muscle strength
Neuroimaging (CT or MRI) if brainstem pathology suspected
fact_text: Sleep studies, blood gases, pulmonary function tests, and brain imaging (CT/MRI) are recommended to differentiate CSA from OSAHS and identify underlying causes

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition

fact_text: CPAP adherence is poor in 30-50% of patients; telemedicine and overnight oximetry can identify non-adherence and support interventions including mask fit, pressure adjustment, humidification, education, and behavioral therapy

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: central sleep apnoea (csa) and nocturnal hypoventilation
condition_aliases: central sleep apnoea (csa) and nocturnal hypoventilation
fact_text: Overnight home non-invasive ventilation (NIV) improves symptoms and prognosis in CSA and nocturnal hypoventilation; sedating medications should be avoided unless palliative

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) delivered by mask every night is the gold standard treatment for OSAHS, improving daytime performance, quality of life, and survival

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Mandibular advancement devices that move the mandible forward and open the pharynx are an alternative treatment for some patients with OSAHS who cannot tolerate CPAP

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Overweight or obese patients with OSAHS should be encouraged to lose weight and consider bariatric surgery or drug therapy if appropriate to improve symptoms and reduce AHI

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Causes of chronic laryngitis include excessive voice use, heavy tobacco smoking, heavy alcohol intake, gastroesophageal reflux disease, repeated acute laryngitis, chronic sinusitis with post-nasal drip, occupational exposure to irritants, and sarcoidosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Causes of laryngeal obstruction include inflammatory or allergic oedema or exudate, laryngeal muscle spasm, inhaled foreign body, inhaled blood clot or vomitus in unconscious patients, laryngeal tumours, bilateral vocal cord paralysis, and fixation of both cords in rheumatoid disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chronic laryngitis is often persistent and poorly responsive to treatment; voice may become permanently impaired. Smoking should be avoided and some patients may benefit from inhaled glucocorticoid treatment or steam inhalations.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Laryngeal obstruction requires urgent treatment to prevent complete airway obstruction; initial management includes up to five sharp back blows if foreign body suspected, followed by abdominal thrusts if ineffective; tracheostomy is required if obstruction persists.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In diphtheria or suspected infection causing laryngeal obstruction, administer antitoxin and appropriate antibiotics; in angioedema, treat with adrenaline 0.5–1 mg IM, chlorphenamine 10 mg IV, and hydrocortisone 200 mg IV.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In laryngeal obstruction, if foreign body causes obstruction, give up to five sharp back blows; if ineffective, give up to five abdominal thrusts; tracheostomy is mandatory if obstruction persists or in pregnant women beyond 12 weeks; direct laryngoscopy may be needed to remove foreign body or insert tube.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Persistent dysphonia from unilateral laryngeal paralysis may improve with injection of bulking agents into the affected vocal cord; bilateral paralysis may require tracheal intubation, tracheostomy, or surgery to reposition or reshape the larynx.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Psychogenic hoarseness or aphonia should be considered when vocal cord movement is voluntarily impaired without organic cause; speech therapy may be helpful after excluding organic pathology.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tracheal obstruction is commonly caused by external compression from lymph nodes in lung cancer or mediastinal tumours, retrosternal goitre, aneurysm of the aortic arch, tuberculous mediastinal lymph nodes, tracheal stenosis post-tracheostomy, prolonged intubation, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, or trauma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Mesothelioma is more common in older individuals due to a long latency period after asbestos exposure, often more than 20 years.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In older adults, spontaneous pneumothorax is almost always associated with underlying lung disease and carries significant mortality.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Rib fractures in older adults are a common cause of pleural-type pain and may be spontaneous (due to coughing), traumatic, or pathological; underlying osteomalacia may impair healing.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tuberculosis should always be considered and actively excluded in older patients presenting with unilateral pleural effusion.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pneumothorax is classified as spontaneous (primary or secondary) or traumatic; primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs without lung disease, secondary occurs with underlying lung disease, and traumatic includes iatrogenic causes and chest wall injury.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically occurs in patients without lung disease, with risk factors including smoking, tall stature, and apical subpleural blebs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in patients with pre-existing lung disease and is associated with higher mortality than primary spontaneous pneumothorax.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
contraindications_or_cautions: Older patients are particularly sensitive to respiratory depressant effects of opioid analgesics
fact_text: Older patients require careful monitoring when using opioid-based analgesia for pleural pain due to increased sensitivity to respiratory depression.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chest X-ray is essential to diagnose pneumothorax, showing a sharply defined lung edge with complete translucency between lung and chest wall; the lung edge is convex in pneumothorax but concave in emphysematous bulla.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Imaging to identify pleural adhesions and lung collapse in complex pneumothorax
fact_text: Imaging is indicated in complex pneumothorax to identify pleural adhesions and lung collapse, aiding differentiation from other conditions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: remove drain after 48 hours of no bubbling
recommended_advice: Patients should be advised not to fly until 7 days after CXR confirms full lung inflation and to stop smoking to reduce recurrence risk.
referral_criteria: consider thoracic surgery referral if lung fails to re-inflate or drain is blocked, kinked, or displaced
fact_text: Chest drains should be removed after 48 hours of no bubbling; if lung fails to re-inflate or drain is blocked/kinked/displaced, consider CT scan and thoracic surgery referral; patients should avoid flying until 7 days after CXR confirms full inflation and be advised to stop smoking to reduce recurrence risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: {"description": "Required for patients with persistent symptomatic pneumothorax after needle aspiration", "medicine_name": "intercostal chest drain"}
fact_text: Patients with persistent symptomatic pneumothorax after needle aspiration require insertion of an intercostal chest drain.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Intercostal drains should be inserted in the triangle of safety, attached to an underwater seal or one-way Heimlich valve, and secured firmly; clamping is dangerous and rarely indicated; the drain should be removed only when the lung is fully re-inflated and bubbling has stopped.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
referral_criteria: consider referral for pleural abrasion or pleurectomy by thoracotomy or thoracoscopy after second pneumothorax
fact_text: After a second spontaneous pneumothorax, surgical pleurodesis is recommended to reduce recurrence risk; this can be achieved by pleural abrasion or pleurectomy via thoracotomy or thoracoscopy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Asymptomatic spontaneous pneumothorax patients can be managed conservatively regardless of size; asymptomatic secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP) patients should be admitted for observation, while asymptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) patients may be discharged with outpatient review.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management algorithm for spontaneous pneumothorax: If mediastinal shift or hypotension (tension pneumothorax) present, immediate decompression and chest drain insertion required; if chronic lung disease and age >50, proceed to needle aspiration or chest drain; if pneumothorax >15% or hemithorax or significant dyspnoea, needle aspiration or chest drain; otherwise observe patient for 6 hours with outpatient follow-up.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Symptomatic spontaneous pneumothorax patients should be assessed for high-risk features (haemodynamic compromise, hypoxia, bilateral pneumothorax, underlying lung disease, age >50, significant smoking history, haemoptysis) and if present, require intercostal chest drain insertion; those without high-risk features may be managed with percutaneous needle aspiration or conservatively based on patient preference and local availability.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: symptomatic spontaneous pneumothorax without high-risk features
condition_aliases: symptomatic spontaneous pneumothorax without high-risk features

fact_text: Percutaneous needle aspiration is a simple, well-tolerated alternative to chest drain for symptomatic spontaneous pneumothorax without high-risk features, with a 60-80% chance of avoiding chest drain insertion.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition

admission_criteria: tension pneumothorax
fact_text: In tension pneumothorax, immediate decompression by cannula insertion into the pleural space is life-saving and should be followed by chest drain insertion.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pathogenic variants in BRCA2 gene tend to be incompletely penetrant, with about 50% penetrance, causing variable expressivity and cancer risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Familial genetic diseases are caused by constitutional variants inherited through the germline, with variable penetrance and expressivity influencing disease severity and clinical manifestations.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene may show variable expressivity, with some carriers having mild features and others developing severe life-threatening aortopathy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Penetrance is the proportion of individuals with a variant who develop the disease phenotype; expressivity describes the severity and variability of clinical features among affected individuals.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Huntington disease is fully penetrant with pathogenic expansion in the HTT gene; all individuals with the expansion will develop the disease if they live long enough.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: Consider alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency in patients with early-onset emphysema or unexplained liver disease
referral_criteria: Refer patients with confirmed PiZZ genotype for specialist respiratory and hepatology assessment
fact_text: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency is an autosomal co-dominant disorder caused by SERPINA1 gene variants p.Glu342Lys (Z) and p.Glu264Val (S), with PiZZ homozygotes having about 90% reduced alpha-1-antitrypsin levels and high risk of emphysema and liver disease; PiSZ compound heterozygotes have intermediate risk and milder disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: duchenne muscular dystrophy (dmd) and becker muscular dystrophy (bmd)
condition_aliases: duchenne muscular dystrophy (dmd) and becker muscular dystrophy (bmd)
recommended_tests: Genetic testing for dystrophin gene mutations
recommended_advice: Counsel families about progressive muscle weakness and early loss of ambulation
Prepare for respiratory support and cardiac care
referral_criteria: Refer to neuromuscular specialist and multidisciplinary care team
warning_signs: Lifespan reduced due to respiratory failure, usually mid-twenties
fact_text: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by dystrophin gene mutations leading to truncated protein, presenting with delayed milestones, speech delay, very high creatine kinase, loss of ambulation by early teens, respiratory failure, and cardiomyopathy; Becker muscular dystrophy is milder with partially functional dystrophin.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Constructing a family tree requires detailed three-generation family history including medical conditions, consanguinity, dates of birth and death, and pregnancy loss or infant death history.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
referral_criteria: Patients with potentially treatable underlying disease
Patients likely to progress to end-stage renal disease (ESRD)
fact_text: Referral to a nephrologist is appropriate for patients with potentially treatable underlying kidney disease and those at risk of progression to end-stage renal disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The 'triangle of safety' for safe chest drain insertion is anatomically defined by the axilla apex, lateral border of pectoralis major anteriorly, lateral border of latissimus dorsi posteriorly, and the 5th intercostal space inferiorly.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bilateral diaphragmatic weakness can occur in peripheral neuropathies such as Guillain–Barré syndrome, anterior horn cell disorders like poliomyelitis, muscular dystrophies, and connective tissue diseases including systemic lupus erythematosus and polymyositis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In advanced chronic kidney disease, physical signs include yellow complexion, pallor, raised jugular venous pressure due to fluid overload or pericardial tamponade, pulsus paradoxus in pericardial tamponade, pericardial friction rub, presence of dual-lumen central venous catheter or arteriovenous fistula for dialysis access, Tenckhoff catheter for peritoneal dialysis, transplanted kidney with overlying scar, 'brown line' pigmentation of nails, excoriation from pruritus, easy bruising, pitting oedema from fluid overload, and peripheral neuropathy characterized by absent reflexes, reduced sensation, paraesthesia, and restless legs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diaphragmatic rupture, usually caused by crush injury, may remain undetected for years; respiratory disorders causing pulmonary hyperinflation like emphysema and those causing small stiff lungs like diffuse pulmonary fibrosis impair diaphragmatic function and predispose to fatigue.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 17.93 Causes of elevation of a hemidiaphragm
fact_text: Elevation of a hemidiaphragm can be caused by phrenic nerve paralysis, eventration, decreased lung volume (e.g., lobectomy or unilateral pulmonary fibrosis), severe pleuritic pain, pulmonary infarction, subphrenic abscess, large gas volumes in stomach or colon, and large liver tumours or cysts.
source_figure_or_table: Box 17.93 Causes of elevation of a hemidiaphragm

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Eventration of the diaphragm is characterized by abnormal elevation or bulging of one hemidiaphragm, usually the left, due to partial or total absence of muscular development; it is often asymptomatic and incidentally detected on chest X-ray in adults but can cause severe respiratory distress in infants if extensive.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: operative correction is rarely performed and usually for cosmetic reasons only
fact_text: Pectus deformities result from abnormal costal cartilage growth causing sternal protrusion (carinatum) or depression (excavatum); pectus excavatum may displace and compress the heart but rarely causes cardiac dysfunction; chest expansion and vital capacity may be reduced; operative correction is rarely indicated and mainly for cosmetic reasons.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
admission_criteria: severe deformity with respiratory failure or cardiac complications
fact_text: Severe thoracic kyphoscoliosis restricts chest wall expansion and diaphragmatic function causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch, which may lead to type II respiratory failure (initially during sleep), pulmonary hypertension, and right ventricular failure; such patients can often be managed successfully with non-invasive ventilatory support.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Repeat renal function tests within 2 weeks in patients with unexpectedly high urea and creatinine or no prior results to exclude acute kidney injury
fact_text: In patients with CKD and unexpectedly high urea and creatinine or no prior renal function results, repeat renal function tests within 2 weeks to exclude acute kidney injury.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Investigations aim to identify underlying cause, reversible factors worsening renal function (e.g. hypertension, urinary obstruction), complications such as anaemia and renal osteodystrophy, and cardiovascular risk factors
fact_text: Investigations in CKD should identify the underlying cause, reversible factors worsening renal function such as hypertension or urinary obstruction, complications including anaemia and renal osteodystrophy, and screen for cardiovascular risk factors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Creatinine and eGFR to assess stability and progression by comparison with previous results
Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria to detect glomerular disease and need for biopsy; proteinuria indicates risk of progressive CKD requiring ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy
Electrolytes to identify hyperkalaemia and acidosis
Calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, and 25(OH)D to assess renal osteodystrophy
Albumin to assess for malnutrition, inflammation, or nephrotic syndrome if low
Full blood count including iron, ferritin, folate, and vitamin B12 to exclude common non-renal causes of anaemia if anaemic
Lipids, glucose, and HbA1c to assess cardiovascular risk and treat risk factors aggressively

Renal ultrasound to evaluate for obstructive urinary symptoms, persistent haematuria, family history of polycystic kidney disease or progressive CKD; asymmetry or small kidneys suggest renovascular or congenital disease
Hepatitis and HIV serology if dialysis or transplant is planned; hepatitis B vaccination recommended if seronegative
Other relevant tests as indicated, especially if cause of CKD is unknown
fact_text: Recommended investigations in CKD include creatinine and eGFR for progression monitoring; urinalysis and proteinuria quantification to detect glomerular disease and guide biopsy and ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy; electrolytes for hyperkalaemia and acidosis; calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, and 25(OH)D for renal osteodystrophy; albumin for malnutrition or nephrotic syndrome; full blood count with iron studies and vitamins to exclude non-renal anaemia causes; lipids, glucose, and HbA1c for cardiovascular risk assessment; renal ultrasound for obstructive symptoms or structural abnormalities; hepatitis and HIV serology if dialysis or transplant planned; and other tests if CKD cause is unknown.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In suspected phrenic nerve paralysis causing hemidiaphragm elevation, diaphragm fluoroscopy can demonstrate paradoxical upward movement on sniffing, and CT of chest and neck is recommended to exclude occult disease affecting the phrenic nerve; supine vital capacity is significantly reduced compared to erect and should be monitored.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Unilateral diaphragmatic paralysis causes approximately 20% loss of ventilatory capacity and significantly reduces supine vital capacity compared to erect posture, though it may be asymptomatic in otherwise healthy individuals.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pulmonary embolism should be suspected in patients presenting with sudden onset chest pain and breathlessness, especially with risk factors such as tobacco exposure and oral contraceptive pill use, even if chest examination is normal.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In patients with pleural plaques and breathlessness, differential diagnosis should include pleural malignancy, especially mesothelioma, particularly with a history of asbestos exposure and occupational risk factors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: CURB-65 score is calculated by assigning one point each for confusion (AMTS ≤8), blood urea nitrogen >7 mmol/L, respiratory rate ≥30/min, blood pressure systolic <90 mmHg or diastolic ≤60 mmHg, and age ≥65 years; total score predicts 30-day mortality and guides treatment setting.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: CT scanning may be required if malignancy is suspected despite negative pleural fluid cytology and bronchoscopy; a staging CT with contrast is preferred over CT pulmonary angiogram for suspected pleural malignancy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In patients with pleural plaques and clinical suspicion of pleural malignancy, diagnostic pleural aspiration under ultrasound guidance is recommended first to confirm effusion presence and minimize complications; fluid analysis should include Light's criteria, cytology for malignant cells, and microbiology for acid-fast bacilli.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: CURB-65 score 0: 0.7% 30-day mortality, treat as outpatient; score 1: 3.2% mortality, treat as outpatient; score 2: 13.0% mortality, consider short hospital stay or close outpatient monitoring; score 3: 17.0% mortality, requires hospitalisation with possible referral; score 4: 41.5% mortality, requires hospitalisation with possible referral; score 5: 57.0% mortality, requires hospitalisation with possible referral to critical care.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pulmonary function tests are not helpful in diagnosing the cause of breathlessness due to pleural effusion and should not be routinely performed in this context.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: sweat test for cystic fibrosis if young patient
fact_text: In a 34-year-old with chronic sputum production, finger clubbing, bilateral basal crackles, and response to antibiotics, bronchiectasis is the most likely diagnosis; initial investigation should include a chest CT scan, and if bronchiectasis is confirmed in a young patient, a sweat test for cystic fibrosis is indicated.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: review inhaler technique and concordance before increasing therapy
recommended_advice: patients with poor asthma control and frequent exacerbations should have inhaler technique and adherence reviewed before stepping up therapy
referral_criteria: consider specialist referral if asthma remains uncontrolled despite good technique and adherence
fact_text: In adults with poorly controlled asthma characterized by excessive reliever inhaler use and frequent exacerbations requiring emergency care, a review of inhaler technique and concordance with therapy is essential before considering escalation of asthma treatment.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the kidney and urinary tract
referral_criteria: presence of pericardial friction rub
confusion due to uraemia or hypertensive encephalopathy
fact_text: Confusion due to uraemia or hypertensive encephalopathy, presence of pericardial friction rub, crepitations indicating fluid overload, and purpuric rash suggest advanced or severe kidney disease and require urgent clinical attention and possible referral.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the kidney and urinary tract

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination of the kidney and urinary tract
fact_text: Clinical examination for kidney and urinary tract disease should include inspection for splinter haemorrhages and 'brown line' nail pigmentation on hands, skin changes such as yellow complexion, bruising, pruritus excoriation, reduced skin turgor, and purpuric rash; measurement of jugular venous pressure (elevated in fluid overload); blood pressure (often elevated); fundoscopy for diabetic retinopathy; brain assessment for confusion due to uraemia or hypertensive encephalopathy; lung auscultation for crepitations in fluid overload; heart auscultation for extra heart sounds and pericardial friction rub; abdominal examination for renal mass, tenderness, arterial bruits, prostate on rectal exam, and bladder enlargement; genital exam for scrotal swelling; assessment for sacral and ankle oedema; peripheral neuropathy signs; and urine analysis for blood and protein with microscopy as indicated. Observation should include assessment of tiredness, respiratory rate and depth (increased in metabolic acidosis), and pallor. Features marked with * indicate advanced chronic kidney disease.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination of the kidney and urinary tract

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Male lower urinary tract demonstrating the relationship of the bladder, urethra, vas deferens and testes
fact_text: The male lower urinary tract anatomy includes the bladder, urethra, vas deferens, prostate gland, seminal vesicle, rectum, ejaculatory duct, epididymis, testis, scrotum, and associated structures, demonstrating their anatomical relationships.
source_figure_or_table: Male lower urinary tract demonstrating the relationship of the bladder, urethra, vas deferens and testes

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Clinical examination techniques to evaluate urological and renal abnormalities
fact_text: Clinical examination of kidney and urinary tract includes: blood pressure measurement, blood tests for creatinine and electrolytes, urinalysis for protein, blood, nitrites and leukocytes, abdominal palpation of kidneys, percussion for renal angle tenderness, digital rectal exam for prostate assessment, and checking sacrum and ankles for pitting oedema.
source_figure_or_table: Clinical examination techniques to evaluate urological and renal abnormalities

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Each kidney is approximately 10–13 cm in length in healthy adults and is located retroperitoneally on either side of the aorta and inferior vena cava between the 12th thoracic and 3rd lumbar vertebrae.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Filtration pressure in the glomerulus is maintained by autoregulation involving muscle contraction in afferent and efferent arterioles and mesangial cells, stabilizing glomerular filtration despite systemic blood pressure variations.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Renin is released by juxtaglomerular cells in response to reduced renal perfusion pressure, sympathetic nervous stimulation, or low sodium concentration at the macula densa; renin activates angiotensin I, which is converted by ACE to angiotensin II, restoring glomerular perfusion pressure.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The glomerulus is a tightly packed tuft of capillaries supplied by an afferent arteriole and drained by an efferent arteriole, surrounded by Bowman capsule epithelium; mesangial cells regulate glomerular filtration rate by contracting and relaxing.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The kidneys receive approximately 20–25% of cardiac output through the renal arteries, which branch into interlobular arteries and then afferent glomerular arterioles supplying the glomeruli.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The right kidney is usually a few centimetres lower than the left due to the liver position; both kidneys rise and descend with respiration.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Acute kidney injury (AKI) occurs in approximately 10% of hospital admissions and is commonly associated with systemic diseases such as diabetes, hypertension, vasculitis, and autoimmune diseases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chronic kidney disease affects 7–10% of the population with prevalence increasing exponentially with age; acute kidney injury occurs in approximately 10% of hospital admissions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diabetic kidney disease is particularly prevalent in North and Central America but also increasingly in Asia and indigenous populations in America and Oceania.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is more common in Black people with recent West African descent.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: IgA nephropathy is more common in East Asia and is a frequent cause of kidney disease in indigenous populations in America and Oceania; it is less common in Black people with recent West African descent.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Membranous nephropathy is more common in Asia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: History taking in kidney disease should include enquiry about fluid intake, vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, and comorbidities such as diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease, with documentation of control status; also enquire about symptoms of undiagnosed systemic diseases (e.g. SLE, vasculitis), urinary symptoms (visible haematuria, frothy urine, oliguria), drug history including nephrotoxic drugs (diuretics, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, etc.), and symptoms of advanced kidney disease such as oedema, appetite loss, and breathlessness.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Heparin is standard anticoagulant during haemodialysis but dose may be reduced if bleeding risk is high
dose_or_duration: Haemodialysis usually 3–5 hours, three times weekly
route_or_site: Vascular access via arteriovenous fistula (AVF) in forearm is preferred; large-bore needles inserted into AVF
contraindications_or_cautions: Confusion due to serum electrolyte changes during dialysis may worsen in elderly with frailty
fact_text: In ESRD, haemodialysis is typically performed 3–5 hours thrice weekly using vascular access via AVF with large-bore needles. Heparin anticoagulation is standard but dose should be reduced if bleeding risk is high. Elderly patients may experience worsened confusion due to electrolyte changes. All patients must be screened for hepatitis B, C, and HIV before dialysis; hepatitis B negative patients should be vaccinated and hepatitis B positive patients segregated to prevent transmission.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: acute kidney injury (aki) and chronic kidney disease (ckd)
condition_aliases: acute kidney injury (aki) and chronic kidney disease (ckd)
recommended_medicines: Dialysis indicated for uraemia with pericarditis or encephalopathy in AKI
Dialysis indicated for uraemic syndrome with anorexia, nausea, lethargy and eGFR <10 mL/min/1.73 m² in CKD
Dialysis indicated for fluid overload causing acute pulmonary oedema in AKI
Dialysis indicated for intractable dependent oedema resistant to diuretics, pulmonary oedema, or severe hypertension in CKD
Dialysis indicated for hyperkalaemia >6.5 mmol/L with ECG changes in AKI
Dialysis indicated for potassium resistant to dietary control and medical intervention in CKD
Dialysis indicated for severe metabolic acidosis (H+ >79 nmol/L; pH <7.1) in AKI
Dialysis indicated for chronic acidosis resistant to bicarbonate therapy in CKD
Dialysis indicated for bleeding diathesis due to uraemia-induced platelet dysfunction in AKI
Dialysis indicated for intractable anaemia despite erythropoietin and iron in CKD
Dialysis indicated for hyperphosphataemia despite binders in CKD
fact_text: Dialysis is indicated in AKI for uraemia with pericarditis or encephalopathy, fluid overload causing acute pulmonary oedema, hyperkalaemia >6.5 mmol/L with ECG changes, severe metabolic acidosis (H+ >79 nmol/L; pH <7.1), and bleeding diathesis due to uraemia-induced platelet dysfunction. In CKD, dialysis is indicated for uraemic syndrome with anorexia, nausea, lethargy and eGFR <10 mL/min/1.73 m², intractable dependent oedema resistant to diuretics, pulmonary oedema, severe hypertension, potassium resistant to dietary and medical treatment, chronic acidosis resistant to bicarbonate therapy, intractable anaemia despite erythropoietin and iron, and hyperphosphataemia despite binders.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: end-stage renal disease (esrd) in older adults
condition_aliases: end-stage renal disease (esrd) in older adults
recommended_medicines: Peritoneal dialysis may avoid problems from fluid and electrolyte status changes in older patients
Conservative therapy without dialysis is appropriate for patients at high risk of dialysis complications or with limited prognosis
avoid_medicines: Avoid dialysis in patients with poor quality of life or significant cardiovascular disease unless benefits outweigh risks
contraindications_or_cautions: Dialysis may worsen frailty and cognitive decline in elderly
Withdrawal from dialysis may be appropriate when quality of life deteriorates irreversibly
fact_text: In older adults with ESRD, dialysis decisions should consider quality of life and cardiovascular disease burden; peritoneal dialysis may reduce fluid and electrolyte complications. Conservative management without dialysis is appropriate for patients with high risk of dialysis complications or limited prognosis. Withdrawal from dialysis may be appropriate if quality of life irreversibly deteriorates.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Podocytes have foot processes that cover the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), forming a key part of the filtration barrier in the glomerulus.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The glomerulus consists of five capillary loops surrounded by Bowman's capsule, with specialized cells including podocytes (epithelial cells), endothelial cells, and mesangial cells embedded in mesangial matrix.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The kidney's functional anatomy includes the renal artery, vein, cortex, medulla, pelvis, calyx, ureter, and bladder, with nephrons comprising afferent and efferent arterioles, glomerulus, proximal and distal convoluted tubules, loop of Henle, and collecting ducts.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Use of NSAIDs and RAAS inhibitors in volume-depleted patients can impair kidney ability to maintain glomerular filtration and may exacerbate pre-renal failure.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction of the efferent arteriole, increasing intraglomerular pressure and thus glomerular filtration rate in the short term.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone release, which enhances sodium reabsorption by the renal tubules, contributing to blood pressure regulation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bladder filling phase involves detrusor muscle relaxation and increased sphincter tone; voiding phase involves detrusor contraction and sphincter relaxation coordinated by pontine micturition centre; bladder volume increase triggers stretch receptors causing reflex relaxation of detrusor and increased sphincter tone.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Renal tubules, loop of Henle, distal tubule and collecting ducts regulate reabsorption of water, electrolytes, acid-base balance, and calcium homeostasis via 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production; failure of erythropoietin production by renal fibroblast-like cells contributes to anaemia in CKD.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Penile erection is controlled by sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves; sympathetic nerves maintain smooth muscle contraction of corpus cavernosum; parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves release neurotransmitters (NO, acetylcholine, VIP, prostacyclin) causing smooth muscle relaxation and lacunar space dilation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Prostate gland surrounds proximal urethra, produces ejaculatory fluid rich in zinc and proteolytic enzymes; seminal vesicles and bulbourethral glands contribute to ejaculate; prostate smooth muscle contraction under sympathetic control propels seminal fluid during ejaculation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bladder stores urine delivered by ureters; detrusor muscle contraction and relaxation are controlled by autonomic nervous system: sympathetic nerves relax detrusor and contract bladder neck to prevent urine release; parasympathetic nerves stimulate detrusor contraction and bladder emptying.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Investigation of renal and urinary tract disease - 18.1 How to quantify glomerular filtration rate (GFR)
fact_text: CKD-EPI 2021 equations estimate GFR from serum creatinine or cystatin C, adjusted for age and sex; creatinine-based eGFR uses constants for female/male and serum creatinine thresholds; cystatin C-based eGFR uses serum cystatin C with defined minimum and maximum values; combined creatinine-cystatin C equations improve accuracy.
source_figure_or_table: Investigation of renal and urinary tract disease - 18.1 How to quantify glomerular filtration rate (GFR)

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Investigation of renal and urinary tract disease - Glomerular filtration rate box
fact_text: GFR is the sum of ultrafiltration rates from plasma into Bowman space in each nephron, reflecting renal excretory function; it is corrected for body surface area and usually expressed as mL/min/1.73m2; direct measurement uses labelled EDTA or inulin clearance; creatinine clearance overestimates GFR due to tubular secretion.
source_figure_or_table: Investigation of renal and urinary tract disease - Glomerular filtration rate box

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: measurement of gfr using labelled markers
condition_aliases: measurement of gfr using labelled markers
source_section: Investigation of renal and urinary tract disease - Glomerular filtration rate box
fact_text: Direct GFR measurement uses labelled ethylenediamine-tetra-acetic acid (EDTA) or inulin clearance; creatinine clearance (CrCl) can be used but overestimates GFR due to tubular secretion; CrCl requires 24-hour urine collection and is inconvenient and often unreliable.
source_figure_or_table: Investigation of renal and urinary tract disease - Glomerular filtration rate box

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Dipstick testing for blood, protein, glucose, ketones, nitrates, leukocytes, urinary pH, and osmolality is recommended for screening renal and urinary tract disease
Presence of glucose on dipstick suggests poor glycaemic control in diabetes mellitus
Leukocytes and nitrites in urine indicate renal tract infection; leukocytes alone may indicate tubulo-interstitial nephritis
High urine specific gravity indicates concentrated urine and possible dehydration

Urine microscopy can detect dysmorphic erythrocytes or red cell casts (suggestive of glomerular disease), white cell casts (suggestive of pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis), and crystals (renal stone disease)
Urine culture is required to confirm infection and identify causative bacteria
Urine collection over 24 hours is used to measure solute excretion (calcium, oxalate, urate) in recurrent renal stone disease
Proteinuria quantification by protein:creatinine ratio on single urine samples is preferred over 24-hour collections
Tubular function tests (e.g., urine concentrating ability, fractional excretion of sodium) are used in specific clinical contexts such as AKI to differentiate causes
fact_text: Urine dipstick testing for blood, protein, glucose, ketones, nitrates, leukocytes, pH, and osmolality is essential for screening renal and urinary tract disease; urine microscopy and culture help diagnose infection and glomerular disease; 24-hour urine collections quantify solutes in stone disease; protein:creatinine ratio is preferred for proteinuria quantification.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Creatinine-based eGFR estimates have wide confidence intervals and limitations: they require stable creatinine, are invalid in acute kidney injury, may misestimate GFR in extremes of muscle mass, are not valid in children under 18 or pregnancy, and have controversial interpretation in older adults with mild reduction without proteinuria.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Autosomal dominant inheritance involves transmission through four generations with affected individuals in each generation; males and females are equally affected; risk of passing disease from affected individual to offspring is 50% regardless of gender.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: More than one sibling born to healthy parents affected by a disease suggests the condition may have arisen 'out of the blue' (de novo mutation) rather than inherited.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Autosomal recessive inheritance requires mutation of both gene copies; affected individuals have two mutant alleles; approximately 25% of children of carrier parents are affected, 50% are carriers; males and females affected equally; consanguinity increases risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In autosomal recessive inheritance, approximately 25% of children of carrier parents are affected, 50% are carriers, and 25% are unaffected; an unaffected child has 50% chance of being a carrier.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Suspect autosomal recessive inheritance in families where males and females are equally affected, parents are consanguineous, and the disease is rare; consanguinity increases likelihood of homozygous variants inherited from both parents.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Mitochondrial DNA disorders are maternally inherited with both sexes affected; transmission occurs only from affected females; all offspring of affected females are expected to inherit the condition.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: X-linked recessive inheritance affects males who inherit the pathogenic allele from carrier mothers; female carriers are usually unaffected but can show symptoms due to skewed X-inactivation; about 50% of cells in female carriers express genes from each X chromosome.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: X-linked recessive inheritance affects mainly males who inherit the pathogenic allele from carrier mothers; affected males cannot transmit the condition to sons but all daughters are carriers; female carriers have 25% chance of affected sons and 50% chance of carrier daughters; skewed X-inactivation can cause female carriers to show symptoms.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 18.3 Stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD)
fact_text: CKD stages 1 to 5 are classified by GFR and kidney damage presence: Stage 1 (GFR >90) normal function, asymptomatic; Stage 2 (GFR 60-89) mild CKD, asymptomatic; Stage 3A (GFR 45-59) mild to moderate CKD, usually asymptomatic; Stage 3B (GFR 30-44) moderate to severe CKD, may have anaemia; Stage 4 (GFR 15-29) severe CKD, first symptoms appear, electrolyte problems and anaemia likely; Stage 5 (GFR <15 or dialysis) kidney failure with significant symptoms and complications.
source_figure_or_table: Table 18.3 Stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD)

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 18.3 KDIGO Prognosis of CKD by GFR and albuminuria categories
fact_text: KDIGO CKD prognosis classification combines GFR categories (G1-G5) and albuminuria categories (A1-A3) to stratify risk: GFR ≥90 (G1) normal/high, 60-89 (G2) mildly decreased, 45-59 (G3a) mild-moderate decrease, 30-44 (G3b) moderate-severe decrease, 15-29 (G4) severe decrease, <15 (G5) kidney failure; albuminuria A1 <30 mg/g normal-mild, A2 30-300 mg/g moderate, A3 >300 mg/g severe. Risk increases from green (low) to red (very high) combining GFR and albuminuria.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 18.3 KDIGO Prognosis of CKD by GFR and albuminuria categories

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In CKD, serum creatinine is raised reflecting reduced GFR; serum potassium and urea levels are often elevated but serum urea has limited value as a GFR measure; abnormalities in routine biochemistry are common in renal disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Normochromic normocytic anaemia in CKD is commonly due to erythropoietin deficiency and bone marrow suppression from retained toxins; other causes include iron deficiency from bleeding and haemolytic anaemia from HUS or TTP; additional abnormalities such as neutrophilia, raised ESR, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia may indicate vasculitis, sepsis, SLE, or bone marrow suppression from myeloma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibodies (ANCAs) may be detected in patients with glomerulonephritis secondary to systemic vasculitis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Antinuclear antibodies and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies may be detected in patients with renal disease secondary to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) antibodies are present in patients with Goodpasture syndrome and low complement levels may be observed in some kidney diseases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Doppler imaging during renal ultrasound can assess blood flow in extrarenal and intrarenal vessels and measure resistivity index, which may be elevated (>0.7) in diseases such as acute tubular necrosis, rejection, or after renal transplant.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Antibodies directed against M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R) are positive in about 70–80% of cases of primary membranous nephropathy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: CTU usually involves an initial scan without contrast, followed by contrast injection to obtain nephrogram images and excretory phase images, replacing intravenous urography (IVU) for upper urinary tract investigation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: non-contrast CT of kidneys, ureters, and bladder (CT KUB)
fact_text: Non-contrast CT KUB is the method of choice for demonstrating stones within the kidney or ureter.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Renal ultrasound is a valuable non-invasive technique to assess renal size and investigate patients suspected of having urinary tract obstruction, renal tumours, cysts, or stones.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Computed tomography urography (CTU) is used to evaluate cysts and mass lesions in the kidney or filling defects within the collecting system, providing detailed imaging and characterization of masses.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Renal ultrasound is operator-dependent and results may be less clear in obese patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
avoid_medicines: Metformin (for 48 hours post-procedure in moderate or high-risk patients)
dose_or_duration: Withhold metformin for 48 hours after procedure
recommended_advice: Hydrate with free oral fluids plus consider IV isotonic saline 500 mL then 250 mL/hr during procedure
Consider alternative imaging if eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m² and risk of nephropathy is high
fact_text: Contrast nephrotoxicity is an acute kidney injury occurring within 48 hours after IV contrast; risk factors include eGFR <45 mL/min/1.73m², ionic contrast, repeated dosing, diabetes, and myeloma. Prevention includes hydration with oral fluids plus IV isotonic saline (500 mL then 250 mL/hr), withholding NSAIDs, and withholding metformin for 48 hours post-procedure in moderate/high-risk patients. If eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m², consider alternative imaging but proceed if benefit outweighs nephropathy risk.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Renal arteriography by catheter insertion into renal artery for investigation of renal artery stenosis or haemorrhage
fact_text: Renal arteriography involves catheter insertion into the renal artery to investigate renal artery stenosis or haemorrhage, and can be combined with therapeutic balloon dilation or stenting to occlude bleeding vessels and promote haemostasis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Percutaneous renal biopsy under local anaesthetic to establish diagnosis, severity, prognosis, and aetiology of renal disease
fact_text: Renal biopsy is performed percutaneously under local anaesthetic to diagnose renal disease, assess severity and prognosis, and determine aetiology when indicated.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Dynamic radionuclide studies with technetium-99m MAG3 to assess tubular secretion and renal plasma flow
Static radionuclide studies with technetium-99m DMSA to assess renal cortical function and scarring
fact_text: Radionuclide studies use gamma-emitting tracers to assess renal function; technetium-99m MAG3 dynamic studies evaluate tubular secretion and detect collecting system obstruction by persistent tracer retention, while technetium-99m DMSA static studies assess renal cortical scarring by uptake in proximal tubular cells.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: MRI for excellent resolution and distinction between tissue types
Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) for imaging renal vessels
recommended_advice: Use MRI and MRA cautiously in patients with impaired renal function due to risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis
contraindications_or_cautions: Gadolinium-based contrast agents may cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in patients with GFR <30 mL/min/1.73m²
