fact_text: Achalasia is defined by a hypertensive lower oesophageal sphincter that fails to relax on swallowing and absent propagated oesophageal contractions causing progressive oesophageal dilatation; diagnosis is confirmed by barium swallow showing tapered narrowing and manometry showing high-pressure non-relaxing sphincter with aperistalsis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Investigations for achalasia include endoscopy to exclude carcinoma, barium swallow showing distal oesophageal narrowing and dilated aperistaltic body, and manometry confirming high-pressure non-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter with poor oesophageal contractions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: pneumatic dilatation 30-35 mm diameter balloon
route_or_site: endoscopic injection into lower oesophageal sphincter
referral_criteria: failure of pneumatic dilatation or high-risk patients
contraindications_or_cautions: botulinum toxin relapse common, repeated injections less effective
fact_text: Endoscopic management of achalasia includes pneumatic dilatation with 30-35 mm balloon improving symptoms in 80% of patients; botulinum toxin injection into the lower oesophageal sphincter induces remission but relapse is common and repeated injections are less effective; per-oral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) is a newer advanced technique performed in specialist centers.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
referral_criteria: symptomatic patients
fact_text: Pharyngeal pouch results from swallowing incoordination causing herniation through cricopharyngeus muscle; diagnosis is by barium swallow showing pouch and aspiration; treatment is indicated in symptomatic patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
route_or_site: laparoscopic or open Heller myotomy with partial fundoplication
recommended_advice: PPI therapy often necessary after surgery to prevent reflux
referral_criteria: specialist surgical centers
contraindications_or_cautions: surgical approach more invasive than endoscopic
risk of gastro-oesophageal reflux post-procedure
fact_text: Surgical treatment of achalasia involves laparoscopic or open Heller myotomy with partial fundoplication to reduce reflux; surgery is more invasive than endoscopic methods and may be complicated by gastro-oesophageal reflux requiring proton pump inhibitor therapy postoperatively.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 21.31 Decision-making algorithm for hospital hyperglycaemia
recommended_tests: HbA1c if random glucose ≥7.8 mmol/L or risk factors present
capillary glucose concentrations hourly or 4–6 hourly depending on clinical status
venous blood gas and ketones if indicated
recommended_advice: Discharge summary must include diagnosis of diabetes or stress hyperglycaemia
Discharge summary must detail medication changes and most recent HbA1c
referral_criteria: Involve diabetes inpatient specialist team if glucose concentrations are abnormal or medication adjustments needed
fact_text: For an unwell patient, check capillary glucose; if random glucose is <7.8 mmol/L without risk factors, no further glucose testing is needed; if ≥7.8 mmol/L or risk factors present (age >40, family history, gestational diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, prediabetes, BMI >25 or >23 if South Asian, long-term glucocorticoids), monitor glucose concentrations 4–6 hourly for 24 hours and request HbA1c; if HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol, treat as newly diagnosed diabetes; if patient is not eating/drinking normally, start fixed rate insulin infusion (FRII) and monitor glucose hourly; if eating/drinking normally, monitor glucose 4–6 hourly and adjust medication accordingly; discharge summary must include diagnosis, medication changes, and recent HbA1c; involve diabetes specialist team as needed.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 21.31 Decision-making algorithm for hospital hyperglycaemia

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: delay in diagnosis increases mortality
referral_criteria: severe cases
difficult cases

fact_text: Oesophageal perforation is a rare but life-threatening condition often caused by iatrogenic endoscopic perforation; diagnosis requires contrast swallow, CT, and possibly endoscopy; delay in diagnosis increases mortality; surgery is mainstay but non-operative management with broad-spectrum antibiotics, nutrition, and endoscopic care may be used in selected cases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Antibodies facilitate phagocytosis by opsonisation and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, and can activate the classical complement pathway and neutralize biological activity of antigens, especially at mucosal surfaces.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Antigen-specific B cells proliferate rapidly via clonal expansion after antigen encounter, undergoing somatic hypermutation to generate higher affinity receptors, differentiating into memory B cells or plasma cells that produce antibodies.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: B-cell activation is initiated by antigen binding to the B-cell receptor, triggering Lyn and SYK kinase activation, phosphorylation of Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK), and requires T-helper cell signals via CD40L and interleukins IL-4 and IL-5 for full activation and antibody production.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Humoral immunity is mediated by B lymphocytes that differentiate from bone marrow stem cells and produce antibodies and antigen presentation, with mature B cells expressing unique B-cell receptors that bind soluble antigen targets.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Immunoglobulins are soluble proteins produced by plasma cells that mediate humoral immunity; the heavy chain determines antibody class (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD) and subclass, influencing antibody function and antigen binding.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The humoral immune response shows immunological memory, with initial IgM antibody production after 5-10 days, followed by class switching to IgG, IgA, or IgE with higher affinity and faster response on re-exposure, without requiring additional T cell input.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 4.6 The structure of an immunoglobulin (antibody) molecule
fact_text: The immunoglobulin molecule consists of variable regions responsible for antigen binding (Fab) and constant regions (Fc) that interact with immune receptors, determining antibody function.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: An individualised diabetes management plan should be established pre-operatively, including optimisation of glucose-lowering therapies, insulin regimens, and glycaemic control, and consideration of starvation period duration.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with high-risk features (e.g., HbA1c >69 mmol/mol) should have suitable pressure relief provided during post-operative nursing to reduce complications.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Plan for the patient to be first on the surgical list to minimize starvation period and reduce the need for VRII and inpatient stay.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pre-operative assessment should consider delaying surgery if HbA1c is greater than 69 mmol/mol, balancing this against surgical urgency.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Acceptable blood glucose range during post-operative VRII management is 6–10 mmol/L (105–180 mg/dL), with an acceptable wider range of 4–12 mmol/L (72–220 mg/dL).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In long starvation or decompensated diabetes (blood glucose >12 mmol/L or HbA1c >69 mmol/mol), stop non-insulin therapies and omit insulin therapies except continue long-acting insulin at 80% of normal dose; use VRII.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In short starvation with good glycaemic control (HbA1c ≤69 mmol/mol), non-insulin therapies on morning of surgery: omit sulphonylureas and SGLT2 inhibitors, continue metformin, thiazolidinedione, DPP-4 inhibitors, and GLP-1 receptor agonists as normal.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In short starvation with good glycaemic control, insulin therapies adjustments: for once daily evening insulin, reduce dose by 20% day before surgery, no change on day of surgery; for once daily morning insulin, reduce dose by 20% day before surgery, no change on day of surgery; for twice daily mixed insulin, no dose change day before or day of surgery; for multiple daily insulin, no dose change day before surgery, omit short-acting insulin and reduce long-acting insulin by 20% on day of surgery.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: People with diabetes admitted for surgery should be considered for admission the night before surgery if they are high risk or require close monitoring to optimize glycaemic control.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Peri-operative management of diabetes requires a personalized approach considering the individual, surgical procedure, and local guidelines; there is no 'one size fits all' approach.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Post-operatively, patients with diabetes should continue fasting until able to eat and drink, maintain a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion (VRII), and have blood glucose and electrolyte levels monitored regularly.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: If ulceration is identified on admission or occurs during hospital stay in a patient with diabetes, immediate referral to the multidisciplinary diabetes foot team is required.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Autonomic neuropathy in diabetes manifests as postural hypotension, gastroparesis, and sexual dysfunction.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chronic hyperglycaemia causes irreversible damage to small vessels of retina, glomerulus, and peripheral nerves, leading to microvascular complications strongly linked to hyperglycaemia and diabetes duration.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diabetes increases risk of certain infections including fungal (Candida), severe forms of infections such as COVID-19, influenza, tuberculosis, and opportunistic infections like emphysematous pyelonephritis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Macrovascular complications of diabetes include coronary circulation disease (angina, acute coronary syndrome/myocardial infarction), cerebral circulation disease (transient ischaemic attack, stroke), and peripheral circulation disease (claudication, ischaemia, ulceration).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Microvascular complications of diabetes include retinopathy (leading cause of visual loss), nephropathy (renal failure, dialysis requirement), and peripheral neuropathy (sensory loss, pain, ulceration, Charcot neuroarthropathy).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Rheumatological complications in diabetes include cheiroarthropathy with limited joint movement, Dupuytren contracture, adhesive capsulitis, and trigger finger.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Skin complications of diabetes include diabetic dermopathy, necrobiosis lipoidica, and xerosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Excess mortality in type 2 diabetes is mainly caused by cardiovascular disease including myocardial infarction, stroke, and cardiac failure.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Life expectancy in type 2 diabetes is similar to the general population of similar socioeconomic status, but those subject to social deprivation have 4-5 years reduced life expectancy due to increased vascular access to care and prescriptions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with diabetes admitted to hospital should have their feet examined for risk of pressure ulceration; those with 'at risk' feet should be fitted with pressure relief aids such as moulded plastic boots with padding or pressure relief pads to off-load heel areas.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: People with diabetes have increased infection risk due to hyperglycaemia impairing innate immunity, including neutrophil and macrophage function, and reduced complement and cytokine levels.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Urogenital infections are common in diabetes, including candidal infections, balanitis, vulvovaginitis, and pyelonephritis; fungal and bacterial infections are more frequent due to immunosuppression and poor glycaemic control.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteomyelitis occurs in about 30% of diabetic osteomyelitis cases, often secondary to foot ulcers or puncture injuries, with mid- and hindfoot involvement common and associated with poor prognosis and high risk of below-knee amputation (~50%).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteomyelitis in the diabetic foot, especially involving the hindfoot, has a poor prognosis with a high risk (~50%) of below-knee amputation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: septic arthritis and discitis in diabetes
condition_aliases: septic arthritis and discitis in diabetes
fact_text: Septic arthritis and discitis are less common than osteomyelitis in diabetes but may occur via direct puncture injury, haematogenous spread, or contiguous spread from adjacent osteomyelitis; Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Plain X-rays are insensitive for early osteomyelitis diagnosis, showing bone changes only after 30-50% bone loss; MRI and bone scintigraphy have higher sensitivity for detecting osteomyelitis in diabetic foot infections.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen in diabetic osteomyelitis; wound swabs are unreliable for diagnosis as they often reflect skin contamination, so bone biopsy for culture is preferred.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Osteomyelitis treatment requires prolonged antibiotic therapy (often weeks to months) with agents that penetrate bone; many antibiotics used for soft tissue infections are inadequate for bone infection, and surgical debridement or amputation may be necessary to control infection.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diabetic nephropathy progression involves initial glomerular hyperfiltration, followed by microalbuminuria, sustained proteinuria, and eventual nephrotic range proteinuria with declining GFR over 10-20 years in type 1 diabetes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Nodular diabetic glomerulosclerosis is characterized by thickening of basement membranes, mesangial expansion, and Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules, which are pathognomonic of diabetic kidney disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Microalbuminuria is defined as urine albumin excretion above normal but below the detection threshold of standard urine dipstick, and should be confirmed by at least two of three first-morning urine samples.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Microalbuminuria is a good predictor of progression to nephropathy in type 1 diabetes and indicates need for ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy to protect kidneys.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Renal function and electrolytes should be monitored after starting or increasing ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy in diabetic nephropathy to detect deterioration due to renal artery stenosis or other causes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Annual testing of urine for microalbuminuria and blood for estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is recommended in all adults with diabetes to detect early diabetic nephropathy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Combining ACE inhibitors and ARBs is not recommended as it offers no additional benefit and may increase risk of renal function deterioration.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are recommended as first-line therapy in diabetic nephropathy to reduce proteinuria and protect renal function, with similar blood pressure control to other antihypertensives.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Addition of other antihypertensive agents such as calcium channel blockers, diuretics, or alpha-adrenoceptor antagonists may be required to achieve target blood pressure in diabetic nephropathy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce progression to end-stage kidney disease and cardiovascular events in type 2 diabetes with overt proteinuria (>300 mg/day) and eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73m2, and are becoming standard add-on therapy to ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of microalbuminuria in diabetes includes strict blood pressure control, reduction of cardiovascular risk factors, and optimization of glycaemic control to reduce progression to nephropathy and cardiovascular disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Renal transplantation is indicated for people with end-stage kidney disease due to diabetic nephropathy and improves survival and quality of life; simultaneous pancreas transplantation should be considered in type 1 diabetes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: clinical features of symmetrical sensory polyneuropathy
condition_aliases: clinical features of symmetrical sensory polyneuropathy
fact_text: Clinical features of symmetrical sensory polyneuropathy include paraesthesia and burning sensations in lower limbs, weakness and atrophy of foot muscles, loss of foot arches, clawing toes, ulceration at pressure points, and neuropathic pain.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diabetic neuropathy is diagnosed clinically by symptoms and signs after excluding other neuropathy causes; electrophysiological testing may be used to confirm diagnosis if uncertain.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is common in type 2 diabetes due to insulin resistance and hepatic fat accumulation, causing steatosis and potentially progressing to inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis; MASLD prevalence is higher than alcoholic liver disease in this group, warranting increased monitoring and liver imaging for diagnosis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Symmetrical sensory polyneuropathy in diabetes is the most common neuropathy type, characterized by diffuse small-fibre involvement with symptoms of paraesthesia, burning feet, and sensory loss, progressing to muscle weakness, foot deformities, and ulceration due to pressure and sensory loss.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: clinical examination and tests for diabetic neuropathy
condition_aliases: clinical examination and tests for diabetic neuropathy
recommended_tests: Electrophysiological tests to demonstrate slowing of motor and sensory conduction
Tests for abnormal vibration sensitivity and thermal thresholds
fact_text: If diabetic neuropathy diagnosis is uncertain, electrophysiological tests may be performed to demonstrate slowing of motor and sensory nerve conduction and assess abnormal vibration and thermal sensitivity thresholds.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Screening for microalbuminuria in diabetes requires early morning urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) measurement, with microalbuminuria defined as ACR 2.5–30 mg/mmol in men or 3.5–30 mg/mmol in women, confirmed by 2 out of 3 positive tests; proteinuria is likely if ACR >30 mg/mmol and confirmed by protein:creatinine ratio (PCR) >45 mg/mmol; nephrotic range proteinuria is PCR >300 mg/mmol.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Chronic kidney disease in diabetes is caused by diabetes-related factors including hyperglycaemia causing diabetic nephropathy, glomerular hyperfiltration, advanced glycation end products (AGEs), and RAAS over-activation leading to inflammation and fibrosis; comorbidities such as acute kidney injury, infections, hypertension, obesity, dyslipidaemia, and chronic inflammation also contribute; medications like NSAIDs, aspirin, ACE inhibitors, and radiological contrast agents affect renal blood flow and can cause idiosyncratic reactions; lifestyle factors such as high sodium diet, sedentary behavior, and smoking worsen hypertension and renal damage.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: Supportive management; partial recovery usually within 12 months
fact_text: Asymmetrical motor diabetic neuropathy (diabetic amyotrophy) presents with severe, progressive proximal lower limb muscle weakness and wasting, severe anterior leg pain, hyperaesthesia, and paraesthesiae; it is thought to result from acute infarction of lumbosacral plexus motor neurons and usually partially recovers within 12 months with supportive care.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Ewing tests (Valsalva manoeuvre, deep breathing, sustained handgrip)
recommended_medicines: Support stockings and fludrocortisone for postural hypotension symptoms
warning_signs: Risk of sudden cardiorespiratory arrest with overt autonomic neuropathy
fact_text: Autonomic neuropathy in diabetes may present with symptoms including dizziness, nausea, vomiting, post-gustatory sweating, urinary difficulties, diarrhoea, and faecal incontinence; examination may reveal postural hypotension with resting tachycardia and pinpoint pupils; diagnosis can be supported by Ewing tests; treatment includes support stockings and fludrocortisone for postural hypotension; overt autonomic neuropathy carries a 50-70% 10-year survival due to risk of sudden cardiorespiratory arrest.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Charcot foot occurs only in diabetic patients with neuropathy and is characterized by bony destruction and deformity visible on X-rays; MRI angiogram may show diffuse arterial atherosclerosis and arterial occlusions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: clawing of toes in diabetic foot
condition_aliases: clawing of toes in diabetic foot
fact_text: Clawing of toes in diabetic foot disease is caused by intrinsic muscle atrophy and muscle imbalance, increasing pressure on metatarsal heads and flexed toes, which raises risk of callus formation and ulceration.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diabetic foot disease in patients with diabetes can result from peripheral neuropathy, peripheral vascular disease, or a combination of both, leading to complications such as clawing of toes, digital gangrene, neuropathic ulcers, dry cracked skin, callus formation, loss of leg hair, and Charcot foot deformity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
dose_or_duration: Usually recovers eventually
fact_text: Mononeuropathies in diabetes are rare but more common than in non-diabetics, often affecting cranial nerves III, VI, VII and femoral or sciatic nerves, presenting as severe, rapid onset mononeuropathy that usually recovers eventually.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Nerve compression palsies such as carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve) and less commonly ulnar nerve palsy are more common in diabetes and may result from glycation-related connective tissue thickening and diabetic microangiopathy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Prokinetic dopamine antagonist antiemetics (metoclopramide, domperidone) for short-term use
avoid_medicines: Long-term use of metoclopramide and domperidone due to adverse effects
recommended_advice: Trial low-fibre, low-residue diet and smaller, more frequent meals
Adjust timing of rapid-acting insulin in multiple daily injection regimens to match delayed gastric emptying
fact_text: Gastroparesis in type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting of undigested food, abdominal pain, and early satiety; diagnosis requires exclusion of mechanical obstruction by upper GI endoscopy and demonstration of delayed gastric emptying by scintigraphy with technetium-99m-labelled meal; treatment includes dietary modification and short-term use of prokinetic antiemetics (metoclopramide, domperidone), avoiding long-term use due to adverse effects; glycaemic control is challenging due to mismatch between insulin action and delayed glucose absorption.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: diabetic foot ulcer complications and referral
condition_aliases: diabetic foot ulcer complications and referral
fact_text: Ulcers that do not heal promptly may progress to osteomyelitis or gangrene; vascular assessment by ultrasound or angiography and possible revascularisation by angioplasty or surgery may be required; severe secondary infection or gangrene may require amputation of affected toe or limb below or above knee depending on severity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Gastric carcinoma typically presents with anorexia and nausea in about one-third of patients; early satiety, haematemesis, melaena, and dyspepsia are less common; dysphagia occurs if the tumor obstructs the gastro-oesophageal junction.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Metastatic spread of gastric carcinoma commonly involves liver, lungs, peritoneum, and bone marrow; occasional spread to supraclavicular lymph nodes (Virchow node), umbilicus (Sister Joseph nodule), or ovaries (Krukenberg tumour) may occur.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Examination in gastric carcinoma may reveal no abnormalities or signs such as weight loss, anaemia, and a palpable epigastric mass; jaundice or ascites indicate metastatic spread.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Foot ulcer risk screening in diabetes requires testing 10 g monofilament sensation at five points on each foot and palpation of dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Systematic screening for foot ulcer risk in diabetes should use a traffic light system: green (normal protective sensation and palpable pulses), amber (reduction or loss of monofilament sensation or moderate risk features), and red (both reduced sensation and absent pulses or foot deformity).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: After endoscopic diagnosis of gastric carcinoma, further imaging with endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) and CT is necessary for staging and assessing resectability; laparoscopy may be required to assess peritoneal metastases before surgery.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is the investigation of choice for suspected gastric carcinoma and should be performed promptly in any dyspeptic patient with alarm features.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: constipation due to autonomic neuropathy in diabetes
condition_aliases: constipation due to autonomic neuropathy in diabetes
fact_text: Constipation in diabetic autonomic neuropathy may be managed with stimulant laxatives such as senna.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Management of diabetic foot ulcers requires urgent multidisciplinary assessment including diabetes specialist, podiatrist, vascular surgeon, and orthotist; treatment includes debridement of necrotic tissue, antibiotic therapy if infection is present, pressure relief with customised insoles or specialised footwear, and total contact plaster cast or irremovable aircast boot.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: diarrhoea due to autonomic neuropathy in diabetes
condition_aliases: diarrhoea due to autonomic neuropathy in diabetes
fact_text: Diarrhoea in diabetic autonomic neuropathy may be treated with loperamide and rifaximin if bacterial overgrowth is suspected.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: dysphagia due to gastric outlet obstruction
condition_aliases: dysphagia due to gastric outlet obstruction
fact_text: Insertion of a nasogastric tube may provide temporary relief of vomiting caused by gastric outlet obstruction in gastric carcinoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Long-term use of dopamine agonists for erectile dysfunction in diabetes is not recommended due to risk of dystonia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Erectile dysfunction in diabetes may be treated with phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors (sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil) orally, prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) injected into corpus cavernosum or intra-urethral administration, vacuum tumescence devices, implanted penile prostheses, and psychological/psychosexual therapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: excessive sweating due to autonomic neuropathy in diabetes
condition_aliases: excessive sweating due to autonomic neuropathy in diabetes
fact_text: Excessive sweating in diabetic autonomic neuropathy may be treated with anticholinergic drugs (propantheline, poldine, oxybutynin), clonidine, or topical antimuscarinic agents such as glycopyrrolate cream.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Adjuvant chemotherapy with 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, and oxaliplatin is recommended for patients with stage II–III gastric cancer who do not receive perioperative chemotherapy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Perioperative chemotherapy with combinations including 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and docetaxel is recommended for patients with T2 or node-positive gastric cancer to improve survival.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Curative resection offers the only hope of cure in gastric carcinoma and can be achieved in about 90% of patients with early disease; total gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy is preferred for most patients.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: For very early gastric tumours, endoscopic mucosal resection or submucosal dissection may be considered as alternatives to surgery.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Palliative gastrectomy may be necessary for patients with bleeding or gastric outlet obstruction who are not candidates for curative surgery.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Patients with proximal oesophago-gastric junction tumours involving the oesophagus require oesophagectomy in addition to gastrectomy.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Small tumours distally located may be managed by partial gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy and Billroth II or Roux-en-Y reconstruction.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Gastrointestinal symptoms due to autonomic neuropathy in diabetes may be treated with dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide, domperidone), erythromycin, botulinum toxin injection into pylorus, or gastric pacemaker for gastroparesis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Molecular stratification guides optimal treatment in metastatic gastric cancer; immune checkpoint inhibitors like pembrolizumab are recommended with chemotherapy for HER2-negative adenocarcinomas with PD-L1 combined positive score ≥5.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Metastatic gastric cancer has poor prognosis with median survival about 4 months with best supportive care; patients with inoperable locally advanced or metastatic disease should be considered for palliative chemotherapy to improve fitness and possibly extend survival up to 12 months.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: peripheral sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathies in diabetes
condition_aliases: peripheral sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathies in diabetes
fact_text: Management of peripheral sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathies in diabetes includes use of tricyclic antidepressants (low-dose amitriptyline, imipramine), anticonvulsants (gabapentin, pregabalin), and if necessary combined with opioid analgesics (tramadol, oxycodone).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: peripheral sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathies in diabetes
condition_aliases: peripheral sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathies in diabetes
fact_text: Other treatments for diabetic neuropathy include tricyclic antidepressants (duloxetine), substances P depleters (capsaicin topical), opioids (tramadol, oxycodone), and antioxidant α-lipoic acid.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Postural hypotension in diabetic neuropathy can be managed with support stockings, fludrocortisone, and midodrine.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage
fact_text: Active diabetic foot ulceration requires rapid referral and management by a multidisciplinary diabetes foot team or direct vascular surgery referral when appropriate.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 21.33 Care of the feet in diabetes
fact_text: Access to podiatry services appropriate to risk level should be available, including multidisciplinary foot teams and specialist podiatrists for urgent referrals and active foot ulcers.
source_figure_or_table: Box 21.33 Care of the feet in diabetes

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 21.33 Care of the feet in diabetes
fact_text: For low risk diabetic foot patients, daily foot washing, regular nail cutting, avoiding soaking, moisturizing dry skin, covering minor cuts with sterile dressings, treating fungal and nail infections promptly, and avoiding hot water or blisters are recommended.
source_figure_or_table: Box 21.33 Care of the feet in diabetes

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Box 21.33 Care of the feet in diabetes
fact_text: For moderate and high risk diabetic foot patients, daily foot inspection, avoiding walking barefoot, wearing well-fitting shoes (e.g. trainers), avoiding over-the-counter corn/callus remedies, not attempting corn removal, checking footwear for foreign bodies, and avoiding extremes of temperature are recommended.
source_figure_or_table: Box 21.33 Care of the feet in diabetes

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage
fact_text: Active diabetic foot disease is defined by presence of active ulceration, infection, with or without ischaemia, gangrene or unexplained hot, red, swollen foot with or without pain.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage
fact_text: High risk diabetic foot also includes presence of more than one risk factor such as loss of sensation, signs of peripheral arterial disease, callus or deformity, inability to self-care, or eGFR <30.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage
fact_text: High risk diabetic foot status includes previous ulceration, amputation or consolidated Charcot foot.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage
fact_text: Low risk diabetic foot is defined by absence of risk factors, with normal sensation, pulses present, no callus or deformity, able to self-care, and eGFR >30.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage
fact_text: Moderate risk diabetic foot is defined by presence of one risk factor such as loss of sensation, signs of peripheral arterial disease, inability to or no help to self-care, or eGFR <30.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage
fact_text: High risk diabetic foot patients should be managed by a specialist podiatrist to prevent ulceration, with annual review of treatment plan and regular provision and review of footwear (orthotics).
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage
fact_text: Low risk diabetic foot patients should have screening every two years by trained healthcare workers with outcome recording, agreement on personal self-care management plan, and footwear review.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage
fact_text: Moderate risk diabetic foot patients require podiatrist assessment and implementation of a management plan, annual screening (every 2 years is insufficient), and consideration of footwear provision (orthotics).
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 21.36 Diabetic foot risk stratification and triage

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Diabetic dermopathy initially presents as small red papules that later flatten into hyperpigmented lesions on the skin in patients with diabetes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Necrobiosis lipoidica is a rare granulomatous skin disorder predominantly affecting women with type 1 diabetes, characterized by reddish plaques with yellowish central atrophic skin and telangiectasia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Xerosis, or abnormal skin dryness, occurs in diabetes as a manifestation of autonomic neuropathy and can lead to skin cracking.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: Refer patient to diabetes team for review of insulin administration and carbohydrate counting before discharge
fact_text: In a patient with DKA and elevated HbA1c but no evidence of sepsis, MI, or pancreatitis, the most likely precipitant is a problem with insulin administration or carbohydrate counting error, requiring diabetes team review before discharge.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table: Causes of hypoglycaemia in insulin-treated diabetes
fact_text: The most common cause of hypoglycaemia in insulin-treated diabetes is incorrect insulin dose, followed by wrong insulin type, wrong timing of insulin, or a combination of wrong timing and dose.
source_figure_or_table: Table: Causes of hypoglycaemia in insulin-treated diabetes

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Administer 20-50 ml of 10% intravenous glucose for hypoglycaemia in conscious patients unable to swallow
dose_or_duration: 20-50 ml of 10% glucose IV
recommended_advice: Treat hypoglycaemia first with fast-acting carbohydrate orally if possible, then follow with longer-acting carbohydrate to prevent recurrence
fact_text: In hypoglycaemia with a conscious patient unable to swallow, the appropriate treatment is intravenous 10% glucose 20-50 ml to rapidly correct blood glucose.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Prescribe Humalog Mix 25 insulin with dose and units clearly written in numbers, not as 'charted'
recommended_advice: Blood glucose charts should specify insulin dose in units, not as 'charted'
fact_text: Humalog Mix 25 insulin prescriptions must specify dose and units clearly in numbers; 'charted' is not acceptable and can cause dosing errors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_medicines: Admit patient pre-operatively for variable rate intravenous insulin infusion (VRIII) if suboptimal glycaemic control and urgent major surgery
recommended_advice: Do not advise patient to take usual morning insulin dose on day of urgent major surgery with suboptimal control
referral_criteria: Admission for VRIII pre-operatively
admission_criteria: Urgent major surgery in patient with suboptimal glycaemic control
fact_text: In patients with type 2 diabetes and suboptimal glycaemic control undergoing urgent major surgery, admission pre-operatively for variable rate intravenous insulin infusion is required; usual morning insulin dose should be withheld on day of surgery.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: manage immune-related adverse events with glucocorticoids as first-line therapy
consider additional immune suppression if glucocorticoids are insufficient
importance of self-tolerance control pathways in limiting immune toxicity
fact_text: Immune checkpoint inhibitors can cause immune-related inflammatory adverse effects commonly involving skin, liver, endocrine, gastrointestinal, lung, and thyroid; glucocorticoids are first-line treatment for these toxicities, with additional immune suppression if needed.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 4.3 Classes and properties of antibody
fact_text: IgA (1.5–4.0 g/L) is highly effective at neutralising toxins and is particularly important at mucosal surfaces, with two subclasses IgA1 and IgA2; it is present in external secretions (++++) but does not activate complement or opsonise.
source_figure_or_table: Table 4.3 Classes and properties of antibody

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 4.3 Classes and properties of antibody
fact_text: IgD is not detected in adult serum, does not activate complement or opsonise, is not present in external secretions, and functions in B-cell development.
source_figure_or_table: Table 4.3 Classes and properties of antibody

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 4.3 Classes and properties of antibody
fact_text: IgE (0.003–0.04 g/L) does not activate complement or opsonise, is mostly bound to mast cells, basophils, and eosinophils, and is important in allergic disease and defence against parasites.
source_figure_or_table: Table 4.3 Classes and properties of antibody

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 4.3 Classes and properties of antibody
fact_text: IgG is the most abundant antibody in adult serum (6.0–16.0 g/L), activates complement via IgG1 and IgG3 subclasses, opsonises pathogens, is present in external secretions, and crosses the placenta; IgG2 is important against polysaccharide antigens.
source_figure_or_table: Table 4.3 Classes and properties of antibody

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Table 4.3 Classes and properties of antibody
fact_text: IgM (0.5–2.0 g/L) strongly activates complement (++++), is highly effective at agglutinating pathogens, but does not opsonise or appear in external secretions.
source_figure_or_table: Table 4.3 Classes and properties of antibody

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Tumour immunology involves immune system surveillance to remove mutated cells; some cancers evade immunity by mutating antigens or exploiting inhibitory pathways, with virus-associated tumours linked to immune suppression and others not linked to viral infection.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_advice: importance of immune checkpoint pathways (CTLA4, PD-1, PD-L1) in maintaining self-tolerance and limiting collateral tissue damage during immune responses
fact_text: Immune checkpoint pathways such as CTLA4, PD-1, and PD-L1 maintain self-tolerance and limit collateral tissue damage during immune responses, and their blockade enhances anti-tumour immunity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Immune checkpoint inhibition in cancer involves blocking PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA4/CD80/CD86 pathways with monoclonal antibodies such as ipilimumab (anti-CTLA4), atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1), and pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) to enhance T-cell activation and proliferation, promoting tumour cell death.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: CD8+ T cells mediate direct killing of infected cells via Fas ligand, TNF-α, and IFN-γ mechanisms after activation and proliferation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The major problem in transplantation is organ donor shortage; cadaveric donors are often unsuitable due to brainstem death and associated complications, making living donor transplantation more common despite ethical and coercion concerns.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: T-cell activation requires antigen-presenting cells (APCs) to process pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) via pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), present antigenic peptides on HLA molecules to T-cell receptors (TCRs), and provide co-stimulation via CD80/CD86 binding CD28 on T cells; CTLA4 competes with CD28 to inhibit activation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: t-cell functional subsets and cytokine profiles
condition_aliases: t-cell functional subsets and cytokine profiles
fact_text: Activated T cells proliferate and differentiate into subsets: Th2 cells (produce IL-4, IL-5, IL-10, IL-13 for B-cell activation), Th1 cells (produce IL-2, TNF-α, IFN-γ for pro-inflammatory responses), Th17 cells (produce IL-17 for mucosal immunity and inflammation), and regulatory T cells (produce IL-10, TGF-β for anti-inflammatory effects).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition

dose_or_duration: Stop intravenous insulin 30 minutes after giving usual subcutaneous insulin dose at evening meal
route_or_site: Subcutaneous insulin at evening meal; intravenous insulin stopped 30 minutes later
recommended_advice: Patients can be converted back to their usual subcutaneous insulin once metabolic parameters normalize and subcutaneous insulin is given at the next convenient meal.
fact_text: In diabetic ketoacidosis management, after metabolic normalization (urea, electrolytes, bicarbonate >18 mmol/L), give usual subcutaneous insulin dose at evening meal and stop intravenous insulin 30 minutes later to maintain insulin levels due to short IV insulin half-life (2.5 minutes).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Clinical examination of the gastrointestinal tract requires systematic observation of hands for clubbing, koilonychia, and signs of liver disease; head and neck for pallor, jaundice, angular stomatitis, glossitis, parotid enlargement, mouth ulcers, dentition, and lymphadenopathy; skin for nutritional status, muscle bulk, subcutaneous fat, signs of weight loss, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum; groin for hernia and lymph nodes; perineum/rectal area for fistulae, skin tags, haemorrhoids, and masses.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: During abdominal examination, observe for distension, respiratory movements, scars, and skin colour; palpate for tenderness, guarding, masses, and enlarged viscera including liver, kidneys, and spleen; percuss for ascites and organ size; auscultate for bowel sounds and vascular bruits.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Presence of multiple surgical scars, prolapsing ileostomy, and enterocutaneous fistulae are clinical examination findings associated with Crohn disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Virchow's node (left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy) is a clinical sign associated with gastric cancer.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Clubbing of the fingers is a clinical sign that may be observed in patients with malabsorption.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a skin manifestation that may be observed in patients with ulcerative colitis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Atrophic glossitis and angular stomatitis are clinical signs that may indicate vitamin B12 deficiency.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Common anal diseases detected on rectal exam include tags, haemorrhoids, polyps, and Crohn disease.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: An epigastric mass on abdominal exam suggests differential diagnoses including gastric cancer, pancreatic cancer, or aortic aneurysm.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Rectal examination may detect extrinsic masses such as tumours, abscesses, prostate enlargement, or uterus/cervix masses.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Generalised abdominal distension may be caused by fat (obesity), fluid (ascites or blood), flatus (obstruction or ileus), faeces (constipation), or fetus (pregnancy).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: A left iliac fossa mass may indicate sigmoid colon cancer, constipation, or a diverticular mass.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: A left upper quadrant mass may be due to splenic or kidney pathology; splenic masses cannot be moved above and move towards the right iliac fossa with dull percussion and a notch, while kidney masses are rounded, can be moved above, move downwards, are resonant to percussion, and ballottable.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Rectal examination can detect prolapse.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: A right iliac fossa mass may be caused by caecal carcinoma, Crohn disease, or an appendix abscess.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: faecal immunochemical test for occult blood
fact_text: Stool examination during rectal exam should assess consistency, colour, steatorrhoea, presence of bloody or black stool, and include faecal immunochemical testing for occult blood.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: A suprapubic mass may be due to bladder pathology, pregnancy, or fibroids/carcinoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
referral_criteria: peritonitis
bowel obstruction
admission_criteria: peritonitis
bowel obstruction
fact_text: Tenderness to palpation with guarding, rebound tenderness, absent bowel sounds, and rigidity indicates peritonitis, while distension with tinkling bowel sounds and visible peristalsis suggests bowel obstruction; these are red flags requiring urgent referral and admission.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Rectal examination may reveal tumours such as polyps or cancer.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The stomach anatomy includes the cardia, fundus, body, antrum, and is innervated by the vagus nerves; the duodenum has first, second, and third parts with the common bile duct entering the second part.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The oesophagus is a muscular tube approximately 25 cm long extending from the cricoid cartilage to the cardiac orifice of the stomach, with the gastroesophageal junction about 40 cm from the incisors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The oesophagus has an upper and lower sphincter; peristaltic swallowing waves propel food boluses into the stomach, which can be measured by oesophageal manometry.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The stomach acts as a 'hopper' that retains and grinds food, then actively propels it into the duodenum.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Swallowing is a voluntary process initiated by tongue propulsion of food into the pharynx, followed by relaxation of the upper oesophageal sphincter, peristaltic activity controlled by brainstem autonomic nerves, and relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter allowing food entry into the stomach.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Plain X-rays to show distended loops of bowel and air-fluid levels with abdominal CT and small bowel MRI to exclude mechanical obstruction
Laparotomy may be required to exclude obstruction and obtain full-thickness biopsies of the intestine
Examination of biopsy material using specialised techniques such as electron microscopy and immunohistochemistry to diagnose diseases of enteric smooth muscle and nerves
recommended_medicines: Metoclopramide or domperidone may enhance motility
Antibiotics are given for bacterial overgrowth
recommended_advice: Nutritional and psychological support is necessary
fact_text: Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction may be primary (familial visceral myopathies/neuropathies, congenital aganglionosis) or secondary to drugs, smooth muscle disorders, myenteric plexus dysfunction, CNS disorders, or endocrine/metabolic diseases; diagnosis requires imaging to exclude mechanical obstruction and biopsy with specialised techniques; treatment includes addressing underlying causes, motility agents (metoclopramide/domperidone), antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth, and nutritional/psychological support.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Colorectal polyps are mucosal growths classified as neoplastic (conventional adenoma, sessile serrated lesion, traditional serrated adenoma) or non-neoplastic (hamartoma, inflammatory, hyperplastic), with neoplastic polyps having malignant potential.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Colorectal polyps have various morphologies including sessile, pedunculated, flat, elevated, and depressed forms.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Neoplastic colorectal polyps include conventional adenoma, sessile serrated lesion, and traditional serrated adenoma; non-neoplastic polyps include hamartoma, inflammatory, and hyperplastic types.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Risk factors for malignant change in colonic polyps include size greater than 2 cm, multiple polyps, serrated polyps (excluding rectal hyperplastic polyps), villous architecture, and high-grade dysplasia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: Oesophageal manometry with pressure sensors at 1 cm intervals to record intra-oesophageal pressure during swallowing
fact_text: Oesophageal manometry involves passing a tube with pressure sensors spaced at 1 cm intervals into the oesophagus to measure pressure changes during swallowing, useful for assessing oesophageal motility disorders.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Bicarbonate ions, prostaglandins, mucins, and trefoil factor family peptides protect the gastroduodenal mucosa from acid and pepsin damage.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Dietary lipids include long-chain triglycerides, cholesterol esters, and lecithin; they are insoluble in water and require lipolysis and incorporation into mixed micelles before absorption by enterocytes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Gastrin is produced by G cells in the gastric antrum and stimulates acid secretion and mucosal growth; somatostatin from D cells inhibits acid secretion; ghrelin from P/D1 cells stimulates acid secretion and appetite.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Gastrin released from antral G cells binds CCK-2 receptors on enterochromaffin-like cells to release histamine, which activates H2 receptors on parietal cells to stimulate acid secretion via H+/K+ ATPase; cholinergic vagal stimulation and gastrin also directly stimulate parietal cells.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine are key stimulants of gastric acid secretion; hydrogen ions are secreted by gastric parietal cells via the H+/K+ ATPase pump, with chloride ions secreted through channels to form hydrochloric acid.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Small intestine functions include digestion (mechanical, enzymatic, peristaltic), absorption of digestion products, water, electrolytes, and vitamins, protection against ingested toxins, and immune regulation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The jejunum begins at the ligament of Treitz and the ileum ends at the ileocaecal valve; small bowel peristaltic activity is stimulated by food entry into the gastrointestinal tract and occurs every 1–2 hours.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Molecular pathways of colorectal cancer include microsatellite instability and chromosomal instability pathways; the serrated neoplasia pathway is associated with faster carcinoma development compared to the classical adenoma-carcinoma pathway.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Up to 50% of colorectal cancers are sporadic and influenced by environmental factors; lifestyle modifications such as reducing smoking, alcohol, and type 2 diabetes risk factors, and increasing fruit and vegetable intake may help prevent colorectal cancer.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The classical adenoma to carcinoma pathway in colorectal cancer involves an initiating loss-of-function mutation in the APC gene, followed by accumulation of mutations in KRAS, DCC (or SMAD4), and TP53 genes, leading to progression from normal mucosa through early, intermediate, and late adenomas to carcinoma.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Colorectal cancer risk factors include: Genetic (multiple small-effect susceptibility genes, accumulation of somatic mutations, hereditary cancer syndromes 3-5%), Diet (increased risk with red and processed meats; decreased risk with dietary fibre, fruits, vegetables, calcium, folic acid, omega-3 fatty acids), Medical conditions (colorectal neoplastic polyps, long-standing extensive ulcerative colitis or Crohn's colitis, ureterosigmoidostomy, acromegaly, pelvic radiotherapy), and Others (increased risk with obesity, sedentary lifestyle, smoking, alcohol, cholecystectomy, type 2 diabetes; reduced risk with aspirin or NSAIDs and possibly statins).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Starch is hydrolysed by salivary and pancreatic amylases into α-limit dextrins (4–8 glucose units), maltose, and maltotriose. Disaccharides are digested by enzymes fixed to the microvillus membrane into monosaccharides glucose, galactose, and fructose. Glucose and galactose are absorbed by energy-dependent facilitated diffusion via GLUT5 transporter and SGLT1 in the small intestine.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fat digestion involves multiple steps: 1) Fatty acids stimulate cholecystokinin (CCK) release from duodenum and upper jejunum, which triggers pancreatic enzyme secretion, gallbladder contraction, and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi to allow bile flow. 2) Bile acids and salts form mixed micelles with dietary fat, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins. 3) Pancreatic lipase and colipase digest triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides. 4) These products are absorbed by enterocytes and re-esterified to triglycerides with cholesterol, phospholipids, fat-soluble vitamins, and apoproteins to form chylomicrons. 5) Chylomicrons enter lymphatics via exocytosis and reach systemic circulation via thoracic duct.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: In healthy individuals, fluid balance is tightly controlled with approximately 100 mL of the 8 liters of fluid entering the gastrointestinal tract daily being excreted in stools.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: absorption of water-soluble vitamins and trace elements
condition_aliases: absorption of water-soluble vitamins and trace elements
fact_text: Water-soluble vitamins are absorbed throughout the intestine. Absorption of folic acid, vitamin B12, calcium, and iron occurs by specific mechanisms described elsewhere (Chapter 24).

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Water and electrolyte absorption in the intestine occurs via two pathways: 1) paracellular route through tight junctions driven by osmotic, electrical, or hydrostatic gradients, and 2) transcellular route via energy-dependent specific transport carriers across apical and basolateral membranes.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Protein digestion begins with pepsin in the stomach, which is quantitatively modest but important. Cholecystokinin (CCK) released from proximal jejunum mucosa stimulates pancreatic proteases including trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, pro-elastase, and procarboxypeptidases. Trypsinogen is activated by enterokinase to trypsin, which activates other pancreatic proteases. These enzymes hydrolyse proteins to peptides and amino acids, which are further digested intracellularly in enterocytes and absorbed into portal circulation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Gastrointestinal mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) constitutes 25% of lymphoid tissue and is central to mucosal immunity, with Peyer's patches containing B lymphocytes that differentiate into plasma cells producing IgA transported into the intestinal lumen to neutralize pathogens.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Intestinal T lymphocytes localize plasma cells to antigen exposure sites and produce inflammatory mediators; macrophages phagocytose pathogens and secrete cytokines mediating inflammation, with mast cells releasing inflammatory molecules upon activation of mast-cell surface IgE receptors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Intestinal defence includes multiple layers: lumen with bacteria and mucins, epithelium with impermeable brush border membranes and tight junctions, and subepithelial immune cells that respond to pathogens via pattern recognition receptors such as Toll-like and NOD receptors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: MAD-CAM-1 peptide expressed on intestinal endothelial cells binds α4β7 integrin on lymphocytes, facilitating lymphocyte homing to intestinal lymphoid tissue, critical for mucosal immune surveillance and response.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 22.7 Fluid homeostasis in the gastrointestinal tract
fact_text: Normal daily fluid volumes in the GI tract include 1500 mL saliva, 1200 mL food and water intake, 500 mL bile, 2000 mL gastric secretions, 1500 mL pancreatic secretions, and 1500 mL small intestine secretions, with 8100 mL absorbed and 100 mL stool excreted, maintaining fluid homeostasis.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 22.7 Fluid homeostasis in the gastrointestinal tract

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Protein digestion involves pancreatic secretion of trypsinogen activated by enterokinase in the small intestine to trypsin, which activates other pro-enzymes to break proteins into peptides, amino acids, and oligopeptides, further digested by brush border enzymes and enterocyte peptidases for absorption into portal circulation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: autonomic nervous system regulation of gut
condition_aliases: autonomic nervous system regulation of gut
fact_text: The autonomic nervous system regulates gut function via parasympathetic pathways (vagal and sacral efferents) that are cholinergic and increase smooth muscle tone and promote sphincter relaxation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
source_section: Fig. 22.48 TNM classification in colorectal cancer
fact_text: The TNM classification for colorectal cancer defines T1 as tumor grown into submucosa, T2 into muscularis propria, T3 into subserosa, and T4 into visceral peritoneum or other structures; N1a/b as cancer cells in 1-3 nearby lymph nodes, N1c as cancer cells in nearby tissues but not lymph nodes, and N2a/b as cancer cells in 4 or more nearby lymph nodes; M1a as spread to one part of the body, M1b as spread to more than one part, and M1c as spread to peritoneal surface.
source_figure_or_table: Fig. 22.48 TNM classification in colorectal cancer

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Secretion, absorption, motility, growth, and differentiation of the gut are modulated by neuronal and hormonal factors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: genetic testing for MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM
fact_text: Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC or Lynch syndrome) accounts for 1-3% of colorectal cancers, has an 80% lifetime risk with mean diagnosis age 45, and requires genetic testing for MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, and EPCAM genes plus microsatellite instability and mismatch repair protein immunohistochemistry to identify affected individuals.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
condition: intestinal microbiota composition and health impact
condition_aliases: intestinal microbiota composition and health impact
fact_text: Human gut microbiota contains 10^14 microbes with gene count 100-fold greater than human genome; microbiota composition is influenced by age, diet, drugs, smoking, stress, and aging, and dysbiosis is linked to gastrointestinal, metabolic, cardiovascular, neuropsychiatric, and psychiatric diseases.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
contraindications_or_cautions: CT colonography is fast and low-risk but less sensitive for polyps <6 mm, requires bowel preparation, and involves ionising radiation exposure.
fact_text: CT colonography offers a fast, low-risk alternative to colonoscopy with equivalent sensitivity for cancer detection but reduced sensitivity for polyps smaller than 6 mm; it requires bowel preparation and exposes patients to ionising radiation, limiting its therapeutic intent.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: pathogenic variant testing for NRAS, KRAS, BRAF V600E
fact_text: Colorectal cancers should be tested for deficient mismatch repair (dMMR) and pathogenic variants in NRAS, KRAS, and BRAF V600E to assess prognosis and guide targeted therapy selection.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
recommended_tests: population-based screening with faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) for people aged 50-74
fact_text: Population-based screening for colorectal cancer using faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) is recommended for people aged 50 to 74 years to detect and remove early or pre-malignant lesions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
contraindications_or_cautions: Colonoscopy requires bowel preparation and carries a risk of perforation (~1:1000).
fact_text: Serial colonoscopy is the screening method of choice in the UK for colorectal cancer, allowing polypectomy and early detection, but it requires bowel preparation and carries a perforation risk of approximately 1 in 1000; many countries lack resources for this approach.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Colon acts as a storage organ with contractile activity; two contraction types occur: segmentation (ring contraction) mixing contents and propulsive (peristaltic) waves moving feces to rectum.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Colon contractile activity is stimulated by gastrocolic reflex via hormones (5-HT, motilin, CCK) after meals.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
contraindications_or_cautions: Bevacizumab and cetuximab are monoclonal antibody therapies targeting VEGF and EGFR respectively; cetuximab is effective only in RAS and BRAF wild-type tumors.
fact_text: Initial palliative chemotherapy for metastatic colorectal cancer includes combinations of 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, capecitabine, oxaliplatin, and irinotecan; monoclonal antibodies bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) and cetuximab (anti-EGFR) are often added, but cetuximab is only effective in RAS and BRAF wild-type tumors; checkpoint inhibitor therapy may be effective in dMMR tumors.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Palliative management of colorectal cancer with metastases includes surgical resection, laser therapy, or stenting of the primary tumor to relieve obstruction or bleeding; palliative radiotherapy is useful for symptom control in pelvic disease, bone or lung metastases; palliative chemotherapy improves symptoms, quality of life, and survival in patients fit enough to benefit.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Ductular cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid to provide an alkaline pH optimum for pancreatic enzyme activity.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Amylase acts on starch and glycogen producing limit dextrans, maltose, and maltotriose; lipase and colipase act on triglycerides producing monoglycerides and free fatty acids; proteolytic enzymes (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, pro-elastase, pro-carboxypeptidases) act on proteins and polypeptides producing short polypeptides.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Exocrine pancreas secretes pro-enzymes activated by pancreatic acinar cells; secretion is stimulated by circulating gastrointestinal hormones.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Investigation of gastrointestinal disease includes tests classified into structure, infection, and function categories to evaluate patients with gastrointestinal symptoms.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Fig 22.10 shows anatomy of terminal ileum, normal colon, rectum, and anal canal with endoscopic views of caecum, terminal ileum, descending colon, and anal canal.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Migrating motor complexes (MMCs) are waves of contraction spreading from stomach to ileum about every 90 minutes or between meals and during fasting, serving to sweep intestinal contents distally in preparation for the next meal and inhibited by eating.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Peristalsis is a reflex triggered by gut wall distension, producing a wave of circular muscle contraction that propels contents from oesophagus to rectum, driven by a basic electrical rhythm from interstitial cells of Cajal in the circular smooth muscle layer.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The ENS can function autonomously using neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine, noradrenaline, 5-HT, nitric oxide, substance P, and calcitonin gene-related peptide, with local reflex loops and loops involving coeliac and mesenteric ganglia.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: The enteric nervous system (ENS) is part of the autonomic nervous system and regulates gut motility, secretion, blood flow, and other key gut functions via two major plexuses: the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus controlling motor function and the submucosal (Meissner) plexus controlling secretion and blood flow.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Barium sulphate contrast X-rays assess anatomical abnormalities and motility; barium sulphate opacifies mucosa and precipitates impaction, while water-soluble contrast is preferred to opacify bowel before CT and in suspected perforation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Plain abdominal X-rays are useful for diagnosing intestinal obstruction or paralytic ileus by showing dilated bowel loops; chest X-rays in erect position can detect subdiaphragmatic free air indicating perforation.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Early recognition and prompt treatment of septic shock is critical to improve patient outcomes; diagnosis and management details are provided in a dedicated chapter.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Acute inflammation is a rapid, complex response involving innate immune cells and soluble mediators causing heat, redness, pain, and swelling, initiated by tissue injury or infection.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: CD4+ T lymphocytes recognize peptides with HLA class II molecules and support CD8+ T lymphocytes and phagocytes by producing cytokines; they are subdivided into Th1, Th2, T-regulatory, and Th17 subsets based on cytokine profiles and functions.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: CD8+ T lymphocytes recognize antigenic peptides with HLA class I molecules and kill infected cells by releasing perforin and digestive enzymes, playing a key role in defense against viral infections.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
fact_text: Resolution of inflammation requires downregulation of inflammatory stimuli and repair of tissue damage, involving neutrophil apoptosis, macrophage phagocytosis of debris, and synthesis of collagen and angiogenic factors to restore tissue homeostasis.

source_title: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 25th Edition
