source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Beta-blockers reduce sympathetic overactivity but may mask signs of severe withdrawal, risking inadequate benzodiazepine treatment.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Inpatient therapy is indicated for moderate to severe withdrawal, prior seizures or delirium tremens, poor outpatient cooperation, comorbidities, or failed outpatient detox; benzodiazepines dosing should be carefully monitored.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Benzodiazepines to decrease withdrawal symptoms and prevent delirium tremens, seizures, and death
Some patients can be treated as outpatients with benzodiazepines

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Treat early disease found by screening test vs treat disease at time of clinical presentation

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

recommended_advice: Use cholinesterase inhibitors
Avoid neuroleptics until DLB diagnosis is evaluated
fact_text: Treat DLB with cholinesterase inhibitors; avoid neuroleptics as they may worsen symptoms.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Diabetes is undiagnosed in 24% of people; 39% have a parent with diabetes; 60-90% concordance in monozygotic twins; lifetime risk is 5-10 times higher in first-degree relatives; obesity is the most important risk factor.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Risk factors for type 2 diabetes mellitus include age ≥ 45, BMI ≥ 25 kg/m², first-degree relative with diabetes, physical inactivity, high-risk ethnic group membership, history of large baby or gestational diabetes, hypertension, low HDL or high triglycerides, polycystic ovary syndrome, vascular disease, and prediabetes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is caused by impaired insulin secretion and resistance, accounts for 90-95% of diabetes cases, and is more prevalent in certain ethnic groups.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Polyuria differential diagnosis includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, primary polydipsia, diabetes insipidus, urinary tract infection, and bladder dysfunction, with specific tests recommended for each.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can affect multiple organs causing cardiovascular, GI, genitourinary, and erectile dysfunction symptoms.

sum total perceived monofilament touches (score 0-8)

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Diabetic diarrhea requires ruling out other causes of chronic diarrhea.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

pregabalin and duloxetine FDA approved for neuropathic pain

fact_text: Tight glycemic control prevents neuropathy; pregabalin and duloxetine are FDA approved for neuropathic pain; other agents include gabapentin, tricyclic antidepressants, venlafaxine, and tramadol.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Any amount of albuminuria increases risk of cardiovascular events.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Diabetic nephropathy is defined by albumin/creatinine ratio with microalbuminuria 30–299 mcg/mg and macroalbuminuria ≥ 300 mcg/mg.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Tight glycemic control reduces incidence of micro- and macroalbuminuria and microvascular complications in diabetes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Diabetic foot infections are classified as mild, moderate, or severe based on extent of erythema, tissue involvement, and systemic inflammatory response signs (SIRS).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Immediate threats to life in dyspnea include coronary syndrome, tamponade, airway obstruction, stenosis, anaphylaxis, and pneumothorax.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: heart failure, pneumonia, obstructive lung disease, pulmonary embolism
condition_aliases: obstructive lung disease (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease/asthma)
heart failure, pneumonia, obstructive lung disease, pulmonary embolism
trigger_evidence: common serious and life-threatening causes of dyspnea
fact_text: Four most common serious and life-threatening causes of dyspnea are heart failure, pneumonia, obstructive lung disease, and pulmonary embolism.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Presence of chest pain, especially pleuritic, helps narrow differential diagnosis of dyspnea to heart failure, pneumonia, PE, or pneumothorax.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Metabolic disorders such as diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperthyroidism can cause dyspnea.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Obesity is a recognized cause of dyspnea.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Pericardial diseases such as tamponade and constrictive pericarditis can cause dyspnea.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: pleuritic chest pain causes (mi, aortic dissection, pe, pneumothorax, arrhythmia, angina, asthma, copd, heart associated lung disease)
condition_aliases: heart associated lung disease with chest tightness
pleuritic chest pain causes (mi, aortic dissection, pe, pneumothorax, arrhythmia, angina, asthma, copd, heart associated lung disease)
fact_text: Pleuritic chest pain with dyspnea suggests diagnoses including MI, aortic dissection, PE, pneumothorax, arrhythmia, angina, asthma, COPD, and heart-associated lung disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is useful to evaluate pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, and pneumothorax in dyspnea patients.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Acute coronary syndrome presents with chest pain and risk factors; ECG, troponin, and angiography recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Anemia presents with pale conjunctiva and bleeding history; hematocrit recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Aortic regurgitation presents with any diastolic murmur and may be associated with chest pain or bicuspid aortic valve.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Aortic stenosis presents with significant systolic murmur and may be associated with bicuspid aortic valve.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: ARDS presents with diffuse crackles and is associated with sepsis, pancreatitis, smoke inhalation, aspiration; chest radiography recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Arrhythmia presents with palpitations and irregular pulse; ECG and Holter/event monitor recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Asthma presents with wheezing triggered by cold or exercise; PFTs with bronchodilator response and methacholine challenge recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: COPD is associated with ≥40 pack years tobacco use, decreased breath sounds, wheezing; chest radiography and PFTs recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Heart failure presents with S3, JVD, crackles on lung exam; chest film, BNP, and echocardiography recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: ILD presents with diffuse lung crackles and risk factors including connective tissue disease and exposures; PFTs and high-resolution chest CT recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Mitral regurgitation presents with holosystolic murmur and may be associated with mitral valve prolapse.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Mitral stenosis presents with any diastolic murmur and is associated with rheumatic heart disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Pneumonia presents with fever, productive cough, and risk factors; chest radiography, HIV, and CD4 testing recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Pneumothorax presents with pleuritic chest pain and pleural rub or decreased breath sounds; chest radiography recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Pulmonary embolism presents with sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and risk factors; D-Dimer, CT angiography, V/Q scan, and leg duplex ultrasound recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Valvular heart disease causing dyspnea shows significant murmur; echocardiography and blood cultures if endocarditis suspected are recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Unilateral pleural effusion causes include pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, malignancy, and heart failure; bilateral effusions suggest heart failure or interstitial lung disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: diseases causing dyspnea associated with abnormal lung fields on chest film
condition_aliases: diseases causing dyspnea associated with abnormal lung fields on chest film
trigger_evidence: abnormal lung fields on chest film
fact_text: Diseases causing dyspnea with abnormal lung fields include pneumonia, malignancy, pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, ARDS, and interstitial lung disease, differentiated by focal vs diffuse infiltrates.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: diseases causing dyspnea with a normal chest film
condition_aliases: diseases causing dyspnea with a normal chest film
fact_text: Diseases causing dyspnea with usually normal chest film include laryngeal edema, airway obstruction, pulmonary hypertension, asthma, anemia, arrhythmia, ACS, and primary arthralgia; occasionally normal chest film seen in heart failure, COPD, interstitial lung disease, and pulmonary embolism.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: shortness of breath with minimal exertion
grade II/VI systolic murmur at apex
recommended_advice: quantify increase in dyspnea from baseline
fact_text: Worsening dyspnea with orthopnea, PND, bilateral crackles, systolic murmur, S3 gallop, and pretibial edema suggests heart failure with volume overload.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Differential diagnosis of dyspnea with pleuritic chest pain includes pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, asthma, COPD, myocardial infarction, angina, aortic dissection, arrhythmia, and pleural effusion.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: findings on point-of-care ultrasound for dyspnea
condition_aliases: findings on point-of-care ultrasound for dyspnea
recommended_tests: lung ultrasound for absence of sliding lung (pneumothorax)
lung ultrasound for B-lines (acute heart failure)
fact_text: Point-of-care ultrasound findings: absence of sliding lung suggests pneumothorax; complete evaluation for pneumonia; B-lines indicate acute heart failure.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: no signs or symptoms suggestive of PE
recommended_tests: echocardiography to document impaired systolic or diastolic cardiac function
pulmonary function tests to determine type of lung disease
fact_text: In patients unlikely to have PE despite elevated D-dimer, echocardiography and pulmonary function tests help evaluate cardiac and lung function to guide diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In men, a total cholesterol–HDL ratio of 2.6–4 is associated with 2–14% greater risk than predicted by total cholesterol or LDL alone; in women, a ratio >5.6 is associated with 25–45% greater risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Colon cancer histology is mostly adenocarcinoma (>90%) with varying differentiation; prognosis varies by stage with overall 5-year survival 64%, stage I 90%, and stage IV 12%.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Colon cancer staging is defined from Stage 0 (carcinoma in situ) to Stage IV (distant metastasis); colonoscopy and pelvic/abdominal CT scan are commonly used for diagnosis and staging.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Total cholesterol and HDL are minimally affected by eating and can be measured in fasting or nonfasting individuals; triglycerides may increase 20–30% by eating and must be measured in fasting state.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Use low- to moderate-dose statin for prevention
fact_text: Adults 40–75 years with ≥1 CVD risk factor and 10-year risk ≥10% should use low- to moderate-dose statin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease per 2016 USPSTF guidelines.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Meta-analyses show statins reduce all-cause mortality by 14% (NNT 138) and cardiovascular events by 25% (NNT 49) over 5 years in primary prevention; no evidence diet alone reduces cardiovascular events.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Pooled Cohort Equations risk assessment tool
fact_text: The ACC/AHA 2013 guidelines recommend using the Pooled Cohort Equations to estimate 10-year risk of first ASCVD event in non-Hispanic whites and blacks; equations may be less accurate in other populations.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: HF affects 6.5 million in US with 900,000 hospitalizations and 75,000 deaths annually; risk higher in men; classified as HFrEF (EF ≤40%) or HFpEF (EF >50%) with distinct causes and pathophysiology.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (hfref)
heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (hfpef)
trigger_evidence: History of MI or poorly controlled hypertension
fact_text: Heart failure diagnosis requires clinical features plus chest radiograph, HCT, and ECG; distinguish HFrEF (EF ≤40%) from HFpEF (EF >50%) based on ejection fraction and clinical features.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Pursue highly specific positive clinical findings such as S3 gallop and JVD to guide diagnosis
fact_text: In dyspnea differential diagnosis, consider heart failure, COPD, PE, and pneumonia; use specific clinical findings like S3 gallop and JVD to guide diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (hfpef)
condition_aliases: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (hfpef)
fact_text: HFpEF is caused mainly by hypertension; less common causes include aortic stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (hfref)
condition_aliases: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (hfref)
fact_text: HFrEF causes include CAD (most common), long-standing hypertension, alcohol abuse, viral/postpartum cardiomyopathy, drug toxicity, persistent tachycardia, and idiopathic cardiomyopathy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: HFpEF involves increased myocardial muscle mass, infiltration, or fibrosis causing decreased LV compliance and impaired filling despite preserved contractility and ejection fraction.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Pulmonary function test abnormalities vary by lung disease mechanism: obstruction shows decreased flows and FEV1/FVC; restriction shows decreased volumes and TLC; vascular embolism shows decreased DLCO.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Treat obvious cause
Consider concomitant causes
Assess risk factors and associated symptoms/signs
fact_text: A structured diagnostic approach to dyspnea includes assessing for common causes (HF, COPD/asthma, PE, pneumonia), evaluating for obvious causes, considering acute must-not-miss diagnoses, assessing clinical findings (chest pain type, JVD, S3, breath sounds, crackles), and incorporating POCUS, chest film, and ECG findings before treatment.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Common causes of LV failure include CAD, hypertension, alcoholic cardiomyopathy
Common causes of RV failure include advanced LV failure and severe pulmonary disease such as COPD
Peripheral edema, JVD, and fatigue may be seen in LV or RV failure
fact_text: Common causes of LV failure include CAD, hypertension, and alcoholic cardiomyopathy; RV failure commonly results from advanced LV failure or severe pulmonary disease; peripheral edema, JVD, and fatigue may be present in either LV or RV failure.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (hfref) and preserved ejection fraction (hfpef)
condition_aliases: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (hfref) and preserved ejection fraction (hfpef)
trigger_evidence: mortality in patients with HFrEF and HFpEF is similar
Patients with ejection fraction of 41–49% are classified as HFpEF borderline
fact_text: Mortality is similar in patients with HFrEF and HFpEF; patients with EF 41–49% are classified as HFpEF borderline; right-sided HF may involve LV, RV, or both; pulmonary edema is common in left-sided HF but not isolated right-sided HF.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: History and classic signs/symptoms support HF diagnosis; absence of signs does not exclude HF; S3 gallop and JVD are highly specific.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: NYHA functional classification grades heart failure severity from Class I (asymptomatic) to Class IV (symptoms at rest).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Heart failure diagnosis is supported by history, exam, and echocardiogram; consider mitral/aortic valve disease and atrial fibrillation as common alternatives; myocardial ischemia must not be missed.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Heart failure complications include stroke, thromboembolism, pulmonary edema, mitral regurgitation, and increased mortality.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: BNP cutoff <50 pg/mL has 97% sensitivity and 44% specificity; <100 pg/mL has 93% sensitivity and 66% specificity for diagnosing heart failure in patients with dyspnea.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: BNP is a sensitive marker for heart failure, elevated in both HFrEF and HFpEF, but can also be elevated in pulmonary embolism.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Jugular venous distention has high sensitivity (39%) and specificity (92%) with LR+ 5.1 for diagnosing heart failure in patients with dyspnea.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Pleural effusions occur in 26% of patients with heart failure and are usually small, transudative, and accompanied by other radiographic signs of heart failure.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Pulmonary venous congestion on chest radiograph has 54% sensitivity and 96% specificity with LR+ 12.0 for diagnosing heart failure in patients with dyspnea.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: HF diagnosis is more difficult in COPD patients; BNP sensitivity is lower; pleural fluid, pulmonary revascularization, and edema are uncommon in COPD without HF.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: POCUS evaluation of inferior vena cava
fact_text: POCUS measurement of IVC diameter and collapsibility can estimate left ventricular filling pressures and help guide volume status assessment in HF.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Routine labs: CBC, urinalysis, BUN, creatinine, electrolytes, lipid panel, glycohemoglobin, liver biochemical tests
fact_text: Two-dimensional echocardiogram is the test of choice to diagnose HF and evaluate systolic and regional function; POCUS can aid in likelihood assessment; cardiac MR is an alternative for detailed evaluation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: POCUS for inferior vena cava evaluation
recommended_advice: Sodium restriction
Diuretics administration
Volume status clinical assessment
Aggressive diuresis if indicated
fact_text: Sodium restriction and diuretics are recommended for all HF patients; volume status assessment is critical and POCUS can aid in evaluating inferior vena cava to guide therapy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Use ACE inhibitors in patients with HFrEF or prior MI to reduce mortality
Use ARBs if ACE inhibitors are not tolerated
fact_text: ACE inhibitors reduce mortality in HFrEF but should be avoided in patients with severe renal impairment or hyperkalemia; ARBs are alternatives.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Use beta-blockers with proven efficacy (carvedilol, sustained-release metoprolol, bisoprolol) to reduce morbidity and mortality
Avoid short-acting beta-blockers in HF
fact_text: Beta-blockers reduce morbidity and mortality in HFrEF but should be used cautiously in reactive airway disease and started at low doses when stable.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Use ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, aldosterone antagonists, and hydralazine combined with nitrates to reduce morbidity and mortality
ACE inhibitors reduce mortality in all patients with HFrEF and may decrease rates of MI
ARBs are indicated in patients intolerant of ACE inhibitors
Beta-blockers reduce morbidity and mortality in all stages of HF, including severe HF (EF < 25%)
Aldosterone antagonists reduce mortality in patients with class II-IV HF and EF > 35%
Angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) may decrease mortality and HF hospitalization compared to ACE inhibitors
Ivabradine may be useful in patients with heart rate > 70 bpm on maximal beta-blocker therapy
Statins should be used in patients with HFrEF and CAD
Hydralazine and nitrates may be useful in patients unable to tolerate ACE inhibitors/ARBs
Digoxin reduces hospitalizations but not mortality in HFrEF
Cardiac resynchronization therapy improves ejection fraction, quality of life, and reduces hospitalizations and mortality in select patients
Implantable cardiac defibrillator reduces sudden death in patients with HF
fact_text: Multiple pharmacologic and device therapies reduce morbidity and mortality in HFrEF, including ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, aldosterone antagonists, ARNI, ivabradine, statins, hydralazine/nitrates, digoxin, cardiac resynchronization therapy, and implantable defibrillators.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Implant wires in atria and ventricles to improve coordinated depolarization
Improves ejection fraction, quality of life, and reduces hospitalizations and mortality
fact_text: CRT improves cardiac function and outcomes in select patients with HFrEF and prolonged QRS duration.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Complications of acute and chronic mitral regurgitation include dyspnea, pulmonary edema, atrial fibrillation, and sudden death.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Chronic mitral regurgitation may present with a holosystolic murmur at the apex, dyspnea, edema, orthopnea, fatigue, or be discovered during atrial fibrillation evaluation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: 5% annual mortality with severe mitral regurgitation
fact_text: Chronic mitral regurgitation progresses slowly, with an annual mortality of 5% in severe cases over about 16 years.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Mitral regurgitation pathophysiology includes compensated phase with LA and LV dilation and decompensated phase with LV systolic dysfunction and possible atrial fibrillation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: blowing holosystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla
fact_text: Physical exam shows a blowing holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, grade 3 or louder murmur, and an S3 gallop in moderate to severe mitral regurgitation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Mitral regurgitation etiologies include primary causes (mitral valve prolapse, rheumatic heart disease, endocarditis) and secondary causes (LV dilation or ischemic mitral regurgitation).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Careful examiner detects early diastolic murmur
fact_text: Patients with chronic aortic regurgitation may present with progressive dyspnea or pounding heart; early diastolic murmur is a key diagnostic clue.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Etiologies of chronic aortic regurgitation include valvular abnormalities (rheumatic carditis, endocarditis, collagen vascular disease, calcific degeneration, medications) and aortic root dilation (hypertension, aneurysm, Marfan, dissection, syphilitic aortitis), plus bicuspid aortic valve disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Optimize HF regimen in secondary mitral regurgitation
Treat hypertension with ACE inhibitors, diuretics, or beta-blockers in mitral regurgitation with hypertension
Treat underlying ischemia
Endocarditis prophylaxis for patients with prosthetic devices or history of endocarditis
fact_text: Serial echocardiography is essential to detect LV dysfunction in mitral regurgitation; valve repair is preferred over replacement when feasible; surgery recommended for severe cases per ACCF/AHA guidelines.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Lifelong anticoagulation with VKA and aspirin for mechanical valves
Short-term VKA followed by aspirin for prosthetic valves
fact_text: Mechanical mitral valve replacement requires lifelong VKA anticoagulation plus aspirin; prosthetic valves require VKA for 3-6 months then aspirin.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: a diastolic murmur is highly specific (98%)
a diastolic murmur is always abnormal and warrants evaluation with echocardiography
recommended_advice: evaluate diastolic murmur with echocardiography
fact_text: A diastolic murmur is highly specific and always abnormal, warranting echocardiographic evaluation for aortic regurgitation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: aortic regurgitant streams may impact mitral valve leaflets causing functional mitral stenosis and a late diastolic murmur over the apex
fact_text: Austin Flint murmur is a late diastolic murmur caused by aortic regurgitant streams impacting mitral valve leaflets, mimicking mitral stenosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: sensitivity for mild to moderate aortic regurgitation is 0-14% among noncardiologist attending physicians
sensitivity for moderate to severe aortic regurgitation is 0-64% among students and residents
sensitivity for moderate to severe aortic regurgitation is 80-95% among experienced cardiologists
fact_text: Sensitivity of auscultation for aortic regurgitation varies widely by severity and examiner experience.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: other causes of wide pulse pressure (anemia, fever, pregnancy, etc)
trigger_evidence: wide pulse pressure causes many classic physical findings
wide pulse pressures defined as systolic BP - diastolic BP > 50% of systolic BP are not specific for aortic regurgitation
fact_text: Wide pulse pressure is a classic but nonspecific finding in aortic regurgitation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: mortality in symptomatic patients without surgery is 10-20% per year
mortality in asymptomatic patients with LV dysfunction is uncertain but worse if symptoms or significant LV dysfunction present
fact_text: Mortality is high in symptomatic aortic regurgitation patients without surgery; prognosis is worse with symptoms or significant LV dysfunction.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: a systolic murmur suggesting aortic stenosis may be heard
increased cardiac output from increased forward flow may exceed capacity of aortic valve to accommodate flow, causing a high-flow systolic murmur
fact_text: A systolic murmur in aortic regurgitation may suggest coexisting aortic stenosis due to increased forward flow.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: serial echocardiography is important to detect LV dysfunction which may occur without symptoms
should be performed regularly with timing based on severity and symptom changes
recommended_advice: perform serial echocardiography regularly based on severity and symptoms
fact_text: Serial echocardiography is important to monitor LV dysfunction in aortic regurgitation and should be done regularly.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: patients with bicuspid valves and aortic root not adequately visualized with transthoracic echocardiography should undergo additional imaging to evaluate aortic root
recommended_advice: perform additional imaging if transthoracic echo inadequate
fact_text: Additional imaging is required to evaluate the aortic root in bicuspid valve patients if transthoracic echocardiography is inadequate.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: echocardiography is the test of choice
should be performed in patients with diastolic murmur and those with dilated aortic root
recommended_advice: perform echocardiography in diastolic murmur or dilated aortic root
fact_text: Echocardiography is the diagnostic test of choice for aortic regurgitation and should be performed in patients with diastolic murmur or dilated aortic root.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: exercise testing can help assess LV function during stress
fact_text: Exercise testing is useful to assess LV function during stress in aortic regurgitation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: valve replacement should be performed before irreversible LV dysfunction and heart failure develop
recommended_advice: perform valve replacement before irreversible LV dysfunction develops
fact_text: Valve replacement is indicated before irreversible LV dysfunction develops in aortic regurgitation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: valve replacement is indicated in symptomatic patients or those with evidence of LV dysfunction
LV end-diastolic diameter > 65 mm or LV end-systolic diameter > 50 mm are criteria for surgery
recommended_advice: valve replacement if symptomatic or LV dimensions exceed thresholds
fact_text: Valve replacement is indicated in symptomatic aortic regurgitation or if LV dimensions exceed defined thresholds.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: ECG with irregular ventricular rate and lack of organized atrial activity
recommended_tests: extended cardiac monitoring (Holter, loop recorder, event monitor)
fact_text: Atrial fibrillation is recognized by irregularly irregular pulse and ECG showing irregular ventricular rate without organized atrial activity; extended cardiac monitoring can detect episodic AF.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Common etiologies of atrial fibrillation include hypertension, heart failure, valvular heart disease, acute coronary syndrome, alcoholic heart disease, pulmonary disease, thyrotoxicosis, and pulmonary embolism.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: anticoagulation to reduce stroke risk
fact_text: Atrial fibrillation causes about one-sixth of all strokes, with stroke risk increased by factors including valvular heart disease, prior stroke, increasing age, hypertension, diabetes, heart failure, and female sex.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: baseline echocardiogram to assess left ventricular function and stroke risk
fact_text: Baseline echocardiogram is recommended to assess left ventricular function and stroke risk in atrial fibrillation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: CT scan has higher sensitivity (94%) but lower specificity (73%) than chest radiograph (60% sensitivity, 94% specificity) for lung cancer screening.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Chest radiograph: 6 randomized trials of chest radiography, with or without sputum cytology, failed to demonstrate a decrease in lung cancer mortality
CT scan: randomized trial showed lung cancer-specific mortality was significantly reduced in the low-dose CT group
fact_text: Chest radiograph screening does not reduce lung cancer mortality, but low-dose CT screening significantly reduces lung cancer-specific mortality.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in both men and women
About 150,000 deaths from lung cancer in 2018
Cigarette smoking responsible for about 85% of lung cancers
recommended_advice: Offer annual low-dose CT screening to adults 55-80 with 30 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit within past 15 years
Discontinue screening if no smoking for 15 years or health problem limits life expectancy or ability to have curative surgery
fact_text: Annual low-dose CT screening is recommended for adults 55-80 with a 30 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years; discontinue if no smoking for 15 years or health limits curative surgery.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) randomized over 53,000 persons aged 55-74 with ≥30 pack-year smoking history
Exclusions: previous lung cancer, other cancer within 5 years, recent chest CT, recent respiratory infection, abnormal chest film
recommended_tests: Annual low-dose CT scan for 3 years
recommended_advice: Screen eligible high-risk patients annually with low-dose CT for 3 years
fact_text: NLST trial supports annual low-dose CT screening for 3 years in high-risk patients aged 55-74 with ≥30 pack-year smoking history, excluding those with recent cancer or chest CT.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: ECG showing irregularly spaced QRS complexes and fibrillatory p waves
fact_text: ECG of atrial fibrillation demonstrates irregularly spaced QRS complexes and fibrillatory p waves.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: cardioversion should be performed immediately in unstable patients
in stable patients, rhythm control or rate control are options
recommended_advice: Cardioversion in unstable patients
Rhythm control attempts to restore and maintain normal sinus rhythm
Rate control allows persistent atrial fibrillation
Rate control recommended in most patients, especially with minimal symptoms
Resting heart rate <110 bpm recommended
Use beta-blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers for rate control
Digoxin may be appropriate in some patients
Avoid beta-blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers in decompensated HF

lymphatic obstruction (primary idiopathic, congenital, secondary neoplasm, surgery, radiation, infections)
localized edema (burns, angioedema, trauma, cellulitis, complex regional pain syndrome type 1)
fact_text: Edema differential diagnosis includes venous obstruction, venous insufficiency, lymphatic obstruction, cellulitis/erysipelas, Baker cyst, and localized causes such as burns and trauma.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Edema results from altered capillary hydrostatic and oncotic pressures, increased capillary permeability, venous obstruction, and lymphatic obstruction.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Treat upper extremity DVT
Treat DVT
Consider alternative diagnoses
Review medication list
Prescribe compression stockings
Stop medication causing edema if possible
Order echocardiogram if edema persists
fact_text: Edema evaluation depends on distribution; unilateral arm or leg edema requires duplex ultrasound and DVT workup; bilateral leg edema requires evaluation for systemic causes and medication review.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis causes architectural distortion of hepatic vasculature and endothelial dysfunction leading to portal hypertension and hepatocyte dysfunction.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: genetic metabolic diseases (wilson disease, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, glycogen storage diseases, porphyria)
fact_text: Common causes of cirrhosis include alcohol, chronic hepatitis B or C, NAFLD, and hemochromatosis; less common causes include drugs, autoimmune hepatitis, genetic diseases, infections, cardiac causes, and biliary cirrhosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In patients with bilateral leg edema, cirrhosis is a leading hypothesis and should be evaluated with liver function tests and imaging.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Caput medusae has a high LR+ (9.5) for cirrhosis; gynecomastia and ascites also have moderate LR+ values (7 and 6.6 respectively) for diagnosis of cirrhosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Low platelet count (<100 x10^3/mcL) and low albumin (<3.5 g/dL) with prolonged INR increase likelihood of cirrhosis; Bonacini score >7 increases likelihood (LR+ 9.4).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Median survival after diagnosis of compensated cirrhosis is 10-13 years; 5-year mortality approaches 85% after decompensation if transplantation is not performed.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Liver biopsy is gold standard but has sampling error and risk; noninvasive tests like serologic fibrogenesis markers and liver elastography are increasingly used with good sensitivity and specificity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Ascites presents as inability to fasten pants, increased abdominal girth, dyspnea, and edema in cirrhosis patients

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: serum creatinine >1.5 mg/dL after diuretic withdrawal and volume expansion
recommended_advice: Liver transplantation is definitive treatment
Limited data on TIPS and vasopressin derivatives for type 1 HRS
fact_text: HRS diagnosis requires cirrhosis with ascites, elevated creatinine, no shock, no nephrotoxic drugs, and no parenchymal kidney disease; liver transplant is definitive treatment

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid analysis and cultures
fact_text: SBP occurs in 10-30% hospitalized cirrhotics; diagnosis requires paracentesis with fluid analysis and cultures; consider secondary peritonitis if multiple organisms cultured

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: VCTE cutoff values for advanced fibrosis: Hepatitis C >9.5 kPa, Hepatitis B >8.1 kPa, NAFLD >9.9 kPa

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: cirrhosis with portal hypertension and clinical decompensation
condition_aliases: cirrhosis with portal hypertension and clinical decompensation
fact_text: Cirrhosis causes portal hypertension and splanchnic vasodilatation leading to reduced effective arterial blood volume and hypotension, which triggers clinical decompensation with fluid sequestration, ascites, hyponatremia, and complications including spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatorenal syndrome, organ failure, and death.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Start empiric antibiotics immediately
Use IV cefotaxime as first-line antibiotic
Consider oral ofloxacin in select outpatients
Administer IV albumin in patients with high bilirubin, BUN, or creatinine
fact_text: Empiric antibiotic treatment for SBP should start before culture results; IV cefotaxime is preferred, oral ofloxacin can be used in select outpatients, and IV albumin reduces mortality in patients with high bilirubin, BUN, or creatinine.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Patient with cirrhosis and mental status changes
fact_text: Hepatic encephalopathy diagnosis requires exclusion of other neurologic/metabolic causes; overt form occurs in 30-45% of cirrhosis patients.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Severe hepatic encephalopathy requiring hospitalization has a 1-year survival rate under 50% and can be precipitated by multiple insults.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and other ascitic fluid conditions
condition_aliases: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and other ascitic fluid conditions
fact_text: Ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear count and culture results help differentiate types of bacterial peritonitis and ascitic fluid infections.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: ascites due to infection or malignancy
fact_text: Serum-ascites albumin gradient ≥ 1.1 g/dL indicates ascites due to portal hypertension; <1.1 g/dL suggests other causes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Large volume paracentesis with volume expansion
fact_text: Large volume paracentesis with volume expansion is done in patients unresponsive to diuretics.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Sodium restriction <2 g/day
Use spironolactone as first-line diuretic
Add loop diuretics if needed
Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs
fact_text: Treat ascites with sodium restriction and spironolactone; add loop diuretics if needed; avoid aspirin, NSAIDs, and certain diuretics.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: TIPS procedure
fact_text: TIPS improves portal hypertension and ascites but has risks including encephalopathy; used as bridge to transplant.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: About 12,900 new cases of cervical cancer and 4100 cervical cancer–related deaths estimated in the United States in 2015
Rates are higher in countries without cytologic screening
Women with preinvasive lesions have a 5-year survival of nearly 100%, with 13% survival for early-stage invasive cancer
93–100% of squamous cell cervical cancers contain DNA from high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) strains
recommended_tests: HPV testing (DNA and RNA-DNA hybrids detection)
recommended_advice: Screen women with no history of CIN2 or more severe lesion, no HIV, and no in utero exposure to DES according to current guidelines
Use cervical cancer screening to reduce mortality by 20–60%
fact_text: Cervical cancer screening with Pap smear and HPV testing reduces mortality; high-risk HPV strains are present in most squamous cell cervical cancers.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: West Haven Criteria grades hepatic encephalopathy from 0 (normal) to 4 (coma) based on consciousness, symptoms, neurologic signs, and EEG abnormalities.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Identify and treat precipitating causes
Treat patients with overt hepatic encephalopathy indefinitely
Focus treatment on reducing intestinal ammonia
Use lactulose to reduce ammonia production and absorption
Use antibiotics to reduce urease-producing bacteria
Consider liver transplantation in patients with hepatic encephalopathy
fact_text: Diagnosis of hepatic encephalopathy requires clinical correlation and exclusion of other causes; treatment focuses on reducing ammonia and precipitating factors.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In liver disease, thrombocytopenia and leukopenia are mainly due to splenic sequestration; anemia is rare and multifactorial.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Hypersplenism is a clinical syndrome in liver disease characterized by splenomegaly and cytopenias due to sequestration and decreased production.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Consider splenectomy or partial splenic embolization for severe thrombocytopenia
Avoid TIPS for thrombocytopenia correction
fact_text: Hypersplenism treatment is usually unnecessary; splenectomy or embolization is reserved for severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Thromboembolic complications due to increased procoagulatory factors and fibrinogen, altered fibrinolytic system, urinary loss of antithrombin III, and increased platelet activity
Relative risk of DVT is 1.7 with an annual incidence of 1.5%; annual incidence of renal vein thrombosis is 0.5%
Relative risk of pulmonary embolism is 1.4 but is 6.8 for patients aged 18–39 years
Risk factors for venous thromboembolism include serum albumin <2.0–2.5 mg/dL, protein excretion >8 g/24 h, and being within 6 months of diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome
recommended_advice: Consider prophylactic anticoagulation in high-risk patients
fact_text: Nephrotic syndrome increases thromboembolism risk due to coagulation abnormalities; risk factors include low serum albumin, high proteinuria, and recent diagnosis; prophylactic anticoagulation may be considered in high-risk patients.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: primary glomerular diseases (including membranous nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, minimal change disease, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, iga nephropathy)
secondary glomerular disease (diabetes, systemic lupus erythematosus, amyloidosis, infections including hiv, hepatitis b, hepatitis c, syphilis, malaria)
malignancies (lung, breast, prostate, colon cancer, hodgkin lymphoma)
drug-induced nephrotic syndrome (nsaids, captopril, tamoxifen, lithium, heroin)
trigger_evidence: Patients with nephrotic syndrome classically have edema (often periorbital), hypertension, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and at least 3.5 g/24 hour of proteinuria.
recommended_tests: Initial laboratory tests: WBC, Hb, HCT, MCV, platelet, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose, albumin, alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin, ALT, AST, PT/PTT, urinalysis, 2+ protein with no cells or casts
Urinary protein excretion >3.5 g/24 hours or spot albumin/creatinine ratio >3000–3500 mcg/mg

Laboratory evaluation including CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, PT/INR, PTT, fasting glucose and HbA1c, antinuclear antibody, HIV, hepatitis B and C serology, serum and urine protein electrophoresis
Renal ultrasound if glomerular filtration rate is reduced
fact_text: Nephrotic syndrome diagnosis requires proteinuria >3.5 g/24h plus hypoalbuminemia and edema; causes include primary glomerular diseases, secondary diseases like diabetes and infections, malignancies, and certain drugs; diagnosis involves lab tests, serologies, and often renal biopsy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: venous insufficiency, pulmonary hypertension, diastolic dysfunction, renal and liver disease
condition_aliases: venous insufficiency, pulmonary hypertension, diastolic dysfunction, renal and liver disease
trigger_evidence: no clinical clues of advanced liver or kidney disease
dependent edema worsened by standing and improves with leg elevation
recommended_tests: right heart catheterization (if pulmonary hypertension suspected)
fact_text: Bilateral edema with long-standing hypertension and dependent edema suggests diastolic dysfunction, venous insufficiency, or pulmonary hypertension; echocardiogram and duplex ultrasound are key diagnostic tests.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Initial symptoms are nonspecific and related to right ventricular dysfunction

Characteristic physical exam findings include accentuated pulmonary component of S2, sustained left lower parasternal movement, increased jugular a and v waves, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, ascites, elevated jugular venous pressure, and edema
fact_text: Symptoms of PH include dyspnea, fatigue, syncope, and dry cough; exam findings include loud P2, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, elevated jugular venous pressure, and edema.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: idiopathic, heritable, or drug related pah
trigger_evidence: Left heart disease is the etiology in about 65% of cases
COPD is the cause in 32-39% of patients with interstitial lung disease
Chronic thromboembolic disease is the etiology in 0.5-2% of patients
fact_text: Most pulmonary hypertension cases are due to left heart disease (65%), with smaller proportions due to idiopathic/heritable PAH, COPD, and chronic thromboembolic disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: group 1: pulmonary arterial hypertension - idiopathic, heritable, drug/toxin induced, connective tissue disease, hiv, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease, schistosomiasis
group 2: pulmonary venous hypertension due to left heart disease - heart failure with reduced or preserved ejection fraction, valvular disease

group 3: ph due to lung diseases and/or hypoxia - chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, interstitial lung disease, sleep disordered breathing, alveolar hypoventilation, chronic exposure to high altitude
group 4: ph due to chronic thromboembolic disease - chronic thromboembolic disease
group 5: ph with unclear multifactorial mechanisms - myeloproliferative disorders, chronic hemolytic anemia, sarcoidosis, glycogen storage diseases, fibrosing mediastinitis
fact_text: Pulmonary hypertension is classified into 5 groups based on etiology including pulmonary arterial hypertension, left heart disease, lung diseases/hypoxia, chronic thromboembolic disease, and unclear multifactorial mechanisms.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: PH is defined as mean PAP ≥ 25 mm Hg by right heart catheterization
fact_text: Pulmonary hypertension is defined as mean pulmonary artery pressure ≥ 25 mm Hg by right heart catheterization.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: ECG findings: right axis deviation, right ventricular hypertrophy, P-pulmonale pattern; sensitivity 55%, specificity 70%
Chest film findings: enlargement of pulmonary arteries and right ventricular enlargement; sensitivity 46%, specificity 63%
Transthoracic echocardiogram is the best first diagnostic test
fact_text: Transthoracic echocardiogram is the best initial diagnostic test for PH; ECG and chest film have limited sensitivity and specificity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Class 1: telangiectasias or reticular veins (nonpalpable subdermal veins up to 4 mm in diameter)
Class 2: varicose veins (palpable, subcutaneous veins > 4 mm in diameter)
fact_text: Skin changes in venous disease are classified as Class 1 (telangiectasias or reticular veins ≤4 mm) and Class 2 (palpable varicose veins >4 mm).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Chronic venous disease is due to venous hypertension caused by reflux through incompetent valves, venous outflow obstruction, or lack of calf muscle pumping due to obesity or immobility
Varicose veins are found in 14–46% of women and 11–29% of men
Prevalence of skin changes is 4–12%; prevalence of skin ulcers is 1–2%
Risk factors include female sex, advancing age, obesity, history of phlebitis or venous thrombosis, serious leg trauma, pregnancy, prolonged standing, and greater height
Postthrombotic syndrome occurs in 33% of patients within 5 years after DVT; long-term use of compression stockings may reduce risk
recommended_advice: Long-term use of compression stockings may reduce risk of postthrombotic syndrome
fact_text: Chronic venous disease results from venous hypertension due to valve reflux or obstruction, with varicose veins common and risk factors including female sex, age, obesity, and history of thrombosis; compression stockings may reduce post-DVT syndrome risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Venous insufficiency can be asymptomatic or manifest just by small visible, but nonpalpable veins
In more severe cases, the patient has large varicose veins and skin changes ranging from edema to fibrosing panniculitis to ulceration
Symptoms include leg fullness or heaviness, aching leg pain, and nocturnal leg cramps
Symptoms are often worse at the end of the day and in heat, and are sometimes relieved by elevation
fact_text: Venous insufficiency can present with visible varicose veins, leg heaviness, aching, cramps, and skin changes from edema to ulceration, often worse at day's end and relieved by elevation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Figure 17-4. Anatomy of the superficial venous system
The superficial saphenous veins join the deep system at the knee (popliteal vein) and the groin (femoral vein)
Perforating veins directly connect the saphenous veins and the deep veins at various points along their parallel courses
Valves within the veins prevent reflux back toward the feet
fact_text: The superficial saphenous veins connect to the deep venous system at the knee and groin, with perforating veins linking them and valves preventing reflux.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: venous insufficiency confirmed by duplex ultrasonography
recommended_advice: Compression stockings are the most important treatment modality
Compression stockings should not be used in patients with peripheral arterial disease or with invasive infection at ulcer site
Alternative compression methods include elastic wraps and intermittent pneumatic compression pumps
Ulcers should be covered with a dressing before applying compression device
fact_text: Compression stockings are the primary treatment for venous insufficiency-related edema and ulcers, with pressure levels tailored to disease severity; duplex ultrasonography is the best noninvasive diagnostic test.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Duplex ultrasonography is the best noninvasive test for diagnosing venous insufficiency and valvular incompetence, with high sensitivity and specificity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Sclerotherapy
Endovenous radiofrequency ablation and laser
Iliac vein stenting
Vein stripping and ligation
fact_text: Interventional therapies for venous insufficiency include sclerotherapy, endovenous ablation, iliac vein stenting, and vein stripping with ligation to reduce ulcer recurrence.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Use occlusive dressing
Leg elevation and compression
Aspirin 325 mg daily may accelerate healing
Pentoxifylline may accelerate healing
Topical antibiotics have no role
Systemic antibiotics only if cellulitis or invasive infection present
fact_text: Venous insufficiency ulcers are treated with occlusive dressing, leg elevation, compression, and possibly aspirin or pentoxifylline; systemic antibiotics only if cellulitis or invasive infection is present.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Cellulitis presents with nonpalpable confluent erythema with indistinct margins, generalized swelling, warmth, and tenderness; systemic symptoms are unusual and suggest more serious infection.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In cellulitis, an entry site is identified in 77% of cases, commonly tinea pedis or other skin breaks like ulcers, trauma, eczema, or abscess.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Risk factors for cellulitis include age, edema, venous insufficiency, obesity, prior cellulitis, injection drug use, homelessness, and breast cancer treatment.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Cellulitis involves deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue; erysipelas is a superficial cellulitis with prominent lymphatic involvement.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Possible venous scarring secondary to radiation
recommended_tests: Clinical exam for cellulitis or erysipelas
CT, MRA, Venography for further DVT evaluation
fact_text: In a patient with unilateral limb edema and risk factors, cellulitis or erysipelas is a leading hypothesis; DVT must also be considered and ruled out with appropriate imaging.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Microbiology of cellulitis varies by location and exposure; common organisms include Staphylococcus aureus, group A streptococcus, and others depending on site and risk factors.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Blood cultures are positive in less than 5% of patients
IDSA guidelines recommend against routine blood cultures, skin surface swab cultures, or biopsy cultures
fact_text: Blood cultures are positive in <5% of cellulitis/erysipelas cases; routine blood, skin swab, or biopsy cultures are not recommended by IDSA guidelines.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Recent hospitalization or long-term care facility residence
Recurrent needle sticks (injection drug use, hemodialysis, insulin use)
fact_text: Risk factors for CA-MRSA cellulitis include recent antibiotics, hospitalization, needle use, homelessness, contact sports, and prior CA-MRSA infection.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Lymphedema and identified portal of entry (primarily tinea pedis) are strongest risk factors
Sudden onset of fever (85% of patients), erythema, edema, and pain
Palpable plaque of erythema extending 2-10 cm/day
recommended_advice: Always treat tinea pedis in patients with cellulitis, erysipelas, or risk factors for these infections
fact_text: Erysipelas presents with sudden fever, erythema with sharply demarcated border, and lymphedema or tinea pedis are key risk factors; treat tinea pedis to prevent infection.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Rapid increase in size of infected area
recommended_advice: Consider necrotizing fasciitis in patients with above signs
fact_text: Necrotizing fasciitis should be suspected with rapid lesion growth, violaceous bullae, severe pain, woody induration, and systemic toxicity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In the D-zone test, inducible clindamycin resistance is indicated by a D-shaped area of no growth next to the erythromycin disk

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Drain abscess
fact_text: If a skin abscess is associated with cellulitis, it should be drained and the fluid cultured

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Clindamycin sensitive/erythromycin resistant isolates should undergo the D-zone test to look for inducible clindamycin resistance

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Cellulitis or erysipelas without associated abscess
fact_text: Cultures are rarely helpful in cellulitis or erysipelas without an associated abscess

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Initial laboratory tests for cellulitis include CBC with differential, blood glucose, and serum creatinine

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: CT or MRI should be done if necrotizing fasciitis is suspected; MRI is more sensitive, CT more specific

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Treatment for both CA-MRSA and beta-hemolytic streptococci needed
recommended_advice: Use clindamycin, TMP-SMX, or doxycycline plus a beta-lactam or linezolid
fact_text: To treat both CA-MRSA and beta-hemolytic streptococci, use clindamycin, TMP-SMX, or doxycycline plus a beta-lactam or linezolid

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Treat with penicillin G or amoxicillin
Other drugs studied include macrolides and fluoroquinolones
fact_text: Penicillin G or amoxicillin is effective in >80% of patients with erysipelas; macrolides and fluoroquinolones are alternative options

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Empiric treatment for beta-hemolytic streptococci with a beta-lactam (cephalexin, amoxicillin, or similar drugs) for 5 days
fact_text: Outpatients with nonpurulent cellulitis should receive empiric beta-lactam treatment for 5 days; treat for CA-MRSA if no response

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Purulent cellulitis associated with purulent drainage or exudate but no drainable abscess
recommended_advice: Empiric treatment for CA-MRSA with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) or doxycycline for 5 days
fact_text: Outpatients with purulent cellulitis should receive empiric treatment for CA-MRSA with TMP-SMX or doxycycline for 5 days; extend treatment if no improvement at 5 days

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: rapidly progressive infection in ill, immunocompromised, or nonadherent patients
condition_aliases: rapidly progressive infection in ill, immunocompromised, or nonadherent patients
recommended_advice: Admit for IV antibiotics including vancomycin, clindamycin, linezolid, or daptomycin
Obtain infectious disease and surgical consultations
fact_text: Patients with rapidly progressive infection who are ill, immunocompromised, or nonadherent should be admitted for IV antibiotics and infectious disease and surgical consultations

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: uncomplicated, slowly progressive infection in a well-appearing patient
condition_aliases: uncomplicated, slowly progressive infection in a well-appearing patient
recommended_advice: Can be treated with oral antibiotics
fact_text: Uncomplicated, slowly progressive cellulitis in a well-appearing patient can be treated with oral antibiotics if no GI upset, limb elevation possible, and serial exams feasible

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Edema present in ~80% of patients in some series
Patients may note numbness, heaviness, paresthesias, pruritus, coldness
fact_text: Pain and edema are common clinical features of UEDVT; other symptoms include numbness, heaviness, paresthesias, pruritus, coldness, and sometimes dilated cutaneous veins.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: oral contraceptives plus factor v leiden or prothrombin g20210a mutation
fact_text: Risk factors for upper extremity deep venous thrombosis include cancer plus central venous catheter (adjusted odds ratio 43.6), inherited coagulation disorder with CVC (~30), cancer alone (18.1), oral contraceptives plus factor V Leiden or prothrombin mutation (13.6), upper extremity surgery (13.1), metastatic cancer (11.5), indwelling CVC (9.7), and upper extremity plaster cast (7.0).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Pulmonary embolism reported in up to 36% of cases
fact_text: UEDVT can cause pulmonary embolism (up to 36%), recurrent thrombosis (2-13%), and postthrombotic syndrome (7-46%).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Duplex ultrasonography is most commonly used noninvasive test
Duplex ultrasound disadvantages: blind spot from clavicle, difficulty interpreting thoracic cavity veins
Magnetic resonance and CT venography sometimes done; sensitivity and specificity unknown
American College of Chest Physicians Guidelines recommend initial duplex ultrasound, follow-up testing with D-dimer or venography if high suspicion, no further testing if negative follow-up
fact_text: Diagnosis of UEDVT is primarily by duplex ultrasonography; venography is gold standard. Follow-up with D-dimer or venography is recommended if ultrasound is normal but suspicion remains high.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Anticoagulation with heparin or heparin analogs followed by at least 3 months of warfarin
Patients with cancer or chronic indwelling central venous catheters should receive anticoagulation indefinitely
Thrombolysis with or without stent placement sometimes done, especially in patients with permanent indwelling catheters
Limited evidence for use of direct oral anticoagulants in UEDVT
recommended_advice: Anticoagulation with heparin followed by warfarin for at least 3 months
Indefinite anticoagulation for cancer or chronic catheter patients
Consider thrombolysis with or without stent in select patients
fact_text: Treat UEDVT with anticoagulation (heparin then warfarin for ≥3 months); indefinite anticoagulation for cancer or chronic catheter patients; thrombolysis sometimes used.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Age is a strong risk factor
Other risk factors include >16 months breastfeeding, 5 or more pregnancies, estrogen exposure, postmenopausal BMI < 23 kg/m2, oophorectomy before age 35
fact_text: Age and reproductive factors such as breastfeeding duration, parity, estrogen exposure, and early oophorectomy influence breast cancer risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Breast density is a risk factor for breast cancer
Density categories: A (fatty), B (scattered fibroglandular), C (heterogeneously dense), D (extremely dense)
Relative risk of breast cancer with Category A density is 2.4–4.5 times lower than with Category D
fact_text: Breast density is a risk factor for breast cancer, with higher density categories associated with increased risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Women with BRCA1/BRCA2 mutation or strong family history
Family members with breast, ovarian, or pancreatic cancer diagnosed at young age
Ashkenazi Jewish descent with breast, ovarian, or pancreatic cancer
recommended_advice: Referral for genetic counseling if high-risk features present
fact_text: Referral for genetic counseling is recommended for patients with BRCA mutations or strong family history of breast, ovarian, or pancreatic cancer.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Women aged 21–29 with cytology (Pap smear) every 3 years
Women aged 30–65 can be screened every 3 years with cytology alone or every 5 years with HPV testing alone
Women older than 65 with adequate recent screening are not otherwise at high risk
recommended_advice: Screening for cervical cancer as per age guidelines
fact_text: USPSTF recommends cervical cancer screening with cytology every 3 years for women 21–29 and cytology every 3 years or HPV testing every 5 years for women 30–65; no screening recommended for women older than 65 with adequate recent screening.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Mammograms are 95% digital and more sensitive in older women and women with low breast density
Sensitivity varies by age and breast density category
fact_text: Mammography sensitivity ranges from 63% to 95% depending on age and breast density, with digital mammograms more sensitive in older women and those with low breast density.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: psychiatric disorders (depression, anxiety, somatization disorder, substance abuse)

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Generalized anxiety disorder diagnosis requires excessive anxiety most days for 6+ months plus at least 3 symptoms: easy fatigability, restlessness, concentration trouble, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Medications that cause drowsiness include tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, imipramine, nortriptyline), other antidepressants (mirtazapine, trazodone, paroxetine), opioids, benzodiazepines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, neuropathic pain agents (gabapentin, pregabalin), alcohol, antihistamines (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, meclizine), and atypical antipsychotics.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Medications that cause insomnia include antidepressants (bupropion, venlafaxine, fluoxetine, sertraline), anticholinergics (ipratropium), CNS stimulants (methylphenidate, modafinil), hormones (oral contraceptives, thyroid hormone, corticosteroids, prostaglandins), sympathomimetic amines (albuterol, theophylline, phenylpropanolamine, pseudoephedrine), antineoplastics (leuprolide, goserelin, pentostatin, interferon alfa), and miscellaneous agents (phenytoin, nicotine, levodopa, quinidine, caffeine, alcohol).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Fatigue requires detailed psychosocial and sleep history; common medical causes to rule out include anemia, hypothyroidism, and diabetes mellitus; basic lab tests include blood count, chemistry panel, and TSH.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Fatigue with anorexia, nausea, edema, and hypertension suggests advanced kidney disease; BUN and creatinine tests are recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Fatigue with anorexia, nausea, edema, jaundice, ascites, and relevant history suggests advanced liver disease; liver function tests are recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Fatigue with dyspnea, symptoms of blood loss, and pale conjunctiva suggest anemia; CBC is recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Fatigue with risk factors and symptoms like polyuria and polydipsia suggests diabetes mellitus; fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c tests are recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: OSA diagnosis is based on AHI or RDI thresholds with symptoms or severity levels: mild (5-14), moderate (15-29), severe (≥30).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: OSA prevalence is 15% in men and 5% in women with AHI ≥5 plus symptoms or AHI ≥15, and 50% in referral populations.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
