fact_text: CBT is first-line treatment for chronic insomnia and includes stimulus control, sleep hygiene, relaxation therapy, sleep restriction, and cognitive therapy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Use pharmacotherapy cautiously with short half-life agents and lowest effective dose
Limit duration and monitor side effects
fact_text: Pharmacotherapy for chronic insomnia should use short half-life agents at lowest effective dose, intermittently, limited to 3-4 weeks, with gradual discontinuation and monitoring for rebound insomnia.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: OSA involves decreased pharyngeal muscle tone and dilator reflexes during sleep, leading to airway collapse and apneas/hypopneas.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: OSA is 2–3 times more common in men than women.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Obesity is the strongest risk factor for OSA, with a 6-fold increased risk per 10% weight gain; enlarged neck circumference and male sex also increase risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: OSA increases risk of motor vehicle accidents, hypertension, heart failure, mortality, coronary artery disease, and can lead to cor pulmonale.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Medications for insomnia include benzodiazepines, BZRAs, antidepressants, orexin receptor antagonists, melatonin agonists, antihistamines, and melatonin with varying dose ranges, half-lives, benefits, and side effects.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Polysomnography is the gold standard for diagnosing OSA, with screening questionnaires useful but less specific.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: OSA treatment includes risk factor modification, CPAP as first-line, oral appliances for mild/moderate cases, limited nasal therapy, and surgery for select patients.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Mammography screening benefits and harms vary by age: deaths avoided per 10,000 women screened for 10 years are 3 (40-49y), 8 (50-59y), 21 (60-69y), 13 (70-74y); false positives and biopsies also vary by age.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Hypothyroidism manifests with metabolic slowing, cardiac effects, and characteristic skin changes including nonpitting edema and dry skin.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Hypothyroidism should be considered in patients with fatigue, constipation, or cold intolerance, especially women and those with autoimmune diseases.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Primary hypothyroidism is mainly caused by autoimmune thyroiditis or iodine deficiency; other causes include thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine therapy, and pituitary or hypothalamic disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Most common cause of chronic hypothyroidism is autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis; prevalence 4-8%, up to 20% in women over 60.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: TSH is bound to thyroxine-binding globulin and albumin; levels of binding proteins can affect total T4 measurement, so free T4 is preferred.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: TSH levels have circadian fluctuations, higher in evening; levels tend to be higher in winter and spring than summer and autumn.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: TSH is the best screening test; if elevated, measure free T4 to distinguish overt from subclinical hypothyroidism.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Once stable, check TSH annually

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use and hypertension are risk factors for diverticular hemorrhage.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Diverticular bleed is the leading hypothesis for brisk self-limited lower GI bleeding with history of diverticuli; colonoscopy is the important test.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

presence of bright red blood per rectum

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: EGD is first-line for GI bleeding unless lower GI bleed is strongly suspected; colonoscopy is used to diagnose diverticular hemorrhage, usually presumptively.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Certain historical features such as NSAID use, vascular disease, or recent procedures can suggest specific causes of GI bleeding.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Volume depletion, orthostatic hypotension, and BUN/creatinine ratio >30 suggest upper GI bleeding; hematochezia can occur in 10-15% of upper GI bleeds.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

endoscopic treatment primarily

colectomy for persistent or large bleeds

endoscopic clipping
angiographic vasoconstrictors or embolization

Consider angiographic intervention rarely
Surgical management for recurrent bleeding
Discontinue long-term antiplatelet therapy if possible

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Patients over 40 with rectal bleeding and no clear anorectal source should have colonoscopy to rule out polyps or cancer.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Sitz baths to relax anal sphincter
Topical analgesics, creams, or short-term topical corticosteroids
Use doughnut cushion for prolonged sitting
Soften stool with increased fluid intake, high-fiber diet, and sodium or mineral oil
Avoid constipation and prolonged sitting on toilet
Surgical removal for internal hemorrhoids that prolapse or continue to bleed
Rapid surgical treatment for thrombosed hemorrhoids
fact_text: Most hemorrhoids and anal fissures are treated conservatively with sitz baths, topical treatments, stool softening, and surgery if prolapse or bleeding persists.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: severe rectal pain with bowel movements
bright red blood on the toilet paper
fissure on be found at the midline, posterior to the anal opening
recommended_advice: Physical exam to identify fissure
Consider other diagnoses if fissures are lateral to the anal opening
fact_text: Anal fissures cause severe rectal pain and bright red blood on toilet paper, usually found at the midline posterior to the anal opening; lateral fissures suggest other diagnoses such as Crohn disease or STDs.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: long-term aspirin, nsaid, or alcohol use
recommended_advice: Determine source of blood loss in occult GI bleeding and iron deficiency anemia
Consider colonoscopy especially in patients with recurrent rectal bleeding
fact_text: All patients with occult GI bleeding or iron deficiency anemia require evaluation of the GI tract to identify bleeding sources, with colonoscopy recommended especially in recurrent bleeding.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Iron deficiency anemia usually due to chronic blood loss
Rarely due to poor iron intake or malabsorption
recommended_advice: Manage menorrhagia carefully
Evaluate for GI bleeding in iron deficiency anemia
fact_text: Iron deficiency anemia is usually from chronic blood loss; menstrual and GI bleeding are common causes, with colonoscopy recommended in women over 40 with menorrhagia or other risk factors.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Pain causes anal sphincter spasm that causes recurrent trauma
Chronic fissures associated with sentinel piles and thickening of the skin
recommended_advice: General supportive care for hemorrhoids
Topical nitrates and injected botulinum toxin
Surgical sphincterotomy if needed
fact_text: Treatment of anal fissures includes supportive care, topical nitrates or botulinum toxin, and possibly surgical sphincterotomy if conservative measures fail.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Negative upper and lower GI tract evaluation
recommended_tests: Deep small bowel enteroscopy (double balloon, single balloon, spiral)
recommended_advice: Repeat endoscopy looking for missed lesions
Use capsule endoscopy if initial endoscopy is negative
Use Meckel diverticulum scan for suspected cases
fact_text: Small bowel bleeding should be considered in patients with GI bleeding and negative upper and lower endoscopy; advanced endoscopic techniques like push enteroscopy and capsule endoscopy help localize the source.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Directed history to identify bleeding source
fact_text: Directed history may provide clues to small bowel bleeding source, including medication use and history of diseases predisposing to GI bleeding.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Repeat endoscopy if initial tests inconclusive
fact_text: Obscure GI bleeding with negative upper and lower endoscopy requires evaluation of the small bowel by capsule endoscopy or advanced endoscopic/radiographic procedures.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Suspected Meckel diverticulum as bleeding source
fact_text: Meckel diverticulum scan uses a nuclear tracer with 75-100% sensitivity to detect Meckel diverticulum as a source of bleeding.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: primary headaches: tension headaches, migraine headaches, cluster headaches

secondary headaches: cervical degenerative joint disease, temporomandibular joint syndrome, cranial neuralgias (primary or secondary), headaches associated with substances or their withdrawal (caffeine, nitrates, analgesics, ergotamine)

new headaches primary: benign cough headache, benign exertional headache, headache associated with sexual activity, benign thunderclap headache, idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri)

new headaches secondary: infectious (upper respiratory tract infection, sinusitis, meningitis), vascular (temporal arteritis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, parenchymal hemorrhage, malignant hypertension, cavernous sinus thrombosis), space-occupying lesions (brain tumors, subdural hematoma)
fact_text: Headache differential diagnosis is framed by distinguishing primary versus secondary headaches and by whether the headache is new or old, with primary headaches including tension, migraine, and cluster types, and secondary headaches including causes such as cervical joint disease, neuralgias, substance-related, infectious, vascular, and space-occupying lesions.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: headaches caused by substance or withdrawal
trigger_evidence: throbbing headache with temporal artery abnormalities
recommended_advice: obtain appropriate imaging if old headache with indications
treat migraine if POUND criteria met
consider lumbar puncture with or without brain imaging if new headache with fever or confusion
prescribe corticosteroids and obtain temporal artery biopsy if temporal arteritis suspected
withdraw substance and monitor response if medication overuse suspected
treat underlying disease if headache is symptom of chronic disease
fact_text: Headache diagnostic approach depends on new vs old onset, presence of neurological signs, fever, temporal artery abnormalities, medication use, and migraine criteria to guide imaging, lumbar puncture, biopsy, or treatment.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: unilateral headache, worst around the orbit or temporal area
associated with conjunctival injection, lacrimation or nasal congestion
recommended_tests: diagnostic criteria and exclusion of secondary headaches
fact_text: Cluster headaches present as unilateral headache around orbit or temporal area with conjunctival injection, lacrimation, or nasal congestion; diagnosis requires exclusion of secondary headaches.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Intracranial aneurysm should be considered in acute or subacute headache; CT angiography, MR angiography, or traditional angiography are important tests.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: aura in about one-third of patients
fact_text: Migraine headaches are unilateral, throbbing, moderate to severe, often with aura that precedes headache and lasts about 20 minutes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: most common in women in their teens or 20s
neural events lead to intracranial vasodilatation
fact_text: Migraine headaches most often present in women in their teens or 20s and are caused by neural events leading to intracranial vasodilatation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: moderate to severe unilateral throbbing headache
recommended_tests: diagnostic criteria and exclusion of secondary headaches
fact_text: Migraine headache is characterized by moderate to severe unilateral throbbing headache sometimes with aura; diagnosis requires exclusion of secondary headaches.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: chronic, pressure-type headache of mild to moderate intensity
recommended_tests: diagnostic criteria and exclusion of secondary headaches
fact_text: Tension headache is a chronic, pressure-type headache of mild to moderate intensity; diagnosis requires exclusion of secondary headaches.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: 50% of patients with migraine have nonpulsatile headaches; 40% have bilateral headaches.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Common migraine aura types include stars or flashes (83%), zigzags (56%), scotoma (40%), sensory aura (20%), aphasia (11%), hemianopsia (7%), and motor aura (4%).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Diagnostic criteria for migraine are helpful but must be used cautiously and not replace clinical judgment.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Duration of migraine aura is <30 minutes in 70% of cases, 30-60 minutes in 18%, and >60 minutes in 7%.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Migraine diagnosis should be considered seriously in any patient with recurrent headaches causing disability.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Patients with migraine are more likely to have had vomiting attacks as children and motion sickness history.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Mnemonic POUNDing helps differentiate migraine from tension headache; nausea is a key distinguishing symptom.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Migraine with aura requires at least 2 attacks with fully reversible aura symptoms and at least 2 characteristics including gradual aura symptom development, duration 5-60 minutes, unilateral aura, and aura followed by headache within 60 minutes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Migraine without aura diagnosis requires ≥5 attacks lasting 4-72 hours, headache with 2 of 4 pain qualities, and ≥1 associated symptom (nausea/vomiting or photophobia/phonophobia).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Cheese precipitation has 38% sensitivity and 92% specificity for migraine diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Chocolate precipitation has 22% sensitivity and 95% specificity for migraine diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Exacerbation by physical activity has 81% sensitivity and 78% specificity for migraine diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Nausea has 82% sensitivity and 96% specificity for migraine diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Phonophobia has 67% sensitivity and 87% specificity for migraine diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Photophobia has 79% sensitivity and 87% specificity for migraine diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Throbbing headache has 76% sensitivity and 77% specificity for migraine diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Unilateral headache has 66% sensitivity and 78% specificity for migraine diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: detailed neurologic exam is completely normal
fact_text: A completely normal detailed neurologic exam supports migraine diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: patients with more than 4 migraines a month
recommended_advice: Lifestyle modifications based on trigger identification
Prophylactic therapy may not need daily use; can be used around predictable migraine times
Effective prophylactic medications include beta-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol, timolol), antidepressants (amitriptyline, venlafaxine), and anticonvulsants (valproic acid, topiramate, gabapentin)
fact_text: Prophylactic therapy for migraine is considered for patients with frequent or prolonged headaches; effective medications include beta-blockers, antidepressants, and anticonvulsants.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: NSAIDs first-line therapy; may be used with antiemetics
Acetaminophen plus aspirin plus caffeine as another first-line therapy
Triptans for moderate to severe migraines; combination with NSAIDs probably more effective
Dihydroergotamine for moderate to severe migraines; may be used with antiemetics
Antiemetics (prochlorperazine maleate or metoclopramide) more effective than hydromorphone
Opioids for moderate to severe migraine; use limited due to risk of rebound and medication overuse
Corticosteroids for rescue therapy in intractable migraines
Butalbital plus aspirin plus caffeine occasional use for moderate and severe migraines
Acetaminophen, dichloralphenazone, and isometheptene occasional use for mild to moderate migraines
fact_text: Recommended abortive treatments for migraine include NSAIDs, acetaminophen plus aspirin plus caffeine, triptans, dihydroergotamine, antiemetics, opioids (limited use), corticosteroids, butalbital combinations, and other occasional use drugs.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Severe headaches occurring in young men, often beginning in their 20s
Unilateral headache around the eye or temporal region
Associated ipsilateral conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion, or rhinorrhea
fact_text: Cluster headaches are severe unilateral headaches with autonomic symptoms, more common in men, and often cause restlessness during attacks.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Recurrent episodes of headache lasting minutes to days
Pain is pressing/tightening in quality, mild or moderate intensity
No nausea, but photophobia or phonophobia may be present
recommended_tests: Detailed history and physical exam to exclude other headache syndromes
recommended_advice: Use simple analgesics (acetaminophen or NSAIDs) for episodic tension headaches
For more severe headaches, use combination medications including caffeine
In frequent episodic headaches, stress reduction including biofeedback is helpful
For chronic tension headaches, detoxification by stopping overused medications is important
Consider amitriptyline or mirtazapine for prophylaxis of chronic tension headaches
Physical therapy and acupuncture may offer some benefit
fact_text: Episodic tension headaches are characterized by recurrent pressing, bilateral headaches without nausea but possible photophobia; treatment includes simple analgesics and stress reduction, while chronic tension headaches require detoxification and prophylactic medications.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Femoral neck is the best site to measure bone density by DXA for hip fracture risk prediction.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Osteoporosis is defined as a bone density T score ≤ -2.5 SD below peak predicted bone density; osteopenia is T score between -1.0 and -2.5.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Relative risk of hip fracture increases 2.5-fold for each SD decrease in femoral neck bone density; vertebral fracture risk increases 1.9-fold per SD decrease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Treatment substantially reduces fracture risk
fact_text: Many studies show treatment substantially reduces fracture risk in osteoporosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Optimal repeat DXA screening intervals depend on baseline T score, ranging from 1 to 17 years.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Screen women aged 65 years or older and younger postmenopausal women at increased risk (≥ 9.3% 10-year risk based on FRAX without BMD or high risk based on OST)
fact_text: USPSTF 2018 recommends screening for osteoporosis in women aged 65+ or younger postmenopausal women at increased risk based on FRAX or OST.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: No studies show screening reduces morbidity or mortality from osteoporotic fractures.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: FRAX calculates 10-year probability of hip or major osteoporotic fracture using femoral neck BMD and clinical risk factors.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: OST score = [weight (kg) - age (years)] × 0.2; patients with score < 2 are considered high risk for low BMD.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: The IHS criteria for a cluster headache are:
The patient must have at least 5 attacks.
The headache must last 15–180 minutes; be severe; and be characterized by unilateral pain that is orbital, supraorbital, or temporal.

The headache is accompanied by at least 1 of the following: ipsilateral conjunctival injection and/or lacrimation, ipsilateral nasal congestion and/or rhinorrhea, ipsilateral eyelid edema, ipsilateral forehead and facial sweating, ipsilateral miosis and/or ptosis, a sense of restlessness or agitation.
Attacks occur anywhere from every other day to 8/day during a cluster.
recommended_advice: Treatment for cluster headaches is similar to the treatment for migraines — either acute abortive or prophylactic therapies may be used.
High-flow oxygen is the treatment with the least side effects and best evidence base.
Triptans, similar to those used in the treatment of migraines, are also effective.
Verapamil is usually considered the first-line therapy for preventing cluster headaches.
Corticosteroids and topiramate have also been used successfully.
fact_text: Cluster headaches are diagnosed by IHS criteria including at least 5 attacks of severe unilateral pain lasting 15-180 minutes with autonomic symptoms; treatment includes high-flow oxygen, triptans, and verapamil for prevention.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: CNS aneurysm may present in 3 ways: asymptomatic detection, acute rupture or expansion, chronic headache.
Few studies of chronic headaches caused by unruptured aneurysms.
Headaches of unruptured aneurysms are nonspecific.
recommended_advice: Treatment of CNS aneurysms can be accomplished with neurosurgical or endovascular procedures.
Repair of aneurysms <1 cm in patients without previous rupture is not recommended due to low rupture rates.
Management decisions are difficult when a small aneurysm and suspicious headache coexist because it is unclear if the aneurysm causes the headache.
fact_text: Unruptured CNS aneurysms may cause nonspecific headaches; diagnosis relies on sensitive neuroimaging (CT/MR angiography), with treatment decisions based on aneurysm size and rupture risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Morning headaches associated with brain tumors
Headaches worse with changes in intracranial pressure
fact_text: In an older patient with new morning headaches, brain tumor is a leading hypothesis and CNS imaging is recommended if history of malignancy or focal neurologic deficit is present.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Tension headaches are chronic, pressure-type headaches of mild to moderate intensity diagnosed by clinical criteria and exclusion of secondary causes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Most common in diabetic persons with recent medication or diet changes
fact_text: Nighttime hypoglycemia is a common cause of morning headaches in diabetics with recent medication or diet changes; confirmed by 2 AM fingerstick glucose.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Obstructive sleep apnea should be considered in patients with morning headaches, obesity, and daytime somnolence; diagnosis confirmed by polysomnogram.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Caffeine withdrawal: worse when sleeping late, often worst on vacations or weekends
Carbon monoxide poisoning: headache that occurs in an exposed cohort and resolves upon leaving site of exposure
recommended_advice: Response to caffeine
Relation to alcohol use
fact_text: Substance exposure or withdrawal (caffeine, alcohol, carbon monoxide) can cause morning headaches; diagnosis guided by history and specific tests like carboxyhemoglobin levels.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Temporal arteritis may present with polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms and temporal artery abnormalities; temporal artery biopsy is diagnostic.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Temporal arteritis presents with throbbing headache and elevated ESR; diagnosis confirmed by temporal artery biopsy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: brain tumors almost never present as isolated headache
fact_text: In patients without cancer history, brain tumors rarely present as isolated headache; noncontrast head CT is a reasonable initial test.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: primary extra-axial tumors (meningioma 80%, acoustic neuroma 10%, pituitary adenoma 7%)
recommended_tests: MRI with contrast (procedure of choice, sensitivity nearly 100%)
recommended_advice: Hospitalize patients with signs of increased intracranial pressure or seizure for rapid diagnosis and treatment
fact_text: Brain tumors classically present with progressive morning headaches and focal neurologic deficits; MRI with contrast is the preferred imaging for diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: headache present in 60% of patients with brain tumors
only 2% have headache as solitary presenting feature
40 patients had preexisting headache disorders but 82.5% had a change in headache pain
fact_text: Headache is common in brain tumors but rarely the sole presenting symptom; changes in preexisting headache patterns are important diagnostic clues.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: daytime somnolence with obstructive sleep apnea (osa)
trigger_evidence: headaches occur predominantly in the morning
fact_text: Morning headaches that improve during the day may be caused by hypoglycemia or sleep apnea rather than intracranial neoplasms.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: new headache in patient with malignancy
fact_text: New headache in a patient with cancer should prompt imaging to rule out intracranial metastasis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: signs of increased intracranial pressure or seizure
recommended_advice: hospitalize immediately for rapid diagnosis and treatment
fact_text: Patients with brain tumors and signs of increased intracranial pressure or seizure should be hospitalized immediately for diagnosis and treatment.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: headaches occur within 24 hours of last caffeine intake
headaches relieved within 1 hour by 100 mg caffeine
headaches resolve within 7 days of withdrawal
recommended_advice: consider caffeine withdrawal if headaches occur with coffee intake changes
caffeine withdrawal should be considered when headaches occur later than usual or on weekends/vacations
fact_text: Caffeine withdrawal headache diagnosis requires daily caffeine intake ≥ 200 mg for > 2 weeks, headache onset within 24 hours of last intake, relief by caffeine, and resolution within 7 days.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: headache with nausea, vomiting, anxiety, coma, cardiovascular collapse
headache occurs only in a single location and resolves when removed from setting
multiple people in same setting have similar symptoms
carbon monoxide poisoning more common in winter
recommended_tests: arterial blood gas with carboxyhemoglobin measurement
fact_text: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes headaches with systemic symptoms; diagnosis confirmed by elevated carboxyhemoglobin and exposure history.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: headaches occurring while asleep or awake
recommended_advice: improve diabetes management
fact_text: Hypoglycemia occurring while asleep or awake can cause morning headaches; consider in diabetic patients with abnormal nocturnal glucose and headaches.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: headache occurring on 15 or more days per month
overuse of headache medication for more than 3 months
headaches resolve when medication overuse is stopped
recommended_advice: stop overused headache medication
fact_text: Medication overuse headache is diagnosed by headache ≥ 15 days/month with medication overuse > 3 months and resolves after stopping medication.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: sleep study for patients with morning headaches and no apparent cause
recommended_advice: improve management of diabetes if hypoglycemia present
continuous positive airway pressure for OSA
carbidopa and levodopa for PLMS
improve pain control for pain syndromes
fact_text: Morning headaches can be caused by primary sleep disturbance (OSA, PLMS), abnormal sleep duration, or secondary to another disease such as chronic pain or depression; sleep study is reasonable if no apparent cause.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: headaches occurring in close temporal relation to substance exposure or withdrawal
recommended_tests: carboxyhemoglobin level for carbon monoxide poisoning
recommended_advice: stop medication overuse
consider caffeine withdrawal if headaches occur with changes in coffee intake
fact_text: Headaches can be caused by acute or chronic substance exposure or withdrawal, including nitrites, carbon monoxide, analgesics, alcohol, caffeine, and opioids.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Table 20-6 lists diagnostic hypotheses for thunderclap headache with associated demographics, symptoms, and important tests.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

recent sudden worst headache of his life
headache slowly resolved over about 2 hours
fact_text: In a patient with a sudden worst headache of life, consider subarachnoid hemorrhage and order appropriate tests to rule it out.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: headache that starts abruptly and reaches maximal severity within seconds
recommended_advice: assume SAH until proven otherwise in thunderclap headache
fact_text: A thunderclap headache reaching maximal severity within seconds should be assumed to be subarachnoid hemorrhage until proven otherwise.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: About 25% of patients with SAH are initially misdiagnosed
Patients with severe clinical presentations are most commonly misdiagnosed
Patients initially misdiagnosed are about half as likely to have a good or excellent outcome
recommended_advice: Maintain high suspicion for SAH in patients with thunderclap headache
Perform lumbar puncture if CT is negative and suspicion remains
fact_text: About 25% of SAH patients are initially misdiagnosed, especially those with severe presentations, leading to worse outcomes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: SAH is primarily caused by rupture of a saccular aneurysm in or near the circle of Willis (~85%)
Aneurysms are present in about 7% of the population
Large aneurysms (>1 cm) rupture at a rate of about 0.5%/year
The vast majority of ruptures occur in persons 40–65 years old
SAH carries a mortality of about 50%
Sentinel headaches are atypical headaches that occur in the weeks preceding SAH
recommended_tests: Lumbar puncture if CT is normal and suspicion remains
CSF examination for RBCs and xanthochromia
recommended_advice: Delay lumbar puncture for 6–12 hours after headache onset for better sensitivity
Perform angiography in all patients with documented SAH
fact_text: SAH is caused by rupture of a saccular aneurysm and presents with thunderclap headache; noncontrast head CT is initial test, lumbar puncture and CSF analysis for RBCs and xanthochromia confirm diagnosis if CT is negative.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Noncontrast head CT sensitivity: 97% in first 12 hours, 93% in 12–24 hours, falls to 80% after 2 weeks
CSF RBCs seen immediately in 100% of patients
Sensitivity of RBCs falls after 24 hours
Spectrophotometric detection of xanthochromia is 100% specific for SAH
Xanthochromia remains positive for over 1 week
recommended_tests: Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis for RBCs and xanthochromia
recommended_advice: Perform lumbar puncture if CT is negative and suspicion remains
Use angiography to assist in surgical planning
fact_text: Noncontrast head CT is highly sensitive for SAH within 12 hours; lumbar puncture with CSF RBC and xanthochromia analysis is required if CT is negative and suspicion persists.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Primary treatment is to occlude the culprit aneurysm to prevent rebleeding
Platinum coils via arterial catheters are usually used
Prevention of cerebral vasospasm is important
Calcium antagonists, primarily nimodipine, decrease risk of vasospasm
recommended_advice: Deploy platinum coils to occlude aneurysm
Use nimodipine to reduce vasospasm risk
Consider neurosurgical clipping if coiling not feasible
fact_text: Treatment of SAH focuses on occluding the aneurysm to prevent rebleeding, usually by platinum coil deployment, and preventing cerebral vasospasm with nimodipine.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: headaches recur over 1-2 weeks then intermittently over years
recommended_advice: Diagnose benign thunderclap headache only after SAH is ruled out
fact_text: Benign thunderclap headaches mimic SAH but lack neurologic signs; diagnosis requires exclusion of SAH by CT and lumbar puncture.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: lumbar puncture to rule out SAH
recommended_advice: Consider primary cough headache if headache starts with cough, sexual activity, or exercise
fact_text: Primary cough headaches are more common in men, last less than 1 minute, and must be distinguished from SAH and Arnold-Chiari malformation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: occurs in young people, often bilateral and throbbing
recommended_tests: Careful evaluation to rule out SAH
recommended_advice: Avoid strenuous activity in hot weather or high altitudes
Use pre-exertion ergotamine, beta-blockers, or NSAIDs
fact_text: Primary exertional headaches occur mostly in young people, are often bilateral and throbbing, and must be distinguished from secondary causes including SAH.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: CT scan and lumbar puncture to rule out SAH
recommended_advice: Consider sexual headache if headache occurs with sexual activity and is short lasting
fact_text: Sexual headaches are more common in men, last less than 3 hours, and include dull, explosive, and postural types; SAH must be ruled out.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Treatment is challenging due to short-lived and intermittent nature
As-needed analgesics are probably the only reasonable therapy
fact_text: Benign thunderclap headache treatment is limited to as-needed analgesics due to its short-lived and intermittent course.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

recommended_advice: Cough headaches: treat with cough suppression and NSAIDs
Exertional headaches: avoid strenuous activity, use pre-exertion ergotamine, beta-blockers, or NSAIDs
Sexual headaches: treat with prophylactic beta-blockers
fact_text: Treatment varies: cough headaches respond to cough suppression and NSAIDs; exertional headaches to activity avoidance and medications; sexual headaches to prophylactic beta-blockers.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Intracerebral hemorrhage accounts for about 10% of strokes, commonly presents with headache and focal neurologic signs, and noncontrast CT and MRI are highly sensitive for diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Seizures are present in about 50% of patients with intracerebral hemorrhage.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Thunderclap-type headache is the presenting sign in nearly 60% of patients with intracerebral hemorrhage.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: temporal arteritis, malignancy, subacute hematoma, intracerebral hemorrhage, infections

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Prolonged workouts including marathons, ultramarathons, sprint and full ironman events
Symptoms range from weakness and nausea to coma, seizures, and death
fact_text: EAH is defined as hyponatremia within 24 hours of physical activity, typically after prolonged endurance events, with symptoms from mild to severe neurologic compromise.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Sustained excessive intake of hypotonic fluid
Inappropriate ADH release in some patients
Manifested by weight gain during the event
fact_text: EAH results from excessive hypotonic fluid intake combined with inappropriate ADH release, often evidenced by weight gain during the event.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Recent completion of a major endurance event (e.g., marathon) with frequent stops for water
fact_text: Exercise-associated hyponatremia is the leading hypothesis in patients with recent major endurance events and frequent water stops; urine osmolality testing helps differentiate from primary polydipsia and ecstasy use.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Athletes should be advised to weigh themselves before and after exercise
Counseled to avoid excessive weight gain (>2 kg)
recommended_advice: Weigh before and after exercise
Avoid excessive weight gain during exercise
fact_text: Prevent EAH by advising athletes to monitor weight and avoid gaining more than 2 kg during exercise.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Individuals who collapse or have neurologic symptoms during or following endurance events should be immediately evaluated for EAH
recommended_advice: Immediate evaluation for EAH and other conditions
Use hypertonic saline for severe symptoms
Avoid hypotonic fluids in symptomatic patients
fact_text: Collapse or neurologic symptoms during endurance events require immediate evaluation for EAH and treatment tailored to symptom severity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Rapid development of hyponatremia causes more severe symptoms at lower degrees of hyponatremia
Falls in serum sodium of 7–10% can produce symptoms
Hyponatremia renders plasma hypotonic relative to brain
Hyponatremia and cerebral edema cause neurologic symptoms including confusion, headaches, vomiting, seizures, coma, herniation, and death
fact_text: Rapidly developing hyponatremia in EAH causes severe symptoms and cerebral edema with neurologic signs including confusion, seizures, and coma.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Severely symptomatic/acute: 100 mL 3% NaCl over 10 min, may repeat x2 if needed
Chronic: depends on etiology, avoid rapid correction
Use desmopressin and fluid restriction to prevent overcorrection
Follow serum sodium hourly in severe cases
fact_text: Hyponatremia treatment depends on symptom severity and duration; severe symptoms require hypertonic saline boluses, chronic cases require slower correction with monitoring.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia renders the serum hypertonic compared to hypotonic astrocytes
causing water efflux, damaging cytoskeleton and DNA, causing cell death and demyelination
recommended_advice: Avoid rapid correction of hyponatremia to prevent ODS
Use desmopressin and D5W to slow or reverse rapid rise in serum sodium in at-risk patients
fact_text: Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome, a life-threatening complication.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Mean urine osmolality 144 ± 23 mOsm/L vs 500 mOsm/L in SIADH
Not all psychogenic polydipsia patients have maximally dilute urine
fact_text: Urine osmolality in psychogenic polydipsia is usually low (~144 mOsm/L) but can be higher than expected.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: other causes of hyponatremia with elevated adh
trigger_evidence: patients with psychiatric history and unexplained hyponatremia
recommended_tests: Water restriction test to assess patient’s access to water and response
recommended_advice: Limit water intake to avoid rapid hyponatremia worsening
Consider psychiatric evaluation
fact_text: Psychogenic polydipsia causes hyponatremia with dilute urine and occurs in psychiatric patients with excessive water intake.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Psychotic episodes may cause transient ADH release or increased renal responsiveness
Psychiatric medications can induce SIADH and increase urine osmolality
fact_text: Psychotic episodes and psychiatric medications can increase ADH activity, complicating psychogenic polydipsia diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: serum creatinine, glucose, potassium, urine, and serum osmolality
fact_text: In hyponatremia with delirium, evaluate serum creatinine, glucose, potassium, urine, and serum osmolality to differentiate causes including psychogenic polydipsia, pseudohyponatremia, and kidney failure.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: low urine osmolality confirms diagnosis of water intoxication
recommended_advice: limit water intake
fact_text: Low urine osmolality with hyponatremia confirms water intoxication; assess duration to rule out risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome and educate patient to limit water intake.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Hyponatremia in cirrhosis results from decreased effective circulating volume causing ADH release and water retention, NSAIDs lowering GFR and antagonizing ADH, and synergistic effects with hyperammonemia increasing cerebral edema.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Hyponatremia occurs in 3% of Child-Pugh class A, 16% class B, and 31% class C cirrhosis patients and is associated with higher frequency of adverse outcomes including hepatic encephalopathy and death.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Patients with cirrhosis and hyponatremia have higher rates of small liver size (85% vs 25%), Child-Pugh class C (60% vs 31%), hepatorenal syndrome (17-85% vs 5%), and hepatic encephalopathy (38% vs 15%) compared to those without hyponatremia.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: History: Heavy alcohol use, hepatitis C or chronic hepatitis B, esophageal varices
Physical exam: Scleral icterus, spider angioma, gynecomastia, ascites (bulging flanks, shifting dullness), splenomegaly
fact_text: Cirrhosis is a leading diagnostic hypothesis for hyponatremia with history of heavy alcohol use, hepatitis, and physical signs such as ascites and splenomegaly; diagnosis supported by liver function tests and imaging.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Ascites is present in 100% of cirrhosis patients with hyponatremia; low urine sodium and NT-proBNP < 1000 pg/mL help distinguish cirrhosis from heart failure.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Hyponatremia associated with increased risk of death
Increased total body sodium and edema
Activation of ADH and renin-angiotensin system
fact_text: Hyponatremia in heart failure is due to impaired free water clearance and increased sodium retention, associated with increased mortality risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Avoid rapid sodium correction
Fluid restriction in symptomatic patients
Avoid vaptans
fact_text: In cirrhosis with hyponatremia, avoid rapid sodium correction; fluid restriction is recommended if sodium <120 mEq/L; vaptans are not recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: ACE inhibitors improve sodium levels by blocking angiotensin receptor
Loop diuretics treat hypervolemia and hyponatremia
Avoid NSAIDs due to worsening kidney function
recommended_advice: Treat underlying heart failure with ACE inhibitors and loop diuretics
Avoid NSAIDs
Use 3% saline and furosemide for severe symptomatic hyponatremia
fact_text: Treat hyponatremia in heart failure with ACE inhibitors, loop diuretics, avoid NSAIDs; use hypertonic saline and furosemide for severe symptoms.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: secondary to systemic disease (e.g., diabetes mellitus, malignancy)
fact_text: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by edema, urine protein excretion >3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia; renal biopsy can help identify underlying disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Risk of overcorrection causing neurologic symptoms
recommended_advice: Correct hyponatremia slowly to avoid neurologic complications
Ensure safe and gradual return of serum sodium to normal
fact_text: In cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome, hyponatremia correction must be slow and carefully monitored to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome and neurologic complications.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Hospitalize patients when therapy is initiated
Monitor serum sodium every 6–8 hours for first 24–48 hours
Avoid use with or immediately after other sodium-raising therapies
Discontinue if patient unable to ingest fluid
fact_text: Vasopressin receptor antagonists require hospitalization and close serum sodium monitoring every 6–8 hours during initial therapy to avoid rapid correction and complications.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: GFR > 50 mL/min who do not respond adequately to water restriction
recommended_advice: Free water restriction
Use vaptans in selected patients with adequate GFR
fact_text: Free water restriction is first-line treatment; vaptans may be effective in patients with GFR > 50 mL/min not responding to water restriction.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Adrenal insufficiency is a must-not-miss diagnosis in hyponatremia, especially with risk factors like corticosteroid use or pituitary disease; serum cortisol and stimulation testing are recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Hypothyroidism is a common alternative diagnosis in hyponatremia presenting with fatigue and cold intolerance; TSH testing is recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: no edema, JVD, gallop, crackles, or ascites
recommended_advice: Review history for cancer, lung disease, HIV, medications
Assess for symptoms of hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency
fact_text: In a patient with hyponatremia and euvolemia, SIADH is the leading diagnosis if urine sodium > 20-30 mEq/L and urine osmolality > 300 mOsm/L, after excluding hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Careful search for signs of hypervolemia (edema, JVD, gallop, crackles, ascites)
Assess for hypovolemia (hypotension, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension)
fact_text: Classify hyponatremia by clinical volume status and urine sodium/osmolality to guide diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In a patient with mid/upper abdominal pain and unexplained hypotension, appendicitis is the leading hypothesis; peptic ulcer and pancreatitis are common alternatives; early bowel obstruction must not be missed; appropriate imaging and endoscopy tests should be ordered accordingly.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

differential diagnosis in patients with abdominal pain and distention

other: adrenal insufficiency, diabetic ketoacidosis, myocardial infarction
differential diagnosis of abdominal pain and unexplained hypotension
fact_text: Differential diagnoses for abdominal pain with unexplained hypotension include intra-abdominal hemorrhage, sepsis-related causes, and other conditions such as adrenal insufficiency and myocardial infarction.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: CT scan of chest and head to evaluate underlying disorder
Evaluate for adrenal insufficiency in suspected cases
recommended_advice: Discontinue medications that may cause SIADH
Treat underlying disorder
Consider fluid restriction < 800 mL/day
Use salt tablets, furosemide with salt tablets, hypertonic 3% saline, and ADH receptor antagonists as therapeutic options
fact_text: SIADH diagnosis requires low serum osmolality, urine sodium >30 mEq/L, inappropriately concentrated urine, and euvolemia; exclude other causes and treat underlying disorder.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: CT scan of chest and head
recommended_advice: Fluid restriction
Salt tablets with furosemide
Hypertonic 3% saline for severe symptoms
ADH receptor antagonists
fact_text: Treatment of SIADH includes fluid restriction, salt tablets with furosemide, hypertonic saline for severe symptoms, and addressing underlying cause.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: clinically euvolemic patient with elevated urine osmolality and urine Na+ > 60 mEq/L
recommended_tests: Screening for autoimmune adrenalitis, HIV, tuberculosis, infections
recommended_advice: Suspect primary adrenal insufficiency in hyponatremic patients with hyperkalemia
Search for underlying cause if SIADH confirmed
fact_text: Primary adrenal insufficiency causes decreased cortisol, aldosterone, DHEA, and catecholamine synthesis leading to hyponatremia with hyperkalemia; secondary adrenal insufficiency results from hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction causing hyponatremia without hyperkalemia.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: abdominal pain (with rigidity or rebound in 22%)
fact_text: Acute adrenal insufficiency often presents with hypotension, unexplained fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Chronic adrenal insufficiency may present with nonspecific symptoms including fatigue, weakness, weight loss, abdominal discomfort, and musculoskeletal pains.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Elevated ACTH with low cortisol and hyponatremia suggests primary adrenal insufficiency; corticotropin stimulation test confirms diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: administer 250 mcg cosyntropin IM or IV if ACTH elevated
fact_text: Morning cortisol levels guide adrenal insufficiency diagnosis; CST is required if cortisol is indeterminate; elevated ACTH suggests primary adrenal insufficiency and warrants cosyntropin administration.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Evaluate etiology and check plasma renin activity (PRA) and aldosterone if primary adrenal insufficiency likely
Evaluate etiology if secondary adrenal insufficiency suspected
Endocrine consultation if normal CST with low ACTH
fact_text: Diagnostic approach to suspected adrenal insufficiency involves checking early morning cortisol, ACTH level, and cosyntropin stimulation test to differentiate primary vs secondary adrenal insufficiency and guide further evaluation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Plasma aldosterone and plasma renin activity (PRA)
recommended_advice: Endocrine consultation advised
fact_text: Evaluation of adrenal insufficiency requires CST interpretation with caution in ICU, imaging and antibody testing for primary causes, and endocrine consultation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Immediate blood tests and hydrocortisone IV
Aggressive fluid resuscitation
Close monitoring of electrolytes and infection
fact_text: In suspected adrenal crisis, draw cortisol and ACTH immediately and start hydrocortisone IV and fluids without waiting for lab results; monitor closely and consult endocrinology.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Long-term glucocorticoid therapy with dose adjustment during stress
Mineralocorticoid therapy if aldosterone deficient
DHEA supplementation in women with symptoms
fact_text: Long-term therapy for adrenal insufficiency includes glucocorticoids with dose adjustment during stress, mineralocorticoids if aldosterone deficient, and possible DHEA for women.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: large pituitary adenoma with signs of hemorrhage
condition_aliases: large pituitary adenoma with signs of hemorrhage
trigger_evidence: MRI showing large pituitary adenoma with hemorrhage
recommended_advice: refer to endocrinology and neurosurgery
fact_text: MRI can reveal large pituitary adenoma with hemorrhage in patients with headache, fever, and hyponatremia

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Thiazide diuretics cause hyponatremia by interfering with sodium transport, causing hypovolemia, increased ADH, and impaired free water clearance; NSAIDs increase risk

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: stop thiazide diuretic
fact_text: Thiazide diuretics are a common cause of hyponatremia, often with symptoms of lethargy, dizziness, vomiting, and confusion; diagnosis is based on history and urine sodium may remain elevated

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: stop thiazide diuretic
careful volume resuscitation with normal saline in hypovolemia
monitor serum sodium closely
fact_text: Treatment of thiazide-induced hyponatremia includes stopping the diuretic, careful volume resuscitation in hypovolemia, and close monitoring to avoid rapid sodium correction

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Hyponatremia may occur in 10% of patients with hypothyroidism but is rarely symptomatic
Hyponatremia arises in part secondary to ADH release triggered by a decrease in cardiac output
Hyponatremia typically develops only in severe hypothyroidism (TSH > 50 mIU/mL)
fact_text: Hyponatremia can occur in hypothyroidism, especially severe cases with high TSH, partly due to ADH release from decreased cardiac output.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: One study reported FE_Na <0.5% 100% sensitive for hypovolemia, 72% specific
False-negative results (elevated FE_Na) may be seen in hypovolemia secondary to diuretics, adrenal insufficiency, or vomiting with metabolic alkalosis
fact_text: FE_Na <0.5% is highly sensitive for hypovolemia, but false negatives can occur with diuretics, adrenal insufficiency, or vomiting-induced metabolic alkalosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Hyponatremia may develop in volume-depleted patients if sodium loss triggers ADH release
Typical urine findings include decreased urine sodium concentration (<30 mEq/L), decreased FE_Na (<0.5%), increased urine osmolality (>450 mOsm/L), prerenal azotemia, and elevated uric acid
fact_text: In hypovolemic hyponatremia, urine sodium is typically low (<30 mEq/L), FE_Na <0.5%, and urine osmolality is high (>450 mOsm/L).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Patients with pseudohyponatremia typically present in 1 of 3 ways depending on underlying cause
Marked hyperlipidemia and marked hyperproteinemia may interfere with sodium measurement causing spuriously low sodium
Actual serum sodium is normal in pseudohyponatremia
fact_text: Pseudohyponatremia occurs when hyperlipidemia or hyperproteinemia cause spuriously low sodium measurements despite normal actual serum sodium.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: For mildly symptomatic patients, normal saline can be used
For severely symptomatic patients with coma or seizures, 3% normal saline can be used
Patients at high risk for ODS require fluid resuscitation to suppress ADH and careful sodium correction
Frequent monitoring of serum sodium is mandatory to avoid overcorrection
recommended_advice: Use normal saline for mild symptoms
Use 3% saline for severe symptoms
Avoid rapid correction to prevent ODS
Monitor serum sodium frequently
fact_text: Hyponatremia treatment depends on severity: normal saline for mild symptoms, 3% saline for severe symptoms, with careful monitoring to prevent overcorrection and ODS.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: patients attending clubs (raves) with anxiety, restlessness, delirium, or seizures
recommended_advice: ICU monitoring usually required for MDMA intoxication
fluid restriction for mild hyponatremia
use hypertonic saline for marked symptoms (coma, seizures)
fact_text: MDMA intoxication causes hyponatremia often with symptoms like anxiety, seizures, and delirium; treatment focuses on hyponatremia management including ICU monitoring and hypertonic saline for severe symptoms.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: frequent drug abuse in young adults
recommended_advice: monitor for severe symptoms
fluid restriction in mild cases
fact_text: Hyponatremia is a common and serious complication of MDMA intoxication, more frequent in women and can cause severe neurological symptoms.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

recommended_advice: treat underlying disorder causing hyponatremia
fact_text: Distinguish true hyponatremia from pseudohyponatremia by measuring serum osmolality and correcting sodium for hyperglycemia; treat underlying cause.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Patients with dementia have increased risk for hypernatremia due to inadequate water intake, especially with superimposed illness
Marked hyperglycemia should be considered a 'must not miss' alternative diagnosis
fact_text: Dementia increases risk of hypernatremia from inadequate water intake; marked hyperglycemia is an important alternative diagnosis to consider.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Clinicians should search for an underlying cause in patients with hypernatremia
Consider hyperglycemia as a cause of free water loss and altered sensorium
Evaluate urine osmolality to differentiate causes
fact_text: In hypernatremia, identifying the underlying cause is essential as it may contribute to delirium; hyperglycemia can cause free water loss leading to hypernatremia.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Urine osmolality, serum electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, and glucose
Evaluate to determine etiology
fact_text: Hypernatremia differential diagnosis includes impaired water intake, osmotic diuresis, rare etiologies like diabetes insipidus, hypothalamic lesions, and increased salt intake; urine osmolality and clinical context guide diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, abnormal subclavicular skin turgor, and dry oral mucosa have variable sensitivity and specificity as findings in hypernatremia.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Approach to hypernatremia involves assessing urine osmolality, administering ADH if low, and differentiating central vs nephrogenic diabetes insipidus based on urine osmolality change.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Classic presentation: abdominal pain initially diffuse then migrates to RLQ
Pain at McBurney point (1.5–2 inches from anterior superior iliac crest toward umbilicus)
Patients often complain of bloating and anorexia
fact_text: Classic appendicitis presents as abdominal pain migrating to RLQ with tenderness at McBurney point.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Elevated WBC counts have variable sensitivity and specificity for appendicitis; WBC >17,000/mcL has high specificity but low sensitivity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Guarding (moderate to severe): sensitivity 46%, specificity 92%, LR+ 5.5, LR– 0.59
Rebound (moderate to severe): sensitivity 61%, specificity 82%, LR+ 3.5, LR– 0.47
Pain migration to RLQ: sensitivity 54%, specificity 63%, LR+ 1.5, LR– 0.7
RLQ tenderness: sensitivity 89–100%, specificity 12–59%, LR+ 1.1–2.2, LR– 0–0.2
fact_text: Moderate to severe guarding and rebound have moderate sensitivity and high specificity for appendicitis; RLQ tenderness is highly sensitive but less specific.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Nausea and vomiting with pain migration to RLQ occurs in about half of appendicitis cases.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Older adults with appendicitis have longer symptom duration and less frequent pain migration to RLQ.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: RLQ pain is the most useful clinical finding with LR+ 7.3–8.5 and LR– 0.0–0.3
fact_text: RLQ pain is the most useful clinical finding for appendicitis diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Absence of fever, severe tenderness, guarding, and rebound does not rule out appendicitis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

hypovolemic shock (hemorrhage: trauma, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, postsurgical/postprocedural bleeding, intra-abdominal causes)

cardiogenic shock (poor contractility: lv failure including mi, myocarditis, metabolic derangements, drug effects, miscellaneous causes; rv failure: mi, pulmonary vascular disease, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction)
outflow obstruction (aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, malignant hypertension, pulmonary embolism)

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

History of fever, rigors, other infectious symptoms
History of CAD or heart failure
Physical exam findings: low cardiac output signs, jugular venous distention, S3 gallop
fact_text: Differentiate hypovolemic, septic, and cardiogenic shock based on history, physical exam, and pulse pressure.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Pulses bounding due to widened pulse pressure
fact_text: Septic shock typically presents with fever, tachypnea, tachycardia, hypotension, bounding pulses, impaired mentation, and decreased urinary output.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

BP should be measured with a manual cuff
Pulse pressure = systolic BP - diastolic BP
Narrow pulse pressure suggests low cardiac output
Wide pulse pressure suggests high cardiac output
recommended_tests: laboratory tests for infection and organ function
fact_text: In hypotension and shock, measure manual BP and pulse pressure to help differentiate hypovolemic, septic, and cardiogenic shock.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
