History of CAD, HF or symptoms of MI
Cold extremities, small pulse pressure, poor refill, JVD, S3 gallop
ECG evidence of MI or positive troponin
Fever, rash, cough, urinary symptoms, wide pulse pressure, brisk capillary refill, warm extremities, focal lung findings, abdominal tenderness, CVAT, skin findings
recommended_advice: Review history, physical exam, and laboratory tests for clues to sepsis, cardiac failure, hypovolemia
Consider echocardiography for shock of uncertain etiology
fact_text: Shock diagnostic approach differentiates hypovolemic, cardiogenic, septic, and uncertain etiology shock based on history, exam, and specific tests including ECG, troponins, echocardiogram, and labs.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Diagnostic hypotheses for Ms. P. include septic shock, hypovolemic shock, and cardiogenic shock, each with specific symptoms and recommended tests.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Lung involvement causes acute respiratory distress syndrome and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
Acute kidney injury secondary to hypotension, renal vasoconstriction, increased tumor necrosis factor
Disseminated intravascular coagulation with decreased protein C
Lactic acidosis due to microcirculatory lesions, hypoventilation, mitochondrial injury, and decreased hepatic lactate clearance
fact_text: Sepsis can cause multiple organ dysfunction including ARDS, acute kidney injury, DIC, and lactic acidosis from microcirculatory and mitochondrial injury.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Infection with bacteria, fungi, mycobacterial, or viral causes
Significant biologic and clinical heterogeneity due to host factors
Noninfectious processes may trigger similar immune response
Hypoperfusion and hypotension mechanisms include vasodilation mediated by nitric oxide, prostacyclin, and low vasopressin levels
fact_text: Sepsis pathophysiology involves infection-triggered dysregulated immune response, vasodilation causing hypotension, and heterogeneity due to host factors and comorbidities.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Comorbidities: AIDS, liver failure, HF, diabetes mellitus, cancer, immunosuppression
Candida, Pseudomonas, or Staphylococcus aureus infection
recommended_advice: Appropriate antibiotics reduce mortality by 50%
fact_text: Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction from infection; septic shock requires vasopressors and elevated lactate, with mortality predictors including age > 40, comorbidities, hypothermia, leukopenia, hospital-acquired infection, and certain pathogens; appropriate antibiotics reduce mortality by 50%.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In emergency patients, fever > 38.8°C is more common in bacteremic patients; 5% of bacteremic patients are normothermic and 13% are hypothermic.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: dopamine or epinephrine or norepinephrine dose
fact_text: Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score uses respiratory, coagulation, liver, cardiovascular, CNS, and renal parameters to assess sepsis-related organ failure severity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Calculate Mortality in Emergency Department Sepsis (MEDS) score to predict mortality risk
fact_text: MEDS score predicts mortality in emergency department patients with suspected infection using 9 clinical variables.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Lactate levels > 4.0 mmol/L in patients with suspected infection predict higher mortality (15%) compared to lower lactate levels (2.5%).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: blood cultures from central venous catheter if present
recommended_advice: consider bacteremia in patients with fever and shaking chills or rigors
obtain blood cultures before antibiotics
evaluate rash in febrile patients for certain infections
fact_text: Absence of fever in bacteremia is linked to increased mortality; chills vary from mild to shaking chills and are sensitive but less specific; rash may indicate certain infections; WBC > 15,000/mcL is only 28% sensitive for bacteremia; normal WBC does not rule out bacteremia.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Injection drug use or acute abdomen increase bacteremia risk; bacteremia incidence is low (2%) without risk factors including temperature > 38.3°C, shaking chills, injection drug use, acute abdomen on exam, or major comorbidities.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Shaking chills have 45% sensitivity, 90% specificity, LR+ 4.7 for bacteremia; injection drug use has 7% sensitivity, 98% specificity, LR+ 2.9; central venous catheter has 23% sensitivity, 90% specificity, LR+ 2.4; acute abdomen has 20% sensitivity, 91% specificity, LR+ 2.2; WBC > 15,000/mcL has 28% sensitivity, 87% specificity, LR+ 2.2; chills (any type) have 88% sensitivity, 52% specificity, LR+ 1.7; comorbidity has 86% sensitivity, 37% specificity, LR+ 1.4.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Procalcitonin is elevated in bacterial infections and attenuated by cytokines in viral infections; elevated levels suggest bacterial infection whereas normal levels may indicate systemic inflammatory response without bacterial infection.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: signs of inflammation at insertion site
erythema present in 3% of catheter-related bloodstream infections
recommended_tests: blood cultures from peripheral site and central catheter
recommended_advice: consider catheter-related infection even without erythema or pus
obtain blood cultures from catheter and peripheral sites
fact_text: Signs of inflammation at catheter insertion site are uncommon; erythema is present in only 3% of catheter-related bloodstream infections; gross pus at catheter site is highly specific for infection.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Serum lactate levels are more sensitive than anion gap for detecting lactic acidosis in sepsis; elevated anion gap is only 44–67% sensitive.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: consider diagnostic threshold and rule out alternatives before confirming sepsis diagnosis
fact_text: In a patient with features suggesting sepsis, confirm diagnostic threshold for septic shock, rule out active alternatives, and consider further tests to exclude other diagnoses.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: obtain cultures as soon as possible
obtain blood cultures peripherally and through central catheter if present
fact_text: Cultures from suspected sources should be obtained as soon as possible; if central catheters are in place, blood cultures should be obtained both peripherally and through the catheter.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: treat underlying cause
prompt volume resuscitation
consider vasopressors, inotropes, intubation, mechanical ventilation, blood products, and others
refer to specialized text for detailed recommendations
fact_text: Treatment of septic shock includes treating the underlying cause, prompt volume resuscitation, and possibly vasopressors, inotropes, intubation, mechanical ventilation, and blood products.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Hematocrit may be normal in acute bleeding due to hemodilution
Hematocrit often elevated in nonhemorrhagic hypovolemia
fact_text: Hematocrit and urine studies help differentiate hemorrhagic from nonhemorrhagic hypovolemia; BUN/Cr ratio > 20 and low urine sodium support hypovolemia.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Postural pulse increment > 30 bpm has high sensitivity and specificity for large blood loss
Supine hypotension has lower sensitivity but high specificity
Dehydration signs include mucous membranes dry and sunken eyes with variable sensitivity and specificity
recommended_tests: Physical examination of vital signs including postural pulse increment, supine hypotension, mucous membranes, sunken eyes
fact_text: Postural pulse increment > 30 bpm is a sensitive and specific sign for detecting large blood loss; mucous membranes dryness and sunken eyes support dehydration diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Volume depletion due to vomiting, diarrhea, inadequate oral intake, or excessive diuresis
Hemorrhage (due to trauma, gastrointestinal or intra-abdominal hemorrhage)
fact_text: Hypovolemic shock typically results from volume depletion or hemorrhage; dehydration-related hypovolemia is common in elderly with specific risk factors.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Orthostatic vital signs are more sensitive than supine vital signs for detecting hypovolemia
Wait 3 minutes before measuring supine vitals and 1 minute after standing to measure upright vitals
fact_text: Orthostatic vital signs, especially postural pulse increment ≥ 30 bpm, are sensitive indicators of hypovolemia.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: cardiogenic shock due to aortic valve failure
cardiogenic shock due to cardiac tamponade
cardiogenic shock due to pulmonary embolism
trigger_evidence: History of bicuspid aortic valve and mechanical aortic valve replacement
No signs or symptoms of sepsis or hypovolemia
fact_text: In a patient with shock and history of aortic valve replacement, cardiogenic shock is most likely; evaluate with ECG, troponin, echocardiogram, chest film, and CTA to rule out active alternatives.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: diffuse infiltrate with acute respiratory distress syndrome
condition_aliases: diffuse infiltrate with acute respiratory distress syndrome
trigger_evidence: After fluid resuscitation, patient developed hypotension, urinary output dropped
Chest film showed diffuse infiltrate consistent with ARDS
recommended_advice: Empiric antibiotics for urosepsis
Mechanical ventilation
IV fluids and norepinephrine
fact_text: In shock with deteriorating oxygenation and diffuse infiltrates, consider sepsis with ARDS; treat with antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors, and mechanical ventilation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Treatment of hypovolemia is restoration of adequate mean pressure by fluid resuscitation
recommended_advice: Restore adequate mean pressure by fluid resuscitation
Identify and stop bleeding in hemorrhagic hypovolemia
Consider transfusions if bleeding is identified
Avoid vasopressors as they may have detrimental effects on cardiac output and perfusion
fact_text: Hypovolemia treatment focuses on restoring adequate mean pressure by fluid resuscitation and controlling bleeding; vasopressors are generally not indicated.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: CRP > 10 mg/L has sensitivity 77% and specificity 37% for appendicitis; likelihood ratios LR+ 1.2, LR- 0.6.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: The Appendicitis Inflammatory Response (AIR) score uses symptoms/signs and lab values to estimate appendicitis probability; score 0-4 indicates low probability.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Ultrasonography sensitivity varies widely and is operator dependent; it should not be used to rule out appendicitis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: CT scan with oral and IV contrast
fact_text: CT scan is the test of choice to rule out appendicitis when diagnosis is uncertain, with high sensitivity and specificity and reduces unnecessary surgery.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Surgical and gynecologic consultation
fact_text: In pregnancy, ultrasonography is preferred to CT due to radiation risk; unenhanced MRI is an alternative for indeterminate cases; gadolinium is not advised.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Observation
Monitor urinary output and vital signs
IV fluid resuscitation
Broad-spectrum antibiotics
Surgery
fact_text: Treatment includes observation, monitoring, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and surgery remains the therapy of choice.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: patients randomized to surgery vs observation with IV antibiotics
recommended_tests: CT scanning to define uncomplicated appendicitis
recommended_advice: Surgery preferred over nonsurgical therapy
fact_text: Trials show surgery is preferred over nonsurgical therapy due to lower rates of emergent appendectomy and recurrence.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: external jugular vein elevation with elevated catheter-measured central venous pressure
recommended_tests: Manual blood pressure cuff measurement for PPP
fact_text: Jugular venous pressure elevation and proportional pulse pressure > 25% are useful diagnostic clues for cardiogenic shock.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: severe reduction in cardiac index (< 1.8 L/min/m2)
elevated filling pressure (LV end-diastolic pressure > 18 mm Hg or RV end-diastolic pressure > 10–15 mm Hg)
recommended_advice: Assess for pericardial effusion
Determine global cardiac systolic function
Identify marked LV or RV enlargement
Immediate catheterization for treatment of acute MI
fact_text: Diagnosing cardiogenic shock relies on recognizing signs of decreased cardiac output despite adequate or elevated filling pressure; bedside ultrasound is useful for assessing cause and cardiac function.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: decreased coronary perfusion lowers cardiac output
catecholamine release causes hypoperfusion and arrhythmia
neurohormonal cascade activation leads to salt and water retention
treatment relies on breaking this cycle
fact_text: Cardiogenic shock pathophysiology involves decreased coronary perfusion, catecholamine-induced hypoperfusion and arrhythmia, neurohormonal activation causing fluid retention, and requires treatment to break this cycle.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Cardiac tamponade physiology involves rising pericardial pressure compressing cardiac chambers, leading to impaired filling, early diastolic RV collapse, and decreased stroke volume.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Tachypnea and dyspnea nearly always present with cardiac tamponade (87-88%).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Cardiac tamponade is classified as acute (trauma or rupture) or subacute (inflammatory or malignancy), with differing presentations and effusion volumes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Common causes of pericardial effusions leading to tamponade include idiopathic pericarditis (20-30%), malignancy (13-36%), and infection (5-21%).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Weakness, hypotension, tachycardia, elevated jugular venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds suggest cardiac tamponade in cardiogenic shock.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: late diastolic collapse of the right atrium
early to mid diastolic collapse of the right ventricle
septal shift toward the left during inspiration and toward the right with expiration
suppression of deep inspiratory collapse of the inferior vena cava
fact_text: Key echocardiographic findings in cardiac tamponade include pericardial effusion with late diastolic right atrial collapse and early to mid diastolic right ventricular collapse.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: exaggerated decrease in BP with normal inspiration
decreased systolic BP despite increased venous return during inspiration
inspiration increases RV filling causing left heart filling to diminish
recommended_advice: manual sphygmomanometer measurement of pulsus paradoxus in quiet location with patience
fact_text: Pulsus paradoxus is an exaggerated decrease in blood pressure with normal inspiration and is a diagnostic clue for cardiac tamponade.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: echocardiography revealed large pericardial effusion with late diastolic collapse of right atrium
patient taken to catheterization lab urgently and 500 mL blood removed
patient improved with BP increase from 110/70 to 110/70 mm Hg and pulse drop to 75 bpm
recommended_advice: urgent pericardiocentesis
fact_text: Urgent pericardiocentesis in cardiac tamponade with large pericardial effusion and right atrial collapse leads to rapid hemodynamic improvement.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Transthoracic echocardiography is the primary diagnostic test to confirm cardiac tamponade.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: pericardiocentesis under ultrasound guidance if needed
recommended_advice: pericardial drainage unless tamponade due to dissection or rupture
symptomatic management with volume resuscitation and oxygen
pericardiocentesis at bedside or ICU if needed
surgical pericardiotomy if loculated effusion or traumatic hemopericardium
fact_text: Treatment of cardiac tamponade requires pericardial drainage unless due to dissection or rupture; symptomatic management and pericardiocentesis under ultrasound guidance are options depending on stability and effusion characteristics.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Anaphylactic shock is suggested by recent new medication or allergen exposure with symptoms like hives, itching, wheezing, angioedema; septic shock presents with fever, rigors, urinary symptoms, cough, diarrhea, abdominal pain and elevated WBC, urinalysis, chest radiograph, blood cultures.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Anaphylaxis involves interaction of antigen with mast cell IgE or direct drug actions causing release of mediators like histamine, leukotrienes, kinins, prostaglandins leading to vasodilation, fluid leakage, bronchoconstriction, and potentially death from hypoxemia or shock.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: acute onset of illness within minutes to hours
fact_text: Diagnosis of anaphylaxis is highly likely if acute onset involves skin plus respiratory or cardiovascular symptoms, or if 2 or more symptoms occur after allergen exposure including skin, respiratory, BP, or GI symptoms.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Individual sensitivities for anaphylaxis findings: diffuse urticaria 39%, pruritus 61%, lip angioedema 49%, tongue angioedema 39%, wheezing 49%.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Lifetime prevalence of anaphylaxis is 0.05–2%; admissions for anaphylaxis have increased, with food as the most common trigger; 57% of anaphylaxis-related deaths are medicine-induced.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Patient history is critical for diagnosing anaphylaxis; respiratory, cardiovascular, and skin symptoms are key clues.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Foods are the most common triggers of anaphylaxis in infants, children, and teenagers; peanut allergies are most common in children, shellfish allergies in adults.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Serum tryptase >2.0 mcg/L between arrival and 1 hour post-discharge supports anaphylaxis diagnosis; test is 75% sensitive but has limited benefit at presentation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Anaphylactic shock is quickly recognized by prompt epinephrine administration and rapid improvement in breath quality.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Prescribe epinephrine auto-injector
Create emergency action plan and provide medical ID
Refer to allergy specialist for evaluation
fact_text: After recovery from anaphylaxis, provide epinephrine auto-injector, emergency plan, medical ID, and allergy specialist referral.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Administer IM epinephrine promptly
Support airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, skin, and body weight
Use antihistamines and corticosteroids as second-line
Position patient supine with elevated legs
Provide respiratory support if needed
Establish IV access and give fluids
fact_text: Initial management of suspected anaphylaxis requires prompt IM epinephrine and supportive care including airway, breathing, circulation, and IV fluids.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Dark, tea-colored urine indicates conjugated hyperbilirubinemia; light clay-colored stools suggest extrahepatic obstruction.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: drug-induced impaired hepatic uptake (rifampin, probenecid, gemfibrozil, azatanavir)
hereditary impaired conjugation (gilbert syndrome, crigler-najjar syndrome)
acquired impaired conjugation (neonates, hyperthyroidism, ethinyl estradiol, liver disease, sepsis)
trigger_evidence: patient with jaundice or abnormal liver enzymes
fact_text: Differential diagnosis of jaundice involves determining if hyperbilirubinemia is conjugated or unconjugated, then considering causes such as increased bilirubin production, impaired hepatic uptake, or impaired conjugation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (>50%) can be caused by increased production, impaired hepatic uptake, or impaired conjugation from hereditary or acquired causes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: extrahepatic cholestasis: common bile duct stone, benign stricture, benign polyp, malignancy (pancreatic cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, ampullary cancer), periportal adenopathy, primary sclerosing cholangitis

intrahepatic cholestasis: hepatitis (viral, alcoholic), intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, cirrhosis, medications and toxins, sepsis, total parenteral nutrition, postoperative jaundice, infiltrative diseases (amyloidosis, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis), primary sclerosing cholangitis, primary biliary cirrhosis
trigger_evidence: alkaline phosphatase more elevated than transaminases
fact_text: Cholestatic pattern with alkaline phosphatase > transaminases suggests intrahepatic or extrahepatic cholestasis with distinct differential diagnoses for each.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Assess conjugated vs unconjugated bilirubin
Evaluate for obstruction or hepatocellular disease
fact_text: First step in hyperbilirubinemia diagnosis is to determine if it is primarily unconjugated or conjugated, then evaluate for obstruction or hepatocellular dysfunction accordingly.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Differential diagnosis of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia depends on liver enzyme patterns: normal enzymes suggest sepsis, rotor syndrome, or Dubin-Johnson syndrome; elevated enzymes suggest hepatocellular or cholestatic causes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Jaundice is detectable on physical exam when total bilirubin is greater than 2.5–3.0 mg/dL; scleral icterus appears before skin jaundice.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: physical exam signs of liver disease
condition_aliases: physical exam signs of liver disease
trigger_evidence: liver edge palpable 7 cm below costal margin
no peripheral edema or abdominal tenderness
fact_text: Physical exam can detect liver disease signs such as scleral icterus, jaundice (detectable when total bilirubin >2.5-3.0 mg/dL), hepatomegaly, and palpable spleen tip.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Figure 26-1 illustrates bilirubin metabolism and excretion pathways including liver conjugation and enterohepatic recycling.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In a patient with hyperbilirubinemia, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and history of alcohol use, alcoholic liver disease is the leading hypothesis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Physical exam sensitivity for jaundice is 78.4% when bilirubin > 3.0 mg/dL and 96.4% when bilirubin > 15.0 mg/dL.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: palpation in supine position highly predictive
fact_text: Palpation of spleen in supine position is highly predictive of splenomegaly; percussion methods have poor test characteristics.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Best historical findings for ascites include increased abdominal girth, recent weight gain, and ankle swelling; physical exam signs include fluid wave and shifting dullness; ultrasonography detects minimal ascites better than physical exam.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: elevated alkaline phosphatase and moderately elevated transaminases
fact_text: Elevated alkaline phosphatase with moderately elevated transaminases suggests cholestatic pattern; AST > ALT suggests alcoholic liver disease; extrahepatic obstruction must be ruled out as common cause of cholestasis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: ultrasound upper limit of normal liver size 13 cm
fact_text: Upper limit of normal liver size on ultrasound is 13 cm; palpable liver edge is not reliable for hepatomegaly if liver is pushed caudally by enlarged lungs.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Key biochemical markers to evaluate liver include AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, GGTP, conjugated bilirubin, serum albumin, and prothrombin time, each reflecting different aspects of liver function or injury.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Elevated serum bilirubin is first classified as >50% indirect or direct; subsequent evaluation depends on anemia, liver tests, pattern of enzyme elevation, and imaging to differentiate causes of hyperbilirubinemia.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: CT scan reveals hypodense fluid collection on right side inferior to cecum
interpretation possible appendiceal perforation versus Crohn disease
fact_text: CT scan showing hypodense fluid collection inferior to cecum suggests appendicitis or appendiceal perforation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: ovarian pathology (ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, ruptured ovarian cyst)
trigger_evidence: CBC reveals WBC of 8700/mcL (86% neutrophils, 0% bands) and HCT of 44%
pain now more severe in the RLQ
moderately tender but still without rebound or guarding
recommended_advice: observe patient
obtain surgical consult
fact_text: Migration of pain to the RLQ with moderate tenderness and elevated neutrophils suggests appendicitis; consider CT scan and surgical consult.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: surgical exploration
removal of necrotic appendix
irrigation of peritoneal cavity
broad-spectrum antibiotics postoperatively
fact_text: In a patient with typical symptom progression and CT findings, surgical exploration and removal of necrotic appendix with antibiotics is appropriate.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: epigastric pain is the first pivotal feature
common causes include PUD, pancreatitis, biliary colic
fact_text: Epigastric pain differential includes PUD, pancreatitis, biliary colic, and Crohn ileitis; time course and multiple episodes help differentiate.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: no history of alcohol, NSAID use, or known PUD
pain not improved with food or antacids
fact_text: In epigastric pain without history of PUD or NSAID use and no relief with food or defecation, consider pancreatitis, biliary colic, bowel obstruction, or nephrolithiasis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Increased risk in men consuming >60-80 g/day for >10 years
Fibrosis develops in 40-60% of heavy drinkers
Cirrhosis develops in 30% of those who continue to drink
recommended_advice: Abstinence from alcohol
fact_text: Cirrhosis risk increases with heavy alcohol use; abstinence improves 5-year survival from 50% to 75%; survival drops to 35% after complications.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Symptoms include fever, hepatomegaly, ascites, encephalopathy, leukocytosis
fact_text: Alcoholic hepatitis presents acutely with fever, hepatomegaly, ascites, encephalopathy, AST:ALT >1.5, malnutrition, and has high mortality; prognostic scores include mDF, MELD, and GAHS.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Signs of cirrhosis (palmar erythema, angioma, splenomegaly)
fact_text: Alcoholic hepatitis diagnosis is supported by alcohol history, hepatomegaly, cirrhosis signs, and confirmed by CT scan, liver biopsy, and AST > ALT.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: chronic hepatitis with fibrosis or cirrhosis
fact_text: ALD has 3 histologic stages: steatosis (generally asymptomatic), alcoholic steatohepatitis, and chronic hepatitis with fibrosis or cirrhosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Alcohol ingestion is the most important risk factor for ALD; beer and spirits are more associated than wine; female sex, African-American and Hispanic ethnicity, obesity, and genetic factors increase risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: gallstones, strictures or polyps, ampullary carcinoma or cholangiocarcinoma
condition_aliases: gallstones, strictures or polyps, ampullary carcinoma or cholangiocarcinoma
trigger_evidence: Lack of pain makes gallstones unlikely but CBD stones can present painlessly
fact_text: Painless jaundice differential includes strictures, polyps, ampullary carcinoma, or cholangiocarcinoma, evaluated by imaging and endoscopy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Pancreatic cancer should be considered in painless or painful jaundice with weight loss and elevated liver enzymes, evaluated by imaging and endoscopy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Exposure to body fluids, needles, or contaminated food
Signs of cirrhosis if chronic hepatitis B or C
fact_text: Viral hepatitis diagnosis is suggested by exposure history and confirmed by hepatitis serologies.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Biomarkers such as GGT, AST, and ALT are not sensitive or specific enough to diagnose ALD
Macrocytosis may be seen but is also insensitive
Alcoholic steatosis diagnosed by fatty infiltration on imaging in patients with excessive alcohol consumption
Alcoholic hepatitis is a clinical diagnosis
Transaminases are elevated but generally < 6–7 times the upper limit of normal
GGTP often elevated, and GGT/alkaline phosphatase ratio often > 2.5
Liver biopsy is the gold standard but not always necessary
recommended_advice: Abstinence from alcohol
Consider corticosteroids if mDF score > 32

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

trigger_evidence: Increase in creatinine without change in GFR may be due to inhibition of tubular secretion of creatinine by drugs (trimethoprim, cimetidine, pyrimethamine)
fact_text: Creatinine increase without GFR change can be caused by drugs inhibiting tubular secretion of creatinine (pseudo-AKI).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Any of cholangitis, jaundice, dilated CBD on ultrasound, elevated alkaline phosphatase, or elevated amylase/lipase suggests choledocholithiasis and warrants CBD evaluation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: CBD stones present in 5-8% of patients without risk factors
fact_text: CT scanning is 75% sensitive but not test of choice; ERCP, MRCP, and EUS are highly accurate for detecting CBD stones.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Cholangitis test: Sensitivity 11%, Specificity 99%, LR+ 18.3, LR- 0.93
Jaundice test: Sensitivity 36%, Specificity 97%, LR+ 10.1, LR- 0.69
Dilated CBD on ultrasound: Sensitivity 42%, Specificity 96%, LR+ 6.9, LR- 0.77
Elevated alkaline phosphatase: Sensitivity 57%, Specificity 86%, LR+ 2.6, LR- 0.65
Elevated amylase: Sensitivity 11%, Specificity 95%, LR+ 1.5, LR- 0.99
fact_text: Cholangitis and jaundice have high specificity and likelihood ratios for choledocholithiasis; dilated CBD and elevated alkaline phosphatase have moderate diagnostic value.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: ERCP for high-risk patients
MRCP or EUS for moderate-risk patients followed by selective ERCP
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy without preoperative CBD evaluation for low-risk patients
fact_text: Risk stratification guides management: ERCP for high-risk, MRCP/EUS then selective ERCP for moderate-risk, and surgery without CBD evaluation for low-risk patients.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic with >90% sensitivity and 99% specificity but carries 1-5% risk of pancreatitis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: EUS is highly sensitive and specific for CBD stones and can reduce ERCP use and complications when used selectively.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: MRCP is a noninvasive test visualizing CBD with 90-100% sensitivity and 88-100% specificity for CBD stones.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Start IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and hydration immediately
Urgent biliary drainage with ERCP in moderate to severe disease
Biliary drainage if no improvement in mild disease after 24 hours
Alternative drainage methods if ERCP unavailable
fact_text: Immediate antibiotics and hydration are essential; ERCP drainage is urgent in moderate/severe ascending cholangitis; alternative drainage if ERCP unavailable.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: history of prostate cancer treated with radiation therapy
recommended_tests: Postvoid residual by bladder scan or catheterization
fact_text: In patients with AKI and hypotension plus infection signs, initial testing should include FENa, urinalysis, BUN/creatinine ratio, urine specific gravity, and ultrasound to differentiate prerenal, ATN, and obstructive causes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Older age, atherosclerosis, chronic hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and certain drugs impair autoregulation of glomerular pressure, increasing AKI risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: 60% of patients who survive recover kidney function over 1-2 weeks
fact_text: 60% of patients surviving ATN recover kidney function within 1-2 weeks; CKD risk is higher in those with preexisting CKD or incomplete recovery.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: ATN accounts for 55-60% of AKI in hospitalized patients; mortality in hospitalized patients with ATN is 15-30%, rising to 40-60% in ICU patients.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: rise in serum creatinine ≥ 0.5 mg/dL or 25% increase from baseline within 48 hours after radiologic procedure
recommended_tests: Mehran Risk Score for contrast-induced AKI
fact_text: ATN is defined by a rise in serum creatinine ≥ 0.5 mg/dL or 25% increase within 48 hours after contrast; serum creatinine peaks at 3 days and may normalize by 10 days.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: ATN etiology includes ischemia from renal hypoperfusion, toxin exposure, and contrast-induced AKI.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: increased creatinine on routine laboratory testing
symptoms of volume overload (edema and dyspnea)
symptoms of uremia (such as anorexia, nausea, delirium, fatigue, and pruritus)
recommended_tests: postvoid residual by bladder scan or catheterization
fact_text: ATN is a common cause of AKI and presents with increased creatinine and symptoms of volume overload or uremia; urine studies and bladder scan help evaluate AKI.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Risk factors for increased mortality in ATN include male sex, advanced age, comorbid illness, malignancy, oliguria, sepsis, mechanical ventilation, multiorgan failure, and severity of illness.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: aki due to liver failure or heart failure
atn due to myoglobinuria or hemoglobinuria
trigger_evidence: FENa < 1% even though the patient has ATN
FENa > 2% even though the patient has prerenal AKI
fact_text: Unexpected FENa results can occur in specific clinical scenarios such as liver failure, heart failure, sepsis-associated AKI, contrast nephropathy, and use of diuretics, affecting interpretation of FENa in AKI diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Orthostatic vital signs: pulse increase > 30 bpm and systolic BP drop > 20 mm Hg have moderate specificity but poor sensitivity for hypovolemia
Dry axilla, dry mucous membranes of mouth and nose, and abnormal skin turgor in subclavicular area are best predictors of hypovolemia
Absence of abnormal skin turgor in subclavicular area and absence of longitudinal furrows on tongue reduce likelihood of hypovolemia
Combination of confusion, nonfluent speech, dry mucous membranes, dry/furrowed tongue, extremity weakness, and sunken eyes is highly predictive of hypovolemia
Patients can be hypovolemic without expected physical exam findings
fact_text: Dry axilla, dry mucous membranes, and abnormal subclavicular skin turgor are best physical exam predictors of hypovolemia; orthostatic vital signs have poor sensitivity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Specific gravity > 1.020 and urine osmolality > 500 mOsm/kg are associated with prerenal states
Osmolality can be falsely low in prerenal states due to impairment of concentrating ability from underlying CKD, osmotic diuresis, diabetes insipidus, or use of diuretics
BUN/creatinine ratio is classically > 20:1 in prerenal states but can be elevated with GI bleeding, corticosteroids, high-protein diet, or infection
BUN/creatinine ratio can be low in AKI secondary to rhabdomyolysis or decreased urea production due to malnutrition or advanced liver disease
fact_text: Urine specific gravity >1.020 and urine osmolality >500 mOsm/kg support prerenal AKI, but these can be affected by CKD, diuretics, and other conditions; BUN/creatinine ratio >20:1 is typical but not specific.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells are classic findings in ATN
No patients with prerenal AKI had > 10 granular casts/hpf or > 6 renal tubular epithelial cells/hpf
Granular casts/hpf has an LR+ of 4.35 for prerenal AKI diagnosis
6-10 granular casts/hpf has an LR+ of 9.68 for ATN diagnosis
> 10 granular casts/hpf is 100% specific for ATN
Hematuria suggests intrarenal or structural kidney disease and is not seen in prerenal AKI or ATN
fact_text: Granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells on urine microscopy help distinguish ATN from prerenal AKI; >10 granular casts/hpf is 100% specific for ATN.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Adjust doses of drugs for kidney impairment as necessary
recommended_advice: Discontinue nephrotoxic agents
Adjust drug doses for kidney impairment
fact_text: Treatment of AKI includes discontinuing nephrotoxic agents and adjusting drug doses for kidney impairment.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: acute urinary retention in older men
condition_aliases: neurologic diseases such as multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injury
acute urinary retention in older men
trigger_evidence: Older men with prostatic hypertrophy causing bladder neck obstruction
Seen in 10% of men in their 70s and up to 33% of men in their 80s
Risk increased with moderate to severe lower urinary tract symptoms
Postvoid residual volume > 30 mL by transrectal ultrasound
fact_text: Acute urinary retention in older men is most commonly caused by prostatic hypertrophy with bladder neck obstruction, especially with low urine flow and high postvoid residual volume.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Two-thirds of adult prostate is glandular, one-third fibromuscular
Smooth muscle of prostate, urethra, and bladder under alpha-1-adrenergic control
fact_text: BPH presents with urinary frequency, nocturia, reduced stream, and dribbling, caused by prostate enlargement and smooth muscle tone under alpha-1-adrenergic control.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Prostatic enlargement causes compression of periurethral area and bladder
Compression occurs due to physical enlargement and increased muscle tone
Increased muscle tone in urethra, prostatic fibromuscular tissue, and bladder neck
fact_text: Prostatic enlargement in BPH causes symptoms by compressing the periurethral area and bladder due to both physical enlargement and increased muscle tone.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: BPH is present in 80% of men in their seventies
Risk factors include increasing age, black race, obesity, diabetes mellitus, high alcohol consumption, physical inactivity
fact_text: Prostate size does not correlate with symptom severity; use IPSS to assess symptoms and response to therapy in BPH.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Cannot ascertain anterior or posterior extension or feel entire posterior surface
Prostate size is underestimated by 25-55% on digital rectal exam compared with transrectal ultrasound
fact_text: Digital rectal exam underestimates prostate size by 25-55% compared to transrectal ultrasound, especially with larger prostates.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Score 0-7 mild BPH; 8-19 moderate BPH; 20-35 severe BPH
fact_text: IPSS questionnaire scores urinary symptoms from 0 to 35 to classify BPH severity as mild, moderate, or severe.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Behavioral interventions advised for all men
Men with mild symptoms generally do not require pharmacologic treatment
Men with moderate or severe symptoms should be treated with pharmacotherapy
recommended_advice: Advise behavioral interventions: avoid fluids before bed or going out, reduce caffeine and alcohol, double voiding
Discontinue diuretics if possible
Use alpha-blockers (terazosin, doxazosin) to relax prostatic smooth muscle
Selective alpha-blockers (tamsulosin, alfuzosin) may have fewer BP effects
Use 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) to reduce prostate size and prevent testosterone conversion
Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) are also effective
Combination therapy with alpha-blocker and 5-alpha reductase inhibitor is more effective than monotherapy
fact_text: Behavioral interventions are first-line; pharmacotherapy with alpha-blockers and/or 5-alpha reductase inhibitors is recommended for moderate to severe BPH symptoms.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: worsening malaise, anorexia, confusion for 3 days
decreased energy and vague abdominal pain for 2 months
history of hypertension, BPH, colorectal cancer
lab results: Na 138, K 4.8, Cl 100, HCO3 20, BUN 90, creatinine 7.2 mg/dL (up from baseline 1.5)
recommended_advice: Stop NSAID medication if implicated
fact_text: In an elderly man with AKI, consider obstruction, NSAID use, and hypovolemia as leading differential diagnoses; use catheterization, bladder scan, postvoid residual, ultrasound, FE_Na, and BUN/creatinine ratio to differentiate causes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Also seen in shock, vascular lesions, severe ATN, or severe GN
fact_text: Anuria (<100 mL urine/day) suggests complete urinary tract obstruction but can also occur in shock, vascular lesions, severe ATN, or severe GN.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Right kidney 11 cm with marked hydronephrosis and ureteral dilation
Left kidney 7 cm with cortical atrophy
fact_text: A significant difference in kidney size on ultrasound suggests unilateral renal disease or obstruction, with the smaller kidney likely nonfunctional.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Upper ureter or renal pelvic lesions can cause flank pain
Obstruction must be bilateral to cause AKI
Incontinence and dribbling common if obstruction is urethral
recommended_tests: Renal ultrasound as first test to look for obstruction
Noncontrast CT to detect sites missed by ultrasound
recommended_advice: Relieve obstruction immediately
Indwelling urinary catheter for bladder neck obstruction
Suprapubic catheter if indwelling urinary not possible
Percutaneous nephrostomy tubes for ureteral obstruction
Ureteral stents if accessible
fact_text: Renal ultrasound is the best initial test for urinary tract obstruction; relief of obstruction should be immediate using catheterization or nephrostomy as needed.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Specificity 65-84% for detecting urinary tract obstruction
recommended_tests: Noncontrast CT scan if ultrasound negative but suspicion remains
fact_text: Renal ultrasound has high sensitivity (90-98%) and moderate specificity (65-84%) for urinary tract obstruction; noncontrast CT can detect obstruction missed by ultrasound.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Rapid decompression of bladder can rarely cause hematuria and hypotension
recommended_advice: Relieve obstruction immediately
Use indwelling urinary catheter for bladder neck obstruction
Use suprapubic catheter if indwelling catheter not possible
Use percutaneous nephrostomy tubes for ureteral obstruction
Use ureteral stents if accessible
fact_text: Immediate relief of urinary tract obstruction is essential; indwelling catheters or nephrostomy tubes are used depending on obstruction site, but rapid bladder decompression may cause hematuria or hypotension.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Stop NSAIDs
Renal biopsy if needed
fact_text: Table 28-7 lists NSAID-induced renal hypoperfusion, interstitial nephritis, and active infection as leading diagnostic hypotheses for AKI, with corresponding risk factors, tests, and treatments.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: AKI caused by NSAIDs is usually asymptomatic and most commonly detected by increased serum creatinine.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: NSAID-induced AKI can occur with nonselective NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors; renal prostaglandins are important in autoregulation of glomerular pressure and GFR.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Urinalysis: 1+ protein, 3 RBCs/hpf, 5-10 WBCs/hpf, no casts
recommended_advice: Stop NSAIDs
fact_text: NSAID-induced renal hypoperfusion typically presents with mild proteinuria, hematuria, pyuria, normal renal ultrasound, and fractional excretion of sodium around 1.5%.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Elevated serum creatinine (1.1 mg/dL baseline, now 1.4 mg/dL)
recommended_tests: Serum Na, K, HCO3, BUN, creatinine
Urine Na and fractional excretion of sodium (FE_Na)
recommended_advice: Stop NSAID medication
Monitor renal function
fact_text: NSAID-induced renal hypoperfusion is a leading hypothesis for AKI in a patient with recent NSAID use, elevated creatinine, and no urinary symptoms; stopping NSAIDs and measuring FE_Na and urine electrolytes help confirm diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Common clinical features of acute interstitial nephritis include arthralgias (45%), fever (36%), rash (22%), non-nephrotic proteinuria (93%), pyuria (82%), microscopic hematuria (67%), eosinophilia (35%), gross hematuria (5%), nephrotic range proteinuria (2.5%), and complete nephrotic syndrome (0.8%).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: classic findings include AKI, hematuria, pyuria with WBC casts, fever, eosinophilia
fact_text: AIN presents with AKI, hematuria, pyuria with WBC casts, fever, and eosinophilia; drug-induced AIN accounts for at least 66% of cases.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: most patients improve within 6-8 weeks and return to baseline kidney function
fact_text: Most patients with acute interstitial nephritis improve within 6-8 weeks and return to baseline kidney function.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: renal prostaglandins not important in normal kidneys
seen within 3-7 days of starting therapy
recommended_advice: stop NSAID exposure
fact_text: NSAID-induced renal hypoperfusion causes reversible AKI seen within 3-7 days of starting therapy and improves after stopping NSAIDs.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Blood cultures if suspect ascending cholangitis
recommended_advice: Cholecystectomy after inflammation resolves in patients with ascending cholangitis
fact_text: No clinical finding is sufficiently sensitive to rule out acute cholecystitis; diagnosis relies on combination of clinical signs, lab tests, and ultrasound.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Pain in epigastrium radiating to the back
15-25% idiopathic cases possibly due to microlithiasis or sphincter of Oddi dysfunction
fact_text: Acute pancreatitis often presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back and is commonly caused by alcohol abuse or microlithiasis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Radioisotope excreted by liver into biliary system
Nonvisualization suggests cystic duct obstruction with 96% sensitivity and 90% specificity
Nonvisualization can also be seen in prolonged fasting, hepatitis, alcohol abuse, prior biliary sphincterotomy
fact_text: HIDA scan nonvisualization of gallbladder is highly sensitive and specific for acute cholecystitis but can be false positive in fasting or liver disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Timing of surgery depends on severity and medical risk
recommended_advice: Admission
Parenteral antibiotics
Cholecystectomy
fact_text: Acute cholecystitis treatment includes admission, parenteral antibiotics, and cholecystectomy with timing based on severity and risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: acute onset of hematuria with red cell casts, proteinuria, elevated creatinine, hypertension, edema
fact_text: Acute GN is caused by immunologically mediated proliferative glomerular disease presenting as nephritic syndrome with hematuria, proteinuria, elevated creatinine, hypertension, and edema; complement testing is important for diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: AKI in rhabdomyolysis results from myoglobin-induced proximal tubule cytotoxicity, distal tubular obstruction by myoglobin precipitation, intrarenal vasoconstriction due to volume depletion, and activation of renal vascular mediators.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: AKI is a serious complication of rhabdomyolysis, occurring in 7-10% of cases in the US, with incidence 13-50% in patients using illicit drugs or alcohol or with multiple causes; survival is about 80% with most recovering kidney function.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: systemic diseases with proteinuria and kidney failure (amyloidosis, myeloma, sarcoidosis)
recommended_advice: Avoid kidney biopsy in multiple cysts, solitary kidney, acute pyelonephritis, uncontrolled blood pressure, uncontrolled bleeding diathesis, uremia, uncooperative patient, obesity (relative contraindication)
fact_text: Kidney biopsy is indicated for nephrotic syndrome, systemic diseases with proteinuria and kidney failure, unclear acute kidney injury, and kidney transplant evaluation; contraindications include multiple cysts, solitary kidney, acute pyelonephritis, uncontrolled blood pressure or bleeding diathesis, uremia, uncooperative patient, and obesity (relative).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Rhabdomyolysis presents with muscle pain, weakness, dark urine, and elevated serum creatine kinase levels.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: exertion (strenuous exercise, seizures, alcohol withdrawal syndrome)
muscle hypoxia (limb compression, major artery occlusion)
infections (influenza, coxsackievirus, epstein-barr virus, hiv, legionella, streptococcus pyogenes, staphylococcus aureus, clostridium, tick-borne infections)
metabolic (hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypocalcemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, nonketotic hyperosmotic conditions)
body temperature changes (heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia, malignant neuroleptic syndrome, hypothermia)
fact_text: Causes of rhabdomyolysis include trauma, exertion, muscle hypoxia, infections, metabolic disturbances, drugs/toxins, body temperature changes, genetic defects, and idiopathic causes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: AKI diagnosis clues include pigmented granular casts, low BUN/creatinine ratio, oliguria, FE_Na <1%, and common electrolyte abnormalities.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis presents with asthma, eosinophilia, granulomatous vasculitis, tissue eosinophilic infiltration, occurs in 30s-40s, mild renal involvement.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Goodpasture syndrome presents with abrupt oliguria, hematuria, kidney dysfunction, 100% anti-GBM antibody positive, bimodal age distribution, ESRD develops in 30%.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis involves upper/lower respiratory tract and GN, >90% cANCA positive, can precede systemic vasculitis onset, 33-50% have eye disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Microscopic polyangiitis presents with constitutional symptoms, hematuria, proteinuria; 50-75% pANCA positive, renal involvement in 80%, pulmonary involvement in 20-55%.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Classic presentation of renal artery thrombosis includes severe flank pain, hematuria, nausea, vomiting, fever, and hypertension.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: sle, poststreptococcal, membranoproliferative, endocarditis, visceral abscesses, shunt nephritis

fact_text: Post-streptococcal GN is the most common postinfectious GN, occurs 10-14 days after infection with nephritogenic group A beta-hemolytic streptococci; supportive treatment only.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Vascular causes of AKI include renal artery thrombosis, thromboembolism, and atheroembolism; these are rare but serious.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Aggressive fluid repletion
Use isotonic or half-normal saline hydration
Alternate saline and bicarbonate if urine pH < 6.5
fact_text: Aggressive fluid repletion with isotonic or half-normal saline is essential in AKI; alternate saline and bicarbonate if urine pH < 6.5 to avoid metabolic acidosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Atheroembolism presents as abrupt kidney injury after an inciting event with 3 syndromes: abrupt injury, subacute worsening, and chronic impairment; risk factors include male sex, age >60, hypertension, smoking, diabetes, and vascular disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: endocarditis, hepatitis b, hemolytic uremic syndrome
fact_text: Hypocomplementemia patterns vary by glomerular disease, with classical pathway activation in lupus nephritis and mixed essential cryoglobulinemia, alternative pathway activation in poststreptococcal GN and related conditions, and reduced complement synthesis in acquired cases.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Nephrectomy if renal infarction occurs
Revascularization or thrombolysis
Observation and medical management sometimes
fact_text: Most patients with renal artery thromboembolism have flank pain with hematuria or anuria; angiogram is gold standard for diagnosis; treatment includes nephrectomy if infarction, revascularization, or medical management.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Kidney or skin biopsy can be used for diagnosis

Best treatment approach beyond supportive therapy is unknown
Avoid anticoagulation
Consider aggressive lipid management
fact_text: Contrast-induced acute kidney injury diagnosis may involve kidney or skin biopsy or fundoscopy; treatment includes avoiding anticoagulation and considering aggressive lipid management, with best approach beyond supportive therapy unknown.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

hypersensitivity syndromes (stevens-johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis)

Presence of comedones, papules, pustules, nodules

fact_text: Acne vulgaris is the leading hypothesis for folliculopapular eruptions with comedones on face, chest, and back in adolescents and young adults; diagnosis is clinical.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Perioral dermatitis presents as monomorphic fine erythematous papules clustered around the mouth; diagnosis is clinical.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Presence of telangiectasias and possibly inflammatory papules
fact_text: Rosacea is an active alternative diagnosis characterized by flushing, telangiectasias, and inflammatory papules in fair-skinned individuals; diagnosis is clinical.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

recommended_tests: Work-up for hyperandrogenism if signs of polycystic ovary disease, virilization, or atypical presentation
recommended_advice: Identify and remedy acne precipitants
Use gentle skin care techniques
Minimize use of moisturizers and cosmetics

Medical therapy aimed at decreasing sebum production, desquamation, and inflammation

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Gradual development of telangiectasias and persistent centrofacial erythema
Inflammatory red papules and papulopustules may be present
fact_text: Rosacea presents with facial telangiectasias, persistent centrofacial erythema, inflammatory papules without comedones, and history of flushing, distinguishing it from acne.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Medical therapy is aimed at the 3 factors involved in acne development: sebum production, desquamation, inflammation
recommended_advice: Topical retinoids (tretinoin, adapalene, tazarotene)
Topical antibiotics (erythromycin, clindamycin, metronidazole, benzoyl peroxide)
Systemic antibiotics (tetracycline, macrolide, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole)
Oral contraceptives for women with strong hormonal component
Spironolactone for adult women with recalcitrant acne
fact_text: Acne treatment includes topical retinoids, topical and systemic antibiotics, and hormonal therapies such as oral contraceptives and spironolactone in women.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Use isotretinoin for nodular cystic acne with caution and appropriate contraception
fact_text: Isotretinoin is reserved for nodular cystic acne and requires experienced prescribers and effective contraception due to teratogenicity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Histopathology is rarely necessary and often nonspecific
fact_text: Rosacea diagnosis is clinical; histopathology is rarely needed and often nonspecific.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Rosacea is characterized by centrofacial persistent facial erythema, telangiectasias, and inflammatory papules and papulopustules.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: rash may worsen with sun exposure
ingestion of spicy foods and thermally hot foods/liquids
fact_text: Rosacea rash may worsen with sun exposure, ingestion of spicy or hot foods/liquids, emotional stress, and exercise.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Rosacea is most common in fair-skinned individuals of northern European descent but can be seen in people with darker skin as well
Women are more commonly affected than men
Complicated disease with sebaceous gland hyperplasia and rhinophyma occurs more often in men
fact_text: Rosacea is more common in fair-skinned northern European descent individuals and women, but complicated forms with sebaceous gland hyperplasia and rhinophyma occur more often in men.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Avoidance of triggers of flushing including sun exposure, spicy and hot foods/liquids, emotional stress
Systemic agents: oral antibiotics of tetracycline class for severe inflammatory lesions
Laser treatment to ablate telangiectasias and improve background erythema
recommended_advice: Sun protection
Avoid triggers of flushing
Topical metronidazole, brimonidine, ivermectin
Oral tetracycline antibiotics for severe inflammation
Laser treatment for telangiectasias and rhinophyma
fact_text: Rosacea treatment includes sun protection, avoidance of flushing triggers, topical metronidazole/brimonidine/ivermectin, oral tetracycline antibiotics for severe cases, and laser treatment for telangiectasias and rhinophyma.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

recommended_tests: Clinical diagnosis for bullous arthropod bites
Skin biopsy and direct immunofluorescence for bullous pemphigoid
fact_text: Differential diagnosis of vesicular rash includes VZV (diagnosed clinically with Tzanck smear/PCR), bullous impetigo (bacterial culture), bullous arthropod bites (clinical), bullous pemphigoid (skin biopsy and immunofluorescence), and Stevens-Johnson syndrome (skin biopsy).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: involvement of first division of trigeminal nerve
vesicles on tip of the nose
fact_text: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus occurs with involvement of the first trigeminal division, especially if vesicles appear on the tip of the nose, and carries a high risk of corneal damage.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: rash over a single, unilateral dermatome
small, tightly grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
lesions become pustular and then crusted
new lesions may appear for up to 7 days
fact_text: VZV (Herpes Zoster) usually presents as a unilateral dermatomal rash with small grouped vesicles on an erythematous base that become pustular and crusted; diagnosis is usually clinical, supported by Tzanck smear or PCR.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Drugs commonly associated with pancreatitis include azathioprine, didanosine, estrogens, furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide, L-asparaginase, metronidazole, opioids, pentamidine, sulfonamides, corticosteroids, tamoxifen, tetracycline, and valproate.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Idiopathic pancreatitis is often due to gallstones or sphincter of Oddi dysfunction; other causes include drugs, trauma, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, infections, pancreatic carcinoma, autoimmune pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, and organ transplantation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Trypsinogen is activated to trypsin in pancreatitis, triggering pancreatic enzyme activation and inflammation; interleukins contribute to inflammation and systemic effects.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: biliary colic, cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, ascending cholangitis, pancreatitis

fact_text: For acute RUQ or epigastric pain, use clinical features and liver tests to guide RUQ ultrasound and further imaging (HIDA scan, EUS, MRCP, ERCP) to diagnose biliary colic, cholecystitis, or choledocholithiasis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: inactivated recombinant vaccine approved for use in the United States
vaccine efficacy 97.2% in patients over age 50
vaccine also effective in older patients (70-79 years 90%, 80+ years 89%)
vaccine recommended for patients over age 50
vaccine should be given 6-12 months after episode
recommended_advice: vaccinate patients over age 50 regardless of chickenpox history
administer vaccine 6-12 months after varicella zoster episode
fact_text: An inactivated recombinant vaccine is recommended for patients over age 50 to prevent varicella zoster; it is effective and should be given 6-12 months after an episode.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: develops on grossly intact skin due to local toxin production
lesions commonly on moist, intertriginous skin
most common superficial skin infection in infants and young children
fact_text: Bullous impetigo presents as flaccid bullae on intact skin, commonly in children, often in intertriginous areas, and is a superficial skin infection caused by local toxin production.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Postherpetic neuralgia is a common and potentially severe neuropathic pain syndrome, especially in the elderly.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Tzanck smear can support but not distinguish VZV from HSV
recommended_tests: viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of vesicle fluid
fact_text: Varicella zoster diagnosis is usually clinical; PCR of vesicle fluid is useful if diagnosis is uncertain; Tzanck smear supports but cannot distinguish VZV from HSV.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

antiviral drugs not beneficial if rash present >72 hours
recommended_advice: supportive care with pain relievers
antiviral agents (acyclovir, famciclovir, valacyclovir) within 72 hours
evaluate eye involvement with ophthalmologist
symptomatic care with soaks and topical antipruritics
fact_text: Varicella zoster treatment is supportive; antiviral agents are most effective if started within 72 hours of rash onset; antiviral drugs are not beneficial if rash present for more than 72 hours.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: histopathology showing edema, subepidermal blister, dermal inflammatory infiltrate with eosinophils
fact_text: Diagnosis of bullous arthropod bites is clinical; histopathology may show edema, subepidermal blister, and dermal eosinophilic infiltrate but is rarely necessary.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Avoid future bites with protective clothing and insect repellants
Eradicate source of biting insects (pets, nests)
fact_text: Bullous arthropod bites present as large tense blisters on exposed skin, are pruritic, and result from hypersensitivity to insect saliva; diagnosis is clinical; treatment includes avoidance and eradication of biting insects.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: blister fluid or moist edge of crusted plaque
recommended_advice: Oral antibiotics active against S aureus for bullous impetigo
fact_text: Diagnosis of bullous impetigo is clinical; culture of blister fluid or moist edge of crusted plaque may confirm diagnosis; oral antibiotics active against S aureus should be prescribed.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Consider possibility of MRSA
Localized nonbullous impetigo may be treated with topical antibiotics: bacitracin, polymyxin, mupirocin

Recurrent infections may indicate staphylococcal carriage; consider eradication measures including daily washing with chlorhexidine gluconate, intranasal mupirocin ointment, oral rifampin and doxycycline
fact_text: Treatment includes oral antibiotics for bullous impetigo; topical antibiotics for localized nonbullous impetigo; consider MRSA and eradication measures for recurrent infections.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: tense bullae arising on skin that may be normal, erythematous, or urticarial
lesions often begin on lower extremities and progress upward
autoantibodies target components of the epidermal basement membrane zone
recommended_tests: Histopathology showing subepidermal blister plane and eosinophils
Immunopathology demonstrating linear deposits of IgG and C3 at dermal-epidermal junction
Circulating IgG recognizing basement membrane zone in 70-80% of patients
recommended_advice: Topical potent corticosteroids
Systemic corticosteroids for extensive disease
Steroid-sparing immunosuppressives to limit toxicity
Alternative anti-inflammatory agents like tetracycline and nicotinamide
Consider plasmapheresis, intravenous gammaglobulin, or rituximab for refractory cases
fact_text: Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense bullae and urticarial plaques, confirmed by histopathology and immunopathology, and treated with corticosteroids and immunosuppressives.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: patient taking a potentially causative medication
rash develops on chest and face after about 1 week of symptoms
flaccid bullae and vesicles develop centrally within preexisting target lesions
bullae rapidly erode leaving red and raw skin
fact_text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome presents with fever and a rapidly evolving blistering rash on chest and face, often after exposure to causative medication.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: stevens-johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
condition_aliases: stevens-johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
fact_text: Medications most commonly implicated include sulfonamide antibiotics, ampicillins, quinolones, cephalosporins, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, valproic acid, piroxicam, allopurinol, and corticosteroids.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: stevens-johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
condition_aliases: stevens-johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
trigger_evidence: Prodromal symptoms: fever, malaise, headache, myalgias, GI and respiratory complaints
Rash starts on face and trunk as pink to red macules and papules
Rash may spread and evolve rapidly with targetoid lesions and coalescing plaques
Flaccid bullae and vesicles develop centrally
Blisters form and rupture leaving raw red skin with gray-white pseudomembrane
Mucous membrane lesions may precede or accompany skin rash
fact_text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis present with prodromal systemic symptoms and a rapidly evolving rash with targetoid lesions, flaccid bullae, and mucous membrane involvement.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: stevens-johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
condition_aliases: stevens-johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis

fact_text: Histopathology supports diagnosis by showing epidermal necrosis with minimal inflammation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: stevens-johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
condition_aliases: stevens-johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis
recommended_advice: Discontinue offending drug
Provide supportive care in a burn unit
Surveillance for secondary infection
Consider immunomodulating drugs early in disease course (benefit unconfirmed)
Systemic corticosteroids use is controversial
fact_text: Treatment includes stopping the offending drug, supportive care in a burn unit, infection surveillance, and cautious consideration of immunomodulating drugs and corticosteroids.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
