Face, ears, and scalp may be involved
Lesions may localize to sites of minor skin trauma or scrapes
Eruption persists for 3–4 months and then remits spontaneously
Frequently preceded by streptococcal throat infection
Increased risk of psoriasis vulgaris in next 3–5 years
Increased incidence of psoriasis in families
fact_text: Guttate psoriasis presents as small, round or oval silvery-scaled lesions on trunk and back, often after streptococcal throat infection, with lesions lasting 3–4 months and increased risk of chronic psoriasis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Pattern of small papules and plaques with points suggesting guttate psoriasis
Scale confluent over surface of lesions
Nummular dermatitis is usually on extremities with pruritus
Secondary syphilis involves palms and soles with thinner plaques without adherent scale
fact_text: Differential diagnosis of papulosquamous eruption includes guttate psoriasis, pityriasis rosea, tinea corporis, nummular dermatitis, and secondary syphilis; clinical features and targeted tests help distinguish them.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Discrete small red papules and plaques with adherent silvery scale
recommended_tests: Identification of fungus with KOH or culture
fact_text: Guttate psoriasis is the leading hypothesis for papulosquamous eruption after acute pharyngitis with discrete small red papules and plaques with silvery scale; important tests include morphology and throat culture.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Remission can be hastened with UV light treatments
If infectious trigger present, give appropriate antibiotics
Topical corticosteroids effective on individual lesions
Avoid systemic corticosteroids due to flare risk
Topical calcipotriene (vitamin D derivative) also effective
fact_text: Guttate psoriasis is a self-limited eruption often triggered by pharyngitis; treatment includes UV light, topical corticosteroids, and possibly antibiotics if infection is present.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Prodrome of malaise, nausea, headache, low-grade fever
Common worldwide, no genetic or racial predilection

Condition resolves in 8-12 weeks
Symptomatic treatment with antihistamines or low potency topical corticosteroids if pruritus present
UVB phototherapy may decrease severity but can worsen postinflammatory pigmentation
fact_text: Pityriasis rosea presents with herald patch and multiple oval plaques; diagnosis is clinical and self-limited, with symptomatic treatment for pruritus.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Overlying scale common, more prominent at border

Systemic antibiotics if secondary infection present
Antihistamines to relieve pruritus
Skin care with bathing practices and emollients
fact_text: Nummular dermatitis presents as pruritic coin-shaped lesions; diagnosis by clinical features and ruling out tinea; treatment includes topical steroids and skin care.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Systemic therapy for hair-bearing sites
fact_text: Microscopic KOH exam and culture confirm Tinea corporis; treatment includes topical and systemic antifungals based on infection extent.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Chronic urticaria (>6 weeks) can be idiopathic or associated with systemic diseases including collagen vascular disease, malignancy, parasitosis, and chronic infection.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Urticaria presents as transient, itchy, red, elevated papules and plaques resolving within 24 hours; differential includes erythema multiforme, insect bites, and bullous pemphigoid.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Consider combination H1-blockers if needed
Add H2-blockers in refractory cases

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Skin biopsy to assess vessel involvement and inflammation
Immunofluorescence or histologic studies for antibody and complement deposits

fact_text: Purpura and petechiae are nonblanching capillary hemorrhages; evaluation includes platelet and coagulation studies, skin biopsy, and immunofluorescence; treatment targets underlying vessel damage and supportive care.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

large tumors can be locally destructive

fact_text: Basal cell carcinoma typically presents as a flesh-colored, translucent or slightly red papule or nodule with rolled border, often friable and bleeding; histologic evaluation is gold standard for diagnosis; Mohs surgery offers lowest recurrence and tissue sparing.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor in humans
Metastasis from basal cell carcinoma is rare
fact_text: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor in humans and rarely metastasizes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Fair-skinned patients with basal cell carcinoma have a high risk (up to 45%) of developing subsequent tumors within 5 years; most tumors occur on sun-exposed skin.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Squamous cell carcinoma presents as firm nodules or plaques that may ulcerate or bleed, often arising from actinic keratoses on sun-exposed skin; in situ lesions are sharply demarcated erythematous scaling plaques.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Exposure to UV light, chronic wounds, immunosuppression, arsenic exposure are risk factors
fact_text: Risk factors for basal cell carcinoma include UV light exposure, chronic wounds, immunosuppression, and arsenic exposure.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Liver biochemical tests with significant elevations of bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, ALT, or AST

fact_text: Lipase > 3 times upper limit of normal is 79% sensitive and 89% specific for pancreatitis; amylase is 72% sensitive and 93% specific; liver tests with significant elevations suggest pancreatitis secondary to gallstones.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Calcium and triglycerides should be ordered to exclude less common causes of acute pancreatitis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Use in patients with severe pancreatitis is controversial
fact_text: ERCP may cause pancreatitis and should be limited to patients with persistent obstruction or cholangitis; its use in severe pancreatitis is controversial.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Preoperative patients with GAP should have CBD evaluation by ERCP, MRCP, or EUS; ERCP is done if stones are found.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: EUS is superior to MRCP for idiopathic pancreatitis, especially for microlithiasis and sludge, with sensitivity 88–96% vs 24% for MRCP.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Abdominal CT is 87–90% sensitive and 90–92% specific for diagnosis of acute pancreatitis
fact_text: Abdominal CT is highly sensitive and specific for acute pancreatitis diagnosis; should be done if diagnosis unclear or complications suspected; IV contrast needed to show necrosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Plain radiography useful to rule out free air or SBO
Transabdominal ultrasound noninvasive and should be performed in all patients with pancreatitis
fact_text: Plain radiography helps rule out free air or SBO; transabdominal ultrasound is noninvasive and should be done in all pancreatitis patients to detect gallstones or CBD dilation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Patients with GAP have high risk of recurrent pancreatitis
recommended_advice: cholecystectomy
fact_text: Patients with GAP have a high risk of recurrent pancreatitis and require cholecystectomy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: Melanoma typically presents as a dark brown or black macule or papule with pigment variation and irregular borders, often on middle-aged persons.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Melanoma subtypes include superficial spreading, nodular, lentiginous, and amelanotic melanoma, with nodular melanoma being the second most common type.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: blue-black, reddish, purplish, or nonpigmented papule or nodule
fact_text: Nodular melanoma often presents on head, neck, or trunk, evolves rapidly over months, and appears as blue-black, reddish, purplish, or nonpigmented papule or nodule.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Eradication of tumor with least disability
Careful evaluation for metastatic disease
Surgical excision
Mohs micrographic surgery
Electrosurgery
Radiation therapy
Local immunotherapy

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Squamous cell carcinoma has about 3% local recurrence risk; metastasis occurs in up to 10% of patients, especially with certain risk factors like location and immunosuppression.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Lentigo maligna melanoma is a rare melanoma type in elderly on sun-exposed head and neck, presenting as flat tumor with irregular borders and color variation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Sun exposure before age 18, light skin pigmentation, freckling, and dysplastic nevi increase melanoma risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Whites have 26 times higher melanoma risk than blacks; familial melanoma accounts for 8-12% of cases with higher risk if 2+ first-degree relatives affected.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Full-thickness incisional or punch biopsy if lesion too large or in sensitive location
fact_text: Excisional biopsy is preferred for melanoma diagnosis; full-thickness incisional or punch biopsy used if lesion too large or in sensitive area.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Assessment of tumor thickness and ulceration
fact_text: Melanoma staging uses TNM system focusing on tumor thickness, ulceration, lymph nodes, and metastases.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

Sentinel lymph node mapping to reduce complications with full lymph node dissection
Adjuvant treatment for advanced disease

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

recommended_advice: Educate patients on UV exposure risks and sun protection.
Encourage routine self-skin exams.
Teach patients the ABCDE criteria for mole evaluation.
fact_text: Melanoma prevention includes patient education on UV risks, sun protection, and routine self-skin exams using ABCDE criteria.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Folliculopapular eruptions: Acne - presents in adolescence with waxing and waning lesions including inflammatory papules, pustules, comedones, and nodulocysts; distribution: face, chest, and back.
Rosacea - presents in adults with telangiectasias and persistent centrofacial erythema, occasionally with inflammatory red papules and papulopustules; distribution: face.
Blistering disorders: Herpes zoster - closely grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, single unilateral dermatome, lesions become pustular then crust over 7-10 days.
Bullous impetigo - flaccid, transparent bullae that rupture easily, shallow moist erosion, usually in children; distribution: intertriginous areas.
Bullous arthropod bites - cluster of large, tense blisters on exposed skin, most common on extremities.
Bullous pemphigoid - seen in elderly, sudden onset of 1-2 cm tense blisters and bright red urticarial plaques, begins on lower extremities and progresses upward.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome - targetoid or macular patches with dusky centers that blister and erode, skin is excoriatingly tender, lips typically eroded and covered with hemorrhagic crust; begins on chest and face and then spreads, palms and soles often involved, mucosal surfaces may be involved.

fact_text: LV failure signs suggest ventricular tachycardia from heart failure; echocardiogram, event monitor, ILR, and EPS are recommended.

fact_text: LV hypertrophy on ECG suggests ventricular tachycardia from heart failure, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or aortic stenosis; echocardiogram, monitoring, and EPS are recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
