source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Wheezing and dyspnea symptoms have high specificity (95-98%) but moderate sensitivity (37-65%) for asthma diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Patient education
Control environmental factors and comorbid conditions such as tobacco use, air pollution, GERD, allergens, and infections
fact_text: Control of environmental factors and comorbid conditions is critical to prevent asthma exacerbations.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Diagnosis of asthma is supported by decreased FEV1, decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, and reversibility defined as ≥200 mL increase in FEV1 and >12% improvement with bronchodilators.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Chest radiography is useful mainly to exclude other diseases in patients suspected of asthma.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Methacholine challenge is useful for diagnosing or excluding asthma in patients with normal pulmonary function tests; a decrease in FEV1 of <20% has a 95% negative predictive value.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Spirometry is recommended for patients with suspected asthma to aid diagnosis and management.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Use a stepwise approach to manage intermittent and persistent asthma
Consider escalation of therapy if short-acting beta-2-agonists are used more than twice a week
fact_text: Asthma treatment follows a stepwise approach from short-acting beta-2-agonists to high-dose inhaled corticosteroids plus oral corticosteroids, with omalizumab consideration for allergies.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: PEF and spirometry to assess pulmonary function
recommended_advice: Prevent chronic symptoms (dyspnea, exercise intolerance, nighttime wakening)
Maintain normal pulmonary function
Maintain normal levels of physical activity
Prevent exacerbations
fact_text: Goals of asthma therapy include preventing chronic symptoms, maintaining normal pulmonary function and physical activity, and preventing exacerbations.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Patients with risk factors for asthma-related death require special attention and consideration for hospitalization
Patients should monitor their own disease and know when to seek physician care
fact_text: Asthma exacerbations require assessment of duration, precipitants, and severity; patients with risk factors for asthma-related death need special attention and possible hospitalization.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In asthma exacerbation, decreased wheezing can indicate either worsening or improving airflow obstruction depending on associated respiratory distress and breath sounds.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Step down therapy when control is achieved
Consider inhaled tiotropium for poorly controlled asthma despite corticosteroids and long-acting beta-2 agonists
fact_text: Refractory asthma may be due to poor adherence, untreated precipitants, or other diseases; step down therapy when controlled and consider inhaled tiotropium if poorly controlled.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Use short-acting beta-2 agonists for immediate relief
Use inhaled corticosteroids for long-term therapy
Use long-acting beta-2 agonists only when inhaled corticosteroids have not adequately controlled symptoms
Consider omalizumab for patients with allergies and asthma not controlled by inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting beta-2 agonists
Consider leukotriene antagonists as another option for patients with allergies and poorly controlled asthma

Consider mepolizumab and reslizumab for patients with allergies and asthma not controlled by inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting beta-2 agonists, especially with multiple asthma exacerbations over the past year
Use systemic corticosteroids for immediate therapy of exacerbations or long-term therapy in patients with refractory asthma
Theophylline is similar to long-acting beta-2 agonists but used less frequently
fact_text: Asthma pharmacotherapy includes short-acting beta-2 agonists for immediate relief, inhaled corticosteroids for long-term therapy, and biologics like omalizumab for refractory allergic asthma.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: severe asthma exacerbation with respiratory fatigue
trigger_evidence: ABGs are useful in patients whose peak flows are not improving with treatment
ABGs during severe exacerbations should reveal a respiratory alkalosis
A respiratory acidosis (or even a normal PCO2 during a severe exacerbation) is very worrisome because it suggests severe airway narrowing and respiratory fatigue
fact_text: ABGs are useful in severe asthma exacerbations not improving with treatment; respiratory acidosis or normal PCO2 indicates severe airway narrowing and respiratory fatigue.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Mild - moderate exacerbation based on symptoms, signs, and PEF/FEV1 ≥ 40% of predicted
Severe exacerbation based on symptoms, signs, and PEF/FEV1 < 40% of predicted
recommended_advice: Mild-moderate: treat with oxygen, inhaled beta-2-agonists, possibly oral corticosteroids
Severe: treat with oxygen, inhaled beta-2-agonists and ipratropium, oral corticosteroids
Impending/actual arrest: intubate and treat with oxygen, inhaled beta-2-agonists and ipratropium, IV corticosteroids
Probable discharge home with beta-2-agonists, oral corticosteroids and initiation or escalation of inhaled corticosteroids if good response
Hospital admission if incomplete response
Intensive care unit admission if poor response
fact_text: Asthma exacerbation management is guided by severity assessed by symptoms, signs, and PEF/FEV1, with treatment escalating from inhaled beta-2-agonists and corticosteroids to intubation and ICU admission based on response.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Chest radiograph is only helpful for identifying the uncommon concomitant infection or complication (eg, pneumothorax)
fact_text: Chest radiograph is useful mainly to identify uncommon complications like pneumothorax during asthma exacerbations.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: A mild exacerbation is defined by symptoms only with activity and a FEV1 or PEF ≥ 70% of predicted
A moderate exacerbation includes symptoms with usual activities and a FEV1 or PEF 40–69% of predicted
In a severe exacerbation, patients have dyspnea at rest and dyspnea that interferes with conversation and a FEV1 or PEF < 40% of predicted
fact_text: Spirometry is crucial for determining asthma exacerbation severity, with thresholds of FEV1 or PEF defining mild (≥70%), moderate (40–69%), and severe (<40%) exacerbations.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: patient improved with low-dose inhaled corticosteroids
able to wean medications after removing carpets
fact_text: Improvement with inhaled corticosteroids and symptom worsening after stopping them supports asthma diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: absence of wheezing on exam does not exclude asthma
presence of exacerbating factors and spirometry results
fact_text: Asthma diagnosis is supported by history of wheezing, childhood asthma, and spirometry; absence of wheezing on exam does not exclude asthma.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: no improvement with beta-agonists and inhaled corticosteroids
PVCM is episodic adduction of vocal cords producing stridor
PVCM does not respond to traditional asthma therapy
fact_text: PVCM should be considered in patients with episodic wheezing or stridor, hoarseness, and no response to asthma therapy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: history of angioedema or risk factors
fact_text: Angioedema presents with acute swelling of soft tissues and often a history of angioedema or risk factors; bowel edema may cause abdominal pain.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Laryngoscopy demonstrating abnormal vocal cord movement
Identification of esophageal and laryngeal abnormalities on endoscopy
Clinical presentation with or without risk factors
fact_text: PVCM diagnosis is supported by laryngoscopy showing abnormal vocal cord movement and must be differentiated from asthma, GERD, and angioedema.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: lack of response to asthma medications
occasional resolution of symptoms during sleep
presence of voice pathology during attacks
preponderance of auscultatory findings in the neck
recommended_advice: Speech therapy focusing on laryngeal relaxation is most effective
Psychiatric intervention if psychiatric illness is present
Acute attacks may be managed with helium/oxygen mixtures (utility uncertain) and instructing patient to lay tongue on floor of mouth and breathe through pursed lips
fact_text: PVCM diagnosis is suggested by lack of asthma triggers, poor response to asthma meds, inspiratory stridor, and confirmed by laryngoscopy; speech therapy is the most effective treatment.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: PVCM can be confused with asthma due to episodic airflow obstruction and stridor
PVCM most commonly occurs in patients younger than 35 years
PVCM associated with anxiety, psychiatric conditions, exercise, airway injury, GERD, neurologic injury
fact_text: PVCM occurs mostly in younger females, often linked to anxiety and other conditions, and shows normal lung function tests during asymptomatic periods.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Angioedema most commonly presents as swelling of lips, tongue, or both
fact_text: Angioedema typically presents as swelling of the lips, tongue, or both.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: nonhistamine-related angioedema (bradykinin-mediated, ace inhibitor therapy, c1-inhibitor deficiency)
trigger_evidence: Onset usually rapid, over minutes to hours
Caused by medications (ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs), allergic reactions, hereditary/acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency
fact_text: Angioedema causes include allergic histamine-related and nonhistamine-related (bradykinin-mediated) types, including ACE inhibitor use and C1-inhibitor deficiency.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Evaluate for autoimmune causes of urticaria if episodes persistent or recurrent
Evaluate for complement deficiency (C4, C2, C1q, C1-inhibitor)
recommended_advice: Counsel on future avoidance if clear allergen
Discontinue medication if medication-induced
fact_text: Use a stepwise approach: assess for allergic symptoms and clear allergen, medication use (ACE-I, NSAIDs), and evaluate for autoimmune or complement deficiency causes to guide treatment and avoidance.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: If angioedema is associated with urticaria, it is not due to ACE inhibitor therapy
fact_text: Angioedema with urticaria is not caused by ACE inhibitor therapy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Most critical management is airway stabilization
All patients receive H1- and H2-blockers and corticosteroids
Patients with airway compromise or intraoral swelling should receive epinephrine
Patients with C1-inhibitor deficiency treated with androgens or C1-inhibitor concentrate
Patients with C1-inhibitor deficiency should avoid estrogen-containing medications
recommended_advice: Airway stabilization
H1- and H2-blockers
Corticosteroids
Epinephrine if airway compromised
Androgens or C1-inhibitor concentrate for C1-inhibitor deficiency
Avoid estrogen-containing medications in C1-inhibitor deficiency
fact_text: Management of angioedema focuses on airway stabilization, antihistamines, corticosteroids, epinephrine if airway compromised, and specific treatment for C1-inhibitor deficiency.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Stat vascular surgery consult if AAA rupture suspected
fact_text: AAA is defined as an infrarenal abdominal aorta diameter ≥ 3 cm; smoking is the most significant risk factor; ruptured AAA has 81% mortality with 32% dying before hospital.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: AAA must not be missed in acute diffuse abdominal pain with orthostatic hypotension and pulsatile abdominal mass; abdominal CT is important for diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Pain out of proportion to exam
fact_text: Bowel ischemia should be suspected with atrial fibrillation, valvular heart disease, heart failure, hypercoagulable state, and abrupt onset pain out of proportion to exam; CT angiography is diagnostic.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Ischemic colitis occurs in older patients with vascular disease and hypotension, presenting with hematochezia and diarrhea; colonoscopy is diagnostic.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Pancreatitis is a common alternative diagnosis in diffuse abdominal pain with history of alcohol abuse or gallstones; serum lipase is diagnostic.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Renal colic presents with flank pain radiating to groin, hematuria, and costovertebral angle tenderness; urinalysis and renal CT are recommended tests.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Lateral neck radiograph or CT scan of the neck
Documentation of foreign body directly or radiographically
recommended_advice: Consider epiglottitis as an airway emergency
Use clinical exam and throat culture to diagnose pharyngitis
Use imaging and laryngoscopy to differentiate epiglottitis and retropharyngeal abscess
fact_text: Epiglottitis is a leading diagnosis in adults with sore throat, muffled voice, stridor, and anterior neck tenderness; it requires urgent airway evaluation and direct visualization.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Admit all patients to ICU for close monitoring
Intubate patients with signs of airway obstruction
Elective intubation preferred due to difficulty in emergency intubation
Some advocate prophylactic intubation
fact_text: Otolaryngology consultation and laryngoscopy are mandatory for suspected epiglottitis; lateral neck films have ~90% sensitivity but do not rule out epiglottitis; airway control with ICU admission and intubation if obstruction signs present is critical.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Lateral neck radiographs to detect thickening of retropharyngeal tissues
CT scan if radiographs normal but suspicion remains
recommended_advice: Surgical drainage as soon as possible
Medical treatment with antibiotics covering polymicrobial flora including clindamycin
fact_text: Retropharyngeal abscess presents with symptoms similar to epiglottitis but often includes a lump in the throat; diagnosis is by lateral neck radiographs or CT scan; treatment includes surgical drainage and polymicrobial antibiotics.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Use antibiotics effective against H influenzae
Third-generation cephalosporins usually recommended
fact_text: Antibiotic treatment for epiglottitis should cover H influenzae, with third-generation cephalosporins usually recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Close monitoring of airway
Do not leave patient unattended
fact_text: Epiglottitis is an airway emergency requiring close monitoring and accompaniment to testing until airway stability is ensured.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Orthopnea is a very nonspecific symptom found in many types of cardiopulmonary disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: COPD presents with progressive dyspnea, decreased exercise tolerance, cough, and sputum production, usually with a long smoking history.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: COPD is a leading hypothesis in chronic dyspnea and wheezing with smoking history; asthma, heart failure, and bronchiectasis are important differential diagnoses with specific tests to distinguish them.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Use of BODE index for prognosis
recommended_advice: Classify patients by GOLD system for severity and exacerbation risk
Assess dyspnea using MMRC scale
fact_text: COPD diagnosis relies on history of smoking, symptoms like chronic cough and dyspnea, and physical exam findings including wheezing; GOLD system and MMRC dyspnea scale help classify severity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Key history features for COPD diagnosis include chronic cough, sputum production > ¼ cup, dyspnea, decreased exercise tolerance, and smoking history > 70 pack-years.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Physical exam findings such as subxiphoid cardiac impulse, absent cardiac dullness at LLSB, diaphragmatic excursion < 2 cm, early inspiratory crackles, and any unforced wheeze have variable sensitivity and high specificity for COPD diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Use BODE index to predict 4-year mortality in COPD patients
fact_text: The BODE index, incorporating BMI, airflow obstruction, dyspnea, and exercise capacity, predicts 4-year mortality in COPD.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Chest radiograph is not useful for diagnosing COPD but is recommended to rule out other causes of symptoms.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Spirometry with bronchodilator response helps distinguish COPD from asthma by identifying reversible airflow obstruction.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency testing is recommended in COPD patients developing disease before age 45 or without smoking history.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: ABG measurement is recommended in COPD patients with FEV1 < 40% predicted or right-sided heart failure.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Chest radiograph to rule out other causes
fact_text: Spirometry is recommended for all patients with suspected COPD; GOLD staging uses postbronchodilator FEV1 with FEV1/FVC < 0.7 to classify severity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Bronchodilator inhalers
Combination long-acting beta-agonist and anticholinergic inhalers
Consider inhaled corticosteroids
Home oxygen for chronic hypoxia or cor pulmonale
Antibiotic prophylaxis with azithromycin for frequent exacerbations
fact_text: Bronchodilator inhalers are recommended for COPD patients with FEV1 < 60%; combination therapy and home oxygen may be needed; inhaled corticosteroids are controversial.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Use anticholinergic and beta-agonist inhalers
Use systemic corticosteroids for up to 2 weeks
Consider pulmonary embolism and heart failure if no cause of exacerbation found
fact_text: COPD exacerbations require bronchodilator inhalers and systemic corticosteroids; chest radiograph is needed to rule out pneumonia; consider pulmonary embolism if no cause found.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Smoking cessation
Avoidance of inhaled toxic agents
fact_text: Smoking cessation is the most effective nonpharmacologic therapy for stable COPD and preserves lung function better than pharmacotherapy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Common bacteria isolated in bronchiectasis sputum include Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Streptococcus pneumoniae.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Bronchiectasis causes include pertussis, tuberculosis, airway obstruction from lymphadenopathy, Aspergillus, Mycobacterium avium complex, cystic fibrosis, and HIV.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: High-resolution CT scan to demonstrate airway damage and dilation
fact_text: Bronchiectasis presents with chronic purulent sputum and airway dilation; diagnosis depends on clinical suspicion and high-resolution CT imaging.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Heavy chronic sputum production suggests bronchiectasis, while purulent sputum in COPD occurs mainly during exacerbations.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Pulmonary function tests (PFTs) including total lung capacity, forced vital capacity, FEV1, FEV1/FVC ratio, DLCO
fact_text: Pulmonary function tests showing airflow obstruction with decreased FEV1 and FVC, normal or low DLCO, support COPD diagnosis when combined with clinical findings.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Administer oxygen carefully to avoid CO2 retention
fact_text: Oxygen therapy is beneficial in severe COPD exacerbations but must be carefully titrated to avoid CO2 retention and respiratory failure.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Diagnosis is made when there is appropriate clinical suspicion and histologic evidence of noncaseating granulomas
Biopsy of accessible lesions or transbronchial biopsy has a diagnostic yield of 85%
fact_text: Diagnosis of sarcoidosis requires clinical suspicion and histologic evidence of noncaseating granulomas, with biopsy of accessible lesions or transbronchial biopsy recommended.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Scadding classification system stages sarcoidosis by chest radiograph appearance
Stage 2: lymphadenopathy and parenchymal lung disease
fact_text: The Scadding classification stages sarcoidosis by chest radiograph from stage 0 (normal) to stage 4 (pulmonary fibrosis) but should not be used for diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: common findings are asymptomatic hilar lymphadenopathy, restrictive lung disease with decreased DLCO, and obstructive lung disease
fact_text: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem inflammatory disease often presenting with lung symptoms including dyspnea, cough, chest pain, or wheezing, with common findings of hilar lymphadenopathy and restrictive or obstructive lung disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Most patients with sarcoidosis do not require treatment
Treatment is generally reserved for clinically active disease
Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment
Methotrexate and infliximab are used for long-term therapy
recommended_advice: Use corticosteroids as main treatment
Consider methotrexate and infliximab for long-term therapy
fact_text: Most sarcoidosis patients do not require treatment; corticosteroids are mainstay when treatment is needed, with methotrexate and infliximab for long-term therapy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Annual rupture risk increases with AAA diameter: 0% at 3.0-3.9 cm, 1% at 4.0-4.9 cm, 1-11% at 5.0-5.9 cm, 10-22% at 6.0-6.9 cm, and 30-33% at >7.0 cm.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Proceed directly to operating room if ruptured AAA suspected
fact_text: Hypotension is a late finding in ruptured AAA; both hypotension and palpable mass are unusual in ruptured AAA patients.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Symptomatic contained AAA presents with abdominal pain in 83%, flank or back pain in 61-66%, syncope in 26%, and abdominal mass on careful exam in 52%.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: CT angiography and bedside emergency ultrasound are highly sensitive and specific for ruptured AAA; ultrasound is preferred for screening.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Proceed directly to operating room for ruptured AAA
Elective repair recommended for AAA ≥5.5 cm or rapid growth
Consider EVAR for lower 30-day morbidity and mortality
fact_text: For ruptured AAA, proceed directly to surgery; elective repair recommended for AAA ≥5.5 cm or rapid growth; EVAR has lower 30-day morbidity but similar overall survival compared to open repair.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: acute kidney injury rare, occurs with bilateral obstruction or solitary functioning kidney
fact_text: Complications of nephrolithiasis include ureteral obstruction, pyelonephritis, sepsis, and rarely acute kidney injury with bilateral obstruction or solitary kidney.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: gross or microscopic hematuria neither very sensitive nor specific for symptomatic nephrolithiasis
fact_text: Gross or microscopic hematuria has limited sensitivity (80%) and specificity (41%) for diagnosing symptomatic nephrolithiasis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: rapid onset of excruciating back and flank pain
pain radiates to abdomen or groin
pain may be associated with nausea, vomiting, dysuria, or urinary frequency
fact_text: Nephrolithiasis presents with rapid onset of severe back/flank pain radiating to abdomen/groin, often with nausea, vomiting, dysuria, and urinary frequency; abdominal tenderness is unusual.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: symptomatic stones develop in 7-13% of people in the US
men affected 2-3 times more than women
positive family history increases risk (relative risk 2.6)
fact_text: Symptomatic nephrolithiasis affects 7-13% of US population, recurs in 35-50% at 5 years, is 2-3 times more common in men, and risk is increased by positive family history.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Nephrolithiasis etiology includes calcium oxalate stones (75%), calcium phosphate stones (5%), uric acid stones (5-10%), struvite stones (5-15%), and others like cystine and indinavir stones.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: stones form when concentration of salts (calcium, oxalate, uric acid) becomes supersaturated in urine
supersaturation secondary to increased urinary salt excretion and inadequate urinary volume
calcium stones: idiopathic hypercalciuria, hyperparathyroidism, immobilization, excessive sodium intake
uric acid stones: uricosuric agents, low urine pH
oxalate stones: increased excretion from diet or malabsorption
infection with urea-splitting organisms causes struvite stones
renal colic develops when stones lodge in kidney and obstruct urinary flow
fact_text: Nephrolithiasis pathophysiology involves supersaturation of urine salts due to increased excretion or low volume; calcium, uric acid, oxalate, and struvite stones have distinct mechanisms including metabolic and infectious causes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: evaluation directed at establishing diagnosis and underlying etiology to prevent recurrence
fact_text: Diagnosis of nephrolithiasis requires evaluation to confirm diagnosis and identify underlying etiology to guide recurrence prevention.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: No known biochemical or structural markers for IBS
Symptoms common in IBS include lower abdominal pain, passage of mucus, feeling of incomplete evacuation, loose or frequent stools at onset of pain, and pain relieved by defecation
Only abdominal pain is very sensitive (90% sensitivity), but specificity is low (32%) and diarrhea pattern is also required
fact_text: IBS diagnosis relies on symptom patterns as no biochemical or structural markers exist; abdominal pain plus diarrhea pattern is required for diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Patients may have pain associated primarily with diarrhea (IBS-D), constipation (IBS-C), or mixed bowel pattern (IBS-M)
fact_text: IBS pain patterns vary and may be associated with diarrhea, constipation, or mixed bowel habits.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: IBS etiology is a combination of altered motility, visceral hypersensitivity, autonomic dysfunction, and psychological factors
Symptoms often exacerbated by psychological or physical stressors
fact_text: IBS symptoms are influenced by altered motility, visceral hypersensitivity, autonomic dysfunction, and psychological factors, often worsened by stress.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Patients complain of intermittent abdominal pain with diarrhea or constipation or both of years' duration
Diarrhea is often accompanied by cramps relieved with defecation
Pain cannot be explained by structural or biochemical abnormalities
Weight loss or anemia should alert clinician to other possibilities
recommended_advice: Evaluate new persistent bowel habit changes thoroughly
fact_text: IBS presents with intermittent abdominal pain and diarrhea or constipation relieved by defecation; new persistent bowel habit changes require evaluation to exclude other diseases.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Emergent bedside ultrasound reveals a massively dilated aorta (9 cm) with 500 mL of adjacent fluid (presumed blood)
Emergent surgery reveals leaking AAA that ruptures intraoperatively
Aorta is cross clamped, repaired, and patient stabilized
recommended_advice: Emergent surgery
Cross clamp and repair aorta
fact_text: Bedside ultrasound can detect leaking AAA; emergent surgery with aortic cross clamping is required for repair and stabilization.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: The absence of hematuria does not rule out nephrolithiasis.
fact_text: Absence of hematuria does not exclude nephrolithiasis; noncontrast renal CT is the test of choice with high sensitivity and specificity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Allopurinol is effective in patients with concomitant hyperuricemia or hyperuricosuria (relative risk 0.59, 0.42–0.84)
recommended_advice: Allopurinol treatment
fact_text: Allopurinol reduces nephrolithiasis risk in patients with hyperuricemia or hyperuricosuria.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Citrate supplementation is effective in patients with and without hypocitraturia (relative risk 0.25, 0.14–0.44)
recommended_advice: Citrate supplementation
fact_text: Citrate supplementation reduces nephrolithiasis risk in patients with or without hypocitraturia.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: NSAIDs treat pain and diminish spasm
Hospitalization for uncontrolled pain, persistent nausea/vomiting, acute kidney injury, or signs of infection
Sepsis or acute kidney injury due to bilateral obstruction or unilateral obstruction in solitary kidney requires emergent drainage
recommended_advice: NSAIDs for pain control
Avoid NSAIDs 3 days before lithotripsy
Opioids second line
Hydration
Hospitalization if uncontrolled pain or complications
Emergent drainage for sepsis or acute kidney injury
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for sepsis
fact_text: NSAIDs are first-line for pain control in nephrolithiasis; hospitalization and emergent drainage are indicated for complications such as sepsis or acute kidney injury.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Nifedipine and alpha-blockers reduce likelihood of stone passage
Lithotripsy or ureteroscopy can remove persistent stones
recommended_advice: Use nifedipine and alpha-blockers to reduce stone passage likelihood
Use lithotripsy or ureteroscopy for persistent stones
fact_text: Nifedipine and alpha-blockers reduce likelihood of stone passage; lithotripsy or ureteroscopy can remove persistent stones.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Increasing fluid intake to >2 L/day decreases risk of recurrent stones
Reducing phosphate-containing soft drinks may decrease recurrences
Thiazide diuretics decrease urinary calcium excretion and reduce risk
recommended_advice: Increase fluid intake to >2 L/day
Reduce phosphate-containing soft drinks
Use thiazide diuretics with potassium supplementation
fact_text: Secondary prevention of nephrolithiasis includes increased fluid intake, reducing phosphate soft drinks, and thiazide diuretics to decrease urinary calcium.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: patients complain of constant gradually increasing left lower quadrant abdominal pain, usually present for several days
diarrhea or constipation and fever often present
guarding and rebound may be seen
fact_text: Diverticulitis presents with constant gradually increasing left lower quadrant pain, diarrhea or constipation, fever, and possible guarding or rebound.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: develops in 5-10% of patients aged > 45 years, 50% in persons > 60 years, and 80% in those > 85 years
low-fiber diets believed to cause diverticula by decreasing stool bulk and increasing intraluminal pressure
fact_text: Diverticulosis prevalence increases with age and is associated with low-fiber diets causing increased intraluminal pressure.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: persistent diarrhea increased likelihood of IBD (LR+, 4.2)
consistent history with abdominal pain or discomfort for at least 3 months
limited work-up to exclude other diseases
recommended_tests: stool for Clostridium difficile toxin and ova and parasites
recommended_advice: limited work-up in young patients without alarm features
consider lactose hydrogen breath testing if lactose intolerance suspected
fact_text: Diagnosis of IBS is based on consistent history, absence of alarm features, and limited work-up to exclude other diseases; CBC and CRP help rule out anemia and inflammation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: treatments effective in IBS include elimination of foods causing symptoms, physical activity, antispasmodics, tricyclic antidepressants, and dietary fiber
recommended_advice: eliminate foods like lactose, beans, cabbage, onions, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, broccoli
increase physical activity
use antispasmodics (hyoscine, peppermint oil)
consider tricyclic antidepressants or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
dietary fiber (psyllium) may be effective
for IBS-D: trial of lactose-free diet, loperamide for diarrhea, rifaximin course, 5 HT3 receptor antagonists (restricted use), probiotics with Bifidobacteria
for IBS-C: lubiprostone, pregnancy test before use in premenopausal women, not recommended in men
fact_text: IBS treatment includes dietary modification, physical activity, antispasmodics, antidepressants, and syndrome-specific therapies such as loperamide for IBS-D and lubiprostone for IBS-C.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: The abdomen is typically nontender even during severe pain episodes
fact_text: Abdomen is usually nontender during severe pain in chronic mesenteric ischemia

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Abdominal pain occurs in 94% and is postprandial in 88%
Pain is typically epigastric or periumbilical
Pain develops in first hour after eating and diminishes 1-2 hours later
fact_text: Abdominal pain in chronic mesenteric ischemia is postprandial, epigastric or periumbilical, and lasts 1-2 hours

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Pain typically begins 1-2 hours after eating and lasts for hours
Associated with food fear, weight loss
Peripheral vascular disease (55%), coronary artery disease (43%), hypertension (37%) common
fact_text: Chronic mesenteric ischemia presents with postprandial abdominal pain, food fear, and weight loss in patients with vascular disease

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Diarrhea is present in about one-third of chronic mesenteric ischemia patients

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: An epigastric bruit has been reported in 63% of patients (range 17-87%)
fact_text: Epigastric bruit is present in about two-thirds of chronic mesenteric ischemia patients

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Weight loss occurs in 78% of patients and is due to food aversion
fact_text: Weight loss in chronic mesenteric ischemia is common and caused by food aversion

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Only 64% of patients with diverticular abscess had temperature ≥ 38.0°C and 62% had WBC > 11,000/mcL
fact_text: Fever and leukocytosis occur in about 64% and 62% of diverticular abscess cases respectively

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Left lower quadrant tenderness increases the likelihood of diverticulitis; LR+, 3.4; LR-, 0.41
recommended_tests: CT scan (test of choice in men and nonpregnant women)
recommended_advice: Outpatient management appropriate for mild attack without marked fever or leukocytosis
fact_text: Left lower quadrant tenderness increases likelihood of diverticulitis; CT scan is test of choice for diagnosis

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: In uncomplicated diverticulitis, only 45% had temperature ≥ 38.0°C or WBC > 11,000/mcL
fact_text: Only 45% of patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis have fever or leukocytosis

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Plain radiographs may demonstrate free air or obstruction
fact_text: Plain radiographs can show free air or obstruction in diverticulitis

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Neither fever nor leukocytosis is very sensitive for diverticulitis or diverticular abscess
fact_text: Fever and leukocytosis are not sensitive to rule out diverticulitis or diverticular abscess

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Colonoscopy can misdiagnose colon cancer as diverticulitis; should be delayed 4-6 weeks after acute inflammation resolves
recommended_advice: Delay colonoscopy until 4-6 weeks after resolution of acute inflammation
fact_text: Colonoscopy should be delayed 4-6 weeks after diverticulitis to avoid misdiagnosis of colon cancer

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: CT scan confirms diverticulitis by showing thickened bowel wall or pericolonic fat stranding, abscess formation, perforation
fact_text: CT scan is test of choice to confirm diverticulitis and evaluate complications

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Recent randomized trial showed no significant benefit of antibiotics in mild diverticulitis
recommended_advice: Antibiotics may not be necessary in mild diverticulitis
fact_text: Antibiotics may not improve outcomes in mild diverticulitis

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Outpatient management appropriate for mild attack without marked fever or leukocytosis
recommended_advice: Outpatient management with oral analgesics and tolerating oral intake
fact_text: Mild diverticulitis without marked fever or leukocytosis can be managed outpatient

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Moderate to severe diverticulitis requires inpatient treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics, no oral intake, CT-guided drainage for abscess >5 cm, and possible surgery
recommended_advice: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
No oral intake
CT-guided drainage for abscess >5 cm
Emergent surgery for peritonitis, uncontrolled sepsis, clinical deterioration, or obstruction with contaminated abscess
fact_text: Moderate to severe diverticulitis requires inpatient care with antibiotics, bowel rest, drainage, and possibly surgery

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: diagnosis of mesenteric ischemia should exclude more common disorders (e.g., PUD and gallstone disease)
recommended_tests: angiography if noninvasive tests suggest vascular obstruction
recommended_advice: consider angiography if noninvasive testing suggests vascular obstruction
fact_text: Symptomatic chronic mesenteric ischemia is rare and diagnosis requires exclusion of more common disorders; CT angiography and MR angiography are important diagnostic tools.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: revascularization by surgical endarterectomy, bypass grafting, or percutaneous endovascular repair
fact_text: Revascularization is the only treatment for mesenteric ischemia.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Calculate anion gap = Na+ - (HCO3- + Cl-)
Normal anion gap is 7-9 mEq/L
Elevated anion gap suggests processes producing acid or unmeasured anions
fact_text: Use anion gap calculation to narrow differential diagnosis of metabolic acidosis; elevated gap suggests acid-producing processes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: If pH < 7.4, primary disorder is acidosis
If pH > 7.4, primary disorder is alkalosis
For acidosis: if HCO3- < 24 mEq/L then metabolic acidosis; if PaCO2 > 40 mm Hg then respiratory acidosis
For alkalosis: if HCO3- > 24 mEq/L then metabolic alkalosis; if PaCO2 < 40 mm Hg then respiratory alkalosis
fact_text: Determine primary acid-base disorder by first evaluating pH, then classify as metabolic or respiratory by HCO3- and PaCO2 levels.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: effect of serum albumin on anion gap
condition_aliases: effect of serum albumin on anion gap
fact_text: Serum albumin level affects the anion gap; lower albumin decreases the anion gap by 2.5 mEq/L per 1 g/dL drop below 4.4 g/dL.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: An increased anion gap suggests the presence of an anion gap metabolic acidosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: lactic acidosis (hypoxia, shock, septic, hypovolemic, cardiogenic, anaphylactic, co or cyanide poisoning, regional obstruction to blood flow, seizures)
toxins and miscellaneous (salicylate, methanol, ethylene glycol, rhabdomyolysis, d-lactic acidosis)
fact_text: Metabolic acidoses with anion gap include ketoacidoses, lactic acidosis, uremia, and toxin-related causes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Metabolic acidoses with nonanion gap include diarrhea, RTA, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, dilutional acidosis, and early kidney disease.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Metabolic alkaloses causes include vomiting, diuretics, hypokalemia, increased mineralocorticoid activity, and licorice ingestion.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: pulmonary diseases (copd, asthma, pulmonary edema, pneumonia, massive pleural effusions, pneumothorax)

neuromuscular diseases (brain stroke, intoxication, sleep apnea; spinal cord trauma, als, polio; nerve guillain-barré syndrome; neuromuscular junction myasthenia gravis; chest wall flail chest, muscular dystrophy)
fact_text: Respiratory acidoses are caused by pulmonary diseases and neuromuscular diseases affecting ventilation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: pulmonary disorders (pneumonia, asthma, pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism, interstitial lung disease, mechanical ventilation)
extrapulmonary disorders (anxiety, pain, fever, pregnancy, cns insult, drugs, cirrhosis)
fact_text: Respiratory alkaloses causes include pulmonary and extrapulmonary disorders such as anxiety and CNS insults.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: An elevated anion gap suggests an anion gap metabolic acidosis even if HCO3- is above normal.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Expected compensation for metabolic acidosis is a decrease in PaCO2 by approximately 1.2 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L decrease in HCO3-.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Metabolic acidosis is identified by decreased HCO3- in acid-base abnormalities.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Expected compensation for metabolic alkalosis is an increase in PaCO2 by approximately 0.7 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L increase in HCO3-.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Metabolic alkalosis is identified by increased HCO3- in acid-base abnormalities.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: more than one simultaneous acid-base disturbance
fact_text: Calculate anion gap and compensation to uncover unexpected acid-base disorders when multiple disturbances coexist.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In acute respiratory acidosis, expected compensation is an increase in HCO3- by 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg increase in PaCO2.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In chronic respiratory acidosis, expected compensation is an increase in HCO3- by 4 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg increase in PaCO2.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Respiratory acidosis is identified by increased PaCO2 in acid-base abnormalities.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In acute respiratory alkalosis, expected compensation is a decrease in HCO3- by 2 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg decrease in PaCO2.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In chronic respiratory alkalosis, expected compensation is a decrease in HCO3- by 4 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg decrease in PaCO2.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Respiratory alkalosis is identified by decreased PaCO2 in acid-base abnormalities.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: metabolic acidosis (anion gap elevated: ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, uremic acidosis, toxin)
metabolic acidosis (anion gap normal: diarrhea, early kidney disease, dilutional)
respiratory acidosis (lung diseases, pleural diseases, neuromuscular diseases)
respiratory alkalosis (pulmonary disorders, anxiety, fever, pain, pregnancy, cns insult, drugs, cirrhosis)
metabolic alkalosis (vomiting, ng suction, diuretics, hypokalemia, increased mineralocorticoid)
recommended_advice: Check compensation formulas to discover acid-base disorders in compensating system
fact_text: Stepwise approach to acid-base disorder diagnosis starts with pH evaluation, then PaCO2 and HCO3- to classify respiratory vs metabolic, followed by anion gap to differentiate metabolic acidosis types.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: A very low HCO3- strongly suggests primary metabolic acidosis; low pH confirms primary disorder is acidosis; ABG measurement documents acidosis and evaluates respiratory compensation.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Tests to identify precipitant (urinalysis, chest radiograph, ECG, imaging as indicated)
fact_text: DKA is suggested by history of insulin-dependent diabetes, noncompliance, precipitating illness, and confirmed by increased anion gap and ketones.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: differential diagnosis of anion gap metabolic acidosis
condition_aliases: lactic acidosis from hypoxemia or shock
differential diagnosis of anion gap metabolic acidosis
recommended_tests: Tests for sepsis (CBC, urinalysis, chest radiograph, blood cultures)
fact_text: Differential diagnoses for anion gap metabolic acidosis include diabetic ketoacidosis, uremic acidosis, starvation and alcoholic ketoacidosis, and lactic acidosis from hypoxemia or shock, each with specific demographic, clinical features, and important tests.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Low HCO3- and PaCO2 indicates primary metabolic acidosis
fact_text: Anion gap metabolic acidosis is diagnosed by low HCO3-, low PaCO2, and elevated anion gap (e.g., 32), narrowing differential to ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, uremia, or toxin.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Marked insulin deficiency causes hyperglycemia by reducing cellular glucose uptake and increasing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; ketoacidosis results from increased glucagon and acetyl CoA production; volume depletion occurs due to osmotic diuresis; potassium loss occurs from diuresis and hyperaldosteronism; hyperkalemia occurs despite total body potassium deficit; hyponatremia results from osmotic diuresis and water loss.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: diabetes secondary to severe chronic pancreatitis and near complete islet cell obliteration
fact_text: DKA occurs primarily in patients with complete or near complete insulin deficiency, including type 1 DM and some type 2 DM cases.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: infection (especially urinary tract infections and pneumonia)
discontinuation of insulin or oral hypoglycemics
medications (corticosteroids, thiazides, cocaine, antipsychotics, sglt2 inhibitors)
fact_text: Most common precipitant of DKA is infection; other precipitants include discontinuation of insulin, new-onset type 1 DM, other infections, MI, cerebrovascular accident, acute pancreatitis, pulmonary embolism, GI hemorrhage, emotional stress, and certain medications.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Glucose > 250 mg/dL (rarely DKA with near normal glucose in pregnancy or SGLT2 inhibitors)
fact_text: ADA criteria for DKA diagnosis include glucose > 250 mg/dL, pH ≤ 7.3, HCO3- ≤ 18 mEq/L, positive serum ketones, and anion gap > 10 mEq/L.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Polyuria and increased thirst are common
Lethargy and obtundation may occur with markedly increased effective osmolality (> 320 mOsm/L)
Abdominal pain is very common and may be caused by DKA or another intra-abdominal process
Abdominal pain frequency increases with severity of DKA
fact_text: Common DKA symptoms include polyuria, thirst, lethargy, and abdominal pain; effective osmolality calculation helps assess neurologic risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: DKA pathophysiology involves insulin deficiency causing hyperglycemia, osmotic diuresis, dehydration, potassium shifts, ketoacidosis, and compensatory Kussmaul breathing.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Serum HCO3- 0-10 mEq/L: 25-75% frequency of abdominal pain, 70% due to DKA, 30% due to intra-abdominal process
Serum HCO3- > 10 mEq/L: 12% frequency of abdominal pain, 16% due to DKA, 84% due to intra-abdominal process
fact_text: Abdominal pain in DKA is more likely due to DKA when serum HCO3- is low (0-10 mEq/L) and more likely due to intra-abdominal process when HCO3- is > 10 mEq/L.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Depressed mental status after 24 hours (adjusted OR 8.6)
> 50 units of insulin required in first 12 hours (adjusted OR 7.9)
fact_text: Mortality in DKA is 5-15%; risk factors include severe coexistent disease, low pH, depressed mental status, high glucose after 12 hours, high insulin requirement, fever after 24 hours, and older age.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Mild leukocytosis common, may be secondary to stress or infection
fact_text: Amylase elevation and mild leukocytosis are common nonspecific findings in DKA and may indicate stress or infection.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Anion gap is elevated in most patients with DKA
In emergency department with glucose > 250 mg/dL, anion gap is 84–90% sensitive and 85–99% specific
recommended_tests: Measure anion gap in patients with suspected DKA
fact_text: Anion gap is elevated in most DKA patients and is a sensitive and specific test when glucose > 250 mg/dL.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Test of choice to evaluate DKA is beta-hydroxybutyrate
fact_text: Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the predominant ketone in severe DKA and is the preferred test for diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: 15% of patients with DKA have glucose levels < 350 mg/dL
fact_text: Glucose level in DKA is variable; 15% of patients have glucose < 350 mg/dL, especially pregnant patients, those with poor oral intake, on SGLT2 inhibitors, or given insulin en route to hospital.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Treatment of DKA includes initial evaluation, fluid resuscitation, insulin, potassium replacement
recommended_tests: Vital signs and orthostatic vital signs
Electrolytes, glucose, serum ketones, serum beta-hydroxybutyric acid, serum lactate, ABG, anion gap, plasma osmolality, BUN, creatinine
Urinalysis and urine culture, CBC with differential, ECG, troponin levels
Other tests as clinically indicated (blood cultures, lipase)
recommended_advice: Fluid resuscitation with evaluation of dehydration, BP, orthostatic BP, pulse, hourly urinary output
IV normal saline 1–2 L bolus initially
Adjust fluid volume based on hypotension and volume depletion
Administer insulin IV bolus followed by continuous infusion
Exclude marked hypokalemia (<3.3 mEq/L) before insulin therapy
Administer treatment in monitored setting
fact_text: DKA treatment involves initial evaluation, frequent monitoring, fluid resuscitation, insulin administration, potassium replacement, and detection/treatment of underlying causes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Abdominal pain and delirium may be complications or causes of DKA
recommended_advice: Always search for the etiology of abdominal pain or delirium in patients with DKA
fact_text: Abdominal pain and delirium may be complications or causes of DKA; always evaluate for underlying causes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: ethanol conversion to acetic acid and stimulated lipolysis
possible pancreatitis, GI bleeding, or infection
fact_text: Alcoholic ketoacidosis occurs in heavy alcohol users with inadequate carbohydrate intake and may have normal or low plasma glucose.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Starvation ketosis occurs with diminished carbohydrate intake, mild acidosis (HCO3- >14 mEq/L), normal glucose and pH.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Acidosis in kidney disease evolves from nonanion gap to anion gap metabolic acidosis as disease advances.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Uremic acidosis causes increased bone calcium loss and skeletal muscle breakdown.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Uremic acidosis results from kidney impairment causing failed bicarbonate regeneration and metabolic acidosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Uremic acidosis occurs in chronic kidney disease with low bicarbonate, high creatinine, BUN, and phosphate, causing fatigue, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and pruritus.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: NaHCO3 replacement
Hemodialysis
fact_text: Treatment of uremic acidosis includes sodium bicarbonate replacement and hemodialysis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: high glucose and diabetic history rule out DKA
recommended_advice: IV thiamine prior to glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy or Korsakoff syndrome
fact_text: High serum ketones with high glucose and diabetic history suggest DKA; normal lactate and large urine ketones suggest alcoholic ketoacidosis; calculate anion gap and respiratory compensation to confirm diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: ECG revealed T wave inversion in leads V1-V4
cardiac catheterization revealed triple vessel disease
recommended_advice: fluid resuscitation
IV insulin
potassium supplementation
beta-blockers and aspirin
cardiac catheterization
fact_text: In DKA with signs of myocardial ischemia, monitor ECG and troponin, treat with fluid resuscitation, insulin, potassium, and cardiac interventions as needed.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: possible urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis
condition_aliases: possible urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis
trigger_evidence: abdominal exam soft without rebound or guarding
lab results: Na 138, K 3.8, HCO3 14, Cl 102, BUN 30, creatinine 1.2, glucose 90
recommended_tests: blood tests including electrolytes and renal function
fact_text: In a patient with nausea, vomiting, urinary symptoms, flank pain, and fever, group symptoms and order urinalysis and blood tests to evaluate for urinary tract infection and acid-base status.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Serum levels of salicylate, methanol, ethylene glycol, serum osmolality
recommended_advice: Assess history for alcohol, moonshine, antifreeze ingestion, salicylate use
Evaluate for signs of infection, shock, and toxin ingestion
Order appropriate labs and imaging based on suspected diagnosis
fact_text: Use ABG pH and serum HCO3- to determine primary acid-base disorder; calculate anion gap to narrow metabolic acidosis differential; consider lactic acidosis, shock, sepsis, alcoholic ketoacidosis, and toxins with appropriate labs and history.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Mortality rate of patients with shock and lactic acidosis is 70%, compared to 25-35% in shock without lactic acidosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: hypoxemia (lung disease, copd, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism)
shock (cardiogenic shock, hypovolemic shock, septic shock)
low oxygen saturation despite normal pao2 (carbon monoxide poisoning, methemoglobinemia)
cellular inability to utilize oxygen (cyanide poisoning)
recommended_advice: Measure serum lactate in critically ill patients with shock regardless of anion gap
fact_text: Serum lactate levels are the gold standard and more sensitive and specific than anion gap increase for diagnosing lactic acidosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: shock with suspected infection and lactic acidosis
recommended_advice: Use lactate levels to risk stratify patients with suspected infection and shock
fact_text: Lactate levels ≥ 4.0 mmol/L in patients with shock and suspected infection indicate higher mortality risk and help identify undetected hypoperfusion.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Adjust metformin dosing based on GFR
Hold metformin before IV radiocontrast
fact_text: Metformin dosing should be adjusted or held based on GFR to reduce risk of lactic acidosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Treatment should target the underlying condition causing lactic acidosis
fact_text: Treatment of lactic acidosis should focus on addressing the underlying cause.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: lactic acidosis as primary acid-base disorder
trigger_evidence: blood and urine cultures grew Escherichia coli
fact_text: Serum lactate > 8 mEq/L confirms lactic acidosis as primary acid-base disorder; blood and urine cultures help exclude sepsis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: PaCO2 expected to fall by 1.2 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L fall in HCO3-
fact_text: In metabolic acidosis, PaCO2 should fall by 1.2 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L fall in HCO3-; deviation suggests respiratory compensation status.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: sepsis with lactic acidosis and respiratory failure
recommended_advice: broad-spectrum antibiotics
IV fluids
norepinephrine
mechanical ventilation
ICU transfer
fact_text: Treatment of lactic acidosis with respiratory failure includes broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV fluids, vasopressors, mechanical ventilation, and ICU care.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: pulse oximetry inadequate to assess ventilation
ABG shows pH 7.22, PaCO2 70 mm Hg, PaO2 55 mm Hg
fact_text: ABG is necessary to assess ventilation adequacy in COPD patients with dyspnea; pulse oximetry alone is insufficient.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: acute respiratory acidosis (pulmonary disease eg copd, pneumonia)
chronic respiratory acidosis (lung disease eg copd)
trigger_evidence: Prior history of intubation or ICU admission
fact_text: Acute respiratory acidosis is associated with decreased pH, elevated PaCO2, near normal HCO3-, and signs such as pulsus paradoxus and worsening symptoms; chronic respiratory acidosis shows decreased pH, elevated PaCO2, and elevated HCO3- with decreased breath sounds.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: acute respiratory acidosis (from pulmonary disease eg copd, pneumonia)
chronic respiratory acidosis (from lung disease eg copd)
trigger_evidence: low pH confirms primary disorder is acidosis
recommended_advice: Ask about history of intubation or ICU admission in patients with asthma or COPD
fact_text: Primary respiratory acidosis is confirmed by low pH and elevated PaCO2 and HCO3-; acute respiratory acidosis is suggested by history of acute pulmonary disease and worsening symptoms, while chronic respiratory acidosis is associated with chronic lung disease such as COPD.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: respiratory acidosis due to lung disease (eg copd, pneumonia, pulmonary edema)
respiratory acidosis due to cns disorders (eg intoxication)
trigger_evidence: Insufficient ventilation results in increased PaCO2
Increased renal HCO3- regeneration over days
Ventilation assessed by arterial PaCO2 and pH
Etiology mostly due to lung disease or CNS disorders
Manifestations due to primary disorder and hypercarbia effects on CNS
recommended_tests: Arterial blood gas to measure PaCO2 and pH
fact_text: Respiratory acidosis results from insufficient ventilation causing increased PaCO2 and compensatory renal HCO3- regeneration; common causes include lung disease and CNS disorders.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Acute respiratory acidosis can be distinguished from chronic respiratory acidosis by evaluating degree of metabolic compensation
Chronic respiratory acidosis associated with more complete compensation (higher HCO3- levels)
Acute respiratory acidosis: increase in HCO3- by 1 mEq/L for every 10 mm Hg increase in PaCO2
Chronic respiratory acidosis: increase in HCO3- by 3.5 to 4 mEq/L for every 10 mm Hg increase in PaCO2
fact_text: Distinguish acute vs chronic respiratory acidosis by degree of metabolic compensation: acute increases HCO3- ~1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg PaCO2 rise; chronic increases ~3.5–4 mEq/L

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: PaCO2 > 45 mm Hg causing respiratory acidosis
Normal PaCO2 occasionally suggests respiratory failure in asthma attacks
fact_text: Normal PaCO2 in asthma attack may indicate respiratory fatigue and impending respiratory failure; PaCO2 > 45 mm Hg usually indicates respiratory acidosis

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Patients are typically quite dyspneic, in distress, sitting upright, leaning forward, and anxious
The cardiac and pulmonary findings depend on the underlying etiology
recommended_advice: Identify and treat underlying disease process
Supplemental oxygen as necessary
fact_text: Respiratory failure is suggested by PaCO2 > 45 mm Hg causing respiratory acidosis; ABG is low threshold test to obtain PaCO2 in respiratory distress

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Tremor, asterixis, slurred speech, and papilledema may be seen
fact_text: Severe respiratory failure may present with PaCO2 > 70–100 mm Hg and neurologic signs such as tremor, asterixis, slurred speech, and papilledema

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Pulsus > 10 mm Hg has sensitivity 53–68%, specificity 69–92%
Pulsus > 20 mm Hg has sensitivity 19–39%, specificity 92–100%
Pulsus > 25 mm Hg has sensitivity 16%, specificity 99%
fact_text: Pulsus paradoxus > 10 mm Hg is moderately sensitive and specific for severe asthma; higher thresholds increase specificity but reduce sensitivity

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Pulsus > 10 mm Hg has sensitivity 53–68% and specificity 69–92%
Pulsus > 20 mm Hg has sensitivity 19–39% and specificity 92–100%
Pulsus > 25 mm Hg has sensitivity 16% and specificity 99%
fact_text: Pulsus paradoxus > 10 mm Hg is specific but not highly sensitive for severe asthma; higher thresholds increase specificity but reduce sensitivity

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: hypercapnia in copd, asthma, or sleep apnea
condition_aliases: hypercapnia in copd, asthma, or sleep apnea
trigger_evidence: Supplemental oxygen occasionally worsens hypercapnia in patients with severe COPD, asthma, or sleep apnea but should never be withheld from hypoxic patients
recommended_advice: Give supplemental oxygen as necessary to prevent hypoxemia
fact_text: Supplemental oxygen may worsen hypercapnia in severe COPD, asthma, or sleep apnea but should not be withheld if patient is hypoxic

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Mechanical ventilation either intubation or biphasic positive airway pressure (BiPAP) is lifesaving in many patients
Indication for mechanical ventilation: pH < 7.1–7.25 or PaCO2 > 80–90 mm Hg or when indicated by patient symptoms
recommended_advice: Initiate mechanical ventilation if indicated
fact_text: Mechanical ventilation is lifesaving in severe respiratory failure with pH < 7.1–7.25 or PaCO2 > 80–90 mm Hg or symptomatic patients

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Decreased effective circulating volume reduces bicarbonate secretion and promotes sodium absorption, increasing bicarbonate reclamation in metabolic alkalosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Increased bicarbonate production and decreased renal bicarbonate excretion (due to decreased renal perfusion) are key mechanisms in metabolic alkalosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Metabolic alkalosis develops only when there is both a source of additional bicarbonate and a renal stimulus that limits its excretion.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Patients with type IV RTA have hypoaldosteronism leading to hyperkalemia and acidosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: drugs (nsaids, ace inhibitors, arbs, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim, heparin, cyclosporine)
fact_text: Type IV RTA is associated with hyperkalemia, mild kidney disease, and multiple causes including drugs and systemic diseases.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Dietary potassium restriction
Loop diuretics
Fludrocortisone
fact_text: Treatment of type IV RTA includes dietary potassium restriction, loop diuretics, and fludrocortisone.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Chloride depletion interferes with HCO3- secretion
Hypovolemia increases proximal NaCl reabsorption limiting distal chloride delivery
fact_text: Chloride depletion interferes with HCO3- secretion by limiting distal chloride delivery, which is necessary for HCO3- secretion.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Hypovolemia increases sodium reabsorption in exchange for hydrogen ion at proximal convoluted tubule
fact_text: In hypovolemia, increased sodium reabsorption in proximal tubule exchanges hydrogen ion, leading to increased HCO3- reabsorption and delivery to bloodstream.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: respiratory acidosis with compensatory metabolic alkalosis
trigger_evidence: Respiratory acidosis promoting compensatory metabolic alkalosis
fact_text: Metabolic alkalosis causes include vomiting, dehydration, diuretics, hypokalemia, hyperaldosteronism, Bartter/Gitelman syndromes, respiratory acidosis, and milk-alkali syndrome.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Hyperventilation induces hypocapnia causing respiratory alkalosis
Common causes include pulmonary diseases, cirrhosis, fever, pain, anxiety
Hypocapnia acutely reduces CNS blood flow
Symptoms include perioral paresthesias, vertigo, dizziness, anxiety, hallucinations, myalgias
Adverse effects include hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, lung injury, seizures, angina, arrhythmias
fact_text: Respiratory alkalosis is caused by hyperventilation leading to hypocapnia, with symptoms including paresthesias and dizziness; common causes include pulmonary disease, cirrhosis, fever, pain, and anxiety.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Volume resuscitation with NaCl in patients with true volume depletion
Replete potassium deficiency
Use carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and low bicarbonate dialysis in severe cases, especially in heart failure patients who cannot tolerate NaCl
fact_text: Treatment of metabolic alkalosis includes volume resuscitation with NaCl, potassium repletion, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors or low bicarbonate dialysis in severe cases.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Therapy is directed at the underlying disorder
fact_text: Treatment of respiratory alkalosis focuses on addressing the underlying disorder.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Calculate delta-delta gap to identify mixed acid-base disorders
fact_text: The delta-delta gap helps identify mixed metabolic acid-base disorders by comparing the increase in anion gap to the decrease in bicarbonate; deviations from 1 suggest additional acid-base processes.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: At the end of 2016, 1,130,000 persons were living with HIV infection in the United States
39,782 new HIV diagnoses in 2016, a 5% decrease from 2011
Sex ratio of new HIV infections is about 4 males to 1 female
Men who have sex with men (MSMs) are disproportionately infected
Racial and ethnic disparities: blacks 44%, whites 26%, Hispanics 25%, Asians 2%
Regional differences in rates of new HIV diagnoses per 100,000 population
fact_text: HIV epidemiology in the US shows high prevalence, male predominance, MSM risk, racial disparities, and regional variation in new diagnoses.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Common modes of transmission include male-to-male sexual transmission, heterosexual transmission, and drug paraphernalia sharing among IDUs
Mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, perinatally, or through breastfeeding is uncommon in the US
Higher viral load increases risk of transmission
Coinfections such as TB or syphilis increase viral load
fact_text: HIV transmission occurs mainly via sexual contact and injection drug use; higher viral load and coinfections increase transmission risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Chronic HIV infection may present in a myriad of ways
Some patients may have symptoms such as chronic diarrhea, seborrheic dermatitis, multiple molluscum contagiosum, poorly responsive psoriasis, and prurigo nodularis
Other patients have conditions strongly associated with HIV infection but also seen in non–HIV-infected persons
fact_text: Chronic HIV infection can present with nonspecific symptoms or conditions strongly associated with HIV but also seen in other diseases, requiring consideration in differential diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Immunologic AIDS is diagnosed when CD4TL count falls below 200 cells/mcL.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: rapid rise in HIV viral load due to humoral and cellular immune responses
viral load set at a level that remains relatively stable after 6 months
fact_text: Seroconversion causes a rapid rise in HIV viral load followed by a stable viral load set point after 6 months.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: negative Epstein-Barr virus (negative EBV viral capsid IgM)
recommended_advice: High index of suspicion for acute HIV diagnosis
fact_text: Acute HIV infection should be considered in mononucleosis-like syndromes with negative EBV and CMV serologies; diagnosis requires high suspicion.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: low-positive viral load in this context should be ruled out as false-positive
fact_text: In primary HIV infection, HIV viral load is almost always >10,000/mcL; low-positive viral load should be ruled out as false-positive.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
