trigger_evidence: ART requires complete suppression of viral replication to prevent new cell infections and resistance mutations
recommended_advice: Effective ART to suppress viral replication and prevent resistance
fact_text: Effective ART requires complete suppression of viral replication to prevent new infections and resistance mutations.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Positive predictive value depends on pretest probability, sensitivity, and specificity
Risk factors include MSM, IDU, multiple sexual partners
Prevalence varies from 0.3% in general US population to >50% in high-risk groups
fact_text: Interpreting HIV test results requires considering pretest probability based on risk factors and prevalence in the population.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Diagnosis of HIV: the 3-step HIV screening sequence
HIV RNA and p24 antigen are present prior to HIV antibodies
fact_text: HIV diagnosis uses a 3-step sequence: initial 4th-gen antigen/antibody test, then antibody differentiation, and if needed, HIV-1 nucleic acid test to confirm infection.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Male and female condoms are about 95% effective in preventing HIV transmission
Blood product screening has eliminated transfusion-associated HIV transmission
Effective ART reduces viral load and transmission risk
Preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a highly effective prevention strategy
recommended_advice: Use condoms consistently
Screen blood products
Start effective ART early
Use PrEP with combination antiretroviral drugs for high-risk individuals
fact_text: HIV prevention includes condom use, blood screening, effective ART to reduce transmission, and PrEP with combination antiretrovirals for high-risk persons.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: HIV RNA becomes detectable about 10 days after infection by nucleic acid test; HIV-1 p24 antigen rises within 4-10 days after initial RNA detection; IgG antibodies become reactive 18-38 days or more after initial RNA detection.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: HIV testing algorithm starts with HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody combination immunoassay; positive results require antibody differentiation immunoassay; indeterminate or negative antibody results with positive antigen require HIV-1 NAT to confirm acute infection.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Refer HIV-infected patients to HIV specialists for comprehensive care and ART management
fact_text: HIV specialists coordinate multidisciplinary care to maximize ART adherence and prevent disease progression and resistance.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Primary care clinician should manage initial HIV diagnosis with counseling and referral
Provide psychosocial support and education
fact_text: Primary care clinicians play a key role in establishing trust, educating patients, addressing misconceptions, and referring HIV-infected patients to specialists.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Routine HIV screening for patients 13-64 years
fact_text: Routine HIV screening is recommended for patients aged 13-64 years in healthcare settings unless prevalence is very low, and universal voluntary screening is the US standard of care.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Serologic tests for syphilis, hepatitis B and C
Tests for T gondii, Chlamydia, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, HPV-related cancers
PPD skin test for latent TB
fact_text: Laboratory evaluation in HIV includes CD4 count, viral load, genotype, screening for coinfections, and PPD testing for latent TB with return visit required for reading.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Advanced research techniques to assess residual viral load
recommended_advice: ART interruption leads to residual viremia and relapse
HIV is not curable with ART alone
fact_text: Even with undetectable viral load by standard tests, residual HIV persists and ART interruption causes relapse; HIV is not curable with ART.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Vaccine response is often suboptimal unless CD4 T cell count > 200 cells/mcL
ART often leads to significant immune reconstitution, improving vaccine response
Recommendations for vaccinations in HIV-infected persons summarized in Table 5-1
fact_text: Vaccine response in HIV is suboptimal unless CD4 T cell count is above 200, and ART improves immune response to vaccines.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Antiretroviral drugs belong to 5 classes
Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors block reverse transcription of viral RNA into DNA by incorporation of chain terminators
fact_text: Antiretroviral drugs include nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors that block viral RNA reverse transcription by chain termination.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Lifelong ART is required for all HIV-infected persons
ART requires complete suppression of viral replication to prevent mutations
Combination tablets with 4 drugs are often used
Complete suppression is realistic in most patients
Lifetime ART is necessary to prevent viral rebound
fact_text: Lifelong ART is required for all HIV-infected persons and is indicated in all patients, with some exceptions for timing in CNS OIs.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: Hepatitis A: Inactivated vaccine recommended in travelers, MSM, and chronic liver disease
Hepatitis B: Inactivated vaccine recommended
HPV: Inactivated vaccine recommended
Influenza: Live vaccine not recommended; Inactivated vaccine recommended annually
Meningococcal: Inactivated vaccine recommended in high-risk young MSM
MMR: Live vaccine safe if CD4 > 200
Pneumococcal 13-valent (Prevnar-13): Inactivated vaccine recommended
Pneumococcal 23-valent (Pneumovax-23): Inactivated vaccine recommended 2 months after Prevnar-13 and every 5 years
TD: Inactivated vaccine every 10 years
TDAP: Inactivated vaccine recommended once and at 28 weeks in pregnant women
Zoster: Inactivated vaccine preferred
fact_text: Vaccination recommendations for HIV-infected persons vary by vaccine type and immune status, with inactivated vaccines generally recommended and live vaccines only if CD4 > 200.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Treatment as prevention prevents new HIV infections
UNAIDS 90-90-90 targets aim for 90% diagnosed, 90% on ART, 90% virally suppressed
Current US rates: 86% diagnosed, 63% in care, 49% retained, 51% virally suppressed
HIV elimination requires reproductive rate of infection below 1
recommended_advice: Maintain ART to keep viral load undetectable and prevent transmission
Achieve and sustain UNAIDS 90-90-90 targets
fact_text: HIV elimination requires sustained viral suppression and reducing new infections below replacement rate; treatment as prevention is key.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Lack of timely access to high-quality healthcare
Poor support for addiction and psychiatric conditions
Poor care of some patients in jail
recommended_advice: Address socioeconomic barriers to improve diagnosis and treatment
fact_text: Socioeconomic barriers such as poor healthcare access, cost, addiction, homelessness, and stigma impede HIV diagnosis and treatment.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: hiv infection with risk of ois
condition_aliases: hiv infection with risk of ois
trigger_evidence: Secondary prophylaxis prevents subsequent symptomatic episodes after initial OI
recommended_advice: Start primary prophylaxis based on CD4T count thresholds
Use secondary prophylaxis after initial OI episodes
fact_text: Use CD4T count to guide primary and secondary prophylaxis for OIs; PJP prophylaxis if CD4T < 200, Toxoplasmosis prophylaxis if CD4T < 100 and IgG positive.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Guidelines recommend monitoring viral load every 3 months and CD4T cell count at intervals.
recommended_advice: Monitor viral load and CD4T cell count regularly
fact_text: Monitor HIV viral load every 3 months and CD4T cell count periodically; goal is undetectable viral load (<20/mcL) by 4–6 months.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Testing performed at baseline to detect transmitted resistance and when viral load is not suppressed on ART
Genotype and phenotype testing available; genotype preferred for cost and speed
Decisions on resistance require expert guidance and databases
recommended_advice: Perform resistance testing at baseline and if viral suppression fails
fact_text: Perform HIV resistance testing at baseline and if viral load is not suppressed; genotype testing preferred.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Adherence of 90–95% required to maintain viral control and prevent resistance
Moderate adherence (50–90%) still has clinical benefits but risk of resistance
Very poor adherence (<50%) does not prevent progression to AIDS
recommended_advice: Promote high adherence to antiretroviral therapy
Address barriers such as substance abuse and mental illness
fact_text: Maintain 90–95% adherence to antiretroviral therapy to prevent resistance and disease progression.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: HIV Care Continuum shows percentages of people living with HIV diagnosed (86%), receipt of care (63%), retained in care (49%), and viral suppression (51%).

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: history of not always using a condom
fact_text: HIV-1/2 Ab combination immunoassay is positive in 99% of HIV infections; CD4 count and viral load help confirm diagnosis; history of multiple partners and inconsistent condom use increase infection likelihood.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: 46-year-old man with AIDS and CD4 80 cells/mcL
fact_text: In HIV-positive patients with headache, fever, and no focal neurologic signs, consider differential diagnosis including opportunistic infections and other causes; detailed clinical evaluation is needed.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: HCV Ab with reflex HCV viral load
recommended_advice: Primary prophylaxis with TMP/SMX
Vaccinations: influenza, TDAP, 13-valent pneumococcal, 23-valent pneumococcal, hepatitis A and B
Start ART
Use barrier precautions
Consider preexposure prophylaxis for HIV-negative partner
fact_text: In HIV patients with CD4 < 200, start TMP/SMX prophylaxis, perform comprehensive blood testing, vaccinate against influenza, pneumococcus, hepatitis A and B, start ART to suppress viral load, and use barrier precautions to prevent transmission.

condition_aliases: bacterial meningitis (neisseria meningitidis, s pneumoniae, listeria monocytogenes)
meningoencephalitis (hsv-1, west nile virus, acute hiv infection)
brain abscess (tuberculous, cryptococcoma, nocardia, bacterial, fungal)
trigger_evidence: degree of immunosuppression (CD4 T cell count)
presence of focal neurologic signs or abnormal neuroimaging
recommended_tests: CT scan of the head to rule out mass lesion before lumbar puncture
Platelet count, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time before LP
Neuroimaging (CT and MRI) to confirm diagnosis and evaluate focal lesions
recommended_advice: Evaluate acuity and immunosuppression status
Perform neuroimaging prior to lumbar puncture if focal signs or mass lesion suspected
Consider broad differential diagnosis based on CD4 count and clinical presentation
fact_text: In HIV patients with headache, assess acuity, immunosuppression (CD4 count), and focal neurologic signs to guide differential diagnosis including infections like cryptococcal meningitis, toxoplasmosis, and PML.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: headache described as frontal, unrelenting, pounding
no history of confusion or seizures
CD4 count 1 year ago was 2 cells/mcL
recommended_advice: Evaluate for active CNS infection or mass lesion
Rule out brain abscess secondary to Staphylococcus aureus
fact_text: In a patient with advanced HIV and severe headache with systemic symptoms, consider meningoencephalitis and mass lesions; neuroimaging and lumbar puncture are essential for diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition: acute cns infections or lesions in hiv
condition_aliases: acute cns infections or lesions in hiv
trigger_evidence: HIV-infected patient with headache or neurologic complaints
acute onset (<3 days) with fever or meningeal signs
presence or absence of mass lesion
recommended_tests: history and physical exam including neurologic and ophthalmologic exam
serum toxoplasmosis IgG, serum cryptococcal antigen, RPR
PT, PTT, platelet count prior to LP
CSF studies including cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain and culture, AFB stain and culture, cryptococcal antigen, VDRL, FTA-ABS
recommended_advice: start empiric antibiotics if bacterial meningitis suspected
start acyclovir if encephalitis suspected
start empiric toxoplasmosis therapy if criteria met
consider brain biopsy if LP nondiagnostic or cannot be performed
fact_text: In HIV patients with headache or neurologic complaints, acute onset with fever or meningeal signs warrants empiric antibiotics for bacterial meningitis and evaluation with CT and LP; CD4 count guides differential diagnosis including toxoplasmosis and lymphoma; empiric toxoplasmosis therapy is started if criteria met, otherwise brain biopsy may be needed.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Basilar meningitis or meningoencephalitis presents with classic meningeal symptoms and signs such as neck stiffness and photophobia in 25–30% of patients.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: MRI for ring-enhancing lesions, mass effect and edema
MRI for white matter nonenhancing lesions
TTE and TEE to search for endocarditis
fact_text: Cryptococcal meningitis is the leading hypothesis in patients with headache and mental status changes, diagnosed by CD4 <100, serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen, CSF PCR, and fungal culture.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis typically presents with subacute headache, malaise, fever, and mental status changes over days to weeks.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: In cryptococcal meningoencephalitis, fever occurs in 65–95%, headache in 73–100%, stiff neck in 22–27%, and photophobia in 18–22% of patients.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_tests: Measure intracranial pressure by lumbar puncture
fact_text: 70% of patients with AIDS meningoencephalitis have increased intracranial pressure > 20 cm H2O, which is associated with increased risk of death and worse symptoms.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: CSF opening pressure of 30 cm H2O
recommended_advice: Order blood cultures and serum CRAG in suspected cases
fact_text: A diagnostic threshold for cryptococcal meningitis includes positive serum CRAG, elevated CSF opening pressure (>20 cm H2O), low CSF glucose, elevated protein, and CSF pleocytosis; CSF VDRL is negative.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Blood cultures positive in 55% in AIDS
Negative serum CRAG makes cryptococcal meningitis unlikely
CSF Gram stain may be positive, India ink detects encapsulated yeast in 60-80% cases
recommended_tests: Lumbar puncture with CSF studies including opening pressure, CSF CRAG, fungal culture, Gram stain, protein, glucose, WBC count
recommended_advice: Include Cryptococcus PCR as part of CSF multi-target PCR panel for diagnosis
fact_text: Serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen testing and CSF fungal culture are highly sensitive and specific for diagnosing cryptococcal meningitis in AIDS; lumbar puncture is required regardless of serum CRAG to confirm diagnosis and manage intracranial pressure.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Mortality increased with abnormal mental status, increased opening pressure, and low CSF CRAG or low glycorrhachia
Induction therapy: IV liposomal amphotericin B (3-4 mg/kg) plus oral flucytosine (100 mg/kg/d) for at least 2 weeks
After induction, high-dose fluconazole (400 mg/day) for 8-10 weeks
Maintenance therapy with lower-dose fluconazole (200 mg/day) for minimum 1 year
In patients with high intracranial pressure, serial lumbar punctures to lower opening pressure by 20 cm H2O or 50% are performed
Optimal timing of ART is controversial; reasonable to delay ART for at least 4 weeks or longer if intracranial pressure remains elevated
recommended_tests: Serial lumbar puncture to monitor and reduce intracranial pressure
recommended_advice: Induction therapy with amphotericin B plus flucytosine
High-dose fluconazole after induction
Maintenance fluconazole for 1 year
Serial lumbar punctures for elevated intracranial pressure
Delay ART initiation for at least 4 weeks
fact_text: Treatment includes induction with IV liposomal amphotericin B plus oral flucytosine for ≥2 weeks, followed by high-dose fluconazole for 8-10 weeks, then maintenance fluconazole for ≥1 year; serial lumbar punctures are needed to manage elevated intracranial pressure; ART initiation is delayed at least 4 weeks.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
fact_text: Common symptoms of TE include frontal headache, seizures, hallucinations, and fever with variable frequency.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: MRI superior to CT in 40% of patients
Lesions: one or more ring-enhancing with mass effect and edema
Lesions located in basal ganglia, thalamus, cortex
Single lesion less likely and increases likelihood of primary CNS lymphoma (PCL)
CT scan abnormal in 87-96% of cases
recommended_advice: Use MRI to differentiate TE from PCL especially with single lesion
fact_text: MRI is the imaging test of choice for TE, showing multiple ring-enhancing lesions with edema, mostly in basal ganglia and cerebral hemispheres; single lesions suggest lymphoma.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Toxoplasma IgG positive in 97% but does not confirm active TE
IgM insensitive (15%) and usually secondary to reactivation
CSF analysis may be normal or nonspecifically elevated
CSF PCR 54% sensitive, 99% specific for CNS toxoplasmosis
CSF abnormalities: WBC >5 cells/mcL in 50%, protein >40 mg/dL in 81%, low glucose in 14%
recommended_advice: Interpret serology and CSF PCR in clinical context
fact_text: Toxoplasma IgG is sensitive but not confirmatory; CSF PCR is highly specific but moderately sensitive for CNS toxoplasmosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Primary infection acquired by eating undercooked meat or ingesting oocysts
TE is secondary to reactivation of latent toxoplasmosis in brain tissue cysts
CD4 T cell count <100 cells/mcL increases risk
Before ART, 33% of AIDS patients with CD4 <100 developed TE
recommended_advice: Consider prophylaxis with TMP-SMX in seropositive patients with low CD4 counts
fact_text: Toxoplasmic encephalitis in AIDS results from reactivation in patients with CD4 <100 cells/mcL; ART reduces incidence and TMP-SMX prophylaxis decreases risk.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: Meningismus is distinctly uncommon in TE
fact_text: Meningismus is uncommon in TE and suggests an alternate or additional diagnosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
condition_aliases: other cns mass lesions in aids patients
trigger_evidence: confusion and mental status changes dominate clinical picture
recommended_tests: Toxoplasma IgG serology (97% sensitive but does not confirm active TE)
Toxoplasma IgM serology (insensitive, usually secondary to reactivation)
CSF analysis including PCR for CNS toxoplasmosis (54% sensitive, 99% specific)
recommended_advice: Consider TE in AIDS patients with CD4 <100 cells/mcL and focal neurologic signs
Use MRI to detect lesions; superior to CT in 40% of patients
Rule out other CNS infections and neoplasms
fact_text: Toxoplasmic encephalitis in AIDS typically presents with focal neurologic signs and multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions; diagnosis supported by positive Toxoplasma IgG and CSF PCR, with MRI as imaging test of choice.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: clinical deterioration within 2 weeks of therapy
recommended_advice: continue empiric treatment if no deterioration
fact_text: If clinical deterioration occurs within 2 weeks of empiric anti-toxoplasmosis therapy, consider brain biopsy with immunoperoxidase staining to rule out other diagnoses.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: single or multiple enhancing mass(es) on MRI
fact_text: PCNSL typically presents as single or multiple enhancing mass lesions on brain MRI in AIDS patients.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition

fact_text: PML shows diffuse scalloped white matter lesions on brain MRI in AIDS patients.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: multiple ring enhancing lesions on MRI
fact_text: Toxoplasmosis typically shows multiple ring enhancing lesions on brain MRI in AIDS patients.

trigger_evidence: diagnostic uncertainty between TE and PCL
fact_text: Brain biopsy is the only method that confirms cerebral toxoplasmosis with certainty and may diagnose concomitant infection; however, it is not routinely done due to complications and imperfect sensitivity.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: diagnosis of any OI in AIDS
recommended_advice: start ART within 2-4 weeks after diagnosis of any OI except CNS cryptococcosis
fact_text: ART should be started quickly within 2–4 weeks after diagnosis of any opportunistic infection in AIDS, except CNS cryptococcosis.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
trigger_evidence: clinical deterioration within 48 hours of therapy
recommended_advice: use corticosteroids only if cerebral edema or midline shift present and clinical deterioration occurs within 48 hours
fact_text: Corticosteroids are only indicated in CNS toxoplasmosis patients with cerebral edema or midline shift and clinical deterioration within 48 hours of therapy.

source_title: Symptom to Diagnosis: An Evidence-Based Medical Guide, 4th Edition
recommended_advice: empiric treatment with pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine or alternatives
fact_text: Empiric treatment for CNS toxoplasmosis is indicated in AIDS patients with multiple brain lesions, CD4 <100, positive Toxoplasma IgG, and no prior prophylaxis.
